entry.title: COP31 opens in Antalya with climate finance — not new pledges — at the centre
entry.content:
The 31st United Nations climate conference, COP31, opens on Monday, November 9, in Antalya, Türkiye, and runs until November 20. It arrives at a difficult moment: wars, trade tensions and an energy crisis triggered by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have pushed climate down the political agenda, even as disasters linked to human-caused global warming multiply — from the tragedy in Nepal and Tibet to deadly heatwaves in Europe.

Expectations for the summit have focused more on its ability to send useful and concrete signals than on the outcome of the formal negotiations. No landmark decision is expected at this transitional COP. That is not a criticism of the gathering so much as a description of where the climate process stands: the big pledges are already on paper, and the question now is whether the system can turn them into delivery, and who pays for it.

A first: two presidents

COP31 is being run under an arrangement the UN climate process has not tried before. Türkiye hosts the conference and holds the presidency, with Murat Kurum, Türkiye's minister of environment, urbanisation and climate change, as COP President. Australia leads the formal negotiations, with Chris Bowen, Australia's minister for climate change and energy, serving as President of Negotiations. It is the first shared presidency in the roughly 30-year history of the talks, agreed at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, after rival hosting bids.

A World Leaders' Summit is scheduled for November 11 and 12, in the first days of the talks. The conference is set to bring together around 60,000 people and several dozen leaders over two weeks on the Turkish Riviera. French President Emmanuel Macron will not attend, according to reporting ahead of the summit.

Before Antalya, a pre-COP meeting was held from October 5 to 8, with Fiji, Tuvalu and Australia partnering to deliver it — an effort to elevate the concerns of small island and climate-vulnerable states ahead of the main event.

The numbers that frame the talks

A UN synthesis published on October 27 shows why the summit matters, and why it is likely to disappoint anyone looking for a breakthrough. The 127 new national climate plans submitted by 154 parties, covering about 71 percent of 2019 global emissions, point to 2035 emissions on average 6 percent below 2019 levels, within a range of 0 to 12 percent. A pathway consistent with 1.5°C needs a cut of about 60 percent.

The Paris Agreement's stated limit of 1.5°C is now slipping. In their fourth letter to the parties, the COP31 presidency team said the world is likely to exceed 1.5°C within a few years, with a peak of about 1.8°C in the best case. The European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service declared on November 6 that 2026 is on track to be the second-hottest year ever recorded, and that cumulative planetary warming from 2023 to 2026 is likely to exceed the 1.5°C threshold set out in the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Those numbers are the backdrop to every negotiation in Antalya. They are also the reason the summit's organisers have billed it as an "implementation COP" — focused on turning previously announced national climate plans into action rather than negotiating new headline pledges.

The five priorities — and the money question

COP31 will focus on five priorities: accelerating electrification, turning climate commitments into bankable projects, mobilising public and private finance, strengthening climate adaptation, and protecting oceans. Food security has been listed alongside those priorities, and a forum on agriculture and food system resilience is scheduled for November 10.

But the central unresolved question is money: who finances climate adaptation in countries that did not cause the problem and cannot absorb its costs. The New Collective Quantified Goal — the finance framework intended to replace the broken $100 billion-per-year promise that developed nations made in 2009 and never fully delivered — is now in its fifth year of negotiation, and as of the summit's opening, no agreed architecture exists.

The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report estimated that developing nations require between $127 billion and $5.8 trillion per year through 2050 for adaptation alone. UNEP's Adaptation Gap Report, released on November 4, estimates that a tripling of adaptation finance would bring it to $85 to $120 billion a year, against estimated needs far higher. The V20 group of twenty climate-vulnerable developing nations is arriving in Antalya with demands for binding finance commitments covering both mitigation support and adaptation finance.

Türkiye's own offer is an electrification pledge: raising electricity's share of final energy consumption from about 24 percent today to 35 percent by 2035. On November 3, Brazil's COP30 presidency published a voluntary roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. Neither is a headline agreement. Both are the kind of incremental, practical step that this COP is built around.

What success looks like

COP31 is unlikely to produce a headline agreement. Its value will depend on whether its smaller decisions make it easier for countries to get money, use it, and show what it delivered. That work continues long after the conference closes on November 20.

It is also the first COP to take place since the United States' withdrawal from the Paris Agreement took effect on January 27, 2026 — a fact that hangs over the talks even if it is not on the formal agenda. With the world's largest historical emitter outside the agreement, the burden of leadership falls more heavily on the countries still inside it.

The test of Antalya, then, is not whether it produces a dramatic final declaration. It is whether, in a crisis-rocked world, the climate process can still send a strong enough message to resonate — and whether the finance architecture that has not kept its promises can finally be rebuilt into something that does.

Sources

  • Le Monde — COP31 conference: Turkey aims to move climate up the agenda
  • BBVA — Countdown to COP31 in Antalya

link.title: COP31 opens in Antalya with climate finance — not new pledges — at the centre

entry.title: DeepMind says its AI agents found two cracks in retired encryption
entry.content:
Google DeepMind says its AI agents have found two previously unknown weaknesses in 1024-bit RSA, the encryption standard that once protected much of the internet and is now considered retired. The work was announced on November 6 by Pushmeet Kohli, DeepMind's vice-president of science, and it is the kind of result that sounds dramatic in a headline and demands careful reading in the detail.

The agents worked under human supervision and alongside academic cryptographers. They found two distinct weaknesses. The first concerns padding — the extra structure wrapped around a message before signing, designed to make forgery harder. According to DeepMind, once an attacker controls about half of the signed block, padding buys almost nothing. Where the attacker controls only a short fingerprint, the agents produced an algorithm DeepMind estimates is around 1,600 times faster than the best published method.

The second weakness is batch factoring. When many keys share a bit length, one expensive precomputation can be spread across all of them, cutting the average cost per additional key by roughly 30 times, according to DeepMind's estimates. Taken together, the two findings suggest that 1024-bit RSA — already retired from serious use — is weaker than cryptographers had believed.

The asterisks matter

Every headline move in this story, as the daily AI briefing that first pulled it together put it, came with an asterisk about who checked it. The capability is real, and the evidence is partial. That is the honest summary.

Both of the big multipliers — 1,600 times faster, 30 times cheaper — are theoretical rather than measured end to end. The part of the work that actually ran was a sandboxed reproduction against a 1024-bit key that an academic team had already broken, published on the IACR ePrint archive in September. In that reproduction, DeepMind reports its agents used 3.5 times less CPU time than factoring the key outright. That is a real, measured result, but it is a much smaller number than the headline figures, and the gap between the two is the gap between a laboratory reproduction and a claim about the general case.

This is not a reason to dismiss the work. Finding previously unknown weaknesses in a well-studied cryptosystem is a genuine achievement, and the fact that AI agents did it — working with humans, not instead of them — is a meaningful signal about where AI-assisted research is heading. It is, however, a reason to describe the result precisely: two weaknesses found, one measured reproduction, and theoretical estimates for the rest.

Why 1024-bit RSA, and why now

RSA with 1024-bit keys has been retired for years. Modern systems use 2048-bit keys or more, or have moved to other algorithms entirely. Nobody's bank account or email was put at risk by this announcement, and DeepMind is not claiming otherwise. The significance is different: it is about what AI agents can now do in a field — cryptanalysis — that has traditionally required rare, specialised human expertise.

Cryptanalysis is a good test case for AI research assistance because it is both deeply mathematical and deeply empirical. An agent that can search a large space of possible attacks, test them, and refine the promising ones is doing something that looks a lot like research. The DeepMind result suggests that agents are getting good enough at that loop to produce results that human cryptographers had not found. That is the story, more than the specific weaknesses in a retired key size.

It is also a story about verification. The cryptography community will now do what it always does with a new claim: try to reproduce it, probe its limits, and decide how much of it holds up. The IACR ePrint archive, where the underlying reproduction was published, is the right venue for that scrutiny. If the findings survive it, they will be folded into the field's understanding of RSA. If parts of them do not, the field will say so. Either outcome is how science is supposed to work.

The wider AI week

The DeepMind result was the front page of a busy week in AI. Google's Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash video model became generally available, with clips running up to 15 seconds instead of 10 and pricing reported to be 30 percent below the previous version. NVIDIA put open-weight checkpoints for its Cosmos 3 world models on Hugging Face on November 5, for driving and robotics simulation. Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Small, a 594-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with roughly 17 billion parameters active per request.

There was also a sobering counterpoint. METR, an independent evaluation nonprofit, published an assessment on November 5 of how much AI is speeding up AI research inside Anthropic, based on on-site work from August 12 to October 29. Anthropic, the report found, is improving model capabilities on well-specified tasks at about twice the rate it managed from March 2024 to October 2025. But Anthropic held unilateral redaction rights and cut a majority of the evidence METR found most informative. The capability is real in every case, the briefing concluded, and the evidence is partial in every case. That sentence applies to the DeepMind result too — and it is worth keeping in mind as AI research accelerates.

Sources

  • BYOBot — AI Daily Newsstand, November 8, 2026
  • The Art of CTO — Daily Sync, November 8, 2026

link.title: DeepMind says its AI agents found two cracks in retired encryption

entry.title: Google turns AI off by default for school accounts — and schools must now choose
entry.content:
Google said on November 3, 2026, that it will switch off Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search for K-12 student accounts until a school administrator turns them on. The announcement, made by Chris Phillips, Google's vice-president and general manager of education, reverses an earlier decision — and it has sparked a debate about how students should learn with AI, and who gets to decide.

In August 2026, Google announced that AI features in its Classroom app for K-12 schools would be turned on by default, giving students access to the Gemini chatbot. Schools told Google they wanted control, and that they were concerned about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork. Google has now reversed course: access will be entirely turned off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn it on. Google says it will share more specifics with schools in the coming months, before the change takes effect.

Schools can now pick each service on its own. If they pick Search, its AI answers come with it. Google posted a clarification the same day confirming that schools can turn on one, two or all of the services, each on its own. The school decides now. Once the change rolls out, a district that does nothing gets none of the four services for its students — Search included.

The backlash: Search is the sticking point

The pilot of Google's newly launched AI learning tools in US schools is drawing online backlash, because K-12 students in schools that opt out of AI features entirely may also lose access to Google Search.

The problem is that Search is, in Google's own description, deeply integrated with AI. If a school banned AI, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available," Phillips was quoted as saying by The New York Times. Schools appear to have no way to disable AI features built directly into Google Search, such as AI Mode, AI Overviews and the new Guided Learning feature — they can only choose whether Search is on or off as a whole.

That has put schools in a difficult position. A school that wants to keep students away from AI chatbots may find it has also taken away the search engine its students use for ordinary research. A school that keeps Search on gets the AI features with it, whether it wants them or not. It is a trade-off that many educators and parents did not expect, and it is the heart of the backlash.

The context matters. In September 2026, school districts in New York City and Los Angeles broadly restricted student access to generative AI on school devices. The demand for control is real, and it is coming from the largest school systems in the country. Google's announcement is, in part, a response to that demand — but the Search complication shows how hard it is to separate AI from the tools schools already rely on.

Guided Learning: the coach, not the answer key

At the centre of Google's announcement is Guided Learning, a learning mode in the Gemini app. Instead of giving the answer to a problem outright, it leads students toward understanding step by step, with hints and questions. It is Google's answer to the shortcut worry: an AI that coaches rather than completes.

Guided Learning began rolling out in Google Classroom worldwide on November 3. It is also coming to Google Search, where it will help students think through homework problems step by step. Google says it will start as a pilot at select US schools later in November, before reaching other districts.

In US cities where AI has not been banned from schools, Google has said it is giving two options for students to use Search from their school-issued accounts. One option is Search with AI Overviews turned on, similar to the current consumer experience. The other is Search via the Guided Learning tool, which walks students through problems instead of giving quick answers to schoolwork.

Google also published results from two studies of Guided Learning. In a randomised controlled trial with more than 300 University of Tokyo students, after a half-day of self-study, students who used only standard online materials raised their scores by 5.3 points, while students who could also use Guided Learning raised theirs by 8.1 points. Google says this amounts to about 1.5 times the gain from a single study session. In the UK, working with the school network Ark, Google tested Guided Learning in Google Classroom at three secondary schools for four weeks across four subjects. These results were published by Google itself and have not been released as a research paper, so they should be read as the company's own evidence, not independent findings.

What schools must decide

Every school with K-12 accounts will now have to decide, service by service, whether students get Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Search. It is a decision that cannot be avoided by doing nothing: doing nothing means all four are off.

For students, the change is a reminder that the tools they use for learning are not neutral, and that the adults around them are still working out the rules. For teachers, it is a new administrative task layered on top of the old one — deciding not just what to teach, but which tools students may use to learn it. And for Google, it is a test of whether an AI company can give schools genuine control without taking away the basic tools of research at the same time.

The Search pilot begins in select US schools later in November 2026. How schools respond — and how students experience the change — will shape the next round of decisions, from Google and from school districts alike.

Sources

  • The Indian Express — Google AI in Schools
  • Think Facility — Google will switch Gemini and Search off for K-12 students

link.title: Google turns AI off by default for school accounts — and schools must now choose

entry.title: Six killed and 15 injured in shooting in Kraków market square
entry.content:
Six people were killed and 15 wounded after a gunman opened fire on Saturday afternoon in a busy market square in Kraków, Poland, according to the Associated Press. The attack took place in one of the city's most visited public spaces, on a Saturday afternoon when the square would have been full of residents, shoppers and tourists.

Polish investigators continued examining the attacker's motives and background on Sunday, November 8. Authorities have not yet announced a confirmed motive, and the investigation remains open. Early reporting described the shooting as being probed as a possible act of terrorism, but no final determination had been made public by the time of this report, and readers should treat the motive as unresolved until Polish authorities say otherwise.

The scale of the attack — six dead and 15 injured — makes it one of the most serious acts of public violence in Poland in recent memory. Kraków, Poland's second-largest city, is known internationally for its historic old town and its market square, one of the largest medieval squares in Europe. An attack in such a place is designed to be seen, and the choice of location is part of why the shooting has drawn attention far beyond Poland.

A city in mourning

Poland is mourning the victims as investigators work through what happened. The immediate questions for police are the practical ones: how the gunman reached the square, what weapon was used, how long the attack lasted, and how the response unfolded. The longer questions — why this place, why these people, and whether anyone else was involved — will take more time, and may never be answered to everyone's satisfaction.

Public shootings of this kind are rare in Poland, a country with strict firearms laws and a comparatively low rate of gun violence. That rarity is part of the shock. When violence of this scale happens in a place where it is not expected, it changes how people use public space, at least for a while. Market squares, stations and concert halls are not places people expect to need an escape plan, and an attack in one of them forces a recalculation that no official statement can undo quickly.

For Kraków itself, the human cost is the story. Six families have lost someone. Fifteen people are injured, some of them seriously, and their recovery will stretch well beyond the news cycle. The city will hold its commemorations, and the square will, in time, fill again. That is how cities recover from such events — slowly, and not because anyone forgets, but because daily life reasserts itself.

What is known, and what is not

It is important to be clear about the limits of what is known. The casualty figures — six killed, 15 injured — have been reported by the Associated Press and carried widely. The location, a busy market square in Kraków, and the timing, Saturday afternoon, are established. What is not established is the motive, and reporting that treats speculation as fact would do the victims and the public a disservice.

Investigators in Poland will be examining the attacker's background, communications and movements in the days and weeks before the attack. They will also be looking at whether the attacker acted alone. Until they report their findings, the responsible course is to wait for their account rather than fill the gap with rumour.

The shooting came on a weekend when the world's attention was pulled in many directions at once — remembrance commemorations in Britain, coalition negotiations in Israel, an unresolved election in New Zealand, and the opening of the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye. Kraków's tragedy stands apart from those stories, but it shares something with them: a reminder that the news agenda is set by events, not by editors, and that a single afternoon in a single square can change a city's year.

The wider picture

Poland's government and security services will face questions in the coming days about prevention and preparedness. Those questions are legitimate, but they are also premature while the investigation is still establishing basic facts. What can be said now is that a public space that should have been safe was not, that six people were killed, and that a city is grieving.

Zentra Daily will update this story as Polish authorities release verified information. We will not publish unverified claims about the attacker's identity, affiliations or motives. If you are looking for the latest confirmed updates, the sources below carry the reporting on which this article is based.

Sources

  • Associated Press, via TFI Online
  • Open Chronicle — Global News Brief, November 8, 2026

link.title: Six killed and 15 injured in shooting in Kraków market square

entry.title: Kyle Larson clinches third NASCAR Cup Series title at Homestead
entry.content:
Kyle Larson is a three-time NASCAR Cup Series champion. The 34-year-old from Elk Grove, California, clinched the 2026 title early in the season finale at Homestead-Miami Speedway on Sunday, November 8, and he did it in the most Larson way possible: by going to the front at a track where he has led more laps than any other driver.

Larson entered the weekend with a comfortable lead over Christopher Bell and Denny Hamlin. All he needed was a handful of stage points — or, without them, a finish of 28th or better — to secure the championship. He left no doubt. He finished fourth in Stage 1 of the 400-mile finale, scoring seven stage points that put Hamlin and Bell out of reach. From that moment, the championship was his, whatever happened in the remaining laps.

Ryan Blaney won the race itself, capturing his fourth victory of the season for Team Penske after a chaotic restart on lap 260 carried him to the lead, which he held to the finish. Tyler Reddick finished second, followed by William Byron, Christopher Bell, Bubba Wallace and Denny Hamlin. Larson finished 12th, a result made mostly moot by the early clinch — but the points told the story of his season: he ended 49 points ahead of Bell and 56 ahead of Hamlin.

A champion at his best track

Homestead-Miami Speedway has long been Larson's place. It is, by the reporting of the day, arguably his best track on the circuit, and he drove it that way on Sunday, putting his No. 5 Hendrick Motorsports Chevrolet to the front and clinching the title before the race was even half run. There is a particular kind of confidence in a driver who can win a championship in the first stage of the final race, and Larson has now done it in the revived Chase format for the first time in his career.

The title is Larson's third in six years, and it makes him the first back-to-back champion since Jimmie Johnson in 2010 — Johnson won five in a row beginning in 2006. Larson is now the 11th driver in NASCAR history to own at least three Cup Series titles, joining a list that includes seven-time champions Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt and Johnson. That is the company a third title buys, and it is not given lightly.

Larson's path to this championship was not a straight line. His career has included early struggles and the kind of setbacks that end lesser drivers' title ambitions. The 2026 season, though, was built on the consistency that championships require: the stage points, the finishes when the car was not at its best, and the ability to be at the front when it mattered most. He entered the finale as the overwhelming favourite to lift the Bill France Cup, with a 67-point lead over Bell, and he needed only nine points to wrap up the title. He got them in the first stage.

The race behind the championship

While Larson's title was decided early, the race itself still had to be run, and Blaney made it worth watching. The Team Penske driver raced to the lead after the lap-260 restart and held it to the chequered flag, winning the season finale and finishing fourth in the final points standings. Reddick, driving for 23XI Racing — the team co-owned by NBA legend Michael Jordan, who watched from pit road — finished second, with Byron third.

For Bell and Hamlin, the two drivers who arrived at Homestead with a mathematical chance of stopping Larson, the day ended in the only way the arithmetic allowed once Stage 1 was over. Bell finished fourth in the race and second in the points; Hamlin finished sixth in the race. Both had strong seasons. Neither had an answer for Larson's points lead.

The finale also closed out the lower series. Kaden Honeycutt won the Truck Series championship at Homestead, and Justin Allgaier, racing for Dale Earnhardt Jr.'s team, won his second O'Reilly Auto Parts Series title on Saturday night by placing seventh. It was a full weekend of championships at Homestead, with Larson's the headline.

What three titles mean

Three championships in six years is a statement. In NASCAR's modern era, sustained excellence is hard: the cars change, the formats change, the competition is deep, and a single bad race in the playoffs can end a season. Larson has now navigated that gauntlet three times, and the back-to-back nature of this latest title — his second consecutive — puts him in the conversation with the sport's greats rather than merely its good drivers.

The question now is what comes next. At 34, Larson is in the prime of a driver's career, with a team in Hendrick Motorsports that has shown it can give him championship-winning cars year after year. A fourth title would put him in still rarer company. For now, though, the 2026 season belongs to him: clinched in Stage 1, celebrated at Homestead, and sealed with a points margin that left no argument about who the best driver of the year was.

Sources

  • USA TODAY — Kyle Larson wins third NASCAR championship
  • CNN — NASCAR phenom Kyle Larson wins 2nd consecutive Cup Series title

link.title: Kyle Larson clinches third NASCAR Cup Series title at Homestead

entry.title: Manchester United salvage 4-4 draw at Villa — but stay in the relegation zone
entry.content:
Manchester United twice came from two goals down to salvage a remarkable 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday, November 8, and potentially save manager Michael Carrick's job. Goals in stoppage time from Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu rescued a point — but United will spend the two-week international break in the relegation zone.

It was, by any measure, a wild game. United conceded twice inside the opening four minutes as Alysson and Nicolas Jackson punished errors from goalkeeper Senne Lammens. At that point, with the team already in the bottom three, the afternoon looked like it might become a rout. Instead, United rallied to level at half-time thanks to a Bruno Fernandes penalty and Youri Tielemans's first goal since moving to Old Trafford from Villa.

The second half brought more of the same: Villa pulling clear, United dragging themselves back. And then, in stoppage time, Zirkzee and Dorgu scored the goals that turned a defeat into a draw. It was the kind of finish that keeps a manager in a job for another fortnight — and the kind that also tells you how deep the problems run, because a team that needs two stoppage-time goals to draw at home is a team in trouble.

A season in the bottom three

The draw keeps United in the bottom three with just eight points from 10 games. Saturday's results had seen them slip into the relegation zone after August for the first time in 40 years — a statistic that captures, in a single line, how far the club has fallen from the standards it set for itself over decades.

Eight points from 10 games is relegation form by any measure. It is not a blip, or a bad month, or a run of hard fixtures. It is a third of a season, and it has left one of the biggest clubs in world football fighting for survival rather than for trophies. The international break now gives Carrick two weeks to work with the players who are not away with their countries, and two weeks for the club's hierarchy to decide whether he is the manager to lead the fight.

Carrick arrived with goodwill and a brief to steady the club. A thrilling fightback from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday had given him a lifeline, and the Villa draw may have given him another. But lifelines are not the same as a recovery, and the table does not care about spirit or fightbacks. It cares about points, and United do not have enough of them.

The goalkeeper question

The opening four minutes will haunt Senne Lammens. Two goals conceded, both punished from errors by the goalkeeper, set the tone for the afternoon and put United in a hole before the game had properly begun. Goalkeepers live with the knowledge that their mistakes are the most visible on the pitch — a striker can miss three chances and score the fourth, but a goalkeeper's error is a goal. Lammens will need the international break as much as anyone.

The broader defensive picture is no better. A team that concedes four goals at home, even in a game it draws, has a defensive problem that no amount of attacking spirit can cover up indefinitely. United scored four and still could not win. That is the sentence that should worry Carrick most.

What the draw does — and does not — change

The draw does not change United's league position. It does not change their points total in any meaningful way — one point instead of none, when the gap to safety is already a concern. What it changes is the mood, and the time Carrick has. A defeat, after the opening four minutes, would have made his position very difficult to defend. A draw, achieved the way it was, gives the club a reason to wait until after the international break before making a decision.

That is how football works at a club in crisis: the manager survives one game at a time, and each survival is presented as a turning point until the day it isn't. Whether the Villa draw is a turning point or merely a postponement will be decided by the games after the break, not by the stoppage-time goals themselves.

For Aston Villa, the draw will feel like two points dropped. They led twice by two goals, and they led in stoppage time. To leave Old Trafford with a point from a game they had won twice is the kind of result that stays with a team. But Villa, unlike United, are not in a crisis. They can afford to be frustrated. United cannot afford anything at all — except, for now, the hope that a 4-4 draw is the start of something rather than the latest chapter in a season that has already made unwanted history.

Sources

  • The New Indian Express — Manchester United salvage 4-4 Aston Villa draw

link.title: Manchester United salvage 4-4 draw at Villa — but stay in the relegation zone

entry.title: Nasdaq slides into correction as AI sell-off wipes trillions from US stocks
entry.content:
Wall Street suffered its worst session since April 2025 on Thursday, November 5. An AI and chip sell-off wiped out the post-election rally and pushed the Nasdaq into a correction — Wall Street's term for a fall of more than 10 percent from a recent high.

The numbers were stark. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,833.06 points, or 3.44 percent, to 51,523.06. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36 percent to 7,353.73. The Nasdaq Composite lost 5.52 percent to 24,315, closing 11.9 percent below its October 6 record. The Nasdaq-100 sank 6.36 percent. All 11 S&P 500 sectors ended lower. More than $2.5 trillion in market capitalisation was wiped out in 24 hours, and the S&P 500 alone lost around $3 trillion in value, according to market reporting of the day.

Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, fell about 9.3 percent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged more than 12 percent. Semiconductor names were the hardest hit across the board: shares of Sandisk, Micron and Western Digital lost 17 to 22 percent on November 5, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 12.1 percent — its second-worst day in history after a 15 percent decline in the early days of Covid.

What triggered it

The sell-off followed the Democrats' sweeping victory in the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3. Investors worried that a Democratic Congress would slow the development of data centres and artificial intelligence, through tighter regulation and greater scrutiny of the infrastructure build-out that has powered the market's rise.

That concern was not abstract. Data-centre and AI-related stocks have fuelled the bull market over the past few years, and opposition to them has grown in step with affordability concerns — the cost of power, land and water for ever-larger data centres, and the question of who benefits from them. The election results made the risk of tighter regulation over AI development feel more real, and the market repriced accordingly.

There was also a company-specific trigger. Disappointing results from Intel, the former semiconductor giant, signalled a slowdown in demand, and that set off the collapse in chip stocks. But the scale of the fall — the Nasdaq's biggest one-day points loss on record, and its worst session since April 2025 — was about more than one company's earnings. It was about a market asking, all at once, whether the AI trade had run too far, too fast.

The correction in context

A correction, in market language, is a fall of 10 percent or more from a recent peak. The Nasdaq entered one on November 5, closing 11.9 percent below its October 6 record. The Nasdaq-100's 6.4 percent fall was its worst single-day return since a 12.2 percent fall in March 2020, in the early days of Covid, and its market-cap decline of $2.2 trillion on the day was its worst ever. Since its 52-week high on October 6, the index has given up gains of more than $5.2 trillion.

The longer view is more sobering still. Since their peaks, Nvidia has lost 25 percent of its value, Micron has dropped 55 percent, and Intel's share price has fallen by a factor of 2.6. The semiconductor index has lost one-third of its value since its June peak. CoreWeave, the heavily indebted data-centre builder, has seen its market capitalisation shrink by more than two-thirds, and Oracle's value has been cut in half. Google is down 30 percent from its peak, Amazon 10 percent. Microsoft has held up, with its share price near record highs.

Wall Street's fear gauge, the CBOE Volatility Index, or VIX, jumped 70 percent on November 5 — the third-highest jump in history, after the "Volmageddon" episode of February 2018 and a 74 percent jump in December 2024. Friday's session ended with a slight rebound, but the sudden drop served as a reminder of the fragility of the sector's growth and profitability expectations.

The fall spread beyond the United States

Asia took the brunt the following day. Tokyo's Nikkei 225 fell more than 6 percent at the open and trimmed losses to 5.7 percent. South Korea fared worse: the Kospi dropped 8.55 percent early, triggering a circuit breaker, and later traded 7.4 percent lower. European shares started strongly, then reversed once Wall Street opened. The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed 0.38 percent lower, and the FTSE 100 closed 0.43 percent lower at 10,782.66.

The Bank of England raised its Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4 percent on the same day — its first increase since August 2023 — adding a further twist to a week in which markets were already unsettled.

What happens next

A correction does not mean the end of the AI trade, and several analysts made that point in the days after the sell-off. But it may signal that the trend is evolving. The questions now are about cost of capital, profitability, and viability: whether the enormous spending on AI infrastructure will generate the returns that justify it, and whether regulation will slow the build-out. Those questions were present before November 5. The midterm results, and the market's reaction to them, made them impossible to ignore.

November 5, 2026, is likely to remain a notable day in market history, given the intensity of the correction and the rising friction around the AI theme. Whether it is remembered as the day the bubble burst, or as a sharp correction inside a longer boom, will depend on what the next few weeks bring.

Sources

  • Gulf News — AI Sell-Off Sparks Market Chaos
  • USA TODAY — Why the midterm blue wave just triggered a red Wall Street

link.title: Nasdaq slides into correction as AI sell-off wipes trillions from US stocks

entry.title: A cat, a kaiju and a Quarter Quell: November at the box office
entry.content:
November is when the year picks back up after the slow comedown September and October usually bring. Last year it was Wicked: For Good and Zootopia 2; the year before, Wicked, Gladiator II and Moana 2 inside one eleven-day stretch. This year there is nothing on the calendar at that size — and that is the story of November 2026 at the box office.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the biggest film of the month, and it is tracking for an opening in the $60–70 million range. That makes November the first month since April likely to finish down on last year, and probably by a fair bit. Last November's four frames did $766 million, with Wicked: For Good's $147 million opening doing a lot of the heavy lifting. There is no $147 million opening coming this year, so the real question is how far down the month lands, and whether the four mid-sized openers — The Cat in the Hat, Godzilla Minus Zero, Ebenezer and the Fockers — can stack up enough to keep it respectable.

If at least three of those four can overperform, and if Sunrise on the Reaping can at the very least match the previous film's $166 million domestic total, then November can still save some face, even if it is still down from previous years. Of the five films, Ebenezer looks least likely to be a hit, with buzz described as decidedly negative. November, in short, is a $1 billion month when it has a Frozen or a Wicked, and a $540–620 million month when it doesn't. This year looks like the second kind.

Weekend one: a cat, a kaiju and a possible record

The first weekend of November, November 6–8, brought two very different openers. The Cat in the Hat, Warner Bros.' animated Seuss feature with Bill Hader voicing the Cat — the first animated Seuss feature since The Grinch — was tracking at $35–45 million according to Boxoffice Pro, with a predicted opening of $30–40 million and a predicted total of $110–150 million. Godzilla Minus Zero, Takashi Yamazaki's return to the franchise and the first Japanese production shot for IMAX, arrived with a 95 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes, a predicted opening of $25–35 million and a predicted total of $70–110 million.

Sony also released Ramayana, the Ranbir Kapoor and Yash epic, in the US on Thursday, November 5, two days before it opened in India — a reminder that the November box office is no longer a purely Hollywood affair, and that major Indian cinema now opens on a global schedule.

What October handed over was thinner. Clayface was tracking at $25–30 million and was the only October release still doing real business through the first half of November. Street Fighter opened to $31.0 million. The month's fortunes, then, rest heavily on the November openers themselves.

Weekend two: the Quarter Quell arrives

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opens on November 13, and it is the biggest opening of the month by a distance. Joseph Zada stars as a young Haymitch, and the film arrives in IMAX with a predicted opening of $50–70 million and a predicted total of $175–250 million. Two hundred million dollars domestic is in play, and if the film reaches it, it will have done more than any other November release to hold the month together.

The same weekend brings a heist film and the return of a familiar star, but the conversation will be about the Hunger Games. The franchise has been one of the most reliable box-office performers of the past fifteen years, and Sunrise on the Reaping is its first outing in several years. Whether it can match the previous film's $166 million domestic total is the number to watch.

The year in context

For all November's softness, 2026 as a whole is running well ahead of last year. The year is already at $7.9 billion and running 20 percent ahead of 2025, and December has Avengers: Doomsday and Dune: Part Three opening on the same day. A down November, in other words, is a pause in a strong year, not a sign of trouble for the industry as a whole.

That context matters for the cinemas, too. A month with four mid-sized openers and one tentpole is a different kind of month from one with a single giant: it spreads the audience across more films, gives smaller titles room to find their audience, and rewards the films that overperform their tracking. The Cat in the Hat and Godzilla Minus Zero could hardly be more different — a family animation and a Japanese kaiju epic — and both have a real chance to beat expectations.

Beyond the box office

The entertainment week was not only about cinemas. The Strokes made their fifth appearance on Saturday Night Live on November 7, performing two tracks from their seventh studio album — with Walton Goggins joining the New York band on bongos. Mark Hoppus, the Blink-182 bassist, made a surprise appearance at the Hollywood Bowl on November 7, joining Jimmy Eat World on stage for a performance of "A Praise Chorus". And Macklemore said on November 6 that nine major American arenas had refused to host his "Free Palestine" benefit tour, accusing venue owners of silencing his support for Palestinians after initially offering available dates.

November 2026, then, is a month of mid-sized bets and one big one — and the box office will tell us, weekend by weekend, whether those bets paid off.

Sources

  • Box Office Watch — November 2026 Preview
  • Brisbane Hustle — Entertainment, November 2026

link.title: A cat, a kaiju and a Quarter Quell: November at the box office

entry.title: Russell Brand sentenced to ten and a half years in prison
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

British comedian Russell Brand has been sentenced to ten years and six months in prison, after a jury in London convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

The sentence was handed down at Southwark Crown Court on Monday, November 9, 2026. Brand, 51, was convicted on Thursday, November 5, following a trial that lasted around four weeks. He had pleaded not guilty and has denied engaging in any non-consensual sexual activity.

The jury found that Brand raped one woman and sexually assaulted three others, in offences committed between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two further counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The sentence

Judge Joel Bennathan imposed separate sentences for each conviction: nine years for the rape, and nine months, 18 months and eight months for the three sexual assaults. The assault sentences run concurrently with each other and consecutively with the rape sentence, giving a total of ten years and six months.

Brand must serve two-thirds of the sentence in custody before he is eligible for release on licence.

In his sentencing remarks, the judge said Brand had believed that "fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live." He also praised the determination and bravery of the women who came forward, noting that they had been confronted and told they had lied or twisted the truth, on Brand's instructions.

The judge took some circumstances into account when setting the sentence, including Brand's lack of previous convictions, the fact that 17 years had passed since his last offence, and the time he has spent helping people struggling with addiction. He said the sentence for the rape would otherwise have been a year longer.

The trial

The trial began on October 12 and featured testimony from six accusers, as well as from Brand himself. Prosecutors told the court that Brand used his celebrity status to pursue women, describing him as a "calculated sexual predator" — a description the judge echoed in his sentencing remarks. Brand testified that he had "misused" his fame to have sexual encounters with women, while maintaining that everything was consensual.

The case began with a joint investigation by The Sunday Times, The Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme in 2023, which reported allegations against Brand spanning 1999 to 2012. Charges were brought in 2025, covering offences said to involve six women between 1999 and 2009.

What happens next

In a statement on November 9, Metropolitan Police Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said Brand "has been held accountable for his crimes" and that he hoped the outcome would give the victims "some measure of closure and allows them to continue rebuilding their lives."

One victim said in a statement that she was grateful to the police and the prosecution "who have been with me throughout this process," while another said she finally felt believed.

London's Metropolitan Police has said Brand remains under investigation over two further allegations of rape, including one involving a woman who was 16 at the time.

Sources

  • USA TODAY (with reporting from Reuters)
  • PEOPLE, reporting the BBC and The Guardian

link.title: Russell Brand sentenced to ten and a half years in prison

entry.title: Seven killed and at least 125 injured as two trains collide south of Cairo
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two passenger trains collided south of Cairo on Sunday, killing seven people and injuring at least 125, Egyptian authorities said. The conductor of one of the trains was among those killed.

The crash happened in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometres (32 miles) south of the capital. According to the Transportation Ministry, a train travelling from Giza to the southwestern province of Fayoum ran into the rear of a train heading from Cairo to the southern city of Aswan. Several carriages derailed in the impact.

Egypt's Health Ministry gave the casualty toll in a statement, saying more than 70 of the injured had already been discharged after receiving treatment. Earlier reports had put the number of injured at 112, before the ministry updated the figure to at least 125 as hospitals continued to treat passengers.

What investigators found

The Chief Prosecutor's office said its investigators reached the site late on Sunday. A preliminary inspection indicated that the Giza–Fayoum train struck the last carriage of the Cairo–Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track and travelling in the same direction, officials said.

Residents of Kafr Girza, near the crash site, rushed to help before emergency crews arrived, pulling survivors from the wreckage and calling ambulances. One resident, Ayman Gamal, said he saw around 80 injured people taken away by ambulance. Some passengers were trapped inside a carriage of the stationary train and were dead when they were pulled out, he said.

Survivors taken to al-Wasta Central Hospital in Beni Suef province described passengers in shock, struggling to breathe in the dust thrown up by the collision. Farha Gamal, a survivor who had been on the Fayoum train, said some passengers appeared dead while others struggled to find their way out of the carriage. "There were other cars that were completely mangled," she said.

Emergency teams and cranes were sent to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services on the line connecting Cairo with Upper Egypt, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.

Investigation ordered

President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash. The public prosecutor's office has opened an inquiry to determine the technical reasons behind the collision.

No final account of the cause has been announced. Authorities have not said whether anyone has been detained or held responsible.

A troubled rail record

Train derailments and crashes are a recurring problem in Egypt, where the railway system has a long history of mismanagement and poor maintenance. The government has announced modernisation programmes in recent years, but serious accidents continue.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district. Egypt's deadliest rail disaster was in 2002, when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train travelling from Cairo to southern Egypt.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Reuters

link.title: Seven killed and at least 125 injured as two trains collide south of Cairo

entry.title: FDA orders vision-loss warning on Ozempic, Zepbound and all GLP-1 drugs
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has ordered makers of every GLP-1 weight-loss and diabetes drug to add a warning about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden, permanent vision loss.

In a drug safety communication issued on Monday, November 9, the agency said it is requiring all glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists — including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro and Zepbound — to carry information about a potential increased risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, known as NAION, in the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

NAION occurs when blood flow to the front of the optic nerve drops, and it can cause sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, sometimes permanently. The FDA describes it as rare and says its underlying cause is not fully understood.

What the FDA found

The review began after a study published in July 2024 in JAMA Ophthalmology examined the risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide. The FDA said that study had limitations, but that the potential risk warranted a closer look, and it undertook a broader evaluation of clinical trial data, animal data and postmarketing reports.

A meta-analysis of 126 clinical trials covering 134,253 patients found 15 probable NAION events — 10 among people taking a GLP-1 drug and five among those on a placebo. That translated to an incidence of 6.4 events per 100,000 person-years in GLP-1 users, compared with 3.8 per 100,000 in people on a comparator drug.

A separate study using the FDA's Sentinel real-world evidence system produced mixed results: it found no statistically significant increase in risk compared with SGLT-2 inhibitors, another class of diabetes drugs, but an increased risk compared with DPP-4 inhibitors.

Importantly, the FDA did not determine that GLP-1 drugs cause NAION. The agency said it found enough evidence of a potential increased risk to require the warning, even though the mechanism — how the drugs might raise the risk — remains unknown. The animal data it reviewed identified no mechanism for the effect.

Which drugs are affected

The warning applies to the entire class, not just the best-known brands. The FDA's list includes semaglutide products (Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy), tirzepatide products (Mounjaro and Zepbound), liraglutide products (Victoza and Saxenda), dulaglutide (Trulicity), exenatide and the combination products Xultophy and Soliqua, as well as orforglipron (Foundayo), approved earlier this year. NAION cases have been reported for every GLP-1 product currently on the market, the agency said.

Warnings about a possible NAION risk are not new everywhere. European labels for semaglutide products have carried them since June, stating the condition may affect up to 1 in 10,000 people taking the drug.

What patients should do

The FDA is telling patients to report sudden, painless vision loss, blind spots, tunnel vision, distorted colours or any other visual change in one eye, and it says doctors should refer patients promptly to an eye specialist if NAION is suspected.

The action is a labelling change, not a recall or withdrawal: no product is being taken off the market. Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly, the makers of the leading GLP-1 drugs, have denied a significant link between their products and NAION, and both companies face lawsuits from patients who say the risk was not disclosed to them.

Sources

  • U.S. Food and Drug Administration
  • Reuters

link.title: FDA orders vision-loss warning on Ozempic, Zepbound and all GLP-1 drugs

entry.title: Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Big Bend, Texas
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United States Supreme Court on Monday, November 9, allowed the Trump administration to move ahead with border wall construction in the remote Big Bend region of West Texas, lifting a lower court's order that had halted the work for the past month.

The court granted the government's emergency request to pause an injunction issued on October 2 by U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone. That injunction had blocked construction of barriers and roads across the Big Bend sector while a lawsuit against the project moved through the courts. The Supreme Court's action lets construction resume while the case continues — it is not a final ruling on whether the project is lawful.

In an unsigned order, the court said Congress has expressed a "clear preference for expeditious border construction," and that the government's interest in border security outweighs "any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm" claimed by the challengers. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent.

The legal fight

The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend river guide and landowner, and Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group working to preserve a historic adobe church in Ruidosa, Texas, that it says is threatened by the construction.

At the centre of the dispute are waivers issued by the Department of Homeland Security that set aside a broad set of environmental and conservation laws — including the Endangered Species Act, the National Wild and Scenic Rivers Act, and the National Park Service Organic Act — to allow the building to proceed. It was the first time such waivers had been applied inside a national park.

The court said the government was "exceedingly likely to prevail" on its argument that a 1996 federal law limits lower courts' ability to review border barrier decisions, meaning Judge Cardone likely lacked jurisdiction to block the work.

A vast, remote stretch

The Big Bend sector spans 517 miles along the Rio Grande — more than a quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border — and includes Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park. It is rugged, sparsely populated terrain, and it records the lowest number of migrant apprehensions of any Southwest border sector. Judge Cardone noted that the sector accounts for only 0.3 to 2.2 percent of apprehensions, despite its size.

The administration says most of the construction, spanning more than 300 miles, will take place on privately owned land, though work is also planned inside the national park. The waivers were issued between February and July by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor Kristi Noem, who designated the region an area of high illegal entry.

The plan has drawn bipartisan criticism, including from lawmakers who object to building through a protected landscape known for its canyons and desert wilderness.

What happens next

The case itself remains alive. The challengers can still press their claims in the district court, and the Supreme Court's order does not decide whether the waivers themselves are lawful. But with the injunction lifted, construction can proceed in the meantime — and environmental groups say the work could cause permanent damage to protected wilderness before the courts reach a final answer.

Sources

  • USA TODAY
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Big Bend, Texas

entry.title: A robot has built a structure in space for the first time — with no astronauts involved
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A robot has assembled part of a structure in orbit for the first time, working entirely on its own — no astronaut had a hand in the build.

The system, called ASTRA, was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology with funding from the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It spent the past six months in space assembling sections of a reflector antenna, testing whether large hardware can be built where it will be used.

Until now, there have been only two ways to get a large structure into orbit: fold it up for launch and unfurl it in space, or send it up in pieces and have astronauts bolt it together over several missions. Both hit a hard limit — the size of a rocket's cargo fairing. ASTRA points to a third option: ship the parts and let a machine do the assembly.

How the build worked

ASTRA, short for Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly, is a robotic manipulator that picks up struts and joints from motorised dispensers and joins them into identical sections, or bays, of a perimeter truss. The target is a reflector antenna 1.4 metres (4.6 feet) across, made from composite fibre tubes, aluminium joints and a Kapton reflective surface.

The roughly one-cubic-metre payload launched on March 30, 2026, from Vandenberg Space Force Base aboard a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission, riding on Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 vehicle. It carried two truss bays assembled on Earth, along with the parts for the rest.

In orbit, controllers released the launch restraints, pushed out the two prebuilt bays, and built a third bay from scratch. Photographs from the payload's 11 cameras confirmed each step. When problems appeared, the team tested fixes first on a twin of the system kept in a Caltech laboratory.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," said Sergio Pellegrino, the Caltech professor who leads the ASTRA team.

An unfinished antenna — and why that still counts

The demonstration did not complete the full antenna. The finished design calls for 11 connected bays; time limits and unexpected difficulties in the space environment meant the team built only the initial section. With the mission due to end in December, finishing all 11 bays now looks unlikely.

The researchers say the partial result still proves the point, and the lessons are shaping a simpler, refined design. Communication was part of the challenge: the ground team gets only seven or eight windows of about 15 minutes each day to talk to the system.

ASTRA is one of only two projects to reach the third phase of DARPA's NOM4D programme, which aims to enable structures "hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale," says programme manager Andrew Detor.

Structures built in orbit could serve as enormous telescope mirrors, giant radio antennas, or solar arrays beaming power back to Earth. "Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino said.

Sources

  • Science Daily
  • phys.org

link.title: A robot has built a structure in space for the first time — with no astronauts involved

entry.title: Russia and Ukraine to resume U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi as Washington signals a wider European security deal
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators are set to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for two days of U.S.-brokered talks, their first direct meeting since February, as Washington signals it is open to a wider agreement with Moscow on European security — a shift that European officials see as an early concession to Russia.

The talks are scheduled to begin at around 6:30 a.m. GMT on Tuesday, November 10, and run for two days, according to officials in Kyiv. Security guarantees are expected to top the agenda, with both sides still far apart on the core questions of territory and the shape of any deal.

A broader deal on the table

The Trump administration believes the only way to end the war is to reach a broader agreement with Russia on Europe's future security arrangements at the same time, U.S. officials said on Monday — accepting a long-standing Kremlin demand the United States and its NATO allies had previously resisted. European officials and experts worry the American call for a wider deal echoes Kremlin talking points.

President Donald Trump raised the prospect himself last week after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin's envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House on November 4. Trump said a broader deal was being discussed. "It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," he said, adding that it might involve all of Europe. On Sunday, he told "60 Minutes" the two sides were "very close" to a deal.

Who is at the table — and who is not

Russia's delegation will again be headed by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky. It will include Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov for the first time, along with senior military officer Yuri Zhigarlovsky. The Ukrainian delegation is headed by Rustem Umerov.

France, Germany and the European Commission are sending officials to Abu Dhabi, but Russia has made clear it does not want the Europeans at the negotiating table. "No one is going to invite them to the negotiating table," Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said. Ukrainian delegates will instead meet separately to brief their European allies on how the discussions are going.

What is still unresolved

The two sides remain far apart. Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from the four regions Moscow illegally annexed early in the war but never fully captured, and has refused a general halt in hostilities. U.S. negotiators believe both leaders may be willing to compromise on territory, a U.S. official told Reuters. Under the proposed deal, Ukraine would get an end to the war, security guarantees and a roadmap to European Union membership.

No details of the broader European security agreement Trump described have been made public, and it is not clear what form it would take or whether European governments would accept it. Previous rounds of talks early this year produced no visible progress, and fighting has continued along the front line.

Sources

  • The Washington Post
  • Reuters

link.title: Russia and Ukraine to resume U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi as Washington signals a wider European security deal

entry.title: House Republican forces vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, moved on Monday to force a House vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war in Iran without congressional approval and of ordering unlawful military strikes abroad.

Massie read eight articles of impeachment aloud on the House floor and filed them as a privileged resolution, a procedural move that requires House leaders to act within two legislative days. A vote could come as soon as Wednesday. It would be the first House impeachment vote against a Pentagon chief in 150 years.

Eight articles

The resolution centers on the war in Iran, which Massie says Hegseth waged without a declaration of war, statutory authorization, or an imminent threat to the United States — and continued even after both chambers of Congress passed a resolution directing U.S. forces to leave. The articles cite three alleged violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, the post-Vietnam law limiting how long U.S. forces can remain in hostilities without Congress's approval.

Other articles cover lethal U.S. strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean, military action in Yemen, and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in a military raid, which Massie called an act of war against a sovereign country.

One article concerns a U.S. airstrike on February 28 on the Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Iran, which killed at least 168 people, most of them children. The Pentagon has not yet released the findings of its investigation into that strike.

A second attempt

This is Massie's second try. He first sought to force an impeachment vote in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home early and the resolution expired before anyone had to vote on it. Massie had to reintroduce the measure to restart the two-day clock.

The new effort comes just days after Republicans suffered historic losses in the midterm elections, which President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have attributed to the unpopular war in Iran and the rise in gas prices that followed. Democrats take control of both chambers when the new Congress convenes in January.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday he was a "hard yes" on the measure, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has endorsed it. Johnson, meanwhile, said Monday it was a "terrible, terrible look" to impeach a defense secretary during hostilities. Massie acknowledged he does not know whether the resolution has enough votes to pass, and warned Johnson could try to sidestep a vote.

What happens next

Even if the House votes to impeach Hegseth, removal is unlikely: a Senate trial would require a two-thirds majority to convict, and Republicans still hold the majority in both chambers until January. Leadership could also try to table the resolution, killing it without a direct vote on the charges — though that, too, would be a recorded vote.

Hegseth, who has vowed to fight the effort, plans a rare press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday morning — his first time taking questions from the briefing room since May 5. Massie, who is leaving Congress at the end of the term after losing a Trump-backed primary, said impeaching Trump himself over war powers was "an impossible hurdle" and that Hegseth was "the better target."

Sources

  • USA Today
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: House Republican forces vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over Iran war

entry.title: California voters reject Proposition 40, the one-time tax on billionaires
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

California voters rejected Proposition 40, a proposed one-time 5% tax on the wealth of the state's billionaires, the Associated Press projected on Monday, ending one of the most expensive ballot fights in the state's history.

The measure was trailing 52.8% to 47.2% when the AP called the race. It would have been the first modern tax on wealth in the United States, where taxes are almost always assessed on income rather than on assets.

What the measure would have done

Proposition 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net assets of California residents worth more than $1 billion, with residency counted as of January 1, 2026. Roughly 200 people would have been affected.

Supporters, led by the Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, estimated the tax would raise about $100 billion over five years, with at least 90% of the money going to health care. The union said the revenue was needed to offset federal Medicaid cuts signed into law last year. The state's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office offered a more cautious estimate, in the tens of billions, and warned the measure could cost the state up to $1 billion a year in income-tax revenue if wealthy residents left.

A record-breaking campaign

Opponents outspent supporters by more than ten to one. Billionaires and business groups poured more than $333 million into defeating the measure, including $102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin — the largest single contribution. Supporters raised roughly $30 million.

Opponents also placed two competing measures on the ballot designed to blunt the tax. One, Proposition 42, would bar the state from taxing personal property and financial assets, effectively banning wealth taxes. Its outcome remained too close to call late Monday.

A split among Democrats

The result exposed a divide inside California's Democratic Party, which backed the measure, along with Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna. Governor Gavin Newsom opposed it, arguing that a wealth tax should be national rather than imposed by a single state.

The union behind the measure vowed to put a billionaire tax back on the ballot in 2028 if the state legislature does not come up with another way to fund the health care cuts by then.

The defeat does not amount to a broad rejection of higher taxes on the wealthy. In the same election, about 60% of voters approved a separate measure making the state's higher income-tax rates permanent for top earners, rather than letting them expire in 2031.

Sources

  • The Associated Press
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: California voters reject Proposition 40, the one-time tax on billionaires

entry.title: Mexico captures alleged Jalisco cartel cell leader 'R2' in DEA-aided raid near Guadalajara
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Mexican security forces arrested Rafael Alvarez, known as "R2", an alleged leader of a Jalisco New Generation Cartel cell, in a raid near Guadalajara on Sunday that drew on intelligence shared by the United States Drug Enforcement Administration.

The operation took place in Zapopan, in the Guadalajara metropolitan area, and was carried out by the Mexican Navy's special operations unit together with the federal security ministry. Mexico's National Intelligence Center also took part. Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Alvarez was wounded in a shootout that broke out during the arrest and is receiving medical care. Nineteen other people were detained in the same operation.

Who the authorities say he is

Alvarez is suspected of heading "Los Rs", a cell of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known as the CJNG, operating in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan. Harfuch said the cell was "mainly linked to extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, illegal deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities", and that its extortion victims included business owners and avocado producers.

The Navy linked Alvarez to the killing of at least 19 people, including Carlos Manzo, the popular crime-fighting mayor of Uruapan in Michoacan state, who was murdered last year. Those are allegations made by the authorities; Alvarez has not been convicted of any offence, and no response from him or from the group has appeared in the reporting.

Alvarez faces an outstanding arrest warrant in Mexico for aggravated homicide and a separate warrant for extradition to the United States. The DEA said he is wanted in the US on federal drug trafficking and firearms charges, describing him as a senior leader of the CJNG "responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico". CBS News reported the same account of the arrest on Monday.

Why the arrest matters

The CJNG is one of Mexico's two main criminal groups and competes with the Sinaloa Cartel for drug trafficking into the United States. The US government designated it a "foreign terrorist organisation" in 2025. Since the death of the group's founder, Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera, in a military operation in February, several of its top leaders have been apprehended.

The arrest is the latest in a run of high-profile detentions, but it does not by itself change the security picture in the region. Reports of kidnapping for ransom continue in the areas where the cartels are active, and an estimated 134,000 people are believed to be missing across Mexico, with Jalisco recording the country's highest numbers of disappearances.

Harfuch described the information released so far as preliminary and said it would be updated as the investigation advances. Officials have not said whether the Mexican case or the US extradition request will proceed first.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Mexico captures alleged Jalisco cartel cell leader 'R2' in DEA-aided raid near Guadalajara

entry.title: China's trade surplus passes $1 trillion — a month earlier than last year's record pace
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

China's trade surplus passed $1 trillion in the first ten months of 2026, official data showed on Tuesday, reaching the milestone a month earlier than last year's record-breaking total — and putting the country on course to beat the $1.2 trillion record it set in 2025.

Exports jumped 35.2 percent year on year in October to $412.3 billion, according to the General Administration of Customs, while imports expanded 41.6 percent to $307.1 billion. The two figures together brought China's cumulative surplus for January to October to $1.04 trillion, up from $964.8 billion over the same period last year.

The engine behind the surge is the global rush to build artificial intelligence infrastructure. Demand for computer chips, data-centre servers and networking equipment has driven overseas sales of high-technology goods, alongside semiconductors, electric vehicles and other advanced products. Semiconductors and computer parts accounted for about 40 percent of the increase in China's exports this year, according to Bloomberg's tally of the data.

Imports grew faster than exports

The monthly picture was more mixed. Because imports grew faster than exports in October, the surplus for the month alone narrowed to $105.3 billion, down from $133.5 billion in September and the smallest monthly gap since April. Imports rose 41.6 percent, far above the roughly 32 percent economists had expected in a Reuters poll, buoyed by purchases of technology products, critical minerals and energy supplies.

Exports to the United States surged 32.9 percent in October, the customs data showed, even as Washington and Beijing remain locked in their long-running trade confrontation. China's surplus with the European Union reached $310.7 billion over the first ten months, up from $241.6 billion a year earlier.

Why it matters

A second straight year above $1 trillion underlines how central China has become to global supply chains — and how large the imbalance has grown. Trading partners have pressed Beijing for greater balance, and the size of the surplus is likely to sharpen tensions and protectionist pressure, including fresh tariff risks.

The figures landed just ahead of another high-stakes meeting between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China next week, where trade is expected to be high on the agenda.

Analysts expect exports to stay resilient through the rest of the year, led by electronics and vehicles, according to Moody's Analytics. On current trends, China is well placed to finish 2026 with a larger surplus than last year's record — a result that would keep its export engine, and the global debate over it, at the centre of the world economy.

Sources

  • The Hindu — China says 2026 trade surplus surpassed $1 trillion in October
  • Reuters — China's trade surplus tops $1 trillion for second straight year

link.title: China's trade surplus passes $1 trillion — a month earlier than last year's record pace

entry.title: U.S. envoys to press Russia to give Europe a seat at future Ukraine peace talks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will press Russia to give Europe a direct role in future negotiations over Ukraine when trilateral peace talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday — the first such meeting between the three sides since February.

The two-day session, mediated by Kushner and Witkoff, is set to open with security guarantees for Ukraine and the future shape of Europe's security arrangements, before turning to territorial questions on the second day. The aim, U.S. officials said, is to keep momentum going rather than to deliver a final ceasefire this week.

Washington wants Europe in the next round

The American envoys plan to argue that this week's meeting should be the last one held without Europe's full participation, and to propose bringing European governments into the discussion once the trilateral round is over. The case, as U.S. officials put it, is that Europeans should hear directly what Washington hears from Moscow, and be able to put their own messages to Russia in person rather than through intermediaries.

Senior European officials are due in Abu Dhabi this week — security advisers from the U.K., Germany and France, plus officials from Italy, NATO, the European Commission and the European Council. But Russia objects to European involvement in the main negotiations, so they will be consulted by Kushner and Witkoff on the sidelines rather than seated at the table.

Who should speak for Europe is itself a divisive question. EU leaders are expected to discuss it at an informal summit in Dublin later this week.

A wider argument about European security

The push for a European seat is part of a broader American argument that ending the war will require a rethink of Europe's security relationship with Russia. European governments worry that President Donald Trump could accept President Vladimir Putin's long-standing demands to roll back NATO's influence in the region. U.S. officials insisted that NATO would remain central to Europe's collective defence, while arguing that the current arrangements are not working and need to be rebuilt. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has been closely involved in the discussions with the U.S. administration, according to the report.

Territory remains the hardest question for Ukraine. Both sides have shown some flexibility in private about the fate of Russian-occupied territory, the report said, and the territorial and security tracks will have to be resolved together.

What is still unknown

Whether Moscow will agree to widen the format at all, who would represent Europe if it does, and what form any new European security arrangement would take are all still open.
