No agreement is expected from this week's talks, and previous rounds earlier this year produced no visible progress while fighting continued along the front line.

Sources

  • POLITICO Europe
  • Kyiv Post

link.title: U.S. envoys to press Russia to give Europe a seat at future Ukraine peace talks

entry.title: Hungary detains former PM Orbán's brother in people-smuggling probe
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Hungarian authorities reportedly detained Áron Orbán, the younger brother of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, on Monday as part of a people-smuggling investigation, in the most politically charged arrest since the country's new government took office.

The news was first reported by Kontroll, a news site owned by Márton Magyar, brother of Prime Minister Péter Magyar. The prime minister shared the report on Facebook, writing that, according to press reports, Áron Orbán had been taken into custody on suspicion of human trafficking. He later confirmed the detention during a speech in Berlin.

Police and Hungary's anti-graft body, the National Asset Protection and Recovery Office, carried out coordinated raids in Budapest and the surrounding Pest county, searching homes and properties linked to Áron Orbán's business associates. Authorities said four people had been detained on suspicion of people smuggling, but they did not name any of the suspects — and police have not confirmed whether Áron Orbán was among those held.

The case behind the raids

According to the authorities, the four detained suspects — one woman and three men — are accused of helping Vietnamese citizens reach Western Europe over several months in 2024. Investigators say the group charged visa applicants a so-called recruitment fee at Hungarian missions in Vietnam and shared the proceeds.

The case has roots in earlier reporting. Last year, an investigation by Hungarian news site Telex linked Áron Orbán, a 49-year-old businessman, and his business associates to an alleged scheme involving visas for foreign guest workers. Counterterrorism officers were reported to have searched a property in Fótliget linked to a company associated with him.

The anti-graft body was set up to investigate alleged corruption during Viktor Orbán's 16 years in power, which he has denied. Three of his former ministers are already in custody, according to Reuters.

Orbán calls it political revenge

Viktor Orbán dismissed his brother's reported detention as political persecution, writing on X that the government was using it to divert attention from other issues.

"I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me," he wrote.

The arrest lands at a sensitive moment. Péter Magyar, a pro-European Union conservative, won a landslide election victory in April that ended Orbán's 16-year rule, after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of power under his predecessor. His government has since launched a broad accountability drive, and the new anti-graft body has taken over several cases involving the sale of political connections to obtain work and residence permits.

What is still unknown

The central fact remains unconfirmed by the authorities: police and the anti-graft body have not said whether Áron Orbán himself was detained, formally identified as a suspect, or charged. What is confirmed is that four people were detained and searches took place at several sites in Budapest and Pest county. Further details from the investigation are expected to follow, and the question of whether the reported detention becomes a formal charge will shape how far the case reaches into the former prime minister's circle.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: Hungary detains former PM Orbán's brother in people-smuggling probe

entry.title: U.S. pulls aircraft from second British base after Iran threat
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United States military evacuated aircraft from a second airbase in Britain on Monday after a reported threat from Iran, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Two U.S. refuelling tankers operating from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk were diverted to Germany early on Monday, and several more tankers stationed at the base were moved to Germany and other locations later in the day, according to the report.

It is the second British base from which American aircraft have been withdrawn in recent weeks. The move follows the removal of U.S. bombers from RAF Fairford in southwest England after a suspected Iran-linked security incident. According to The National, that incident involved seven arrests.

Security raised at two bases

The U.S. also raised the security posture at RAF Mildenhall and the nearby RAF Lakenheath to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the second-highest defensive threat level in the U.S. Department of Defense system. The level is used when intelligence indicates that a form of terrorist action is likely.

RAF Mildenhall hosts U.S. Air Force personnel and units, including the tankers that support long-range operations. RAF Fairford had been used by U.S. bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had previously declared Fairford and similar bases legitimate targets, The National reported.

The precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among U.S. officials, according to the Wall Street Journal. It is not clear whether the threat was imminent or whether the move was precautionary.

What is still unknown

No U.S. or British official has publicly described the threat in detail, and neither government has confirmed the exact number of aircraft moved. What is confirmed is that tankers left Mildenhall for Germany and other locations on Monday, and that the alert level at Mildenhall and Lakenheath has been raised. Further clarity is likely to come from official statements in the coming days.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The National

link.title: U.S. pulls aircraft from second British base after Iran threat

entry.title: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' and new strikes are unlikely
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the war with Iran could end "fairly soon" and that further U.S. military action now looks unnecessary, in his clearest signal yet that Washington is turning toward a diplomatic end to the nine-month conflict.

Speaking to reporters at the White House after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Trump said Tehran was "talking very politely" with Washington and that momentum was building toward an end to the fighting. "We're seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it's going to be ending fairly soon," he said.

Trump described Iran as defeated in military terms, pointing to the destruction of its navy and an economy hollowed out by surging inflation. "Iran militarily is effectively over," he said. "We're just keeping it the status quo."

Strikes still on the table

The president was careful to keep the military option open. He said the United States was "locked and loaded" and ready to resume strikes if circumstances changed, and that a renewed campaign could be far larger than the ones already carried out. At this point, however, he said that looked "quite unlikely."

In a message posted on Truth Social after the meeting, Trump said regional governments including the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar all favoured maintaining the current approach — keeping the U.S. naval blockade of Iran in place — rather than launching further attacks.

A deal, with conditions

Trump said he wanted to give negotiations a chance and that there was a "good chance" of a deal, but warned he could reverse course if Tehran did not treat the talks seriously. He repeated that Iran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, calling that point non-negotiable.

The U.S. naval blockade remains firmly in place, and a new American task force known as Operation Iron Gate, announced on November 7, is tasked with restricting Iran's overland trade in weapons, dual-use technology and sanctioned materials.

Iran, for its part, has pushed back. Its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, called on the United States to accept Tehran's seven conditions for ending the conflict, accusing Washington of spreading "fake news" about imaginary talks.

The conflict began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched missile strikes on Tehran, killing several of Iran's top leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. It has since driven a surge in fuel prices felt across the global economy.

No ceasefire or formal agreement has been announced, and it remains unclear what terms either side would accept. For now, the war appears to be on hold — with the blockade and the threat of renewed strikes both still in force.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • The National

link.title: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' and new strikes are unlikely

entry.title: France blames Iran for supermarket fridge hack and warns of sanctions
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

France summoned Iran's ambassador on Tuesday after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets across the country, in a diplomatic escalation that Paris says could lead to European sanctions and a cyber response of its own.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said France would push for EU sanctions over what he called an "attack of unprecedented scale and aggression in our country". Speaking on France Info television, he warned that Paris would take whatever measures it judged proportionate, including some it would not discuss publicly, to deter further attacks and punish those responsible.

Tehran blamed for October disruption

French officials said on Monday that Iran's Revolutionary Guards were behind the attacks, which disrupted commercial refrigeration systems in early October. The foreign ministry confirmed that the ambassador's summoning, announced the previous day, took place on Tuesday morning.

The supermarket hacks were among the most disruptive cyberattacks since the war with Iran began in February, a conflict marked by sporadic episodes of suspected digital sabotage. Other incidents in that pattern have included hacks targeting the Los Angeles transit system in March and US water treatment plants in July.

The attacks were relatively unsophisticated in technical terms — the refrigeration systems were connected to the internet, which left them exposed — but their scale made them a national problem. Hundreds of stores were affected, and the disruption put chilled and frozen stock at risk across the country.

A relationship already under strain

Iran's mission to the United Nations did not respond to requests for comment on Monday. Iran routinely denies carrying out malicious cyber operations.

Relations between Paris and Tehran have been strained for years over Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, its regional activities and the detention of several French nationals. Ties improved after those detainees were released and France distanced itself from the US war on Iran, but they deteriorated again over the summer, after Iran arrested and later expelled two French diplomats. France responded by expelling Iranian diplomats.

French officials say Tehran has become increasingly hostile towards France, notably over its support for Iranian civil society.

What is still unknown

France has not published technical evidence linking the attacks to the Revolutionary Guards, and no details of any planned sanctions or cyber response have been disclosed. Barrot said France's cyberdefence doctrine gave authorities a range of options, but he did not say which, if any, had been chosen.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: France blames Iran for supermarket fridge hack and warns of sanctions

entry.title: Anthropic pulls back IPO terms sent to banks in filing mix-up
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, sent bankers an IPO prospectus on Monday showing a share sale of about 867 million shares priced at $70 to $80 — then pulled it back hours later, saying the details were inaccurate.

The circulated document implied a fundraising of up to $69.3 billion at the top of the price range. A follow-up email told recipients the pricing details were wrong and that an updated filing would follow, without saying which figures were incorrect. An Anthropic spokesperson declined to comment.

A clerical error before a giant listing

The retracted document was an updated prospectus sent by Anthropic's outside counsel in Canada, according to The Information, citing people familiar with the matter. The counsel later told the banks that some of the details were inaccurate and that the filing would be updated.

The mix-up landed just as Anthropic was preparing to begin formal marketing of what would be one of the largest public listings ever. Marketing is expected to start on Tuesday morning, according to IFR, with one-on-one and group meetings between management and investors around the world, in person and virtually. Retail investors may receive as much as 20% of the available shares, people familiar with the matter have said.

If the timetable holds, Anthropic would price the offering and debut on the Nasdaq Global Select Market in the week of November 16 — before the US Thanksgiving holiday on November 26, the company's apparent deadline.

A nervous market for AI stocks

The error added last-minute drama to an already jittery market. AI-related stocks sold off sharply last week, briefly pushing the Cboe Volatility Index — Wall Street's "fear gauge" — above 25, a level at which companies typically postpone listings.

The valuation debate is unresolved. Some potential investors have discussed a range of about $1.1 trillion to $1.3 trillion, well below where talks had been focused a month earlier, during which time the Nasdaq 100 index fell 14%. The retracted $69.3 billion figure would have fallen short of an earlier goal of matching SpaceX's record-setting debut.

Anthropic also faces questions about its growth: its quarterly revenue growth slowed at the end of the third quarter, and the data centres powering its models could face pressure after the Democrats' midterm election gains — the trigger for last week's sell-off.

Still, advisers say the deal's sheer size may insulate it. "It's such a big deal and such a unique asset that if the company wants to move forward, they can," Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at IPO research firm Renaissance Capital, said. "It just becomes a matter of where it prices."

What is still unknown

It is not clear which details in the retracted filing were wrong — the share count, the price range, or both — and Anthropic has not said when the corrected filing will arrive. The final size and pricing of the offering remain unsettled, and the company has not confirmed the marketing schedule publicly.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Edge Singapore (Bloomberg)

link.title: Anthropic pulls back IPO terms sent to banks in filing mix-up

entry.title: SoftBank posts $7.1 billion quarterly loss as US data-centre bet backfires
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

SoftBank Group reported a net loss of ¥1.12 trillion — about $7.1 billion — in its fiscal second quarter on Tuesday, its first quarterly loss in almost two years and a sharp reversal from the profit analysts had expected.

The Tokyo-based investor, one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, had been forecast to post a profit of ¥129 billion on average. Instead, it absorbed a $3.7 billion writedown on its American data-centre projects and watched the value of several of its largest listed holdings fall.

The writedown relates to non-refundable advance payments SoftBank made to secure power-generation equipment for its US data-centre build-out, including an eight-gigawatt campus in Ohio. Having rushed to reserve manufacturing capacity amid fears of shortages and long lead times, the company later revised its procurement plans as the requirements of its existing and planned projects changed. In total, it had paid about $9.5 billion upfront for power-generation equipment by the end of September.

Falling holdings added to the damage

The data-centre charge was not the only drag. Declines in the share prices of chipmakers Arm Holdings and Intel, along with South Korean e-commerce group Coupang, further weighed on the bottom line. SoftBank recorded a loss of about ¥270 billion on its Intel holdings and related derivatives.

The result underlines the tension at the heart of founder Masayoshi Son's strategy: building the infrastructure needed to support artificial intelligence at enormous speed, even as the cost of hardware and financing rises. SoftBank has committed roughly $65 billion to OpenAI, and a potential new funding round that could value the chatbot maker at $1.25 trillion has not yet been reflected in its results — any revaluation will wait until that round closes, chief financial officer Yoshimitsu Goto said.

A proxy for AI sentiment

SoftBank is increasingly treated by investors as a proxy for sentiment towards OpenAI and the wider AI sector, and its shares have fallen by more than half from their record high in June. They rallied 13.9 percent on Tuesday, alongside broader strength in Asian technology stocks, before the results were released.

The loss is one of the first hard writedowns on AI data-centre spending by a top-tier backer, and it lands in a market already asking whether the vast sums being poured into AI infrastructure will generate the returns to justify them. SoftBank's answer, for this quarter at least, is that the bill has arrived before the payoff.

What is still unknown

It is not clear how much of the equipment SoftBank has already paid for can still be used, or what rebates it may recover on future purchases. The company has also not said whether it will slow the pace of its data-centre spending, or how the Ohio project will proceed now that its procurement plans have changed.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Japan Times

link.title: SoftBank posts $7.1 billion quarterly loss as US data-centre bet backfires

entry.title: US measles elimination status under review as cases pass 5,000
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

An international panel of health experts meets behind closed doors in Washington this week to decide whether the United States keeps the measles elimination status it has held since 2000. The review comes as the country has confirmed at least 5,182 measles cases so far this year, spread across 45 states and Washington, D.C.

The meeting, scheduled for November 10 to 13, is run by the Pan American Health Organization's independent commission for monitoring measles and rubella elimination in the Americas. The commission, made up of experts in epidemiology, public health, virology, pediatrics and immunization, meets at least once a year to assess whether countries in the region still qualify as having eliminated the disease.

The question is whether the spread never stopped

Elimination does not mean measles vanished entirely. It means the virus was not spreading continuously within the country for at least 12 months. The United States earned that designation in 2000, when annual cases had fallen to 85.

The review turns on what happened after the first cases of the current surge were confirmed in a small town in western Texas in January 2025. From there, measles spread to neighbouring Texas counties and to other states, including Utah, Arizona, South Carolina and Pennsylvania.

If the evidence shows genetically identical strains linking the large outbreaks back to the Texas strain, that would support a finding of a full year of continuous transmission — and the loss of elimination status. If the outbreaks turn out to be separate and unlinked, the country would keep its status.

A record year, by a wide margin

The scale of the resurgence is now clear. The United States recorded 2,289 confirmed cases in 2025, the first time the annual total had passed 2,000 since 1992. This year's count of more than 5,000 is already more than double that.

Pennsylvania alone has recorded more than 1,500 cases this year, according to the state's health department. Eleven measles deaths have been confirmed over the past nearly two years, largely among people who were unvaccinated or too young to be vaccinated.

Canada lost its own measles elimination status last year after a year-long outbreak it could not contain, and the wider Americas region has already lost its measles-free designation as a result.

A decision that is largely symbolic — and still stings

Health experts who spoke to ABC News said losing the status would change little in practice, because measles transmission is already widespread. But they described the moment as a serious marker of how far the disease has come back.

Dr. Paul Offit called the possible loss "a tremendous loss" and, "at best… a call to arms." Dr. Peter Hotez put it more bluntly: "Measles is back."

What is still unknown

The commission will weigh the evidence during its four-day meeting, but there is no public timetable for a decision. Its conclusions go to PAHO's director, who formally communicates the classification to national authorities, so a public announcement may come days after the meeting ends.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ABC News
  • PAHO

link.title: US measles elimination status under review as cases pass 5,000

entry.title: US inflation ran hotter than expected in October, strengthening the case for a December rate hike
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Tuesday — a slower pace than September's 0.6% increase, but hotter than the 0.3% rise economists had expected, and enough to keep the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates at its December meeting.

The report's underlying measures were stubborn too. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% for a third consecutive month, again above the 0.2% forecast. Housing did much of the work: shelter costs rose 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the month's overall increase, according to the bureau. Food prices rose 0.5%, while energy prices rose 0.7% — a sharp easing from September's 5.2% jump, but still rising.

One figure was missing entirely. The bureau did not publish an annual inflation rate for October, because last year's federal government shutdown prevented it from collecting the consumer price data for October 2025 that a year-on-year comparison requires. The last published annual reading, for September, was 3.7%.

A rate hike now looks near-certain

The October data all but settles the question hanging over the Fed's December 9 meeting. Traders now put the odds of a rate hike at more than 98%, according to CME FedWatch, with a quarter-point move to a 4% to 4.25% range the most likely outcome. Higher rates would make borrowing more expensive for households already stretching to cover groceries, rent and other everyday costs — and real average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, the bureau reported separately, meaning pay did not keep pace with prices.

The report lands days after midterm elections in which frustration over the cost of living was a major issue for voters. For the central bank, the dilemma is familiar: inflation is cooling from September's pace, but it is not cooling fast enough, and the missing annual figure leaves policymakers without their usual headline yardstick.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear how large December's move will be, or how the Fed will frame its next steps given the gap in the annual data. The bureau is scheduled to publish the November inflation report on December 10 — one day after the Fed's decision — so the central bank will act on October's figures and its own projections rather than fresh data.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics

link.title: US inflation ran hotter than expected in October, strengthening the case for a December rate hike

entry.title: Stanford's century-long AI study finds AI has gone mainstream — and the public had little say
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A landmark study that tracks artificial intelligence every five years has concluded that AI has gone mainstream — and that the public has had almost no say in how it got there.

The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence, known as AI100, released its third report on Tuesday, titled "AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI." Administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence and led by an international panel chaired by Oxford professor Michael Wooldridge, the report assesses AI's development and societal impact across technical, ethical, economic and governance questions.

Scaling — building systems with ever more data and computing power — powered the chief advances of the last five years, the panel found. But that approach is now running into data and compute constraints, pushing the frontier toward reasoning and inference-time computing instead.

The report compares AI's disruption to that of the World Wide Web. Creative industries, mathematics and software development — fields that believed themselves beyond its reach — are already being transformed, joining journalism, music and retail among the sectors upended by technology over the past three decades. Science is moving fastest of all: AI is compressing research timescales from years to months or weeks, a shift recognised by the 2024 Nobel Prizes in physics and chemistry.

Concentration, conflict and trust

The panel's warnings are as striking as its account of progress. Capital investment in AI infrastructure is unprecedented in scale and speed, propping up parts of the US economy and dominating capital markets — while fuelling fears of a financial bubble and straining energy and freshwater supplies. Frontier AI development is concentrated among a small number of US and Chinese actors, raising questions about who will ultimately own and have access to leading-edge systems.

Military AI, the report says, has gone from a hypothetical point of speculation to a transformative force in active conflicts. Cybersecurity has emerged as a major area of risk for AI abuse. And AI-generated imagery, audio and video have ended the century-old assumption that evidence based on photographs and recordings is inherently trustworthy.

Governance, meanwhile, is fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus on its direction. Risks once seen as pure science fiction are now emerging, the panel warns, while existing ethical concerns demand ever more attention.

A watershed, already dating

Wooldridge said that since 2021, powerful general-purpose AI tools had gone "from being a point of speculation to an everyday reality, used by millions of people." Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee and a professor at the University of Toronto, called the last five years "a watershed moment in the history of AI."

The panel's twelfth and final takeaway is a warning about its own shelf life: the pace of development over the past five years was unprecedented, few people predicted where AI would be today even five years ago, and if the current pace is sustained, the next five years should surprise us just as much. The report concedes it will be out of date by the time most people read it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Max-Planck-Gesellschaft
  • Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI

link.title: Stanford's century-long AI study finds AI has gone mainstream — and the public had little say

entry.title: Indonesia's vice president signals he will step down as eligibility questions mount
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Indonesia's Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka told President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday that he intends to resign, a presidential spokesperson said, as lawmakers weigh whether the education documents he submitted to stand for office disqualified him.

Gibran, 39, raised the matter during a meeting with the president, spokesperson Prasetyo Hadi said. The president did not decline the request, Hadi added. It was not immediately clear whether a formal resignation letter had been submitted, or when any resignation would take effect.

A probe parliament is weighing

Parliament reconvened on Tuesday with lawmakers considering an investigation into Gibran's eligibility, amid a widening rift between his father, the hugely popular former president Joko Widodo, and Prabowo. House Speaker Puan Maharani said lawmakers had received many opinions on the issue during a one-month recess and that the next steps would be discussed. Asked about the vice president's future, she declined to speculate, saying it was better to respond calmly and avoid raising public concern over things that had not yet happened.

The dispute centres on Gibran's qualifications. Last month, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled that the education documents he submitted did not meet election requirements. The Constitutional Court added that it did not have the power to disqualify him, saying that responsibility belonged to other institutions. Some lawmakers are now seeking an investigation, which analysts believe could be the first step towards impeachment proceedings.

A partnership under strain

Gibran's presence on the ticket helped Prabowo win the 2024 election by a large margin, but he has kept a low profile as vice president, and his public appearances alongside Prabowo have been infrequent during their first two years in office. The eligibility question has now become a visible strain on the partnership between the president and the family of his predecessor.

It remains unclear whether Prabowo will accept the resignation, whether parliament will press ahead with its probe, or what either decision would mean for the coalition that brought the pair to power. What is certain is that the question hanging over the vice presidency — whether Gibran was ever eligible to hold it — is now being asked in the open, by the institutions that would have to answer it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • Reuters

entry.title: Rivian bets its future on the R2 and self-driving tech, calling 2027 an inflection year
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Rivian's chief executive, RJ Scaringe, says 2027 will be "an inflection year" for the electric-vehicle maker, as it ramps up production of its cheaper R2 SUV and rolls out new driver-assistance technology. He made the remarks in an interview with CNBC on Tuesday, five years to the day since Rivian listed on the Nasdaq.

The anniversary is a sobering one for shareholders. Rivian's shares have fallen more than 80% from their initial public offering price of $78, including a drop of nearly 30% this year. Scaringe's argument is that the next twelve months change the story: the R2, a midsize SUV aimed at a far broader market than Rivian's first models, is now the company's best-selling vehicle by volume, and its cheapest version is expected to cost about $45,000.

The numbers behind that claim are the strongest the company has reported. Rivian delivered a record 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter of 2026, up 46% on a year earlier, with the R2 driving the growth in its first full quarter of sales. The company has raised its full-year delivery forecast to between 67,000 and 70,000 vehicles. The R2 has also collected early honours, including TopGear's SUV of the Year award for 2027.

Autonomy is the second bet

The other half of Scaringe's plan is self-driving technology. Rivian is preparing a limited release of "point-to-point" driving — in which the vehicle navigates between destinations while the driver supervises — before the end of this year, with a general release to subscribers of its Autonomy+ service in 2027. The company says it will share more detail about its artificial-intelligence and autonomy plans at an investor event on December 9.

Rivian is also building a multibillion-dollar factory in Georgia to support the R2's expansion, and it estimates its available future liquidity at about $13 billion, including credit lines, funding from its partnerships with Volkswagen and Uber, and a $4.5 billion US Department of Energy loan for the Georgia plant.

What is still unknown

Investors have not yet seen Rivian's 2027 delivery or profit targets, and funding remains a live concern: Deutsche Bank analyst Edison Yu flagged the company's cash needs after its October 30 earnings report. Rivian's automotive division is on course to end 2026 with positive gross margins, its interim finance chief told investors last week — a milestone that would give the 2027 plan a firmer footing, but one the company still has to deliver.

Illustration — not a photograph.

entry.title: Relief at the pump as U.S. gas falls below $4 a gallon for the first time since July
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The average price of regular gasoline in the United States fell below $4 a gallon on Tuesday, the first time it has done so since July 20, according to data from motor club AAA. The national average stood at $3.97 a gallon, down from $4.14 on Election Day a week earlier.

The drop caps a slide that began in late September, when the national average peaked near $4.48, and it follows a sharp fall in crude oil. Brent crude, the global benchmark, plunged 13% last week — its steepest one-week decline since April 2020 — then slid a further 5% on Monday to its lowest point since August 31. On Tuesday it briefly traded below $90 a barrel.

Two forces are pushing prices down. The first is seasonal: the summer driving season has ended and the clocks have gone back, both of which cut demand for gasoline. The second is geopolitical. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global supply, and markets are betting that the midterm election results increase pressure for a diplomatic end to the war in Iran. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the war was "effectively over" militarily, and his administration is meeting mediators over Tehran's nuclear programme.

Relief — with limits

For drivers, the change is real but partial. Gas prices remain more than 30% above where they stood before the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, and roughly 40% higher than at the start of the year. Diesel, used by heavy trucks and farm equipment, is still expensive: it fell from $6.28 a gallon on Election Day to $6.15, but remains above $6.

The picture also varies sharply by state. Twenty-six states already average below $4 a gallon, with North Carolina the cheapest at $3.26. At the other end, Nevada, California and Hawaii are still averaging close to $6.

What happens next

Analysts expect further declines in the near term. Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, expects the national average to reach about $3.75 by Thanksgiving, and AAA notes that prices typically fall by 10 to 30 cents a gallon over the winter months. Whether the sub-$4 level holds into spring will depend largely on whether negotiations in the Middle East continue — and on whether the recent easing in oil markets lasts.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • NBC News

link.title: Relief at the pump as U.S. gas falls below $4 a gallon for the first time since July

entry.title: Russia and Ukraine hold first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months, calling day one 'very productive'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Russia and Ukraine held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on Tuesday, meeting in Abu Dhabi for nearly four hours in a renewed push to end a war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The session, the first direct meeting between the sides since February, is scheduled to continue for a second day on Wednesday. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the opening day "very productive," while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described it as "constructive and quite substantive."

Neither Rubio nor Zelenskyy attended the talks in the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Washington was represented by President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, who are trying to broker a settlement. Russia's chief negotiator is Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky; the Ukrainian delegation is headed by Rustem Umerov.

Humanitarian questions first

According to Zelenskyy, the first day was largely about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and the return of Ukrainian civilians held in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. The two-day session was also expected to take up future security guarantees for the warring countries, the White House said before the discussions began.

Hopes of a breakthrough are tempered by the record so far. Three previous rounds of talks earlier this year produced no significant breakthroughs, and the two sides remain far apart on the core questions of territory and the shape of any deal. Russia wants Ukraine to pull back troops and abandon its bid to join NATO — terms Zelenskyy has rejected.

Fighting goes on

The talks did not pause the war. Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's air force said, and analysts and humanitarian organizations say the conflict has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

The Trump administration has signalled it believes ending the war may require a broader agreement with Moscow on Europe's security — a position European officials see as an early concession to Russia. Trump said last week that a wider deal was in the works and would "involve more than Ukraine."

Whether a second day of talks produces anything concrete remains to be seen. For now, the fact that the two sides are in the same room again — after nine months apart — is the news.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Nikkei Asia

entry.title: House Republicans choose Jim Jordan as their next leader after midterm losses
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

House Republicans have chosen Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their next leader, handing the party's top House post to one of its most combative conservatives a week after voters stripped the party of its majority.

Jordan, the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee and a founder of the conservative Freedom Caucus, defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a closed-door secret ballot on Tuesday. The vote was 106 to 73, according to two Republican lawmakers in the room.

Jordan will serve as minority leader in the next Congress, when Democrats take control of the chamber after winning at least 11 Republican-held seats in last week's midterm elections. The Associated Press projected Democrats will hold at least 255 seats to at least 166 for Republicans, with some races still uncalled.

A changing of the guard

The result is a clear break with the party's recent leadership. Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana announced on Monday that he was stepping down from the leadership team after three years in the top role, and Jordan now succeeds him as the House's senior Republican.

Scalise, who had spent a decade in leadership and held the No. 2 post since 2019, was the establishment choice. Jordan's victory signals that the conference, now facing life in the minority, preferred a fighter known for confrontation with Democratic leaders and for his close alliance with President Donald Trump.

Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota was re-elected as whip and will be the second-ranking House Republican in the next Congress.

A rematch with history

Tuesday's contest was a rematch of the leadership struggle that followed the ouster of then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy in 2023. Scalise defeated Jordan 113 to 99 in that closed-door race for the party's nomination, but withdrew the following day after failing to secure enough support to win a vote of the full House. Jordan's own bid for the speakership then collapsed as well.

This time the path was simpler: the minority leader is chosen by the party conference alone, so Jordan needed only a majority of his colleagues, not the full House.

What comes next

The new Congress is sworn in in January, when Jordan will formally take up the minority leader's post and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is expected to become speaker. The immediate test for Jordan will be holding together a smaller, bruised conference while Democrats, with a commanding majority, set the House agenda — and while the party decides how to rebuild after a midterm defeat that cost it both chambers.

For now, the message from the conference is unmistakable: after a sweeping loss, House Republicans have chosen their most prominent brawler to lead them.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NBC News
  • USA Today

entry.title: Anthropic's seven founders will each cash out about $250 million in the IPO
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic's seven co-founders will each take home about $250 million when the artificial intelligence company goes public next week, according to an updated filing — a modest cash-out next to the stakes they will keep, worth roughly $18 billion apiece.

The filing, published on Tuesday, shows each founder plans to sell 3,378,378 shares in the offering. At the midpoint of Anthropic's $70-to-$78 price range, that works out to just under $250 million each, or about $1.75 billion combined. At the low end of the range each would receive just over $236 million; at the high end, just under $264 million. Anthropic itself receives none of the money from the founders' sales.

The seven are chief executive Dario Amodei; his sister Daniela Amodei, the company's president and chair of the board; chief compute officer Tom Brown; Jack Clark, who heads the company's public-benefit institute; chief science officer Jared Kaplan; chief architect Sam McCandlish; and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah.

A small slice of very large stakes

The sales amount to only about 1.5 percent of each founder's holding. After the offering, each will still own about 3.2 percent of Anthropic's Class A shares — roughly 22 percent between them — with the stakes valued at around $18 billion each at the midpoint of the price range, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The founders have also agreed to transfer restrictions lasting up to a year after the offering, limiting further sales in the near term.

A record-setting debut

The cash-out figures underline the sheer scale of the listing. Anthropic is offering 825 million Class A shares, which would raise between $57.75 billion and $64.35 billion, and is seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion in total once a private placement to large investors is included. At the top of the price range, the company would be valued at about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than a month earlier. The offering is expected to be priced on November 18, with shares beginning trading on the Nasdaq the following day under the ticker "ANT."

Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million of shares through his donor-advised fund, according to the filing.

What comes next

The listing will be one of the largest public offerings ever and the biggest test yet of investor appetite for AI companies at trillion-dollar valuations. For the founders, the message of the filing is restraint as much as reward: they are selling a sliver of their holdings while keeping the overwhelming majority — and the voting control that comes with it — for the long term.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • The Wall Street Journal

entry.title: CoreWeave beats revenue forecasts as AI demand lifts its order book to $133 billion
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

CoreWeave, the cloud provider that rents out Nvidia-powered computing for artificial intelligence work, reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results on Tuesday, easing some of the market's recent nerves about the AI infrastructure boom.

Revenue for the quarter reached $3.66 billion, ahead of Wall Street's expectation of $3.54 billion and up 168 percent on the year. Adjusted operating income rose 75 percent to $379 million, although the adjusted operating margin narrowed from 16 percent to 10 percent.

The results landed after a rough stretch for the stock, which had fallen by roughly half over the previous month as investors questioned whether the company's debt-fuelled expansion could keep pace with demand. Shares rose in after-hours trading following the report.

A backlog that keeps growing

The headline that mattered most to investors was the order book. CoreWeave's revenue backlog — signed contracts not yet delivered — grew to $133 billion, up from $104 billion at the end of the second quarter.

The company's growth rests on its close relationship with Nvidia, which is a 9 percent shareholder, a customer and its most important supplier. CoreWeave rents out Nvidia servers in the cloud, and that access has translated into large contracts with heavyweight customers including Microsoft and Meta Platforms.

The company also gave solid guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year, particularly for adjusted operating income, suggesting management expects the momentum to continue into the end of 2026.

The cost side of the boom

The report also laid bare the price of growing this fast. Interest expenses reached $846 million in the quarter, up from $310 million a year earlier, more than wiping out the operating profit. Debt and lease liabilities rose by $14.6 billion in a single quarter, to $66 billion.

Chief executive Michael Intrator said the company was moving away from unsecured public debt in favour of delayed-draw facilities it has used before, a shift aimed at lowering its borrowing costs.

That financing question is now the central test for CoreWeave. Demand for AI computing shows no sign of slowing — the backlog proves that — but the company must convert those contracts into revenue on schedule while keeping its borrowing under control. This quarter, the top line did its part. The balance sheet remains the thing to watch.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Barron's
  • CNBC

entry.title: French police searched the Ritz in Paris as part of the Al Fayed trafficking inquiry
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

French police searched the Ritz hotel in Paris and two other properties linked to the late billionaire Mohamed Al Fayed in mid-October, the Paris prosecutor's office confirmed on Tuesday, as part of an investigation into an alleged trafficking network.

The searches took place on October 13 and 14 at the Ritz in Paris, at Villa Windsor in the city's 16th arrondissement, and at Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez on the French Riviera. Officers from London's Metropolitan Police were present during the operation in France, though they did not take part directly. The French investigation is being conducted in coordination with British authorities.

Several people were taken into police custody for questioning following the searches and have since been released pending further investigation. Investigators seized computers, phones and other digital material, which prosecutors said is being analysed. No current member of Ritz staff was arrested, according to The Observer.

An inquiry into alleged accomplices

The French investigation was opened in the summer of 2025 into allegations of aggravated human trafficking, procuring prostitutes and rape. Its focus is on identifying possible accomplices of Mohamed Al Fayed and his late brother, Salah Al Fayed, rather than on the businessman himself, who died in 2023 aged 94 without ever being charged.

France's specialist anti-trafficking unit has interviewed at least five complainants. Victims cited the Ritz and Villa Windsor as locations where alleged abuse took place, according to prosecutors.

The inquiry runs parallel to a British investigation. More than 20 women told the BBC in 2024 that Al Fayed had sexually abused them, some alleging rape, and Harrods — which he owned until 2010 — apologised the same year. Since the BBC documentary aired, more than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Mohamed Al Fayed and his brother, and at least 157 people have reported allegations directly to the Metropolitan Police taskforce, known as Operation Cornpoppy.

What remains unknown

No charges have been announced in the French case, and prosecutors have not disclosed what the seized digital material contains. The searches themselves do not establish that anyone assisted the alleged offending.

The Ritz has condemned the alleged behaviour. The investigation continues under the supervision of the Paris prosecutor's office.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Observer

link.title: French police searched the Ritz in Paris as part of the Al Fayed trafficking inquiry

entry.title: Apple's iCloud outage knocks out Mail, Calendar and Photos; account sign-in still down
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Apple confirmed an outage affecting several of its iCloud services on Tuesday, November 10, leaving some users unable to reach their mail, calendars and photos for part of the day.

The disruption was reported by 9to5Mac on Tuesday afternoon, and Apple's own System Status page listed a string of iCloud services as affected. By the early evening, most of them had been restored — but two problems were still active.

What went down

According to Apple's System Status page, the outage touched iCloud Mail, iCloud Calendar, iCloud Contacts and Photos, along with Game Center, iWork for iCloud, Apple Music and Podcasts. As of 5:07 p.m. Pacific time on Tuesday, each of those was listed as resolved.

Two services were still showing problems at that time. iCloud Account & Sign In remained in outage, and Find My was listed as having an issue. Other iCloud services — including iCloud Drive, iCloud Backup, iCloud Keychain, iCloud Notes and iCloud Web Apps — were shown as available.

The status page does not say how many people were affected or when the outage began, and Apple has not given a cause for the disruption.

What is still affected

The continuing outage in iCloud Account & Sign In means some users may still have trouble signing in to iCloud or reaching account-related features. The ongoing issue with Find My may affect locating devices through the service.

For most users, the practical effects of the earlier outage were interruptions to everyday tools: mail not syncing, calendar entries not updating across devices, and photos not uploading. iCloud sits at the centre of how Apple devices share data, so even a partial outage can be felt across an iPhone, a Mac and the web at the same time.

What remains unknown

Apple has not said what caused the outage, how widespread it was, or when the two remaining problems will be cleared. The company's status page is the main public record of the incident, and it lists only whether each service is available, affected or in outage — not the number of users involved.

Users still seeing problems can check the System Status page for the latest state of each service, and the page is updated as incidents are resolved.

Illustration — not a photograph.

entry.title: US charges three Iran-backed suspects over plots including RAF Fairford incident
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The US Department of Justice has charged three men it says were involved in a string of plots in the United States and Europe, including an alleged terrorist plot at RAF Fairford in England in September.

An eight-count indictment was unsealed on Tuesday. It names Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national; and Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen. The charges have not been proven in court.

What the US alleges

According to the Justice Department, the three men planned attacks in Europe carried out under the name of a purportedly new group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya — the Islamic Movement of the People of the Right Hand, known as HAYI.

The department said 18 attacks in the spring of 2026 in Europe were claimed in HAYI's name, seven of them in the UK. Those attacks involved arson and explosives, and in one case a near-fatal stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green, north London, in April — one of them a dual US-British citizen. A suspect in that stabbing is due to stand trial next year.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the accused were involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iran-backed Iraqi militia Kataib Hezbollah. He said the indictment showed Iran's determination to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the US.

One of the men, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, is accused of communicating with contacts in the UK from a prison in New York, where he is awaiting trial on previous charges. The other two are accused of communicating from Iran. Patel said one of the three allegedly sent coded messages from detention to assist in future acts of violence.

The RAF Fairford incident

A major incident was declared on 27 September near RAF Fairford in the Cotswolds, Gloucestershire, after three suspicious vans were seen near the airbase. No explosive materials were found in the vans, but a quantity of petrol was seized.

The Justice Department said Iranian agents most recently orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom. It alleges that in August, al-Hassani directed and paid associates in the UK to take preparatory steps for the plot, including paying one person on 22 August to carry out surveillance of the base's perimeter.

In September, the department alleges, he paid several people to help prepare — procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching chemical accelerants including large quantities of potassium chloride, and buying metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. The vans were made to look as though they belonged to a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On 26 September, al-Hassani allegedly told individuals to drive the three vans, some carrying barrels of fuel, to the base, staying in frequent contact with the drivers. At least two of the vans met a security roadblock on the way to the perimeter and were turned back. In the early hours of 27 September, a local farmer spotted the vans and called the police.

Seven men have been arrested in the UK over the incident, and two British nationals appeared in court last month in connection with the alleged plot.

Wider context

RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force for decades, and in recent months the US flew B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East for strikes on Iran. The US removed all its bombers from the base last month after the incident, with President Donald Trump citing threats to the base. In July, Iran said any base used for aggression against Iranian territory was a legitimate target.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the Fairford incident. The Iranian embassy in London said it categorically rejected what it called unfounded and malicious speculation linking Iran to it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News

link.title: US charges three Iran-backed suspects over plots including RAF Fairford incident

entry.title: Latvia and Lithuania warn of drone threat as NATO jets scramble
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Latvia and Lithuania warned residents to take shelter on Tuesday night after an unidentified object was detected in Belarus flying towards the Baltic states, and NATO fighter jets on the Baltic air defence mission were scrambled in response.

In Latvia, the National Armed Forces issued an orange-level air threat alert for Ludza municipality, on the border with Belarus, telling residents to take cover immediately. The alert was later extended to the Krāslava and Augšdaugava regions before being called off about an hour later. No injuries were reported.

Latvia uses a two-level mobile alert system. A yellow alert is an informational message about a possible threat that requires no immediate action; an orange alert means a confirmed threat in the airspace and residents in the affected areas must follow instructions at once. People in the areas covered by the warning received the alert on their mobile phones.

Lithuania's alert

Lithuania issued its own warning after the object was spotted in Belarus heading towards its territory. A code yellow alert was broadcast at around 11pm local time, urging people in the counties of Vilnius and Utena to head for their nearest shelter.

Vilnius Airport and the airspace around it were shut down while the alert was in force, and reopened once it was called off. The head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT that the object had yet to be identified.

A drone detected in Belarusian territory was also reported to have crossed the border into Poland, according to reports carried by Israeli outlet Ynet, and Lithuania later widened its alert in the border area with Belarus.

A recurring pattern

The incident is the latest in a series of airspace scares across northern Europe. Drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in recent months, and Latvia reported a brief intrusion near its borders with Belarus and Russia just over a week ago, on 1 November.

Ukraine has been attacking Russian oil shipping ports on the Baltic Sea, and some of its drones have missed their targets and triggered security warnings in neighbouring countries. Moscow has accused Kyiv of using NATO airspace as cover for attacks, a charge Kyiv rejects.

Neither Latvian nor Lithuanian authorities said on Tuesday night what the object was, where it came from, or whether it ever entered their airspace. Both countries lifted their alerts within about an hour, and residents in Ludza were told they could leave their shelters.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Latvia and Lithuania warn of drone threat as NATO jets scramble

entry.title: Bank of Canada raised rates to curb inflation risk, minutes show
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Senior Bank of Canada policymakers agreed it was prudent to raise interest rates to dampen the risk of higher inflation, even with considerable uncertainty hanging over the economy, according to minutes of the central bank's most recent policy deliberations published on Tuesday.

The Bank lifted its target for the overnight rate to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase in more than three years. Officials now expect consumer-price inflation to stay above 3% until late 2027 and only gradually return to the Bank's 2% target by mid-2028.

The deliberations, which began on October 20 and involved all six members of the Bank's policy-setting governing council, centred on an energy shock that officials expect to last. With the war in the Middle East continuing and little sign that oil-tanker traffic would soon speed up, the minutes said the risk that high inflation could persist and spread across the economy had grown.

"The prolonged energy shock and a resilient economy meant that the risk that high inflation could persist and become broad-based had increased," the minutes said. On that basis, officials decided "to raise the policy rate to 2.5% to reduce the risk that persistently high energy prices would lead to broader price increases."

Uncertainty, but not inaction

The case for holding rates was not ignored. Canada's economy has slack, and inflation outside energy remains close to target — consumer prices excluding gasoline were running at 2.2%, with core measures near 2%.

But the council judged that uncertainty was not a reason to stand still. Officials pointed to U.S.-Canada trade friction, the U.S.-Iran war, and the speed at which firms might raise prices to recoup higher input costs. "Uncertainty did not mean inaction," the minutes said, though officials agreed they would need to proceed carefully.

The minutes reinforced Governor Tiff Macklem's message that further increases could be needed, with each decision taken one meeting at a time.

A softer backdrop since the hike

Since the October decision, the economic picture has softened. Statistics Canada said the economy stalled in August, with early estimates pointing to a slight decline in September — putting growth on track for about 1.3% annualised, below the Bank's estimate of 2%.

October jobs data showed the economy shedding jobs for a third straight month, unemployment rising, and average hourly wage growth slowing. Traders have scaled back expectations for a follow-up rate increase at the Bank's next decision, on December 9.

For Canadian borrowers, the hike means higher costs on variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit. Whether December brings another increase will depend on whether the economy's slowdown cools price pressures faster than energy costs push them up.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Wall Street Journal
  • Reuters

entry.title: SpaceX unveils Starlink Mini 2 with a swappable battery for $999
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

SpaceX has unveiled the Starlink Mini 2, a new version of its smallest portable satellite internet terminal — and the headline change is power. For the first time, the laptop-sized dish carries its own battery, so it can get online without an outlet, a vehicle, or an external power bank nearby.

The terminal combines a satellite dish, a Wi-Fi router and now a removable 71 Wh battery in a single unit. SpaceX says the pack delivers up to 4.5 hours of connectivity on a full charge, and owners can hot-swap in a spare while the terminal stays online. The battery clips on with a quick-release mechanism that needs no tools, has its own LED indicators, and charges over USB-C at up to 60 watts. It can also send up to 60 watts back out over USB-C to charge other devices.

The redesign is slimmer and tougher than the original Mini, which launched in June 2024 at $599 and always needed an external power source. The Mini 2 is 23.1 mm thick, down from 38.5 mm, weighs about 3.5 pounds with the battery and kickstand attached, and carries an IP67 rating against dust and water. SpaceX says its built-in Wi-Fi can connect a user within 60 seconds.

Price and availability

Preorders opened on November 10 by invitation only, for select customers in the United States, at $999 plus tax. That price covers the hardware and a full year of Roam Unlimited service, which SpaceX values at $2,100. Customers reserve with a $100 refundable deposit, with the remaining $899 charged when the device ships. SpaceX expects the first shipments to begin in mid-December.

Most buyers will have to wait. SpaceX has not announced when general sales will open, what the terminal will cost without the year of service, or what it will cost in other countries. Its website lists more customers and countries as "coming soon", with no dates attached.

Why it matters

The original Mini's biggest practical limit was its dependence on power: in the field it had to stay tethered to a vehicle, a power station, or a wall. A built-in, swappable battery makes the terminal genuinely portable for travellers, campers, remote workers, and anyone needing connectivity during a power cut — a use case SpaceX has leaned into in its announcement. The bundle pricing also matters: with a year of service valued at more than twice the $999 package price, the launch is effectively a service-led offer, and the standalone hardware price remains unknown.

What is still unknown

The 4.5-hour figure is SpaceX's own claim, and no independent test of it has been published yet. Spare batteries will be sold separately, but SpaceX has not said what they will cost. Separately, code spotted on Starlink's website before the announcement hinted at a $249 kit and a $50 spare battery, but SpaceX has not confirmed either figure, and they should not be confused with the $999 invitation package.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • Interesting Engineering
  • Tesla Oracle

entry.title: House votes 211–204 to shelve Hegseth impeachment effort
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The House of Representatives voted 211–204 on Tuesday evening to send Rep. Thomas Massie's eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Judiciary Committee, effectively ending the effort for the remainder of this Congress.

The referral means there will be no floor vote on whether to impeach Hegseth. The articles now sit with the Republican-led Judiciary Committee, which is not expected to take them up before the current Congress ends on January 3, when they will formally expire. Democrats would need to start over with a new resolution if they want to pursue the matter next year.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, was the only member of his party to vote against sending the articles to committee. He had reintroduced the eight-article resolution on Monday as a privileged resolution, a procedural move that forced House leaders to act on it within two legislative days.

What the articles alleged

The resolution accused Hegseth of waging war in Iran without congressional approval, in violation of the War Powers Resolution, and of continuing the campaign even after both chambers of Congress passed a measure directing U.S. forces to withdraw. The remaining articles covered lethal U.S. strikes on suspected drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean, military action in Yemen, and the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in a military raid.

The push came a week after Republicans suffered heavy losses in the midterm elections, with some in the party blaming Hegseth's handling of the Iran war. Ahead of the vote, Axios reported that House Republican leaders expected enough defections from lawmakers with little left to lose to make the outcome uncertain. In the end, the party held together, with Massie alone breaking ranks.

Hegseth and the White House pushed back

Hegseth dismissed the effort as a "farce" and a "political spectacle" earlier on Tuesday, and the Trump administration issued a statement opposing the impeachment push shortly before the vote. Vice President JD Vance weighed in on X, calling the question of whether Hegseth had committed impeachable crimes "absurd." President Donald Trump celebrated the result on Truth Social after the vote, saying the attempt had failed and praising every Republican except Massie.

Why it matters

The vote spares Hegseth an impeachment vote for now, but the reprieve is likely short-lived. Democrats won majorities in both chambers in the midterm elections and take control in January, and they are widely expected to revive the impeachment effort in the new Congress. Even if the House were to impeach Hegseth then, removing him would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate — a much higher bar.

Only two cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached by the House in American history, and neither was convicted by the Senate. If Hegseth were impeached, he would become the third.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • The Times
