entry.title: NASA opens astronaut applications for Moon base and Mars missions
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

NASA has opened applications for its next class of astronauts, giving Americans a short window to apply for a job that could take them to the surface of the Moon.

The space agency announced the recruitment drive on Saturday, November 7 — the first time it has sought new astronauts since 2024. Applications close at 11:59 p.m. EST on Thursday, December 3, and must be submitted through the federal jobs site USAJOBS.

Those selected will join NASA as it works to return astronauts to the Moon and build a permanent base there, while laying the groundwork for the first crewed missions to Mars. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the new recruits could walk on the Moon, live and work at the planned Moon Base, and help develop the systems that will eventually carry crews to Mars.

Who can apply

Applicants must be U.S. citizens with a master's degree in a science, technology, engineering or mathematics field — including engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics — from an accredited institution. Most candidates also need at least three years of professional experience related to their degree, or 1,000 to 1,500 flight hours as a pilot. All must pass NASA's long-duration flight physical.

There is no official age limit. NASA says past selectees have ranged from 26 to 46 years old.

The job pays $164,395 a year under the 2026 federal pay schedule, though NASA notes the rate could be adjusted for 2027 and 2028. Selected candidates will train at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas.

A long shot, by the numbers

The odds are steep. When NASA last opened applications in 2024, more than 8,000 people applied. Ten candidates were chosen in 2025 and are now partway through nearly two years of training. NASA currently has 32 active astronauts.

The agency expects to announce its final selections late next year, with training for the new class to begin soon after.

Why it matters

The recruitment drive is tied to NASA's Artemis program, which aims to return humans to the Moon in 2028 — the first time since 1972. The plan calls for a sustained presence at the lunar south pole, where rotating crews would live and work while preparing for the longer journey to Mars. Before that landing, the Artemis III crew is scheduled to fly a test mission in low Earth orbit in 2027 to practise docking with the lunar landers built by Blue Origin and SpaceX.

For the handful of people eventually chosen, the application closing on December 3 is the first step toward a career that could end with footsteps on another world.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NASA
  • USA Today

link.title: NASA opens astronaut applications for Moon base and Mars missions

entry.title: Europe demands a seat at the Ukraine peace table as G7 meets Rubio in Paris
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

European foreign ministers told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Paris on Monday that Europe must have a say in any deal to end Russia's war on Ukraine, as US-mediated talks between Moscow and Kyiv got under way in Abu Dhabi.

The appeal came at a two-day G7 foreign ministers' meeting — Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States — which ends on Tuesday. Ministers from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, South Korea and Brazil are also attending.

It was Rubio's first meeting with allies since last week's midterm elections, in which Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses. It gave Washington's allies a chance to raise their concerns directly, amid unease about Trump's talk of a new security architecture for Europe.

"Europe belongs at this table"

Germany's Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul was blunt after his talks with Rubio, saying it was "certainly neither necessary, nor right, nor appropriate to make a fundamental change" to Europe's security architecture.

"Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe — only with Europe," he added.

France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot had said on Sunday that Europeans would be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks. The Paris meeting overlaps with the talks between Russia and Ukraine, scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday.

Wadephul said the Abu Dhabi talks must show whether Russia is "genuinely prepared to negotiate", urging Moscow to "give up maximalist demands" and warning against any "negotiation show". With Russian attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure continuing, he said, "we see no substantial contribution whatsoever toward negotiations gaining any serious momentum" from Moscow.

Ukraine: "No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs"

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha is set to join a session on Ukraine in Paris on Tuesday. Before departing, he said: "No one has the right to decide our fate behind our backs."

The Paris meeting comes as G7 members have grown uneasy with the direction of US policy, including Washington's scaling back of support for Ukraine and of sanctions on Russia, and its increasingly unilateral course. Europe fears Kyiv could be forced to accept disadvantageous terms, and that Washington could offer Russia new security guarantees over the Europeans' heads.

Iran is also expected to feature prominently on Tuesday. Washington's G7 allies have repeatedly voiced scepticism about the US and Israeli war on Iran, fearing further US military action could deepen the crisis rather than resolve it.

Why it matters

The two tracks are now running in parallel, and the question hanging over both is whether Europe will have a formal role in whatever emerges. Al Jazeera's correspondent in Paris reported that day one ended with little clarity on US policy after the midterms — and that the bigger question is the future of the multilateral system that has shaped relations among these countries for decades.

What remains unknown is whether the Abu Dhabi talks produce anything concrete — and whether Europe's demand is answered with a place at the table or with assurances alone.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • The Korea Times

link.title: Europe demands a seat at the Ukraine peace table as G7 meets Rubio in Paris

entry.title: Iran lifts its 2,000km missile-range cap as it shifts to an 'offensive' doctrine
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Saturday that it has lifted its self-imposed 2,000-kilometre (1,250-mile) limit on the range of its ballistic missiles, in the clearest sign yet that Tehran is widening the scope of its war with the United States and Israel.

"This limitation has been lifted for us," IRGC spokesman Brigadier-General Hossein Mohebbi told a news conference in Tehran. He did not say whether Iran already has missiles that can fly beyond the cap, saying Tehran would show its capabilities "through action rather than statements". He added that Iran has shifted towards an "offensive" military doctrine.

The announcement came days after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned that "any kind and level of threat" from the United States or Israel would be met with a response unlimited by geography.

What the cap meant

For years, the 2,000km limit was presented as a reassurance to Europe — a promise that Iranian missiles would not be aimed beyond the Middle East. It was self-imposed, not a treaty obligation, and the United Nations curbs in Security Council Resolution 2231 expired in October 2023.

For Iran's Gulf neighbours, little changes: they already sit well within the 2,000km range and have come under repeated Iranian missile fire since the war began on February 28. Beyond that line, Iran's existing arsenal can already reach the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt, plus parts of southeastern Europe, including Greece, Bulgaria and Romania.

What Iran can — and cannot — reach

Iran currently has no intercontinental ballistic missiles. But a 2019 British, French and German assessment put a lighter-warhead version of Iran's Khorramshahr missile at roughly 3,000km.

In March, the United Kingdom accused Iran of firing missiles towards the joint US-UK base at Diego Garcia, some 4,000km from Iran. Tehran denied targeting the base. Before the war, Iran held the largest ballistic missile stockpile in the Middle East, estimated at between 2,500 and 6,000 missiles.

Why now

Analysts read the move as both deterrence and bargaining. As a warning, it tells Washington — and European governments hosting US aircraft — that renewed strikes could bring a wider response. As leverage, the cap can now be offered back as a concession at the negotiating table. Muhanad Seloom of the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies argued Tehran sees a narrow window before the new US Congress convenes in January, in which President Donald Trump will want a deal he can present as a success. Trump said on Monday there was "positive momentum" towards ending the hostilities after talks with the Qatari prime minister in Washington. Seloom called the announcement "worrying … but not alarming" for Europe, since missiles would have to travel far to reach the mainland, giving NATO members early warning and time to intercept them.

What remains unknown

Whether Iran actually fields a missile that can fly beyond 2,000km is unproven — Mohebbi offered no evidence of one. Iran has also claimed it has built underground "missile cities" to keep weapons production running under bombing, a claim that cannot be independently verified.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Iran lifts its 2,000km missile-range cap as it shifts to an 'offensive' doctrine

entry.title: CoreWeave's earnings beat steadies the AI trade as tech futures climb
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Technology stocks steadied on Wednesday after CoreWeave, the AI data-centre company at the centre of recent market anxiety, reported quarterly results that beat expectations and raised its outlook for the year. Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 0.8 percent, S&P 500 futures rose 0.4 percent and Dow futures were higher by 33 points, or about 0.1 percent, according to CNBC's live market coverage.

The rebound followed a rough Tuesday on Wall Street. All three major averages fell more than 1 percent: the Dow dropped 553 points, or 1.2 percent, the S&P 500 fell 1.1 percent and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1.6 percent. The trigger was hotter-than-expected September inflation data, which raised doubts about whether the Federal Reserve will be able to cut interest rates as quickly as investors had hoped.

CoreWeave's numbers gave the market something firmer to hold on to. The company reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 168 percent from about $1.36 billion a year earlier and ahead of the $3.55 billion analysts had expected. Its adjusted loss narrowed to 95 cents a share, better than the $1.16 loss Wall Street had forecast, although the company still posted a net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 a share.

A raised outlook

The company also lifted its guidance for the full year. It now expects 2026 revenue of $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion, up from $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion in August, and adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion. Its order backlog reached about $133 billion, more than double the level a year ago, according to market reporting of the results. CoreWeave shares advanced in extended trading after the report.

The relief spread beyond the United States. In Asia, Japan's Nikkei rose 1.6 percent, South Korea's Kospi gained 1.2 percent and Hong Kong's Hang Seng climbed 1.8 percent. Europe's Stoxx 600 was up 0.6 percent.

Why this report mattered

CoreWeave has become a bellwether for the AI infrastructure boom — and for the doubts about it. The company rents out computing power for training artificial-intelligence models, and its heavy borrowing to build data centres made it a focal point when investors began questioning whether AI spending would pay off. Those doubts helped drive last week's sell-off, which pushed the Nasdaq into correction territory and erased trillions of dollars in market value.

A single earnings report does not settle that debate. CoreWeave remains loss-making, its debt load is still large, and the broader market still faces the same questions about inflation and interest rates that sank stocks on Tuesday. But the beat-and-raise gave investors evidence that demand for AI computing is still growing, and for one morning at least, that was enough to steady the trade.

Illustration — not a photograph.

entry.title: Millions strike across Spain in first general strike in 14 years over housing costs
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Millions of workers across Spain stopped work on Wednesday in the country's first general strike in 14 years, demanding that the government act on a housing crisis that has pushed rents out of reach for many — less than three weeks before a snap national election.

The strike, backed by Spain's two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, along with tenants' associations and other labour groups, was expected to disrupt public transport and slow or close businesses, factories and shops across the eurozone's fourth-largest economy. Picket lines formed in the early hours despite stormy weather in much of the country, and the unions reported widespread participation.

A decade of rising rents

Housing is at the centre of the protest. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters. According to the Youth Council of Spain, the average rental price of €1,176 a month is equivalent to about 98.7 percent of a young person's average monthly salary.

Spain also faces a shortage of roughly 750,000 homes, according to the central bank — a gap expected to grow to more than a million by 2028.

The strike was called by the tenants' movement and quickly won union backing. Its official slogan is "Salaries. Housing. Prices." The housing activists are demanding several measures, including the elimination of tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation, and protection for renters through automatic lease renewals. The unions are also seeking more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum-wage agreement negotiated with employers.

A death that became a symbol

The campaign gained force after the eviction of an 87-year-old woman known as Maricarmen, who was removed from her home in Madrid's Retiro neighbourhood on September 23. Her subsequent death drew further public anger and made her a symbol for Spaniards who feel they pay too much on rent and cannot imagine ever owning a home.

The last general strike in Spain was on November 14, 2012, called against the austerity measures of the government of the time. This time the initiative came from the housing movement rather than the unions alone.

Politics days away

The timing is pointed. The strike comes 18 days before a November 29 general election, and on Thursday — the day after the strike — the Congress will vote on two housing decrees, including measures that would allow some tenants to request up to two additional years of rent and suspend evictions of vulnerable households without housing alternatives.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has defended the right to strike. Analysts say the protest puts housing — and the cost of living more broadly — at the centre of the election campaign, in a vote that could bring the far right to power.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News — via The Week
  • Reuters — via Free Malaysia Today

link.title: Millions strike across Spain in first general strike in 14 years over housing costs

entry.title: Adobe opens Photoshop and Premiere to outside AI assistants
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Adobe has announced it will open its flagship creative apps to outside AI assistants, letting tools such as ChatGPT and Claude edit projects directly inside Photoshop, Premiere Pro, Illustrator and After Effects. The change, unveiled on Tuesday at Adobe MAX in Miami Beach, is the most significant opening of Creative Cloud since the subscription service launched in 2012.

The connection uses the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that lets AI assistants plug into other software. It will run locally on the user's own computer, so an assistant works directly with native project files — layered Photoshop documents, Premiere sequences, vectors and bins — and those elements stay editable afterwards. Adobe says the integrations will enter private beta in early 2027.

A wave of tools arriving now

Most of the other announcements are available from today. In Photoshop, a new Relight tool lets users add, move and resize light sources in an image non-destructively, while Generative Restyle generates style variations from a text prompt that can be fine-tuned with sliders. The beta app gains features including Mockups, Camera Angles and a tool that converts text in a flattened image into an editable type layer.

Following Adobe's acquisition of Topaz Labs, two new enhancement models arrive: Wonder 4, which combines upscaling, denoising, deblurring and sharpening in one step, and Image HDR, which converts standard images to HDR.

Premiere Pro gets a new colour-grading tool, Color Mode, starting today, alongside a Generative Media tool that can create missing b-roll, sound effects, soundscapes and music from inside the timeline, drawing on Adobe's Firefly models or partner models from Google, Kling, Runway and Luma. Audio tools including Enhance Audio and Separate Crosstalk aim to clean up messy recordings, and a Generative Remove tool in beta can erase unwanted objects such as boom microphones directly on the timeline.

Firefly and the agent push

Adobe is also reorganising Firefly, its generative AI brand, around new pieces: Firefly Video for organising scenes and assembling clips, Firefly Design, a single canvas combining illustration, image editing, animation and 3D, Firefly Graph for reusable creative workflows, and Firefly Builder, in private beta, which turns a natural-language idea into a working website or app prototype.

The company's own Adobe Creative Agent is expanding across Creative Cloud, with AI assistants now in beta in Illustrator, Premiere, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io, as well as the Photoshop beta app. The assistants handle multi-step jobs from natural-language prompts — in Premiere, for example, applying effects across a whole sequence. Adobe is also previewing always-on agents in Firefly that can handle recurring chores such as organising assets, with a beta due in early 2027.

What is still unknown

Adobe has not said whether any of the new tools will cost extra or require a higher subscription tier, and the third-party integrations are still months from their private beta. Whether outside assistants editing native files becomes a daily workflow, or a niche for power users, will only become clear once the beta opens in early 2027.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac
  • Computerworld

link.title: Adobe opens Photoshop and Premiere to outside AI assistants

entry.title: Dua Lipa to become first British woman to headline Coachella in 2027
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Dua Lipa will headline Coachella in 2027, becoming the first solo female British artist to top the bill at the California festival.

Coachella announced its 2027 line-up on Tuesday, with Lipa closing the Friday bill on both weekends, on 9 and 16 April. The Australian psych-rock band Tame Impala will headline the Saturday shows, and the American singer SZA will close out both Sundays. The festival returns to the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California, across two weekends — 9 to 11 April and 16 to 18 April — with more than 100,000 fans expected to attend each day.

A first for a British woman

Lipa, whose hits include "Training Season", becomes the first British woman to headline Coachella. Charli XCX performed on the main stage in 2025, but ahead of that year's headliner, Green Day. Lipa's booking ends weeks of speculation about the 2027 headliners, after reports last month that she had been in advanced talks with the organisers.

The announcement also sets up a reunion with SZA: the two singers both headlined Glastonbury in 2024, and will now share top billing across the two Coachella weekends.

Who else is playing

The line-up reaches well beyond the three headliners. Madonna is set to appear in the dance tent, alongside a bill that includes Daddy Yankee, Zara Larsson, Steve Lacy, Kehlani, JISOO of BLACKPINK, Peggy Gou and Giorgio Moroder. Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer, Tiësto, Martin Garrix, Role Model, Kygo, The Neighbourhood and Becky G are also on the roster, with Diljit Dosanjh among the international acts.

SZA's headline slot had been widely anticipated after she appeared to confirm it herself on social media in the run-up to the announcement, posting about the other two headliners in a public comment.

What happens next

Detailed stage assignments and individual set times have not yet been released, and are expected to follow closer to the festival. For now, the headline news is the bill itself: three acts from three different corners of pop, with a British first at the top of it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • BBC
  • Wikipedia

entry.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with no breakthrough — but Washington wants Europe at the table next time
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The second day of U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine ended in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday with no breakthrough on the war's core questions — but with a new push from Washington to bring Europe into the room next time.

The session lasted just under two hours behind closed doors, after an opening day on Tuesday that ran about four and a half hours. It was the first direct meeting between the two sides in nine months.

The one concrete result was humanitarian: agreement on a large prisoner exchange, with figures of 1,000 for 1,000 or 1,500 for 1,500 under discussion, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. On the bigger issues — territory, a ceasefire and security guarantees — the gap remains wide.

Europe's missing seat

The most pointed question was not what was discussed, but who was allowed to discuss it. European security advisers from Britain, France, Germany and Italy, along with EU and NATO officials, were in the city for separate consultations — but Russia kept them out of the main talks.

That is now the focus of the American effort. Politico reported, citing U.S. officials, that Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, will press Moscow to accept European participation in the next round — and want this week's meeting to be the last one held without Europe at the table.

"We need Europe at the table," one official told Politico, describing a proposal to bring European representatives into the discussions after this trilateral round. The envoys are also trying to speed up the process, leaving European governments little time to decide who would speak for them.

Moscow has shown no sign of agreeing. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov accused European leaders of trying to "buy time for Ukraine" and suggested they "stay at the hotel" in Abu Dhabi, and the Kremlin said its delegation held no contacts with European representatives.

What happens next

Zelenskyy said Europe must decide by the end of November who will represent it, and expressed hope the decision could be reached at a November 19 meeting of the coalition of the willing in Germany. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has ruled herself out, saying European institutions should take part instead. Finnish President Alexander Stubb has been mentioned as a possible representative; he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre both spoke to Putin by phone on October 27.

Witkoff and Kushner could travel to Moscow and then Kyiv after the Abu Dhabi round, Western media reported, as Washington tries to keep the momentum going.

Both sides spoke positively without claiming progress on substance. Kushner said he was "encouraged by the constructive discussions," Zelenskyy called Wednesday "the most crucial day for negotiations," and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who did not attend, called the opening day productive but cautioned that much work remained.

For now, the war goes on while diplomacy circles the same obstacles: Russia's demand that Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas, the shape of any security guarantees, and whether Europe gets a seat at a table deciding its own security.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Politico
  • Kyiv Post

link.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with no breakthrough — but Washington wants Europe at the table next time

entry.title: Hoax bomb emails force hundreds of Italian schools to evacuate as threats spread across Europe
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Thousands of schools across Italy, the United Kingdom and Ireland received threatening emails on Wednesday, forcing more than 300 Italian schools to evacuate as a precaution. Police in all three countries quickly assessed the messages as hoaxes, and no credible danger was found.

In Italy, the disruption was the widest. Schools in Rome, Naples, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and Vicenza were among those to receive the emails, and pupils were sent home while police checked the buildings. Parents were called to collect their children, and classes were interrupted for much of the morning.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said the alerts posed no danger and that police and other public bodies were monitoring the situation. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara told Italian television that about 300 schools had received the threats, and described them as presumed hoaxes linked to cyberattacks rather than a genuine risk.

The UK and Ireland were hit too

The same wave reached schools well beyond Italy. Police Scotland said at least 470 schools received the email, while more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland reported the same message. Police in the Republic of Ireland said a generic message had been sent to a number of schools and assessed it as not credible, advising against evacuations.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland said the email originated outside the United Kingdom and was being treated as a hoax. "Our enquiries are ongoing, however, at this stage we consider risk to the public as low," Assistant Chief Constable Anthony McNally said.

Police Scotland likewise told schools that the email alone did not warrant evacuation or keeping children at home, though a small number of schools activated their emergency plans anyway. Pupils at Queensferry High School in Edinburgh were sent home, and a primary school in County Down evacuated children to a nearby church.

A familiar signature, no attribution

A copy of the message seen by Reuters was signed "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan," and included a threat against Prime Minister Meloni. The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.

Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said Wednesday's threats were part of a clear strategy "to spread fear and create anxiety," according to the Adnkronos news agency. But authorities have not attributed the emails to any group or state, and no evidence has emerged linking them to a government.

The incident is the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks targeting infrastructure and organisations across Europe, including supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic and television broadcasters. Northern Ireland schools were hit by a similar hoax wave last month, when more than 300 schools received fake bomb threats.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Hoax bomb emails force hundreds of Italian schools to evacuate as threats spread across Europe

entry.title: Scientists sink ghost-particle detectors into Lake Superior in a freshwater first
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Scientists are lowering a set of giant sensor frames to the bottom of Lake Superior to hunt for neutrinos, the near-invisible particles physicists call "ghost particles." The project, known as the Experimental Neutrino Detector, is the first time neutrino detectors have been placed in a freshwater lake.

The effort is led by the University of Minnesota Duluth, working with the U.S. Department of Energy and two national laboratories. Its lead investigator is Alec Habig, a professor of physics and astronomy at the university.

The detectors arrived by an unusual route. The Neil Armstrong, a 238-foot ocean research vessel from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts, sailed across the Great Lakes and into Duluth this week. Crews spent Tuesday preparing the equipment at the Clure Terminal Expansion pier in Duluth.

On Thursday, the ship was to cruise about three miles out from Two Harbors, Minnesota, and crane the sensors onto the lakebed, about 200 metres below the surface. Crews will then lay fibre-optic cables connecting the detectors to a temporary facility on shore near Two Harbors.

Five frames, 90 sensors

The installation consists of five frames, each about three stories tall and weighing roughly 8,000 pounds. Each frame holds 18 spherical sensors about the size of a beach ball, filled with phototubes. The sensors, called digital optical modules, are designed to catch the faint blue flashes of light produced when a neutrino interacts with matter.

Neutrinos almost never interact with anything, which is why they are so hard to study — and so useful. Trillions pass through every person, and through the Earth itself, every second without leaving a trace.

This experiment targets neutrinos from a beam generated at Fermilab outside Chicago, fired since 2005 and aimed underground toward northern Minnesota, passing under Wisconsin and by Lake Superior off Two Harbors. The Lake Superior detectors are designed to pick the beam's neutrinos out from the solar and other natural neutrinos that are always present.

Why it matters

Physicists study neutrinos to answer fundamental questions about the universe, including why it is made mostly of matter rather than antimatter. A freshwater lake offers a vast, dark, naturally shielded volume in which to watch for the rare flashes that betray a neutrino's passage.

The project is sponsored by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, at a cost in the tens of millions of dollars, project leaders said. DARPA program manager John Bruzzese said the agency does not have a specific application in mind for the work.

The Fermilab beam is scheduled to shut off in February, because scientists have built a newer beam. When the Lake Superior experiment ends, the underwater sensors will be retrieved and sent to Europe for neutrino research deep in the Mediterranean Sea.

Minnesota has a long neutrino history: a former detector sat deep in the Soudan Underground Mine near Ely, and a laboratory still operates at Ash River outside Voyageurs National Park.

Sources

  • MPR News
  • Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

link.title: Scientists sink ghost-particle detectors into Lake Superior in a freshwater first

entry.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal but no path to ending the Ukraine war
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two days of U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine ended in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday with agreement on a large exchange of prisoners of war — but no breakthrough on ending a war that is nearing its fifth year.

The meeting was the first direct encounter between the two sides since February. Hopes for a significant step toward peace had been low, and the delegations left still far apart on the question that matters most: territory.

The one concrete result

Both sides confirmed they had agreed in principle to a large-scale prisoner swap. Russia's chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, said mutual understanding had been reached on some issues, while U.S. envoy Jared Kushner called the planned release "the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners" and said the numbers would be finalised on Thursday.

Russia's state-run news agency TASS reported the exchange should take place within two to three weeks. A Russian military intelligence official said the aim was to go past 1,000 people on each side — which would make it the largest swap of the war, topping the 1,000-for-1,000 exchange in May last year. Prisoner swaps have continued through the war even as diplomacy stalled: the two sides freed 200 prisoners each in March, and large exchanges followed three rounds of talks in Istanbul from May to July.

No movement on the core dispute

On the substance of a settlement, neither side moved. Kushner said "progress" had been made on a post-war security framework for Ukraine, but added that no deal could be signed until the territorial dispute is settled — and he described territory as the hardest issue to resolve. Russia continues to demand that Ukraine give up land it still holds, including parts of the Donbas, a demand Kyiv has refused.

Ukraine's peace negotiator, David Arakhamia, said there was "good momentum" toward reaching a solution before the end of the year, and argued the next round should be multilateral, with Europe represented. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who did not attend the talks, said on Wednesday that European security could not be discussed "without Europe". Medinsky said Moscow was not opposed to European participation in future talks, though he questioned what Russia and the EU would discuss.

What happens next

Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin and relay what was discussed, then fly to Dublin to meet Zelenskyy. Kushner said the envoys saw "some openings and some opportunities" in Moscow, and that the meetings would also address whether Europeans can be brought into the format.

The round's modest outcome keeps the diplomatic process alive without resolving it. The prisoner exchange, if it goes ahead at the scale discussed, will be a real humanitarian step — but the war itself, and the territorial question at its centre, remains where it was when the delegations arrived.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Associated Press

link.title: Abu Dhabi talks end with a prisoner-swap deal but no path to ending the Ukraine war

entry.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A criminal court in Cairo has adjourned the retrial of Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Egypt's leading independent news site Mada Masr, until 18 November, after her lawyers asked for the presiding judge to step aside.

The defence argued the judge had already made up his mind against her, Mada Masr said, citing its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar. The judge took a recess at Wednesday's opening hearing and then adjourned proceedings for a week to consider the request.

A fine, a shutdown order — and a sentence she did not know about

The retrial stems from a case in which Attalah was sentenced in her absence in 2024 to a year in prison for spreading false news and running a website without a licence. She only learned of that sentence after last month's separate trial, even though she was in Egypt when it was issued. She is now being retried in that case before the same judge.

Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of operating a website without a licence — a licence she said she had tried for years to obtain without success. It fined her 3 million Egyptian pounds (about $56,000) and ordered Mada Masr to close. Her appeal against that conviction is due to be heard on 25 November.

The UN warning

On Tuesday, the United Nations human rights office warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists." Its spokesperson, Thameen Al-Kheetan, said Attalah's case raised fresh concerns about due process and a fair trial, and called on Egypt to end the harassment of journalists and media outlets and to overturn the measures suppressing Mada Masr and the fact-checking platform Matsda2sh.

In September, six journalists from Matsda2sh — the platform's entire newsroom — were arrested in home raids and held incommunicado for nearly a week. They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism. Their lawyers say several were beaten and subjected to electric shocks in detention, and that prosecutors have presented no evidence linking them to the Brotherhood.

A shrinking space for independent news

Attalah told the BBC the crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left." Mada Masr was set up 13 years ago and is widely regarded as Egypt's leading independent news outlet.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' 2026 press freedom index, which says at least 26 journalists arrested in recent years remain in detention.

What is still unknown

It is not yet known whether the court will agree to replace the judge when the hearing resumes on 18 November, or how the appeal on 25 November will rule. The charges against the Matsda2sh journalists have not yet been tested in court.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'

entry.title: Ancient rocks pinpoint when Earth's tectonic engine switched on
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Researchers at Curtin University say they have found the clearest evidence yet for when plate tectonics — the slow engine that builds continents, opens oceans and helps steady Earth's climate — began working much as it does today: about 2.5 billion years ago.

Pinning down that date has long frustrated geologists. Plate tectonics destroys much of its own evidence, dragging old crust deep into the planet and recycling it. The team got around that problem by looking for something subtler: a chemical fingerprint left behind when new crust forms by melting older rock.

A fingerprint that vanishes

Lead author Dr. Janne Liebmann, a research fellow in Curtin's Timescales of Mineral Systems Group, and colleagues searched for the fingerprint in thousands of rocks from around the world, spanning almost 4 billion years of Earth's history.

They found it consistently in rocks older than 2.5 billion years, showing those rocks were derived from a pool of ancient crust that formed about 4 billion years ago. But after 2.5 billion years ago, the fingerprint disappears from the geological record — and despite examining thousands of rocks, the team never sees it again.

"That tells us something fundamental changed in the way Earth's crust was being formed and transformed," Liebmann said, "marking a transition toward the dynamic tectonic system we see today."

The study, "Loss of ancient crustal reservoirs marks a shift in Earth's geodynamic regime," was published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

From reworking in place to recycling on a grand scale

Before the shift, Earth's early crust was repeatedly melted and reworked more or less where it sat. After it, the planet became capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale — the kind of conveyor-belt system that defines modern plate tectonics, with old crust sinking at plate boundaries and new crust forming elsewhere.

Study co-author Professor Chris Kirkland, also of Curtin's Timescales of Mineral Systems Group, said the finding helps explain when Earth acquired one of the features that sets it apart from tectonically quiet neighbours such as Venus and Mars.

"Plate tectonics is fundamental to the way Earth has evolved over billions of years," Kirkland said, "continually reshaping the continents and oceans and influencing the planet's atmosphere and climate."

Why the timing matters

The date matters beyond geology. Plate tectonics regulates the carbon cycle, shapes the magnetic field that shields the surface from solar radiation, and builds the continents where most life lives. Knowing when the modern system switched on gives scientists a firmer starting point for understanding how Earth became habitable — and stayed that way.

What is still unknown

The study identifies when the transition happened, not what caused it. The precise trigger for the change remains an open question, and the onset of plate tectonics is still actively debated — other studies have argued for some form of plate motion earlier in Earth's history. What this work adds is a sharp, globally consistent marker in the rock record: a 4-billion-year-old fingerprint that is everywhere before 2.5 billion years ago, and nowhere after.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org

link.title: Ancient rocks pinpoint when Earth's tectonic engine switched on

entry.title: Ten lines of AI code put an indie hit at the centre of an awards fight
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A ten-line bug fix has become one of the sharpest arguments in indie gaming. House House, the studio behind Big Walk, has confirmed it used a chatbot to help solve a stubborn engine problem late in development — and 19 Independent Games Festival jurors say that alone should disqualify the game from awards consideration.

The studio says the chatbot was used sparingly, only for technical problems, and the AI-assisted code is well under 0.1% of the game. No generative AI touched art, writing, music or gameplay.

The bug that started it

The problem was in Unity's rendering pipeline: in some situations, shadows stretched to what the studio called infinite length, halving performance for about 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. House House says it researched the issue extensively, and a Unity engineer concluded a fix was not possible.

Out of options, the developers put the problem to a chatbot. After a few dead ends it suggested a fix, which the team reworked heavily into about 10 lines of code.

House House had disclosed the AI use when submitting for festival consideration, which asks about all forms of AI use. It had not mentioned it on Steam, saying Valve does not ask developers to disclose code or chatbot help — its form covers AI-generated content, not coding assistance.

The jurors' line

On Monday, 19 members of the festival's 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI "in any capacity". They cited a sharp rise in AI-built submissions and ecological, economic, psychological and labour harms, urging the festival to bar games containing any AI-generated work.

Not every juror agrees. Liz Ryerson said she did not find the minimal use personally disqualifying. But Austin Walker and Damon Reece said even a small amount of AI use outweighed their regard for the game; Reece wrote that jurors had their hands on the lever and needed to speak clearly for human creativity and labour.

What House House said

In a statement added to the game's public FAQ, the studio said it was disclosing the use because it had become a matter of public interest, and apologised that it "may not meet their standards" for some. It stressed the disclosure was not an endorsement of AI tools, however minimal, and said it supports efforts to limit generative AI's harm — while worrying that voluntary disclosure might itself help normalise the technology.

The fallout has been swift: more than 400 negative reviews have hit Big Walk's Steam page, though Steam's anti-review-bombing tools appear to have limited the damage to its overall "Very Positive" rating.

What is still unknown

The festival has not said whether it will adopt the stricter policy, or how it would police AI use. The dispute leaves a wider question open for the industry: should the line sit at AI-generated content, or at any AI assistance at all — including debugging help many developers now use routinely?

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Ars Technica

link.title: Ten lines of AI code put an indie hit at the centre of an awards fight

entry.title: Congo Ebola cases pass 11,000 in the deadliest outbreak the country has faced
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo have passed 11,000, government data showed on Tuesday, in an outbreak that is now the second-largest and deadliest ever recorded anywhere in the world.

The data put confirmed infections at 11,042, with 5,387 deaths. Only the 2014–2016 West African epidemic, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000, was larger.

The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the Ebola virus, was declared in mid-May. There are no approved treatments or vaccines for this species of the virus, which sets it apart from the better-known Zaire strain, for which vaccines exist.

Eight provinces affected

The virus has now reached eight of Congo's 26 provinces, and many of the deaths have occurred outside treatment centres — a sign that cases are being detected late, or that sick people are not reaching care at all.

Health officials have pointed to three forces driving the spread: delayed detection, conflict, and health services stretched thin. Together, they have allowed the virus to move faster than in previous outbreaks.

The geographic reach is also unprecedented. The disease has now been reported in East, Central and West Africa, giving this outbreak the widest spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

Why this strain is harder to fight

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of a sick person, or with surfaces and materials contaminated by them. Outbreaks are usually contained through rapid case-finding, isolation, contact tracing and safe burials.

The Bundibugyo species complicates that work. Because it is rare, there is far less experience fighting it, and the tools developed for other Ebola strains — including vaccines — are not approved for use against it. That leaves the response dependent on the basics: finding cases early, isolating the sick, tracing their contacts, and protecting health workers.

The International Organization for Migration has separately warned that a funding gap risks leaving the outbreak out of control, with dozens of cases already detected along travel routes out of the affected areas.

What is still unknown

The government figures are confirmed cases only, and the true scale of the outbreak may be larger, given the deaths occurring outside treatment centres and the difficulty of surveillance in conflict-affected areas. How quickly the case count is still rising, and whether the response can close the funding and detection gaps, will determine whether the outbreak stays the second-largest on record — or closes in on the West African epidemic it now trails.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Congo Ebola cases pass 11,000 in the deadliest outbreak the country has faced

entry.title: Apple ends its 28-year-old Support Community forum, closing the door on November 20
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Apple is shutting down its official Support Community, the user-to-user forum where customers have traded troubleshooting advice for 28 years. The company posted a notice on the forum on Tuesday night saying it will close permanently on November 20, 2026, and that the site is now read-only: no new questions or replies can be posted.

"The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state," the notice said, directing users to Apple's official Support site for help. The final message posted to the forum appears to have gone up at 5:49 p.m. Pacific Time on Tuesday, minutes before posting was switched off.

A forum that predates the iPhone

The community is one of the oldest fixtures of Apple's online presence. It launched in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange, when the company was still rebuilding after Steve Jobs' return and the iMac was brand new. It became Apple Discussions in 2000, was relaunched as the Apple Support Communities in 2011, and took its current name in 2022.

For most of that time it worked the same way: a user with a broken Mac, a misbehaving iPhone or a puzzling software bug could post a question and get an answer from another user, sometimes with an Apple employee stepping in with a fix or an update. Millions of threads accumulated into a searchable archive of fixes that often turned up in search results before Apple's own support pages did.

Apple has not given a detailed public explanation. The company told MacRumors it decided to retire the forum "after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs," and its notice points users toward official support channels instead. Alternatives for peer help include independent forums such as the MacRumors Forums and Reddit.

What happens to the archive

What remains unclear is what happens to nearly three decades of archived discussions after November 20. Apple has not said whether the threads will stay readable, be taken offline entirely, or be preserved in some other form. The login button on the forum now routes to an internal employee page, suggesting staff access will continue even as public posting ends.

The move follows a similar step by Verizon earlier this year, which also switched its community forum to read-only before closing it. For Apple users, the practical effect is immediate: the fastest route to an answer from another customer is gone, and the official support site — with its articles, chat and phone options — is now the company's only front door for help.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Ars Technica
  • MacRumors

link.title: Apple ends its 28-year-old Support Community forum, closing the door on November 20

entry.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

United Airlines said on Wednesday it will stop personal artificial-intelligence agents from booking flights on its customers' behalf, making it the first major US airline to draw a line against the fast-growing class of AI travel assistants.

The carrier is updating its booking and ticketing policies to block what it calls unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents and assistants. The restriction applies directly on United's own website and app, and indirectly through travel agencies and flight aggregators that sell its tickets.

United framed the move as a matter of security and compliance. Letting an AI assistant act for a traveler means handing it the keys to the account: login credentials, payment details and frequent-flyer miles. The airline said that sharing those credentials with a third-party assistant can expose sensitive information and lead to purchases a customer never intended, changes to an account, or miles spent without the traveler's knowledge.

There is also a regulatory angle. Some steps in air travel legally require the traveler to act in person — checking in, for example, involves confirming that checked luggage holds no banned items. United said an automated tool performing those steps on a customer's behalf could run afoul of federal aviation and transportation rules.

The assistants keep growing

The ban lands as AI agents move from answering questions to carrying out transactions. Millions of consumers now use assistants such as Meta's Muse and OpenAI's dots to research products, track down deals and complete purchases, and travel is one of the most obvious next frontiers.

For United, there is a commercial motive as well as a safety one. Aviation analyst Henry Harteveldt of Atmosphere Research Group told CBS News that the airline wants to keep control of its own booking process and avoid a surge in automated flight searches, which cost carriers money with every query. "Flight searches cost airlines money," he said.

Travelers will not lose the ability to compare United's fares. Its tickets will still be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, and finding a good fare should not get any harder. What changes is that an AI agent cannot complete the purchase on United's systems — and, by blocking the bots, United will not make it any easier for them to find its fares either.

The move puts United on a different path from at least one rival. Southwest Airlines has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can reach the airline's website through the AI app — a reminder that the industry has not yet settled on a single answer to the agent question.

What is still unknown

United has not published a timetable for the new restrictions or explained how it will detect and stop unauthorized agents, including those reaching it through agencies and aggregators. It is also unclear whether other major carriers will follow with outright bans or take a different approach, such as authorizing selected assistants under formal partnerships. For now, United says it has no partnerships with third-party AI agents.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CBS News

link.title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers

entry.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat in a historic upset
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Democrat Scott Colom has won election to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi, according to a race call by the Associated Press, narrowly defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the country's closest Senate contest.

The call came on Wednesday, more than a week after election day, once officials had finished counting the outstanding absentee and provisional ballots that had left the outcome in doubt. Colom won by just a few thousand votes.

A week of counting

The race was too close to settle on the night itself. With ballots still being counted for days afterwards, both campaigns waited while local officials worked through the remaining absentee and affidavit ballots. When the count finished, the margin was small enough to make it the tightest Senate race in the country — and a result few forecasters had predicted. The Cook Political Report had rated the contest as Likely Republican going into election night.

A historic first

Colom's victory carries two historic firsts. He is the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Mississippi in more than 40 years, and the first Black senator elected from the state since Reconstruction.

Mississippi has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40% of the electorate, yet President Donald Trump carried the state by 23 points in 2024. NPR described the result as part of a midterm full of upsets for Democrats, driven in the South by a surge in Black voter turnout.

How the race turned

Colom, a district attorney, made the cost of living the centrepiece of his campaign, branding his opponent "Cindy High-Prices" and arguing that rising prices had hit Mississippi's rural, agriculture-heavy economy especially hard.

A remark by Hyde-Smith — a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner — became a turning point. Asked earlier this year about high beef prices, she suggested voters had "so many other proteins to choose from." Colom's campaign turned the line into a viral advertisement, with voters reacting in disbelief before the ad closed on its message: it was time to "pick another senator."

Unlike most other contested Senate races, Mississippi drew little national money or attention until the closing days. That changed in the final week, when Trump flew in to headline a rally for Hyde-Smith, while former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock campaigned for Colom.

Colom himself had criticised the national Democratic Party's late arrival. "The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he told NPR earlier this month, saying the party had spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states and "almost nothing in Mississippi."

What is still unknown

The final certified vote totals have yet to be published, and Hyde-Smith has said little publicly since election night beyond expressing confidence while votes were still being counted. What the result means for the balance of the Senate, and how Colom positions himself once seated, will become clearer in the weeks ahead.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NPR
  • CNN

link.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate seat in a historic upset

entry.title: First black hole image stands up to a fully independent re-check
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The first picture ever taken of a black hole's shadow has survived its toughest test yet. A team of Australian researchers has reanalysed the original telescope data with a completely independent method — and produced almost exactly the same glowing ring.

When the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration released the image in 2019, it became one of the most recognisable pictures in modern science: a bright orange ring around a dark centre, the shadow of the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87, known as M87\*. But the image was a reconstruction, stitched together from radio signals collected by telescopes across the planet, and some researchers argued the ring shape might be an artefact of the way the data had been processed. One alternative analysis even produced a shapeless blob instead of a ring.

The new study, published in Nature on 11 November, set out to answer that doubt. The team — Samuel Lai, Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong and F. Diakogiannis, from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency — built a fresh imaging pipeline that works differently from the original in almost every respect.

A different way of combining the data

The original analysis combined measurements from pairs of telescopes. The new approach, called GenDIReCT, groups the telescopes in threes. Combining three signals at a time preserves information about the object's structure while cancelling out errors caused by the atmosphere and by the instruments themselves — errors that have troubled radio astronomers for decades.

The team also trained its machine-learning algorithm only on images unrelated to astronomy, so the software had no preconceived idea of what a black hole should look like. "Our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," lead author Samuel Lai said.

Applied to the original 2017 observations — and to later data from 2018 and 2021 — the method recovered a compact ring in every epoch, in close agreement with the 2019 image. It is, the researchers say, the first truly independent validation of the landmark picture.

Why it matters

The stakes go beyond one famous image. The ring's size and shape matched predictions from Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity, which first predicted black holes more than a century ago. A reanalysis that produced a different shape would have raised questions not only about the image but about the physics it appeared to confirm.

M87\* sits about 55 million light-years from Earth and has a mass roughly 6.5 billion times that of the Sun. What the telescopes actually capture is not the black hole itself — no light escapes it — but the glow of hot matter swirling around it, bent into a ring by the black hole's gravity.

What is still unknown

The new result confirms the ring's shape, but it does not end the work. The Event Horizon Telescope continues to observe M87\ and the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, Sagittarius A\, with the aim of sharper images and, eventually, moving pictures of matter orbiting the edge of a black hole.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Nature
  • Phys.org

link.title: First black hole image stands up to a fully independent re-check

entry.title: Toyota brings back Scion — with a tiny 25-mph kei truck built in Indiana
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Toyota is bringing back Scion, but not as the youth-focused car brand Americans remember. The revived nameplate, now called Scion by Toyota, will serve as an experimental mobility brand — and its first vehicle is a tiny Japanese-style kei truck, assembled in Indiana and limited to 25 mph.

The truck, the KEI-01, is scheduled to reach customers in the second half of 2027. Toyota will assemble it at its plant in Princeton, Indiana, backed by a $34 million investment and about 50 new jobs. The vehicles will arrive as kits from Japan for final assembly in the United States.

Small by design

The KEI-01 follows the Japanese kei-truck formula almost to the letter. It measures just over 11 feet long and less than five feet wide, with a 660cc three-cylinder engine, a continuously variable transmission and standard four-wheel drive. Its cargo bed folds down on three sides and can carry up to 600 pounds. It keeps its right-hand-drive layout, just like the kei trucks sold in Japan.

The catch is the speed. Toyota designed the KEI-01 to meet the federal safety standard for low-speed vehicles, FMVSS No. 500, which caps its top speed at 25 mph and restricts it to roads with speed limits of 35 mph or less. It is a work vehicle for campuses, farms and local roads — not a highway pickup.

That trade-off is the point. Kei trucks have become a quiet cult favourite in the United States, with more than 30,000 used examples imported since 2020, largely for farm and utility work. Toyota is now the first major automaker to offer one officially, built and sold through its own network rather than through independent importers.

A fleet experiment first

Most Americans will not be able to buy a KEI-01 at first. Toyota is launching it as a fleet-focused pilot programme, aimed at corporate campuses, farms, municipalities and local delivery operators, sold through a small group of existing Toyota dealers. The company says limited retail sales could follow if demand supports it. No price has been announced.

The revival is a sharp turn for a badge that once meant cheap, quirky cars for young buyers. Scion launched in 2003 and was discontinued in 2016 after sales faded. Toyota now describes the new Scion as a "freedom lab" — a place to test vehicles and ideas that would not fit its mainstream lineup. Alongside the KEI-01, it showed two concepts: a hybrid side-by-side off-road vehicle and a compact electric mobility concept.

What is still unknown

Toyota has not said what the KEI-01 will cost, how many it plans to build, or when — or whether — retail buyers will get access. The pilot's results will decide whether the tiny truck becomes a niche fleet tool or the start of a broader Scion experiment.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Verge
  • Autoblog

link.title: Toyota brings back Scion — with a tiny 25-mph kei truck built in Indiana

entry.title: Grand Theft Auto VI pre-orders pass $1 billion a week before launch, estimates show
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Grand Theft Auto VI has already crossed an estimated $1 billion in pre-order revenue, a week before the game is due to launch on November 19 — a milestone its predecessor needed three days on sale to reach.

Analytics firm Sensor Tower puts pre-orders at about 10.31 million copies, according to reports published on November 11. The figures are estimates, not official sales numbers: neither Rockstar Games nor its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, has confirmed them.

What the estimates say

PlayStation 5 accounts for roughly three-quarters of the pre-orders, at an estimated 7.73 million copies worth about $751 million, with Xbox Series X|S making up the remaining 2.58 million. Sensor Tower has tracked pre-orders on both consoles since they opened on June 25, and has not published the methodology behind its figures.

The pace has been quickening as launch approaches. On November 9 alone, the estimate grew by about 620,000 copies and roughly $59.5 million, according to the firm's tracker.

Take-Two reported its quarterly results on November 9 and gave no pre-order number, but chief executive Strauss Zelnick said demand was running "far in excess" of the company's expectations. The company expects net bookings of $8 billion to $8.2 billion for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, and $3.35 billion to $3.5 billion in the quarter in which the game launches.

A record-breaking run-up

Sony has confirmed that Grand Theft Auto VI is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of the PlayStation Store, with Microsoft reporting a similar record on Xbox. Digital pre-loading opened on November 10, letting buyers download the game — a roughly 208GB install — ahead of release day.

The comparison with Grand Theft Auto V underlines the scale. Take-Two said in 2013 that GTA V generated more than $800 million in its first 24 hours and passed $1 billion within three days. But the two numbers are not measured the same way: the GTA V figure was the company's own estimate of sales in shops, while the GTA VI figure is an outside estimate of digital pre-orders on two consoles.

What is still unknown

The first official figure will come from Take-Two after November 19, and it may not match Sensor Tower's estimate. The game arrives after two delays — it was first slated for fall 2025, then pushed to May 2026, and finally to November 19 — and expectations are high enough that analysts say a breakout launch would likely force the company to raise its earnings guidance.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • GamesBeat
  • NDTV

link.title: Grand Theft Auto VI pre-orders pass $1 billion a week before launch, estimates show

entry.title: A universe nearly twice as old as thought passes key tests — without dark matter or dark energy
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

An alternative picture of the cosmos — one in which the universe is 26.7 billion years old and neither dark matter nor dark energy exists — has survived a series of major observational tests, according to a new study from the University of Ottawa.

The standard model of cosmology, known as ΛCDM, puts the universe at about 13.8 billion years old and holds that dark matter and dark energy make up roughly 95 percent of everything there is. Neither has ever been directly detected, and the model has struggled to explain the surprisingly large, mature galaxies the James Webb Space Telescope keeps finding in the very early universe.

The new work, published in the journal Universe, tests a framework called CCC+TL — short for "covarying coupling constants plus tired light" — developed by adjunct physics professor Rajendra Gupta and postdoctoral researcher Nikolaos Samaras. Instead of invisible matter and energy, the model says the effects attributed to them come from fundamental physical constants that change over time. It also rewrites the Einstein and Friedmann equations that describe gravity and cosmic expansion, so the researchers had to build new equations and computer code for every test.

What the tests found

The team's results, gathered during 2025 and 2026, agreed with several pillars of observational cosmology. The model's predictions for the amounts of hydrogen, helium and other light elements forged shortly after the Big Bang matched those of the standard model. It also agreed with cosmic-chronometer measurements, which reconstruct the history of cosmic expansion from the ages of galaxies at different distances.

In a separate paper in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers applied the model to all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found it could reproduce their rotation curves — the speeds at which stars orbit galactic centres — without any dark matter at all. A study of time dilation in supernova observations also supports the model, although that paper is still under review.

The team also looked at the Bullet Cluster, where the extra gravitational effect the model predicts follows the galaxies rather than the hot, X-ray-emitting gas. The researchers describe that result as an early proof of concept that needs more study.

More time for early galaxies

The older universe may also resolve one of the standard model's most awkward problems: galaxies that look too grown-up, too early. In the standard picture, the universe was only about 300 million years old during cosmic dawn. Under CCC+TL, it would already have been about 4.6 billion years old at the same observed redshift — giving galaxies far longer to grow. In the researchers' calculations, early galaxies come out about 12 times larger in size and mass than the standard model predicts.

"Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies," Gupta said. The model even predicts galaxies beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached so far — a claim the telescope's GLIMPSE programme may soon test by searching for galaxies at redshifts that could exceed 50, where the standard model may not leave enough time for massive galaxies to form.

What is still unproven

Passing tests is not the same as being right. The biggest remaining check — the cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the Big Bang — has not yet been published for this model, although Gupta says the team's findings meet that challenge. The supernova result is still under peer review, and the Bullet Cluster work is preliminary.

"The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the universe beyond ΛCDM limits," Gupta said. For now, the 26.7-billion-year universe is a serious contender, not a settled fact — and the next round of telescope observations will help decide whether it stays one.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • Science Daily

link.title: A universe nearly twice as old as thought passes key tests — without dark matter or dark energy

entry.title: Google Wallet can now hold your house key — if your lock speaks Aliro
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Your house key can now live in Google Wallet. Google has begun rolling out support for digital home keys on Android, letting a phone unlock a compatible smart lock — a feature Apple has offered in Apple Wallet for years.

Once a home key is added to Wallet, tapping the phone against the lock opens the door. The tap uses NFC and works even when the phone's screen is locked, by default — although that can be changed in the Wallet app to require a screen lock or biometric check first. Any Android phone running Android 9 or newer can use the tap-to-unlock mode.

There is also a hands-free option, called Unlock on Approach, which opens the door as you walk up. That needs an Aliro-compatible phone with ultra-wideband, plus an Aliro-compatible lock — Google names the Pixel 10 Pro series and above, and selected ultra-wideband Samsung Galaxy phones. Smartwatches are left out for now: Wear OS is not supported at launch.

One key for the whole home

The key is tied to the home in the Google Home app, not to a single lock. That means one digital key in Wallet works with every compatible Aliro lock in the household, and it syncs automatically across other Android phones signed into the same Wallet account. Keys are added through the Home app, which prompts you to save one after a lock is set up, or from Home settings under Google Wallet key. The card in Wallet shows a Google Home logo with the home's name in the top-right corner.

Aliro is the open smart-lock standard from the Connectivity Standards Alliance, the group behind Matter. Its arrival in Wallet matters because it breaks the pattern of each lock brand needing its own app: any lock that follows the standard should, in principle, work with any phone wallet that supports it.

A short list, for now

The catch is how few locks qualify at launch. Only three models are supported to start: the Aqara u400, which handles both ultra-wideband and NFC; the Schlage Sense Pro, with NFC now and ultra-wideband to follow; and the Nuki Keypad 2 NFC. Google says support for more models is coming.

The rollout is also staged. It reaches Google Home Public Preview members first, then widens to all users over the coming weeks. So most Android owners with a smart lock will have to wait — and, if their lock is not one of the three, wait longer still.

Still, the direction is clear. Car keys, hotel keys and transit passes already live in phone wallets; the front door was the obvious next step. For the small group with the right lock and the right phone, the keyring just got one item lighter.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • 9to5Google
