entry.title: Australian teen found alive after six days lost in Victorian bushland
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A 17-year-old boy missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive, ending a search that drew in more than 100 people across Victoria's east.

William, whose surname has not been released, was spotted by a Victoria Police AirWing helicopter crew on Thursday morning, six days after he strayed from his camp near Walhalla, about 180 kilometres east of Melbourne. He was lying in a dry creek bed when the crew found him, and was winched to safety before being flown to a search base at Cowwarr and reunited with his family.

A week in the bush with almost nothing

William disappeared last Friday afternoon while on a camping trip with a friend at Walhalla East, a former gold-mining town in the Gippsland region. He was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, between Cowwarr and Walhalla, at about 4pm on November 6. He had walked to another part of the campsite and failed to return.

He was wearing only shorts and work boots, and had left his food, water and phone behind at the camp. Overnight temperatures in the area fell as low as 3C during the six days he was missing, and police said they held grave fears for his welfare. William has autism, and police said he may have become disoriented and lost his way in the steep, heavily forested terrain.

The search grew into one of the biggest the region has seen in recent years. Police divers, the dog squad, mounted officers and helicopters worked alongside State Emergency Service volunteers, combing the bushland around Walhalla for six days.

"Grounded for life"

His mother, Elizabeth Barkley, was at the police staging ground in Cowwarr when the helicopter brought him in, and the two were reunited on Thursday morning. She told reporters her son had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy, joking that he was now "grounded for life" and would never be leaving the house again.

Victoria Police said William was "in good spirits and, for the most part, in good health". Rescuers gave him a doughnut and a bottle of water before he was taken to hospital for a check-up.

Officers involved in the search said they were emotional at the outcome. "It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said.

What is still unknown

Police have not said how William survived the six nights, including whether he found water or shelter, or exactly how far he travelled from the campsite. His hospital check-up was precautionary, and no details of any treatment have been released.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • AAP

link.title: Australian teen found alive after six days lost in Victorian bushland

entry.title: Hera closes in on the asteroid NASA struck — first close look at a planetary-defence test
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A European spacecraft has begun its close inspection of the asteroid NASA deliberately struck four years ago, opening the first detailed examination of whether a spacecraft impact can reliably deflect a dangerous space rock.

The European Space Agency announced on Wednesday that its Hera spacecraft is now studying the Didymos asteroid system from just 25 to 30 kilometres away. Didymos is a 780-metre-wide asteroid orbited by a smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, about 151 metres across — the body NASA's DART probe slammed into in September 2022 in the first test of planetary defence.

What Hera has seen so far

Hera, a car-sized spacecraft launched in 2024, sent back its first close-up view of the system on November 5, photographed from 60 kilometres away. The image showed a side of Didymos that DART's camera never captured before impact: a rugged, boulder-strewn hemisphere marked with craters and what may be grooves or ridges across its surface. Dimorphos was partly hidden in shadow at the lower edge of the frame.

The spacecraft will move closer still. Next month it is due to approach to within 20 kilometres of the pair, and the agency plans to release the first detailed, full-resolution images of both asteroids on November 25.

Why the follow-up matters

DART — short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test — struck Dimorphos at about 6.6 kilometres per second on September 26, 2022, and shortened the moonlet's orbit around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes. The impact sent rubble and boulders flying off Dimorphos, adding extra momentum beyond the blow itself.

But the size of the crater, and whether the impact reshaped Dimorphos as a whole, could only be guessed at from Earth. Hera's job is to measure what actually happened: it will weigh Dimorphos, map the crater and chart changes across both bodies, turning a successful demonstration into a technique scientists understand well enough to repeat if Earth ever faces a real threat.

Two small companions to come

After its initial survey, Hera will release two shoebox-sized CubeSats, Milani and Juventas. Milani will carry out mineralogical analysis of the asteroids' surfaces, while Juventas will probe Dimorphos's interior with the first ground-penetrating radar ever flown to an asteroid.

The system sits about 197 million kilometres from Earth, an 11-minute one-way radio delay — close enough to study in detail, far enough that every command takes patience.

What is still unknown

The detailed images due on November 25 should settle whether DART reshaped Dimorphos or merely cratered it. Until Hera's measurements are complete, the exact mass of Dimorphos, the depth of the impact crater and the internal structure of the rubble-pile moonlet remain estimates.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Astronomy Now

link.title: Hera closes in on the asteroid NASA struck — first close look at a planetary-defence test

entry.title: Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang's future as shares slide after fresh reports
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Nvidia's board met late on Wednesday to decide the future of Jensen Huang, the founder and only chief executive the chipmaker has ever had, after a week of damaging reports about his conduct sent the company's shares sharply lower.

Shares in Nvidia fell more than 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, dropping to about $158.78 from a regular-session close of $173.73. The slide followed a report in the Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, that the board was preparing to remove Huang. Reuters, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that the board was meeting late on Wednesday to decide whether to oust him.

The immediate trigger was a New York Times report, published earlier on Wednesday, that Huang had a relationship with a Nvidia executive who reports directly to him. The executive is Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of healthcare. The Times cited unidentified people who worked at the company, and the Journal subsequently confirmed the reporting. Neither Nvidia nor Powell had responded to requests for comment by late Wednesday, and the board had issued no statement.

A crisis that has built over days

The reports cap a week in which Huang's position has come under growing pressure. On Sunday, Huang told Nvidia employees in a letter that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship. The same day, the board opened an independent investigation into reports that Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

That investigation concerns Huang's reported relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman US authorities have described as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board has retained the law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead the inquiry, and the FBI is also examining the matter. The board had previously said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised, and had expressed confidence in Huang.

The political fallout has spread beyond the company. Lawmakers in Washington have called for briefings and new restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, and at least one senator has publicly called for Huang's resignation. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Huang, who told him he had no idea the woman was a spy, and that he believed him.

Investors have reacted swiftly. Nvidia's shares had already fallen a combined 9.5% on Monday and Tuesday, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars from its market value, before recovering 2.9% in Wednesday's regular session — only to plunge again after the closing bell. Shares in rival chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom rose in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

What is still unknown

No decision has been announced. The board has not said when it will conclude its deliberations, and it is not clear whether a successor has been identified. That matters: analysts note Nvidia has no public succession plan, and Huang has led the company since founding it in 1993, overseeing a rise in its share price of more than 700,000% as it became the dominant supplier of the processors that power artificial intelligence.

For now, the company's leadership — and the centre of the AI industry — hangs on a board decision that had not been made public by late Wednesday night.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Reuters

link.title: Nvidia board weighs Jensen Huang's future as shares slide after fresh reports

entry.title: Yankees' Cam Schlittler takes AL Cy Young unanimously after a breakout season
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Cam Schlittler is the American League's best pitcher, and nobody who voted disagreed. The New York Yankees right-hander was named the unanimous winner of the 2026 AL Cy Young Award on Wednesday, collecting all 30 first-place votes from the Baseball Writers' Association of America.

Schlittler, 25, went 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA across 33 starts in his first full major league season. He led the American League in ERA and in pitching WAR (7.0), and struck out 239 batters in 193⅔ innings. His 1.95 ERA was the lowest in the league since 2022 and the third-lowest in Yankees history among qualified pitchers, behind Spud Chandler's 1.64 in 1943 and Ron Guidry's 1.74 in 1978.

Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease finished second with 110 points, and Cleveland Guardians rookie Parker Messick placed third. Schlittler finished with 210 points, the maximum possible under the voting system.

The award puts Schlittler in rare company. He is the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the Cy Young, joining Bob Turley (1958), Whitey Ford (1961), Sparky Lyle (1977), Guidry (1978), Roger Clemens (2001) and Gerrit Cole (2023). He is the youngest Yankee ever to win it, and only the third in club history to do so unanimously, after Guidry and Cole. Clemens, a seven-time winner himself, announced Schlittler as the winner during the awards ceremony in Las Vegas.

A rapid rise to the top of the rotation

Schlittler's path to the award was fast. A seventh-round draft pick, he debuted on July 9, 2025, and made 14 starts that season before stepping into a full-time rotation role this year. Since his debut, he has posted the majors' best ERA (2.23) while tying for the most starts in baseball, and he allowed one run or fewer in an MLB-best 21 starts this season.

The numbers tell the story of a pitcher who took over the Yankees' rotation in his second year. He pitched the second-most innings in the American League, and his 239 strikeouts ranked among the league's best. He is also the first homegrown Yankees Cy Young winner since Guidry in 1978.

The other half of the night belonged to the National League. Milwaukee Brewers right-hander Jacob Misiorowski also won unanimously, taking all 30 first-place votes in his first full season. It is only the second time both Cy Young winners were in their second major league seasons.

For the Yankees, the award caps a season in which Schlittler went from a promising arm to the undisputed ace of the staff. He remains under team control through the 2031 season, with two seasons still to go before he is even eligible for arbitration — a detail that will shape the club's offseason planning as much as the trophy itself.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • Reuters

link.title: Yankees' Cam Schlittler takes AL Cy Young unanimously after a breakout season

entry.title: Two killed, 17 hurt as Brooklyn building collapses into excavation pit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two people were killed and at least 17 others were injured on Wednesday afternoon when a three-story building in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood partially collapsed into an open excavation pit at the construction site next door, fire officials said.

The collapse happened at about 4 p.m. near the intersection of Flatbush Avenue and Bedford Avenue. The building, at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, had a business on the ground floor and apartments above. It fell into the excavation at 2625 Bedford Avenue, the lot beside it, where construction work was underway.

The first 911 call came in at 4:01 p.m., and firefighters arrived within a minute, the Fire Department of New York said. Two people were pulled from the rubble soon after the collapse, and crews kept searching through the night with drones, search dogs and their hands, looking for anyone still trapped.

At a news conference on Wednesday night, the fire department said two people had died and at least 17 people were hurt, four of them in critical condition. Seven children and a firefighter were among the injured, officials said. The others suffered less serious injuries. The identities of the two people who died had not been released.

Officials warned the toll could still rise. The fire department said it did not know how many people were inside the building when it fell, or whether everyone had been accounted for.

What caused it is not yet known

No cause had been determined as of Wednesday night, and an investigation is underway. The city's Department of Buildings said inspectors were at the scene to help with the recovery and to check the structural stability of surrounding buildings. Law enforcement is leading the investigation into the cause, NBC New York reported.

Attention is likely to fall on the excavation next door. City records show work at the site began in September and included blasting rock, NBC New York reported, and investigators have not yet established whether the excavation or the work supporting it played any role in the collapse. The news outlet said it had left messages with the architect, the property owner and the general contractor listed in city records.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a post on social media that people should avoid the area so rescue crews could keep working. The city's Office of Emergency Management also advised drivers to expect road closures and delays around the site. ABC7 reported that a reception center for displaced families was opened at the Flatbush YMCA.

For the neighborhood, the collapse is a sudden rupture in an ordinary street: a corner building that held homes and a shop, gone into a pit in an afternoon, with the search for survivors stretching into the night and the question of why it happened still unanswered.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NBC New York

link.title: Two killed, 17 hurt as Brooklyn building collapses into excavation pit

entry.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns as diploma dispute splits the ruling alliance
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Indonesia's vice president, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, resigned on Thursday, ending two years in office after court rulings cast doubt on his education credentials and lawmakers moved toward impeaching him.

Gibran, 39, handed his resignation letter to parliament leaders in Jakarta on Thursday morning after a meeting of about 20 minutes, Ahmad Muzani, speaker of the People's Consultative Assembly, told reporters. He had also sent one to President Prabowo Subianto, who said hours later at a press conference alongside Gibran that he had accepted it with a "heavy heart."

Gibran is the eldest son of former President Joko Widodo, known as Jokowi, whose backing helped carry Prabowo to the presidency in 2024. His resignation closes a chapter on the alliance between the two men and leaves the government under pressure amid widespread public dissatisfaction over the economy, corruption and wildfires.

The immediate cause was a dispute over his eligibility. Last month, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted about his overseas education did not meet election requirements, fuelling questions over whether he held a valid senior high school-equivalent diploma. On Wednesday, 120 lawmakers from all eight parties in parliament filed a motion that could have led to his impeachment.

A swift reversal

The resignation came a day after Gibran had vowed to fight the court rulings in the State Administrative Court and the Supreme Court. But at a meeting with Prabowo on Tuesday, he offered to resign, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy.

Muzani, reading from the letter, said Gibran had acted "through my own volition ... for the interests of the government and nation." The five-paragraph letter cited "growing public sentiment" and personal reasons, senior ministers said. Muzani added that Gibran gave no reason in the letter he sent to Prabowo.

Jokowi moved quickly to steady the fallout. Speaking outside his home in Solo, central Java, the former president said he would continue to support Prabowo's administration, "especially programmes that serve the interests of the broader public." The show of support may soothe signs of strain, though some observers say Gibran may have been pressed to step down rather than quitting freely.

What happens next

Under Indonesia's Constitution, a vice-presidential vacancy does not trigger a new election. The People's Consultative Assembly must first hold a session to formally declare the office vacant, and the president will then nominate two candidates. The assembly elects a replacement within 60 days.

Gibran had served two years of a five-year term after taking office in October 2024. His candidacy was controversial from the start: a Constitutional Court ruling changed the election rules so he could stand, and Jokowi was accused of influencing that decision. The questions that surrounded him — about eligibility, courts and political dynasties — are likely to shape the contest to replace him.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times

link.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns as diploma dispute splits the ruling alliance

entry.title: Americans head into the holidays carrying a record $1.29 trillion in credit card debt
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Americans are heading into the holiday shopping season carrying record credit card balances. Total card debt reached $1.29 trillion in the three months ending in September, up $22 billion from the prior quarter, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest quarterly report on household debt and credit, released November 10.

The figure is 67% higher than in the first quarter of 2021, when pandemic restrictions were still limiting spending on travel and dining out. Total household debt — including mortgages, student and auto loans, credit cards and home equity lines of credit — rose by $334 billion in the third quarter to $19.1 trillion, about $5 trillion more than at the end of 2019.

The buildup comes as household budgets face pressure from several directions at once. Prices are up roughly 30% since 2019, and the savings rate has dipped below 4% of total income, well below pre-pandemic levels. Disposable personal income, adjusted for inflation, grew less than 1% in September, the slowest reading since April and the third consecutive monthly slowdown, according to Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis data.

Signs of strain

Spending is showing signs of slowing after a resilient year. A monthly gauge published by CNBC and the National Retail Federation found retail sales rose just 0.2% last month, the slowest pace in nearly a year, with the figure held up by a strong Halloween season and early holiday promotions.

Even McDonald's has struggled despite $5 and $6 meal deals: U.S. same-store sales fell 0.2% in the third quarter, its first quarterly drop since early last year. Chief executive Chris Kempczinski said lower-income customers in particular were looking for entry-level value the chain had not fully delivered.

The pressure is also visible in demand for help with debt. Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency, said the past two months had been the busiest for debt management plan sign-ups in more than 15 years. "Household budgets are reaching a breaking point," he said.

A labour market holding the line

There is one counterweight: jobs. The labour market remains in a low-fire, low-hire pattern, and job growth has shown signs of stabilising — employment grew by an average of 137,000 a month over the past three months, compared with an average loss of 45,000 a month during the same period in 2025. Many economists believe that as long as most people stay employed, consumer spending is unlikely to fall off a cliff.

The picture is not uniform, though. About 2 million Americans have been out of work for six months or more, accounting for 27.6% of all unemployed workers — the highest share since December 2021.

What happens over the holidays will be the next test: with balances already at a record, how much more households put on their cards may say a lot about where the economy heads next.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NBC News
  • PYMNTS

link.title: Americans head into the holidays carrying a record $1.29 trillion in credit card debt

entry.title: U.S. envoys land in Moscow for Putin talks after Abu Dhabi round stalls on territory
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, the latest leg of a fast-moving American diplomatic push to end the war in Ukraine.

The two men were met at the airport by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and driven to central Moscow, where their meeting with Putin was scheduled for the first half of the day. It is the tenth time Witkoff has met Putin in person. After Moscow, the envoys planned to fly to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later the same day.

The visit follows two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian delegations — the first direct negotiations between the two sides in nine months. That round ended on Wednesday with agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange, but no breakthrough on the questions that have blocked a settlement for more than four years.

What Abu Dhabi produced — and what it did not

The one concrete result from Abu Dhabi was humanitarian. Both sides agreed in principle to a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, which Kushner described as potentially the biggest release of the conflict. The numbers were still being finalised, and no date was announced.

On the substance of a settlement, neither side moved. Russia continues to demand that Ukraine give up territory in the eastern Donbas, including land Kyiv still holds — a demand Ukraine has refused. Kushner said progress had been made on a post-war security framework for Ukraine, but added that no deal could be signed until the territorial dispute is settled, describing it as the hardest issue to resolve.

The Moscow meeting is the American attempt to carry that unfinished business forward. Kushner said on Tuesday that the U.S. had seen "some openings and some opportunities" and would try to make progress with Putin. Zelenskyy, speaking in Ireland, said there was a "window of opportunity" to reach a deal this year, and said he hoped the Americans would return from Moscow with "specifics."

Europe's seat at the table

The other question the envoys are carrying to Moscow is who gets to take part in the next round. Kushner said the U.S. wants European representatives included in future discussions, particularly on questions of continental security, and urged Europe to pick a single person to speak for it in the negotiations.

Russia has opposed European participation, pointing to Europe's support for Kyiv. European security advisers were in Abu Dhabi for separate consultations this week but were kept out of the main talks, and Moscow has shown no sign of changing that position.

Whether Putin agrees to let Europe in — and whether the Moscow session produces anything beyond the prisoner-exchange plan — will shape what happens next. The envoys' same-day trip to Dublin means Zelenskyy will hear the outcome within hours, but the core dispute over territory remains unresolved, and neither side has signalled a concession on it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Reuters

link.title: U.S. envoys land in Moscow for Putin talks after Abu Dhabi round stalls on territory

entry.title: Webb catches a 'forbidden' glow that eluded laboratories for 40 years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The James Webb Space Telescope has picked up a whisper of light that physicists have been chasing for four decades — the faint rotational glow of the trihydrogen ion, a molecule so central to interstellar chemistry that it had never been seen shining, anywhere in the Universe or in a laboratory.

The detection was made with Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument, trained on a turbulent patch of sky known as Herbig-Haro 168, or HH 168, in the star-forming region Cepheus A. There, a jet from a young star slams into the surrounding gas, heating it in a violent shock. Buried in the infrared light from that hot gas, a team led by David Neufeld of Johns Hopkins University found a series of extraordinarily faint spectral lines — 26 of them, each matching the wavelengths predicted for the trihydrogen cation, H₃⁺. The strongest line registered at 72 sigma, leaving virtually no doubt about the detection.

A prediction from 1986

The signal was predicted in 1986, when astrophysicists Fu-Shih Pan and Takeshi Oka of the University of Chicago calculated that the trihydrogen ion should emit a very faint amount of light as it rotates. The transitions involved are so weak that physicists call them "forbidden" — not impossible, but so improbable that the light they produce is vanishingly faint.

For forty years, that prediction stayed unconfirmed. The signal was too faint to catch, even in laboratory experiments designed to look for it. Webb's sensitivity finally changed that, and the wavelengths the team measured matched Pan and Oka's forty-year-old calculations.

It was not a one-off. When the researchers examined archival Webb observations of another Herbig-Haro object, HH 211, they found the same telltale emission there too — a second confirmation that the signal is real and not a quirk of one patch of sky.

Why a faint glow matters

H₃⁺ is one of the most important ions in astrochemistry. It forms readily in cold molecular clouds and drives much of the chemistry that builds more complex molecules in space. Its newly detected rotational lines give astronomers a fresh way to measure ionisation in shock-heated gas — the kind of gas that surrounds newborn stars — and to test how those violent regions evolve.

There are limits to what the result can yet say. The work is available as a preprint on arXiv and has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, but the interpretation still rests on incomplete knowledge of how energetic collisions excite H₃⁺. Models of the shock in HH 168 do not yet fully match the observed brightness, so the physics behind the glow remains partly open.

What is settled is the detection itself: after forty years, a signal once thought too faint to ever see has finally been caught — twice, in two different stellar nurseries.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceAlert
  • Horizon Lab

link.title: Webb catches a 'forbidden' glow that eluded laboratories for 40 years

entry.title: American Cancer Society now urges routine prostate screening for many men
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The American Cancer Society has changed its advice on prostate cancer screening for the first time in 16 years. The organisation now says most men should get a blood test for the disease, rather than weighing the option with a doctor.

Under the new guidance, published Thursday, men at average risk should have a prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, blood test every two years between the ages of 50 and 69. Doctors should still explain the benefits, limits and possible harms before testing begins. The previous guidance, issued in 2010, left the decision entirely to the individual after a discussion with a clinician.

Earlier and more frequent testing for higher-risk men

The recommendations are stronger for men at higher risk. Black men, and men with a strong family history of the disease, should now be tested every year from the age of 45 through 69. Black men face a 67 percent higher incidence of prostate cancer than white men and nearly double the death rate, according to the society.

For men aged 70 to 74, the decision becomes individual, made with a clinician, because the balance of benefit and harm is less clear at that age. Routine screening is not recommended from 75 on, and should stop after 80 or when life expectancy is under 10 years — though very healthy men aged 75 to 79 with a rising PSA may choose to continue after talking with a doctor.

A clearer path between a high reading and a biopsy

The update also tightens what happens after a test comes back high. A PSA level of 3.0 nanograms per millilitre or higher counts as elevated for men aged 45 to 69; for men aged 70 to 74, the threshold is 6.5. That is lower than the 4.0 figure many American laboratories still print as normal.

Rather than moving straight to a biopsy, the guidance calls for a second blood test to confirm the result, then an MRI scan or a validated biomarker test. The aim is to cut unnecessary biopsies and to catch slow-growing cancers that can safely be watched rather than treated at once.

Why the society changed its mind

The shift reflects new evidence and better tools. A long-term European study published in 2025 found prostate cancer deaths were 13 percent lower among screened men. MRI scans and biomarker tests now also let doctors sort out which raised readings need a biopsy — far harder in 2010, when the test's lack of specificity led to false alarms, unnecessary procedures and treatment of tumours that would never have caused harm.

The society estimates about 333,830 American men will be diagnosed in 2026, and about 36,320 will die from it — the second most common cause of cancer death in men.

One influential body has not yet moved. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, whose recommendations determine which preventive services insurers must cover, still advises individual decision-making. It has announced an update is coming.

Sources

  • STAT
  • USA Today

link.title: American Cancer Society now urges routine prostate screening for many men

entry.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief as board names Colette Kress interim CEO
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday as president, chief executive and a member of the board of Nvidia, effective immediately, ending a 33-year run as the founder and only chief executive the chipmaker has ever had. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and said it had begun a search for a permanent successor, considering internal and external candidates. It also appointed longtime director Harvey C. Jones as its first board chairman.

The resignation came a day after Nvidia's board met to consider removing Huang, following reports in the New York Times and the Wall Street Journal about two extramarital affairs. One involved a Singapore-based technology executive whom United States intelligence officials suspect of spying for China; the other involved a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. On Sunday, Huang told employees in a letter that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without giving details.

An inquiry that is still running

On November 8, Nvidia said its independent directors, assisted by outside legal counsel, would oversee an investigation into whether Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation. The inquiry is being led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton, and the FBI is also examining the matter. The board had previously said it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised, and had expressed confidence in Huang.

The political fallout has spread beyond the company. Lawmakers in Washington have called for briefings and new restrictions on advanced chip exports to China, and at least one senator has publicly called for Huang's resignation. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Huang, who told him he had no idea the woman was a spy, and that he believed him.

Investors have reacted swiftly. Nvidia's shares have fallen sharply this week, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars from its market value, and the stock slid again after Thursday's announcement, rattling other technology stocks. Huang, 63, owns about 3.6 percent of the company and is one of the world's richest people.

What happens next

Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 and has led its finance operations since. She will keep her roles as executive vice president and chief financial officer while serving as interim chief executive. Nvidia said it would still report its third-quarter results for fiscal 2027 on November 17, as previously scheduled.

The board's statement gave no reason for the resignation and disclosed no terms of any agreement with Huang. The independent investigation continues, and the board has given no timeline for naming a permanent successor — a notable gap, since Huang has said he does not believe in succession planning and Nvidia has no public plan for replacing him.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • USA Today

link.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia chief as board names Colette Kress interim CEO

entry.title: US jobless claims rise to 200,000, but layoffs stay rare and the labour market holds firm
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

More Americans applied for unemployment benefits last week, the Labor Department reported on Thursday, but the increase was small and claims remain at levels that have historically pointed to a tight labour market, with layoffs rare and most workers enjoying unusual job security.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits rose 9,000 to a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ended November 7, the department said. That was above the 195,000 economists polled by Reuters had forecast. The previous week's figure was revised up by 2,000 to 191,000.

The broader picture has barely changed. Claims have stayed at or below 200,000 for nine straight weeks and have not topped 230,000 in any week this year. They remain close to the 189,000 level reached in mid-July, the lowest since 1969. The four-week moving average, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, was unchanged at 195,250.

There was also a sign of steady hiring underneath the headline. Continuing claims — the number of people still receiving benefits after an initial week of aid — fell 20,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million in the week ended October 31. The insured unemployment rate held at 1.1%.

A stable backdrop for the Fed

The figures fit with the wider jobs picture. The government reported last week that nonfarm payrolls surged in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2% in September. Economists read the claims data as consistent with a stable, or even strengthening, labour market — a backdrop that lets the Federal Reserve focus on fighting inflation rather than worrying about a wave of layoffs.

That stability matters because the claims report is the most timely read on the jobs market, arriving weekly rather than monthly. A single week's rise of 9,000 is well within the normal noise of the series, and at 200,000 the level is far below the readings that have historically signalled trouble.

What is still unknown

Economists expect layoffs to stay low through the end of the year, but seasonal volatility around the holiday season could produce some spikes in the weekly data. Whether claims hold near current levels into December will be the next test — for now, the rise looks like a blip in a calm series rather than the start of a turn.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Reuters

link.title: US jobless claims rise to 200,000, but layoffs stay rare and the labour market holds firm

entry.title: US envoys wrap up Putin talks in Moscow with no breakthrough, but a new round is set
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ended talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday, closing a week of diplomacy that restarted direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine but produced no breakthrough on ending the war.

The Moscow meeting followed two days of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi between Russian and Ukrainian delegations — the first direct contact between the two sides since February. That round ended on Wednesday with an agreement in principle on a large prisoner exchange, though the exact number of detainees has yet to be settled, and no clear resolution on the war itself.

Speaking to reporters at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport shortly before departing, Witkoff struck an upbeat note. "I think progress was made. I think it was made earlier today," he said. "People didn't think that we were going to restart trilateral. We've restarted it. We've set a new meeting."

Kushner, who holds no official role in the Trump administration despite acting as one of its top diplomats, described the discussions as "very fulsome and detailed" and said they would inform the next round of multilateral talks.

Europe's seat at the table

One of the envoys' goals in Moscow was to secure Putin's backing for European representatives to join the negotiations, which are also looking at the continent's broader security arrangements. Witkoff said European officials would take part in the next round. "They're our partners, and it's important for them to be involved," he told reporters.

Putin's foreign policy aide, Yuri Ushakov, confirmed that the three-way talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States would continue, but appeared to play down the prospect of European participation. "They are making every effort to get involved in the negotiations, but, as our president has said, they need to decide whether they want peace or a continuation of the war," Ushakov said.

Putin himself told the envoys that Russia had "never objected (to) pursuing dialogue" with Europe. "You want this peace to be a durable and lasting one, and I confirm that I subscribe to that, and I'd say more. I want this peace to be eternal, for good," he said.

Moscow has so far resisted European governments sitting at the main negotiating table. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov criticised the presence of European officials in Abu Dhabi earlier in the week, calling it not a "promising approach," and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said no contacts had taken place between the Russians and any EU representatives there.

What happens next

The U.S. envoys are now expected to fly to Dublin, where they will meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and brief him on the Moscow meeting. Zelenskyy was already in the Irish capital on Thursday for a summit of the European Political Community, where the Abu Dhabi talks and additional sanctions on Russia were on the agenda.

The diplomacy has not brought Ukraine any respite from the fighting. Moscow launched a ballistic missile and drone attack overnight into Thursday, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, and at least one person was killed in Kyiv on Thursday morning, local authorities said.

Zelenskyy also warned on Thursday of renewed disruptions to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk's Starlink service that is critical to Ukraine's military operations, saying the service had faced "significant disruptions" that were hampering Kyiv's ability to shoot down Russian drones. SpaceX, which owns Starshield, told CNN there had been no change in its service.

The war is approaching its fifth year: large-scale hostilities began on February 24, 2022, following fighting that first broke out in eastern Ukraine in 2014.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Associated Press

link.title: US envoys wrap up Putin talks in Moscow with no breakthrough, but a new round is set

entry.title: US home sales fall to a 16-year low as high mortgage rates freeze buyers
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Sales of existing homes in the United States fell sharply in October to their lowest level in more than 16 years, the National Association of Realtors reported on Thursday, as high mortgage rates and still-elevated prices kept would-be buyers on the sidelines.

Existing-home sales dropped 5.5% from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the realtors' group said. That was the weakest pace since August 2010, when sales were falling after the end of a homebuyer tax credit, and it came in below the 3.85 million rate economists polled by Reuters had expected. Sales were down 8.8% from a year earlier.

The drop ended a three-year stretch in which sales had hovered near the 4 million mark, moving within a narrow range from month to month. The main culprit, by the realtors' own account, is the cost of borrowing: the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.33% in October, the highest since 2000 apart from a single month in 2023.

"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said Lawrence Yun, the association's chief economist. "As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010."

More homes, fewer buyers

The market is not short of homes to buy. There were 1.59 million homes on the market in October, up 4.6% from a year ago, a supply of about 5.1 months at the current sales pace. The median price of an existing home held at $416,700.

That combination — more choice, but fewer deals — points to affordability rather than supply as the binding constraint. Sales are counted when a contract closes, so October's figures largely reflect deals agreed in August and September, when rates were already climbing.

Economists do not expect a quick rebound. Nancy Vanden Houten, lead U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, said she expects sales to stay below 4 million until late next year. Yun said he expects total sales for 2026 to come in somewhat below last year's, and is waiting until December, after the midterm elections, before forecasting 2027.

What is still unknown

Whether rates ease from here is the open question. If they stay near current levels, the freeze is likely to persist into the winter, traditionally the slowest season for housing. If they fall, the homes already sitting on the market could move quickly — the demand, by most accounts, is waiting rather than gone.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • WSJ

link.title: US home sales fall to a 16-year low as high mortgage rates freeze buyers

entry.title: Four tankers hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said on Thursday, adding that the vessels had ignored warnings and sailed into areas it considers restricted.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two supertankers were disabled by explosions on Wednesday after they ignored warnings against using what it described as an unauthorised route. Iranian state media reported that the two vessels exploded after hitting naval mines and broadcast what it said was video footage of the incidents. The Guards said the two supertankers were carrying a combined total of more than four million barrels of oil and were left ablaze.

Later on Thursday, Iran's army said two other tankers had hit mines in the eastern part of the strait after ignoring warnings and disabling their radar systems, according to state television. The statements did not name the tankers or give their nationalities, and no casualty figures were reported.

Reuters, which first reported the Iranian statements, said it could not immediately verify the Iranian account.

A strait still under attack

The incidents come despite a rebound in shipping traffic through the strait and expectations of a de-escalation in the conflict between the United States and Iran — expectations that had been reflected in falling oil prices. The Strait of Hormuz normally carries about one-fifth of the world's oil, and the United States has responded to the attacks with a naval blockade of Iranian ports while helping tankers cross the waterway.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said in reports on Thursday that a vessel had been hit by an unidentified projectile about 14 nautical miles northwest of the United Arab Emirates emirate of Ras Al-Khaimah on Wednesday while leaving the strait.

Attacks on shipping in the strait have continued at a rapid pace. At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October — the highest monthly tally since the conflict began in late February, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

What is still unknown

The cause of the explosions has not been independently established, and the names and nationalities of the four tankers have not been released. It is also unclear whether the vessels are still burning or have been towed, and whether the latest incidents will disrupt traffic through the strait or push oil prices higher in the coming days.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Arab News

link.title: Four tankers hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran says

entry.title: Euclid maps 900 million galaxies in its biggest look at the dark universe
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The European Space Agency has released the first major collection of data from its Euclid space telescope, covering observations of more than 900 million galaxies as scientists work to understand the dark matter and dark energy that shape the universe.

Unveiled on Thursday, it covers a sweep of sky equal to about 9,500 times the size of the Moon as seen from Earth — around 13 months of observations totalling 1.7 petabytes of data.

Launched from Florida in 2023, Euclid aims to build the largest-ever three-dimensional atlas of the cosmos, spanning more than a third of the sky, by 2031. This haul still covers just 14 percent of the area it is due to survey in visible and near-infrared light over six years.

Mapping the cosmic web

Euclid does more than photograph galaxies. It also measures their distance, adding a third dimension to the map and placing each galaxy in space and time across 10 billion years. That lets scientists reconstruct the cosmic web — the vast network of filaments along which galaxies cluster, separated by near-empty voids — and track how it has grown.

The web's shape depends on dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary matter makes up only about 5 percent of the universe; dark matter, known only from its gravitational pull, may account for 27 percent, and dark energy, thought to drive the universe's accelerating expansion, 68 percent. Neither can be observed directly.

"It marks a major milestone for ESA's Euclid mission and for everyone involved," said Valeria Pettorino, the agency's Euclid project scientist.

Lenses that weigh galaxies

One of the sharpest tools in the new data is gravitational lensing. Light from distant galaxies is bent as it passes massive objects in the foreground, and the strength of that bending reveals how much matter a galaxy contains — including the invisible kind.

The release includes about 15,000 strong gravitational lens candidates, more than the total found in the previous half century. Euclid combines breadth with sharpness: ground telescopes cover wide areas but are blurred by the atmosphere, while Hubble and the James Webb telescope image only tiny patches sharply. Euclid does both at once.

Euclid has also pinpointed 60 million quasars — brilliant galactic cores powered by supermassive black holes — including some whose light set off around 13 billion years ago, when the universe was just 5 percent of its current age.

What comes next

The release will be completed next year, when the first results on dark energy and dark matter are expected.

What is still unknown

The new data does not yet answer the central questions: what dark matter and dark energy actually are. Those first results are expected next year, and the full survey will not be complete until 2031.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Euclid maps 900 million galaxies in its biggest look at the dark universe

entry.title: Microsoft 365 outage knocks out Outlook, Teams and Copilot for millions
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Millions of people were cut off from their email and workplace tools on Thursday after a major Microsoft 365 outage knocked out Outlook, Teams and several other services for much of the day.

The disruption began on Thursday morning in the United States and spread worldwide, hitting Exchange Online — the cloud service behind business Outlook accounts — along with Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, Office for the web, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Defender XDR. Microsoft first described the problem as affecting the Americas before widening it to "any region."

Outage tracker Downdetector recorded just under 130,000 reports for Outlook around 1:09 p.m. Eastern Time, the day's peak. Reports for Microsoft 365 itself topped 46,000, while Teams peaked at about 4,600 reports and Copilot at nearly 6,000. By late afternoon the numbers were falling, with roughly 54,000 Outlook reports still outstanding at 4:20 p.m.

Servers "unexpectedly unavailable"

Microsoft said the failure was not caused by a surge in demand. Instead, it said "a large number of servers" had become "unexpectedly unavailable," pushing extra load onto the systems that remained and triggering automated health-check failures.

"We've determined that the elevated load isn't driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure," the company said in its service-health updates.

The company logged the incident under reference EX1550543 and labelled it a "service degradation" for Outlook. It said it was redistributing traffic across its infrastructure, moving users off the affected systems and restarting the failed servers. By around 4 p.m., Microsoft said some servers had been "successfully returned to service," though it had not declared the incident over at the time of reporting.

A day of disruption

The outage reached well beyond office workers. OpenAI said it was investigating broken Microsoft connectors, and Anthropic said an issue with an upstream provider was affecting its own Microsoft 365 connector. The State of Michigan said its email and other Microsoft applications were affected by the widescale outage.

Microsoft also said it had paused deployment and configuration changes while it reviewed the incident's telemetry.

There is no evidence the outage was caused by a cyberattack. Nothing Microsoft has published points to one, and the company has described the cause in infrastructure terms — servers failing, not an external intrusion. A full root cause will only come with Microsoft's post-incident review, which it has not yet published.

What is still unknown

Microsoft has not said what made so many servers unavailable at once, nor given a firm time for full recovery. Separate from the main outage, the company said earlier on Thursday that it had restored a shorter Teams disruption in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity problems.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • TechCrunch

link.title: Microsoft 365 outage knocks out Outlook, Teams and Copilot for millions

entry.title: Spain's parliament ratifies housing decree a day after nationwide strike
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Spain's interim lower house ratified a package of housing measures on Thursday, a day after a general strike and major street protests over the housing cost crisis. The vote was decided by a single ballot: 35 in favour, 34 against.

The measures extend eviction protections for tenants judged by social services to be in a precarious position, as long as regional authorities cannot offer an alternative home. That protection runs until 2030. The package also freezes rent increases above the government's reference price for the neighbourhood, and caps other annual rises at 2 percent until the end of 2027.

It also bars property companies from buying homes below 70 percent of their value, to stop cheap wholesale purchases resold at a markup, and adds a 10 percent tax on tourist apartments, tax incentives for leasing, and government-backed loans for buyers' down payments.

A second decree falls

The government had split its plan into two decrees, expecting one to fail. The second — automatic renewal of residential leases, with landlords who refused owing a year's rent in compensation — was rejected 34-35, after a centre-right Basque party that backed the first decree switched sides. Many lawmakers argued automatic renewal would push owners to pull homes from the rental market and drive prices higher.

The measures were first attempted in October, after anger over soaring rents erupted following the televised eviction — and subsequent death — of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Conservative parties blocked them, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez responded days later by calling an early election. The government then waited to try again with the smaller interim parliament, where it and its allies held a slightly more favourable balance. That interim lower house has 69 members, against 350 in the regular parliament, dissolved when the election was called.

Everything now turns on November 29

How long they last will likely depend on the national election on November 29. The leading opposition party, the conservative Popular Party, says it will repeal the measures if it takes power — which polls suggest is a real possibility — and has instead pledged one million new homes plus cuts to taxes and red tape for developers.

"Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box," interim Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez told lawmakers.

The stakes are high: average rents have almost doubled in a decade, and the average monthly rent of €1,176 now equals about 98.7 percent of a young person's average monthly salary, according to the Youth Council of Spain. The central bank puts the housing shortfall at roughly 750,000 homes, expected to pass one million by 2028.

What is still unknown

The decree is now validated law, but a change of government on November 29 could repeal it. The Popular Party has not said how quickly it would act, or what it would offer tenants covered by the new protections instead.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • SpainGuru

link.title: Spain's parliament ratifies housing decree a day after nationwide strike

entry.title: Mysterious eight-minute radio pulses traced to a dead star and its Sun-like companion
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

For nearly a year, a radio telescope in the Australian outback kept picking up the same uncanny rhythm: a burst of radio energy arriving like clockwork every eight minutes, then silence. Now astronomers say they have found what is behind it — a dead star spinning beside a star much like our own Sun.

The signal, catalogued as GPM J071507−114153, was first detected in late 2024 by the Murchison Widefield Array in Western Australia. Between December 2024 and September 2025 the telescope recorded 214 pulses from the source, and researchers classified it as a long-period transient — a recently recognised class of cosmic radio signals that switch on and off over minutes or hours.

In a study published on Thursday in the journal Nature Astronomy, the team reports the most likely source: a binary star system made up of a white dwarf — the dense, collapsed core left behind when a star dies — orbiting a G-type star similar to the Sun. It is the first time radio pulses have been detected from a white dwarf paired with a Sun-like star rather than a smaller, cooler red dwarf.

A clockwork signal 5,000 light-years away

The system sits about 5,000 light-years from Earth. The eight-minute beat, the researchers found, is set by the white dwarf's own rotation. Because the pulses were unusually clear, the team could watch the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion — the first time that has been possible for this kind of object.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," said lead author Sam McSweeney, an astronomer at Curtin University in Australia, "so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself."

The pulses did more than reveal the pair. They also let the team catch stellar flares erupting on the Sun-like companion — storms on a star thousands of light-years away, picked up through radio waves. Follow-up optical observations with the Keck Observatory in Hawaii confirmed the companion is indeed a G-type star. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away," said Natasha Hurley-Walker, a corresponding author of the study and an astronomer at Curtin University.

Why it matters

Long-period transients are still a young field. The first hints of such signals appeared in 2005, but astronomers only began studying them in earnest in 2022, when a signal pulsing roughly every 18 minutes was found; another, with a 21-minute period, followed a year later. Around a dozen are now known, and at least four of them turned out to be binary systems pairing a white dwarf with a red dwarf — but it was never clear which star was producing the long radio pulses.

This discovery breaks that pattern. It shows that white dwarfs can generate these pulses while orbiting Sun-like stars too, widening the hunt: future detections of long-period transients could now help astronomers find white dwarfs that ordinary telescopes cannot see.

What is still unknown

The exact mechanism that produces the radio pulses is not settled. The researchers believe the emission comes from near the white dwarf, but whether it is generated by the white dwarf itself or by the interaction between the two stars remains an open question — one that further observations of this system and others like it may answer.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Gizmodo
  • ICRAR / Curtin University

link.title: Mysterious eight-minute radio pulses traced to a dead star and its Sun-like companion

entry.title: SpaceX plans more than $74 billion for two AI supercomputing campuses in Texas and Arizona
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

SpaceX said on Thursday it plans to invest more than $74 billion in two supercomputing campuses, one at its Starbase site in Texas and another in Cochise County, Arizona, in a major expansion of its artificial intelligence business.

The company expects to spend more than $24 billion on the Starbase campus and roughly $50 billion on the Arizona site, it said in a statement. The campuses are designed to train frontier AI systems, the large models used for research, manufacturing and national security work.

Two sites, two different builds

The Starbase facility, near the company's rocket base on the Gulf Coast, would generate its own electricity rather than draw from the public grid. SpaceX has described a gas-fired power plant for the site, and the Starbase City Commission is due to consider a property-tax abatement for the project on December 9.

The Arizona campus is the larger of the two. The company says it would draw up to 6 gigawatts of power at full build-out, delivered in four phases across nine large compute buildings. It would create about 5,500 construction jobs at peak and 1,000 permanent jobs, according to SpaceX. The site would use dry cooling, with no planned industrial use of groundwater, and the company says it could cut power bills for local cooperative members by up to 20%.

Approval still to come

Neither project is a done deal yet. The Arizona campus needs approval from Cochise County, and a petition with about 2,400 signatures has asked officials to deny the permit. The county's planning commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing on December 9.

The announcement underlines how central AI computing has become to SpaceX. The company's AI segment generated more than half of its revenue in the third quarter, Reuters reported, alongside its rocket launches and Starlink satellite internet business.

SpaceX has not disclosed which chip suppliers it will use, or a commissioning schedule for either campus. The $74 billion figure is the company's planned investment; it is not contracted capacity or revenue, and both sites remain subject to the local decisions due in December.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: SpaceX plans more than $74 billion for two AI supercomputing campuses in Texas and Arizona

entry.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong wins NL MVP unanimously after a historic 40-40 season
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Pete Crow-Armstrong is the National League's Most Valuable Player, and the vote was not close. The Chicago Cubs center fielder was named the unanimous winner of the 2026 NL MVP Award on Thursday, collecting all 30 first-place votes from the Baseball Writers' Association of America.

Crow-Armstrong, 24, put together one of the finest all-around seasons in recent memory. He hit .280 with 45 home runs and 41 stolen bases, becoming just the seventh player in major league history to reach the 40-40 mark in a single season — and the first Cub ever to do it. He tied for the major league lead in home runs, led baseball with 119 runs scored, and piled up 357 total bases and 84 extra-base hits.

The advanced numbers were just as emphatic. Crow-Armstrong led the majors with a 9.8 WAR by Baseball-Reference's measure and a 10.6 WAR on FanGraphs, finishing well clear of the rest of the league. He was also the game's best defensive center fielder, winning both the Gold Glove and the Platinum Glove, which goes to the top overall defender in each league. He is the first player ever to win an MVP and a Platinum Glove in the same season.

Ending Ohtani's run

The award ends Shohei Ohtani's streak of three consecutive MVP wins. Ohtani, the Dodgers' two-way star, finished second after earning 26 of the 30 second-place votes, for 264 points. Milwaukee's Brice Turang placed third. Crow-Armstrong's 420 points were the maximum possible under the voting system.

It is the fourth consecutive season in which the National League winner was unanimous, and the 11th unanimous NL MVP in history. Crow-Armstrong is the ninth Cub to win the award and the first since Kris Bryant in 2016 — and the first in franchise history to win it unanimously.

The season also brought him the Players Choice Awards for Player of the Year and NL Outstanding Player, voted on by his fellow players, along with the Hank Aaron Award as the league's top offensive performer.

A unanimous year across baseball

Crow-Armstrong's win came on the same night Houston's Yordan Alvarez won the American League MVP, also unanimously. The two are the third pair of unanimous MVP winners in the same year, and 2026 is the first season in which all four MVP and Cy Young winners were unanimous choices.

For the Cubs, the award is the payoff on a player they committed to early: Crow-Armstrong agreed to a six-year, $115 million contract in March, before the season that turned him from a promising young outfielder into the game's most complete player.

Sources

  • BBWAA
  • USA Today

link.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong wins NL MVP unanimously after a historic 40-40 season

entry.title: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen trades raw power for speed in agentic work
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Google on Wednesday introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a new model in its Gemini 4 family built for speed rather than maximum reasoning power, aimed at everyday coding and the multi-step jobs AI agents carry out alone. It is rolling out now across Google's developer tools, the Gemini app and Google Search.

Hydrogen sits a tier below the family's frontier models, Carbon and Argon, designed for deep, long-horizon reasoning on hard problems. The idea is that the most powerful model is not always the right tool: for routine work — writing code, running tests, verifying changes, carrying research through several steps — a faster, cheaper model that is still capable can be the better choice. Google calls Hydrogen its daily driver for agentic workflows.

On Google's own numbers, the trade-off is small. At its default high thinking setting, Hydrogen scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, edging out Argon at 50, and reaches 54 at its highest level, a new "xhigh" tier. It completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, the fast model it replaces, and on Terminal-Bench 4.1, a test of agentic terminal work, it scores 57 percent against Flash's 18.2 percent, cutting fabricated claims by more than five times. On multi-step tasks such as deep research and broad code navigation, it ranks fifth on Agent Arena.

Search gets the biggest upgrade

The most widely felt change may be in Google Search, where Hydrogen is rolling out to all users — Google calls it its biggest model improvement to Search yet. The model is meant to handle complicated questions better — ones with several parts, highly specific requirements or confusing typos — and to give more helpful links and visual responses in AI Mode. Its improved reasoning also sharpens Search's fan-out technique, which breaks one prompt into several subqueries, and users should see more images, structured answers, comparison tables and custom tools as visual responses.

Pricing, thinking levels and teamwork

Hydrogen offers four thinking levels — low, medium, high as the default, and the new xhigh tier — so users pay and wait only for the reasoning depth a task needs. Pricing is flat across its full one-million-token context window — $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens — with native one-million-token input and up to one million output tokens.

The model is also designed to work in teams. Alongside it, Google introduced Orchestrator in Antigravity, its development platform, which switches between models inside one session: Carbon can coordinate while Hydrogen powers worker and verifier agents building and testing changes in parallel. Hydrogen is available now in all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, the Gemini app, Search, and for paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Antigravity.

One caution: every benchmark cited here is Google's own, measured on tests Google chose. Independent evaluations have yet to publish, and they will be the real test of whether the speed comes with the reliability Google claims.
