entry.title: Wolfenstein 3 officially in production at MachineGames, Xbox confirms
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames, Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma announced on Wednesday, ending nearly a decade of waiting for the next entry in the alternate-history shooter series. The confirmation came as Xbox marked its 25th anniversary in Seattle, closing out an eight-city FanFest tour in the city where the brand began.

Sharma shared the news in a post on X, calling Wolfenstein "one of gaming's most important franchises" and praising the studio's work in carrying it forward. The post included a photo of a script page for the game's first chapter, titled "Nazitraz," according to Insider Gaming's account of the announcement. MachineGames followed minutes later with its own post: "His reputation precedes him. Wolfenstein 3 is in production."

Xbox's official recap of the anniversary announcements added a key detail: actors Brian Bloom and Debra Wilson are reprising their roles as BJ Blazkowicz and Grace Walker, the hero and the resistance leader of the modern series.

Finishing the trilogy

MachineGames rebooted Wolfenstein in 2014 with The New Order, followed by The New Colossus in 2017. Studio director Jerk Gustafsson has said publicly that the team wanted to finish the story as a trilogy, while declining to say when. Wednesday's announcement is the first formal confirmation that the third game is actually being made.

It is also the first Wolfenstein title developed by MachineGames while the studio is under Xbox ownership, following Microsoft's acquisition of Bethesda parent company ZeniMax.

What we still don't know

For all the excitement, the announcement was a confirmation, not a reveal. There is no trailer, no gameplay footage, no release date, no confirmed platforms and no subtitle beyond the chapter title on the script page. Xbox has said only that the game is in production and that it looks forward to sharing more.

A casting call reported earlier this year suggested performance capture was scheduled to run into 2027, pointing to a long wait — though none of that has been confirmed as part of the finished game.

Part of a bigger anniversary day

Wolfenstein 3 was the headline gaming announcement in a day of Xbox news. Sharma also confirmed id Software's next project is in development, Halo's cooperative Firefight mode is coming to Halo: Campaign Evolved, and 25 original Xbox games are now available on PC. New Fable gameplay was shown as well.

For Wolfenstein fans, though, the day belonged to a single sentence: the trilogy is back on. After nine years of silence since The New Colossus, the third game is no longer a hope or a rumour. It is in production.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Xbox Wire
  • Insider Gaming

link.title: Wolfenstein 3 officially in production at MachineGames, Xbox confirms

entry.title: Investors pile into Anthropic's market debut as orders run about six times the shares on offer
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Investor orders for Anthropic's initial public offering have reached about six times the shares available, Bloomberg News reported on Thursday, in a sign of intense demand for what could become the largest first-time share sale in history.

The AI company behind the Claude chatbot and some of its existing shareholders are aiming to raise up to $64.4 billion by selling 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each, according to the reporting. At the top of that range, the listing would value Anthropic at up to $1.4 trillion — slightly below what some investors had expected, but still a figure that would place the company among the most valuable ever to go public.

Bankers have told prospective investors that Anthropic will give priority to its existing backers when shares are allocated, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter. That means some would-be buyers are likely to receive smaller allocations than they asked for, even with demand running far ahead of supply.

A test of confidence in the AI boom

The listing is shaping up as a key test of Wall Street's confidence in the artificial intelligence boom. Anthropic is one of the leading developers of large AI models, and its debut comes as investors weigh whether the sector's rapid growth — and the enormous spending behind it — can be sustained.

The company's filing showed a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of October 31, up from $65 billion at the end of July, according to CNBC TV18. A separate private placement of about $26 billion is running alongside the IPO, anchored by cornerstone investors including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Nvidia alone agreed to buy about $10 billion of shares, the filings showed. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the offering, with 20 other banks taking part.

Shares are expected to start trading on the Nasdaq on November 19 under the ticker symbol "ANT."

What is still unknown

The six-times figure is a snapshot, not a final result. The report cautioned that details of the IPO, including the level of demand, could still change before the shares are priced, and order books in a listing of this size can move quickly in the final days. Anthropic could not immediately be reached for comment on the report.

The final price, the exact allocation of shares and the first day of trading will show whether the early enthusiasm holds — and whether the market is willing to pay a record price for a stake in the AI race.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNBC TV18

link.title: Investors pile into Anthropic's market debut as orders run about six times the shares on offer

entry.title: Canada gives Stellantis 30 days to fix Brampton plant deal or face a lawsuit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Canada has given automaker Stellantis 30 days to fix alleged breaches of a 2022 funding agreement — or face a lawsuit to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in public money. The ultimatum follows the company's decision to sell its idle assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, and move planned vehicle production to the United States.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on Thursday that Ottawa had served the world's fourth-largest carmaker with a formal notice of default. "We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days or else. Of course, we'll sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto. She is seeking a response by December 12.

The dispute centres on a 2022 agreement under which the federal government committed up to C$529 million — about US$380 million — to help Stellantis retool its Brampton and Windsor plants for electric and gasoline-powered vehicles, with Ontario pledging a further C$513 million. About C$222 million in federal money had been disbursed as of December 2025.

What Ottawa says Stellantis did wrong

Joly's letter to Stellantis Canada chief executive Trevor Longley lists several alleged breaches: the suspension of the Brampton retooling in February 2025, the relocation of planned Jeep Compass production to Illinois, and the planned sale of the plant itself. The agreement required the company to maintain its footprint in Ontario through 2035, and barred closing Brampton before 2033 unless the plant was commercially unviable.

Stellantis announced on Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton site to Roshel, a Canadian maker of armoured vehicles, for an undisclosed sum. The plant has been idle since 2023, when production stopped for retooling, and the shift leaves more than 2,000 Canadian workers without jobs.

The company has offered to voluntarily return $24 million in federal support received for the original Brampton retooling plan — far less than the hundreds of millions Ottawa is seeking. If Stellantis stays in breach, Joly warned, it could face termination of the funding deal and a demand to repay all or part of the money it received, plus interest.

A flashpoint in the trade war

The row has become one of the sharpest flashpoints of the US–Canada trade war. Prime Minister Mark Carney has accused Stellantis of betraying Canadian workers, and Unifor — the union representing more than 9,000 Stellantis workers across Canada — said the sale broke the federal government's promise to protect autoworkers. Its president, Lana Payne, said the company had "betrayed" its unionised workforce.

Joly met the company, the union and Ontario Premier Doug Ford in Toronto before issuing the notice.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether Stellantis will try to remedy the alleged breaches within 30 days, offer a larger repayment, or let the dispute go to court. The company has not disclosed the price of the Roshel deal. What is certain is the deadline: December 12.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: Canada gives Stellantis 30 days to fix Brampton plant deal or face a lawsuit

entry.title: Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate majority leader
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced on Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for the job of Senate majority leader, opening a leadership contest inside a Democratic Party that has just won back the Senate.

Van Hollen, 67, made the announcement in an interview with MS NOW host Jen Psaki and in a post on X, saying voters had sent a clear message in the midterm elections. "This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people," he said, describing the midterms as a "huge outburst of democracy" and a rejection of the status quo.

Democrats flipped eight seats in the midterms and will enter January with at least 55 senators, possibly 56. The caucus will choose its leader by secret ballot, with the vote scheduled for December 1.

A challenge from the left

Van Hollen framed his candidacy as a break with business as usual. He said he would use the "full power" of the Senate to respond to voters' demands to end the war in Iran and to lower the cost of living — two issues he has pressed for months.

The Maryland senator has emerged as a vessel for progressives and newer members who want more forceful leadership, or at least want to push Schumer toward a more aggressive posture. Sen. Bernie Sanders said this week he would not support Schumer for another term as leader, and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who has said for weeks he could back Van Hollen, welcomed the announcement.

Van Hollen's move is a sharp reversal from just days ago. On Saturday he told CNN that seeking the leadership job was "not my focus," noting that he was also interested in running for president in 2028. As of Thursday afternoon, he said he was "still actively listening to members" — before declaring his candidacy hours later.

Schumer says he has the votes

Schumer, 75, a five-term senator from New York, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade and says he is confident he will win. In a statement on Thursday, he said he welcomed a discussion about the caucus's future and repeated his assurance that he had the votes to continue as leader.

"I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

Schumer has faced sustained criticism from parts of the party over his handling of the Democratic caucus during the Trump presidency, and the leadership race will test how much of that discontent reaches the ballot box. Even if Schumer wins, the contest could raise questions about his authority at the start of a new majority.

What is still unknown

No other senator has entered the race, and it is not yet clear how many of the incoming freshmen — most of whom have declined to publicly back Schumer — will vote for Van Hollen. The closed ballot means the outcome will not be known until the December 1 vote.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NPR
  • CNN

entry.title: Finland says it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Finland's military said on Thursday that its forces had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland the day before, in what would be the first attack of its kind on a Russian vessel in the Baltic Sea since the war in Ukraine began.

A spokesperson for the Finnish Defence Forces said in an email to Reuters that its forces "detected … a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation." The spokesperson added that Finland was not under "any immediate military threat," and declined to give further details about where or when the strike happened, or how it was detected.

Ukraine's Security Service has said it carried out the attack, according to Finnish public broadcaster Yle. The service said it targeted the Naro-Fominsk, a Buyan-M class missile corvette of Russia's Baltic Fleet, as part of a wider drone operation against the oil export port of Ust-Luga on the Russian side of the gulf. It did not say what weapon was used or provide evidence of damage.

What the neighbours saw

Estonia's defence minister, Martin Herem, told public broadcaster ERR that an explosion occurred aboard a Russian Baltic Fleet vessel in the gulf at about 5:30 a.m. local time on Wednesday. Estonian media reported that the ship later returned to St Petersburg.

A senior Finnish official told Yle that the attack took place near Gogland, a Russian-held island in the gulf about 40 kilometres off the Finnish coast near Kotka. Brigadier General Markku Viitasaari of Finland's defence ministry told the newspaper Helsingin Sanomat that Finnish sensors recorded flashes and smoke coming from the ship in international waters, and that officials at first thought the vessel was firing at Ukrainian drones before sensor data pointed to at least one explosion on board.

Neither Finland nor Estonia has named the attacker, and Russia has not publicly confirmed that any warship was hit.

A wider night of drone attacks

The strike came during a broader Ukrainian drone operation against Russia's north-western Leningrad region, which includes St Petersburg and the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, a major export outlet for oil and grain. Russia said it had intercepted at least 146 Ukrainian drones in the region in recent days, and the regional governor confirmed a fire in the Ust-Luga port area after a drone attack.

The same night, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania issued warnings telling residents to take shelter after drones entered their airspace, and NATO warplanes were scrambled in response. Some Ukrainian drones have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states before, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries bordering Russia.

Diplomacy in parallel

The incident came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised mediation efforts led by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who have been shuttling between Kyiv and Moscow in an effort to advance talks on ending the war. The envoys' diplomacy has so far produced no breakthrough, and the fighting — including long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia — has continued alongside it.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether anyone was hurt in the strike, how badly the vessel was damaged, or whether the ship Finland and Estonia observed was the Naro-Fominsk. The Finnish military has not said how it detected the strike, and Russia has not confirmed a hit on the warship by name. Until those details are confirmed, the episode stands as a detected strike with a claimed attacker — and a sign of how close the war now runs to NATO's northern flank.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: Finland says it detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland

entry.title: California braces for 50-foot waves as a week of storms rolls in
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

California is bracing for a week of storms that will bring the season's first prolonged stretch of rain, wind, snow and towering surf, with waves of up to 50 feet expected along parts of the coast this weekend.

The storms are arriving as the waters off California are unusually warm and El Niño continues to strengthen, a combination forecasters say is pushing tides higher than normal and making the surf hit the shore harder.

Towering surf this weekend

The National Weather Service has issued a high surf warning for the Bay Area coast from 6 p.m. Friday, November 13, to 4 a.m. Sunday, November 15, with breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet and sets of 40 to 50 feet at favoured spots. The warning covers nearly all of the Northern and Central California coast and much of the Oregon coast.

Waves at Ocean Beach in San Francisco could top 40 feet, and at Mavericks, the famed surf break about 20 miles south of the city, they are expected to reach 60 feet or higher. Beaches in Central California could see waves of 25 feet, while Los Angeles and San Diego are forecast to get waves of eight to 12 feet.

Forecasters warned of dangerous conditions at beaches across the state, especially in Northern California, where an unexpectedly large wave can pull a person standing on shore into turbulent water. Sneaker waves and rip currents are expected through the weekend, and a coastal flood advisory covers the Bay Area coast from midnight Friday night to 6 p.m. Saturday, with waves topping seawalls and flooding low-lying roads.

Rain and Sierra snow

The first storm will bring rain up and down the state on Friday, arriving in the North Bay as early as late Thursday night. The heaviest rain is likely in the North Coast region, where up to six inches could fall over the next week. The San Francisco Bay Area could record up to two inches, while Los Angeles is likely to get less than an inch.

The storms are also expected to deliver the first significant snow of the season in the Sierra Nevada, with half a foot to more than a foot expected through Sunday morning. The Weather Service issued winter storm warnings across the mountain range, including for the Tahoe area, and warned of travel delays on mountain roads through the weekend.

More storms on the way

After a brief break, a second storm is expected to move across the state between Sunday and Tuesday, with the rain again focused over Northern California. A third storm is likely next week, though forecasters said on Thursday it was not yet clear when it would arrive.

The flooding risk from the rain is predicted to be low. The storms will replenish reservoirs and rivers and soak the landscape enough to reduce the threat of wildfires, experts said.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • The Weather Channel

link.title: California braces for 50-foot waves as a week of storms rolls in

entry.title: Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress as Nvidia scandal widens
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify before the United States Congress about his reported affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, days after the revelations forced him out of the chipmaker he led for more than three decades.

Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott, a South Carolina Republican, wrote to Huang and to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Thursday, asking both men to appear before the panel in December. Scott warned that the committee could issue a subpoena if Huang does not appear voluntarily. Separately, three House committees — Intelligence, Foreign Affairs and the panel on China — have called Huang for a closed-door interview on 1 December. The Senate has asked him to appear voluntarily on 3 December.

The affair at the centre of the inquiry

Huang, 63, admitted on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years, Lori Huang, after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre company. The two are not related. American intelligence has reportedly suspected Alice Huang of being an asset of Chinese intelligence — an allegation Beijing has rejected as a smear and which has not been established. The Justice Department said on Thursday it had not yet reached any conclusions about whether she was engaged in espionage for Beijing.

A second alleged affair was reported on Wednesday, involving Kimberly Powell, a long-time Nvidia executive who reported directly to Huang. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation into whether its former chief executive was "the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The company said it had "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised," while pledging that the inquiry would examine all available information.

Fallout for Nvidia and Lutnick

The scandal has shaken the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom. Nvidia has lost about $550bn (£415bn) in market value in five days — its steepest five-day fall since it went public 27 years ago. Chief financial officer Colette Kress was named interim chief executive on Thursday.

Lutnick faces questions of his own, over whether the Commerce Department stalled efforts to tighten export controls on advanced AI chips bound for China. A department spokesperson said he had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate committee. Unnamed administration officials have told American media that Lutnick slowed moves to toughen the controls.

What is still unknown

Much remains unresolved: whether subpoenas will be issued, what lawmakers knew and when, and whether any Nvidia technology or secrets were compromised. Nothing published so far establishes that secrets were passed on, and the espionage allegation against Alice Huang remains unproven.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • The Straits Times

link.title: Jensen Huang summoned to testify before Congress as Nvidia scandal widens

entry.title: Dutch government on the brink as wealth-tax row splits coalition
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Dutch government is on the brink of collapse less than nine months after taking office, after a row over wealth taxes split Prime Minister Rob Jetten's three-party minority coalition.

Jetten will meet his coalition partners on Friday in an attempt to hold the government together, a day after parliament narrowly passed a 2027 tax plan that one of the governing parties had voted against.

The dispute centres on a deal struck on Wednesday between Jetten's centrist D66 party and the Christian Democrats, the CDA, and left-wing opposition parties. In exchange for opposition support for the annual tax package, the two governing parties agreed to a small increase in wealth taxes — a shift of part of the tax burden from income to wealth.

The right-wing, pro-business People's Party for Freedom and Democracy, the VVD, the third member of the coalition, opposed the change and ultimately voted against its own government's tax plan. The plan still passed with a narrow majority, carried by opposition votes.

The "millionaire tax"

The most contested element is a levy on the wealthy that critics have dubbed the "millionaire tax". It would tax annual returns on assets above €60,000 at 38.5 per cent, one of the highest rates in the euro area, while the rate on returns below that threshold would fall to 35.5 per cent.

Supporters say the package raises taxes on the very wealthy while cutting them for people on lower incomes. The VVD called it a bad deal for the Netherlands and a breach of the coalition agreement the three parties negotiated earlier this year.

VVD parliamentary leader Ruben Brekelmans described the result of the vote as "disillusioning" and said his party would have to seriously reconsider its position. The party had threatened to quit the coalition if the amendment passed.

A government without a majority

Jetten, 38, became the youngest prime minister in Dutch history when he took office in February, after his D66 party unexpectedly won last year's election on a campaign promising a break from the divisive previous government. But his coalition has never held a majority in either house of parliament, and has needed opposition support to pass every proposal.

He skipped a summit of European Union leaders in Ireland on Thursday to attend the parliamentary debate. After the vote, he said he would do all he could to hold the coalition together and would seek "a new start" at Friday's meeting with the leaders of the VVD and the Christian Democrats.

If the VVD walks out, the government would almost certainly fall. A crisis could trigger new elections — which would be the fourth in the Netherlands in five years — although parties could also try to form a new government from the current parliament. That route would probably produce another minority government, an option the left-wing opposition party Pro has already ruled out.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Bloomberg

link.title: Dutch government on the brink as wealth-tax row splits coalition

entry.title: North Korea shortens its flag for the first time since 1948
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

North Korea has changed the proportions of its national flag for the first time since the state was founded in 1948, making the flag noticeably shorter and squarer under a revised constitution published this week.

Article 166 of the revised constitution, posted on Naenara, the state's external propaganda website, now sets the flag's height-to-width ratio at 1 to 1.65, replacing the 1-to-2 ratio that had stood for 78 years. The change was reported on Friday by South Korea's Yonhap news agency, citing the amended text.

Everything else about the flag stays the same. It keeps its broad red stripe across the centre, narrow white stripes above and below it, blue stripes along the top and bottom edges, and a red five-pointed star inside a white circle near the hoist. The flag is still wider than it is tall — just less stretched than before.

A new shape, the same symbols

The constitution also restates what each element of the flag is meant to stand for. The red stripe represents the blood shed by fighters against Japanese rule during the 1910–45 colonial period. The white circle and stripes stand for loyalty to the country's leader and the ruling Workers' Party of Korea. The blue stripes represent the people's revolutionary spirit, the pursuit of peace and friendship, and national sovereignty.

The proportions rule had survived untouched in the law until now, including through a constitutional revision in September 2023. Its first change in nearly eight decades comes as leader Kim Jong Un works to put his own stamp on the state he inherited — building a distinct governing style and national identity while keeping the symbols of his predecessors in place.

Part of a wider redefinition

Observers see the flag change as one piece of a broader redrawing of North Korean identity. The revised constitution also drops language about reunification with the South and instead defines South Korea as a separate, hostile state — a position Kim set out in late 2023 and early 2024. In 2024, the lyrics of the national anthem were also revised, replacing a phrase referring to the whole Korean Peninsula with words meaning "this world."

Analysts quoted in regional coverage described the flag revision as an attempt to craft a new national image for the Kim era: the familiar colours and the red star remain, but the specifications are now his.

What is not yet clear is how quickly the new proportions will appear on flags in everyday official use. The change exists so far in the constitutional text and on the Naenara website; Pyongyang has issued no separate public statement about it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Yonhap News Agency
  • The Straits Times

link.title: North Korea shortens its flag for the first time since 1948

entry.title: From courtrooms to hospitals: the Microsoft outage, felt in 74 countries
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A Microsoft outage that began on Thursday has now touched at least 74 countries, and the list of places feeling it reads like a tour of public life: courts, hospitals, parliaments, police forces and stock exchanges.

The failure was first detected after midday on the U.S. East Coast on Thursday, 12 November. Microsoft 365 services — including Outlook email, Teams and the AI assistant Copilot — have been suffering connectivity problems ever since, and the company had not restored full service by Friday morning.

Microsoft has said the cause was "elevated load" on its infrastructure across several regions, after a number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable" and pushed extra traffic onto the machines still running. A Microsoft executive, Charles Lamanna, said the incident was not caused by a cyberattack. The company has also warned that its early fixes were not working "as expected".

The disruption, country by country

In the United States, staff in the House of Representatives were unable to use Outlook, and court communications were delayed from Los Angeles to Texas. The City of Austin reported its Outlook email was unavailable, though phone lines and the 911 emergency service were unaffected. Workhorse Group, an electric-vehicle maker, pushed back its third-quarter results from 12 November to 16 November.

In Canada, Unity Health Toronto declared a "code grey" — its alert for infrastructure failure — while stressing that patient care was unaffected. In Japan, some companies went back to the fax machine, and government systems were disrupted in both Japan and Singapore. The Philippines Supreme Court reported delayed email responses, and users in India reported disrupted Teams calls and email.

Australia's spy and federal police agencies were affected, though the impact was described as minimal and largely confined to email. In Europe, the stock-exchange operator Euronext advised listed companies to use the phone, while in Britain, GPs, police, pharmacies and members of parliament were among those hit. The UK Parliament said it was working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible, with alternative ways of communicating in place.

The outage also spilled beyond Microsoft's own products: both OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems, because their tools connect to workplace files and email through Microsoft 365.

Why one failure travelled so far

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft, so a fault in the shared infrastructure behind Outlook and Teams reaches far beyond office workers. The same cloud services now carry court filings, hospital administration, government correspondence and the tools other companies build on top of.

That is also why the recovery is slow. Microsoft says it is carefully reintroducing traffic as it brings servers back, and that capacity has not yet returned to normal. There is still no time given for a full restoration.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News
  • The Week

link.title: From courtrooms to hospitals: the Microsoft outage, felt in 74 countries

entry.title: Mauricio Pochettino confirmed as Manchester United head coach
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Manchester United have confirmed Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach, ending a week of speculation over who would succeed the sacked Michael Carrick.

The 54-year-old Argentine has signed a two-and-a-half-year deal and will officially take charge on Wednesday, November 18. He will first complete his final duties with the United States men's national team, coaching their two Concacaf Nations League quarter-final ties against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday, before crossing the Atlantic.

His first match in charge will be one of the biggest in the English calendar: a Premier League trip to Liverpool on Sunday, November 22.

A club in crisis

Pochettino inherits a side in deep trouble. United sacked Carrick on Thursday after the club's worst start to a league campaign in four decades, with one win and eight points from their opening ten games leaving them in the relegation zone.

The club said it had reached an agreement with the U.S. Soccer Federation for Pochettino and his staff to be released after their national-team commitments. In its announcement, United described its new head coach as "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players."

According to The Times, the appointment was recommended by director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada, and approved by minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. British media reported United will pay U.S. Soccer £7.5 million in compensation to release Pochettino from a contract that had been due to run until the 2030 World Cup.

Return to the Premier League

Pochettino is no stranger to English football. He previously managed Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea before taking over the United States in 2024. With the U.S., he guided the World Cup co-hosts to the last 16 on home soil earlier this year before their campaign ended in defeat by Belgium.

He was the only coach United spoke to directly about the job, according to the Press Association, and his appointment is understood to have the unanimous endorsement of the club's leadership and ownership.

United said details of the staff who will join Pochettino at Old Trafford will be confirmed in the coming days. His long-time assistant Jesus Perez is widely expected to be among them.

What is still unknown

The full composition of Pochettino's backroom team has not been confirmed, and neither the club nor U.S. Soccer has disclosed the exact compensation figure officially. How quickly the Argentine can lift a squad short on confidence — starting with a trip to Anfield — will be the first real test of the appointment.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Mauricio Pochettino confirmed as Manchester United head coach

entry.title: Wholesale inflation hit its fastest annual pace in nearly four years in October
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US wholesale inflation accelerated in October to its fastest annual pace in nearly four years, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday, as rising food, fuel and electronics costs pushed producer prices higher for a second straight month.

The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% from September and 6.5% over the 12 months ended in October — the largest yearly increase since November 2022, when prices rose 7.4%. The monthly gain was slightly smaller than the 0.4% economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected, and the annual figure came in just below the 6.6% forecast. Even so, the yearly rate climbed from 6.3% in September, extending a run of hot readings.

Food did much of the pushing. Food prices rose 1.3% in October, the fastest monthly increase since July 2022, after a 1.1% rise in September. Wholesale prices for fresh and dry vegetables jumped 26.7%, following a 30.7% leap the month before. Goods prices overall rose 0.5% in October, after a 2.5% jump in September, and were up 10.2% over the year — their largest annual rise since October 2022.

Energy remained a pressure point. The war in Iran and the resulting supply shock have sent gas and diesel prices markedly higher in recent months, and high diesel costs are now lifting transportation and warehousing costs as well.

Stripping out food and energy, core producer prices rose 0.3% on the month and 5% over the year, matching a pace last seen in January 2023. One standout was electronic components and accessories, up 4.2% in the month — a six-month high — and 31.7% from a year earlier, the fastest annual rate in bureau records going back to December 1966. The surge is tied to massive investment in artificial intelligence technology and equipment.

What it means for the Federal Reserve

The report is the last major inflation reading before the Federal Reserve's December meeting, and it points in the same direction as this week's hotter-than-expected consumer price data. Markets expect a quarter-point rate hike, although Fed Governor Christopher Waller has said a half-point move could be necessary. Nationwide senior economist Ben Ayers said lingering fuel-price effects could stretch into 2027 and warrant further tightening.

Producer prices tend to lead consumer prices, so the report raises the prospect that the factory-gate inflation now showing up in wholesale data will reach household budgets in the months ahead — a concern for families already stretching to cover groceries, rent and everyday costs.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether December brings a quarter-point move or something larger, or how much of the wholesale increase will be passed on to consumers rather than absorbed by businesses. The bureau is scheduled to publish its November inflation report on December 10 — one day after the Fed's decision — so policymakers will act on October's figures and their own projections rather than fresh data.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Reuters

link.title: Wholesale inflation hit its fastest annual pace in nearly four years in October

entry.title: Scientists map 8 million brain cells in the most detailed atlas of the basal ganglia yet
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Scientists have produced the most detailed molecular map yet of the basal ganglia, the cluster of structures deep inside the human brain that governs movement, motivation, habits and decision-making. The atlas, published on November 12 in the journal Cell, charts about 8 million individual cells and identifies 60 distinct cell types and the communities they form.

The work was led by the University of California, Irvine, under Xiangmin Xu, a professor of anatomy and neurobiology and director of the university's Center for Neural Circuit Mapping. Using brain samples from four neurotypical donors, the team combined two spatial transcriptomics techniques — MERFISH+ and Stereo-seq — to link each cell's molecular identity to its precise location in the tissue. That combination let them see not only which cells are present, but how they are arranged into neighbourhoods inside the basal ganglia.

The basal ganglia is a small region with an outsized role in health. Its circuits are implicated in Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease, as well as in psychiatric conditions and addiction. Until now, researchers studying those disorders lacked a fine-grained reference for what a healthy basal ganglia looks like at the level of individual cells.

Part of a much larger mapping effort

The atlas is one of two papers led by UC Irvine in a coordinated publication package from the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, known as BICAN. The wider package involved hundreds of scientists from 55 institutions across nine countries, and the Irvine team also contributed to four additional papers in Cell. A second Irvine-led paper, published in Cell Systems, describes the programme that procured and prepared the donated brain tissue used across the project.

The main paper — "Multiscale spatial atlas of human basal ganglia cell types and communities," led by Bereket Tesfay Berackey — was produced through UC Irvine's Center for Multiomic Human Brain Cell Atlas project, working alongside the Salk Institute, UC San Diego and Washington University in St. Louis.

Why it matters

For researchers, the atlas is a baseline. Comparing tissue from people with Parkinson's or Huntington's against this healthy reference should make it easier to spot which cell types and communities go wrong first — and where a future treatment might need to act. The same reference could also help scientists test whether experimental therapies reach the right cells.

What is still unknown

The map covers one region, not the whole brain. BICAN's stated goal is a complete parts list of every cell type in the human brain, and the basal ganglia atlas is described as a first major milestone toward it. The four-donor sample also means the atlas captures a snapshot of healthy variation, not the full range across ages and populations — a gap future mapping work will need to fill.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Medical Xpress
  • Allen Institute

link.title: Scientists map 8 million brain cells in the most detailed atlas of the basal ganglia yet

entry.title: Microsoft says November security updates may break printing
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Microsoft has warned customers that its November 2026 security updates may break printing for documents with complex formatting, in the latest problem to surface from this month's Patch Tuesday release.

In a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, the company said printing "might fail for documents containing images rendered with a height or width value of zero at the selected printing resolution" after the November updates — or later updates — are installed. The issue affects devices running Windows 10 or later and Windows Server 2016 or later.

The bug mainly hits people printing Microsoft Word documents through the Windows Graphics Device Interface, the system that handles how documents are drawn on screen and on paper. Microsoft said printing from other applications could also be affected.

The trigger is easy to miss. The zero-sized images at the heart of the problem can sit inside a document even when no graphic is visible — they are used in some complex formatting, such as invisible images added as watermarks, layout anchors, or by document-generation tools. A file can look perfectly normal on screen and still fail to print.

A troubled update

The printing fault is not the only problem with the November release. Microsoft has also confirmed that the updates fail to install on some Windows 11 machines that took October's non-security preview update, leaving affected devices repeatedly retrying the install or showing error codes 0x80070306, 0x800f0989 or 0x800f0993. The company said it would repair affected devices automatically within 24 to 48 hours, with no action needed from users.

The same batch of updates has also triggered Windows activation and licensing failures, with error code 0x80041008, and Microsoft has acknowledged performance and stability problems in SQL Server on systems updated since October's Patch Tuesday.

It is a familiar pattern. Windows updates in March and July 2025 caused printing problems of their own — the first made some USB printers print random text, the second broke the "Print to PDF" feature — and August 2026 .NET Framework updates broke printing and PDF export in apps built on the Windows Presentation Foundation framework.

What is still unknown

Microsoft said it is investigating the printing issue and will share more information when it has it. It has not announced a permanent fix, a workaround, or a date for one, so users who hit the problem have little to do for now but watch for an updated advisory — and check whether a document that will not print contains the kind of hidden formatting that triggers the bug.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BleepingComputer
  • How-To Geek

entry.title: Hidden companion found behind a star's 15 years of fake supernovae
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Astronomers using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory have solved a mystery that has puzzled them for 15 years: a giant, unstable star that keeps exploding like a supernova — without ever dying.

The star, known as AT 2016blu, sits in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, 30 million light-years from Earth. It is a luminous blue variable, a class of hot, massive stars known for dramatic swings in brightness. Its surges are so bright they resemble a supernova, the violent death of a massive star — but the star survives each blast, which is why astronomers call it a "supernova impostor."

Between 2012 and 2026, telescopes recorded at least 27 bursts of visible light from the star, arriving roughly every 113 days. The regularity was the clue that something was driving the eruptions on a schedule — but for years, nobody could say what.

A companion hiding in the glare

The answer, published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, is a hidden companion orbiting the giant star: either a stellar-mass black hole or a neutron star, the dense core left when a massive star dies. The pair travels an oval orbit, swinging close together every 113 days. At closest approach, the companion pulls material off the giant star; the captured gas whips around near light speed, heating until it shines in X-rays, and that energy heats the surrounding gas until it glows in visible light.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," said Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia, who led the study. "Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn't figure out what was making this happen."

Catching the star at the right moment was the hard part. The team timed a Chandra observation for a predicted outburst in early 2026, confirming the flare with optical telescopes — the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory network and more than 30 amateur astronomers. Chandra observed in March 2026 and found the star at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in 2001 and 2002, before the outbursts began.

A first on two counts

It is the first X-ray detection of this class of erupting star, and the first found with a black hole or neutron star companion. AT 2016blu is also bright enough in X-rays to qualify as a candidate ultra-luminous X-ray source, a rare and poorly understood class of bright X-ray objects.

The discovery may reach beyond one strange star. Astronomers suspect many stars that brighten before exploding as supernovae sit in similar systems — a massive star orbiting a compact object or another massive star. The hidden companion may be a common culprit behind some of the sky's most dramatic behaviour.

What remains unknown is which kind of companion it is: the observations confirm a compact object but cannot yet say whether it is a black hole or a neutron star. That will need further observations — and the next outburst is never far away.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NASA
  • Newswise

link.title: Hidden companion found behind a star's 15 years of fake supernovae

entry.title: El Niño drives record-shattering ocean heat off the San Francisco coast
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The water off the San Francisco coast is warmer than it has ever been this late in the year — by a wide margin. Near the Farallon Islands, normally the centre of Northern California's famously cold upwelling zone, sea temperatures have passed 66°F, roughly 10 degrees above what is normal for November.

The warmth is not a local quirk. Climate scientist Daniel Swain of UCLA reports that water within 20 to 30 miles of shore is running more than 10°F above average in one unbroken stretch from central Baja California north to Sonoma County, with 5- to 8-degree anomalies reaching the Oregon border. The readings are the warmest on record for the date along nearly the entire California coast — and in many places they would break the record for any week of the cool season, November through April, in the satellite era that began in 1981.

The cause is a pile-up of warming forces: an extreme El Niño, already among the strongest ever measured, building on a marine heatwave amplified by long-term ocean warming. NOAA puts the chance of a "historic" El Niño this winter at about 60%.

Seas running a foot high

Warm water takes up more space, and the effect is already visible in sea level. Swain estimates that thermal expansion accounts for about 12 inches of a persistent 12- to 18-inch rise in coastal ocean height, with more to come as coastally trapped Kelvin waves arrive through the season. That leaves the coast exposed: king tides, the year's highest astronomical tides, fall on November 23–25, December 23–25 and January 21–22, and even a moderate storm during one of those windows could push water a further foot or two higher.

The warming reaches well below the surface. Researchers at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute recorded 64.72°F at a depth of 200 feet in Monterey Bay on October 26 — the warmest reading at that depth in nearly 40 years of monitoring, beating a record set during the powerful 1997 El Niño. The temperature there was more than 7°C above the long-term average, and tropical species are already appearing where they have never been seen.

For now, the immediate consequence is weather. The same warm water is feeding extra moisture and energy into a run of Pacific storms now arriving on the coast. Forecasters expect three or four systems over the coming days, with the first significant rain of the season reaching Northern California on Friday. San Francisco could see one to five inches of rain over two weeks — against a November average of about 2.6 inches for the whole month.

Swain's seasonal outlook suggests the extreme warmth is likely to persist at least into January or February. Splitting the contributions — El Niño, the background marine heatwave, human-caused warming — will take attribution studies. What is already clear is that the ocean off California has never been this warm, this late, in the modern record.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • KQED
  • Weather West

link.title: El Niño drives record-shattering ocean heat off the San Francisco coast

entry.title: SignDrop zero-day turns a Windows security feature into a path to SYSTEM access
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A security researcher has published working exploit code for a new Windows zero-day that turns one of Microsoft's own defences against itself. The proof of concept, called SignDrop, lets a standard local user escalate to SYSTEM — the highest privilege level on a Windows machine — by abusing the log-file authentication feature Microsoft added to the Common Log File System (CLFS) driver.

The code and a detailed write-up were posted to GitHub on Tuesday, November 10, the same day Microsoft shipped its November security updates. The researcher, who publishes under the name MSNightmare and has since been identified as Abdelhamid Naceri, says the flaw sits in how the CLFS driver creates a companion authentication file — a .cnpf file — when a privileged process opens a prepared log.

The mechanism is a study in unintended consequences. CLFS, the logging subsystem built into Windows, has long been a favourite target for privilege-escalation attacks. To close that door, Microsoft added an authentication check to CLFS log files in October 2025, so the driver only parses logs it wrote itself. SignDrop abuses the new step that check introduced: by preparing a log in a folder the user controls and redirecting paths with symbolic links, the attacker gets a privileged process to create the companion file in its own security context — but with permissions the standard user can still write to. In the published code, that privileged process is Microsoft Defender itself, triggered through its signature-update interface.

No patch, no CVE — and a warning not to switch the defence off

Microsoft has not confirmed the claimed flaw, assigned it a CVE identifier, or released a fix, and nothing about SignDrop appeared in the November security updates. There is no evidence the exploit has been used in real attacks, and it does not appear in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue.

The researcher tested the exploit on Windows 11 26H2 and Windows Server 2025 Experimental builds, and estimates — unverified — that around 80 percent of Windows installations could be in scope, since systems older than 90 days typically move from the mitigation's learning mode into enforcement automatically. Independent testing by Heewon Song of the PurpleHound team at Korean security firm 78researchlab confirmed the exploit works, but found it does not run reliably enough for operational use. Defender must also be enabled for the published chain to succeed.

For now, researchers advise leaving the CLFS authentication mitigation switched on. Turning it off would take a system outside SignDrop's claimed attack surface, but it would also reopen the memory-corruption flaws the protection was built to prevent.

SignDrop is the latest in a series of Windows and Defender exploits from the same researcher since April; Microsoft confirmed and patched two earlier ones, RoguePlanet and ShieldBreak. The difference this time is the target: where those exploits raced Defender's file handling, SignDrop goes after the CLFS driver's own authentication feature — a defence that, in the researcher's words, was implemented correctly but whose logic "allows abuse."

Sources

  • Ars Technica
  • The Hacker News

link.title: SignDrop zero-day turns a Windows security feature into a path to SYSTEM access

entry.title: Tanker slams into docked cruise ship on the Mississippi, tipping it on its side as rescues unfold
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A tanker slammed into a docked river cruise ship on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, tipping the smaller vessel on its side and partly submerging it as rescue crews pulled passengers from the water.

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines' American Heritage at about 12:30 p.m. local time while the ship was docked at the Port of New Orleans, port officials said. About 129 passengers were aboard, along with crew members. The ship had docked about two hours earlier to begin letting passengers off.

Video from CNN affiliate WDSU showed the tanker ramming the docked cruiser and pushing it over until it lay on its side, partly underwater, near the Crescent City Connection bridge. Twelve people were reported in the water in the first hours after the collision, and WDSU reported that a dozen people were taken to hospital. The Port of New Orleans said the number of injuries had not yet been confirmed.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel all responded to the scene, according to a port news release. Passengers were escorted into the Port of New Orleans Administration Building, where they could be medically evaluated and given assistance.

A rescue still unfolding

American Cruise Lines said its guests and crew had been evacuated and that it was in close coordination with the Coast Guard and local authorities. "We are deeply concerned for everyone involved," the company said in a statement.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was aware of the incident and would be heading to New Orleans. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno's office said multiple people had been rescued and that search-and-rescue operations were continuing into the afternoon.

The cause of the collision is not yet known, and investigators were still working to establish how a tanker under way on the river came to strike a ship tied up at the dock. Officials have not said whether all passengers and crew have been accounted for, or how badly the American Heritage was damaged.

What is still unknown

This remains a developing incident. The Port of New Orleans said its immediate priority was the safety of passengers, crew members and first responders, and that the situation was still evolving. The number of people injured, the condition of those taken to hospital, and the cause of the collision are all still to be confirmed by officials.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • WDSU
  • CNN
