entry.title: FAA halts all U.S. departures in rare nationwide ground stop after air-traffic communication failure
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday, halting every departing flight in the United States after a communication problem spread across the country's air traffic control centers.

The order, issued just before 4 p.m. Eastern time, told all departing aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice. In its advisory, the FAA cited "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the stop at 4:16 p.m., saying it followed a communication issue affecting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers, and that FAA technicians were investigating.

Flights already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land. International flights heading to the United States were to be handled on a case-by-case basis. Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 reported that about 3,100 aircraft were airborne and bound for U.S. airports when the order took effect, with no additional aircraft taking off.

The disruption rippled through the system quickly. Reuters reported that nearly 7,000 flights across the country had been delayed or canceled because of the stop. The FAA's advisory listed an effective period beginning at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and running to 11:30 p.m. Eastern, but the directive itself said departures should stay grounded until further notice, and the agency gave no estimate for when normal operations would resume.

Reports pointed to problems beginning at about 3:30 p.m. Eastern at the FAA's Kansas City Air Traffic Control Center before spreading to other centers. Flightradar24 linked the order to an equipment outage, and the National Weather Service also reported a national radar outage. The FAA has not named a cause, and officials have not said whether a cyberattack is suspected.

Only the third stop of its kind

A nationwide halt of all departures is exceptionally rare. The only comparable events were September 11, 2001, when U.S. airspace was closed after the terrorist attacks, and January 11, 2023, when the FAA's system for distributing critical flight safety notices failed and departures were grounded for hours.

That history underlines how seriously the agency treats a loss of reliable communication with aircraft. Controllers depend on radio contact to keep planes separated in the sky, and a failure that touches every control center at once leaves the system with no safe way to launch more flights.

What is still unknown

This is a developing story. The FAA has not said what caused the communication failure, how long the ground stop will last, or when departures will resume. Passengers with flights scheduled for Friday evening were advised to check with their airlines, as delays and cancellations were expected to continue even after the stop is lifted.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • USA Today

link.title: FAA halts all U.S. departures in rare nationwide ground stop after air-traffic communication failure

entry.title: U.S. measles cases pass 5,400 as deaths reach 10 in worst outbreak since 1991
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Measles cases in the United States have climbed past 5,400 this year, and the number of deaths linked to the disease has reached 10, according to state health departments — the worst outbreak the country has seen in more than three decades.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 5,412 cases for 2026 as of November 12, an increase of 230 in a single week. It was the 14th consecutive week in which the CDC recorded a triple-digit weekly rise. Cases have now been reported in 45 states and the District of Columbia.

The death toll tells a more complicated story. State health departments have reported 10 measles-associated deaths this year, while the CDC's own count stands at six. The federal agency has consistently lagged behind state reports and says its total is subject to change.

Two of the deaths were reported this week. Wisconsin's health department said a child in Grant County, in the state's southwestern corner, had died of measles complications, a week after a baby in the state also died. Pennsylvania officials confirmed that an unvaccinated resident of Montour County had died after testing positive for measles. Each state has now recorded seven measles-associated deaths this year, and New York has recorded one. At least four of this year's deaths were children.

Pennsylvania remains the epicentre

Pennsylvania is still the hardest-hit state, with 1,542 cases this year — more than any other state. Wisconsin reported the most new infections over the past week, with 174, bringing its total to 651. Ohio added 61 cases this week for a total of 372.

The outbreak is being driven overwhelmingly by gaps in vaccination. People who have not been vaccinated, or whose vaccination status is unknown, account for 96 percent of reported cases, according to the CDC. The hospitalization rate remains at 11 percent, with 591 people hospitalized this year.

There are signs the surge in Pennsylvania may be slowing. The state's vaccination campaign has pushed monthly measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) doses far above normal — about 56,000 in September and 61,000 in October, against a typical monthly average of roughly 25,000 — including home visits to under-immunized communities.

Elimination status at risk

The outbreak now threatens a public health milestone the United States has held for more than a quarter of a century. Measles was declared eliminated in the country in 2000, meaning the virus was no longer spreading continuously within its borders. Cases have now risen above 5,000 for the first time since 1991.

A commission of the Pan American Health Organization is meeting this week to decide whether the United States — and Mexico — should lose that elimination status, following Canada, which has already lost it. A decision is expected on November 17. Infectious disease experts say the virus is effectively spreading again across North America, driven by falling vaccination rates.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ABC News
  • CIDRAP

link.title: U.S. measles cases pass 5,400 as deaths reach 10 in worst outbreak since 1991

entry.title: Europe to send united front to potential Ukraine peace talks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Europe will take a seat at any future talks on ending the war in Ukraine, speaking with one voice through the European Union and five of its biggest states, European leaders agreed in Dublin on Friday.

European Council President Antonio Costa announced it after an informal European Council meeting and a European Political Community summit that brought 47 European leaders to the Irish capital. Under the plan, the EU will jointly represent Europe alongside France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom.

It answers a demand European and Ukrainian leaders have pressed for years: no settlement about Ukraine's future without Europe in the room. Russia has long resisted a European role, and the United States under President Donald Trump had previously appeared indifferent. That position now appears to be shifting.

A shift after Moscow

The announcement followed a diplomatic sequence that began with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday. On Thursday, US envoys Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff met President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, then travelled to Dublin to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner said late on Thursday that a deal could not be concluded without the Europeans at the table, and that Putin was willing to give the expanded format a try. Witkoff told reporters that Europeans would be present at the next round of meetings.

But the shape of Europe's presence is far from settled. Russia and the United States have called for a single European representative, while several European nations favour a diplomatic team. Who would speak for the EU itself is also open. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said she is the one representing Europe on foreign and security policy; she and Costa are the two names most often tipped.

Moscow is sending mixed signals. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said European participation was not discussed during the Moscow talks. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia needed to understand the EU's real intentions before deciding on an expanded format, while chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky claimed Russia had received no concrete peace proposal from European countries after the Abu Dhabi talks.

Merz warns Trump against surprises

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz used the Dublin meeting to send Washington a public message. With Trump expected to meet Putin again at an APEC summit in China next week, Merz asked for no surprises, warning against a repeat of last summer's Russia-US talks in Anchorage, Alaska, whose outcome Europe viewed as favouring Putin. He said Germany's involvement in any future talks was a given.

Kallas struck a similar note of caution, saying a ceasefire must come first and warning against walking into what she called Russian traps. She argued that Moscow does not want a strong figure at the table because it wants to push through its maximum demands.

The Dublin agreement puts Europe's claim to a seat on the record. Whether Russia accepts it, and in what form, is the next question — nearly five years into the war.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • DW

link.title: Europe to send united front to potential Ukraine peace talks

entry.title: SpaceX Starship booster catch fails; ship presses on toward first-ever catch attempt
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 lifted off from Texas on Friday evening with an ambitious goal: to become the first fully reusable orbital rocket by catching both of its stages at the launch tower. It got halfway there.

The 15th test flight of the world's largest rocket launched at 5:47 p.m. EST from SpaceX's Starbase site in Boca Chica, Texas. Minutes later, the plan for the Super Heavy booster began to unravel. A technical problem a little more than six minutes after liftoff prevented the booster from returning to the pad, and flight controllers diverted it to the Gulf of Mexico, where it splashed down and promptly burst into flames as residual propellant ignited.

It was a setback for a manoeuvre SpaceX had already pulled off three times. The last successful tower catch of a Super Heavy booster came in March 2025, and this flight was the first attempt with a new version of the booster — and the first catch try at the flight's launch pad.

The ship is still flying

The upper stage, known as the Ship, fared better. After an 18-minute coast on an initially sub-orbital path, a single Raptor engine reignited for a short 10-second burn that pushed Starship into its planned orbit.

It then released its cargo: 26 upgraded Starlink V3 internet satellites, the second time a Starship flight has carried operational satellites to orbit. All 26 were deployed and confirmed in contact. Three of the satellites carry cameras to photograph the ship's heat shield in orbit, giving engineers a look at its condition before the return.

The Ship is now on a roughly 22-hour mission, circling Earth about 14 times. If it stays healthy, SpaceX will attempt something never tried before: catching an orbital upper stage at the launch tower. A single Raptor is expected to fire on Saturday afternoon to begin the de-orbit, followed by a 56-minute belly-first re-entry and a return to Starbase. If anything looks wrong, the ship will be ditched in the ocean instead.

Why it matters

Full reusability is the core of SpaceX's case for Starship. Catching and reflying both stages would slash the cost of putting mass into orbit, which the company needs to expand its Starlink network and, eventually, to fly cargo and crew to the Moon and Mars.

Friday's flight showed both sides of that bet in a single evening: a booster lost to a fault minutes into flight, and a ship that reached orbit and delivered its payload as planned. Whether the mission ends as a partial success or a landmark depends on what happens when the Ship comes home on Saturday.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CBS News

link.title: SpaceX Starship booster catch fails; ship presses on toward first-ever catch attempt

entry.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 26 years, health panel rules
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, an independent panel of experts has determined, ending a public health milestone the country has held since 2000.

The commission, which reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization, concluded that the United States no longer qualifies as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The decision had been widely expected after years of falling vaccination rates and surging case counts.

Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000, meaning the virus was no longer spreading continuously within the country's borders. Outbreaks still occurred, usually started by travellers bringing the virus in from abroad, but high vaccination rates kept them small and short-lived. That changed in 2025 and 2026, when the virus found more unvaccinated families and communities to spread through.

The evidence behind the decision

The committee considers an infection endemic when the same strain is passed from person to person for at least a year within a country. A key piece of evidence came from Utah, where scientists found the same strain had circulated for more than a year, accounting for more than 95 percent of the state's cases and causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026. Sustained outbreaks have also been reported in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York.

More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the United States this year — the highest number since 1991 — most of them linked to 43 new outbreaks. Nearly all have been in people who had not received the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. Roughly one in nine reported cases has led to hospitalisation, according to the CDC, and at least 10 people have died, according to state reports.

What losing the status means

"Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system," said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the CDC. "Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges."

The consequences fall hardest on people who cannot be vaccinated — infants too young for the shot and people with weakened immune systems — who now face a higher risk in outbreak areas than they did two years ago. The MMR vaccine remains highly effective: two doses cut an exposed person's chances of falling ill by 97 percent compared with someone unvaccinated.

The road back

The United States can regain its elimination status, but only after showing that outbreak transmission has been interrupted for at least 12 months. Experts say that will not be easy, pointing to diminished public trust in vaccines, rising nonmedical exemptions in schools and declining MMR coverage among kindergarten students.

The United States is not alone in slipping backwards. Canada lost its elimination status last year after a lengthy outbreak, and Mexico, which has had several large outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing the designation.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN

link.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 26 years, health panel rules

entry.title: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first-ever three-way meeting at APEC in Shenzhen
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia will meet together for the first time next week, the White House confirmed on Friday, in an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's three biggest nuclear powers.

President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are scheduled to sit down on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese technology hub hosting this year's gathering. The meeting will close Trump's visit to China.

The White House said Trump wants to use the session to discuss reducing nuclear weapons stockpiles and to raise the war in Iran. A senior U.S. official, briefing reporters on condition of anonymity, said Trump does not plan to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine at the three-way meeting, and that those negotiations are on a separate track.

Low expectations, high symbolism

Officials on all sides have been careful to play down what the meeting might produce. The senior U.S. official described it as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" on nuclear disarmament, and said no agreements are expected to be announced. Analysts quoted by the Associated Press said the talks are likely to be heavier on symbolism than substance.

The backdrop gives the symbolism weight. The last nuclear arms pact between the United States and Russia expired in February, removing caps on the world's two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than half a century. China, which holds more than 600 nuclear warheads according to Pentagon estimates — far fewer than the estimated 5,000-plus held by each of the United States and Russia — has long resisted joining formal arms-control talks, and U.S. officials acknowledged that persuading Beijing to engage will be difficult.

For the Kremlin, the meeting is a coveted chance to present Russia as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing. For China, it carries a complication: the trilateral could undercut Beijing's effort to portray itself at APEC as a defender of free trade and multilateralism.

The Ukraine question

The decision to keep Ukraine off the agenda has already drawn a reaction in Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the meeting could become a venue for discussing a possible Ukraine settlement behind his country's back, and Ukrainian officials have objected to any suggestion that the three leaders might decide the war's outcome between themselves.

The Kremlin has pushed back on comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference, where the Allied leaders redrew Europe. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said any understandings reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries.

The APEC summit itself runs on November 18 and 19, and the trilateral meeting is expected to overshadow much of the gathering's trade agenda.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press

link.title: Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first-ever three-way meeting at APEC in Shenzhen

entry.title: Rubio says economic pressure on Iran makes new strikes unnecessary — for now
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United States sees no need to resume major military operations against Iran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday, arguing that sanctions and a naval blockade are doing the work that airstrikes would otherwise do.

"The economic campaign against Iran is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations," Rubio told reporters in Paris after two days of meetings with foreign ministers from the Group of Seven. "That's what I told our allies here today."

Rubio said President Donald Trump had reached the same conclusion: the United States can achieve its objectives "by economic means" for the time being, and choosing not to strike is not the same as accepting a stalemate. "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure. That's not stalemate," he said.

A pause, not a settlement

The remarks mark a shift in tone after eight months of war between the United States and Iran. Hours earlier, Trump had spoken of "positive momentum" toward resolving the conflict, and on Monday he said he would hold off on new strikes for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including Qatar's prime minister during talks at the White House.

But the restraint comes with a warning. Rubio said that if Iran crossed the "red lines" set by Washington, the U.S. military "stands ready" and Tehran would pay a "terrible price." The pressure campaign itself has escalated beyond sanctions: Washington has imposed a counter-blockade on Iranian ports and in August announced what it called an "economic asphyxiation" campaign aimed at financially strangling Iran, already battered by years of sanctions.

The war has also carried a political cost at home. Trump has acknowledged that the Iran conflict was part of the reason Republicans were humbled in last week's midterm elections, with the economic fallout from the fighting weighing on voters.

The Hormuz question

At the centre of the standoff is the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow exit route for Gulf energy exports. Iran has been blockading the strait, sending oil prices soaring, and Tehran says its offer to reopen the waterway within two days — if Washington agrees to a raft of conditions — remains on the table.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, has said the conflict "will not be resolved through military means, nor by intensifying sanctions," and has pressed Washington to address Tehran's demands. Iran also maintains that no direct negotiations are under way, only contacts through intermediaries such as Qatar and Pakistan.

For now, Washington's message is that economic pressure is compounding daily and the clock is on its side. Whether that patience holds will depend on what happens at Hormuz — and on whether either side's red lines are tested.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Hindu
  • The Korea Times (AFP)

link.title: Rubio says economic pressure on Iran makes new strikes unnecessary — for now

entry.title: Lauren Boebert loses Colorado seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's 4th Congressional District on Friday, the Associated Press projected, unseating a three-term Republican and one of Congress's most prominent MAGA voices in a seat Donald Trump carried by 18 points in 2024.

With nearly all votes counted, Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, led Boebert 48.8% to 47.9% — a margin of roughly 3,400 votes out of more than 384,000 cast. She becomes the first Democrat to win the eastern Colorado seat since 2008.

Laubacher declared victory on Monday, days before the race was called, and was so confident of the outcome that she travelled to Washington to attend orientation for incoming members of Congress. Boebert, by contrast, has not conceded. She has said ballots remained uncounted, including military and overseas votes, and her campaign attorney, former Colorado Secretary of State Scott Gessler, said he expects the race to head to a recount "one way or another," citing what he called unusual voting patterns.

The margin is outside Colorado's threshold for an automatic recount, but state law allows Boebert to request one at her own expense. She has until November 25 to do so.

A stunning upset in a deep-red seat

Boebert was first elected to Congress in 2020, representing western Colorado's 3rd District, and survived re-election in 2022 by just 546 votes. In late 2023 she switched to the more conservative 4th District, which had been in Republican hands since 2011, and won it in 2024. Trump endorsed her 2026 run, calling her "a MAGA Warrior" days before the election.

Her defeat is one of the most striking results of a midterm cycle shaping up as a sweeping Democratic wave — the Associated Press described it as one of the most lopsided elections in half a century. Colorado's House delegation will now favour Democrats 7–1, and Boebert is the third Colorado Republican to lose a re-election bid this cycle.

Boebert has said she would not run for the seat again in 2028 if she lost, and attributed her defeat to the financial backing Laubacher received. Laubacher, who served on President Joe Biden's National Security Council, is expected to join the new Congress when it convenes in January 2027.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Colorado Public Radio

link.title: Lauren Boebert loses Colorado seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher

entry.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska governor's race, first since 1998
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Alaska voters have elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, the Associated Press projected on Friday, handing former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins a win in one of the most Republican-leaning states in the country.

Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, defeated three Republicans — Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — and will become the youngest governor in Alaska's history. He will also be the youngest sitting governor in the United States when he takes office. His running mate, independent Zac Johnson, will serve as lieutenant governor.

The result was decided on first-choice votes. Kreiss-Tomkins cleared just over 50 percent, enough to avoid a ranked-choice runoff under Alaska's voting system. Final ballot counting is scheduled for November 18, with certification expected by November 25, and he is due to be sworn in on December 7.

A win built on crossover appeal

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, won in a state where Democrats make up only about 11 percent of registered voters. He campaigned as a pragmatic coalition-builder, pledging to work across party lines and to appoint a cabinet drawn from Republicans, Democrats and independents.

It is a political comeback three years after he left the state House, where he served for a decade after first winning a seat at age 23. He finished first in August's open primary; the second Democrat in the race, Tom Begich, later withdrew.

He succeeds Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy, who was barred by term limits from seeking another four years. Wilson, a former talk-show host who owns a garbage-collection company, was the Republican backed by President Donald Trump.

Part of a wider midterm wave

The Associated Press described the Alaska result as part of a national midterm wave that delivered sweeping wins for Democrats in state governments. With Alaska, Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control, among them Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

The state's last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving two terms. Kreiss-Tomkins told supporters that Alaskans had "voted for change," and said he would take office facing a short-term budget surplus driven by higher oil prices.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • NBC News

link.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins Alaska governor's race, first since 1998

entry.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop as U.S. flights resume after hours-long halt
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Federal Aviation Administration lifted its nationwide ground stop on Friday evening, allowing departing flights to resume after a communications failure kept planes on the ground across the United States for about five hours.

The agency announced at 8:15 p.m. Eastern time that the order had been lifted, after issuing it at 3:54 p.m. The stop was the first nationwide grounding since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system failed, and officials described it as the longest such halt in 25 years.

The disruption began when communications problems hit all 22 of the FAA's air route traffic control centers, which guide aircraft traveling between airports. The agency said there had been a temporary telecommunications outage and halted all departures out of an abundance of caution. Flights already in the air were allowed to continue to their destinations and land, and officials said every flight had been accounted for. Flights within Alaska and Hawaii were not affected.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA had restored full functionality at its air traffic control centers and reopened the airspace, but warned that it would take time to resume normal operations. Administration officials said new equipment being added to the air traffic control system had overwhelmed older hardware, causing intermittent communications and radar gaps. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication the failure was triggered by a threat to the country, and the FBI does not believe a cyberattack or criminal activity caused it.

A system out of position

Even with departures resuming, airlines could not return to normal schedules immediately. Thousands of aircraft and crews were left out of position by the halt, and officials said the backlog could take days to clear. They said they expected the system to be back to normal in time for the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The scale of the disruption was large. FlightAware data cited by CBS News showed more than 10,000 flights delayed and over 4,000 canceled. About 4,042 aircraft were in the air and heading toward U.S. airports when the ground stop was ordered, according to Flightradar24. Aviation analytics firm Cirium reported that at least 827 flights had been diverted by early evening, with most sent back to the airport they departed from.

Airports moved quickly to restart operations once the order was lifted. Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the world's busiest, said on Friday night that its flight operations were resuming. Delta Air Lines issued a travel waiver for its passengers, and airlines urged travelers to keep checking with their carrier for the latest information.

What is still unknown

Officials have not given a detailed account of exactly which piece of equipment failed, or why the new technology overloaded the older systems. Duffy said he could not guarantee the problem would not happen again. The FAA said its technicians were investigating.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Indian Express

link.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop as U.S. flights resume after hours-long halt

entry.title: EU leaders insist on a seat at Ukraine peace talks, but leave open who will speak for Europe
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

European Union leaders meeting in Dublin on Friday agreed that Europe must speak with one voice in any future Ukraine peace talks, but they left open the question of who would do the speaking.

The leaders said the structure of European security should not itself be a subject for negotiation between Ukraine and Russia. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz put the position plainly to reporters: "There will be no discussions about Ukraine without Ukraine, and no discussions about Europe without Europe. Furthermore, there is no need to talk about European security architecture. We have that already."

Russia has pressed for a broad agreement on Europe's security framework before tackling the specifics of the war, and U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner said on Thursday that he had begun discussions with European partners on the subject. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the Russian calls risked diverting attention from the need for a ceasefire, and Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs called such discussions "a trap."

A seat at the table, still undefined

The question of representation remains unresolved. EU leaders broadly agreed that Europe needed a single voice, but they did not settle on one person to provide it, and Merz said discussions would continue.

Merz pointed to the options already in use. "There are established institutional forms of (EU) representation — Kaja Kallas, for instance, is part of this — but the E3 format has also proven very effective," he said, referring to the informal grouping of France, Germany and Britain. "Moreover, we always include Italy and Poland," he added.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Britain, one of Europe's top three military powers, certainly had to be included, and that five countries plus EU institutions would make sense. "I'm quite flexible on that, so I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room," he said.

A day earlier, forty European countries meeting as a broader group in Dublin signed a declaration saying that any matter affecting European security should be decided with Europeans involved.

Moscow's conditions

The Kremlin said on Friday that it would be open to European countries taking part in the talks if it saw they were ready to contribute to the peace process. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said a decision on an expanded format would come once Moscow understood their "genuine intention and readiness to contribute."

That position stops short of a commitment. U.S. negotiators had said on Thursday that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to European participation, but Peskov said no concrete discussions about European involvement had yet taken place. Putin said on Thursday that the United States must work with its European allies to understand whether they wanted peace or war in Ukraine.

Representatives from Britain, France, Germany and Italy, along with the EU, attended Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week — the first such meeting in nine months. Both Moscow and Kyiv cited some progress, though there was no sign of a breakthrough on key issues such as territory.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Reuters

link.title: EU leaders insist on a seat at Ukraine peace talks, but leave open who will speak for Europe

entry.title: Europe names five-nation team to speak for it at Ukraine peace talks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

European leaders have settled the question that hung over their Dublin summit: who speaks for Europe at the next round of Ukraine peace talks. The answer is a team, not a single envoy — the European Union's institutions together with five countries: Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.

European Council President António Costa announced the arrangement on Friday, at the end of an informal summit of EU leaders in Dublin. The five are the largest military powers in the loose "coalition of the willing" backing Ukraine.

The decision came a day after the same leaders had agreed that Europe must speak with one voice in any talks, but left the question of who would do the speaking unresolved. Costa said the team would work with all 27 EU member states.

Who exactly sits in the chairs is still to be decided. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas laid claim to the envoy role on Friday, saying she is the one who represents Europe on foreign and security policy, and that it is not up to Russia to decide who speaks for the EU. No individual names have been confirmed for the national seats.

Moscow has not yet said yes

The bigger unknown is whether the Europeans will be admitted to the room at all. The Kremlin said on Friday that it would be open to European participation if it saw the Europeans were genuinely ready to contribute to the peace process — but it has not confirmed that they will join the next round.

U.S. negotiators had said on Thursday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to European involvement, but Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no concrete discussions had taken place. Moscow continues to press for a broad agreement on Europe's security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

European leaders pushed back. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called the Kremlin's comments "the same old game" and said there would be no discussions about Ukraine without Ukraine, and none about Europe without Europe. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there could be no revision of Europe's security architecture — which, he said, was what Putin was demanding.

A week of shuttle diplomacy

The decision caps a week of shuttle diplomacy. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, then flew to Dublin to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Representatives from Britain, France, Germany and Italy, along with the EU, attended Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi earlier in the week — the first direct meeting between the two sides in nine months. Both sides cited some progress, but no breakthrough on territory or a ceasefire.

A day earlier, 40 European countries meeting in Dublin signed a declaration saying any matter affecting European security should be decided with Europeans involved. EU leaders next meet on November 26–27 to discuss Ukraine's financing needs for 2027 and beyond. No date has been set for the next round of peace talks.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Reuters

link.title: Europe names five-nation team to speak for it at Ukraine peace talks

entry.title: Blood test offers first glimpse of CTE in living patients — but it is only a first step
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

For the first time, scientists have found a signal in the blood that points to advanced chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, in living people. The disease, linked to repeated blows to the head, can today only be confirmed by examining the brain after death, leaving former athletes, soldiers and their families without a diagnosis while alive.

The clue is a protein fragment called eMTBR-tau243. Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis were studying it as a marker of Alzheimer's disease, where a protein called tau builds into toxic tangles inside brain cells; the fragment's levels in blood had already been shown to track those tangles. Testing autopsy-confirmed samples, the team found one patient with unexpectedly high levels — but no Alzheimer's. That person's records showed the brain had advanced CTE instead.

The team then tested stored blood from 11 people whose CTE had been confirmed after death. Levels were higher than in healthy people, rose with disease severity, and distinguished advanced CTE from healthy participants with high accuracy. The study, published Friday in the journal JAMA, drew on 229 participants, with collaborators at the University of California, San Francisco.

Why it matters

If larger studies confirm the finding, clinicians could one day use a blood test to monitor people at risk — former football players, boxers and combat veterans — and drug developers would finally have a way to tell whether a treatment is working. Co-senior author Kanta Horie said the work could "potentially open a new door for diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients."

The limits are large

The result is very preliminary. The CTE finding rests on just 11 autopsy-confirmed cases, and the test could not reliably identify early-stage disease. Levels in CTE were also much lower than in Alzheimer's, which makes the measurement harder, and the fragment rises in Alzheimer's and other diseases involving the same toxic protein — so on its own it cannot tell CTE apart from them, a real problem since the two often occur together.

Outside experts urged caution. Dr. Rudolph Castellani, a neuropathologist at Northwestern University who was not involved in the research, called it an interesting but very preliminary finding that needs far larger studies. The university has licensed the measurement technology to C2N Diagnostics, a university startup, but the test has not been validated for diagnosing CTE and is not available to patients.

For now, nothing changes for people worried about CTE: no clinic can test for it until large validation studies are done. What the study offers is a direction — a measurable clue, found almost by accident, that a disease long visible only after death may one day be seen in life.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Washington University School of Medicine

link.title: Blood test offers first glimpse of CTE in living patients — but it is only a first step

entry.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage that hit millions
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Microsoft said on Saturday that its services had fully recovered, bringing to an end a global outage that cut millions of people off from their email and workplace tools for more than 24 hours.

"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X. The message covered Teams, Outlook, Copilot and its other products, and Microsoft's service-health page showed all products operational on Saturday morning.

The outage was one of the longest in the company's history. Reports began climbing at about 5:25 p.m. GMT on Thursday, according to Ookla, the parent company of outage tracker Downdetector. By the end of the incident, Downdetector had logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute — more than 1,500 times normal levels. The disruption reached users in 74 countries, hitting businesses, government offices, hospitals and courts.

Servers "unexpectedly unavailable"

Microsoft said the failure was tied to Exchange Online, its cloud-based email and scheduling hub, which left Outlook, Teams and Copilot struggling while unconnected applications kept working. The company said a large number of servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable" after an earlier network-capacity upgrade, and a further change to its systems then left the remaining servers unable to cope with the load.

On Friday, Microsoft said an earlier round of fixes had not worked as expected, and it was rolling out broader software fixes to stabilise the system. Consumer services were reported fully recovered at 4:10 p.m. UTC on Friday, while enterprise services continued to come back through the night before the company confirmed full restoration on Saturday.

Microsoft has said there was no indication of a cyberattack or malicious activity, and it ruled out artificial intelligence as a cause of the incident. That distinction mattered to customers: the outage was a failure of capacity and configuration, not of security.

A second disruption this year

The incident is the second disruption to Microsoft's services in 2026, and its scale underlined how much of daily work now runs through a handful of cloud platforms. Outlook and Teams are among the most widely used workplace applications in the world, with hundreds of millions of users, and the outage blocked basic tasks such as sending email, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday, a muted market reaction to a disruption that, for a day, left much of the working world waiting on its inbox.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Straits Times
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Microsoft says services fully restored after global outage that hit millions

entry.title: Cash buried in forests: Hungary recovers nearly $20m in graft probe of ex-minister
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Hungarian investigators have recovered nearly $20 million in cash — some of it buried in forests — during a bribery investigation into a former minister who served under Viktor Orbán.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said late on Friday that searches over two days, on November 12 and 13, turned up about $19.5 million hidden in Budapest and three other parts of the country. The agency, known by its Hungarian initials as the NVVH, was set up by the new government to pursue suspected misuse of public money during Orbán's years in power.

The haul was spread across an unlikely set of hiding places: bundles of banknotes dug out of woodland, stashed in farm buildings and warehouses, kept in a home, and locked inside a high-value safe in a secluded location. Finance Minister András Kármán said 12 treasury workers spent eight hours counting the money with five banknote counters.

Cash in three currencies

The total came to 5.07 billion forints — about $15.33 million — plus €2.66 million and $1.26 million. The mix of currencies, and the spread of locations, suggests the cash was deliberately scattered rather than kept in one place.

The discovery is part of criminal proceedings against Miklós Seszták, who was Orbán's development minister from 2014 to 2018. He is suspected of receiving more than $37.2 million in bribes and kickbacks linked to overpriced secondhand bus purchases by a state transport company and to government construction projects. Seszták has denied wrongdoing.

A new government's anti-graft drive

The case is the most visible result so far of the anti-corruption drive promised by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, whose centre-right Tisza party ended Orbán's 16 years in power in an April election. Magyar has called the clampdown "Operation Purgatory", and a poll by the Median agency published this month found 70% of respondents considered the drive "very important".

Two other former ministers from Orbán's government and former central bank chief György Matolcsy are under arrest over graft accusations in separate investigations.

For Magyar, who pledged to mend ties with the European Union after years of conflict under Orbán, the recovery is also a political statement: his government argues that corruption was rampant during the previous administration, and that recovering the money proves the new institutions work.

What is not yet known

The authorities have not said whether Seszták will face formal charges, or how much of the recovered cash prosecutors will be able to link to the alleged bribes. The investigation is continuing, and the money — now in state hands — is evidence in a case that is still being built.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Cash buried in forests: Hungary recovers nearly $20m in graft probe of ex-minister

entry.title: Zelenskyy says U.S. raised NATO membership tied to a Donbas withdrawal
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. negotiators raised the idea of Ukraine withdrawing from its eastern Donbas region in exchange for joining NATO, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday — the first time Washington had put the question to Kyiv in talks aimed at ending the war with Russia.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks released by his office. "This was the first time this had been raised."

The question came after two days of U.S.-brokered talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi, which ended on Wednesday without a major breakthrough. Zelenskyy said the idea put NATO membership back on the negotiating agenda — while warning the conversation would be extremely difficult, given President Vladimir Putin's longstanding position that Ukrainian membership of the alliance is a red line for Moscow.

Kyiv's conditions

Zelenskyy repeated that Kyiv is not prepared to give up territory. But he said that if Western countries confirmed a comprehensive package — security guarantees, a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and money to rebuild — he would put the question to the Ukrainian people.

"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?" he said. "I have no right to make that decision on my own."

The account rests on Zelenskyy's description of the exchange. The United States has not publicly confirmed it, and the remarks were given to reporters on Friday under embargo until Saturday, after Zelenskyy met European leaders in Dublin following the Abu Dhabi round.

A week of shuttle diplomacy

The Abu Dhabi talks did produce one concrete result: the two sides agreed to a prisoner exchange involving more than 1,000 people, though final numbers were still under discussion. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner then met Putin in Moscow on Thursday, and Zelenskyy in Ireland later the same day, having pledged to raise an energy ceasefire with Putin — but there was no news of progress. Zelenskyy said Putin "personally does not support a ceasefire" and that Russia had rejected a halt to strikes on energy targets.

Zelenskyy also pushed back against Moscow's call for a broad agreement on European security to come before the specifics of ending the war, echoing European leaders who met in Dublin on Friday. "We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first," he said.

What is still unknown

Whether Washington will confirm the security package Zelenskyy described, whether any referendum would ever be held, and whether Moscow would accept any arrangement involving NATO membership are all unresolved. The U.S. envoys told Zelenskyy that all sides had agreed Europe would have a seat at the table in forthcoming talks, and EU leaders in Dublin agreed a team of five major military powers — Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland — would speak for Europe. No date or format for the next round has been announced.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Hindu

link.title: Zelenskyy says U.S. raised NATO membership tied to a Donbas withdrawal

entry.title: 98-million-year-old mantis found in amber wore leaves on its abdomen
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

In the mid-Cretaceous, a tropical rainforest in what is now Myanmar was dripping with sticky tree resin. One drop caught a very peculiar praying mantis — and held it for 98 million years. Scientists say the insect is the earliest clear evidence in the fossil record of a mantis mimicking plant leaves.

The fossil's abdomen carries leaf-like extensions that closely resemble the fronds of an extinct clubmoss, Selaginella grimaldii, which is itself known from amber found in the same region. Researchers have named the insect Folimantis hyalinala in a paper published in the journal New Phytologist.

The name is descriptive: the genus Folimantis translates literally as "leaf mantis", while hyalinala refers to the glass-like transparency of the creature's wings. Lead author Hongru Yang and colleagues note that this style of mimicry has never been reported before, and no living mantis is known to copy Selaginella.

A disguise that started at the back

Modern mantises are famous for their camouflage. The orchid mantis of Southeast Asia looks and even sways like a flower. But when F. hyalinala lived, flowering plants had not yet taken over the landscape, so the insect evolved to look like leaves instead.

There is something odd about this fossil, though. Modern plant-mimicking mantises wear leaf-like features across different parts of their bodies. F. hyalinala carries them on its abdomen only. The researchers suggest this could be a hint that plant mimicry began at the rear, with changes to the wings and thorax emerging later in mantis evolution.

The likeliest explanation is the usual one: a mantis that looked more like its host plant had a better chance of sneaking up on prey while staying hidden from its own predators. That is an evolutionary interpretation of the anatomy, not behaviour observed in the fossil.

The discovery also pushes the known history of this trick back a long way. Mantises share an ancestor with cockroaches that lived around 274 million years ago, and the first distinct mantises are thought to have emerged about 185 million years ago, during the Jurassic. This specimen shows leaf mimicry was already part of their toolkit at least 98 million years ago — and other insect groups, including cockroaches, grasshoppers and stick insects, were evolving plant-like features around the same time.

The amber question

The find comes with an ethical footnote. Amber mining in Myanmar's Kachin region is linked to ongoing conflict, and there are concerns the trade helps fund abuses the United Nations has condemned. Myanmar banned fossil exports in 2015, though specimens embedded in amber have fallen into a legal grey area, and in 2021 the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology called for a moratorium on publishing research on amber fossils obtained from Myanmar sources after January that year.

This specimen predates those lines. It was acquired in 2015 by collector Fangyuan Xia, who donated it later that year to the insect evolution laboratory at Capital Normal University in Beijing, where the research was carried out.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceAlert
  • Eastern Herald

link.title: 98-million-year-old mantis found in amber wore leaves on its abdomen

entry.title: Voyager 1 is about to become the first human-made object one light-day from Earth
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

NASA's Voyager 1 is about to set a distance record no human-made object has ever reached. On Wednesday, November 18, the spacecraft will sit one light-day from Earth — 16.09 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometres) away, the exact distance light travels in 24 hours.

The crossing is expected at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern time. From that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth will take precisely a full day to reach the probe, and its reply will take another day to come back. Every exchange with the spacecraft will now take about 48 hours.

Voyager 1 launched from Cape Canaveral on September 5, 1977, on what was planned as a five-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn. It flew past both planets in 1979 and 1980, then kept going. In August 2012 it crossed the heliopause — the boundary where the Sun's wind gives way to the space between stars — becoming the first human-made object to enter interstellar space.

It is still travelling at roughly 38,000 miles per hour (61,000 km/h), and it has held the title of most distant human-made object since 1998, when it overtook Pioneer 10. Its twin, Voyager 2, launched two weeks earlier but on a slower trajectory, will not reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

A yardstick, not a border

Nothing on the spacecraft will change when it crosses the line. The milestone is symbolic — a way of picturing a distance that is otherwise hard to grasp. A light-day is about 173 times the distance between Earth and the Sun. At its current speed, Voyager 1 would need around 18,000 years to cover a full light-year, and more than twice that before it comes near another star.

The probe's longevity is itself the story. Its computers hold about 69 kilobytes of memory, its transmitter puts out roughly 23 watts, and it still sends science data home from beyond the solar system. To keep it alive, NASA has switched off instruments over the years, most recently the low-energy charged particle instrument in April 2026, leaving the magnetometer and the plasma wave instrument still operating.

Project manager Suzanne Dodd, who leads the mission at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, called the spacecraft "a national treasure" and "really extraordinary" — a machine launched 49 years ago that is still working, still talking, and still setting records.

How NASA is marking the day

NASA is inviting the public to take part. After sunset on Tuesday, November 17, people around the world are asked to shine a light toward the sky, flashing "VGR" — the mission's call sign — in Morse code as part of an event called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day." On Thursday, November 19, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory will host a moderated discussion with mission members about the twin probes and the challenge of keeping them operating.

Voyager 1's most famous moment came in 1990, when it turned its camera back toward home and took the "Pale Blue Dot" photograph — Earth as a speck of light seen from beyond Neptune, the most distant picture of our planet ever taken. Thirty-six years later, the same spacecraft is still moving away, one light-day at a time.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • NASA

link.title: Voyager 1 is about to become the first human-made object one light-day from Earth

entry.title: Webb finds ice around a young star that may be older than the star itself
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The James Webb Space Telescope has found water and carbon dioxide ice swirling around a young star — and the ice appears to be older than the star itself.

The discovery comes from Beta Pictoris, a star about 64 light-years from Earth that is only around 20 million years old, a newborn by cosmic standards. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming; astronomers have already found three worlds there. A team led by Sarah Betti of the Space Telescope Science Institute pointed Webb's Near Infrared Spectrograph at the disk on December 7, 2023, and recorded the light from two spots roughly 100 astronomical units from the star, on opposite sides.

In both places, the spectra showed the unmistakable fingerprints of frozen water and frozen carbon dioxide. Water ice absorbs light strongly near a wavelength of 3 micrometres; carbon dioxide leaves its mark at 4.27 micrometres, with a second signal at 4.39 micrometres from the heavier carbon-13 form. Earlier searches had come up empty, finding neither water vapour nor the 3-micrometre ice signature. Webb's sensitivity made the difference.

What makes the find striking is the ice's condition. The water ice is almost entirely glassy — amorphous, like frozen glass, rather than arranged in an orderly crystal lattice. Less than 7 percent of it is estimated to be crystalline. Glassy ice can only survive if it stays colder than about 100 Kelvin (minus 173°C), which means this material has spent its life in deep cold, undisturbed by the heat of a forming star.

The carbon dioxide is also telling. Rather than sitting in separate grains, it is trapped inside the water ice, and it makes up about 11 percent of the mixture — slightly more than one carbon dioxide molecule for every ten water molecules. That proportion falls squarely within the range measured in comets in our own Solar System, which carry between 2.5 and 30 percent carbon dioxide.

A leftover from before the star

Taken together, the clues point to an origin that predates Beta Pictoris itself. The researchers concluded the ice most likely formed in the interstellar medium, building up on dust grains in cold, dense, water-rich clouds during the earliest stages of star formation — before the star and its planets began to take shape. The disk we see today is, in effect, still carrying the frozen raw material of its birth cloud.

That matters because Beta Pictoris is one of the best-studied young systems in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for watching planetary systems grow. If its building blocks arrived pre-frozen from interstellar space, the same may be true for other young stars — including, long ago, our own Sun.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Ars Technica
  • Science

link.title: Webb finds ice around a young star that may be older than the star itself

entry.title: U.S. air travel should be back to normal by Sunday after historic ground stop, FAA says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. air travel should be back to normal by the end of Sunday, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration said on Saturday, as airlines worked through the backlog from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said carriers would "still have delays and cancellations" on Saturday, but promised that the "worst is behind us."

The ground stop lasted more than four hours on Friday, halting every departing flight in the country after air traffic control centres lost reliable radar and communications. It was the first nationwide stop since January 2023, when a computer system that sends notices to pilots failed, and only the second since the attacks of September 11, 2001. FlightAware counted nearly 25,000 delayed flights and more than 9,000 cancellations on Friday; by Saturday morning, more than 4,000 further cancellations had been recorded — about 14 percent of flights departing the United States, according to aviation data firm Cirium.

Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, causing intermittent gaps in communications and radar. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor had been replacing a section of the system's old copper wiring with new fibre, and that the work somehow triggered the overload. The contractor is L3Harris, a long-time FAA supplier, which was carrying out routine maintenance at a remote FAA location. Duffy said some of the routers involved were manufactured in 2001, and officials were investigating whether the fault came down to contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment. "Our contractor didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.

Bedford said there was no evidence of anything nefarious or of any AI-related problem, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence the failure was an attack. The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as SMART, but its maker, Air Space Intelligence, said the ground stop was not based on or a result of its product.

The disruption rippled far beyond Friday. Aviation consultant Andrew Charlton said the stoppage affected about a quarter of the roughly 45,000 flights that operate in the United States each day, and the knock-on effects — aircraft and crews out of position, passengers stranded — were expected to linger for days. Duffy said on Friday night that he expected the system to be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving." In a detail that underlined the department's struggling systems, his Saturday news conference began with audio troubles that forced last-minute microphone swaps.

Bedford said airlines told officials they expected "full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday." The FAA is still investigating the exact error that set off the cascade. L3Harris did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • NPR

entry.title: Pope Leo XIV draws 1.5 million to Mass in the Peruvian city where he was bishop
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

About 1.5 million people gathered in and around Chiclayo, in northern Peru, on Friday as Pope Leo XIV celebrated an outdoor Mass in the city where he once served as bishop. The Vatican estimated that roughly one million people lined the streets along his route, while about 500,000 more attended the Mass itself at the Pampas de Pimentel, a wide open space outside the city.

It was the central event of the pope's 12-day tour of South America, and by several accounts its most emotional stop. Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, spent about 20 years as a missionary in Peru and was bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. Earlier in the week he described the country as his homeland, and crowds in Chiclayo still call him by his old name, Father Robert.

In his sermon, Leo said it was a blessing to be back in his adopted home exactly one month after undergoing surgery for lung cancer. He had an operation for lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, on October 13. Addressing the crowd, he thanked God that he was alive to see them, and told them that all Christians are called to be missionaries.

People arrived on foot and in lines of vehicles at the arid field outside Chiclayo, enduring heat of about 31 degrees Celsius (87 Fahrenheit) to attend. Leo arrived from Lima on Friday morning aboard a plane decorated with "#LeoXIVFliesHome" stickers. The stop in Peru is the final leg of a three-nation tour that also took him to Uruguay and Argentina; the Vatican estimates that about 12 million people have turned out for public events across the trip so far.

Leo is due to remain in Chiclayo until Sunday before the tour moves on. For the city, the visit was a homecoming as much as a papal event: the diocese he led has about 1.5 million inhabitants, nearly all of them Catholic, and his return had been anticipated for days.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • EWTN Vatican

entry.title: Italy fines Meta €805 million over Facebook's access to Android photo galleries
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Italy's data protection authority has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) after finding that the Facebook app on Android phones accessed users' photographs and videos without their specific consent.

The regulator, known as the Garante, said on Saturday that the app had reached into the photo galleries of Italian Android users, taking in pictures, videos and the information attached to them, without properly informing them or obtaining the consent the law requires. About 20 million people in Italy may have been affected.

At the centre of the case is a Facebook feature called "Get suggestions from gallery when browsing Facebook", which offers pictures and videos from a phone's gallery as ideas for posts while the user is browsing. The authority said the feature breached the Italian law that implements Europe's ePrivacy rules, which protect information held on a person's own device. Consent had been collected through a single, generic app-wide authorisation, and the feature was switched on by default.

The fine is the largest the Italian regulator has ever imposed, and amounts to roughly 0.47 percent of Meta's global revenue. The authority said Meta's lack of cooperation during the proceedings and an earlier violation, which drew a fine in 2019, were among the factors behind the size of the penalty.

Meta now has 60 days to switch the feature off by default and to ask users for separate, specific consent before reading their galleries. The company had not publicly commented by Saturday afternoon and has the right to appeal.

The investigation began in July 2025, after a complaint from a consumer protection centre in Bolzano, and included a technical analysis of the Facebook app. The Garante also rejected Meta's argument that the case should have been handled by another European regulator, saying the ePrivacy rules do not provide for the European Union's usual "one-stop-shop" mechanism, under which a company answers mainly to the authority in the country where it is based.

The proceedings did not examine whether any of the material was used to train artificial intelligence models — a practice Meta denies. The authority said it reserved the right to look separately at a newer feature, launched in 2026, that allows content from users' galleries to be processed in the cloud.

The ruling lands as regulators across Europe continue to test the limits of how much access apps can take to the most personal material on a phone, and what clear consent has to look like before they take it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Italy fines Meta €805 million over Facebook's access to Android photo galleries

entry.title: Brain implants give people with ALS a voice that can speak — and sing
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Brain implants are giving people who have lost the ability to speak a voice again — one that can carry pitch, emphasis and even a tune. New results presented at Neuroscience 2026, the Society for Neuroscience's annual meeting, show brain-computer interfaces moving closer to everyday use for people with paralysis.

The most striking finding came from the University of California, Davis. Researcher Maitreyee Wairagkar presented a brain-computer interface that turns brain activity into a synthetic voice capable of capturing pitch variations — the rises and falls that make speech expressive, letting a listener hear a question, an emphasis or a mood. The system improved how well listeners understood the patient, and it allowed the patient to sing.

The work builds on a voice-synthesis neuroprosthesis the UC Davis team described in the journal Nature in 2025. Four microelectrode arrays implanted in the brain's speech area decode a person's attempted speech in real time and turn it into audible words. The participant in that study has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, a progressive condition that gradually takes away voluntary muscle control, including speech.

Two other results presented at the meeting point in the same direction. At Massachusetts General Hospital, Daniel Rubin reported that a person in a completely locked-in state — unable to move or speak — has been communicating independently for more than a year using an interface that decodes intended movement from brain activity. And at Georgia Tech and Emory University, Chethan Pandarinath presented a portable brain-to-text interface that decodes brain activity into written words accurately and reliably, even running on an iPhone.

Cynthia Chestek, a biomedical engineer at the University of Michigan who moderated the session, said the ability to turn brain activity into spoken or written words could be life-changing for people with paralysis, and that the new work moves the technology closer to reaching people outside clinical trials.

The technology is still largely experimental. The UC Davis voice work involved a single participant, and the systems are investigational devices, not treatments available to patients generally. They do not cure or slow ALS; they offer a new route to communication. Even so, interest is growing fast: the global brain-computer interface market is projected to rise from $1.7 billion in 2022 to $6.2 billion by 2030.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Medical Xpress
  • Nature

entry.title: Bomb found at Peoria ethanol plant forces evacuation of thousands; FBI joins the search
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A bomb found at an ethanol plant in central Illinois forced more than 5,000 people to evacuate part of a city for about a day, as police and federal agents searched a sprawling industrial site for further threats. The evacuation order was lifted on Saturday afternoon, roughly 24 hours after the device was discovered, and no injuries were reported.

The device was found on Friday at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria, a city of about 110,000 people roughly 130 miles southwest of Chicago. The plant sits in an industrial area along the Illinois River, just southwest of downtown, and makes ethanol — a highly flammable liquid used in fuel, beverages and hand sanitiser.

The incident began shortly after 1 p.m. local time on Friday, when the plant told police it had received a bomb threat by email. Officers found a suspicious package at about 2 p.m. and, at about 6:45 p.m., determined it posed a credible threat. Bomb technicians rendered the device safe at about 9:12 p.m.

Because of the materials stored at the plant, officials set a one-mile blast radius around the site. An evacuation order took effect at 7:02 p.m. on Friday, covering parts of downtown Peoria and the Warehouse District and crossing the Illinois River into neighbouring East Peoria. Shelters were opened at Manual Academy High School in Peoria and the EastSide Centre sports complex in East Peoria.

The order stayed in place through Saturday morning while investigators searched the facility, which Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon said is the size of about 44 and a half football fields. By Saturday afternoon the search was complete, nothing further had been found, and the evacuation order and blast radius were cancelled.

The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives assisted in the investigation, including with bomb technicians and explosives specialists. Officials said they were still searching for whoever was responsible. No arrests have been made, and no motive or suspect has been identified.

Dixon said he would not call the device a bomb while the process of determining its composition was still under way, a caution that reflects how much of the investigation remains open. BioUrja, based in Houston, Texas, bought the plant from Archer Daniels Midland in late 2021. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Reuters

entry.title: Peltola widens her lead in Alaska's Senate race as the count nears its end
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Democrat Mary Peltola widened her lead over Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska's Senate race on Friday, as the latest release of ballots moved her closer to a majority — but the contest, the last uncalled Senate race in the country, is still not decided.

With about 96 percent of expected ballots counted, according to the Associated Press, Peltola held 138,240 votes, or 49.8 percent, against 127,828 votes, or 46.1 percent, for Sullivan — a lead of 10,412 votes. Friday's update added roughly 22,500 ballots to the count, and Peltola's margin has grown with each release since election night, when she led by just a few hundred votes.

The race remains uncalled. Under Alaska's ranked-choice system, if neither candidate finishes with more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, the lowest-placed candidates are eliminated and their supporters' next preferences are counted. That official tabulation is scheduled for November 18, after the deadline for ballots mailed from overseas to arrive, and the state aims to certify the result by November 25. A New York Times analysis found Peltola on track to eventually prevail, and her campaign has said victory is near. Sullivan's campaign is waiting for every ballot to be counted. "We're still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we'll see what happens from there," a Sullivan spokesman, Nate Adams, said on Friday night.

Two other candidates were on the ballot alongside Peltola and Sullivan: Gerald L. Heikes, a Republican, and Dan J. Sullivan, an unaffiliated candidate whose name closely resembles the senator's. Together they have taken about 4 percent of the vote so far.

What a Peltola win would mean

Peltola, a former congresswoman who campaigned as a centrist under the slogan "fish, family and freedom," would be the first Alaska Native ever elected to the United States Senate, and the first Democrat to win a Senate seat from Alaska in nearly two decades.

The stakes extend beyond Alaska. Democrats have already won 55 Senate seats in the midterm elections, and a Peltola victory would give them 56 — their largest Senate majority since 2008. The result is striking in a state Donald Trump carried by about 14 percentage points in 2024, though Alaska has drifted gradually leftward in presidential elections over the past quarter-century.

Why the count has taken so long

Alaska's slow count is partly a matter of time allowed for mail ballots to arrive and be verified, and partly a feature of the state's ranked-choice system, which requires a full tabulation once the first-choice count is complete. Voters rejected a ballot measure that would have repealed the system, so it remains in place for this election.

Until the tabulation runs, the outcome is a projection, not a certification. But with her lead now above 10,000 votes and only a small share of ballots outstanding, Peltola's position has strengthened with every update — and the count, eleven days after the midterms, is nearly done.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • WION
