entry.title: Germany hands its spy agencies sweeping powers to strike back at cyberattacks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Germany's parliament has approved the biggest overhaul of the country's intelligence laws in decades, giving its spy agencies powers to act against espionage, sabotage and cyberattacks rather than merely watch and report.

The Bundestag passed the reform package on Friday, with the governing coalition of the conservative CDU/CSU and the Social Democratic Party voting in favour. The vote was 309 in favour, 190 against, with 71 abstentions.

Under the new rules, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), which handles foreign intelligence, will be allowed to answer cyberattacks from abroad with counterattacks of its own. The measures can range from deleting and manipulating data to shutting down entire systems and, if necessary, destroying physical weapons such as drones deployed against Germany.

The domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, gains operational powers for the first time. Until now it has been limited largely to gathering information and monitoring. Under certain conditions its officers will be permitted to enter homes and business premises covertly, for example to prepare surveillance operations, and to act against explosives and weapons. They will not be allowed to use force against people.

An independent oversight board is to be established to monitor the agencies' new powers.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the reform, has described it as a generational change. "Anyone who attacks us in this way must know that we are prepared to strike back," he said. The government argues the changes are needed because of growing hybrid threats, pointing to the activities of Russia, China and Iran, as well as drone sightings and sabotage.

The head of the Federal Criminal Police Office, Holger Münch, has argued that modern hybrid attacks are blurring the old line between police work and intelligence gathering. He pointed to figures showing crime originating abroad rose by 24 percent in the first six months of 2026 compared with the same period last year.

Opposition lawmakers and legal experts warn the reform blurs the post-war separation between police and intelligence services, a principle meant to prevent the concentration of unchecked power. Critics are expected to challenge the law before the Federal Constitutional Court. Most provisions are due to take effect on December 31, after the Bundesrat, the upper house, considers the bill.

Sources

  • DW
  • LaPresse

link.title: Germany hands its spy agencies sweeping powers to strike back at cyberattacks

entry.title: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage for the first time after a day in orbit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

SpaceX caught its Starship spacecraft with the mechanical arms of its launch tower in Texas on Saturday, completing the first-ever recovery of the rocket's upper stage after a trip to orbit.

The spacecraft, known simply as the Ship, descended through the atmosphere after circling Earth 14 times over about 22 hours, then eased between the tower's two "chopstick" arms at the company's Starbase site. Crowds watching from a nearby beach cheered as it settled into its cradle high above the ground.

"We caught a Starship and now, everything changes," SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said after the catch.

A day in orbit

Flight 15 lifted off on Friday afternoon, November 13, at 4:47 p.m. Central time. The Super Heavy booster separated about two minutes into the flight and sent the Ship on toward orbit, where it deployed 26 of SpaceX's newer Starlink V3 internet satellites.

It was only the second time a Starship had reached full orbit. This time the spacecraft kept going, completing 14 laps of the planet at about 165 miles (265 kilometres) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. SpaceX said everything on board, including the vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

The return began on Saturday afternoon. The Ship fell back through the atmosphere, performed its sideways "belly flop" descent, then flipped upright, fired its engines for a landing burn and came to rest in the arms of the Mechazilla tower at about 3:20 p.m. Central time.

Only half the plan

The catch was one half of an ambitious goal. SpaceX had hoped Flight 15 would achieve a first double catch: the booster returning to the tower minutes after launch, followed a day later by the Ship.

The booster part failed. After separation, the Super Heavy was initially cleared to return to the launch site, but it diverted instead toward the Gulf of Mexico, where its flight termination system triggered and it exploded before hitting the water. SpaceX said early signs pointed to the booster's boostback burn ending early because of a low fuel mass alarm, and that the root cause was still under investigation.

SpaceX had caught Super Heavy boosters three times before. But catching the Ship was far harder: it falls much faster and from much higher than a booster does, after surviving the heat of re-entry.

Why it matters

Recovering both stages is the core of SpaceX's plan to make Starship a fully reusable rocket — a goal the company says would cut the cost of reaching space sharply and allow far more frequent launches. The same system is central to NASA's plans to return astronauts to the Moon and, eventually, to send people to Mars. NASA welcomed Saturday's news.

Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown, standing 407 feet (124 metres) tall. Saturday's flight was its 15th full-scale test since 2023. SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Space
  • Associated Press

entry.title: Jupiter and Mars meet in Leo for their closest pairing in years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two of the night sky's most familiar planets are about to put on a brief show together. On the night of November 15–16, Mars and Jupiter will appear a little over one degree apart in the constellation Leo — roughly the width of a little finger held at arm's length — in their closest apparent pairing in years.

Their closest approach comes at 9:04 p.m. Eastern time on Sunday, November 15, according to calculations from In-The-Sky reported by Space.com. At that exact moment, though, the pair will still be below the horizon for most of the United States. The real viewing window opens later: the planets rise over the eastern horizon around midnight local time, and the best views run through the hours before dawn on Monday, November 16. Face east once they are up, and look for Leo — the blue-white star Regulus will be glowing just below the pair.

No equipment is needed. Jupiter will dominate with a bright, steady glow, while Mars will show its familiar reddish tint nearby. A pair of 10x50 binoculars will frame both planets at once for anyone who wants a closer look, and a small telescope can pull out Jupiter's cloud bands and Mars as a small ochre disk.

A trick of perspective

The closeness is entirely an illusion. In reality, Mars and Jupiter are separated by more than 368 million miles (592 million kilometres), and the light from Regulus below them has travelled some 79 light-years to reach Earth. The two planets simply happen to line up from our vantage point as Mars, on its faster inner orbit, catches up with Jupiter — an event astronomers call an appulse. It happens roughly once every two to two-and-a-half years, but this one is unusually tight: the pair will not look this close again until July 2029, when they meet in Virgo.

The pairing also arrives just ahead of another November sky event. The Leonid meteor shower peaks on the nights of November 17–18, so anyone out in the small hours after the conjunction may catch a few early shooting stars as well.

Clouds on the 16th need not spoil it. Mars and Jupiter will still sit close together on the mornings either side, and the two planets will drift apart only gradually over the following weeks.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Space.com
  • StarWalk

link.title: Jupiter and Mars meet in Leo for their closest pairing in years

entry.title: China's 3.95-billion-year-old rocks point to an early start for plate tectonics
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Rocks found in northern China and dated to 3.95 billion years ago are among the oldest ever discovered — and they carry chemical clues that a process resembling modern plate tectonics may already have been at work nearly 4 billion years ago.

The rocks, a trondhjemitic gneiss from the Shimen Complex in Hebei province, were analysed by a team led by Hangqiang Xie of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences in Beijing. The team collected three samples and dated them by studying tiny zircon crystals trapped inside the rock. Uranium in the crystals decays into lead at a known rate, which let the researchers pin the rock's formation to 3,951 million years ago, give or take 3 million years. The findings were published in the journal Nature on November 11.

Earth is about 4.5 billion years old, but rocks from its earliest chapter are extremely rare: most have long since been destroyed by the same geological churning they would record. Until now, the only rocks older than 3.9 billion years confirmed beyond doubt came from the Acasta Gneiss Complex in Canada. Scientists have searched China for rocks older than 3.8 billion years for decades.

A journey down, then back up

The team wanted to know more than the rocks' age. Analysing the chemistry of the zircon crystals — including different forms of oxygen and hafnium — and running computer models of the conditions under which the rocks formed, they found that the material had once been in contact with water at or near Earth's surface. That same material was then carried more than 50 kilometres (31 miles) below the surface, where intense heat and pressure partly melted it.

The researchers propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event: one section of Earth's crust sinking beneath another, as happens in plate tectonics today. In other words, the machinery that now builds mountains and recycles ocean floor may already have been switching on in at least one part of the planet nearly 4 billion years ago.

A second chemical clock points even further back. Analysis of hafnium isotopes in the zircon crystals suggests that the process of separating new crust from Earth's mantle had begun more than 4.3 billion years ago, during the Hadean eon — hundreds of millions of years before these rocks formed.

If the interpretation holds, it pushes the timeline for Earth's crust formation and early tectonics back substantially. But the authors describe the event as transient, and a single site in one craton cannot prove the process operated worldwide. The discovery is a new data point in a long-running debate about when plate tectonics began — not the end of it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • Nature

link.title: China's 3.95-billion-year-old rocks point to an early start for plate tectonics

entry.title: U.S. shifts focus to direct talks between Europe and Russia as Ukraine peace effort continues
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United States is now working to arrange direct engagement between Russia and its European partners, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said on Saturday, as Washington pushes to keep the Ukraine peace effort moving after a week of shuttle diplomacy.

Kushner said the focus had shifted to setting up talks between Moscow and European governments and preparing the agenda for the next round of three-way negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. He made the remarks in a post on X, after he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff held separate meetings this week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The meetings followed the first round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi, which concluded on Wednesday. It was the first direct contact between the two sides since February. The round ended with plans for a prisoner exchange and further talks, but no wider agreement on ending the war, which has now lasted more than four and a half years.

Kushner said the envoys had stayed in close consultation with Russia, Ukraine and European partners since the Abu Dhabi round, and that new ideas from the discussions were being explored. He added that a lasting peace would require credible security guarantees for Ukraine and detailed postwar arrangements to reduce the risk of another war.

Europe's place in the process

European governments have been pressing for a seat at the table, and the question of their role has been one of the most contested parts of the diplomacy. Russia has long resisted European participation in the main negotiations, though Putin told the U.S. envoys this week that Russia had never objected to pursuing dialogue with Europe.

European leaders moved on Friday in Dublin to select five nations — the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy and Poland — to send representatives to future rounds of talks, according to TRT World. The move suggests the European side is organising itself for a formal role even as the terms of its involvement are still being negotiated.

Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said on Saturday that American envoys had raised the prospect of Ukraine giving up territory in exchange for NATO membership, TRT World reported. The claim underlines how difficult the substance of any settlement remains, even as the format of the talks expands.

What happens next

The next round of trilateral talks has not yet been scheduled publicly, and no date has been announced for the direct European-Russian engagement Kushner described. For now, the diplomacy amounts to a framework in search of content: the parties are talking again after a nine-month gap, and the circle of participants is widening, but the central questions — territory, security guarantees and the terms of any ceasefire — remain unresolved.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CBS News
  • The Kyiv Independent

link.title: U.S. shifts focus to direct talks between Europe and Russia as Ukraine peace effort continues

entry.title: GTA 6 is the first in the series built to encourage empathy, Rockstar says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Grand Theft Auto VI will be the first game in the series designed to encourage empathy, Rockstar Games has said, five days before the long-awaited release on November 19.

In a hands-on interview with The Guardian, published in the paper's Saturday magazine, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson said the change grows out of the story the game is telling rather than from any rule imposed on the player. "We've tried for the first time in a GTA to provide mechanisms that encourage it, for those who want to," he said.

The heart of that approach is the relationship between the game's two protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a young couple trying to make their way in the fictional state of Leonida. "The relationship is yours to nurture or yours to lose," Nelson said — a marked shift for a series long defined by consequence-free chaos.

A slower kind of crime

The interview describes a more deliberate opening than fans may expect. Jason and Lucia begin as small-time criminals, hotwiring cheap cars and scraping by, rather than arriving as established kingpins. In the demo shown to The Guardian, the first person the pair meet outside their apartment is a woman walking her dog — and Jason asks her permission before petting it.

Players can also listen in on passers-by's conversations, and interrupting them can draw a puzzled reply or a stream of abuse. The game, the report says, steers players toward acting in character rather than going on aimless rampages, in a similar spirit to Red Dead Redemption 2.

That does not mean the old Grand Theft Auto is gone. Nelson was clear that crime remains fundamental to the game and that Rockstar is not punishing players for playing the way they always have. The empathy mechanics are optional, and actions will affect how the game plays out rather than locking anyone into a moral path.

Not an honour system

The approach is distinct from the honour system in Red Dead Redemption 2. A separate system, called the Criminal Profile, tracks how violently and maliciously players commit crimes over the course of the story — independently of Jason and Lucia's relationship. Rockstar has not explained in detail how the two systems interact, or how far the consequences of a player's choices will reach.

Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar's head of publishing, told The Guardian the studio resisted making a safer sequel. "They could have made GTA 5.5, and done it faster," she said. Take-Two confirmed development was complete on November 9, and the game launches on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19, thirteen years after GTA V.

Sources

  • TechPowerUp
  • OutputLag

link.title: GTA 6 is the first in the series built to encourage empathy, Rockstar says

entry.title: Years of warnings preceded Friday's nationwide flight shutdown
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The nationwide ground stop that halted every departure in the United States on Friday did not come out of nowhere. The Federal Aviation Administration had been warned for years that the ageing network at the heart of air traffic control was at risk of failure, according to reporting by the Washington Post — and the warnings are documented in the public record.

The stop began on Friday afternoon, November 13, after communication problems struck several regional centres that guide aircraft between airports. It lasted more than four hours before departures resumed at about 8:15 p.m. Eastern time. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, the first since January 2023, and only the second since September 11, 2001.

More than 3,000 flights already in the air landed safely, and officials said no one was in danger. On the ground, the disruption was vast: reports put it at more than 11,000 flights affected, with cancellations running into the thousands.

What failed

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed overloaded, decades-old network equipment. Contractor L3Harris Technologies was replacing sections of the system's old copper wire with new fibre when it overloaded, he said. The ageing switches and routers began feeding control centres inconsistent information, prompting the decision to stop traffic.

"We use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said at a White House briefing on Friday night. "It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials had seen no evidence of a cyberattack.

The warnings on file

The fragility of the system was no secret. A review commissioned by the FAA in 2023 called the agency's telecom network obsolete and predicted more outages "due to an underfunded migration to IP-based telecommunications." In March 2025, the air traffic controllers' union testified to Congress under the heading "The FAA's Looming Telecommunications Crisis."

Government auditors added their own. A September 2024 assessment by the Government Accountability Office identified 105 air traffic control systems as unsustainable or potentially unsustainable. And on September 14 this year, auditors warned the FAA lacked a reliable cost estimate for modernisation and had not integrated the schedules of more than 11,000 individual projects.

There is also a question about Friday's work itself. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, the union representing the agency's technicians, said the FAA normally asks them to assess the risks of upgrades or repairs in advance — but that did not happen in this case.

What is still unknown

No official root cause has been announced, and the FAA has not published a detailed account of what failed or why several centres were affected at once. Duffy said he could not guarantee the problem would not happen again.

The administration is pressing Congress for money to replace the system. A formal request sent the week of the outage sought $30.1 billion for airport and air traffic modernisation, while Duffy has floated a $50 billion emergency overhaul. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said air travel should be back to normal by the end of Sunday: "the worst is behind us."

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Washington Post
  • Associated Press

link.title: Years of warnings preceded Friday's nationwide flight shutdown

entry.title: Saudi coalition intercepts missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh as Yemen fighting escalates
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Saudi-led coalition forces said early on Sunday they had intercepted two ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh, allegedly fired by Yemen's Houthis, in the latest cross-border attack as fighting intensifies across several front lines in Yemen.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X that air defences had intercepted and destroyed the two missiles. He said on Saturday that two suspected Houthi drones had been brought down in Riyadh and the southern regions, and on Sunday the coalition said three more drones were shot down in the Eastern region — five drones in all over the weekend.

Saudi authorities say at least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks inside the kingdom since September 23. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh's King Khalid international airport, as well as oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.

A downed aircraft, claimed by the Houthis

The Houthis gave their own account of the weekend's fighting. Their military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said the group had shot down an armed coalition reconnaissance aircraft operating over al-Jawf, describing it as the fifth aircraft brought down since the escalation began. He said Houthi fighters had repelled Saudi formations using Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles, and that the group had fired ballistic missiles at Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of Lahij governorate.

On the ground, Yemeni government forces said they had made gains in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf as fighting intensified around Marib. The government said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 operations across Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf, and that 117 military vehicles had been destroyed. The Houthis, for their part, said the coalition had launched 72 air strikes against them in the past 24 hours. Houthi-affiliated media reported that two women and two children were wounded by artillery shelling in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa.

Displacement and a U.S. warning

The International Organization for Migration says more than 340,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen since August, as the conflict grinds on with no settlement in sight.

As the fighting escalated, the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise "heightened vigilance", citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks. The embassy said attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure had caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruption, and warned that hostilities could spread rapidly.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Saudi coalition intercepts missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh as Yemen fighting escalates

entry.title: Judge blocks Trump's plan to close and rebuild Washington's East Potomac golf course
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal judge on Saturday temporarily blocked President Donald Trump's plan to close East Potomac Park in Washington and rebuild its public golf course, ruling one day before the park was due to shut for 15 months of renovation.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, in a 30-page decision, said the administration's stated reasons for closing the park — safety concerns — were "pretextual," and that the government likely violated at least two federal laws in its haste to meet what she called an "arbitrary deadline." The order keeps the park open during the hours it was open as of November 14. The government does not have to keep running golf operations there, Reyes wrote, but it "cannot use the absence of golf operations as a reason to exclude the public." The order runs through November 28, or until the court orders otherwise.

The park sits near the Jefferson Memorial, about two miles south of the White House. It holds three golf courses totalling 36 holes, a miniature golf course and a paved loop popular with cyclists and runners. Trump's plan would replace them with a single 18-hole championship course that he has said could host events such as the U.S. Open and the Ryder Cup while remaining open to the public. In an October 18 social media post, Trump said the closure would last 15 months and would transform the park's golf offerings into "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World."

The lawsuit was brought by the DC Preservation League, a historic preservation group, along with two local golfers. They argue the redevelopment would violate federal environmental and administrative laws and would change the character of an accessible public course, making it unaffordable — a claim the president denies. In a statement after the ruling, the Justice Department said it would "always vociferously defend the Trump Administration's agenda in court," and noted that nothing in the order stops planning for the golf course from continuing.

The ruling is the latest in a series of setbacks for the project in Reyes's court. In October, she blocked the removal of trees and other irreversible changes after more than 400 trees were cut down with minimal notice. She has also ordered an inquiry into whether Justice Department lawyers misled her about the closure timeline, and the department's attempt to have her removed from the case failed.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether the administration will appeal or ask a higher court to lift the order, or how quickly the underlying lawsuit will move. The case, DC Preservation League v. Department of the Interior, will decide whether the redevelopment itself can go ahead — Saturday's order only pauses the closure while that question is litigated.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • Reuters

link.title: Judge blocks Trump's plan to close and rebuild Washington's East Potomac golf course

entry.title: Pope Leo returns to remote Andes town and warns of villages emptying as people leave
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Pope Leo XIV returned on Saturday to a remote town high in Peru's Andes mountains, where he once served as a bishop, and used the visit to speak about the poverty and migration that are emptying the region's villages.

The pope arrived by helicopter in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, a town of about 6,000 people in the Cajamarca region of northern Peru, and was greeted by singing and cheering crowds before touring in a popemobile and celebrating an outdoor Mass. About 20,000 people attended the visit, according to the Vatican — more than three times the town's population.

In his sermon, the pope spoke of the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future" and of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages." He also criticised the unequal distribution of the land's resources, and said he felt joy at visiting the small town again.

The visit was a homecoming of sorts. Leo, who was born in the United States and elected pope in May 2025, lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023, became a Peruvian citizen in 2015, and served as bishop of Chiclayo — the diocese that includes Santa Cruz de Succhabamba — from 2015 to 2023.

The town's struggles are the region's struggles. More than 40 percent of people in Cajamarca live in poverty, the highest figure in Peru, according to official data. The region has also lost more people to internal migration than any other in the country: some 729,000 people born in Cajamarca now live elsewhere in Peru, many of them in coastal cities such as Lima and Trujillo.

Peru is the longest stop on the pope's first tour of Latin America, a 12-day trip that also included Argentina and Uruguay. He was scheduled to leave Chiclayo on Sunday for Cusco, then visit a Peruvian sector of the Amazon rainforest, before the tour concludes on Monday with his return to Rome.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear what, if anything, will follow from the pope's remarks on migration and rural poverty, or whether the visit will bring new attention — or funding — to the Cajamarca region. The Vatican has not announced any new initiatives for the area tied to the trip.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Pope Leo returns to remote Andes town and warns of villages emptying as people leave

entry.title: Rifle-carrying robot dogs join the retaking of Haiti's national stadium
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

El Salvador's president has released video showing four-legged robots fitted with rifles taking part in an operation to retake Haiti's national stadium from gang control, in what appears to be the first time armed robot dogs have been used in a live security operation in the Americas.

The footage, posted by President Nayib Bukele on Thursday, shows the machines moving down a hallway and up a set of stairs inside the Sylvio Cator Stadium in Port-au-Prince, rifles mounted on their backs. Soldiers are seen in the same video sweeping the stadium's stands and fitting the weapons onto the robots on the pitch.

The stadium had been under gang control for more than two years, forcing Haiti's national team to play its home matches abroad. Under a bilateral agreement between the Haitian government and the government of El Salvador, a joint operation involving the Haitian National Police, the Haitian Armed Forces, a government task force and Salvadoran special forces took control of the ground and secured it.

What the robots did — and did not — show

Exactly how the robot dogs assisted in the operation is not clear from the footage. Bukele did not elaborate on their role, and no robot is shown firing a weapon or engaging a target. The video also does not identify the robots' make or model, or the type of rifle mounted on them. Open-source analysts have suggested the machines resemble a commercially sold Chinese quadruped, but that identification has not been confirmed by any official source.

Bukele said "several human skulls" were found inside the stadium during the operation, a claim that has not been independently confirmed. He said forces would now establish an operational base at the stadium to advance deeper into gang-held territory, adding that his forces now have "the upper hand on the ground."

Before the operation, Bukele had demanded that gang members leave the area, warning that those who stayed to fight would face the consequences.

Why Salvadoran troops are in Haiti

El Salvador's involvement follows an ambush in October in which Salvadoran nationals were seized. Bukele sent troops to Haiti under the bilateral security agreement, and the stadium operation is the most visible result so far. Haitian police have also claimed credit for the recapture, and the two accounts have not been fully reconciled in public reporting.

The use of armed robots raises questions that go beyond this one operation. The machines are built on commercially available platforms, and the footage shows how quickly off-the-shelf technology can be adapted for military use. Neither the manufacturer of the robots nor the rules governing their use in the field have been disclosed.

For Haiti, the stadium's recapture is a symbolic win in a much larger fight. Gangs control large parts of Port-au-Prince, and reclaiming a national landmark — one the country hopes to use again for its own matches — matters to a public that has watched the state lose ground for years. Whether the stadium base becomes a springboard for a wider offensive, as Bukele promises, remains to be seen.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Fox News
  • Jamaica Observer

link.title: Rifle-carrying robot dogs join the retaking of Haiti's national stadium

entry.title: UPS cargo jet and Copa passenger plane collide on a Miami taxiway
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, leaving two people with minor injuries and both aircraft damaged, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said.

The collision happened at about 9:15 p.m. local time at the intersection of two taxiways. Copa Airlines Flight 427, a Boeing 737-800 that had just arrived from Panama City with 166 passengers and six crew members aboard, was taxiing toward its gate. UPS Flight 358, a Boeing 767 freighter, was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia. The wingtip of the Copa jet struck the nose of the UPS aircraft, according to the FAA.

Air traffic controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way and let the arriving Copa flight pass before continuing toward the runway. Radio recordings of the exchange show the UPS crew acknowledging the mistake moments after the impact. After the Copa crew reported that somebody had hit them, the controller asked the UPS crew whether they had hit the aircraft. The UPS pilot replied: "Yeah, we went too far and then he... he clipped us with the wing."

The Copa pilot later told controllers: "It seems that we are missing the left wingtip."

Two treated at the scene

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue treated two people at the scene for minor injuries. Neither needed to be taken to hospital, airport communications director Greg Chin said. All 166 passengers and six crew members aboard the Copa flight later disembarked after the aircraft was moved back to the terminal, the airline confirmed.

The airport said the collision had no effect on its overall operations, with aircraft redirected to other taxiways while the two planes were dealt with. UPS said its crew was safe and that it was committed to working with the authorities to determine what happened.

Investigation under way

The FAA has opened an investigation into the collision. No official cause has been established yet, and the extent of the damage to either aircraft has not been officially confirmed, although images posted on social media show significant damage to the nose of the UPS jet.

There is a suggestion that a runway change may have added to the UPS crew's workload shortly before the collision. During the radio exchange, one of the pilots said the crew was in the middle of a checklist for a runway change. That has been reported as a possible factor, not as a finding — the investigation will determine what happened.

The incident came a day after a rare nationwide ground stop brought departures across the United States to a halt for more than four hours on Friday, following problems with the air traffic control network.

Sources

  • Simple Flying
  • The Statesman

link.title: UPS cargo jet and Copa passenger plane collide on a Miami taxiway

entry.title: Earth's frozen regions have moved past safe planetary limits, study finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The frozen parts of the planet have moved beyond the safe limits that sustained human civilisation, according to a major new study published in the journal Science and presented at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye.

The research, led by the Stockholm Resilience Centre at Stockholm University and involving more than 30 scientists, assessed the cryosphere — the planet's ice sheets, mountain glaciers, sea ice, permafrost and snow cover — against a "safe operating space" defined by the relatively stable conditions of the past 11,700 years, the Holocene epoch in which human societies developed.

Its conclusion is stark: three of the four measures it tracked have already crossed that boundary, and the fourth is heading the same way.

What has already passed the limit

Sea ice area, snow cover and permafrost temperature have all moved beyond the safe operating space, the study finds. Land ice — almost 90 per cent of which sits in Antarctica — is still within the range today, but the authors warn that ice loss set in motion now commits the planet to centuries of further decline, so it should be treated as departing the safe zone as well.

"The cryosphere has already exceeded its planetary safe operating space, threatening the frozen foundations of our planet that have supported human civilisations for millennia," said Dr Bo Su, the study's lead author and a researcher at the Stockholm Resilience Centre and Beijing Normal University.

The degradation is driven predominantly by human-caused climate change, the paper finds, alongside regional pressures such as black carbon emissions and industrial and infrastructure expansion in frozen regions.

Why frozen ground matters

The cryosphere plays an irreplaceable role in the planet's energy, water, carbon and methane cycles. Ice sheets and glaciers store fresh water, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space, snow cover regulates seasonal water supplies for billions of people, and permafrost locks away vast stores of carbon and methane that warming can release.

Losing those functions does not just mean higher seas. The study argues that cryosphere decline systematically threatens the Earth system conditions on which humanity depends, from water security in mountain regions to the stability of coastlines and the pace of warming itself.

What happens next

The findings arrive during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye (November 9–20), and in the middle of the UN Decade of Action for Cryospheric Sciences (2025–2034). The authors propose folding the cryosphere into the planetary boundaries framework — the science-based limits used to track how humanity is doing on climate, biodiversity and other global systems — so that frozen regions get the same structured attention as the atmosphere and oceans.

Two major UN-backed reports released last week reached a similar conclusion from a different angle: significant cryosphere losses are already unavoidable, and the question now is how far the overshoot goes.

The study does not set a single deadline for action. Its message is that the frozen foundations of the planet are no longer a stable backdrop — they are an active part of the climate crisis, and they are already moving.

Sources

  • Science X
  • Stockholm University

link.title: Earth's frozen regions have moved past safe planetary limits, study finds

entry.title: The Nvidia scandal has exposed the backdoor route sending US AI chips to China
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The scandal that ended Jensen Huang's 33-year run at Nvidia has exposed a backdoor route that has kept advanced American AI chips flowing to China despite years of US export controls.

At the centre of the story is Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that in three years went from an inactive offshoot of a Chinese gaming firm to one of Asia's biggest buyers of cutting-edge US semiconductors. Trade records show it has bought more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia since 2023.

US officials suspect Megaspeed of exploiting a gap in the controls Washington imposed in 2022 to stop China's access to its most advanced chips. Instead of selling chips onward, Megaspeed builds data centres across Southeast Asia and rents out the computing power. "If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari… I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari," said Alex Capri of the National University of Singapore. "It's the car dealership that you have to control."

The scale of the wider problem is hard to pin down, but researchers estimate that between 290,000 and 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors reached China in violation of export controls last year. Blacklisted buyers have kept obtaining chips directly: Northwestern Polytechnical University, on the US Entity List since 2001, bought four H200 chips in October for $250,000, according to procurement records on its own website that have since been deleted.

Megaspeed is also at the heart of the scandal that cost Huang his job. He resigned on Thursday after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang — no relation — a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing calls the claim groundless, and US intelligence has not established that she acted as a spy. The FBI has investigated for at least a year without reaching conclusions. Megaspeed says it has cooperated with Commerce Department inspections and hired a US law firm to verify its compliance; it says Alice Huang left the company in August 2025.

The case has also exposed a rift in Washington. Megaspeed has not been placed on the Entity List or subjected to purchase limits — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, CNN reported. Lawmakers are now demanding greater oversight, with Huang called to testify behind closed doors on December 1 and Lutnick due before the Senate Banking Committee next month.

Nvidia's shares fell 12.75 per cent in the week to Friday's close, wiping out about $573 billion in market value. Finance chief Colette Kress has been named interim chief executive.

What happens next is unclear. Singapore is investigating Megaspeed and its controllers over possible false declarations about server purchases and their final destinations, and Taiwan is moving to criminalise unauthorised exports of advanced AI chips to China. The scrutiny comes days before President Donald Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • CNN

link.title: The Nvidia scandal has exposed the backdoor route sending US AI chips to China

entry.title: Bahrain says it shot down Iranian attacks as Tehran claims a strike on a U.S. base
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Bahrain said on Sunday that its air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks before they could reach their targets, in the first such interceptions by the kingdom since September.

The Bahraini military said the attacks were stopped before reaching their targets and accused Tehran of continuing a hostile approach towards the kingdom. The interceptions followed two warnings of potential threats that urged residents to seek shelter.

Tehran gave a different account. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a U.S. military base in Bahrain in retaliation for what it called hostile American actions, according to Iran's Fars news agency. Iranian state-run Press TV said the Guards launched six drones targeting U.S. air-defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base.

There was no immediate confirmation of that claim from U.S. or Bahraini authorities, and no casualty or damage figures were reported for Sunday's incident. Bahrain said the attacks were intercepted before reaching their targets.

Bahrain's interior ministry urged citizens and residents to remain calm and to move to the nearest safe location. The Gulf kingdom is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, which oversees American naval operations across the Middle East.

A second incident in three days

It was the second reported Iranian attack on Bahrain in three days. Two days earlier, the Revolutionary Guards said they had struck a U.S. early-warning radar facility in the kingdom. The U.S. military denied that account, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage.

The exchanges come amid uncertainty over efforts to end a conflict now in its ninth month. Diplomatic efforts have yet to produce a breakthrough, and sporadic attacks have continued despite a broader lull in fighting between the United States and Iran.

The war began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and then spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on U.S. military bases in Gulf countries.

President Donald Trump said in recent days that he might hold off from attacking Iran if the United States faced no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a U.S. naval blockade, Reuters reported on Saturday.

Fighting continues on a separate front

The Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition continued exchanging attacks over the weekend. The coalition said on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.

What is still unknown

The central dispute remains unresolved: Tehran says it struck a U.S. base in Bahrain, while Bahrain says the attacks were intercepted and Washington has not confirmed any strike. Until U.S. or Bahraini officials give a fuller account, it is not possible to say whether any drone reached its target, or what, if anything, was damaged.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • Haaretz

link.title: Bahrain says it shot down Iranian attacks as Tehran claims a strike on a U.S. base

entry.title: Carney says Canada–U.S. trade talks are advancing, but no deal yet
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday that Canada and the United States are making progress toward a trade deal, after negotiations broke down in August. He made the remarks to reporters in Manila, where he is attending a summit of Southeast Asian leaders.

"I had quite a long, substantive conversation with President Trump just before leaving for this trip," Carney said. "We are making progress. There is the possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal. But we're not yet there."

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller also took part in the call, Carney said.

The auto industry is the sticking point

Carney drew a clear line around Canada's car industry, which he called one of the most difficult issues still on the table. He said his government would not accept an agreement that undermines the sector, which has been hit hard by U.S. tariffs.

Canada walked away from trade talks in August after what Ottawa described as last-minute American demands it considered unacceptable. Washington then imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, and Canada answered with retaliatory tariffs in September. The two sides have since returned to the table.

Canada and the United States share one of the largest trading relationships in the world, and a deal could lower tariffs on key sectors including steel and aluminum. President Donald Trump said before the U.S. midterm elections that the two countries were "very close" to an agreement, while Carney said Washington had dropped demands touching on Canadian culture, French-language protections and Canada's freedom to strike trade deals with other countries.

Carney looks to Asia as talks continue

Carney used the Manila visit to announce progress on a second front. Canada has substantially concluded free-trade negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a bloc of nearly 700 million people, and has completed separate negotiations with the Philippines. Both agreements are expected to be signed next year.

Ottawa estimates the ASEAN agreement could add nearly 2 billion Canadian dollars (about US$1.4 billion) to the Canadian economy and create almost 14,000 jobs, mostly in agriculture and manufacturing. The Philippines deal covers more than 90 per cent of tariff lines, and the Canadian government said it could help triple Canadian exports to the Philippines by 2035.

The announcements fit Carney's stated goal of doubling Canadian exports to countries other than the United States by 2035, reducing Ottawa's dependence on its southern neighbour during the trade war.

What is still unknown

No timetable for a Canada–U.S. deal has been given, and the auto issue remains unresolved. It is also unclear how far U.S. tariffs would fall under any agreement: Carney has acknowledged that Canada faces a choice between accepting a deal that cuts some tariffs but leaves others in place, or holding out for freer trade while the U.S. Congress prepares to challenge the tariffs.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Reuters

link.title: Carney says Canada–U.S. trade talks are advancing, but no deal yet

entry.title: Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night of November 17–18
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Leonid meteor shower reaches its peak this week, with the best viewing in the dark hours before dawn on Wednesday, November 18. Skywatchers under a clear, dark sky can expect roughly 10 to 15 meteors an hour — a modest show by Leonid standards, but one arriving under unusually good conditions this year.

The shower is active from November 6 to November 30, as Earth passes through a trail of dust left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. The peak is expected late on Tuesday, November 17: the International Meteor Organization puts the maximum at about 11:49 p.m. UTC (6:49 p.m. Eastern), and the American Meteor Society forecasts the peak around midnight UTC on November 18. In practice, the meteors worth watching for come after midnight, as the constellation Leo — the shower's radiant — climbs higher in the eastern sky and is highest at dawn.

The Moon is out of the way this year

This year the Moon is cooperating. It reaches its first-quarter phase on November 17 and sets around midnight, leaving the sky dark for the prime viewing hours. That matters more than the raw meteor rate: a bright Moon can wash out the fainter meteors, and this year it will be gone before the best of the shower arrives.

Fast meteors with glowing trains

Leonids are known for their speed. The dust grains strike the atmosphere at about 44 miles per second, and the brighter meteors often leave glowing trains that linger for a few seconds after the streak fades. The meteors appear to radiate from Leo, near the star Regulus, but they can streak across any part of the sky — the radiant is a starting point for the eye, not a place to stare.

A shower with a dramatic past

The Leonids have produced some of the most famous meteor displays in history. In 1833 the shower was so intense that witnesses described the sky as falling, and in November 1966 observers in parts of the United States saw thousands of meteors per minute over about 15 minutes. Storms on that scale returned in 1999 and 2001. Nothing like that is expected this year — forecasters describe 2026 as an ordinary Leonid year — but that history is why the shower still draws a crowd every November.

How to watch

No equipment is needed. Find the darkest sky you can, away from streetlights, and give your eyes 20 to 30 minutes to adapt. Lie back, look up, and be patient: the meteors come in bursts, and a quiet stretch does not mean the show is over. The shower is visible from both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. As a bonus, Mars and Jupiter sit close together near Leo this week, a short distance apart in the pre-dawn sky.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Boston Globe
  • timeanddate.com

link.title: Leonid meteor shower peaks on the night of November 17–18

entry.title: Space data centers could make satellites the brightest lights in the night sky
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The night sky as we know it may not survive the race to put artificial intelligence into orbit. A new report warns that sprawling networks of space-based data centers could make stargazing far more difficult — in many places, satellites could become the most visible lights in the sky, outnumbering the stars themselves.

The report, "Space-Based Data Centers Roadmap: The Case for Caution," was published this week by the Innovation for Cool Earth Forum and led by David Sandalow of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy. It argues that companies and policymakers should proceed with great caution before launching large numbers of AI-powered data centers into orbit: the risks are not yet understood — or governed.

A sky full of satellites

The warning is not about a handful of satellites. Some orbital data centers are already operating, and the filings are enormous: SpaceX has applied for one million data-center satellites, Starcloud for 88,000 and Blue Origin's Project Sunrise for 51,600, according to the Secure World Foundation. Investment tied to orbital data centers reached $197 million in 2025 and $1.11 billion so far in 2026, per market research firm Quilty Space.

In the report's night-sky chapter, Sandalow and Columbia Climate School dean Alexis Abramson write that such constellations could dramatically transform night skies worldwide, with satellites outnumbering visible stars in many places — though technical fixes could soften the effect, with trade-offs.

The launch bill — and the other risks

Putting the hardware up there is itself a vast undertaking: placing just 10 percent of the AI data centers anticipated by 2030 into orbit would require more than 700 launches of large rockets a year — about two a day, indefinitely. The centers would run on solar power, but those launches would produce greenhouse gases and black carbon.

The night sky is only one concern. The report also points to debris fields in low Earth orbit, collisions with thousands of facilities travelling at about 17,000 miles per hour, damage from satellites falling back to Earth, ozone depletion, and the possibility that the centers could become military targets. Existing governance, the authors write, cannot manage risks that need coordination on a global scale.

"Slowly and with care"

Sandalow told Axios there are still "unknown unknowns" about the effects, and that deployment "should happen slowly and with care." The report proposes guardrails in the meantime: brightness limits, mandatory impact assessments before launch, required mitigation, caps on satellite numbers, and international standards.

It also urges policymakers not to allow large constellations until there is more operational experience, citing Deepwater Horizon and Fukushima as reminders of what happens when a technology scales faster than understanding of its risks.

Not every filing will become a launch — Quilty Space cautions that companies often apply for far more satellites than they intend to deploy. But the report's central point stands: what the night sky looks like a decade from now is being decided in filing cabinets and boardrooms today, largely out of public view.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • Columbia University

link.title: Space data centers could make satellites the brightest lights in the night sky

entry.title: A common amino acid may help the immune system spot cancer and viruses
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A nutrient the body already makes — and that most people get from protein-rich food — may play a surprisingly direct role in whether the immune system notices cancer cells and viruses. New research from Rockefeller University, published in the journal Cell, traces the connection to a single amino acid: arginine.

When arginine runs low, the study found, cells struggle to produce a protein called MHC-I, which acts as a display window on the cell surface. MHC-I shows fragments of what is happening inside a cell to passing T cells, the immune system's scouts. If a cell has turned cancerous or been infected by a virus, those fragments are the signal that triggers a response. Without enough arginine, the signal fades — and abnormal cells can slip past unnoticed.

A stalled assembly line

The researchers, led by Sohail Tavazoie and first author Qiushuang Wu, traced the breakdown to the cell's protein-building machinery. MHC-I is rich in arginine, and when the amino acid is scarce, the ribosomes that assemble proteins stall partway through making it. In cell cultures deprived of arginine, 414 proteins fell to unusually low levels — but the most striking effect involved the three genes that produce MHC-I.

The team had already shown in 2023 that starving colon cancer cells of arginine caused them to accumulate more mutations. The new work suggests the deficiency also weakens the immune system's side of the equation. Arginine was the most depleted amino acid across the disease models the team examined: colon cancer, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2.

Fewer tumors, milder infections — in mice

The findings held up in animal studies. Mice fed a low-arginine diet developed more colon tumors; mice given more arginine developed fewer. In models of influenza and SARS-CoV-2, an arginine-rich diet meant milder symptoms — and giving mice arginine after a flu infection had already started improved their outcomes, a result the researchers said they had not expected.

A moderate dose, roughly equivalent to a couple of over-the-counter tablets, was enough in laboratory experiments to restore the genes involved in MHC-I production. The researchers say that makes arginine a realistic candidate for testing alongside immunotherapy, or for high-risk groups exposed to viral infections.

Why age may matter

The results may also help explain a familiar pattern: arginine levels naturally decline with age, and older people are more vulnerable to certain cancers and respiratory viruses. The researchers suggest that falling arginine could be one reason the immune system grows less sharp at recognizing abnormal cells as people get older — a "perfect storm," in Tavazoie's words, for the initiation of colon cancer.

One important caution: the evidence so far comes from laboratory and animal studies, not from people. Human trials would still be needed before anyone could say arginine supplements prevent cancer or treat viral infections. But because arginine is inexpensive and widely available, the researchers hope those studies can begin soon.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Science Daily
  • Cell

entry.title: The 700-pound grizzly they call 'the Boss' still rules Banff — and his fame may be his biggest risk
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park, he is grizzly bear 122. To almost everyone else in and around Canada's oldest national park — and to many of its 4.5 million annual visitors — he is simply the Boss.

The Boss weighs about 700 pounds and rules a territory of roughly 2,000 square kilometres across Banff and the neighbouring parks. He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect and shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and ate a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his territory. His battles with a rival known as Split Lip are local legend — he caused the split lip. Each spring, his emergence from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.

When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, traffic stops and "bear jams" follow. Galleries in Banff and neighbouring Canmore sell giant photographs of him around the world. A local restaurant is named for him. Yet the people who know him best say his fame, not any rival, may be what ends his reign.

A vegetarian who eats 200,000 berries a day

For all his fearsome reputation — and four-inch claws — the Boss is mostly a vegetarian. Berries, roots and other plant material make up about 90 percent of the diet of Banff's grizzlies, according to David Laskin, a Parks Canada wildlife ecologist. Keeping 700 pounds fed on plants takes serious work: the Boss can put away about 200,000 buffaloberries a day, and in 2012, while wearing a tracking collar, he travelled some 1,400 kilometres in search of food.

About 75 grizzly bears roam Banff's 6,641 square kilometres of mountains, rivers and valleys. The Boss stands out partly because his home turf overlaps with the park's main tourist gateway, so he is seen far more often than bears in remote valleys. Laskin says the danger most grizzlies pose is overstated. "Bears need to be respected," he said. "Getting close to a bear: there's a risk for you but also for the bear especially."

Old age, and the cost of celebrity

Now in his mid-20s, the Boss is getting old for a wild grizzly, and his body is showing it. His teeth are worn, though Laskin says that is not unusual for a bear his age. Earlier this year he was found in a trap set for another study bear, sedated and examined, and fitted with a collar that soon fell off, most likely in a fight. Grizzlies typically peak physically at about 10 and then gradually shrink — but Laskin said there is no sign of that in the Boss.

Under the park's bear management plan, the Boss is classed as "habituated," meaning he does not much care about people as long as he is left alone. When trail cameras and sightings suggest he is heading toward Banff, Canmore or a campground, park workers gently steer him elsewhere and clear visitors from his path.

Paul Kalra, a gas station owner and nature photographer widely credited with naming the bear more than 20 years ago, worries the attention itself is the problem. "Give him a break," he said. "Even the movie stars that are most famous, they go incognito with sunglasses when they go to have a burger, you know? I want the same thing for the Boss."

As winter approaches, the question in Banff is whether the old bear will emerge from hibernation in the spring — and whether the crowds that love him will give him the space to keep ruling.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • Nature World News

entry.title: Bessent says Nvidia needs an outside CEO and a 'dramatic shakeup'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for its next chief executive, arguing that the chipmaker needs a "dramatic shakeup" after the sudden resignation of founder Jensen Huang last week.

"This makes me think that as the board conducts a search for a new leader that they need to go outside the company, that just with what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shakeup," Bessent told Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures" show.

Huang stepped down on Thursday after 33 years at the helm, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy. The company's board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and appointed longtime director Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chair. Nvidia has said it will consider both internal and external candidates for the permanent job.

Ten days to answer on export compliance

Bessent also put a deadline on a second front. He said Nvidia's board and its outside counsel should answer within 10 days questions about the company's culture of compliance with export restrictions — including whether it pursued chip sales to China that appeared to break the rules.

Bloomberg reported that the questions concern sales routed through Singapore shell companies, and that Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for stalling the trade-blacklist listing of Megaspeed, the Singapore firm at the centre of the affair. Huang has acknowledged a relationship with Alice Huang, the former chief executive of Megaspeed, who has been identified in media reports as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Megaspeed has said Alice Huang left the company in 2025 and denied wrongdoing.

The Financial Times reported on Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Rene Haas, chief executive of British chip designer Arm Holdings, as a possible successor.

A company in transition

The intervention is the sharpest yet from Washington since Huang's departure plunged the world's most valuable chipmaker into crisis. Nvidia, valued at about $4 trillion, reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday — its first report without Huang at the helm.

Huang has also agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees on December 1, and the Senate Banking Committee has asked him to testify the same week.

What happens next rests with the board: whether it follows Bessent's advice and hires from outside, and what its answers on export compliance show when the 10-day clock runs out around November 25.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Bloomberg
  • Reuters

link.title: Bessent says Nvidia needs an outside CEO and a 'dramatic shakeup'

entry.title: Six months on, Congo's Ebola outbreak is still out of control, MSF warns
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Six months after Ebola was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the outbreak is still out of control, Médecins Sans Frontières warned on Thursday, with cases going undetected, hospitals in some areas spreading the virus, and front-line workers left without pay, fuel or basic equipment.

MSF's international president, Javid Abdelmoneim, said staff were "often left speechless by dysfunctions" in the response, and called for urgent improvements in oversight, staffing and operational support. The organisation said the resources mobilised for the outbreak were not reaching the patients, communities and medics who need them.

The numbers underline the warning. More than 11,000 confirmed cases have been recorded, with over 5,400 deaths, according to Congo's National Institute of Public Health. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species of the virus — for which there are no approved treatments or vaccines — is the second-largest ever recorded, behind only the 2014–16 West African epidemic.

But the case count is only part of the picture. Epidemiologists tracking the outbreak believe only about half of infections are being detected. MSF's emergency coordinator, Anna Halford, said most cases arriving at treatment centres were "surprise cases" with no known link to another infection — a sign, she said, that contact tracing is not keeping up with the spread.

"While that remains the situation, it is an absolute sign that we do not have this under control," Halford said. "You should not have the majority of your cases coming out of nowhere."

Money that never arrived

Figures cited from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention indicate that of $962 million passed on to organisations dealing with Ebola, $700 million was unaccounted for. On the ground, MSF describes surveillance teams with motorbikes but no fuel, community awareness workers who have not been paid, and health workers without supplies or technical support.

The outbreak began in the eastern provinces of North Kivu and Ituri and has since spread to eight provinces, five of which are still active. The World Health Organization declared it a public health emergency in May.

Conflict compounds the crisis

Insecurity has become one of the biggest obstacles to containing the virus. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus acknowledged delays in paying health workers this week and pointed to attacks on health facilities. An attack in the town of Cantine-Aloya in North Kivu last week killed 66 civilians, including three health workers.

Despite the failures, MSF said there had been progress — better information flow, new diagnostic facilities and stronger community engagement. The organisation employs nearly 1,500 staff in the country, more than eight in ten of them Congolese.

For the wider world, the risk remains low: Ebola is not airborne and is not highly contagious. But inside Congo, the spread is slowly growing rather than slowing — and six months in, the response is still catching up.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The National
  • Reuters
