entry.title: Israel abducted two Iranian generals in the hunt for a missing airman — a lead it now says was wrong
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

For nearly forty years, Israel searched for Ron Arad, an air force navigator who vanished over Lebanon in 1986. A New York Times investigation published on Sunday reports that the search included the abduction of two senior Iranian generals — and was built on a premise Israeli officials now say was mistaken: that Iran was holding him.

Arad bailed out of his plane during an operation in southern Lebanon and was captured by the Shiite Amal movement. Signs of life reached his family in the first two years, the last a letter dated May 5, 1988. Israel declared him dead in 2008, but the search never stopped.

The investigation, based on interviews with dozens of Iranian, Israeli and American officials, says Israeli intelligence became convinced Iran had taken Arad from Lebanon. In 1994, commandos abducted Mustafa Dirani, a senior Amal member who had held Arad. Dirani told interrogators he had taken Arad to the village of Nabi Chit, where guards left him alone to fight nearby Israeli troops — and when they returned, he was gone. He also claimed an Iranian official had told him the Revolutionary Guards had taken Arad to Iran. Some in Israel treated that as proof; others dismissed it as uncorroborated and extracted under duress.

Two generals, two abductions

In 2006, Mossad agents kidnapped General Alireza Asgari, a senior Quds Force officer who had served in Lebanon shortly after Arad disappeared, from Istanbul. Three former American officials told the Times that agents questioned him for weeks aboard a boat, then killed him and dumped his body in the Black Sea after finding no evidence he knew anything about Arad. Israel has denied any involvement.

Fifteen years later, in September 2021, agents abducted General Abdullah Saberi in Damascus while he was out on a morning run. Saberi had been tasked by Iran with overseeing the search for evidence of Arad's whereabouts. He was taken to Israel and interrogated, then released in Johannesburg, South Africa, according to one account. Then-Mossad chief David Barnea later acknowledged authorising a daring but unsuccessful operation.

The lead that did not hold

A 2006 review by Israel's Shin Bet concluded that neither Iran nor Hezbollah had held Arad, but the government and the Mossad largely set its findings aside. A joint investigation by Iran and Hezbollah concluded that Arad had died in Nabi Chit in 1988 and was buried there. A 2016 report by the Mossad and Israeli military intelligence said he had likely been dead since 1988.

Israeli officials told the Times the prevailing assessment now is that Iran never held Arad — and that the assumption was likely mistaken from the outset. The leading theory is that he was killed in 1988 in revenge for the death of a fighter involved in his capture.

In March this year, Israeli commandos raided Nabi Chit looking for his remains, with airstrikes that local officials said killed at least 41 people. The raid found nothing. Arad's widow later said the family did not want soldiers' lives put at risk to recover his remains.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Times of Israel
  • Haaretz

link.title: Israel abducted two Iranian generals in the hunt for a missing airman — a lead it now says was wrong

entry.title: Vulcan rocket fails minutes after liftoff, destroying 40 Amazon internet satellites
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon internet satellites failed about 10 minutes after liftoff from Florida on Sunday, destroying its payload in the first outright failure of a ULA rocket since the company was formed in 2006.

The 214-foot Vulcan lifted off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station at 12:40 p.m. EST. Its six strap-on solid rocket boosters appeared to work normally, burning out and falling away about a minute and 40 seconds into flight. But the first stage's methane-burning BE-4 engines appeared to fire longer than planned, and something went wrong during the burn of the hydrogen-fueled Centaur upper stage.

About 50 minutes after liftoff, ULA confirmed the loss. "Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," the company said in a statement. It said it would work with Amazon and other organizations to find the cause, determine the corrective action and return to flight as quickly as possible.

Sunday's flight was only the fifth for Vulcan, ULA's replacement for its Atlas 5 fleet, and its first in nine months. ULA had spent that time fixing problems with the nozzles on the strap-on boosters that marred two earlier flights, in 2024 and this past February. The boosters appeared to work normally on Sunday. Instead, the trouble came later: the first stage separated from the Centaur later than expected, and telemetry showed the upper stage making unusual orientation adjustments early in its burn.

The launch had already been difficult: Friday's attempt was scrubbed after problems knocked out a plant supplying gaseous nitrogen to the pad, and Saturday's was called off over network problems between the rocket and ground systems. On Sunday, controllers held the countdown at T-minus 20 seconds over an unexplained technical issue before clearing the rocket to fly. It is not yet known whether that issue played any role in the failure.

A setback for Amazon's satellite internet plans

The mission, known as LV-01, was the first of 38 Vulcan flights Amazon has purchased to build out Leo, its satellite internet constellation and rival to SpaceX's Starlink. The 40 satellites were the largest batch Amazon has flown on one rocket, and their loss leaves the constellation waiting on ULA's investigation before it can try again on Vulcan. Amazon has also booked Leo launches on Blue Origin's New Glenn, Europe's Ariane 6 and SpaceX's Falcon 9; its next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission with 36 satellites, targeted for November 23 at the earliest.

More than 3,300 Leo satellites will be needed to complete the constellation. Sunday's flight would have pushed the total launched to date to 436.

What caused the failure is not yet publicly known. ULA said it is committed to full transparency with its customers during the investigation, and NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman offered the space agency's help with the investigation and remediation.

Sources

  • Spaceflight Now
  • GeekWire

link.title: Vulcan rocket fails minutes after liftoff, destroying 40 Amazon internet satellites

entry.title: Estonia to close all crossings with Russia on December 1 after foiled attack on drone maker
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Estonia will close every border crossing with Russia from December 1, its government announced on Sunday, after what Tallinn says was an attempted arson attack on a drone manufacturer ordered by Russian military intelligence.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced the closure in a post on X, writing that Estonia would shut "all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December" and citing what he called "clear evidence" that Russia's GRU military intelligence service had ordered the attack. He did not say how long the closure would last.

The decision follows an attempt on Saturday night to set fire to the premises of Threod Systems, a defence company in Viimsi, just north of the capital, Tallinn. The company makes reconnaissance and attack drones. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the GRU had ordered a "sabotage attempt" at the plant, adding that "extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement" and that "the attackers have been detained."

Security forces arrested eight people who live in Latvia, chief prosecutor Astrid Asi told journalists. Tsahkna said he had informed his Finnish, Latvian and Lithuanian counterparts of the closure decision.

Estonia currently has three open crossings with Russia — at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula — which admit pedestrians and freight. All three will close under the December 1 measure.

Tallinn has blamed Moscow for a pattern of sabotage against its defence industry. Michal described the weekend incident as "part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia," adding: "We will not be intimidated." Tsahkna said "Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences" and that "attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will not go unanswered."

Moscow has not commented on the latest accusations or the border decision. Russia regularly denies involvement in sabotage operations in Europe.

It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence firm that Tallinn has attributed to Russia. In August, the defence subcontractor Milrem, based in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack, and Latvian nationals were arrested.

What is still unknown

Estonia has not said when — or whether — the crossings will reopen, and no end date has been set. The government has also not released further details about the eight people detained, or the evidence behind its claim that the GRU ordered the attack. The attribution rests on the findings of Estonia's Internal Security Service and has not been independently verified.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • France 24
  • Reuters

link.title: Estonia to close all crossings with Russia on December 1 after foiled attack on drone maker

entry.title: Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly Greek Orthodox church attack
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A military-run court in Jordan sentenced three men to death on Sunday for a gun attack on a Greek Orthodox church last month that killed nine people, the Jordanian military said in a statement.

The State Security Court handed down death sentences by hanging after convicting the men on terrorism charges. They were found guilty of carrying out terrorist attacks that resulted in death, as well as weapons offences, conspiracy to commit terrorist acts and promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation.

The three men — two Jordanian brothers and a relative by marriage — fled after the attack and were arrested three days later, according to the authorities.

The attack in Karak

On October 23, gunmen stormed a funeral at St George's Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud village, in Jordan's southern Karak governorate, and opened fire. Nine people were killed and 25 wounded, Al Jazeera reported.

The shooting was one of the deadliest militant attacks in Jordan in years. King Abdullah II vowed after the attack that those responsible would face the harshest penalties.

A swift verdict

The ruling came 23 days after the attack, an unusually fast timetable for a terrorism trial. The Jordanian military announced the court's decision in a statement on Sunday, saying the State Security Court had sentenced to death "the three criminals who carried out the terrorist attack" at the church.

The verdict underscores how seriously Jordan's government has treated the attack, which struck a Christian congregation during a funeral and rattled a country that has largely been spared the kind of sectarian violence seen elsewhere in the region.

No date for the executions was announced, and the reports did not say whether the men would appeal.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Jordan sentences three men to death over deadly Greek Orthodox church attack

entry.title: Lower blood pressure target cuts heart risk after stroke, large trial finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Pushing blood pressure lower than the usual target cut the risk of further heart attacks, strokes and deaths in people who had already had a stroke, according to a large trial presented on November 7 at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago and published the same day in the New England Journal of Medicine.

The OPTIMAL-STROKE trial enrolled 4,368 adults at 30 centres in Brazil between 2019 and 2022. All had previously had an ischemic stroke or a transient ischemic attack — a brief, stroke-like episode — and had systolic blood pressure, the top number in a reading, between 130 and 180. Half were randomly assigned to intensive treatment aiming for a systolic reading below 120; the others received standard treatment targeting below 140.

Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, the intensive group averaged a systolic pressure of 122, against 135 in the standard group — a gap of about 13 points. Major cardiovascular events, a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal heart attack or stroke, or hospital admission for unstable angina or heart failure, occurred in 10.9 percent of the intensive group and 13.5 percent of the standard group, a relative reduction of about 21 percent. Strokes alone fell from 6.4 percent to 4.7 percent.

The question had been open because earlier intensive-control trials, including the landmark SPRINT study, excluded people who had already had a stroke. Current American Heart Association guidance recommends systolic pressure below 130, and below 120 for people at higher cardiovascular risk; the new results give that lower target direct evidence in stroke survivors for the first time.

The benefit came with cautions. Kidney function declined more often with intensive treatment — the composite renal outcome occurred in 3.9 percent of the intensive group versus 2.2 percent — and low blood sodium was more common. Serious adverse events overall were similar between the groups, and injurious falls were slightly less frequent with intensive treatment. The researchers said tighter control needs closer monitoring, particularly of kidney function.

What is still unknown

A twin trial in people with diabetes, OPTIMAL-DIABETES, found no significant difference between the two targets, so the benefit is not universal. Experts also noted the intensive group averaged 122 rather than actually reaching below 120, so it is not yet clear whether the specific number matters or simply getting pressure lower. Guidelines may revisit the post-stroke target, but for now the decision belongs with a patient's own doctor.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • American Heart Association
  • Medical Xpress

link.title: Lower blood pressure target cuts heart risk after stroke, large trial finds

entry.title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of the Guadalajara cartel, dies at 80
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, the trafficker known as the "Boss of Bosses" who built the Guadalajara cartel into the dominant force in Mexico's drug trade, has died in hospital in Guadalajara. He was 80.

Jalisco state security authorities said Félix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the city on November 13 and died of multiple organ failure at around 2 p.m. on Sunday, November 15. Prison police had secured the hospital where he was admitted earlier in the week.

Born in 1946 in Culiacán, Sinaloa, Félix Gallardo worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor before co-founding the Guadalajara cartel. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, he became one of the architects of Mexico's modern drug trade.

An alliance that reshaped the trade

Félix Gallardo's defining move was to forge an alliance between Mexican trafficking groups and the Colombian cartels, above all Pablo Escobar's Medellín cartel. The partnership combined cocaine production in the Andes with Mexican transport routes across the border into the United States.

At one point, an estimated 80 percent of all cocaine entering the United States came from the Medellín cartel, and Félix Gallardo's organisation played a major role in smuggling it in. At its height, the Guadalajara cartel's influence reached deep into Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships, according to the BBC.

The cartel's power began to unravel after the 1985 torture and murder of Enrique "Kiki" Camarena, an agent of the US Drug Enforcement Administration. Camarena had angered the cartel after discovering and destroying a vast marijuana plantation in Chihuahua. His death set off one of the biggest manhunts the US government has ever launched in North America.

Arrest, prison and a lasting legacy

Félix Gallardo was captured in 1989 and sentenced to decades in prison. He remained in state custody from then on, and in ill health he was placed under house arrest in 2022. A federal court later imposed a further 37-year sentence in connection with the Camarena case.

His arrest broke up the Guadalajara cartel, but the organisation he built did not disappear. In the 1980s he had introduced Joaquín "El Chapo" Guzmán to the trade and put him in charge of handling logistics. The Sinaloa cartel emerged from the break-up of Félix Gallardo's organisation, led by Guzmán, who was sentenced to life in prison in the United States in 2019.

His story later reached a wide audience when actor Diego Luna portrayed him in the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. The BBC's Will Grant wrote that his name "will echo through the annals of drug-trafficking history more than any other except perhaps Pablo Escobar's."

entry.title: Prince Harry visits wounded veterans in Lviv on unannounced Ukraine trip
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Britain's Prince Harry made an unannounced weekend visit to Ukraine, meeting wounded veterans and medics in the western city of Lviv and telling them they would win the war against Russia.

The Duke of Sussex, 42, arrived on Saturday for a two-day trip that was kept secret until he had left the country for security reasons. It was his fourth visit to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and his second this year.

In Lviv, Harry visited the Superhumans Center, a specialist clinic that treats wounded military personnel and civilians, many of whom need prosthetic limbs. He also spoke at a conference for medics organised by the clinic, where he praised the work being done for injured soldiers and acknowledged the risk of travelling to a country at war.

"You're going to win the war and then you're going to be set up for success," he told the conference on Saturday, adding that he had "taken a risk to come here."

Trials for the Invictus Games

Harry also attended Ukraine's National Invictus Games trials, watching wheelchair rugby and pickleball players compete for a place on the team for next year's games in Birmingham, England. Around 500 athletes registered to compete for the 60-member squad — the largest team Ukraine has ever planned to send to the event.

Harry founded the Invictus Games in 2014 to support wounded, injured and recovering military personnel through adaptive sport. He told veterans in Lviv that when the war is over and Ukraine wins, he would be ready to support holding an Invictus Games in the country.

During the trials he met competitors including Valery Odainyk, a leg amputee and still-serving soldier who competed at the games in Canada last year, and Kostiantyn Vlasenko, who was the first Ukrainian soldier airlifted by drone from the front lines.

A growing veteran population

Ukraine has about 1.4 million combat veterans, more than 10 percent of whom have disabilities, according to figures cited during the visit. Lviv, close to the Polish border, has become a hub for the medical treatment and rehabilitation of wounded soldiers.

Harry, a British Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, described the wounded veterans he met as role models and said they must continue to receive support from Kyiv. His visit wrapped up on Sunday, with the details of his movements only reported after he had departed.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Associated Press

link.title: Prince Harry visits wounded veterans in Lviv on unannounced Ukraine trip

entry.title: Japan's economy shrinks for the first time in a year as household spending stalls
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Japan's economy shrank in the July–September quarter, government data showed on Monday, ending a year of growth as households pulled back on spending while prices stayed high.

Gross domestic product contracted at an annualised rate of 0.1%, the first decline in four quarters. The reading missed the median market forecast of 0.3% annualised growth in a Reuters poll, and followed a revised 1.7% expansion in the previous quarter. On a quarterly basis, the economy shrank 0.02%, against expectations of a 0.1% rise.

The weakness came from consumers. Private consumption, which accounts for more than half of Japan's economic output, fell 0.3% — a sharper drop than the 0.2% decline economists had expected. Household spending was squeezed by persistent price pressures and disrupted by poor weather, including heavy rain and typhoons during the quarter. Demand for cars and air conditioners also faded after a temporary boost in the previous quarter from tax and regulatory changes.

Business investment held up

Not everything in the report pointed down. Capital spending, a key driver of private demand, rose 1.6%, slightly above the 1.5% forecast, supported by investment in labour-saving technology and artificial-intelligence-related projects. Policymakers are unlikely to read the contraction as a break in Japan's moderate recovery, with resilient corporate activity and rising real wages still underpinning growth.

Trade was the other drag. Net external demand — exports minus imports — knocked 0.6 percentage point off growth, worse than the 0.4-point drag economists had expected. Imports rose sharply as oil and other energy purchases recovered after Japan diversified its procurement following disruptions linked to the war in the Middle East.

What it means for the Bank of Japan

The data will be closely watched by the Bank of Japan as it judges whether the economy can withstand further interest-rate increases. With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflation, the central bank has tightened policy this year, raising rates in June and September.

Economists still expect only modest growth ahead. A monthly survey by the Japan Center for Economic Research of 37 economists put growth at 0.89% in fiscal 2026 and 1.02% in fiscal 2027. Longer-term challenges remain in focus too: the International Monetary Fund projects Japan will slip to the world's sixth-largest economy in nominal dollar terms in 2027, overtaken by India and Britain. Japan is currently the world's fourth-largest economy, after Germany.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNBC

link.title: Japan's economy shrinks for the first time in a year as household spending stalls

entry.title: Apple opens a 200,000-person study to learn how people actually use health AI
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Apple is taking a research-first route into health AI. The company announced on Saturday the launch of the Apple Health AI Usage Study, a virtual research project in the United States that will enrol up to 200,000 participants to find out how people ask health questions of an AI assistant — and whether the answers actually help.

The study is run in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. Participants use a dedicated study app to ask everyday health questions, as they would in a chatbot, and receive simplified answers grounded in peer-reviewed medical literature from sources including the New England Journal of Medicine, the Journal of the American Medical Association and Nature. Each response carries linked citations; participants rate the answers and take monthly surveys. They can also choose to share HealthKit data — resting heart rate, activity, sleep or lab results — so researchers can see whether personal context changes how useful the answers are.

A study, not a product launch

Apple is careful to draw a line between the study and a consumer feature. The app is not meant to diagnose or treat any condition, and participants are told to consult a doctor about health concerns or to verify medical information. Safety guardrails are designed to detect certain concerning questions and suggest following up with a provider.

"At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding," said Sumbul Desai, Apple's vice president of Health and Fitness. "Conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life."

The research is open to adults aged 21 and over in the United States who have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone — an iPhone 15 Pro or later running iOS 26 or later. Apple aims to run the study for more than 12 months. The app is available to download now for US users.

Privacy is the centrepiece

The study's privacy terms are unusually strict. Data is anonymised before it leaves the phone for a secure third-party cloud provider, it will not be used to train any AI models, and OpenEvidence deletes query and response data after 24 hours. Participants keep control over whether they share any HealthKit metrics or survey responses.

Earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking more than 300 million health-related queries each week. Apple has not said whether the capability will eventually reach its Health app or Siri — for now, the study itself is the product, and its findings are meant to guide the responsible design of health AI.

"Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds," said Robert M. Wachter, professor and chair of the Department of Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco. "When patients and doctors draw on versions of the same trustworthy tools, patients arrive prepared, conversations improve, and next steps happen seamlessly."

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Apple
  • TechCrunch

link.title: Apple opens a 200,000-person study to learn how people actually use health AI

entry.title: Asian shares fall and US futures slip ahead of Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's debut
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Asian shares fell on Monday and US stock futures slipped, as investors braced for a week that could decide whether the artificial-intelligence rally still has further to run. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday, and Anthropic — the company behind the Claude chatbot — is due to start trading on Thursday.

The selling was broad across Asia. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped 1.9%, dragged down by a 4.7% tumble in Taiwan and a 3% fall in South Korea. Japan's Nikkei fell 1.7% after data showed the economy unexpectedly shrank last quarter. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the main maker of Nvidia's AI chips, fell 4%, and China's blue-chip shares slid 0.6%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was the exception, rising 0.8%.

US futures pointed lower as well. S&P 500 futures slipped 0.2% and Nasdaq futures lost 0.4% on Monday, while European stock futures were up 0.2%.

Nvidia's first test without Huang

Tuesday's results will be Nvidia's first earnings report since the shock departure of chief executive Jensen Huang last week. The chipmaker, the poster child of a four-year US bull market, has seen its market value fall to $3.9 trillion as of Friday, from about $5.8 trillion in early October, according to LSEG data, as investors rushed for the exits.

Analysts expect earnings growth of about 90% on revenue of $109 billion in Nvidia's fiscal third quarter. But the numbers may matter less than the message: all eyes are on whether the new management, led by interim chief executive Colette Kress, will stick to the chipmaker's bullish outlook for next year. Options markets imply a move of roughly 7% in either direction on the day.

"Nvidia may well deliver another exceptional beat and raise at tomorrow's earnings, but investors are increasingly trying to value a business in FY2028 and FY2029 potentially without the individual who architected its competitive advantage," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone.

Anthropic's debut follows two days later

Trading in Anthropic is scheduled to begin on Thursday, just two days after Nvidia's results, setting up a real-time barometer for sentiment on the AI trade. The listing is expected to raise as much as $64.4 billion, at a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, according to a filing — and Reuters reported the IPO has drawn more institutional interest than SpaceX.

The week holds other tests for markets. Minutes from the US Federal Reserve's October policy meeting are due on Wednesday, and futures markets now treat a quarter-point interest rate hike next month as essentially locked in. In commodities, Brent crude fell 0.7% to $95.14 a barrel, while gold eased 0.2% to $3,872 an ounce.

For investors, the sequence is unforgiving: two verdicts on the AI trade, three days apart, with the Fed's thinking in between. By Friday, the market will know whether the rally's two biggest names still command the confidence they did a month ago.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • CNBC
