entry.title: US banks hit by outages as Chase blames a software bug
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Customers at some of the largest banks in the United States reported problems reaching their accounts and moving money on Monday afternoon, in an outage that appeared to be easing by the early evening.

JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and US Bank all drew customer complaints, with the disruption showing up in online banking, mobile apps and, in some cases, in branches and at ATMs. By 6 p.m. Eastern time, the volume of reported problems had fallen for Chase, Bank of America and US Bank.

Chase, the country's largest bank, said a software bug in its hardware systems may have been behind the glitch. The bank described the problem as temporary and said it was not systemic or cyber-related. It said some transactions were taking longer than usual, but that customers still had access to their accounts and funds. The exact nature of the bug was not clear.

Outage tracker Downdetector recorded almost 5,000 reports about Chase alone. Customers said they struggled to sign in, view balances and complete transactions, including transfers and wire transfers. One customer in Texas said she could not deposit a cheque at a Chase branch in Dallas and was told the transaction could not be completed. Another was told by a teller that the system was down.

Bank of America customers reported trouble at ATMs and with mobile banking. US Bank customers using the Zelle payment service received error messages saying payments could not be sent. Zelle said its own service was operating as it should, and that problems at other banks could affect payments. US Bank said some of its systems were not directly affected.

Customers also reported problems at Truist, PNC and Capital One, but all three told the BBC they had not been affected.

The scale of the disruption reflects how central the affected banks are to everyday American finance. Chase serves more than 86 million customers through 5,000 branches and 7.4 million small businesses, and is the top credit card issuer in the United States.

What is still unknown

Service had not been described as fully restored for all of the banks by Monday evening, and it was not clear how long the remaining problems would take to clear. Chase has not said when it expects the bug to be fully fixed.

The banking outage came on the same day as a separate technology problem at United Airlines, which disrupted departing flights for a few hours before being resolved. That outage was also described as a technology issue rather than a cybersecurity incident, and was unrelated to the banking problems or to the nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: US banks hit by outages as Chase blames a software bug

entry.title: Judge strikes down DHS rule limiting how long foreign students can stay in the US
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal judge in Boston has struck down a Trump administration rule that would have put a fixed time limit on how long international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists can stay in the United States.

U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV issued the final ruling on Monday, November 16, 2026, vacating the Department of Homeland Security rule in full. He described the policy as "arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and otherwise not in accordance with law," and granted the plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment while denying the government's.

Published in the Federal Register on July 17, 2026, the rule would have ended "duration of status" — the system under which international students have been admitted for decades for as long as they pursue their programme and maintain their status. In its place, F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors would have been admitted for fixed periods of no more than four years, and would have had to apply to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services for more time. The grace period after a programme ends would have fallen from 60 days to 30, and foreign journalists on I visas would have faced shorter stays.

The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, but Judge Saylor blocked it one day earlier, on September 14, finding that the department had failed to show a rational connection between the restrictions and their stated objectives. Monday's ruling turns that temporary pause into a final judgment on the merits.

The lawsuit was brought by a coalition of universities, educators and unions, including the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA and the American Federation of Teachers.

The judge found that the department had not properly assessed the rule's costs and benefits, had not produced enough evidence that it was needed to prevent fraud or protect national security, and had not seriously explored less restrictive alternatives — including greater use of the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), which already tracks students through their schools.

The court also rejected the department's claim of broad discretion to define a course of study, noting it would have barred extended programmes, including PhDs, joint degrees and changes of concentration. "Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," the judge wrote, adding that "the statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program."

The decision restores the status quo for students and scholars already in the country: admission for the length of their programme, with the 60-day grace period intact.

What is still unknown

The dispute is not necessarily over. The government's appeal of the September preliminary injunction remains pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit, and the administration can appeal Monday's final ruling as well. As of publication, the Department of Homeland Security had not said whether it would do so.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Economic Times

link.title: Judge strikes down DHS rule limiting how long foreign students can stay in the US

entry.title: More than 7,000 LAUSD students walk out to protest immigration raids
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

More than 7,000 students in the Los Angeles Unified School District walked out of class on Monday, November 16, 2026, to protest federal immigration enforcement operations and demand stronger protections for immigrant families.

Organisers had expected students from around 60 schools to take part, and reports indicated some schools outside the district joined as well. About 200 students walked out at Thomas Jefferson Senior High School in South Los Angeles, and dozens more at Huntington Park High School. The district itself did not immediately provide participation figures; the estimate of more than 7,000 came from a school police source.

Hundreds of students reached Los Angeles City Hall in downtown Los Angeles and marched through the surrounding streets for much of the day. More than 100 others reached Huntington Park City Hall in south-east Los Angeles County before continuing on to Pacific Boulevard.

The students called for an end to all Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and for the city and the school district to do more to protect immigrant communities. A central demand was the establishment and funding of campus "dream centers" on every campus — spaces that provide food, clothing, information on immigration law, mental health support and room for student organising. Some students at Bravo Medical Magnet High School also used the walkout to oppose reinstating the SAT and ACT as requirements for University of California admissions.

The district already operates 19 dream centers on high school campuses, funded by $5 million approved by the Los Angeles Board of Education in June 2025. In recent months it has also offered know-your-rights training, home-to-school bus pickups, alerts when immigration agents are reported near campuses, and neighbourhood patrols by staff and volunteers.

The march was described as largely peaceful, though a brief brawl broke out near the downtown Federal Building. Those involved and what caused it were not immediately clear.

Students taking part cited fear for undocumented relatives, against a backdrop of record immigration arrests and deportations reported under the Trump administration. It was not the first such action this year: thousands of students walked out in January and February over similar fears.

What is still unknown

No final participation count has been released, and the district has not said whether it will expand the dream center programme to every campus, as the students demanded. It is also unclear whether students who left class without permission will face any consequences, though California law allows an excused absence for a civic or political event when a school is notified in advance.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Los Angeles Times

link.title: More than 7,000 LAUSD students walk out to protest immigration raids

entry.title: 75 baby sea turtles reach the Pacific after California's first recorded nesting
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Seventy-five baby olive ridley sea turtles have made it into the Pacific Ocean from the first sea turtle nests ever recorded on the US West Coast, after two months of careful incubation at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.

The first 54 hatchlings came from a nest at Seal Beach and were released on the same beach in the dark early hours of Saturday, November 14. A second group of 21, from a nest near Huntington Beach Pier, followed early on Sunday morning. All of the released hatchlings reached the water.

The story began in September, when two olive ridley turtles were seen nesting on Orange County beaches — one at Seal Beach on September 16, the other near Huntington Beach Pier three days later. It was the first recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the West Coast. Until then, the northernmost known olive ridley nest was roughly 700 miles south, in Baja California Sur, Mexico.

Because a tropical storm was approaching and the nests faced high tides and flooding, biologists moved all 204 eggs — 104 from Seal Beach and 100 from Huntington Beach — to the Aquarium of the Pacific on September 25. The eggs spent 58 days in temperature- and humidity-controlled incubators under sand.

A Saturday morning eruption

Aquarium staff first noticed signs of hatching on November 12, when the sand in the Seal Beach incubation container began to crack and dip. The first turtle emerged at about 7:15 p.m. on Friday, November 13, and 54 had surfaced within about two hours.

"It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles," Dr. Lance Adams, the aquarium's director of veterinary services, said at a press conference on November 14.

The hatchlings are tiny — under two inches long, each roughly the size and weight of a large strawberry. They were released before sunrise so they could navigate toward the ocean using moonlight, then began a "frenzy period" of swimming continuously for 24 to 48 hours. About 50 eggs from the Seal Beach nest had still not hatched at the time of the press conference, and staff were continuing to monitor them. By Monday afternoon, the aquarium said 94 hatchlings had hatched and been released in total.

Why did they nest in California?

Scientists think unusually warm Pacific water is the main reason. The ongoing "super" El Niño has raised sea surface temperatures, and one theory is that the mother turtles lost their way because of a hurricane. A biologist with the US Fish and Wildlife Service also pointed to decades of conservation work: olive ridley populations have grown substantially, putting more turtles along the California coast to take advantage of the unusual conditions.

Olive ridleys are the smallest sea turtle species, growing to about two to three feet long and weighing 70 to 100 pounds as adults. They can live for 50 years, but only about one in a thousand hatchlings survives to adulthood.

A third nest was found on November 1 at San Buenaventura State Beach in Ventura County, about 100 miles north, but it was destroyed by high tides.

What is still unknown

Scientists do not yet know whether the California nests are a one-off event or the start of a new pattern. DNA testing of shell fragments is planned to identify which Mexican breeding colonies the mother turtles came from, and staff are still watching the remaining eggs to see how many more hatch.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • Smithsonian Magazine

link.title: 75 baby sea turtles reach the Pacific after California's first recorded nesting

entry.title: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Russian ballistic missiles struck two of Kyiv's main bridges overnight, the city's mayor said, in an attack that damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted water, power and heating supplies in parts of the Ukrainian capital.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, which span the Dnipro River, had been hit. Loud explosions were heard across the city shortly before midnight, and Klitschko said soon afterwards that infrastructure systems had been damaged. Some of the city's above-ground subway services were also damaged, officials said, after residents were told to take shelter in civil defence shelters. Kyiv's underground stations are routinely used as shelters during air raids.

No casualties were reported in the capital from the bridge strikes themselves. Three people were injured in a separate Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

Why the bridges matter

Eight major bridges cross the Dnipro, linking western and eastern Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on them. Several were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October.

A day after the largest drone attack

The strikes came a day after Russia said it had faced the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began. Russian officials said the military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours. Moscow's mayor was cited as saying around 600 drones flew toward the Russian capital alone.

The attack also followed a round of online talks between Ukrainian, US and European officials aimed at ending the war. President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned earlier that Moscow might launch further strikes on Monday night. In an address on Monday evening, he described the talks meeting as "difficult" and said Moscow was receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.

US envoy Jared Kushner said after Monday's meeting that Washington was committed to providing Ukraine with "strong, credible security guarantees" and a path toward EU membership, with preparations under way for a further multilateral meeting. Zelensky said Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will take part in negotiations with Moscow.

Elsewhere overnight, the Moscow-installed governor in Crimea said Ukraine had struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea again, for a second consecutive day, and that traffic across the bridge had been suspended. The severity of the latest strike on that bridge was still unclear.

What is still unknown

The BBC report did not say how badly the two Kyiv bridges were damaged, whether either crossing is closed, or how long repairs might take. It also did not report casualties in Kyiv from the overnight attack. Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022; about a fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation, and Kyiv has refused Moscow's demand to give up areas of the eastern Donbas that remain under Ukrainian control.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says

entry.title: Ukraine says second strike on aid shelter killed 72 as rescuers came under fire
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

At least 72 people were killed in the Ukrainian village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November, Ukrainian officials say, after a second strike hit a shelter where residents had fled following an initial attack on a humanitarian aid distribution. Ukraine says rescue workers were then struck repeatedly as they tried to reach the survivors.

Local people had gathered at the aid centre after a message in a local Telegram group said food and supplies would be handed out between 10:00 and 12:00. Ukrainian authorities say the first strike came at 09:45, hitting buildings above ground and killing one woman. About an hour later, a second strike hit the underground shelter where people had taken cover. Ukraine says it involved a 3,000 kg aerial bomb.

Police bodycam footage examined by BBC Verify shows people freeing a casualty after the first strike, radio warnings of a second attack growing more urgent, and people running for the shelter before a large explosion. Later footage shows bodies being recovered from a large crater above the shelter.

Rescue workers 'hit again'

Ukraine's State Emergency Service told BBC Verify there were several Russian strikes during the rescue operation, injuring three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs and damaging five vehicles. Work had to be suspended repeatedly because of the threat of further shelling, the service said.

An intelligence officer investigating the incident, identified only as Oleksiy, said the rescue vehicles were clearly marked and accused Russia of deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment and of terror against civilians. BBC Verify confirmed Ukrainian police videos showing rescue workers shouting warnings about a drone and running for cover the day after the attack.

Bomb disposal expert Trevor Ball and former UK National Crime Agency investigator Chris Proops both said the crater and damage were consistent with a FAB-3000, a 3,000 kg Russian bomb capable of destroying underground structures. Both also confirmed that verified photographs of munition fragments obtained from Ukrainian authorities show part of a glide-bomb guidance kit compatible with the weapon.

What Russia has said

BBC Verify said it asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks and received no response. A general ministry statement on 2 November said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

The article notes there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha, but that the village lies close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations, and that it had previously been reported struck on 28 October.

International law experts Ben Saul of the University of Sydney and Samuel Moyn of Yale told BBC Verify that knowingly attacking rescue workers or civilians would be a war crime or a gross violation of international humanitarian law — stated conditionally, as an assessment of the law rather than a finding on this incident.

What is still unknown

The death toll may still change: bodies were still being recovered from the rubble, and funerals have been held almost daily for aid workers, people collecting aid, and soldiers officials say came to help with the rescue. The casualty figure and the account of strikes during the rescue come from Ukrainian authorities, and the claim that rescuers were deliberately targeted is Ukraine's allegation, not a BBC finding. The toll would make it one of the deadliest single incidents since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Ukraine says second strike on aid shelter killed 72 as rescuers came under fire

entry.title: Third U.S. carrier reaches the Gulf as Iran warns shipping and a tanker is hit in Hormuz
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Gulf, sharpening a nine-month standoff with Iran, as Tehran steps up threats against U.S. forces and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt entered the region on Sunday, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington. Three carrier strike groups in one theatre is an unusually large concentration of American naval power, with more than 50,000 U.S. personnel now in the region, per The Wall Street Journal.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy warned shipping companies off the U.S.-backed southern route through the strait, calling it fully closed and a "minefield of fire." Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia said the strait would not reopen until "the enemy accepts Iran's conditions."

A tanker struck

On Tuesday, the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations agency said a tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Strait of Hormuz and subsequently caught fire. The agency did not say who was responsible and urged vessels to transit with caution. No casualties were reported. Security monitor Vanguard identified the vessel as the Panama-flagged ON PHOENIX, struck three nautical miles off Oman.

Separately, the Iranian navy said four oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire in the eastern strait over the previous 24 hours. Those claims could not be independently verified. Iran has also said it will not allow inspectors into its damaged nuclear sites until the conflict ends.

The escalation follows an Iranian drone attack on Sunday against a U.S. air-defence radar at Bahrain's Riffa air base — the second attack Iran has claimed against the kingdom in three days. Bahrain said it intercepted several of the attacks, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned them on Monday.

CNN also reported new U.S. intelligence indicating Iran was developing plans that could target senior Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington. CNBC said it could not immediately verify the report, and CNN characterised it as developing options rather than evidence of an imminent attack. The White House said there were "no credible threats to the homeland."

Mixed signals from Washington

President Donald Trump has sent mixed signals, alternating between declaring the war could soon end and warning of renewed large-scale strikes if talks fail. The conflict began in late February, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran; indirect talks through Qatar have since appeared to stall.

Ian Bremmer of Eurasia Group said Iran was likely to keep disrupting shipping to pressure Washington into concessions, while Washington would probably expand its blockade of Iran's trade routes. Brent crude slipped 0.7% in Asian trading, to $91.8 a barrel.

What is still unknown

It is not yet known who fired the projectile that struck the tanker, or whether the mine strikes claimed by Iran's navy took place as described — or whether the third carrier's deployment signals preparation for renewed strikes or deterrence while talks stall.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • The National

link.title: Third U.S. carrier reaches the Gulf as Iran warns shipping and a tanker is hit in Hormuz

entry.title: Crimea bridge closed after reported Ukrainian strike as Kyiv crossings shut
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The bridge linking Crimea with Russia has been closed after reports of a Ukrainian strike, in an overnight exchange that also shut two of Kyiv's main crossings over the Dnipro River.

Crimea's Moscow-backed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed on Telegram that traffic across the bridge had been suspended. Images circulating online, shared by a former adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, purport to show a section of the span collapsed into the water, but the BBC said it had not independently verified them, and the full extent of the damage remained unclear on Tuesday morning. Russian state media reported that officials were due to meet during the day to discuss the situation.

The reported strike came a day after Ukraine began its latest attempt to disable the crossing. Two people were killed in a strike overnight on Sunday, at the start of that attempt, according to the Russian-installed governor.

Built by Russia after its annexation of Crimea in 2014 and opened by President Vladimir Putin in 2018, the bridge is both a supply route and a potent symbol of the occupation. It has been attacked repeatedly during the war and is protected by layers of air and sea defences.

Kyiv crossings hit

In the Ukrainian capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges — two of the eight major spans carrying about three million residents across the Dnipro — were closed after Russian ballistic missile strikes.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv shortly before midnight. Klitschko said the strikes damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted heating and water supplies, and officials said some above-ground subway services were also affected after residents were told to take shelter.

Three people were injured in a separate Russian missile attack in the Cherkasy region, according to local officials.

Diplomacy continues

The exchange came as diplomats pressed on with efforts to end the war. President Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the run-up to a meeting of the Chinese, US and Russian leaders in Shenzhen on Thursday.

After talks on Monday between US, Ukrainian and European officials, US envoy Jared Kushner said Washington was committed to strong, credible security guarantees for Ukraine and a path toward EU membership, adding that NATO would remain a critical pillar of European security. Zelensky described the meeting as "difficult" and said more was needed to defend against Russian ballistic missile strikes, which he said were being supplied by North Korea.

What is still unknown

It is not yet confirmed how badly the Crimea bridge has been damaged, how long it will stay closed, or precisely what struck it. The images said to show the collapsed section remain unverified, and neither side has given a full account of the overnight exchange.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Crimea bridge closed after reported Ukrainian strike as Kyiv crossings shut

entry.title: BMI alone misses millions of obesity cases, major study finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Body-mass index, the height-and-weight formula doctors have used for decades to diagnose obesity, is missing millions of people who have the condition — and wrongly labelling millions more, according to a large international study published in the journal Nature.

The research compared BMI-only diagnosis against a newer framework across 844,108 adults in four groups covering China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain. BMI alone missed obesity in up to 8.6 percent of participants, while wrongly classifying up to 3.1 percent as having obesity when they did not meet the newer criteria. Scaled up, the authors say, that is millions of people with the wrong diagnosis.

BMI divides a person's weight by their height squared, and it has long been criticised as too blunt an instrument: it cannot tell muscle from fat, and it says nothing about where fat sits in the body or whether it is doing harm. The newer framework, put forward by experts in 2025, keeps BMI as a starting point but adds waist circumference, waist-to-height ratio and body fat scans, and checks for signs of organ damage or difficulty with everyday activities.

Two kinds of obesity

A central part of the new approach is the split between clinical obesity, in which excess fat is actively damaging organs, and preclinical obesity, in which a person carries excess fat but it has not yet begun to harm bodily functions.

The study found that up to a third of obesity cases were clinical — an active disease that should be treated as such, according to Francesco Rubino, a bariatric surgery consultant at King's College London who led the work. Most people with preclinical obesity remained free of clinical obesity for a decade.

The difference matters for survival. Being clinically obese was associated with a 69 percent higher risk of dying during follow-up periods of more than a decade, compared with 19 percent for preclinical obesity — a gap that traditional BMI diagnosis would not flag.

"Preclinical obesity should therefore be neither treated automatically as active disease nor dismissed as harmless," Rubino said. "Some people may need preventive treatment, but its intensity should match their individual risk."

What could change

If the framework is adopted more widely, the researchers say treatments such as GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could be directed to the people who genuinely need them, rather than to everyone classified as obese under BMI rules.

There are caveats. Some outside experts have questioned whether the ethnicity-specific thresholds used are the best global definition, and the study relied on diagnostic codes as stand-ins for organ damage rather than direct clinical assessments. The team is planning further studies to refine the techniques and test how the criteria work in practice.

"The marked differences in prognosis between clinical and preclinical obesity, consistently observed across countries and ethnic groups, support global adoption of the new framework," said epidemiologist An Pan of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in China, a co-author of the study.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceAlert

link.title: BMI alone misses millions of obesity cases, major study finds

entry.title: School cellphone bans show small learning gains, new study finds — but it's complicated
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Strict bans on mobile phones in schools are linked to small but measurable improvements in pupils' test scores, according to a large new study — though the researchers themselves, and outside experts, warn the picture is far from settled.

The study, a joint effort by Harvard University's Center for Education Policy Research, Dartmouth College and the testing organisation NWEA, looked at more than 3 million elementary, middle and high school students over the past five school years. It compared student-level maths and reading scores at 844 schools that use Yondr lockable phone pouches with similar schools that did not adopt them. More than 3,300 schools across the United States began using the pouches between the 2019–20 and 2025–26 school years.

The researchers found that the strictest bans — phones locked away in pouches for the whole school day — were associated with gains equivalent to one to two weeks of extra learning per year. Co-author Tom Kane of Harvard framed the result as plugging about half of the estimated two to three weeks of learning lost each year since around 2013. The gains did not fade after the first year, the study found, and appeared to continue for up to three years after a school adopted the pouches.

The cost is part of the pitch. Kane put the price of the pouches at roughly $25 per student — far less, he argued, than paying teachers for an extra week or two of instruction.

The caveats

The new study has not been peer-reviewed, and it arrives alongside a very different result. An earlier peer-reviewed study published in April, by a team including Brian Jacob of the University of Michigan and Tom Dee of Stanford, pooled school-level average scores from several thousand Yondr schools and found close to zero overall impact, with no statistically significant benefit. That study did find significant gains in high school maths, but they were offset by learning losses in middle school.

The two teams used different methods: the new study worked with finer-grained student-level data from fewer schools, while the April study used school-level averages from a much larger group. Dee cautioned against extrapolating the new study's small, sensitive estimates over just a few years of bans, describing the early results as largely disappointing and saying continued study is needed. Jacob said the new findings were encouraging if the benefit persists and accumulates — but "we'll just have to wait and see."

For schools and districts weighing a ban, the evidence now points in the same direction but with different force: locked-away phones may buy a little learning back, at modest cost, yet the size of that gain — and whether it lasts — is still an open question.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NPR

link.title: School cellphone bans show small learning gains, new study finds — but it's complicated

entry.title: Trump lands in Manila to open Asia trip, with trade deals and a Xi–Putin summit ahead
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, opening a three-day Asia trip that mixes trade deals and alliance meetings with a planned three-way summit in China alongside Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Manila, the Philippine capital, is the first stop. The visit is Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in the midterm elections, and it comes as the White House contends with the fallout from the departure of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and a major disruption to the United States aviation industry.

After landing, Trump met the leaders of the Quad — the United States, Australia, India and Japan — for the first time since his return to the White House. The group will conduct an exercise featuring maritime patrol aircraft and launch an accelerator to speed the development of artificial intelligence, the president announced.

On Tuesday evening, Trump is the guest of honour at a gala for the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Before the dinner, he will join a special summit with ASEAN leaders to discuss deeper trade and security ties, the long-running violence in Myanmar and disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims almost in its entirety. ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China over the contested waters, where clashes between Chinese and Philippine forces have escalated in recent years.

Trade deals on the agenda

Trump is scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, one of the agreements he has pursued since launching a trade war last year. Under a framework announced last October, Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, while spending more than $18 billion on American aircraft and buying farm goods and liquefied natural gas.

The deal follows a winding path. The United States Supreme Court overturned in February the 19 per cent tariff Trump had placed on goods from Thailand; the administration then sought replacement tariffs in July, levying a 12.5 per cent tax on Thai imports for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labour.

Protests in Manila

About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from Washington. They waved red flags and held a large streamer reading "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" and planned to burn an effigy of Trump, as riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby. Nearly 23,000 police personnel and other law enforcers, including SWAT teams, were deployed to secure the ASEAN summit.

On Wednesday, Trump receives a red-carpet welcome and full military honours from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet at the Malacañang presidential palace. From Manila, he heads to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and the three-way nuclear talks with Xi and Putin. He has also said a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un is possible, though nothing has been confirmed.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News

link.title: Trump lands in Manila to open Asia trip, with trade deals and a Xi–Putin summit ahead

entry.title: Options traders brace for a $335 billion swing in Nvidia after earnings
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Options traders are pricing in a roughly $335 billion swing in Nvidia's market value after the chipmaker reports third-quarter earnings on Tuesday afternoon — the latest sign of how much uncertainty now hangs over the world's most closely watched stock.

The options market implies an 8.5% move in either direction on Wednesday, the day after results, according to Susquehanna. That is more than double Nvidia's average post-earnings move over the past eight quarters, and only just short of the 8.74% jump that followed its previous report. The implied swing is larger than the entire market value of about 90% of the companies in the S&P 500.

Nvidia arrives at earnings in the middle of a steep slide. Its market value stood at about $3.9 trillion on Friday, down from roughly $5.8 trillion in early October, according to LSEG data. Shares fell a further 4% on Monday and are down nearly 17% this year, while the S&P 500 is up 8% over the same period.

A leadership crisis on top of a market one

The selloff accelerated after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned last week, following reports that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and with a subordinate at the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor.

President Donald Trump has said he would not oppose Huang's return, and a petition calling for him to come back has gathered more than 178,000 signatures, including from prominent Silicon Valley executives. But Nvidia's board is not weighing a return for Huang, three people told Reuters.

Investors have responded by trimming their holdings ahead of earnings — while continuing to buy call options and call spreads, contracts that would pay off if the stock rebounds, said Chris Murphy, co-head of derivatives strategy at Susquehanna. "Earnings are the main catalyst over the next three days, but that pricing also captures ongoing headline risk — including new company developments and Trump comments — rather than earnings alone," he said.

What investors will be listening for

Sentiment toward chipmakers and the AI infrastructure buildout has turned negative, with rising borrowing costs and concern that growth in the sector could slow after Democrats swept the midterm elections. The question now is whether Nvidia can reassure the market that demand for AI infrastructure remains strong.

"It will be forward-looking statements about the order book, customers possibly canceling and pushing out, whether data center regulatory issues mean that data centers are going to take longer than we thought," said Chris Grisanti, chief market strategist at MAI Capital Management.

Grisanti added that the underlying case for the stock may be simpler than the noise suggests: "There's less here than meets the eye, in the sense of data center growth will continue in '27. Nvidia is the monopoly provider of chips, and it's not hard to connect the dots to a higher stock price with those two things."

What is still unknown

Tuesday's report is the company's first since Huang's departure, and the first earnings call led by Kress. Whether the numbers and guidance are enough to steady a stock that has lost nearly a third of its value from its October peak — or whether the options market's big swing materialises to the downside — will be clear by Wednesday's open.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Options traders brace for a $335 billion swing in Nvidia after earnings

entry.title: US confirms criminal investigation into Megaspeed over Nvidia chips bound for China
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The US government has confirmed it is investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based computing firm suspected of helping advanced Nvidia AI chips reach China despite American export controls.

In a joint statement on Monday, the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce said the investigation was under way and that it was in the public interest to provide an update. The departments said the government would pursue the matter to the full extent of the law, describing semiconductors as among the most valuable and strategic technologies.

Megaspeed is described as the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia. US officials suspect the company of diverting high-end AI chips to China, in breach of controls Washington imposed to limit Beijing's access to the most advanced semiconductors.

The investigation began in 2024 over potential export-control breaches, according to the BBC. In May 2025, Commerce Department investigators asked Nvidia for records about direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security later acted alongside Singaporean law-enforcement officers, after which the Justice Department took the lead in the criminal investigation.

A scandal that has already cost Nvidia its chief

The confirmation comes days after the resignation of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, who stepped down as chief executive last week after revelations about two affairs, including one allegedly with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, including the House Select Committee on China.

The case has also exposed a rift inside the US government. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday blamed the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to oversee the chip exports properly. Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month.

The White House said on Monday that it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms such as Nvidia.

What is still unknown

No monetary figures or chip quantities were given in the announcement, and Megaspeed itself was not quoted in the BBC report. A related report notes the company saying the suspected spy left the firm in 2025. Singapore does not prohibit transferring advanced AI chips to companies abroad, but such transfers can still breach US export controls — and it is that gap, rather than Singaporean law, that the US investigation is testing.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News

link.title: US confirms criminal investigation into Megaspeed over Nvidia chips bound for China

entry.title: Congo Ebola deaths climb at twice West Africa's pace as outbreak passes six months
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Six months after Ebola was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the outbreak is not slowing down — it is accelerating. Infections and deaths are rising at double the rate recorded in the first six months of the West African epidemic of 2014–16, the largest Ebola outbreak ever seen, according to government data reported by Reuters.

More than 11,000 people have been infected and more than 5,500 have died since the outbreak was declared on May 15. It is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record anywhere in the world, and the deadliest of the 17 that Congo has faced. The virus is the rare Bundibugyo species, for which there are no approved vaccines or treatments. Congo's previous largest outbreak, in 2018–20, ended with 3,481 cases and 2,299 deaths — figures this outbreak has already left far behind.

Why it is not under control

The response is struggling on several fronts at once. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80 per cent of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections are never tracked by the authorities. The virus had already been circulating undetected before the outbreak was announced: 43 deaths had been recorded by the time of the declaration in mid-May.

Insecurity is a major obstacle. Health workers, vehicles and surveillance teams have come under attack in communities that distrust outsiders, and the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières says vital resources and supplies still are not reaching hot spots outside the original epicentre in Ituri province. Health workers have gone on strike over conditions and unpaid salaries, and some have not been paid since August, officials say. Some $2.9 billion has been pledged for the response, but less than half of it has been disbursed, according to Africa CDC.

Children hit hardest

Children have borne a disproportionate share of the toll. According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35 per cent of deaths recorded through November 4. Children under five made up 21 per cent of all deaths, and nearly 72 per cent of infected children in that age group died. Experts say most affected children have not received specialised care, and that pre-existing conditions such as malnutrition have made them more vulnerable.

Public health experts cited by the Associated Press said there was little chance of bringing the outbreak under control within the next year. On its current course, the death toll is on track to surpass the roughly 11,000 people who died in the West African epidemic.

For the wider world, the risk remains low: Ebola is not airborne and spreads only through direct contact with the bodily fluids of a sick person. But inside Congo, six months in, the outbreak is still growing faster than any before it — and the response is still catching up.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Associated Press

link.title: Congo Ebola deaths climb at twice West Africa's pace as outbreak passes six months

entry.title: Bessent and Lutnick clash over Nvidia chip curbs as White House split spills into public view
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The White House's split over China policy broke into the open on Monday, as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick fought publicly over how far the United States should go in cutting off China's access to advanced Nvidia chips.

Just hours after the White House ordered the Commerce Department to crack down on a loophole that allegedly allows Chinese companies to remotely access the chips, President Donald Trump softened the move, telling reporters as he left for Asia that he understood "both sides" of the debate.

"If you did do something, you could have a blow-up with China," Trump said on Monday morning.

Trump's reluctance to settle the question underscores the deep divisions inside his administration — and leaves unresolved a power struggle among his top economic advisers over how far to go in restricting Beijing's access to the technology fuelling the artificial intelligence race.

At the centre of the fight are Bessent and Lutnick, two of Trump's closest economic aides, who have sparred over the scope of export controls on Nvidia's most advanced processors. Bessent has publicly criticised the Commerce Department for not taking a tougher approach, saying other agencies pushed for restrictions but that "Commerce has the pen." Trump had previously directed Lutnick to pursue restrictions, according to The Washington Post, but the Commerce chief resisted, arguing a crackdown would risk a trade war with China. The rivalry between the two men extends back to the presidential transition.

The fight flared with a new federal rule aimed at closing the remote-access loophole — the latest flashpoint in the scandal that led to the ouster of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang last week.

Nvidia's board is investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, after reports of his close relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence officials believe passed information to China. Alice Huang is not related to Jensen Huang. Beijing has called the accusations groundless, and the Justice Department has said it has reached no conclusions.

Congress has widened its own inquiry. Three Republican House committee chairmen have asked Huang to attend a closed-door interview on December 1, with Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter due the following day; the Senate Banking Committee has separately sought testimony from Huang and Lutnick. Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee have written to Lutnick demanding a halt to advanced chip exports and answers by December 1 on what senior officials knew.

Huang's ties to Trump have coincided with several favourable policy decisions for Nvidia, including a decision in April 2025 to back off restricting exports of certain Nvidia chips to China, and a December 2025 decision to allow exports of its H200 processors with a 25 percent fee. Trump has defended Huang, saying he believes the chief executive did not know the businesswoman was a suspected spy.

Trump has not said which side he will back, and the December hearings will test how much the administration knew about Megaspeed and when.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Washington Post
  • Rappler

link.title: Bessent and Lutnick clash over Nvidia chip curbs as White House split spills into public view

entry.title: US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Washington has moved to close one of the last open routes by which Chinese firms gain access to advanced American chips, announcing new interim rules that put data-centre operators across South East Asia and Brazil under US licensing controls.

Under the rules, firms in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil will need a US licence before buying advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. Licences will be decided case by case, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said, warning the five countries present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion to China.

The controls go beyond physical exports to target access to computing power itself: Chinese companies have increasingly rented capacity in overseas data centres to train AI models, after earlier US export bans cut off direct supplies. The Bureau said the measures aim to stop sensitive US technology being circumvented through remote computing arrangements in third countries.

The announcement lands as the Megaspeed affair continues to reverberate. The Singaporean data-centre firm, the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia, is accused of smuggling chips to Chinese companies. Megaspeed denies the allegations, calls its business legitimate and lawful, and says it has hired external lawyers to investigate. Its former director Alice Huang, suspected by US officials of passing information to China, left the firm last year. The scandal intensified after Nvidia chief Jensen Huang admitted an affair with her and resigned.

The stakes are large. The US-based Institute for Progress projects that at least 30 percent of China's advanced AI computing power will come from rented overseas capacity or smuggled chips in 2027, and estimates the best American AI models lead their Chinese rivals by only about six and a half months.

Reactions split along familiar lines. China's foreign ministry called the rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing would take the necessary steps to protect its interests. Singapore said it was talking to US authorities to understand the rules and keep trusted access for local firms. Brazil said it was closely monitoring developments, while Malaysia has said it will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls. The BBC said it had contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.

Analysts cautioned that the region's data-centre boom is unlikely to stop. Trade expert Naoise McDonagh of Edith Cowan University said Malaysia and Thailand, where the build-out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers, could be hit hardest. Reema Bhattacharya of Verisk Maplecroft said investment backed by major tech firms should stay relatively resilient — but the rules have taken away one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to frontier computing power.

The rules come just as President Donald Trump heads to China to meet President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week. Tighter controls may also push Chinese firms further toward domestic semiconductors, a field Beijing has made a national priority. No start date for the new licensing regime has been stated.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News

link.title: US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China

entry.title: Anthropic wins Nasdaq approval as its blockbuster IPO looks set to price above range
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic has been cleared to list its shares on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT, according to a regulatory filing on Tuesday, taking the artificial-intelligence company a step closer to one of the largest public offerings on record — with reports suggesting it could price above its marketed range.

The Economic Times reported the approval, citing the filing, and said the proposed price range of $70 to $78 a share is unchanged. The offering covers 825 million Class A shares. At the top of the range it would raise about $64 billion, with a further $26 billion coming through a concurrent private placement.

Demand has been running far ahead of supply. Bloomberg News reported that bids for the shares total nearly seven times the number on offer, and that Anthropic is giving priority to existing investors when allocating shares, meaning some new buyers may get smaller holdings than they asked for.

CNBC reported on Tuesday, citing multiple sources, that Anthropic is likely to price above the $70-to-$78 range. The company planned to close its order books at 4 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday to lock in total demand, with the final price expected to be set on Wednesday and trading to begin on Thursday.

At $78 a share, Anthropic would be valued at about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis — up from the $965 billion valuation set in a private funding round in May.

The filing shows that growth in stark terms. Revenue for the nine months to the end of September reached $33.24 billion, roughly 1,200 percent higher than the same period last year, driven in large part by demand for Claude Code, its coding tool. The annualised revenue run rate hit $81 billion by October 31, up $10 billion in a single month.

The same filing shows the other side of the ledger. Anthropic posted a net loss of $104 billion over the nine months, against $25.1 billion a year earlier, largely from changes in the value of convertible notes and derivatives as its valuation rose. It also faces about $71 billion of commitments falling due in the year to September 30, 2027, mostly for computing capacity and semiconductors.

The private placement is part of the same bet: AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC have committed to buy $26 billion of a separate class of shares at the final IPO price. The money is earmarked for general corporate purposes, including computing capacity, AI infrastructure and hiring.

Anthropic has been courting investors in the run-up to pricing, including a livestreamed conversation on Friday between chief executive Dario Amodei and JPMorgan chief Jamie Dimon. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, who attended in person, told Bloomberg he was impressed, calling Amodei "a very thoughtful, measured CEO."

Nothing is final until Wednesday evening, when the price is set. But with the books nearly seven times covered, the year's biggest AI listing is already taking shape.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Economic Times
