entry.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge, sending a section of the Crimea link into the sea
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge before dawn on Tuesday, collapsing a section of its road span into the sea in what Kyiv described as its most significant attack yet on the link between Russia and occupied Crimea.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the operation "unprecedented", saying Ukrainian forces had spent weeks wearing down Russian air defences around the bridge before bombarding it overnight. Ukraine's General Staff said an arch and a span of the road section had collapsed, severing the road link, while the railway line was still standing, though its arch was damaged.

"The symbol of the occupation has cracked," the General Staff said in a statement.

The 19-kilometre bridge, opened by Vladimir Putin in 2018, is the only bridge connecting Crimea — illegally annexed by Russia in 2014 — to the Russian mainland, and a key supply route to the peninsula. A graphic published by The New York Times, based on imagery from the Ukrainian Security Service, showed a collapsed section of about 700 feet, with debris in the water below.

Zelenskyy said the attack was the seventh and final stage of an operation carried out over several weeks: Ukrainian forces first knocked out air-defence systems, radars and electronic-warfare equipment, then domestically developed long-range drones struck the road section and Neptune missiles targeted the rail section, with Flamingo precision-guided missiles delivering the final blow.

Russia confirmed the attack. Its Investigative Committee said drones had struck the bridge and caused damage, without elaborating. Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea, said traffic was halted but rail traffic had been restored by Tuesday afternoon. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would be restored, "even better than it was before".

It is the latest in a series of Ukrainian attempts to destroy the bridge: a truck bomb in 2022, unmanned naval vessels in 2023, and explosives planted on its undersea supports two years later — none of which put it out of action for long.

Timing, and a night of strikes in both directions

The attack came two days before Putin is due to meet Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday, where the war in Ukraine is expected to be discussed. Trump has said he plans to raise the war with both leaders.

The same night, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at two of Kyiv's main bridges over the Dnipro, killing at least two people in the capital, according to Zelenskyy. Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight — the second straight night of record interception claims.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • Associated Press

link.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge, sending a section of the Crimea link into the sea

entry.title: NASA's Curiosity finds 'potato chip' crystals on Mars — and drills in for answers
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

NASA's Curiosity rover has found something odd in the rocks of Mars: crystal forms shaped like potato chips. The rover drilled into the bedrock at a site nicknamed "Nazca" to collect samples, and scientists are now working out what the shapes are made of — and what they reveal about the planet's watery past.

The find was reported in NASA's Curiosity mission blog on November 11. The site is an area of bedrock "containing disk-shaped (or, in a liberal interpretation, potato-chip shaped) crystal forms," the blog said. One of the mission's key objectives, it added, is to "better characterize these chip-shaped features."

The formations are small — close-up images taken by the rover's hand-lens camera from just inches away show irregular, curled shapes embedded in the rock. Early thinking among the team is that they may be pseudomorphs: later minerals that replaced the original crystals while keeping their shape. How those first crystals grew, and in what kind of environment, is still an open question.

Drilling in for chemistry

Curiosity spent last week completing its drill campaign at Nazca, on the slopes of Mount Sharp, the mountain it has been climbing since 2014. Samples from the drill hole were delivered to the rover's onboard laboratory, the Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument, which can read the chemical makeup of Martian rock.

The rover also aimed its laser instrument, ChemCam, at crystal formations nicknamed "Colca" and "Ahi Veremos" to probe their chemistry from a distance, and photographed the shapes at night with its hand-lens camera under white-light and ultraviolet lamps.

The shapes matter because crystal forms can record history. Disk-shaped minerals often grow where water once flowed, so the chips may hold clues to a wetter Mars — but scientists are waiting for the SAM results before claiming more.

Polygons up ahead

Curiosity has already moved on. In its latest update, published November 17, the mission team described nearby rocks crisscrossed with small, regular polygons ringed by raised ridges. Patterns like these can form when minerals lose water, when temperatures cycle, or when buried rock is compacted and then exposed again — each a clue to how Mars' habitability changed over time.

The rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2012, will keep climbing Mount Sharp, documenting the chemistry and textures of the rocks it meets. From orbit, the layers ahead look much like the polygon fields it has just crossed. As the mission's deputy project scientist put it, after more than 5,000 Martian days of exploring, "Mars is full of surprises."

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Fox News
  • NASA Science

link.title: NASA's Curiosity finds 'potato chip' crystals on Mars — and drills in for answers

entry.title: FAA halts new router rollout as ground-stop inquiry continues
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Federal Aviation Administration has paused the installation of new telecommunications routers across its air-traffic network while investigators determine how a routine equipment upgrade triggered Friday's nationwide ground stop.

The pause, first reported by The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday and confirmed by the FAA to CNN, halts the rollout of Juniper routers that contractor L3Harris Technologies has been installing to replace the agency's ageing copper-wire communications system. The FAA said it had also disabled a broadcasting function on the routers involved — and on more than 60 others — as a precaution.

The FAA said it believed disabling that function had addressed the initial cause of the disruption.

Four hours on the ground

Friday's failure held departing flights across the country for more than four hours and led to more than 10,000 cancellations. It was the longest nationwide halt to US flight departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks. Pilots reported static and interference before the FAA ordered the ground stop at 3:47 p.m. Eastern.

Federal officials have traced the breakdown to a router installed by L3Harris at a radio transmitter site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the device flooded the FAA's communications network, overwhelming other routers and disrupting radio and radar feeds. He said the router was making about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. A second site, a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, was also identified as a source of excess network traffic.

In all, the failure affected communications and radar feeds at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route air-traffic control centres.

Defect or configuration?

Investigators have not yet determined whether the router was defective or improperly configured. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, the parent company of Juniper Networks, said its equipment was working as configured. L3Harris says it is cooperating, and the FBI said on Tuesday it was working with the Department of Transportation, the FAA and L3Harris. Duffy said investigators had found no evidence of a cyberattack or foreign interference.

The pause follows a letter on Tuesday from 13 Democratic senators on the Senate Commerce Committee, led by Maria Cantwell, asking the FAA to halt its plan to replace thousands of routers until the investigation is complete. The senators questioned whether the equipment had been adequately tested and why backup systems failed. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote.

The scale of the programme underlines what is now on hold: L3Harris plans to convert 3,648 routers to Juniper devices, with 400 installed so far and 69 operational. More than 60 had been installed since July without major problems before Friday's daytime installation triggered disruption shortly after 3 p.m. Eastern.

Duffy is separately seeking $50 billion from Congress to overhaul the nation's air-traffic control system, a request President Donald Trump has also backed. For now, the FAA says it is assessing the configuration and performance of all the infrastructure involved.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • CNN

link.title: FAA halts new router rollout as ground-stop inquiry continues

entry.title: Iran's third strike on Bahrain in five days ends Gulf lull as US hits back
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Iran fired drones at a US radar installation in Bahrain on Tuesday, the third Iranian attack on American military targets in the Persian Gulf kingdom in five days — and the United States answered hours later with a strike of its own.

The exchange broke a roughly two-month lull in fighting in a war that began on February 28, when the US and Israel attacked Iran. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the drones. The US military said the attack caused no damage to American equipment and no injuries to American personnel.

Hours later, a US fighter jet struck a missile launch site on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, belonging to Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, a US official said. The official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations, said "precision munitions" were used and that the US was responding to "aggression" toward its personnel. A local official, Ahmad Nafisi, said the strike caused no damage to residential or commercial areas or infrastructure.

A week of strikes

Tuesday's attack followed two earlier ones. On Friday, Iran targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain, and on Sunday it fired at a radar system at an American helicopter base there. Iran said it was retaliating for US strikes on Iranian communications towers and ongoing drone surveillance.

Why the lull ended

Analysts say the renewed attacks reflect mounting pressure on Tehran. Iran has been living under a US-enforced naval blockade in and around the Strait of Hormuz, which is curbing the flow of Iranian crude and damaging its economy. Negotiations to end the war have stalled despite intensified mediation by Qatar, and Tehran-based analyst Mostafa Najafi told the Associated Press the attacks could signal a shift in Iranian strategy, from waiting and retaliating to targeting the operational capability of bases.

Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates each condemned the attack, calling it a violation of Bahraini sovereignty. Qatar said the continued attacks "undermine diplomatic efforts."

A larger US naval presence

The US has also expanded its forces in the region. With the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group, American naval assets across the region now exceed the force deployed when the war began, according to a new analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies. The Roosevelt joins the USS George H.W. Bush and the USS George Washington, along with smaller Navy ships maintaining the blockade of Iranian shipping.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether this week's exchanges mark a brief flare-up or the start of a sustained escalation. "Tehran knows it needs to do something, but I wouldn't overestimate what we saw against Bahrain this week," said Sascha Bruchmann, a Bahrain-based defence analyst. Iranian officials have described the current situation as "no war, no peace" and vowed to end it, while saying they remain open to a negotiated deal.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Associated Press
  • NPR

link.title: Iran's third strike on Bahrain in five days ends Gulf lull as US hits back

entry.title: Britain sanctions Israeli settlement firms in push to protect two-state solution
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Britain has imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in a move London says is aimed at protecting the two-state solution.

The measures, announced on Tuesday by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, include asset freezes and disqualifications for company directors. Britain said the action would disrupt the firms' access to finance and support for further construction in the West Bank.

Among the companies named are Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd, and S.A.G. (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which build and develop homes in the territory.

Timed to the E1 tender

The announcement came shortly before the final deadlines for the E1 tender, a settlement project that would bisect the Israeli-occupied West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, fragmenting land Palestinians hope will form the heart of a future state.

Miliband said protecting the two-state solution was the guiding principle of the government's approach, and warned companies against taking part in the project: "do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."

Aid-blocking group also sanctioned

Britain also sanctioned Tzav 9, an Israeli activist group the government said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks carrying food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.

The move drew a sharp response from Israel. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar described the sanctions as a hostile act against private, law-abiding companies and said Israel would respond with countermeasures.

The Palestinian Authority welcomed the decision and called on other countries to take similar action.

The sanctions are Britain's first targeting Israeli firms working in the West Bank, and they come as international pressure grows over settlement expansion, which most countries consider illegal under international law — a position Israel disputes.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Britain sanctions Israeli settlement firms in push to protect two-state solution

entry.title: China and Canada widen tariff relief as Carney and Xi meet in Shenzhen
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Canada and China agreed on Tuesday to widen tariff relief between the two countries, as Prime Minister Mark Carney met President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief worth about 400 million Canadian dollars (US$280 million) on Canadian exports, including C$116 million of frozen pork cuts and C$285 million of fish and seafood — among them shrimp and prawns, geoduck, sea cucumber and Greenland halibut. In return, Canada will extend for two years tariff remission measures on certain Chinese steel and aluminium products that were due to expire at the end of 2026, and add remissions for 32 more steel and aluminium items for which Canadian supply is insufficient.

The measures build on a preliminary trade arrangement the two leaders struck in January, after Carney's visit to Beijing — the first by a Canadian prime minister since 2017. Under that deal, Canada cut its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles a year into the country, a cap set to rise to 70,000 over five years. China, in turn, lowered tariffs on Canadian farm goods and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for two more years. Carney's office said Canada has now restored market access for more than 90 per cent of the trade previously hit by tariffs — nearly C$7.5 billion of exports.

The deal comes as Carney makes diversifying Canada's trade beyond the United States a central part of his economic strategy, with US tariffs hitting Canadian auto, steel and aluminium producers and trade talks between Ottawa and Washington having broken down in August. A day earlier, in Cambodia, Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese carmakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry — remarks that drew a sharp response from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who asked whether Carney was threatening to "play China off the US".

Xi said stronger ties served both countries' interests and supported global stability and prosperity, calling it "the right choice". Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 per cent by the end of the decade. Carney said on Saturday he had spoken with US President Donald Trump and senior officials and that, while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.

Carney also met Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement. The two leaders noted a 19 per cent rise in merchandise trade in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: China and Canada widen tariff relief as Carney and Xi meet in Shenzhen

entry.title: Navy nominee Hung Cao tells Senate the Iran war is straining the fleet
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao told the Senate Armed Services Committee on Tuesday that the war with Iran is straining the United States Navy, as senators from both parties pressed him on long deployments, shrinking weapons stockpiles and the welfare of sailors at his confirmation hearing.

"This war, again, I know it's a strain on our Navy," Cao said, while arguing that the joint military campaign had "really set China back on their heels". The hearing was his bid for the permanent top civilian job. President Donald Trump nominated him in September, and he has served as acting secretary since April, after the departure of his predecessor, John Phelan.

The war is now in its ninth month. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited estimates that the naval blockade of Iranian shipping costs about $32.5 million a day, and that Iranian strikes on the Navy's regional headquarters in Bahrain caused at least $400 million in damage. Cao confirmed the blockade figure but said he could not assess the Bahrain damage in full.

Much of the hearing focused on the crew of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln. Cao confirmed that eight sailors in the carrier strike group attempted suicide during an extended deployment supporting the war — a figure he had disclosed to lawmakers in a letter in September. "You see it as eight suicide attempts; I see it as eight suicide mitigations," he told Senator Richard Blumenthal, pointing to the mental-health staff aboard. The Lincoln returned to San Diego in early October after a record-breaking deployment of more than eight months, and the United States is currently massing three carrier strike groups in the region.

Senators also pressed Cao on weapons. The conflict has drawn down stockpiles of air defence interceptors and Tomahawk cruise missiles, and lawmakers questioned whether the Navy can keep supplying the blockade while preparing for a possible conflict with China. Cao said production had risen sharply — the Navy now makes "well above 60" Tomahawks a month, against 125 a year when he was in uniform — and said unmanned vessels could eventually relieve destroyers on blockade duty.

Cao's path to confirmation is not straightforward. He retired from active duty in October 2021, so he needs a congressional waiver from the law requiring seven years out of uniform before a former officer can lead a military service — an exemption that needs 60 votes in the Senate. He also faced questions about the Navy quietly removing the entire leadership team of the submarine USS South Dakota after an underwater collision in October, without telling Congress. Committee chair Roger Wicker voiced support for the nomination; ranking Democrat Jack Reed said he was troubled by Cao's leadership record.

The hearing came days after Trump said further strikes on Iran were "quite unlikely" and the military phase of the war "effectively over", while adding that US forces remain "locked and loaded" if conditions change. Whether the Senate grants Cao the waiver is still to be decided.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Hill
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Navy nominee Hung Cao tells Senate the Iran war is straining the fleet

entry.title: US soldier accused of spying for Russia handed to American military custody
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A senior American soldier assigned to NATO who was arrested in Britain last week on suspicion of spying for Russia has been transferred to United States military custody, British police said on Tuesday.

The 41-year-old, identified by American officials as Lieutenant Colonel Brandon Tyner, was arrested by British counterterrorism police on November 10 near Gloucester in southwest England. He had been held in British police custody since then, and was handed to the US military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.

Tyner was based at Imjin Barracks near Gloucester, the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, a 20-nation high-readiness force led by the British Army. He served there as a senior human resources officer. He joined the US Army in 2008 and had previously been deployed to Afghanistan, Qatar and Iraq.

He was arrested on suspicion of offences under Sections 1 and 3 of the UK's National Security Act 2023. Section 1 covers obtaining or disclosing protected information; Section 3 covers assisting a foreign intelligence service. British police had previously said the foreign state linked to the allegations was Russia.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said London had passed the investigation to its American partners "in line with existing international protocols", after an extensive investigation and discussions between British prosecutors and US officials.

"These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Taylor said. He added that British police would continue to support their US colleagues as they take the matter forward.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the officer was in US custody as a result of a joint espionage investigation involving the FBI's Philadelphia field office and its London legal attache, alongside UK Counter Terrorism Policing, MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence and the US Army Counterintelligence Command.

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, who commands the Army Counterintelligence Command, said the case sent a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath". The case is believed to be the first time a US soldier has been suspected of spying for a foreign government while in the United Kingdom.

The Kremlin has denied any connection to the officer. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow had "nothing to do with it" and that he was unaware of what the arrest was connected to.

It remains unclear what information, if anything, was passed on, and no charges have been publicly announced. The case now proceeds under US military jurisdiction, with British authorities continuing to cooperate.

The case is the latest involving suspected Russian espionage in Britain and elsewhere in Europe, and comes amid heightened tensions between Moscow and European capitals since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Channel News Asia

link.title: US soldier accused of spying for Russia handed to American military custody

entry.title: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Kuwait's military said on Tuesday night that its air defences were intercepting hostile drone attacks, as the United States and Iran traded strikes across the Gulf in a widening exchange.

The Kuwaiti armed forces said in a statement posted on X that any explosion sounds heard across the country were the result of air defence systems intercepting hostile attacks, and urged the public to follow safety instructions. It did not say where the drones came from, or whether there were casualties or damage.

Earlier on Tuesday, the United States carried out several attacks on Iran's southern island of Qeshm, in the Strait of Hormuz, hours after Iran said it had launched a drone attack on a US radar system in Bahrain. A US official told Al Jazeera the strike hit a missile launch site on Qeshm, in response to Iran's earlier attack on a US base in Bahrain.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had carried out a "precision operation" with drones on the US-operated radar at the Sheikh Isa air base, describing it as a response to what it called repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones.

US Central Command said Iranian drones aimed at a US radar system at an air base in Bahrain "were intercepted without any damage to US equipment or personnel". Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, said its air defences intercepted the attack, and blasts were heard over the capital, Manama, according to the AFP news agency.

It was the third Iranian drone attack on Bahrain in five days, after a lull of several weeks. Friday's strike was the first Iranian attack on a Gulf country since early September, AFP reported.

Iranian media reported that the US strikes on Qeshm caused no damage to infrastructure. Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Iran's southern Hormozgan province, told the official IRNA news agency that the situation was under control and relief agencies were on full alert. IRNA reported five to six explosions on the island on Tuesday evening.

The exchange comes as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil, faces growing disruption. Iran's armed forces said three oil tankers struck naval mines while trying to cross the strait on Tuesday, while the US military said it had cleared the main routes of mines. The war began on February 28, and the US has responded to Iranian pressure on shipping with a naval blockade of Iranian ports and tanker escorts.

Diplomacy continued alongside the fighting. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and his Omani counterpart, Badr Albusaidi, discussed safeguarding shipping and diplomatic options in Muscat. A third US aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, arrived in the Middle East on Monday, and US President Donald Trump is due to hold a three-way summit on Thursday in China with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, where the Iran war is on the agenda.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Kuwait reports drone attacks as Iran, US trade attacks on Qeshm and Bahrain

entry.title: Trump heads to China for first three-way talks with Xi and Putin
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump departs on Wednesday for China, where he will join Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for an unprecedented three-way meeting, with nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine at the top of the agenda.

The meeting takes place in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled technology hub hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Trump arrives from Manila, where he attended the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, and will take part in the APEC summit on Thursday before sitting down with Xi and Putin, then returning to the United States.

Trump has signalled that he wants to take an improvised approach to the trip, leaning on personal relationships rather than a scripted agenda. It is a bet that his unscripted style of diplomacy can produce a legacy-defining moment in the final two years of his presidency, at a time when much of the world is on edge over the wars in Ukraine and Iran and the rapid transformation brought by artificial intelligence.

The president said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. That raises a question about what is actually on the table: before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be part of the trilateral meeting. It is not yet clear how that difference will be resolved once the three leaders are in the room.

Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting. A first-ever three-way gathering of the American, Chinese and Russian leaders is historic in itself, but the gaps between them — on Ukraine, on trade, on the military use of artificial intelligence — are wide, and a single session is unlikely to close them.

Trump has also floated the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un while he is in Asia. Neither has been confirmed beyond the president's own remarks, and it remains unclear whether either will happen.

The trip comes at an awkward moment at home. A series of technical outages back in the United States has put the administration on the defensive, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepping in to reassure the public on Trump's behalf. Trump, meanwhile, has been keen to project strength abroad, presenting the China visit as a demonstration of American technological leadership.

What the meeting produces, if anything, should become clear on Thursday, when the three leaders meet and then face reporters. Until then, the most that can be said with confidence is that the meeting itself — three leaders, one table, no precedent — is the news.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News

link.title: Trump heads to China for first three-way talks with Xi and Putin

entry.title: Peltola wins Alaska's Senate race, completing Democrats' nine-seat midterm sweep
entry.content:
Democrat Mary Peltola defeated two-term Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, the Associated Press called on Tuesday night, resolving the last uncalled Senate race of the 2026 midterm elections and completing a Democratic sweep of nine Republican-held seats — the party's largest midterm gain since 1958.

With nearly all ballots counted, Peltola held about 50 percent of the vote to roughly 46 percent for Sullivan, two weeks after Election Day on November 3. The result gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate when the new Congress convenes in January, reversing the 53-47 Republican edge the party entered the midterms with.

Peltola, who is Yup'ik, will be the first Alaska Native ever elected to the United States Senate and only the fifth Democrat to represent Alaska in the chamber since statehood. The most recent was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan defeated in 2014. Peltola previously held Alaska's lone House seat, becoming the first Alaska Native to serve in Congress, before losing her re-election bid in 2024.

The campaign was one of the most expensive and contentious of the cycle, with more than $140 million spent, and it was upended in its final days by an allegation that members of Peltola's campaign helped recruit a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to siphon votes from the incumbent. The New York Times first reported the claim less than a week before the election. Peltola denied any involvement, and the retired teacher at the centre of it, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., finished with about 1.7 percent of the vote and has denied running at the Democrats' behest.

President Donald Trump called for Peltola's prosecution after the report, and the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification if Sullivan lost, pending an investigation into possible voter confusion. A federal judge dismissed the case, though the department appealed, and it has confirmed a criminal investigation is under way. Trump and Vice President JD Vance each travelled to Alaska in the month before the election to campaign for Sullivan.

An "Alaska first" campaign

Peltola ran as a centrist under the slogan "fish, family and freedom," leaning into Alaskans' frustrations with high fuel prices and the cost of food and supplies that must be barged or flown into remote communities. She sought to distance herself from national Democrats, while Sullivan and his supporters tried to tie her to "Lower 48 liberals" they said wanted to restrict oil, gas and mining development.

The result is striking in a state Trump carried by wide margins, including about 13 percentage points in 2024. Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998. The Associated Press has not yet called the state's House race, where independent Bill Hill is challenging Republican Representative Nick Begich. Legal challenges to the Senate result remain possible, but with the count effectively complete, the contest that drew national attention for a ballot quirk and a federal lawsuit has delivered Democrats their ninth pickup — and a majority larger than any they have held since 2008.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Peltola wins Alaska's Senate race, completing Democrats' nine-seat midterm sweep

entry.title: Rubio says 'zero evidence' links wave of US outages to cyberattacks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved on Tuesday to calm a jittery public, saying the United States has found no evidence that a string of outages across the country is connected — or the work of hackers or a foreign state.

"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio told reporters in Manila, where he is travelling with President Donald Trump ahead of meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen.

Rubio, also Trump's national security adviser, was blunt: the failures are not linked to each other. "We have no indication, no evidence, and no reason to believe at all that any of these incidents are related to each other," he said. "In essence, the Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago." "We are not under systemic attack," he added.

The reassurance follows a remarkable run of disruptions. It began on Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other workplace tools went down for millions of users; the company blamed a network capacity upgrade. On Friday, flights were grounded nationwide in the longest ground stop since 9/11; the Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade. By Monday, customers at several major banks reported trouble reaching online accounts after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase rippled through the system. Chase called it a software bug, "not cyber-related." United Airlines fixed an internal systems outage the same day. On Tuesday, an internal National Security Agency network used for classified communications went offline during what the agency called routine maintenance.

Officials point to a common theme rather than a common culprit: security and capacity upgrades hitting unexpected problems. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the government was "looking very diligently across the landscape" and "not seeing this as a cyber attack incident." The FAA's preliminary investigation into the ground stop likewise found no indication of a cyberattack, and Senator Mark Warner, the Senate Intelligence Committee's vice chairman, also said there was no sign of a coordinated cyberattack or foreign interference.

Not everyone is satisfied. Trump was dismissive in Asia, saying of the Chase outage that "things like that happen." Former press secretary Karoline Leavitt advised the White House that "transparency is key" and said a senior official should explain what is known after Trump returns from Asia. Commentator Laura Loomer claimed without evidence the outages were "very clearly a coordinated cyber attack," while former Homeland Security spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin said Americans "want and deserve to know what's really going on."

For now, the administration says the country suffered unrelated technical failures, not an attack. What remains unknown is when fuller findings will be published — and whether that will settle the scepticism.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • TRT World

link.title: Rubio says 'zero evidence' links wave of US outages to cyberattacks

entry.title: Nvidia stops shipping AI chips to China despite US approval
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Nvidia has stopped shipping its licensed Hopper artificial intelligence chips to China, the world's leading AI chip supplier said on Tuesday — a decision that closes off a market Washington had only recently cleared it to serve.

Colette Kress, the company's interim chief executive, told analysts on an earnings call that Nvidia's outlook contains no licensed Hopper data centre products for China and that shipments of those chips have ended. The announcement came even though the US government gave Nvidia permission last year to sell a version of the Hopper model into China under licence.

The move draws a line under a fraught chapter for the chipmaker. Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of licensed Hopper products to China in the third quarter, showing that demand in the country remained strong even as the political ground shifted beneath the business. That revenue will now fall away from future guidance.

Nvidia's position in China has been squeezed from both directions. In Washington, the company's access to the Chinese market has become a political flashpoint: the administration's decision to allow licensed sales drew criticism, and the loopholes that let Chinese firms reach advanced chips through overseas data centres have drawn scrutiny in Congress. In Beijing, meanwhile, officials have pushed domestic buyers toward homegrown alternatives, leaving Nvidia's licensed products in an increasingly narrow lane.

The decision also lands in the middle of a leadership transition at Nvidia. Kress is running the company on an interim basis after the departure of Jensen Huang, the co-founder who built Nvidia into the dominant supplier of the chips powering the AI boom. The board is weighing who should lead the company next, and the China question is one of the most consequential files on the new chief executive's desk.

For the wider chip industry, Nvidia's exit from licensed Hopper sales in China sharpens a divide that has been widening for years: a US-led AI hardware ecosystem and a Chinese one, each increasingly sealed off from the other. Chinese customers will now have to rely on domestic suppliers or on older, less capable hardware, while Nvidia gives up one of its largest single markets in the name of a cleaner position with Washington.

What remains unclear is whether the halt is permanent or a pause while the company and the government settle on new terms. Kress gave no indication of a timeline for resuming sales, and Nvidia did not say whether it is seeking approval for a different, more restricted chip design for China.

Investors will be watching the company's next set of results for the full cost of the decision — and whether the booming demand for AI hardware elsewhere is enough to absorb the loss of $2.4 billion a quarter in Chinese sales.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Bloomberg

link.title: Nvidia stops shipping AI chips to China despite US approval

entry.title: White House pulls Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the FDA
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The White House has withdrawn Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration, a White House official told the Guardian on Tuesday — ending her bid to run the agency a day before the Senate health committee was due to vote on whether to advance it.

Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Donald Trump in August. Her selection was seen as an attempt to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the agency after a tumultuous year under the president's first FDA commissioner, Marty Makary. Overton has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or for conservative groups aligned with his agenda.

Her confirmation prospects had been narrowing for weeks. Senators from both parties questioned whether she would act independently of the president, particularly on his unsupported claims about the dangers of childhood vaccines. Senator Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, had called her support for Trump's plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot — "almost disqualifying," and pressed her during a September hearing on her scientific independence and her willingness to push back against Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic.

The arithmetic was unforgiving. With Democrats expected to oppose her, Overton needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the 21-member committee to advance to the full Senate. Cassidy said earlier on Tuesday that he remained undecided ahead of the vote scheduled for Wednesday. After the withdrawal, he said the White House had abandoned a viable confirmation path, adding that his conversations with Overton had convinced him she would follow the science.

Abortion policy also hung over the nomination. As FDA commissioner, Overton would have overseen the agency that regulates medication abortion. In a 2023 brief for the America First Policy Institute, she argued that Congress should strictly regulate the abortion pill mifepristone, criticized the mailing of abortion pills, and wrote that abortion "is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly."

The withdrawal leaves the FDA without a permanent leader. The agency is currently being run on an acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, according to Reuters, and the White House has given no timeline for naming a new nominee. Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas, who recently lost his reelection bid, has expressed interest in the role, according to people familiar with the matter.

Overton is the latest health nominee the White House has pulled amid crumbling Republican support, following nominees to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the surgeon general's office. Republicans are racing to confirm the president's remaining nominees before handing power to Senate Democrats in January, and the FDA vacancy now looks likely to stretch well into next year.

---

Sources

  • The Guardian

link.title: White House pulls Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the FDA

entry.title: AI researchers uncover critical Java flaw hidden for 12 years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A cyber-security start-up says it has used artificial intelligence to uncover a critical vulnerability in Java, one of the world's most widely used programming languages, that had gone unnoticed for more than a decade.

The flaw, named Java4Shell, sits in Java's memory functions. It could allow an attacker to remotely run unwanted commands against a system's memory — one of the most common routes hackers use to exploit or crash a system. The researchers say the bug had been hiding in plain sight for 12 years.

The discovery was made by Calif, a tech start-up that recently found a similar flaw in the web language PHP. In this case, the system probing Java was GPT-6 Cyber, an OpenAI model that has not yet been released to the public. Computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh said AI is now exposing flaws far more quickly, including ones so obscure that people alone might never have found them. He noted that managing memory safely is central to what Java is for, which is what makes this flaw so unlikely — and so serious.

Java matters because it sits underneath so much of the modern economy. First released in 1995, it is used by nearly all of the world's largest companies, along with banks, hospitals and governments, and it underpins banking, national security, aviation and telecommunications. Calif describes the language as the "beating heart of the modern economy." Cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said the flaw could compromise critical financial systems and customer data, noting that in Australia almost every bank relies on Java to manage critical transaction data.

Oracle, which owns Java, has not acknowledged the bug, but on Tuesday it released a "critical patch update" containing security vulnerability fixes. The BBC said it had contacted Oracle for comment. It is not yet clear whether any company or platform has been affected, and experts warn that hackers could now try to identify the bug themselves if it is not fixed.

The discovery comes after a run of serious technology failures. A major Microsoft outage, Apple services going down, a network failure that grounded flights across the United States, and thousands of customers at major US banks — including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America — reporting trouble accessing their accounts. The US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday for what it called scheduled routine maintenance. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related.

The Java find follows Calif's earlier discovery in PHP, which Professor Alan Woodward of the Surrey Centre for Cyber Security said left about 30 million websites vulnerable. OpenAI's president, Greg Brockman, said earlier this month that the company is moving a quarter of its staff to focus on cyber-security work.

---

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: AI researchers uncover critical Java flaw hidden for 12 years

entry.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launches after a 13-year wait
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

After 13 years, one of entertainment's biggest releases is finally here. "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon.

The game becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, so players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its release in the United States. New Zealand is among the first countries where players can get in.

The scale of the launch is hard to overstate. The game file is 212 gigabytes, and one New Zealand network expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its system as downloads begin.

The expectations are enormous, too. The "Grand Theft Auto" franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Pre-orders for the new game are estimated to have already passed $1.5 billion, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictional version of Miami, with two new protagonists and a sprawling Florida-inspired world. At the centre of "GTA VI" are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar's fictional version of Florida. Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from "Grand Theft Auto V," which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida.

Miami has leaned into its connection to Vice City ahead of the release. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant "Welcome to Vice City" display atop the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center. The campaign has not been universally welcomed — some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity.

Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation. The first "GTA VI" trailer drew more than 93 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, and the second generated more than 475 million views across platforms in a day. The game has also received eight nominations for the Game Awards, including game of the year, with the awards presented on December 10. Rockstar also commissioned an original adaptive score from Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice, with a 30-track soundtrack due December 11.

Despite years of trailers and promotional material, Rockstar has kept significant portions of "GTA VI" under wraps, including the full voice cast. Those answers will begin emerging first from players in Asia and Europe as midnight arrives in their regions, followed by North America hours later.

---

Sources

  • AP News

link.title: Grand Theft Auto VI launches after a 13-year wait

entry.title: Xi and Putin push back on tariffs and sanctions as Trump lands in Shenzhen for APEC
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

China's president used the opening of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Wednesday to make the case for open trade, hours before Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen for a first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders.

Xi Jinping told business executives gathered in the southern Chinese technology and financial hub that the Asia-Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth if it is to remain stable and dynamic. He promised China would cut tariffs, widen market access and push ahead with reforms to rules, regulations and standards, presenting Beijing as a steady partner for global investors.

"While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development," Xi said, adding that China had brought "stability and predictability to world economic growth."

The message landed as a deliberate contrast with Washington. Trump's "America First" approach of tariff hikes and other trade barriers runs counter to APEC's long-term aim of a Pacific Rim free trade zone, and US limits on China's access to leading-edge technology — including the Nvidia chips that power artificial intelligence — remain a constant source of strain. Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia or the United States directly, according to analysts at the summit.

Russian President Vladimir Putin followed Xi on stage with a sharper attack on Western economic pressure. He described sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions as "instruments of economic dominance" that have "outlived their usefulness and have largely lost their intimidating effect." It was his first in-person appearance at an APEC leaders' meeting since 2017. Putin said the Asia-Pacific now accounts for more than half of Russia's total trade, and that Moscow has submitted a bid to chair APEC in 2035.

Trump arrived on Wednesday from the Philippines, where he attended the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. The three leaders are due to meet behind closed doors on Thursday, in a trilateral encounter that could touch on Russia's war in Ukraine, the US war in Iran, trade, artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons.

The gathering comes with real pressures behind the pageantry. China's economy is still growing at more than 4 per cent, but retail spending and investment have dragged during a prolonged property market slump, and its trade surplus is on track to exceed $1 trillion for a second straight year — a figure that has drawn backlash from trading partners. Friction with Washington is also pushing other countries to hedge: on Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met Xi and the two agreed to cut tariffs on each other's goods.

The 21 APEC economies account for 60 per cent of global economic activity, half of global trade and 40 per cent of humanity. The forum takes no binding decisions, but over 37 years it has served as a place to build consensus on cooperation and more open trade — and this week's meeting will test whether that consensus still holds.

---

Sources

  • AP News

link.title: Xi and Putin push back on tariffs and sanctions as Trump lands in Shenzhen for APEC

entry.title: Amazon and Google could soon hold more than a third of Anthropic
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Amazon and Google could soon own more than a third of Anthropic, with a combined stake worth roughly $400 billion at the price the artificial intelligence company is expected to set for its stock market debut.

An updated prospectus filed on Tuesday lays out the scale of the two technology giants' holdings. Google will own 1.8 billion Anthropic shares once the initial public offering and a concurrent private sale are complete, according to Barron's analysis of the filing. At $74 a share, that stake would be worth about $133 billion.

Amazon will start with 1.9 billion shares. It also holds Anthropic debt that it can choose to convert into stock. If it exercises that option in full, Amazon would hold as many as 3.5 billion shares, valued at about $260 billion at the same $74 price.

Together, the pair will own 28.4 per cent of Anthropic's outstanding capital stock, and an estimated 36 per cent if Amazon converts the bonds. Both companies will hold Class N shares, a class designed for Anthropic's business partners.

The stakes are the product of years of backing. Alphabet, Google's parent, first funded Anthropic by buying convertible debt that has since been converted into equity, and this year agreed to invest up to $30 billion more. Amazon agreed earlier this year to invest $20 billion, of which $5 billion has already gone in, with a further $15 billion tied to computing capacity milestones. About $6.2 billion of Amazon's earlier convertible debt was still outstanding at the end of June.

The relationship runs both ways. Amazon and Google are also Anthropic's critical cloud-service providers, supplying the data-centre capacity that trains and runs its Claude models. Anthropic is committed to more than $475 billion in compute capacity agreements over the next seven to 10 years, and Alphabet and Amazon are each set to receive around $110 billion of that spending.

The filing lands as Anthropic's listing reaches its final hours. The company is telling prospective investors it expects to price its shares at the top end of its $70 to $78 range, or even above it, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter. The final price is expected late on Wednesday, with the shares due to begin trading on Thursday.

Anthropic is also selling shares at the IPO price to a group of large technology companies, including Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

What remains uncertain is whether Amazon will convert its debt in full — the decision that determines whether the pair's combined stake stops at 28.4 per cent or rises to about 36 per cent — and the final IPO price, which will fix the dollar value of both holdings.

---

Sources

  • Barron's

link.title: Amazon and Google could soon hold more than a third of Anthropic

entry.title: Grand Theft Auto VI earns near-perfect reviews as its worldwide release begins
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The reviews are in, and Grand Theft Auto VI appears to have lived up to its hype. The game has averaged 99 on Metacritic across 100 critic reviews, putting it — at least for now — level with the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which scored 99 when it launched in 1998.

IGN awarded the game a perfect 10 out of 10, describing it as "exquisitely detailed" and "uncompromisingly engineered". The New York Times called it a "dense game filled with friction", saying it "matures beyond its memorable car crashes and stick-ups with a game about love, relationships and nurturing your partner". The lowest confirmed reviews so far give the game 90, according to the BBC. Slant Magazine was less effusive, giving four and a half stars and noting "flaws" in its creative approach.

The verdicts arrived as the game began its staggered worldwide release. It unlocks at midnight local time in each region, so players in New Zealand were the first to get in, at 11:00 GMT on Wednesday. The full release follows the clock around the world, reaching the UK at midnight GMT on Thursday, November 19.

Early players in New Zealand were quick to praise it. Connor Cattermoul, a 27-year-old from New Zealand who finished the game's 45-minute introductory mission in the early hours, told the BBC it was "amazing" so far with "beautiful" graphics. Staying up, he said, was "pretty worth it".

The launch has already drawn a huge live audience. More than 2.4 million people were watching gamers play GTA VI on Twitch within hours of the New Zealand release, according to the BBC.

The game is the first new entry in the series in 13 years, and it carries the weight of that wait. Set in Leonida, Rockstar's fictional version of Florida, it returns players to Vice City, its take on Miami, and follows two protagonists — Lucia, the series' first playable female lead in a 3D and HD setting, and her partner Jason — on what the BBC describes as a "Bonnie and Clyde-esque adventure". It is available on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, priced at £69.99 in the UK and $79.99 in the US. There is no news yet on a PC version, or on whether it will come to Nintendo Switch 2.

The release follows two delays, after the game was initially due to launch in autumn 2025. Its predecessor, GTA V, sold around 235 million copies and made Rockstar $1 billion in just three days.

Not all reviews are in yet, and the final score may shift as more critics publish their verdicts — some outlets want more time with a game whose main story is estimated to take around 50 hours. But with countless reviewers handing out perfect marks, Rockstar has delivered on what the BBC called its "truly monstrous hype".

---

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Grand Theft Auto VI earns near-perfect reviews as its worldwide release begins

entry.title: Target posts its strongest sales growth in five years as shoppers return
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Target reported its strongest quarterly sales growth in more than five years on Wednesday, a result the retailer credited to new products, price cuts and faster delivery — and a sign that its long turnaround effort is finally gaining traction with shoppers squeezed by inflation.

Net sales rose 7.1% in the three months ended October 31, to $27.07 billion from $25.27 billion a year earlier, the company's best performance since the fourth quarter of 2021. Comparable sales — from stores and digital channels open at least a year — climbed 5.6%, well ahead of the roughly 3.8% analysts had expected, as comparable traffic rose 5%. Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10%, while in-store comparable sales rose 4.6%.

Profit rose sharply. Target earned $1.21 billion, or $2.65 a share, against $689 million, or $1.51 a share, in the same period last year. The figure includes a 50-cent-per-share benefit from government tariff refunds. Analysts had expected earnings of about $2.07 a share on sales of roughly $26.5 billion, according to FactSet.

A turnaround finding its footing

The quarter overlapped with the back-to-school season, and the company said a refreshed product lineup, expanded same-day delivery and lower prices on thousands of items brought customers back. Chief executive Michael Fiddelke, a 20-year veteran who took the top job in February, has made reviving the stores and merchandising the centre of his turnaround plan.

Target's shares have risen 63% so far in 2026, though the stock remains about 40% below its record closing high of $266.39, set in November 2021. The question now is whether the momentum survives the holiday season, the retailer's toughest test of the year.

Outlook raised again

Encouraged by the quarter, Target raised its full-year guidance for the second time this year. It now expects net sales growth of around 6%, one percentage point higher than the guidance it gave in August, and full-year earnings per share of $10.65 to $11.40, up from a prior range of $9.90 to $10.90. That earnings range includes about $2.14 a share in tariff refund benefits recognised so far.

The company also projected a full-year operating income margin of about 6.2%, including roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds, and said it plans to spend $5 billion to $6 billion on capital investments in 2027.

Target said November sales so far are in line with its full-year outlook.

What is still unknown

The headline beat comes with a caveat. A large part of the profit jump — the 50 cents a share in tariff refunds this quarter, and $2.14 across the full-year guidance — is a one-off benefit, not a gain from selling more goods. Average transaction amounts grew by less than 1%, suggesting shoppers are visiting more often but still spending carefully. Whether the traffic gains hold once the refund boost fades will decide whether this is a durable recovery or a strong quarter flattered by timing.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • Barron's

link.title: Target posts its strongest sales growth in five years as shoppers return

entry.title: Harry Styles, Billie Eilish and Sam Fender to headline Glastonbury 2027
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Glastonbury Festival will return in 2027 with Harry Styles, Sam Fender and Billie Eilish headlining the Pyramid Stage, the organisers announced on Wednesday. Cher will play the coveted Sunday afternoon legends slot, becoming the oldest act ever to take it, at 81.

Sam Fender will open the headline run on Friday night, Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on Saturday, and Eilish will close the festival on Sunday. The three are the youngest group of Pyramid headliners since 1997 — Fender and Styles are both 32, Eilish is 24.

For Styles, it will be a Glastonbury debut. He arrives fresh from a 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden in New York. Fender, who last played the festival in 2022, takes a top spot for the first time, while Eilish returns to headline for a second time after her 2022 set made her the youngest solo artist ever to top the Pyramid bill.

Cher's legends slot is often treated as a fourth headline set. She will be 81 by the time of the festival, passing Rod Stewart, who played the slot at 80 in 2025. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.

The festival runs from Wednesday, June 23 to Sunday, June 27, 2027, at Worthy Farm in Somerset, with music on the main stages starting on Friday, June 25. It is the first Glastonbury in two years: the festival took 2026 off as a fallow year, the periodic break that lets the farm's pastures recover from hosting more than 200,000 people.

Tickets had already sold out before any headliner was named — in 42 minutes last month. Organiser Emily Eavis said the team was happy to be returning after the fallow year and wanted to offer fans an early taste of what is to come.

The first wave of names goes well beyond the headliners. Electronic pioneers Kraftwerk will headline the West Holts stage, and the bill so far also includes Massive Attack, Chase & Status, the xx, Lily Allen, The Streets, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream, Sombr, Sienna Spiro and Adéla. More names, stage-by-stage schedules and set times are expected in the New Year, along with a spring resale of any returned tickets.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • The Independent

entry.title: Xi meets Trump on the tarmac in Shenzhen — a hug that broke with decades of protocol
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

China's President Xi Jinping broke with decades of diplomatic convention on Wednesday, waiting on the tarmac at Shenzhen's airport to greet Donald Trump in person as the US president stepped off Air Force One. The two men shook hands at the foot of the aircraft's stairs, then embraced, before walking together along a red carpet lined with performers waving pom-poms, flowers and flags.

The welcome at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport was a deliberate piece of stagecraft, and a pointed one. Xi paid Trump a special honour by meeting him on arrival, reciprocating the gesture Trump made in September, when he personally greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews during the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington. American presidents typically receive visiting heads of state at the White House, not on the runway.

Chinese leaders almost never greet foreign counterparts at the airport. Xi did not do so when Trump visited Beijing in May, and his surprise appearance in Shenzhen made him the first Chinese paramount leader in decades to welcome a visiting leader on arrival, according to AFP.

The contrast with the day's other arrival was hard to miss. Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Shenzhen earlier on Wednesday, but he was met by Cai Qi, Xi's chief of staff, rather than by Xi himself — despite the two leaders' longstanding friendship and their frequent public displays of closeness.

The warmth on the tarmac sets the tone for a consequential 24 hours. On Thursday, Xi is due to host Trump and Putin for a first-of-its-kind trilateral meeting, expected to touch on nuclear arms control, Iran, Ukraine, trade and the AI chips at the heart of the US-China technology rivalry. Trump arrived in Shenzhen from the Philippines, where he had attended the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Whether the personal rapport on display at the airport translates into anything concrete is an open question. The greeting was choreographed to signal that Beijing values its relationship with Washington — and that Xi is willing to break his own protocol to say so. The talks that follow will show whether the gesture was the start of a deal, or only a photograph.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • AP News

entry.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat, completing Democrats' nine-seat sweep
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Democrat Mary Peltola has defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska's Senate race, the last contest of the 2026 midterms to be decided — and a result that gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the chamber.

The Associated Press called the race on Tuesday night, two weeks after Election Day. With 99 percent of the vote counted, Peltola held 50.1 percent to Sullivan's 45.8 percent, clearing the majority threshold Alaska's ranked-choice voting system requires for an outright win.

Peltola, who is Yup'ik, becomes the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. Senate. She previously made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning the state's sole House seat in a special election. She lost that seat in 2024, then rebuilt her campaign around a deliberately local message: lower costs, high fuel prices, and putting Alaska first.

Her victory is the ninth Senate seat Democrats flipped from Republicans in this year's midterms, the party's largest midterm Senate gain since 1958. Republicans entered the election with a 53-47 majority; Democrats now emerge with a 56-44 margin when the new Congress convenes in January. It is also the first time in more than a decade that a Democrat has won a Senate seat in Alaska — the last was Mark Begich, whom Sullivan unseated in 2014.

The race was one of the most closely watched and most bitterly fought of the cycle. It drew national attention after an investigation alleged that people linked to Peltola's campaign had helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. — who shares the incumbent's name — to run and siphon votes from the Republican senator. Peltola has denied any knowledge of the alleged decoy-candidate plan. Days before the result was called, the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results if Sullivan lost; Sullivan had pledged to accept the election outcome.

In a statement after the race was called, Peltola said there was "no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs and put Alaska first."

Alaska also elected a Democrat as governor for the first time since 1998, with former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeating three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. The Associated Press has not yet called the state's House race, where independent Bill Hill is challenging Republican Representative Nick Begich.

Legal challenges to the Senate result are still possible, and the final certified count may adjust the margins. But the outcome itself is now settled: the Senate's last open seat has gone to the Democrats, closing out a midterm that delivered the party its strongest position in the chamber in 16 years.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Associated Press

link.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat, completing Democrats' nine-seat sweep

entry.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a distance of one light-day from Earth — about 16 billion miles — becoming the first human-made object ever to travel that far from home.

NASA calculated that the probe crossed the mark on Wednesday at 5:16 a.m. ET, more than 49 years after it left Earth. Because a signal from the spacecraft now takes a full day to reach us, engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will have to wait about a day for the data confirming the crossing, and the agency has scheduled an event for Thursday to discuss the milestone.

A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours. At Voyager 1's distance, a radio message sent from Earth now needs an entire day to arrive, and another full day for a reply to come back — stretching a round trip to 48 hours. The probe sits roughly 173 times as far from the Sun as Earth, more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, sixteen days after its twin, Voyager 2, on a mission originally meant only to fly past Jupiter and Saturn. It completed those encounters in 1979 and 1980, then kept going. It crossed the heliopause — the outer edge of the Sun's protective bubble — in August 2012, becoming the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and it has been the most distant human-made object since 1998, when it passed the Pioneer 10 probe. It is still travelling at nearly 38,000 miles per hour.

Remarkably, the spacecraft is still working. Its remaining instruments are sending back continuous measurements of magnetic fields, cosmic rays and plasma waves from a region no other mission has explored, and have even detected the faint hum caused by vibrations of small amounts of gas in interstellar space. Recent power-saving measures could keep the two Voyager spacecraft in communication with Earth for three to four more years, with enough power to run the current instruments through the 50th anniversary of their launches next year.

"Reaching one light-day is an astounding feat, one that I never expected to see," said Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager.

Voyager 1 is headed in the direction of the star Gliese 445, which it is expected to pass within about 1.7 light-years of in roughly 40,000 years. Its twin is not far behind on the same scale: Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day from Earth in November 2035. Both spacecraft carry the Golden Record, a gold-plated copper disc engraved with sounds and images representing life on Earth.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NBC News
  • Smithsonian Magazine

link.title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth, a first for any human-made object

entry.title: GTA 6 earns near-perfect reviews, tying a 28-year-old record
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

After 13 years of waiting, the verdict on Grand Theft Auto 6 is in — and, according to the first reviews, it was worth it. The game averages 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, the review-aggregation site, tying the record held since 1998 by Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The reviews landed on Wednesday, a day before the game's worldwide release on Thursday, November 19. Critics were near-unanimous in their praise, describing an open-world game of unusual scale and polish from Rockstar Games, the studio behind the series.

IGN called the game "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable". Eurogamer awarded it five stars, with reviewer Chris Tapsell writing that Rockstar had pushed back the horizon of video games once again, while noting there were still nits to pick. Bloomberg's Jason Schreier, also in a five-star review, called it a "masterpiece" and wrote that there is nothing else like it. The Washington Post said the game "raises the bar at every level".

Much of the praise centred on Leonida, the Miami-inspired setting, and on the two lead characters, Jason and Lucia. The Guardian described Leonida as so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, and said the leads feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to the player's whim. Forbes reviewer Paul Tassi wrote that he had never seen a better video game relationship than the one the pair share. The New York Times' Yussef Cole struck a more measured note, saying the game had matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups, while questioning whether its realism might dull some of the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Gaming journalist Jordan Middler, who played for around 100 hours to reach the credits, called it the "game of a generation", adding that it can slow down at times because of how much is happening on screen.

The scale of the production is reflected in its cost, though Rockstar has not disclosed a figure. Some estimates put it north of $1 billion (£760 million). Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, saw its shares rise on the news, and analysts estimated preorders at $1.65 billion, according to Sensor Tower figures cited by Barron's.

The game has already been recognised by the industry before a single copy has been sold: it received eight nominations at The Game Awards, including game of the year and best music, announced on Tuesday. One of those nominations also confirmed Manni L Perez as the actress behind Lucia.

Not everyone is swept along. Some posters on gaming forums have pushed back against what they see as ultra fan-boy hype. But with more than 140 critic reviews counted and the score holding at 99, the early consensus is clear: the most anticipated game in years has, for most critics, lived up to it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News
  • Barron's
