entry.title: Israeli tanks push into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Israeli tanks advanced into central Gaza on Wednesday, in the first broad ground operation since the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas was signed more than a year ago, hospital officials and witnesses said.

Three Palestinians were killed during the day's fighting, according to hospital officials. Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground reported Israeli tanks operating near Salah al-Din Street, east of the Nuseirat refugee camp and north of the Bureij camp, while witnesses told Reuters that some tanks had rolled onto the main road itself, west of the so-called Yellow Line.

The Yellow Line, established under the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, marks the boundary of the area of Gaza still under Israeli military control — roughly two-thirds of the territory. The tanks' advance across it was described by residents as the first ground raid since the ceasefire took effect.

What the Israeli military said

Earlier on Wednesday, the Israeli army said the operation aimed to "eliminate a threat" to its forces operating in the area of the Yellow Line, and that it was targeting Hamas infrastructure outside the areas it controls.

"We reserve the freedom to act and manoeuvre whenever necessary to eliminate any immediate threat in the Gaza Strip," the military said in a statement.

An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News the operation was aimed at Hamas infrastructure west of the Yellow Line in central Gaza, and said forces had also struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier in the day.

Families flee as shells fall

Palestinians began fleeing parts of central Gaza as the operation got under way. Al Jazeera's Hind Khoudary, reporting from Gaza City, said people in eastern Maghazi and Bureij and those living close to Salah al-Din Street were evacuating amid explosions, live ammunition and artillery shelling.

An Israeli air strike targeted the town of al-Mughraqa, north of Nuseirat, killing one person and wounding several others, an official at al-Awda Hospital told Al Jazeera. Two further people were killed in separate drone attacks before the operation was announced — one in the Sheikh Ijlin neighbourhood of southwestern Gaza City and one in Deir el-Balah, hospital officials said.

Gaza's Ministry of Health said hospitals had recorded seven deaths and received 15 wounded people in the previous 24 hours.

Hamas calls it a ceasefire violation

Hamas condemned the operation as a "flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement", saying forced evacuation orders and displacement under the threat of bombardment amounted to a war crime. The group said it held Israel and the United States responsible for the repercussions of the operation.

The October 2025 ceasefire halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, but it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas' disarmament. Whether Wednesday's ground push marks a limited raid or a wider return to ground operations remains unclear, and neither side has said how long the operation will last.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: Israeli tanks push into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire

entry.title: Duffy keeps pointing at L3Harris as FAA ground-stop cause stays unknown
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy continued on Wednesday to blame contractor L3Harris for the failure that forced the Federal Aviation Administration to ground flights nationwide last Friday — even though investigators still have not determined the root cause.

L3Harris owns and maintains the FAA's telecommunications network. A section of old copper wire in El Dorado, Arkansas, was being replaced with fiber-optic lines when the incident happened.

Speaking on "The Morning Meeting" on Wednesday, Duffy said a contractor failed to identify and isolate the router problem quickly enough. "The monitoring of the network matters," he said. New installations of the same routers have been paused, and technicians have disabled the function linked to Friday's outage. The FAA offered no update on the investigation on Wednesday.

A single router, a nationwide stop

Officials have said a Juniper router installed as part of the upgrade in El Dorado suddenly began sending thousands of inquiries every few seconds, overwhelming the older parts of the network. That produced inconsistent radar and communications signals at 17 of the FAA's 22 key air traffic control centers, and the agency grounded planes. It was only the second nationwide ground stop since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

It is still a mystery why this device behaved differently from the 68 previous copper-to-fiber upgrades across the FAA's network, none of which caused a problem. Officials have suggested the router may have been configured incorrectly, but Bedford said the technician was a highly trained Air Force veteran who had done the same job dozens of times before.

"Blame me"

Bedford, speaking at a separate event hosted by The Hill, pushed back on the idea that the contractor alone should carry the blame. He said his agency is ultimately responsible for what happened, even if L3Harris was doing the work.

"I am the chief accountability officer. I take full responsibility for it," Bedford said. "I wish people would lay off the secretary. He's got a lot of work to do, but I'm the guy they hired to get this done. So, blame me."

L3Harris has not commented since a Saturday statement pledging to support the investigation, and declined to say more on Wednesday.

The $50 billion question

The FAA nearly doubled its funding request to Congress to $50 billion after Friday's ground stop, to pay for the rest of the overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. The agency received $12.5 billion last year to start the project. Only about $10 billion of the new request would go to air traffic control technology; the rest would fund runways, airport towers and aging control centers built in the 1960s.

Several key lawmakers said on Tuesday that Congress is unlikely to approve the full amount right now, since the FAA has not spent all of last year's money. Bedford said he understands why members of Congress might be having "some indigestion associated with that."

Airlines for America president Chris Sununu praised Bedford for briefing airline chief executives within half an hour of the stop and staying on the phone through the night. He warned this might not be the last technical problem during the project, because the work is akin to trying to get an iPhone to talk to a flip phone.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Fast Company

link.title: Duffy keeps pointing at L3Harris as FAA ground-stop cause stays unknown

entry.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, setting up a record AI debut
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed, in one of the largest stock-market debuts on record and the first by a major developer of frontier artificial intelligence models.

The shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT. The company had planned to sell 825 million shares, and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters the size of the offering has increased, though the final share count has not been made public. At $83, the original 825 million shares alone would raise about $68.5 billion, valuing the maker of the Claude chatbot at roughly $1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

The pricing follows a roadshow that drew demand several times the shares on offer, despite questions about the company's ability to sustain its rapid growth. It is the second mega-IPO this year centred on AI, following SpaceX's record-setting listing in June. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead underwriters, heading a 22-bank syndicate; the same two banks led the SpaceX offering.

Anthropic's growth has been driven by surging demand for its Claude models, particularly Claude Code, its coding agent that has become popular among software developers. Its annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from September 30, according to its IPO filing. It had 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 a year as of September 30, up from more than 1,500 at the end of last year.

But sustaining that growth is becoming expensive. Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing capacity and infrastructure in the first half of 2026, nearly four times the amount a year earlier, and incurred a further $5 billion in computing costs in the third quarter. Revenue rose 47 percent in the third quarter to $16.96 billion, while the company reported an operating loss of $567 million, compared with operating income of $974 million in the second quarter.

The company has committed to nearly $900 billion in computing spending with infrastructure partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google. Its prospectus warns that some of those partners depend on third-party financing to acquire chips and build capacity, and that if such financing became unavailable or more costly, contracted capacity could be delayed, repriced, reduced or not delivered.

The debut is also a test of the AI boom at a more difficult moment for the sector. Chipmakers and cloud companies central to the business have come under pressure in recent weeks over valuation concerns and mounting infrastructure costs. Anthropic's closest rival, OpenAI, is expected to pursue a public listing as early as next year.

Anthropic also faces questions over how it will balance its commercial ambitions with its emphasis on AI safety. Chief executive Dario Amodei has called for the industry to slow the pace of developing and releasing increasingly powerful models, warning that advances in AI could outstrip society's ability to manage the risks.

Anthropic declined to comment on the pricing. Bloomberg News first reported it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 a share, setting up a record AI debut

entry.title: Nvidia's interim chief tells staff to move forward at first all-hands since Huang exit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Nvidia's interim chief executive, Colette Kress, told employees to move on from the departure of founder Jensen Huang at the company's first all-hands meeting since his resignation, promising pay rises and extra equity in December as the board pushes ahead with finding a permanent leader.

"Let's move forward," Kress told staff at the meeting in Santa Clara on Wednesday, according to people familiar with the matter. The hour-long gathering was held in person and streamed to employees on Microsoft Teams. Kress was joined by Harvey Jones, the newly appointed chair of Nvidia's board, and Ian Buck, who leads the company's hyperscale and high-performance computing business.

Kress moved quickly from her opening message to pay. She told employees they could expect salary increases and additional equity awards in December, months ahead of the company's normal compensation cycle. "The best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp," she said, according to the reports.

Pay was the most common subject among roughly 700 questions employees submitted before the meeting, with board transparency second. Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer since 2013, has spent her first days as interim chief trying to steady a workforce rattled by the sudden exit of the man who built the company into the world's most valuable chipmaker.

Jones used his part of the meeting to repeat the board's position: it unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him. He told staff the board would not settle for a "Jensen clone" and would not compromise its requirements for the sake of speed, while accepting suggestions from employees during the search. The board has retained the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles and says it will consider internal and external candidates.

The message lands against open dissent inside the company. An online petition calling for Huang's return has gathered nearly 200,000 signatures, more than 10,000 of them from people claiming to be current Nvidia employees, and some staff have publicly pressed for his reinstatement. Huang himself said on Tuesday that he would be "honoured" to return. Kress told CNBC the same day that "the board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen."

Huang resigned after reports about his personal conduct, including an admitted affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset, which the board described as a lack of candour. His departure came days after Nvidia reported another record quarter, with third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion and guidance well above Wall Street expectations. Shares fell 2.9 percent on Wednesday, as investors weighed whether the company can sustain its momentum without its founder at the helm.

Kress closed Tuesday's earnings call, her first as interim chief, with an upbeat note: "Our customers and our partners are with us. And employees are committed. We've got this." Wednesday's meeting was the first test of whether employees agree.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • New York Post

link.title: Nvidia's interim chief tells staff to move forward at first all-hands since Huang exit

entry.title: Flu activity rises across the US as six states reach high levels, CDC data shows
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The US flu season is off to an unusually early start, and it is gathering speed. New data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows six states now at high or very high levels of flu activity, with illness spreading fastest across the South and West.

Five states — California, Tennessee, Oregon, South Carolina and Texas — are in the CDC's high-activity category. Louisiana stands alone in the very-high category. Three more states — New York, Massachusetts and Hawaii — are at moderate activity. The figures come from the CDC's weekly FluView update for the week ending November 7.

The agency said seasonal flu activity is higher than typically observed at this time of year, and that it continues to increase in many parts of the country. About 11% of flu specimens tested at clinical laboratories were positive in the week ending November 7, and that share was still rising. More than 3% of doctors' office visits were for flu-like symptoms.

The CDC's first estimates of the season put the toll so far at at least 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations and 2,100 deaths. Five flu-associated deaths among children have been reported this season. The most frequently reported virus in the week ending November 7 was influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, a descendant of the strain behind the 2009 swine flu pandemic that has circulated seasonally ever since.

Health experts cautioned that the early surge is real but its ultimate severity is not yet known. The CDC noted that an earlier increase in activity does not necessarily lead to a higher seasonal peak or greater overall severity, and said it is too early to know which flu viruses will dominate this season. In an October media briefing, Dr. Anna Durbin of Johns Hopkins University said the flu hospitalization rate in mid-October was the highest recorded that early in autumn in more than 15 years.

Dr. Fred Lopez, an infectious diseases specialist at the LSU Health Sciences Center in New Orleans, said the season was taking off and was only likely to increase over the next month or two. Louisiana, where he practices, is seeing the worst of it so far.

The CDC recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone aged six months and older, and says prescription antiviral drugs should be started as early as possible, especially for people at higher risk of complications.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Fox News

link.title: Flu activity rises across the US as six states reach high levels, CDC data shows

entry.title: The billion-year gap in Earth's rock record may finally have an explanation
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

More than a billion years of Earth's history is missing from the rock record, and scientists say they may finally have an explanation. A study published November 4 in the journal Nature traces the gap to slow movements deep inside the planet, which lifted ancient continents into the path of grinding ice sheets and then let them sink again.

The gap is known as the Great Unconformity. In a normal sequence, rock layers stack up with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top. But in places including the Grand Canyon, northern Europe and northern China, sedimentary rock about 540 million years old sits directly on crystalline basement rock that is more than a billion years old — in places up to two billion. Everything that should have been laid down in between is simply absent. At the Grand Canyon, researchers estimate the missing record spans roughly 1.2 billion years, as much as a quarter of Earth's entire history.

Geologists first described the feature in the late 1800s, at the Grand Canyon. For about 150 years the cause stayed an open question. One leading idea blamed the Snowball Earth period, roughly 720 to 635 million years ago, when the planet may have been largely frozen and moving ice could have scraped the rock away. But if ice covered the globe, it should have erased the record everywhere — and the gap is not everywhere.

The new work, by Santosh Dhungana and Nicolas Flament of the University of Wollongong in Australia, tested a different suspect: the mantle, the 2,900-kilometre-thick layer of hot, slowly flowing rock between the crust and the core. Using the Gadi supercomputer, they ran six simulations of mantle convection over the past billion years. In every model, the currents lifted three ancient continental cores — Laurentia, now much of North America; Baltica, in northern Europe; and North China — from around a billion years ago until about 540 million years ago.

That uplift overlapped with the Snowball Earth freeze, and raised land erodes far faster under moving ice than flat land does under rivers. The researchers argue the ice ground away the exposed rock. Then, over the past 540 million years, the same regions slowly sank and were buried under fresh sediment, sealing the sharp boundary seen today.

The gap ends just before the Cambrian explosion, around 530 to 540 million years ago, when animal life diversified rapidly. The erosion may have released elements such as potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the oceans, which could have helped marine life develop shells and added oxygen to the atmosphere — though that link remains a hypothesis.

The finding does not close the book: the evidence is a computer model, and the primary proof is rock that is no longer there. But it is the first quantitative test of the mantle-driven idea, and it ties two long-standing suspects — deep-Earth movement and ice — into a single sequence.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Smithsonian Magazine

link.title: The billion-year gap in Earth's rock record may finally have an explanation

entry.title: Heavy rain floods both U.S. coasts as Florida braces for more
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A slow-moving storm system dumped heavy rain on both American coasts on Wednesday, flooding roads across South Florida and grounding flights in San Francisco, with forecasters warning more rain is coming in Florida.

In South Florida, preliminary figures from the National Weather Service showed 15.3 inches of rain fell in a 24-hour period ending Wednesday in parts of Broward County. The city of Hollywood declared a state of emergency, and Mayor Josh Levy urged motorists to stay off the roads, calling it a historically significant rainfall event. Portions of Interstate 95 and the Florida Turnpike in Hollywood were closed because of high water and stalled vehicles, and the city said it received more than 300 calls for service overnight.

Heavy rain caused the roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood to collapse. No injuries were reported. Cars were submerged along roads across the region, and in Fort Lauderdale the 5.72 inches that fell in a downpour ending early Wednesday broke the daily record of 1.8 inches set in 1959. Farther north, a warning was issued for minor flooding along the St. Johns River.

The Florida Division of Emergency Management warned on Tuesday night that potentially catastrophic amounts of rainfall could cause flash flooding and life-threatening rip tides. The threat was expected to last through Friday along Florida's Atlantic Coast, with another 12 inches of rain possible in places. NBC News reported that about 11 million people between Miami and Jacksonville faced flooding risks.

Forecasters link the deluge to El Niño, the warming cycle that has disrupted Florida's typical October-to-May dry season, steering low-pressure systems toward the southeastern United States and bringing repeated rounds of heavy rain. It is the second major flooding episode to hit Florida this month, after record rain in early November.

A new concern looms ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. A low-pressure system is expected to form near the northern Bahamas and could become a subtropical or tropical storm, bringing more rain to parts of the southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts into early next week, according to the National Hurricane Center in Miami.

California was hit by the same coast-to-coast pattern. Heavy rain and high winds grounded planes at San Francisco's airport, disrupted ferry service and flooded roads in Napa County and other wine-country areas north of the city. Along San Francisco's Embarcadero, waves crashed over flood barricades near the Ferry Building, and several ferries were canceled. Highways were blocked by flooding or debris in Napa, Marin, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties.

The Los Angeles County Fire Department issued an evacuation warning on Wednesday for the Palisades, Hurst and Sunset burn-scar areas, citing a risk of debris flows as the storm approaches. The warning runs from Wednesday evening through Friday morning. Wind gusts up to 50 mph were forecast for San Francisco's East Bay and 70 mph for the Altamont Pass, with as much as four feet of snow expected through Friday in the highest Sierra Nevada.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • National Weather Service

entry.title: A blood test may predict Alzheimer's-related decline years before symptoms
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A simple blood test may one day tell a healthy older adult how likely they are to develop memory and thinking problems, according to a new Mayo Clinic study.

The research, published November 16 in JAMA Neurology, found that a blood marker called phosphorylated tau 217 — p-tau217 for short — can help estimate a cognitively healthy person's risk of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over the next five or ten years. The approach combines the blood measurement with age, sex and genetic risk. Higher levels of the marker and older age were both associated with greater risk.

P-tau217 is a protein fragment linked to Alzheimer's disease, in which tau proteins build into toxic tangles inside brain cells. Its level in the blood can rise as Alzheimer's-related changes take hold, years before everyday memory is affected.

The researchers studied 2,178 adults aged 60 to 90 with no cognitive impairment at the start: 1,644 in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging and 534 in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. All had p-tau217 blood measurements, genetic testing and repeated cognitive assessments. The team built its risk estimates from the Mayo Clinic group, then confirmed the link between higher p-tau217 and greater risk of decline in the second group.

The numbers show how much the estimate can vary. For a 75-year-old woman who did not carry APOE e4, a common genetic risk variant, the estimated five-year risk of mild cognitive impairment was 5 percent with a relatively low p-tau217 level — and 16 percent with a higher one. Her estimated ten-year risk rose from 12 percent to 35 percent. Age mattered too: at the same high p-tau217 level, the estimated five-year risk ranged from 6 percent at age 65 to 37 percent at age 85.

The work builds on earlier Mayo Clinic research that used PET brain scans to measure amyloid, a protein that accumulates in the brain in Alzheimer's disease. A blood test is less invasive and potentially more scalable. It could matter more if therapies now being studied can prevent or delay decline before symptoms appear: two prevention trials, AHEAD 3-45 and TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 3, are testing amyloid-targeting treatments in people without symptoms and used blood biomarkers to help identify participants.

The researchers stress the test is not ready for routine use. The estimates were developed in the Mayo Clinic Study of Aging, whose participants come largely from southeastern Minnesota, and need further study in more diverse populations and with other p-tau217 blood tests. Biomarker testing is not currently recommended for people without symptoms, and there is no approved treatment for people who carry Alzheimer's-related changes but have no symptoms. A higher result does not mean dementia is certain — some people with Alzheimer's-related brain changes never develop symptoms.

"Absolute risk gives the biomarker result clinical context," said Clifford Jack Jr., a Mayo Clinic neuroradiologist and the study's senior author. "If preventive treatments become available, this kind of information could help patients and clinicians have more informed conversations about treatment."

Illustration — not a photograph.

entry.title: House Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker, putting him on course to make history
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

House Democrats have formally nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be Speaker of the House, putting the New York lawmaker on course to become the first Black person to lead the chamber.

Jeffries won the nomination in a closed-door caucus vote on Wednesday, November 18, by 251 votes to 11. No other candidate stood against him, but 11 members voted against his nomination — a small group of holdouts that included newly elected members from the party's left wing. Seven incoming lawmakers issued a joint statement explaining their opposition, arguing that the party needed new leadership after its time in the minority.

The nomination is the first formal step. The full House will elect its Speaker on January 3, when the new Congress convenes and Democrats take control of the chamber after their midterm election victory. Jeffries will need 218 votes on the House floor to win the gavel. Democrats are projected to hold at least 257 seats in the new Congress — comfortably above that threshold — with seven midterm races still uncalled.

If elected, Jeffries would make history as the first Black lawmaker to serve as Speaker, one of the most powerful roles in American government and second in line to the presidency. The Congressional Black Caucus noted the potential milestone as the nomination was announced.

Jeffries, 56, represents a Brooklyn district and has led House Democrats since 2023, when he succeeded Nancy Pelosi as the party's leader in the chamber. He had the option of being nominated by acclamation, with no ballots cast and no count taken, but instead asked for a recorded vote — a choice that put the 11 dissenting votes on the record.

His election as Speaker is widely expected, though the nomination vote showed that a small part of the caucus remains unconvinced. How those members vote on the House floor in January will be closely watched, even if the outcome is not in serious doubt.

On the Republican side, House Republicans have nominated Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan as their candidate for Speaker, setting up a contest between the two parties' leaders when the new Congress convenes.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • Reuters

entry.title: Astronomers watch a star swallow its companion in the Andromeda galaxy
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Astronomers have watched a star swallow its companion whole — and, for the first time, pieced together the entire event from beginning to end.

The pair, formally known as AT 2025abao and nicknamed Bao, sits on the outskirts of the Andromeda galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun. Its companion was a puffy supergiant roughly seven times the Sun's mass, 350 times its radius and 18,000 times as bright. When the giant swelled up, it engulfed the smaller star, which spiralled inward through its outer layers until the two became one.

What makes this merger special is the record around it. Researchers first noticed unusual activity in the system in 2023 and kept watching. The system erupted in October 2025 — the flash was spotted by amateur astronomer Koichi Itagaki and picked up by the Zwicky Transient Facility — and NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed it just 47 days after the eruption peaked, on December 24, 2025. That is the earliest follow-up ever made of an event like this, and it gave the team the final piece needed to reconstruct what happened before, during and after the merger.

The findings, published Wednesday in the journal Nature, describe a surprisingly fast end. Once the smaller star touched the giant's surface, the two merged after only about seven orbits — roughly seven years — far quicker than other known mergers of two smaller stars. The process is known as common-envelope evolution: the two stars briefly share a single outer layer of gas before becoming one, possibly rejuvenated, star.

The result matters because binary stars are common, and their mergers shape the objects astronomers see across the universe — from unusual bright stars to the progenitors of some supernovae. Standard models have struggled to explain how energy moves around inside a shared envelope, and Bao's unusually complete timeline gives theorists a rare test case to check their work against.

There is still room for doubt. Dust thrown off by the eruption currently hides the merged star itself, so the merger is an inference drawn from the light, the dust and the simulations — strong, but indirect. A separate modelling study, published as a preprint in October and not yet peer-reviewed, argues the two stars' cores might have survived in orbit without fully merging. Future observations will be needed to settle that question for good.

For now, Bao stands as the best-observed stellar merger yet: a slow-motion collision, caught on camera across three years, in the galaxy next door.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • MIT Kavli Institute

link.title: Astronomers watch a star swallow its companion in the Andromeda galaxy

entry.title: World court to decide whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United Nations' highest court will deliver its judgment on Thursday in a case accusing Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority — a ruling that could make legal history.

The International Court of Justice will begin reading its judgment at 10 a.m. local time (09:00 GMT) at the Peace Palace in The Hague. Judge Yuji Iwasawa, the court's president, will read the decision in a session expected to last up to 90 minutes.

The case was brought by The Gambia, a small West African nation, in November 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It accuses Myanmar of violating the 1948 Genocide Convention during a military crackdown in Rakhine State in August and September 2017 that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya — most of them Muslim — across the border into Bangladesh. Survivors have described killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A United Nations fact-finding mission in 2018 concluded that the campaign included "genocidal acts".

Myanmar denies the charge. It says its forces were responding to attacks by armed Rohingya militants on police posts, and argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya as a people.

That question of intent is the heart of the case. Under the Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of a specific intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part. The Gambia has argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from the scale and pattern of the 2017 operation. The court held hearings on the merits from January 12 to 29 this year.

If the court finds against Myanmar, it would be the first time the International Court of Justice has held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, the court found that Serbia had failed to prevent the Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed — but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide. The Myanmar judgment would be the court's first ruling on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.

The judgment will be final, with no right of appeal. But the court has no way to enforce its decisions. The Gambia has asked it to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, pay reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely. If Myanmar ignores the ruling, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.

For the Rohingya themselves, the wait has been long. About 1.2 million now live in the Cox's Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, and roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, where they face restrictions on movement, healthcare and livelihoods. A finding of genocide would formally recognise the harm they suffered, even if it brings no immediate change on the ground.

What is still unknown

The outcome itself is not yet public, and the court could stop short of a genocide finding — for instance, by ruling that Myanmar failed to prevent or punish genocide without committing it. Whatever it decides, the judgment settles the legal question; whether it changes anything for the refugees in Cox's Bazar will depend on what states and the Security Council do next.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: World court to decide whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

entry.title: Musk calls his record $446m midterm spending 'pretty foolish'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Elon Musk has said he feels "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent backing Republicans in the US midterm elections, after voters handed the party sweeping defeats.

Musk was the election's biggest individual donor, giving $446 million (£339 million) to support President Donald Trump's party, much of it aimed at races in Texas, where many of his companies are based. Speaking virtually on Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit in New York, he said the money had bought him little.

"I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it," he said, adding that the result showed campaign cash alone could not decide an election. He added that, given the chance to do it again, he would probably have spent less.

It was a striking change of tone from a man who, at a Trump rally in 2024, joked that he was "not just Maga, I'm dark Maga". On Wednesday he distanced himself from the movement altogether. "I'm not Maga," he said, adding that if the label meant "blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

The scale of the spending was without precedent for a donor who was not a candidate. According to BBC analysis, at least $45 million of Musk's money went to support Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for a US Senate seat in Texas — who lost to Democrat James Talarico. In the Texas governor's race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of Republican control of the state. Musk described Hinojosa as "going to be quite moderate".

The defeats were part of a wider Democratic sweep. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, flipping seats in places Republicans had held for decades, in a bruising defeat for Trump.

Musk had backed Trump's second White House bid and served for several months at the start of Trump's second term as an unpaid special government employee, leading the Department of Government Efficiency.

The new Democratic majorities have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including controversial data centres. Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX — which has gained an estimated $10 billion in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected — should be investigated.

For Musk, the midterms were an expensive lesson in the limits of political money. He spent more than any private donor in history on a single election cycle, and the candidates he backed most heavily lost anyway. Whether he returns to big political spending is now an open question — and one his own remarks suggest he will think twice about.

What is still unknown

It is not yet clear whether Musk will scale back his political donations permanently or simply redirect them — he gave no firm commitment about future spending. How the new Democratic Congress handles its promised scrutiny of SpaceX also remains to be seen.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Reuters

link.title: Musk calls his record $446m midterm spending 'pretty foolish'

entry.title: Waymo pulls driverless cars off US freeways after California safety ban
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Waymo has paused driverless taxi rides on freeways across the United States, days after California's motor vehicles department banned its self-driving cars from the state's highways over safety concerns.

The Alphabet-owned company said it has "temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service". The pause, implemented last Wednesday, covers the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin — the five areas where Waymo offered freeway rides. Rides on city streets continue as normal.

The California Department of Motor Vehicles imposed its ban effective November 11, after two incidents in early November. On November 5, three Waymo vehicles drove into an active construction zone on US Route 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco. The next day, a Waymo car on Highway 280 in San Francisco sped towards two California Highway Patrol cars and tried to pass them while their lights were flashing during a traffic break. Video of the second incident spread widely online.

The department said Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose "an imminent hazard to public safety" because of "recurring incursions" into active construction zones, putting road workers, vehicles and equipment at risk. It said the restrictions will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates it has taken "effective corrective actions". The regulator noted that similar incidents had occurred on May 18, and that this is the second time this year Waymo has faced highway restrictions in California — it paused freeway operations in May in San Francisco and Los Angeles to improve how its vehicles respond to construction zones.

Waymo said the November 5 construction-zone incident caused no injuries or collisions, and that it is working with the California DMV and other state officials to resume freeway operations. Freeway testing continues with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel, and the company says the pause will let it "evaluate our performance". Waymo, which completes about half a million trips a week, points to its own data showing 95 percent fewer crashes resulting in serious injuries than human drivers.

The pause matters because freeway driving was a key step in Waymo's expansion beyond city streets, and because it is the sharpest regulatory intervention the company has faced. Robotaxis have already drawn scrutiny from safety investigators over red-light running, driving into oncoming traffic and failing to respect emergency road closures — a June CNN analysis found hundreds of such incidents. Waymo has described most of those as isolated, and says the overwhelming majority of its rides are smooth and uneventful.

What is still unknown

Neither Waymo nor the DMV has given a timeline for when freeway rides will resume, or said what specific corrective actions would satisfy the regulator. It is also unclear whether other states will follow California's lead, or whether the pause will slow Waymo's plans to expand into new cities.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • CNN

link.title: Waymo pulls driverless cars off US freeways after California safety ban

entry.title: Trump, Xi and Putin open first-ever three-way summit in Shenzhen
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The presidents of the United States, China and Russia opened the first trilateral meeting of the three countries' leaders on Thursday in Shenzhen, a gathering Donald Trump described as "really making history."

Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin sat down at the Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the two-day APEC leaders' meeting in the southern Chinese tech hub. Xi, hosting the talks, called them of "groundbreaking significance" as the session began. Trump said the three leaders had a "great deal to discuss" and carried a "special responsibility" as leaders of three of the world's largest countries.

The meeting is the first time the three leaders have met as a group. Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and with Xi earlier in the visit. He called Putin his "friend" and said the two have a "great relationship," and said after meeting Xi that the United States and China "want to see an end to the Ukraine war."

The agenda is crowded. The leaders were expected to discuss the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade and artificial intelligence. Trump said the talks would cover "a lot of things including denuclearisation," and said after the Xi meeting that Iran "cannot have a nuclear weapon."

There are limits to what the meeting is expected to produce. US officials have said they do not expect a formal agreement, describing the session as an initial conversation. China has long been reluctant to join nuclear disarmament talks, pointing to the gap between its arsenal and those of the United States and Russia, and Beijing has resisted efforts to put the Ukraine war on the agenda.

The timing adds weight to the encounter. The last US-Russia nuclear treaty expired in February, leaving the world's two largest nuclear arsenals without caps for the first time in more than half a century. The three leaders' talks come as the APEC summit brings 21 Pacific Rim economies together in Shenzhen, a forum that takes no binding decisions but has long served as a place to build consensus on trade and cooperation.

Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday from the Philippines, where he attended the ASEAN summit. His bilateral meeting with Xi was their fourth since he returned to office in 2025, and their third this year. Putin's appearance at the APEC gathering was his first in person since 2017.

Whether the three-way format becomes a regular fixture, or a one-off piece of pageantry, will depend on what follows the handshakes. For now, the meeting itself is the news: three leaders who have never sat down together have done so, in a room where the world's largest economies, its biggest nuclear arsenals and two ongoing wars were all on the table.

---

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Trump, Xi and Putin open first-ever three-way summit in Shenzhen

entry.title: AI in African classrooms: promise, pitfalls, and the policies that decide which wins
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Artificial intelligence is arriving in African classrooms faster than the rules for using it. A new analysis published by the World Economic Forum argues that whether it helps or harms students will depend less on the technology itself than on the policies, languages and teachers around it.

The stakes are high. More than 80 percent of students in sub-Saharan Africa cannot read by the age of 10, according to the piece, and around 1.2 billion young people in emerging and developing economies will reach working age between 2025 and 2035. Education systems need to equip them with job skills at a scale that traditional methods have struggled to reach. Technology alone, the authors note, has not done the job: a review by the Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel found that interventions focused only on infrastructure or hardware did not improve learning outcomes.

Used well, AI could change that equation. The analysis points to tools that automate routine administrative work, support teachers' professional development, and give students personalised guidance as they learn. But it warns that the technology is often oversold as a cure-all and pitched without regard for a country's norms, policies, stakeholders or culture — and when that happens, it can falter, or actively harm teaching, learning and students' sense of identity.

The risks are concrete. Large language models still perform far better in English than in the low-resource languages many African students speak, and their outputs can carry culturally irrelevant content. In Guinea-Bissau, where the government used Anthropic's Claude with World Bank Group support to draft learning-assessment questions and help with grading, Portuguese prompts returned lower-quality results than English ones, and the model used uncommon surnames and the European Portuguese word "aldeia" for village instead of the Bissau-Guinean term "tabanka". The team caught the errors and did not use the output verbatim — but the authors warn that using such a chatbot to train more than 6,000 teachers nationally could have real consequences if it kept suggesting the wrong content.

Even good tools can stall on logistics. In Seychelles, an open-source AI tutor for secondary maths and geography was piloted in schools that already had free internet, yet the team struggled to fit it into the timetable: schools had to decide what activity it would displace, who would supervise the sessions, and how participation would be sustained.

The authors' conclusion is that success depends more on policy and cultural relevance than on computing power. The Beijing Consensus has already called on countries to adjust existing regulations or adopt new ones for responsible AI in education. Evidence from South Africa points the same way: a World Bank Group programme studied 46 higher education institutions and found that about half had their own policies or guidelines for ethical AI use. Among those with policies, 78 percent were integrating AI into the curriculum — roughly three times the rate of institutions without one. The study's authors caution that this does not prove fragmented policies alone can mainstream AI, and that more research is needed on how policy, institutional size and resources interact.

The message for governments and schools is to treat AI as one tool in a broader toolkit, not as something above human systems. That means building policy, culture and people into every deployment — including training language models on the under-represented cultures and languages they are meant to serve.

---

Sources

  • World Economic Forum

link.title: AI in African classrooms: promise, pitfalls, and the policies that decide which wins

entry.title: Anthropic's record $107 billion listing values the AI maker at $1.5 trillion
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has raised more than $107 billion in the largest initial public offering in history, valuing the five-year-old company at about $1.5 trillion. Its shares begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT.

The company said on Wednesday that it sold 956 million shares at $83 each, above the $70 to $78 range it had marketed to investors. Its seven co-founders sold a further 23.6 million shares. The public sale alone raised about $81.3 billion. A separate $26 billion private placement, with shares bought by companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia, lifts the total to more than $107 billion.

The deal tops the previous record set by SpaceX, which raised $75 billion when it listed in June. On a fully diluted basis — counting stock options and restricted shares as well as shares outstanding — Anthropic is valued at about $1.5 trillion. Counting only shares outstanding, the figure is about $1.08 trillion.

The listing is the first by a frontier AI lab, a company building the most powerful general-purpose AI models. Anthropic was founded in 2021 by researchers who left OpenAI over concerns about AI safety, led by chief executive Dario Amodei. It launched Claude in early 2023, months after OpenAI released ChatGPT, and the two companies have competed closely ever since.

The financials show remarkable growth. Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached about $81 billion by the end of October, up $10 billion in a single month. Revenue in the first half of the year was $16.3 billion, up 1,300 percent on the same period a year earlier, and adjusted operating income was $1.6 billion, against a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.

But the debut also arrives amid doubts. Tech shares linked to the AI boom have been volatile, and the Nasdaq is down more than 11 percent since early October as investors question whether the vast spending on AI infrastructure will pay off. Analysts quoted by NPR called the listing a test of sentiment towards the AI trade. Anthropic's own prospectus runs to dozens of pages of risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI systems.

The company has also drawn political scrutiny. Earlier this year it clashed with the Pentagon over restrictions on how its models could be used by the military, and the Pentagon later designated it a "supply chain risk". Its chief executive has himself warned that frontier AI development should slow down — even as his company races ahead.

For now, investors have voted with their wallets. Whether the valuation holds will be decided from Thursday, when the shares start trading and the market gets its first chance to price the most expensive AI bet yet made.

---

Sources

  • Axios

link.title: Anthropic's record $107 billion listing values the AI maker at $1.5 trillion

entry.title: World court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority during a military crackdown in 2017, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.

Judges in The Hague found that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, carried out widespread acts of sexual violence and extreme violence against children, and attacked people as they fled in large numbers to Bangladesh. The court said the only reasonable explanation for the scale and nature of the violence was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State.

The case was brought by The Gambia in November 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which obliges states to prevent and punish genocide. The court's decision, reached by nine votes to six, is final and cannot be appealed.

The ruling closes a case that has run for seven years. In August 2017, Myanmar's military launched what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State after attacks by Rohingya militants on security posts. More than 730,000 Rohingya fled across the border into Bangladesh in the weeks that followed, in one of the fastest mass displacements in modern history. Most remain in refugee camps there today.

The court acknowledged that the militant group known as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army had attacked security outposts and civilians. But it found that the military's response went far beyond anything that could be explained as punishment or counter-insurgency, pointing in particular to indiscriminate killings, the separation and execution of men, sexual violence, and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.

The judgment is only the fourth time since the Second World War that an international court has found the legal threshold for genocide to have been met. Human rights groups called it a rare victory for survivors. Amnesty International said the finding gave formal legal recognition to atrocities that had been documented for years.

The ruling binds Myanmar under international law, but the court has no police force or enforcement arm of its own. Whether it changes anything on the ground will depend on what other states and United Nations bodies do next. Separate proceedings at the International Criminal Court, which deals with the criminal responsibility of individuals rather than states, are still open: in 2024 its prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar's military leader, Min Aung Hlaing.

For the Rohingya, a stateless Muslim minority that has faced decades of discrimination in Myanmar, the judgment is the first time an international court has said plainly that what happened to them in 2017 was genocide.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: World court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

entry.title: Trump, Xi and Putin challenge the International Criminal Court at Shenzhen summit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The leaders of the United States, China and Russia used their first three-way summit on Thursday to take aim at the International Criminal Court, agreeing in a joint declaration that the Hague-based court "must not abuse" its jurisdiction.

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin met for 80 minutes at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China. Afterwards they issued a four-point "declaration toward peace" — the first statement the three leaders have ever signed together.

The declaration covered reform of the United Nations, increased supplies of refined oil, a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, and the court. On the court, the three leaders said the consent of states and respect for the immunity of state officials were of paramount importance, and agreed that the court and similar bodies "must not abuse their jurisdiction."

Trump went further in the meeting's public opening, describing the court as a rogue globalist organisation that had exceeded its authority and was "out of control", and grouping it with other bodies he said undermined national sovereignty.

The language carries a pointed edge for Putin. The court issued an arrest warrant for the Russian president in March 2023 over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children, and the warrant remains in force. None of the three countries — the United States, China or Russia — is a member of the court.

For all its symbolism, the summit settled little else. The declaration named no nuclear cap, mentioned neither Ukraine nor Iran, and no deal emerged on the wars that filled the agenda. The statement was released through Chinese state media and later by Russia; no US version had been issued when the meeting ended.

The three leaders reaffirmed that "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought", and promised talks on reducing nuclear risks. Whether the declaration marks a durable alignment — or a one-day show of unity — will be judged by what, if anything, follows it.

Sources

  • Politico

link.title: Trump, Xi and Putin challenge the International Criminal Court at Shenzhen summit

entry.title: UK Covid inquiry finds early containment was 'doomed to fail'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The United Kingdom's early efforts to contain Covid-19 were doomed to fail, the public inquiry into the pandemic has concluded, because the country had no test, trace and isolate system able to cope with a fast-moving outbreak when the virus arrived.

The finding comes in the inquiry's seventh report, a 245-page assessment of border controls through contact tracing. Community testing and contact tracing were abandoned in mid-March 2020, after which the virus spread virtually unchecked. Ministers said testing capacity was being overwhelmed, and the four UK nations were effectively blind to how quickly Covid was spreading. The absence of a robust system from the start, it says, helped force harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures.

Testing capacity did eventually grow: NHS Test and Trace, launched two months later, became one of the largest testing services in the world relative to population. More than £30 billion was spent across the UK on testing, tracing and isolating. But the inquiry questions why testing capacity in hospitals, universities and the private sector was not used from the start, instead of relying only on 12 government laboratories.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared, learning from countries with experience of other outbreaks, such as Sars — notably Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan, which had systems ready to go. UK simulation exercises had already flagged problems with test, trace and isolation that appear not to have been fully acted on.

Support for people told to self-isolate was also criticised. Many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial help, the report says, and in the early months estimates suggested less than half of people complied with isolation rules. Fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for non-compliance, and £500 payments to help people on low incomes stay at home did not arrive until September in England — later in Scotland and Wales.

On borders, the inquiry found the UK lacked a clear early strategy. Suspending all flights from China in February 2020 could have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems, Baroness Hallett said; that did not happen. By April 2020, 93% of countries had put in place measures such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions. The UK, by contrast, only asked travellers from high-risk areas to self-isolate for 14 days, and introduced no further border measures until June 2020.

The report is more positive about smartphone apps, saying digital tools can significantly reduce the spread of infection. But three separate apps were developed — one for England and Wales, one for Scotland, and one for Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland — which took up valuable time. In summer 2021, around 7% of all UK adults were told to self-isolate over a seven-day period, an episode the press dubbed the "pingdemic". Treasury estimates suggested that may have reduced economic growth by as much as 0.3% that month.

The recommendations include putting international border control measures in place at the earliest stages of a future pandemic, and developing a single UK-wide digital tool rather than separate apps. The overall message: the UK should have had a robust, ready-to-go test, trace and isolate system, learned from other countries and its own exercises, and provided better practical and financial support for isolation.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: UK Covid inquiry finds early containment was 'doomed to fail'

entry.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A wooden boat carrying about 100 migrants capsized off the coast of Senegal in the early hours of Wednesday, leaving dozens of people missing and prompting a search that stretched into a second day.

The pirogue went down near the village of Yenne, south of the capital Dakar, at around 02:00 local time, according to a representative of the village chief. A survivor questioned by police said about 100 people had been on board, including five women. The badly damaged boat later washed ashore on a beach near Yenne, where identity documents, several mobile phones and a school enrolment document were found among the belongings left behind.

Initial reports said one person had died, but some local media reported that at least four bodies had been recovered. Dozens remained unaccounted for as search operations continued through Wednesday and were due to resume on Thursday. "Cries could be heard coming from the pirogue that were audible even from the beach," Oumar Sow, the village chief's representative, told the AFP news agency.

The sinking came less than two weeks after a shipwreck off the north-western town of Thieppe killed at least 39 people, in what was described as one of Senegal's deadliest migration disasters. The two tragedies underline a renewed surge in dangerous sea crossings from West Africa, with migrants increasingly setting out in overloaded wooden pirogues bound for Spain's Canary Islands.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Diomaye Faye expressed concern about the renewed increase in irregular departures by migrants hoping to reach Europe. He instructed the interior ministry to prepare a report examining the factors driving the dangerous journeys and proposing measures to tackle the problem. After the earlier tragedy, Faye had urged Senegalese people not to risk their lives attempting the crossings.

The scale of the danger is stark. The UN migration agency, the International Organization for Migration, said last month that it had recorded at least 454 deaths and disappearances off the West African coast this year alone — and warned the true figure was likely higher, because many boats vanish without survivors or any trace.

The pressure at the other end of the route is also rising. On 7 November, El Hierro, the smallest of Spain's Canary Islands, declared a state of emergency after more than 3,300 people arrived in about 30 boats since the beginning of the month. For those who set out from Senegal's beaches in the dark, the journey remains one of the most perilous migration routes in the world.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Dozens missing after boat carrying 100 migrants sinks off Senegal's coast

entry.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A painting Vincent van Gogh made in the final weeks of his life has sold in New York for $190.4 million (£144.8 million), the highest price ever paid at auction for a work by the Dutch artist.

Châtaigniers en fleurs — Chestnut Trees in Blossom — went under the hammer at Sotheby's on Wednesday, fetching $165 million before fees took the total to $190.4 million. The result beat the pre-sale estimate of $180 million and shattered Van Gogh's previous auction record of $117.2 million, set in 2022 when his 1888 Orchard with Cypresses sold at Christie's in New York. It also ranks as the fourth-most expensive painting ever sold at auction.

Van Gogh painted the work in 1890, in the final two months of his life, during a burst of creativity after his release from a psychiatric asylum that May. He died two months later. The canvas had spent decades out of public view, held in the collection of Argentina's Blaquier-Arrieta family, who acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century.

The sale almost did not happen. In the days before the auction, representatives of the heirs of Samuel Fischer — the German-Jewish publisher who bought the painting in Paris in 1909 — argued that the family had been forced to part with it under Nazi persecution. Fischer died in 1934, and the painting was sold in 1936, after the family had suffered financial losses under the Nazis. The heirs' lawyer had called on Sotheby's to show the work had been sold at its market value, and to postpone the sale until it did.

On Tuesday, a day before the auction, Sotheby's announced that an agreement had been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of Fischer's legal descendants, allowing the sale to go ahead. The terms were not disclosed. Sotheby's said the two families had reached "a mutually satisfactory resolution" in recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust. The Fischer heirs said they were grateful for a negotiation that made it possible to acknowledge that suffering.

The painting's journey traces a century of European history. After Fischer acquired it in 1909, it was deposited with the dealer Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933, then passed to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936. Four further owners followed before the Blaquier family bought it in 1975.

Sotheby's did not immediately name the buyer. The painting was the most valuable lot offered across New York's auction houses this season, and its sale helped drive a strong week of marquee sales in the city.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history

entry.title: Houthi missile damages Riyadh's tallest tower in strike on financial district
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, was damaged on Thursday by a suspected Houthi missile, in the second strike on the capital's financial district in less than two weeks.

The strike hit the Public Investment Fund Tower, an 80-storey building standing 385 metres high in the King Abdullah Financial District. Witnesses said the blast blew out windows across seven to eight floors and bent parts of the tower's metal facade. Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency confirmed the attack caused material damage but no casualties, and said damage to several floors of the tower and nearby buildings was being assessed.

The early-morning blast was heard across the capital, and journalists in Riyadh reported a powerful explosion before Saudi authorities issued an emergency warning that was lifted minutes later. Entrances to the financial district were closed and people were evacuated, while ambulances and fire trucks were sent to the scene.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had addressed a missile threat launched towards Riyadh. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said an initial assessment pointed to the impact of falling debris, with material damage still being surveyed. Three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters the building had been hit by an incoming Houthi missile. The Houthis issued no immediate statement on the strike, and the Public Investment Fund acknowledged receiving a request for comment.

The tower is the centrepiece of the King Abdullah Financial District, a showcase for Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions that also houses the Saudi stock exchange and offices of international firms. The fund it hosts manages assets worth more than $900 billion and finances major projects intended to reduce the kingdom's dependence on oil. Witnesses told AFP that most of the building's employees had been working remotely since early September.

The attack follows a strike on state oil giant Aramco's building in the same district on November 8, and comes amid a surge in Houthi attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighbouring Yemen's civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Iran-backed Houthis. Saudi Arabia has also launched retaliatory strikes in Yemen in recent days, with Houthi media reporting deadly strikes across territory the group controls.

It was not immediately clear whether the tower had been evacuated before the attack, and officials did not immediately confirm the full extent of the damage. The strike underlines how the renewed fighting in Yemen is reaching into the heart of Saudi Arabia's financial centre, eleven days after the previous landmark was hit.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AFP
  • Reuters

link.title: Houthi missile damages Riyadh's tallest tower in strike on financial district

entry.title: Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge for third time in a week
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Ukraine struck the bridge linking Russia to Crimea for the third time in a week on Thursday, forcing a halt to train services across the crossing hours before President Vladimir Putin met President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping at a trilateral summit in China.

The latest attack was the third on the Kerch Bridge in four days. The first, on Monday, caused more minor damage. On Tuesday, Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section, and video and images verified by Reuters showed the main road arch crumbling into the sea and leaving a yawning gap in the roadway.

Russian authorities said the Thursday attack forced a suspension of train services across the bridge. Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed governor of Crimea, said in a video message that rail travel would resume later in the day, adding that Crimea would overcome the damage. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the latest attack and that specialists were assessing the damage, without giving an extent for Thursday's strike.

Satellite images from Monday and Thursday show a collapsed section of the bridge, according to the report. The Tuesday strike was described as likely to make it harder for Russia to supply the peninsula, home to nearly 2.5 million people, and to put pressure on Russian military logistics in parts of southern Ukraine held by Moscow.

The 12-mile bridge is the longest in Europe. Opened by Putin in 2018, it has become a symbol of Russia's attachment to Crimea, which Moscow annexed from Ukraine in 2014 and which hosts its Black Sea Fleet. The crossing carries both road and rail traffic and has been a repeated target since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.

There was no immediate comment on the latest attack from Ukraine or from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, according to the report. Zelenskyy was due to hold talks in Berlin later on Thursday with United States peace envoys, while the three leaders in Shenzhen were meeting for the first time in the trilateral format.

The bridge attacks have come in a week of intense diplomacy around the war, with the Shenzhen summit and the Berlin talks both taking place on the same day. Whether the damage to the crossing changes the course of those discussions remains unclear, and neither side has said when full road and rail traffic across the bridge will be restored.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NBC News

link.title: Ukraine strikes Crimean Bridge for third time in a week

entry.title: New York City's horse-drawn carriages will end in 2028 as Mamdani signs ban into law
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

New York City's horse-drawn carriages, a fixture of Central Park for more than 150 years, will disappear from the city's streets by June 2028. Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the ban into law on Thursday at City Hall, closing a chapter that generations of visitors have associated with the park.

The law, known as Romanch's Law, stops the city from issuing new licences for carriage horses, horse-drawn cabs and their drivers, and every existing licence expires on May 31, 2028. From June 1, 2028, no horse-drawn carriage will be allowed to operate on New York's streets. The City Council passed the bill on October 22 by a vote of 40 to 7.

The law is named for Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old visitor from India who died on June 17, 2026, after the horse pulling his family's carriage bolted during a ride in Central Park. The bill was sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte and had been debated for years before the fatal accident gave the campaign new urgency.

"For generations, horses lived and worked here in New York City," Mamdani said at the signing ceremony, adding that the city had changed and its laws needed to change with it. He signed the bill in City Hall's Blue Room, flanked by Council Speaker Julie Menin and former Mayor Bill de Blasio, who had pushed for the change for years.

The phase-out affects about 200 people: carriage drivers, stable hands and medallion owners. The administration says it will support them through a new Horse Carriage Worker Industry Program, with medallion buybacks for owners, stipends for drivers and stable hands, workforce training, career counselling and help starting new businesses. A full transition plan is due by April 2027. The law also requires the horses to be rehomed humanely, and forbids selling them for slaughter or transferring them to other carriage companies.

The ban is not going unchallenged. Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents the drivers, filed a federal lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block the law, arguing that it is unconstitutional. The case will decide whether the phase-out timetable survives.

New York is now the largest metropolitan area in the United States to ban horse-drawn carriages. Supporters of the ban point to decades of accidents and the welfare of the horses; opponents say the city is ending a living tradition and the livelihoods that go with it. Both sides now wait on the courts — and on the transition plan due next spring.

Sources

  • USA Today

link.title: New York City's horse-drawn carriages will end in 2028 as Mamdani signs ban into law

entry.title: TSMC cuts off advanced chipmaking for Chinese AI designers as new US rules bite
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Taiwan's TSMC is tightening restrictions on Chinese chip designers, suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders and generally limiting affected customers to older chipmaking technology, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The world's largest contract chipmaker has instructed that orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below be halted unless customers obtain US export licences, the people said. Chinese designers will generally be limited to older 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided their chips do not use high-bandwidth memory or require advanced packaging, according to TSMC guidance reviewed by the two people.

The move could close one of the last remaining routes for Chinese companies to produce powerful AI processors, complicating Beijing's efforts to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC. Most leading AI chips are produced using 7-nanometre processes or smaller, which allow faster and more energy-efficient performance. High-bandwidth memory lets processors handle the vast data volumes AI applications require, while advanced packaging integrates chips and memory to boost computing power.

The restrictions follow new US Commerce Department rules that took effect on Thursday, removing a compliance route that had allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced manufacturing services without individual export licences. Previously, TSMC could check the computing power and other technical characteristics of certain Chinese chip designs to determine whether they fell outside US export controls. Under the new rules, TSMC can no longer use that verification process for affected Chinese customers. Their advanced chips are instead presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless an exception applies.

The Financial Times first reported on Thursday that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following the new restrictions.

The measures could particularly affect Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia's processors, including independent chip designers and technology giants that have developed in-house chips. A US government list of approved chip designers includes Nvidia, AMD, Apple and Taiwanese companies MediaTek and Realtek — but no mainland Chinese firms.

Some Chinese AI chip designers still had access to TSMC's 7-nanometre manufacturing technology before Thursday, a separate source with direct knowledge of the matter said. Reuters could not independently verify the arrangements under which those chips were manufactured.

TSMC's guidance also requires closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers and shipping routes, the people said. The checks extend to orders placed through overseas subsidiaries or intermediaries, including entities in Taiwan, the US, Europe, Japan and Southeast Asia.

Whether the US grants export licences for the halted orders, and how Beijing responds to the tighter controls, remains to be seen.

---

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: TSMC cuts off advanced chipmaking for Chinese AI designers as new US rules bite

entry.title: Muslims projected to outnumber Christians by 2035, Pew finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Islam is on course to become the world's largest religion by 2035, according to new projections from the Pew Research Center, ending centuries in which Christianity has held that position. The shift is expected to happen within a decade — but it is not a story of one faith shrinking while another grows. Both are getting bigger; one is simply growing faster.

Pew projects that by 2035 there will be about 2.57 billion Muslims worldwide, compared with 2.52 billion Christians. In 2020, the starting point for the study, the figures were roughly 2.02 billion Muslims and 2.27 billion Christians. Looking further ahead, the gap widens: if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians by 2070. Muslims would rise from 26 percent of the world's population in 2020 to 36 percent, while Christians would hold fairly steady at 29 percent.

The main driver is births, not conversion. Muslims have the highest fertility rate of any major religious group, at 3.1 children per woman in the 2020–2025 period, compared with 2.5 for Christian women and 1.6 for all other women combined. Muslims also tend to be younger on average, which means more women of childbearing age in the decades ahead.

The numbers behind that are stark. Between 2020 and 2070, Muslims are projected to gain 1.6 billion people through natural population change — births minus deaths — against an increase of 792 million for Christians. Religious switching plays a much smaller role: Pew expects Islam to lose a net 8 million people through switching over the period, and Christianity to lose a net 105 million, mostly people becoming religiously unaffiliated. Movement directly between the two faiths is expected to roughly cancel out.

Most of the growth will happen where each faith is already established.
