About three-quarters of the projected growth in the Muslim population is expected in the 53 countries where Muslims were already the majority in 2020. Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to double, from 227 million in 2020 to 461 million in 2070, making it home to the world's largest Muslim population. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Christian population is expected to roughly triple, from 92 million to 299 million.

Not every Christian population is growing, however. The United States, which had the world's largest Christian population in 2020 at 217 million, is expected to see the biggest decline, falling to 174 million by 2070, as deaths outnumber births among an older population and some people leave the faith.

Pew is careful to describe its figures as projections, not predictions. The study covers 201 countries and territories, accounting for 99.98 percent of the world's population, and assumes recent patterns of births, deaths, migration and switching continue. It does not model wars, epidemics, economic shocks or religious revivals, any of which could change the picture.

Pew's 2015 projections had the two religions reaching near parity only around 2050 — about fifteen years later than the new crossover date.

---

Sources

  • Pew Research Center

link.title: Muslims projected to outnumber Christians by 2035, Pew finds

entry.title: US approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to China, House panel reveals
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The US Commerce Department approved sales of more than 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies over a six-month stretch, according to documents released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee — putting hard numbers on a trade Washington has spent years trying to restrict.

The approvals, granted by the department's Bureau of Industry and Security between December 2025 and May 2026, covered chips made by Nvidia and AMD, including Nvidia's H200 and AMD's MI325X. The committee published the figures after its chairman, Brian Mast, used powers under the Export Control Reform Act to make normally confidential licence information public.

The breakdown named some of China's largest technology companies. Tencent was approved to receive 150,000 chips, Alibaba 75,000, Baidu 43,000 and the carmaker BYD 4,000. All four are on the Pentagon's list of companies alleged to have links to the Chinese military. Companies had applied to ship 3.4 million chips to China in total during the period, so roughly a quarter of the requested volume was approved.

What the documents do not show is how many of the approved chips were actually shipped. The committee said that was not immediately clear. Nvidia said the approvals came with "strict conditions and limited volumes" and added that, despite receiving some licences, it has since stopped shipping H200 chips to China.

The disclosure also raised questions about how chips reach their buyers. Mast said two entities appearing on Nvidia's licence applications, New Matrix and Maginfra, were suspected smuggling fronts, and the committee said Nvidia had sought to rely on possible smuggling fronts to move advanced chips into China. The committee described the release as the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act. Its ranking Democrat, Gregory Meeks, took part in the vote to make the records public.

The figures land in the middle of a long-running debate over whether US export controls are working. The controls are meant to slow China's development of advanced artificial intelligence and military technology by cutting off access to the most powerful processors. Critics of the licensing system argue that approvals on this scale undercut that goal; supporters of the current approach say licences are granted case by case, with conditions attached, and that a blanket ban would hand the market to Chinese chipmakers instead.

The same week brought a reminder that the net is tightening elsewhere: new US rules have pushed TSMC, the world's largest chipmaker, to halt advanced manufacturing orders for Chinese AI designers. Approvals and restrictions are moving in opposite directions at once — and the newly published numbers give Congress, and the industry, a concrete basis for arguing about which direction is winning.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: US approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to China, House panel reveals

entry.title: Mortgage rates jump to 7.28%, snapping a month of relief for homebuyers
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Mortgage rates are climbing again, ending a brief stretch of relief for American homebuyers after touching a three-year high.

The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.28% this week, up from 7.11% last week, according to Freddie Mac. It is the largest one-week jump since the week of October 1, and it ends four weeks of declines that had briefly eased borrowing costs.

The increase also widens the gap with a year ago. At this time last year, the average 30-year rate stood at 6.26% — more than a full percentage point lower than today.

Mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year Treasury yield, which moved higher recently after a hotter-than-expected inflation report raised the odds that the Federal Reserve could raise its benchmark interest rate at its December policy meeting. When investors expect the Fed to tighten, long-term borrowing costs usually rise with it.

Rates have now stayed above 7% since late September. Outside of a single month in 2023, that is the highest they have been at any time since 2000.

The higher costs are weighing on an already stalled housing market. Pending home sales — deals that have been agreed but have not yet closed — collapsed in October to a record low, according to a report released Wednesday by the National Association of Realtors. Pending deals fell 4.7% between September and October, and nearly 17% compared with a year earlier.

"It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million," Lawrence Yun, the association's chief economist, said in a statement. "Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans."

For would-be buyers, the turn in rates is a reminder of how quickly affordability can shift. A four-week slide had raised hopes that borrowing costs were finally easing after years of elevated rates. This week's jump shows that relief is far from assured — and that the path of inflation, and the Fed's response to it, will decide what happens next.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN

link.title: Mortgage rates jump to 7.28%, snapping a month of relief for homebuyers

entry.title: Trump grants posthumous pardon to Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he has posthumously pardoned Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader, more than two years after the player's death and a year after Major League Baseball restored his eligibility for the Hall of Fame.

Trump announced the pardon in a social media post written aboard Air Force One as he flew home from a trip to Asia. "I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND," he wrote, citing Rose's record of 4,256 hits — a career total collected over 24 seasons, not in a single season as the post suggested.

Rose, who died on September 30, 2024, at the age of 83, was one of the most accomplished and most controversial figures in the sport. A three-time World Series champion with a .303 career batting average, he was nicknamed "Charlie Hustle" for the way he played. But he was banned from baseball in August 1989 after an investigation led by John M. Dowd concluded that he had bet repeatedly on the Cincinnati Reds while playing for and managing his hometown team from 1985 to 1987.

The pardon covers only the federal case that followed. On April 20, 1990, Rose pleaded guilty to two counts of filing false federal income tax returns, admitting he had failed to report $354,968 over a four-year period. He was sentenced that July to five months in prison, served his time at a federal camp in Marion, Illinois, between August 1990 and January 1991, paid a $50,000 fine, completed 1,000 hours of community service and repaid the Internal Revenue Service $366,042.

Trump had been promising the pardon for more than a year. In March 2025 he said he would sign one "over the next few weeks," and he repeated the pledge on November 9 — yet no pardon for Rose appeared on the Justice Department's list of clemency grants, last updated on October 20, 2026.

The pardon does not, by itself, change Rose's standing with baseball. That question was settled separately in May 2025, when Commissioner Rob Manfred removed Rose from the permanently ineligible list, ruling that a lifetime ban ends with a person's death. Manfred later acknowledged that Trump's urging, in an April meeting at the White House, had influenced the decision. The next opportunity for Rose to be voted into the Hall of Fame comes in December 2027, with the earliest possible induction in 2028.

Trump used the announcement to renew his criticism of baseball's handling of Rose, writing that he had been "treated terribly" by the league. The pardon closes the legal chapter of a career defined as much by its ending as by its record. For the Hall of Fame, the wait continues.

Sources

  • NBC Sports
  • Reuters

link.title: Trump grants posthumous pardon to Pete Rose, baseball's all-time hits leader

entry.title: Europe demands a seat at the table as Ukraine allies meet in Berlin
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

European leaders closed ranks in Berlin on Thursday, telling Washington and Moscow that no peace deal for Ukraine can be struck without Europe and Kyiv at the table — hours after Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping held a three-way summit in China.

The Coalition of the Willing, the group of nearly 40 countries backing Ukraine, met in the German capital with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, alongside NATO chief Mark Rutte, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

In a joint statement, the leaders of Germany, France, Britain and Ukraine said they were committed to a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, and that the security of Europe depended on it. They condemned Russia's missile and drone attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, pledged long-term support with air defence the priority, and promised more pressure on Russian oil and gas revenues and the shadow fleet carrying them.

The statement also set out what Europe wants in a settlement: robust and legally binding security guarantees once a ceasefire takes effect, a European-led multinational force for Ukraine backed by the United States, and direct talks between Kyiv and Moscow with the US and Europe involved. As a first step, the leaders called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire for the winter. They also insisted that Ukraine's right to choose its own security arrangements must be fully respected.

Merz was blunt about the Shenzhen meeting, calling it a "photo op" and warning that a "Yalta format cannot bring peace". He said the war's outcome would shape European security for years to come, and pointed to 45 billion euros earmarked by the European Commission for Ukraine next year. Kushner, speaking after Trump joined the Berlin meeting by phone, said Europe was "very united and very, very strong" in its support, and that Russia was "comfortable" with the idea of NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine.

Macron said the immediate priority was helping Ukraine defend itself, including air-defence systems and interceptors, and argued that the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO should be reopened. Zelenskyy said it was crucial that the United States use its influence on Russia, which he said had rejected every proposal for de-escalation. Britain announced a 260 million pound winter support package, including 1,000 long-range strike drones and long-range cruise missiles.

No date has been set for negotiations, and the leaders acknowledged they were preparing for the possibility that talks fail. But the message from Berlin was consistent: Europe intends to be in the room when the war's end is negotiated — while preparing Ukraine for a winter of war.

Sources

  • DW
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Europe demands a seat at the table as Ukraine allies meet in Berlin

entry.title: BepiColombo closes in on Mercury, two days from orbit
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

After eight years in space, the European-Japanese BepiColombo mission is two days from entering orbit around Mercury, with the spacecraft due to be captured by the planet's gravity on Saturday, 21 November.

BepiColombo is a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). It carries two orbiters — ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, known as Mio — still travelling together as one stacked spacecraft. It will be the first mission to orbit Mercury with two spacecraft at the same time, and only the second mission ever to enter orbit around the planet, after NASA's MESSENGER, which circled Mercury from 2011 to 2015.

The journey has been long by design. BepiColombo launched on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou in French Guiana on 20 October 2018, and has since travelled roughly 9.9 billion kilometres, using nine planetary flybys — one of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury itself — to shed speed. Mercury is the hardest planet to reach in the Solar System in one sense: falling towards the Sun, a spacecraft must lose a great deal of energy before the planet's weak gravity can capture it.

Arrival was originally planned for December 2025. In April 2024, engineers found that the transfer module's electric thrusters could not deliver full power, and ESA recalculated the route, pushing arrival back by almost a year. The Mercury Transfer Module, which had powered and steered the spacecraft for most of the journey, separated from the two orbiters on 3 September 2026, more than 200 million kilometres from Earth.

Since then, the mission team has been working through a long checklist. On 24 September, MPO fired its axial thrusters for the first time in the new configuration, an eight-minute, 42-second burn that delivered a precise 11.4 metres-per-second course correction. On 15 September, all of MPO's instruments were switched on together for the first time since the transfer module separated: the laser altimeter BELA fired its laser in space for the first time, emitting more than 700,000 pulses over 21.5 hours, and the science camera SIMBIO-SYS took its first image. On 29 October, the mission control team in Darmstadt completed its final simulation of the arrival sequence, rehearsing the separation of Mio's sunshield and interface structure, an operation scheduled for 16 December.

Saturday's orbit insertion is the pivotal moment, and it will happen largely on its own. Mercury is about 150 million kilometres from Earth — roughly eight light-minutes away — so no command from the ground can steer the burn in real time. If the thrusters fire as programmed, the two orbiters will be captured into a polar orbit together.

What follows is a months-long sequence. MPO and Mio are due to separate on 9–10 December, moving into their own science orbits: MPO into a close polar orbit, about 480 by 1,500 kilometres above the surface, to map Mercury and study its composition and interior; Mio into a much wider orbit, about 590 by 11,640 kilometres, to study the planet's magnetic field and the plasma around it. Full science operations are set to begin in April 2027.

Mercury is the least explored of the Solar System's rocky planets, and the two-orbiters-at-once approach is the point of the mission: surface and magnetic-field measurements taken simultaneously should finally explain how a planet so small sustains a magnetic field at all, and what its cratered surface reveals about the early Solar System. By coincidence, Mercury is also at its widest angle from the Sun in the morning sky this week, so the planet itself is visible low in the east before dawn on the day its new visitor arrives.

ESA notes that exact dates can still change for operational reasons. Confirmation that the capture burn worked is expected hours after the event, on the agency's arrival-updates page.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • ESA

link.title: BepiColombo closes in on Mercury, two days from orbit

entry.title: Trump names Kirsten Davies as new national cyber director
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump has named Kirsten Davies as the White House's new national cyber director, replacing Sean Cairncross in a shake-up of the administration's technology leadership.

Davies currently serves as chief information officer at the Pentagon, a Senate-confirmed role she has held since December 2025. She will take over the cyber director's job in an acting capacity, according to multiple reports. Axios first reported the appointment on Thursday.

The national cyber director leads the Office of the National Cyber Director, which advises the president on cybersecurity policy and coordinates cyber strategy across the federal government. The position requires Senate confirmation, and Davies has already been through that process once, for her Pentagon post.

Cairncross had led the office since August 2025, after being confirmed by the Senate that month. Accounts of his departure differ. Two sources described it to Axios as amicable, saying Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. But two White House officials told the outlet that Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, sought the change, saying Cairncross lacked the strong cyber credentials the job requires. A source close to the White House told CNN that Trump fully supported removing him. A White House spokesperson confirmed Cairncross is leaving the administration, but his exact last day has not been made public.

The change comes after a difficult week for American technology systems. Outages disrupted Microsoft services, air-traffic routing systems run by the Federal Aviation Administration, banking services at Chase, and internal systems at the National Security Agency, among others. The disruptions have cost hundreds of millions of dollars and rattled air travel, banking and workplaces. Administration officials have said there is no evidence the outages were the result of a coordinated cyberattack.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly congratulated Davies on Thursday, writing that he looked forward to working with her to strengthen American cybersecurity.

The appointment is part of a broader overhaul of Trump's artificial intelligence and technology team. The same day, the president's nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, Michael LoSapio, appeared at his Senate confirmation hearing — a process that has drawn scrutiny of its own.

What happens next is not yet settled. The White House has not said when Cairncross will formally leave, or whether Davies will be formally nominated to hold the cyber director's job permanently rather than in an acting role. Her Senate-confirmed status at the Pentagon is expected to smooth any path to confirmation, but the timing remains unclear.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • CNN

link.title: Trump names Kirsten Davies as new national cyber director

entry.title: GTA 6 tops $2 billion in estimated first-day sales
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Grand Theft Auto VI has made an estimated $2.36 billion in its first day on sale, according to analytics firm Sensor Tower, putting Rockstar Games' long-awaited sequel on course to be the biggest video game launch in history.

Sensor Tower estimates that 24.58 million copies were sold by Thursday evening, with the total still climbing as players rushed to download the game after it went live at midnight. The figure dwarfs the record set by its predecessor: Grand Theft Auto V sold about $800 million worth of copies on its first day in 2013, widely regarded as the best-selling video game in its first 24 hours.

The numbers make GTA 6 the fastest-selling entertainment release ever measured on day one, comfortably ahead of the biggest film openings. Much of the total came from pre-orders, which Take-Two Interactive, the game's publisher, has described as unprecedented.

Take-Two has remained tight-lipped about demand since pre-orders opened in June, limiting its public comments to saying demand has been "unprecedented" or "far exceeding expectations". Chief executive Strauss Zelnick struck a cautious note on the company's earnings call earlier in November, saying: "The title is so widely anticipated, consumers appear very, very excited, and all the press so far has been universally positive, but we still aren't ready to declare victory."

"We tend to avoid claiming success before it occurs," he added.

The launch is the payoff for one of the most expensive entertainment projects ever made. Take-Two is estimated to have spent $1 billion or more on producing GTA 6. Its marketing campaign was equally sprawling: Sensor Tower estimates that the game's promotional trailer, "Extended Look", released on Netflix in August, helped drive a sixfold jump in pre-orders. In Miami, the city Vice City is based on, the local NBA team celebrated the release with a Vice City-themed match, and the company is hosting a launch-weekend music festival featuring Cardi B, Metro Boomin and Travis Scott.

The figures come with an important caveat. They are third-party estimates, not official sales data: neither Rockstar nor Take-Two has released its own numbers, and the totals do not account for refunds.

Attention now turns to what comes next. Investors have been waiting for Take-Two's plans for a PC version of GTA 6 and the rollout of its online multiplayer mode, which analysts expect in 2027. The online component matters most for the long term: it turns a one-off purchase into a recurring revenue engine, and brokerage TD Cowen has named Take-Two one of its "Best Ideas" for 2027 on that basis.

For now, though, the first-day numbers alone put GTA 6 in a league of its own — a launch thirteen years in the making, and one that has already rewritten the record books.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Straits Times
  • BBC

link.title: GTA 6 tops $2 billion in estimated first-day sales

entry.title: Pancreatic cancer pill shows tumours vanishing in early trial
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A daily pill taken alongside chemotherapy has produced striking early results against one of the deadliest cancers, with tumours shrinking or disappearing on scans in six out of ten patients in a small trial.

The drug, daraxonrasib, was tested with two standard chemotherapy drugs — gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel — in 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for the advanced disease. The results were presented at a cancer therapeutics symposium in Barcelona by the trial's lead researcher, Dr Wungki Park of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York.

Across the group, tumours shrank significantly or became undetectable in 60.7 percent of patients. In 8.2 percent — about one in twelve — tumours vanished entirely from scans, a result known as a complete response. Overall, the treatment stopped tumours growing in 90.2 percent of patients.

The benefits also appeared to last. Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer started growing again — roughly double the five to six months typically seen with chemotherapy alone. After a year, 76.6 percent of patients were still alive, compared with the roughly one in four pancreatic cancer patients who usually survive beyond twelve months.

Daraxonrasib works by switching off RAS, a family of proteins that acts like a stuck accelerator in cancer cells. More than nine in ten pancreatic cancers carry a RAS mutation, most commonly in the KRAS gene, which drives cells to divide relentlessly. The drug blocks the active form of the protein, cutting the signal that tells tumours to grow.

The trial's leaders are urging caution despite the excitement. The study was small and early-stage, with no comparison group receiving chemotherapy alone, so it cannot yet prove the pill improves survival. Side effects were in line with the known effects of the drugs involved — mainly rash, diarrhoea, fatigue and low blood counts — and five percent of patients stopped the drug because of side effects.

A larger, randomised phase III trial is now under way to test daraxonrasib, alone and with chemotherapy, directly against standard treatment. Cancer Research UK has described the findings as the biggest leap forward for pancreatic cancer patients in decades, while stressing that more trials are needed before the treatment can be considered for routine use.

For now, daraxonrasib remains experimental, but the results suggest that switching off RAS — long considered an untargetable driver of cancer — may finally be within reach.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Bioengineer.org

link.title: Pancreatic cancer pill shows tumours vanishing in early trial

entry.title: Xi hails 'comprehensive turnaround' as China and Australia reset ties
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

China and Australia have completed a "comprehensive turnaround" in their relationship, President Xi Jinping said on Friday, after meeting Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

"Since you took office as prime minister in 2022, we have met four times. I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive turnaround in China-Australia relations," Xi said, according to Reuters.

Xi said China was willing to work with Australia to expand cooperation, set aside differences and build on the recent improvements, taking the partnership to a new stage of development. In the meeting he suggested greater cooperation in agriculture, energy, the green economy and artificial intelligence, as well as stronger exchanges between the two countries' peoples, according to China's official Xinhua news agency.

The reset caps a four-year repair job. Ties with China, Australia's top trade partner, soured under the country's previous centre-right coalition government, which called for an inquiry into the origins of COVID-19, angering Beijing. China responded with a series of barriers on Australian exports. It has since lifted many of them, though tensions have flared from time to time — including after a Chinese missile test into the Pacific and Beijing's arrest of Chinese-born Australian nationals on spying charges.

Albanese struck a careful note after the meeting. Differences would be discussed "constructively and directly", he said, and a stable relationship was in the interests of both nations.

"It is important that Australia continues to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them. And we, today, were able to discuss a full range of issues," Albanese said.

The diplomacy continues in Beijing. Albanese was expected to travel there later on Friday to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang, accompanied by several top Australian business executives — including Rio Tinto's head of iron ore, Matt Holcz, and BHP's Australia boss, Geraldine Slattery — for a CEO roundtable with Chinese company executives.

But one hard negotiation still hangs over the reset. Australia's top miners are in increasingly fraught talks with China's state iron ore buyer, China Mineral Resources Group, whose centralisation of purchasing increases Beijing's bargaining power in contract negotiations. Australian Resources Minister Madeleine King said this week that any potential manipulation of trade in iron ore would be against international rules and a threat to government revenues.

The language from both leaders marks how far the relationship has travelled since 2022. The iron ore talks, and the differences both sides say they will keep managing directly, show the reset is still being negotiated in practice.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Xi hails 'comprehensive turnaround' as China and Australia reset ties

entry.title: COP31 draft drops fossil-fuel language as Antalya talks near deadline
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Climate negotiators at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, have stripped all mention of ending fossil fuel use from a slimmed-down draft of the summit deal, published on Thursday as the talks approached their scheduled Friday close.

The first draft, published on Monday, had contained two references to fossil fuels and to limiting their use — a subject that divides countries at the climate talks almost every year. The revised text removes both. In their place, the draft encourages countries to scale up technologies that pull carbon out of the atmosphere, a shift in emphasis from cutting fossil fuels at the source toward capturing emissions after the fact.

The draft still acknowledges that global warming could pass the 1.5 degrees Celsius threshold countries have sought to preserve, and it calls for "deep, rapid and sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions. What it no longer says is anything about winding down the fuels that produce most of those emissions.

Australia, which is leading the negotiations under a split presidency arrangement with Türkiye, had said on Monday that the opening draft was always meant to be a broad document that would then be narrowed down. The latest text is expected to be revised further before anything can be agreed, and the final wording may yet change.

The conference is scheduled to end on Friday, but that deadline is rarely kept. In recent years, efforts to secure consensus among the nearly 200 countries taking part have regularly run more than 24 hours past the scheduled close.

The need to limit rising temperatures is widely accepted among the delegations in Antalya. They disagree on how to do it, who should pay for it, and how quickly the world needs to act — and the fate of the fossil-fuel language is the clearest measure of that disagreement.

The talks are taking place as the effects of a warming climate — heatwaves, floods and droughts — grow more severe and more regular, even as they compete for policymakers' attention with wars and rising living costs.

What happens next is still open. Negotiators have a day of scheduled talks left, and the draft will go through further revisions before any deal is put to the nearly 200 participating countries. Whether fossil-fuel language returns in a later version, and what the final text says about paying for the transition, will decide how the summit is judged.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: COP31 draft drops fossil-fuel language as Antalya talks near deadline

entry.title: Russia hits three Kyiv bridges in overnight ballistic attack
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Russian ballistic missiles damaged three bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv overnight, striking crossings that link the two halves of the capital and disrupting traffic across the city.

The Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and South bridges were all hit in the early hours of Friday, November 20, as a series of explosions sounded across Kyiv and Ukrainian air defences responded. The strikes damaged the bridge decks and sparked fires in at least three districts.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said traffic from the right bank to the left bank was suspended on the Podilskyi Bridge while engineers assessed the damage, and the Darnytskyi Bridge was also under assessment. The South Bridge stayed partly open, carrying vehicles only from the left bank to the right bank, with weight limits of 10 tons for ordinary vehicles and 18 tons for public transport. Klitschko urged residents to avoid unnecessary car travel and called on businesses to allow remote work where possible.

Falling missile debris set fire to a three-story building in the Obolonskyi district, in the north of the city. Another building caught fire in a nonresidential area of Podilskyi, and in Holosiivskyi a strike hit the grounds of an infrastructure facility, with preliminary reports that an office building there had caught fire. No casualties from the overnight attack were reported in the Kyiv Post's account.

Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had struck road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to the battlefield, Reuters reported. The ministry said the strikes were part of a wider round of attacks on energy and transport infrastructure across Ukraine, including port facilities in the Odesa region and sea vessels used for military purposes.

The three crossings carry the daily flow of commuters and freight between Kyiv's banks, and the damage leaves the city with one bridge closed, one under assessment and the third running in a single direction under weight limits. The full extent of the structural damage, and how long repairs will take, was not yet clear as authorities continued their assessments on Friday morning.

Sources

  • Kyiv Post

link.title: Russia hits three Kyiv bridges in overnight ballistic attack

entry.title: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil match Earth-grown yields
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Scientists have succeeded in growing nutritious potatoes in simulated lunar soil that are safe to eat, bringing a future moon base one step closer to feeding itself.

The research, supported by NASA and led by Oregon State University plant biologist Aymeric Goyer, was published on Thursday in the journal npj Microgravity. The team grew Modoc, an early-maturing potato variety with red skin and white flesh, in a greenhouse under sunlight and artificial light, at 72 degrees Fahrenheit (22 degrees Celsius) during the day and 64 F (18 C) at night.

The soil on the moon's surface, properly called lunar regolith, is crushed rock and dust — often sharp and glass-like — formed over billions of years by meteorite impacts. Unlike Earth soil, it contains no organic material and no nitrogen. "Lunar regolith does not contain any nitrogen, so no crop would grow without supplementing it," Goyer said.

The researchers mixed the simulated regolith with vermicompost, a nutrient-rich substance produced when earthworms break down organic waste. Potatoes planted in regolith with no vermicompost produced almost no roots or tubers. A mixture of just 5% vermicompost produced some roots and tubers, and at 30% vermicompost the yield was identical to potatoes grown under the same conditions in Earth soil — specifically soil from Hermiston, Oregon, a region known for impressive potato yields.

The compost also solved a second problem. Lunar regolith carries high levels of heavy metals such as copper, and without organic matter the potatoes took up too much of them. "Organic matter helps make heavy metals less available to the plants, so plants do not overaccumulate them," Goyer said.

There are limits to the result. The plants were grown in small pots, so the potatoes they produced were small — generally less than a third of an ounce (10 grams), even in Earth soil. A second study using larger pots has already produced potatoes of the size typically seen in stores, Goyer said. And nobody has tasted the lunar-grown crop yet: the harvest was used for laboratory analyses.

The work matters because both the United States and China intend to send astronauts to the lunar surface in the coming years, with plans for long-term bases. A local food source is considered vital, since transporting all needed food from Earth is impractical. Potatoes are a strong candidate: they provide more calories per land area than many other crops, are rich in vitamin C and potassium, and have a high satiety index.

Other crops are being tested too. A study published in March documented chickpeas grown in lunar regolith supplemented with vermicompost, and researchers are also working with tomatoes, lettuce and legumes such as alfalfa.

The research may also pay off on Earth. Study co-author David Handy, an Oregon State space biologist, said the techniques could help produce food in regions of low agricultural output that rely on shipments, such as inner cities and desert communities, and could help remediate contaminated soils.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Potatoes grown in simulated moon soil match Earth-grown yields

entry.title: Frequent night shifts linked to subtle changes in heart structure, large study finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

People who regularly work night shifts show small but measurable differences in the structure of their hearts and in blood markers linked to cardiovascular health, according to a study of more than 42,000 people published on November 19 in the European Heart Journal — Cardiovascular Imaging.

The research is the first large-scale study to combine detailed cardiac MRI scans with extensive blood-marker analysis to look at how night-shift work may relate to the heart. Around one in five workers worldwide performs regular night-shift work, and earlier research has already linked it to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and death. Working against the body's circadian rhythm can disturb sleep, metabolism, inflammation, blood pressure and blood-vessel function, though why the link exists is not fully understood.

What the scans showed

The team analysed 42,671 men and women from the UK Biobank, with a mean age of 52. Of those, 1,322 reported frequent night-shift work; people who already had cardiovascular disease were excluded.

Compared with day workers, frequent night-shift workers tended to have slightly thicker heart walls relative to the size of the main pumping chamber, and somewhat smaller heart chambers. There was also a subtle difference in one measure of how the heart muscle contracts. The researchers found no significant difference in ejection fraction, the standard measure of the heart's overall pumping function.

Blood tests told a similar story: lower levels of DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid that supports heart and blood-vessel health, and of some measures linked to "good" cholesterol (HDL), alongside higher levels of markers relating to triglycerides and inflammation.

Small differences, not a diagnosis

The researchers stress that the differences they observed were small average differences at a population level. They do not mean that all night-shift workers will develop heart disease or heart failure.

The study was observational, so it cannot establish whether night-shift work directly damages the heart, and it measured the heart at a single point in time — it cannot say whether the differences grow with longer exposure or ease if night work stops. Those questions need prospective studies that track shift patterns and heart imaging over time.

There are other limits. The UK Biobank population is predominantly white European and made up of healthy volunteers, which limits how far the results generalise. Participants whose shift-work information was unavailable were excluded, and they tended to be older and to have more cardiometabolic disease, so some selection bias is possible.

Study author Dr. Muwei Li, from Zhengzhou University, said people who regularly work at night should "pay particular attention to taking care of their cardiovascular health" — not smoking, staying active, keeping a healthy diet and weight, sleeping enough on a regular schedule, and keeping blood pressure, cholesterol and blood glucose controlled. Doctors, he added, may wish to note night-shift work in a patient's history, particularly alongside established cardiovascular risk factors.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Medical Xpress
  • European Heart Journal — Cardiovascular Imaging

link.title: Frequent night shifts linked to subtle changes in heart structure, large study finds

entry.title: Rohingya refugees greet genocide ruling with tears, prayers and hope of return
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

In the crowded refugee camps of Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, news of the International Court of Justice's genocide ruling arrived on mobile phones, laptop screens and communal televisions — and was met with tears, prayers and celebration.

Umme Ruman had been waiting for the verdict since the afternoon, watching from her shelter in Camp 1E. Poor internet kept interrupting the live broadcast, so she opened Facebook and saw the headline: the court had confirmed that Myanmar committed genocide. Overwhelmed, she jumped up and rushed to hug her sister-in-law, breaking down in tears before she could explain what had happened.

"I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us," she said.

On Thursday, the court in The Hague found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which it found more than 10,000 people had been killed. The case was brought by The Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, and the decision — reached by nine votes to six — was the first time in the court's history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.

Across the camps, people followed the announcement together, many of them on Facebook and YouTube. Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched on a laptop with his community teacher and friends. "Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah," he said. His first thought was that the verdict could open the door for the Rohingya to return home. "Just imagining that made me so happy," he said. When he told his mother, she said they had won and would be able to return to their homeland.

The celebrations came amid difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal — a reminder that recognition had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a young Rohingya man, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories of 2017 and the home he had to leave behind. Activist Rohimullah described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope — but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.

Nasir Uddin, an anthropology professor at the University of Chittagong who studies the crisis, called the judgement essential to establishing global justice. Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council said it would shape negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar over refugee returns, and that Dhaka would need stronger assurances of a safe return.

What the ruling does not settle is whether the refugees will actually be able to go home. The court has no police force of its own, so enforcement depends on other states and UN bodies. For the Rohingya, the hope is accountability, restored rights and citizenship, and a safe, dignified return. "We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more — that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity," Nurul Amin said.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: Rohingya refugees greet genocide ruling with tears, prayers and hope of return

entry.title: Judge orders USDA chief to stop sending religious emails to staff
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A federal judge has ordered Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins to stop sending religious messages to employees from her official account, finding that her holiday emails likely violated the First Amendment's ban on government establishment of religion. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson of the Northern District of California issued the preliminary injunction on Thursday, November 19, writing that "the Secretary must recognize certain boundaries when communicating religious messages" — and expressing no view on what Rollins may do in her personal capacity.

The ruling focused on two messages sent to all department employees: a Christmas email on December 23, 2025, that included a video calling Jesus Christ "our Savior," and an Easter email on April 5, 2026, carrying an illustration of a stone rolled away from Jesus' tomb with the words "Christ is Risen." Thompson found that both went too far.

At the heart of the case was not the secretary's faith, but her authority. Her messages reached every employee through an official account that staff are expected to read, and used language such as "we," "us" and "our" that assumed every recipient shared her Christian beliefs. No comparable messages marked other religions' holidays. Even without singling out anyone who disagreed, the judge found, the "immense social pressure" of such messages from a superior could amount to coercion.

The lawsuit was filed in May 2026 by the National Federation of Federal Employees, a union representing more than 100,000 federal workers, along with six individual USDA employees. They said the messages favored employees who shared the secretary's beliefs and pressured others to hide their own — a Buddhist employee who no longer felt safe discussing a holiday she celebrates, an atheist who felt silenced, and a Pagan employee who felt pressure to appear Christian to advance. They are represented by Americans United for Separation of Church and State, Democracy Forward and Bryan Schwartz Law.

The department had argued the emails were not coercive because Rollins was sharing her personal views on holidays, not compelling conformity. Thompson rejected that framing for messages sent in an official capacity, and ordered Rollins to follow the department's own guidance on religious expression at work: stop if a colleague asks, do not create a hostile work environment, and do not use official authority to pressure subordinates.

The injunction is preliminary, not a final ruling — it holds while the case continues, and the government can ask an appeals court to lift it. The administration is considering an appeal, according to reports. Thompson also dismissed the plaintiffs' Administrative Procedure Act claims, finding the emails did not amount to an official agency rule.

The order arrives just weeks before Christmas, when the next round of seasonal messages would ordinarily go out. It does not restrict Rollins's private religious expression. As the judge put it, the Founders understood that independence requires freedom of conscience — and the Establishment Clause bars the government from using its authority to sway how a person practices their faith.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Judge orders USDA chief to stop sending religious emails to staff

entry.title: Magnitude 4.4 earthquake rattles Los Angeles area before dawn
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake shook the Los Angeles area in the early hours of Friday morning, waking residents across the region and sending fire department helicopters into the sky to check for damage.

The tremor struck at 3:25 a.m. local time, with its epicentre about a kilometre north-northwest of Commerce, a city roughly five miles east-southeast of downtown Los Angeles, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. It originated about 10.6 miles (17 kilometres) below the surface.

The quake was first measured at magnitude 4.2 and later revised upward to 4.4 after seismologists at the California Institute of Technology's seismic network reviewed the data. Shaking was reported across Los Angeles County, from Whittier and the San Gabriel Valley to communities nearer the coast, and social media filled quickly with posts from people woken by the jolt.

There were no immediate reports of injuries or serious damage. The Los Angeles Fire Department sent helicopters over the city shortly after the shaking to look for signs of structural damage, and the Geological Survey's automated assessment issued a green alert, indicating a low likelihood of casualties or significant economic losses. Officials urged anyone who felt the tremor to report it through the survey's "Did You Feel It?" programme, which helps scientists map how widely shaking is felt.

The earthquake was the strongest to shake the Los Angeles area in about a year, according to Geological Survey records. Southern California sits atop a network of active faults, and moderate quakes of this size are not unusual — but one centred so close to the city centre is enough to rattle nerves and set phones buzzing across the region.

The Los Angeles tremor was not the only seismic activity in California overnight. A separate cluster of more than a dozen earthquakes rattled Central California near Pinnacles National Park late on Thursday into early Friday, the strongest of them also measuring magnitude 4.4, according to the Geological Survey.

Damage assessments were continuing on Friday morning, and it was not immediately clear whether the Commerce quake had caused any injuries or structural harm. Seismologists typically watch for aftershocks after a quake of this size; smaller tremors in the hours and days that follow are common, though most are too weak to be felt.

Sources

  • The Weather Channel

link.title: Magnitude 4.4 earthquake rattles Los Angeles area before dawn

entry.title: Astronomers find a triple-star system that 'shouldn't exist' just 28 light-years away
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Astronomers have found a trio of stars just 28 light-years from Earth that, by the known rules of how stars live and die, should not exist at all.

The system, named Welopōʻai, contains two white dwarfs — the dense, cooling embers of dead sun-like stars — and a single red dwarf, a star far dimmer than our sun. It is the closest known triple-star system containing two white dwarfs, and no comparable system is known within 100 light-years of Earth.

The discovery was made by an international team led by the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, and is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. The team was not looking for a triple star at all. They were hunting for planets around a nearby red dwarf, watching for tiny wobbles in its speed that an orbiting planet would cause.

What they found was far stranger. The red dwarf's speed relative to Earth varied by about 10 miles per second — more than a thousand times larger than the wobble a planet would produce. After years of follow-up observations, the team concluded the unseen companion had to be more massive than half our sun, yet almost impossibly faint. The only plausible explanation was the remnant of a dead star.

High-resolution images from the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea confirmed it: a faint white dwarf orbiting close to the red dwarf, with a second, already-known white dwarf circling the pair at a much greater distance. The inner pair orbits roughly every 9.8 years, a little less than Jupiter's distance from the sun, while the outer white dwarf sits far beyond them.

The puzzle is how the red dwarf survived. Before becoming a white dwarf, its companion was a star about 40 percent more massive than the sun. As it died, it would have swollen into a giant hundreds of times its original size — an expansion that, in most similar systems, swallows the companion star or drags the two into a merger. Against all expectations, Welopōʻai's red dwarf is still there, in a surprisingly wide and stable orbit.

"This system should not exist," said Patrick Dufour, a professor at the Université de Montréal who specialises in white dwarfs and co-authored the study. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here. That is the question driving our next observations."

The discovery also gives astronomers an unusually precise measurement. The team weighed the newly identified white dwarf with an uncertainty of less than one percent — about 0.62 times the mass of the sun — making it one of the most precisely weighed white dwarfs within 65 light-years and a valuable test of stellar-evolution models.

The system's Hawaiian name, chosen through the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center's naming programme, combines "welo", meaning a family trait, and "pōʻai", meaning a circular path — a nod to the orbital dance of its three stars. Further observations, including from the Webb telescope, may help explain how such a family formed.

Sources

  • The Times
  • Phys.org

link.title: Astronomers find a triple-star system that 'shouldn't exist' just 28 light-years away

entry.title: UK and EU seal Brexit reset deal on food trade, youth mobility and carbon markets
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The United Kingdom and the European Union have sealed the first stage of a reset in their relations, a decade after British voters chose to leave the bloc.

After a summit in Brussels on Friday, Downing Street said negotiations on three agreements had concluded. "The deal is done," a UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera. "Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa at the summit, the second such meeting since the two sides launched a renewed partnership in May 2025. "This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham told the EU chiefs as the talks began.

The three agreements cover food trade, young people and carbon markets. A sanitary and phytosanitary deal will remove checks and paperwork on food and animal goods traded between Britain and the EU, a change the UK government estimates is worth £5.1 billion ($6.7 billion) a year to the British economy. A youth mobility scheme will allow up to 100,000 young people from each side to live, work or study in the other's territory for up to three years. And linking the two sides' emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other's carbon border levies.

Burnham said the package could add 0.5 percent to Britain's economy. Downing Street said both sides had agreed timelines for putting the measures into practice, with details to be published in a joint statement.

The deal is not the end of the story. University tuition fees remain unresolved: Brussels wants students from EU countries to pay the same rates as British students at UK universities, rather than the far higher international fees charged today. The two sides have given themselves six months to reach agreement, and the deals will be signed once that is settled. Britain is also seeking access to the EU's "Made in Europe" rules, notably for cars.

Legal processes in both the UK and the EU must still run their course, and Al Jazeera reported that months or years of negotiations lie ahead before any deeper reset takes effect.

The summit comes ten years after the 2016 referendum in which 52 percent of British voters backed leaving the EU. Burnham has previously said all options for the future relationship should be on the table, including rejoining the now 27-nation bloc, while stressing that reversing Brexit is far from imminent.

The agreements drew a swift attack from Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who called Burnham "naive" and accused the EU of strong-arming the prime minister. But for Burnham, who has argued that Britain lost more than it gained from Brexit, the summit marks the most concrete step yet towards rebuilding ties with Brussels.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: UK and EU seal Brexit reset deal on food trade, youth mobility and carbon markets

entry.title: Russian missile lands in Poland as Tusk calls incursion a deliberate provocation
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Russia violated Polish airspace overnight, with three objects — probably two missiles and a jet-powered drone — coming down in south-eastern Poland, Warsaw said on Friday. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the incursion appeared to be a deliberate provocation.

"There has been a violation of Polish airspace and an incursion by objects from the Russian Federation," Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told a press conference. One of the objects was a Kh-101 cruise missile, he said; a second was probably also a missile, and the third was most likely a jet-powered drone.

The objects came down at three sites: Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem. At Nowy Lipowiec, about 60 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, an object about seven metres long fell at 05:40 GMT, sending up black smoke. A resident described hearing a whistling sound, then a dull thud. Debris was scattered across farmland at Mołodycz, about 50 kilometres to the south. At Rudnik nad Sanem, a traffic controller heard a loud bang near railway premises, though no damage to the railway was found, and air traffic controllers were evacuated at the airport in Rzeszów. No injuries were reported in Poland, and schools near Nowy Lipowiec suspended classes for the day.

The timing is what Warsaw is pointing to. The objects fell as Poland prepared to host "Coalition of the Willing" military exercises on Friday, with defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom and the Baltic states and eight chiefs of staff in the country. Kosiniak-Kamysz said the convergence of the incursion and the exercises "is no accident". Tusk said there was no doubt the objects were Russian, and added: "It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation." He stressed, however, that the link to the exercises remained a hypothesis.

Tusk said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday, and Poland would ask the alliance for more support in securing its eastern flank. The exercises will go ahead as planned, Kosiniak-Kamysz said. The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

The incursion came during a large overnight Russian attack on Ukraine that killed three people, injured nine and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure, according to the Associated Press. Drones and missiles have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of NATO's eastern-flank countries during the war, fuelling fears the conflict could spread. Investigations are under way at the three Polish sites, and prosecutors have opened an inquiry into the airspace violation.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Associated Press

link.title: Russian missile lands in Poland as Tusk calls incursion a deliberate provocation

entry.title: Taung Child redated to 3 million years, and the human family tree looks more tangled than ever
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A century after its discovery changed the story of human origins, the Taung Child has a firm new age — and the result complicates the family tree it once seemed to anchor.

The fossil skull of a young early human relative, found in a South African lime quarry in 1924, is now dated to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years old, according to a study published on November 5 in the journal npj Palaeoecosystems. The work was led by Gabriele Macho of the Vrije Universiteit Brussel, and announced by the university on November 9.

Dating the child has been difficult because its exact position in the quarry was lost during mining, leaving earlier estimates scattered from under a million years to 3.03 million. The team dated a sheet of mineral rock known as flowstone, lying above the fossil-bearing deposit, using uranium-lead dating. That gave a minimum age of 2.962 million years, give or take 59,000. Combined with a maximum age from earlier magnetic evidence, it pins the child to 2.96–3.03 million years ago, firmly in the Pliocene.

The child is the type specimen — the reference fossil — for Australopithecus africanus, the species named from it in 1925. It provided the first concrete evidence that human origins lay in Africa. Yet no clear criteria were ever set for sorting later discoveries into the species, and the child remains the only fossil that can be assigned to it without dispute.

That is the problem the new study presses on. Comparing the child's teeth and brain development during growth with adult fossils, the researchers found that several adults traditionally grouped under Australopithecus africanus do not fit the child's developmental trajectory. Differences in brain development were especially telling, suggesting that more than one hominin species lived in the Sterkfontein region, either side by side or one after another. The authors describe Australopithecus africanus as a poorly defined taxon.

The team ties the variety to a changing climate. Fossilised pollen shows the child lived in a much wetter, more wooded landscape than the region's semi-arid savanna today, with trees that now grow hundreds of kilometres to the north-east. Between about 4 and 2.5 million years ago, wet and dry cycles repeatedly reshaped southern Africa's habitats. As populations followed the shifting landscape, they were split apart and brought back together — diverging, and sometimes interbreeding, along the way.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," Macho said. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk — it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts."

The study does not name a new species or redraw the tree. The authors write that no clear picture yet emerges of the child's relationship to other hominins, and that the Taung Child must stay at the centre of future work on how the diverse populations of three million years ago eventually gave rise to our own genus, Homo.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • Discover Magazine

link.title: Taung Child redated to 3 million years, and the human family tree looks more tangled than ever

entry.title: Dark energy may be the work of the force that holds atomic nuclei together
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

For nearly three decades, physicists have known that the universe is not just expanding but speeding up — yet no one could say what is doing the pushing. A new study proposes an answer hiding in plain sight: the same force that binds atomic nuclei together.

Dark energy, the name given to whatever drives that acceleration, accounts for roughly 70 percent of the universe's total energy budget. Proposed explanations usually invoke new, undiscovered fields or particles — none of which has ever been detected.

Researchers at the University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield now argue that no new ingredients are needed at all. In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal, they trace dark energy to quantum chromodynamics, or QCD — the established theory of the strong nuclear force, which binds quarks inside protons and neutrons.

The key is that empty space is not truly empty. In QCD, the vacuum is a busy environment of subatomic fields and quantum energy, with topological properties that can reach across vast distances. The team proposes that as the universe expands, this vacuum structure responds differently over time, producing a small energy shift — just strong enough to drive cosmic acceleration.

Crucially, the numbers fall out of physics that is already known. The energy scale predicted by combining the QCD vacuum with gravity lands close to the dark-energy scale astronomers actually observe, emerging from known physical constants without any extra fitting parameters or ad hoc fields.

The paper was led by Dong Ha Lee, a doctoral researcher at the University of Sheffield, building on theoretical ideas developed by Ariel Zhitnitsky, a physics and astronomy professor at the University of British Columbia. Ludovic Van Waerbeke, also at UBC, worked on the analysis.

To test the idea, the Sheffield team compared the model with real astronomical data — light from distant exploding stars, or supernovae, and the leftover radiation from the early universe. The model matched the observations about as well as the standard cosmological models, while also offering a physical origin for dark energy, something the standard picture does not provide. In the standard model, dark energy is treated as a cosmological constant: a number that fits the data but explains nothing about where the energy comes from.

The authors frame this as a proposal, not a proof. Their next steps are to refine the calculations and test the framework against data from next-generation space telescopes, which are expected to map the universe's expansion history in unprecedented detail over the coming years.

If it holds up, the result would tie the largest-scale mystery in cosmology to the smallest-scale force in physics — the same force holding every atomic nucleus together.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • University of British Columbia

link.title: Dark energy may be the work of the force that holds atomic nuclei together

entry.title: Senate approves sweeping permitting bill aimed at cutting energy costs
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Senate on Thursday passed a sweeping bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for energy and infrastructure projects, clearing the chamber 62–33 as lawmakers face pressure over rising electricity prices and surging demand from artificial intelligence.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which runs to more than 400 pages, would shorten deadlines for federal environmental reviews, narrow the window for lawsuits challenging projects, and limit the circumstances in which approvals can be withdrawn. It covers power plants, transmission lines, mines and data centers, and would require data centers to pay for the transmission costs they create.

The bill was written by two Republicans — Senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah — and two Democrats — Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island. Fourteen Democrats and one independent joined most Republicans in supporting it; two Republicans voted against.

Supporters framed the vote as a response to household costs. The price of a kilowatt-hour has risen more than 6 percent in the last year and 39 percent in the last five years. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the bill would "cut through decades of red tape," while Capito said its passage was a major step toward addressing "the affordability concerns of the American people." Whitehouse said Americans would "quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit." An analysis by the Rhodium Group estimated the bill would cut household electricity bills by $50 to $78 a year by 2040.

But the bill drew sharp opposition from environmental groups and many Democrats. The Sierra Club and the National Wildlife Federation argue it will weaken environmental accountability, and critics say it will make it easier to approve oil and gas projects and energy-hungry data centers while weakening protections for clean air and water. Some senators also raised concerns about tribal rights, and amendments from Oregon's senators — including one to ban data centers on public land — were not adopted.

Some climate advocates support the measure, arguing the country needs to build renewable energy projects and transmission lines faster and that the bill will help solar, wind and battery projects get built.

The bill now heads to the Republican-controlled House, where its prospects are uncertain. President Trump has urged Congress to approve it, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE."

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NPR
  • Reuters

link.title: Senate approves sweeping permitting bill aimed at cutting energy costs

entry.title: Oregon reports first human bird flu case of 2026 in a Morrow County dairy worker
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Oregon has confirmed its first human case of bird flu this year: a dairy worker in Morrow County who caught the virus from infected cattle and developed only mild symptoms.

The Oregon Health Authority announced the case on Thursday, November 19. Its epidemiologists had received confirmation from the Oregon State Public Health Laboratory the day before. The worker, who was in contact with an infected herd, developed conjunctivitis and upper-respiratory symptoms, was treated with the antiviral medicine oseltamivir, and did not need hospital care. People in the worker's household were offered the drug as a precaution.

The case was found through routine monitoring. Weekly testing of milk from dairies across Oregon flagged the virus in the Morrow County herd earlier in November — the state's first detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza in dairy cattle, confirmed on November 10. The farm was placed under quarantine, and the state agriculture department supplied protective equipment and safety training to workers. Genetic sequencing links the Oregon outbreak to dairy herds in Washington's Yakima Valley, where dozens of herds have recently tested positive.

Health officials say the response will stay in place for weeks. The state epidemiologist, Dean Sidelinger, said health workers will keep working with the farm for at least six more weeks, offering testing and early treatment to catch any further human cases. The agriculture department and Morrow County Public Health are monitoring people who were exposed to the virus.

This is not Oregon's first encounter with the virus in people. Public health officials have monitored more than 300 people exposed to sick animals since 2022, and one human case was identified in 2024 in connection with a commercial poultry outbreak.

For the general public, officials say the risk remains very low. The virus is not known to spread from person to person, and the health authority described the risk to the public as "extremely low." Melissa Sutton, the authority's medical director for respiratory viral pathogens, said the case was evidence the surveillance system was working: "This is not cause for alarm. Rather, it is evidence that the surveillance and response system we have in place is working. Our goal is to ensure that all symptomatic farm workers receive prompt testing and treatment to prevent severe disease."

The seasonal flu vaccine does not protect against avian influenza, though it can lower the risk of catching a human flu virus at the same time, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The exact strain involved has not been publicly named, and officials have not released details about the worker, which is standard practice to protect patient privacy.

Sources

  • Statesman Journal
  • KATU

link.title: Oregon reports first human bird flu case of 2026 in a Morrow County dairy worker

entry.title: Trump vows 'tremendous tax' on US firms building AI data centres abroad
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump said on Friday that American companies building data centres outside the United States will face steep penalties, in a warning aimed squarely at the tech firms driving the artificial intelligence boom.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country," Trump said at a White House news conference, his first since returning from two days in China, where he held talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers."

He said companies that build abroad anyway would face a "tremendous tax". He gave no detail about how such a penalty would work — no rate and no timetable — and it was not immediately clear whether the threat would become a formal policy.

Trump's argument was about competition with China. If American firms are allowed to build overseas, he said, they will all build in China, and the United States would lose the industry in the same way he said it lost chip manufacturing when production moved abroad. "The next thing we know, they'll build them in space," he added. "That could happen, too."

He said the facilities should be built in the United States instead, naming Texas and California and adding that if firms would not build there, "they're going to go in West Virginia. We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places."

The warning lands as several large American firms are expanding abroad. Alphabet announced earlier this month that it plans to invest $15 billion in data-centre infrastructure in Malaysia in 2027 and 2028, and CoreWeave has said it plans to expand across Australia, India, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and the United Arab Emirates. Oracle has also been building capacity outside the United States. Data centres supply the computing power the AI buildout runs on, and developers often place them close to users to keep delays and transmission costs down.

At home, the facilities have become a political flashpoint of their own. Data centres have faced bipartisan backlash in communities that blame them for noise and higher electricity prices, and a Gallup poll in August found that 7 in 10 Americans do not want one in their community. Industry groups have countered that the facilities do not raise costs. Trump told communities to take advantage of the boom rather than shut it down: "Make them pay you. Make them pay your community."

Trump also praised Anthropic's stock-market debut and said he and Xi had agreed to work on joint guardrails for AI.

For now, the threat is words, not policy. Whether it becomes a tax, a restriction or simply pressure to keep the next big builds at home — and whether the administration can legally penalise a company for where it builds — is what firms and investors will be watching.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • USA Today

link.title: Trump vows 'tremendous tax' on US firms building AI data centres abroad

entry.title: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as Nasdaq wipes out its 2026 gains
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US stocks fell sharply on Friday, dragging the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average into correction territory and wiping out the Nasdaq Composite's gains for the year, as a sell-off in artificial-intelligence shares gathered pace.

The S&P 500 fell 3.7%, its seventh straight daily decline — its longest losing run since 2020. The Dow dropped 1.9%, or more than 900 points. The Nasdaq plunged 5.2%, or more than 1,200 points, its second-largest one-day points fall on record.

Both the S&P 500 and the Dow are now more than 10% below their recent record highs, the threshold generally used to define a correction. The Nasdaq has been in correction territory since November 5 and is now down nearly 3% for the year. The other two major indexes have kept less than 1% of their 2026 gains.

The week was the market's worst since the first week of April 2025, when President Donald Trump's reciprocal-tariff announcement sent stocks into a tailspin. The Dow finished the week down 8%, the S&P 500 down 8.6% and the Nasdaq down 10%. Just six weeks ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading at record highs.

The slide was driven by the unravelling of the AI trade. Anthropic, the AI lab whose stock-market debut on Thursday was the biggest initial public offering on record, fell nearly 9% to around $89 on its second day of trading, giving back much of its first-day gains. The shares debuted at $111.50, well above the $83 IPO price, but closed Thursday at about $97. The listing had been seen as a test of confidence in AI shares; investors took little comfort from it.

Chip stocks, hit hard in recent weeks, fell again. Nvidia, the AI bellwether, dropped 14% and led the Dow's decliners. The company has lost a third of its value in the past two weeks as investors weigh the impact of Jensen Huang's departure from the chief executive role. Advanced Micro Devices fell 13%, while Broadcom, Marvell Technology and Micron all posted double-digit declines. Memory-chip makers were among the day's biggest losers in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq: SanDisk fell 16%, and Seagate and Western Digital each dropped 12%.

Wall Street's fear gauge, the Cboe Volatility Index, jumped 26% to near 36, its highest mark since last year's tariff turmoil.

The retreat spread beyond equities. Bitcoin traded at $58,100, its lowest level since June. Gold futures fell 4.5% to $3,525 an ounce, their lowest since September 2025. Oil moved the other way, with West Texas Intermediate crude up 1.1% to $84.10 a barrel, while the yield on the 10-year Treasury note fell to 4.94% from 5.05%.

What happens next will turn on whether AI shares stabilise and whether the S&P 500 can hold above 7,000 — a level traders have been watching as a line of support. For now, a rally that carried stocks to records six weeks ago has given back almost everything it gained this year.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Investopedia
  • Barron's

link.title: S&P 500 and Dow close in correction as Nasdaq wipes out its 2026 gains

entry.title: SEC scrutiny turns to Nvidia's accounting as the chip giant's crisis deepens
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia's accounting practices, according to two people briefed on the matter, adding a regulatory investigation to the legal troubles already facing the chip giant.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the SEC was looking into Nvidia, without establishing the focus. Reuters is the first to report that the focus is accounting.

A spokesperson for the SEC declined to comment, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It is not yet clear when the inquiry opened, or exactly which accounting issues are being examined. An investigation is not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action.

The probe lands as Nvidia, a linchpin of the artificial-intelligence boom, reels from a crisis that has sent its shares tumbling by more than a third.

At the centre of that crisis is the ousting of chief executive Jensen Huang, following revelations about his extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy — a claim China has denied.

Alice Huang led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was historically a large customer for Nvidia chips. US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the Justice and Commerce departments said this week.
