One area now drawing renewed attention is how Nvidia reports where its sales come from. Last year the company changed its geographic revenue reporting to use customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, a change that removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown. The Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing company accounts, that Nvidia made the change even as sales in Singapore soared to almost half of its global revenue.

Analysts and investors have also grown concerned about circular financing deals in the AI industry, in which chipmakers have used complex arrangements to help customers pay for their chips and to fund the data centres that use them. Critics say such deals can make it harder for investors to judge the quality of a chipmaker's revenue and its true financial exposure.

On the company's earnings call on Tuesday, interim chief executive Colette Kress — previously Nvidia's chief financial officer — said the company would be far more selective going forward about financing deals in the sector. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy the open-source platform Hugging Face, alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company.

The SEC's enforcement chief, David Woodcock, said last month that the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to make sure they give investors the full picture of potential risks. Under President Donald Trump the SEC has pulled back on enforcement more broadly, saying it will concentrate on bread-and-butter securities fraud, including accounting violations.

What the SEC finds remains unknown. For now, the accounting focus adds a new front to a crisis that has already cost Nvidia its chief executive.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: SEC scrutiny turns to Nvidia's accounting as the chip giant's crisis deepens

entry.title: GTA VI posts $3.79 billion in first-day sales, the biggest entertainment launch ever
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Grand Theft Auto VI took in $3.79 billion in retail sales in its first 24 hours, developer Rockstar Games said on Friday, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history by a wide margin.

The figure, announced by Rockstar and its parent company Take-Two Interactive, covers sales through the end of Thursday, November 19, the game's first full day on sale worldwide. It sets a record for any entertainment release across any medium — ahead of the biggest film openings and far ahead of any previous video game launch.

The game also sold 32.5 million copies before its official release, a record for pre-orders across all platforms, according to the companies. The launch comes after thirteen years of anticipation since the previous entry in the series, and the game earned a near-perfect score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.

The official total is considerably higher than the estimates that circulated on launch day. Analytics firm Sensor Tower had put first-day sales at about $2.36 billion, based on 24.58 million copies sold by Thursday evening. The Rockstar figure is the company's own estimate of what shoppers spent at retail, and it includes the record pre-order volume that built up before release.

For comparison, Grand Theft Auto V, the previous game in the series, sold about $800 million worth of copies on its first day in 2013 — then a record for the industry. GTA VI has nearly tripled the number of copies its predecessor sold in its first 24 hours. The $3.79 billion total is also more than the highest-grossing film in history has earned across its entire theatrical run.

The scale of the launch reflects one of the most expensive entertainment projects ever made, with production costs estimated at $1 billion or more. The game went on sale for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, and Take-Two said demand had been unprecedented since pre-orders opened.

Rockstar president and founder Sam Houser said the studio was grateful to players as it begins a new chapter with the release. Attention now turns to what follows: investors are watching for Take-Two's plans for a PC version and for the game's online multiplayer mode, which analysts expect in 2027 and which could turn a one-off purchase into a longer-running revenue stream.

For now, the first-day numbers alone put GTA VI in a league of its own — a launch thirteen years in the making, and one that has already rewritten the record books for the entertainment industry.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Business Wire

link.title: GTA VI posts $3.79 billion in first-day sales, the biggest entertainment launch ever

entry.title: Man convicted of starting the fire that became the deadly Palisades blaze
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal jury in Los Angeles has convicted the man accused of starting the blaze that became the Palisades Fire, one of the deadliest and most destructive wildfires in the city's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty on Friday of two federal charges: destruction of property by means of fire, and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce. Each count carries up to 20 years in prison. He is due to be sentenced on March 17, 2027, when he faces a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 40 years in federal prison.

The verdict came at a retrial, five months after a first jury deadlocked 10-2 in favour of acquittal and a mistrial was declared. The second trial, before U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang, lasted 14 days, with jurors deliberating for nearly three days.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht deliberately lit a small brush fire shortly after midnight on January 1, 2025, in a clearing on Hidden Buddha Hill near the Skull Rock Trailhead above Pacific Palisades. The fire, known as the Lachman Fire, was quickly suppressed by firefighters — but it kept burning underground, smouldering in the dense root systems below the surface.

Six days later, on January 7, fierce winds drove the hidden fire back above ground. It spread rapidly through Pacific Palisades and Malibu, killing 12 people and destroying 6,837 structures, with damage estimated at about $25 billion. Prosecutors called it the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

At trial, prosecutors relied on surveillance footage and location data from Rinderknecht's phone, which they said showed he was the only person near the ignition site when the fire began. They also told jurors that in a January 2025 interview with investigators, he lied about where he had been when he first saw the blaze; phone records placed him in a clearing about 30 feet from the fire as it grew.

Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver and onetime Pacific Palisades resident, has been in federal custody since his arrest in Florida in October 2025. He declined to testify in either trial, but said in a court declaration filed in March that he had not wilfully started any fire. His defence argued that holiday fireworks had triggered the New Year's Day blaze, and that the inferno a week later was a separate fire set by someone else. His lawyer also argued that prosecutors lacked enough physical evidence to prove the case, and suggested his client was being blamed for failures by the Los Angeles Fire Department.

The Palisades disaster struck on the same day as another catastrophic wind-driven fire in Eaton Canyon, about 30 miles to the east, which killed 19 people in Altadena. Investigators later concluded that fire was sparked by an electrical transmission tower. Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire calamity in Los Angeles County history. Rinderknecht is the only person criminally charged in connection with either fire.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • U.S. Department of Justice

link.title: Man convicted of starting the fire that became the deadly Palisades blaze

entry.title: Trump weighs renewed Iran strikes as military warns of strain on forces
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump is weighing a new round of military strikes against Iran, even as American military planners warn that U.S. forces risk becoming overextended if the standoff drags into the new year, the Financial Times reported on Friday.

The report said hawkish officials in Washington and Israel are pressing Trump to resume military action, while planners caution that sustaining the current deployment is becoming harder the longer the confrontation continues.

A separate report in The New York Times, published on Wednesday, said Trump has not yet made a decision, but is considering fresh Israeli intelligence warnings that Tehran has rebuilt parts of its missile and drone arsenals and made progress on chemical and biological weapons programmes.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is urging Washington to join Israel in a four-to-seven-day air campaign, according to the Times report. A senior Israeli official disputed that Netanyahu had pressured Trump to act.

The discussions intensified last week, when Mossad director Roman Gofman travelled to Washington for meetings with senior administration officials, including CIA director John Ratcliffe. Israeli military intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Shlomi Binder has also advocated resuming operations, the report said.

The prospect of another major campaign has exposed divisions inside the administration, both over the reliability of the intelligence and over the wisdom of renewed strikes. Some officials question whether the emerging threats justify a new offensive, particularly after the Republican Party's defeat in the midterm elections. The war, which began on February 28, has lasted nearly eight months, contributing to rising prices at home without delivering the swift victory Trump initially promised.

Trump recently instructed Vice President JD Vance to abandon efforts to reach a negotiated settlement with Tehran, the Times reported, favouring sustained economic pressure aimed at forcing Iran to give up its nuclear programme. One U.S. official argued, however, that further major military operations were unnecessary because the economic pressure campaign had already severely weakened Iran.

The report came hours after Trump told Fox News that American intelligence had indications Iran was exploring chemical and biological weapons as alternatives to nuclear weapons.

"Well, there is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Trump told the network's White House correspondent, Jacqui Heinrich.

The president also confirmed that contacts with Tehran were continuing. "They want to make a deal, but I want a deal that can be lasting," he said. Asked whether he would keep American troops in the region until an agreement was reached, he replied: "Yeah, I'm going to finish it off. Yeah, soon. I mean, one way or the other, we'll finish it off."

His remarks left open whether Washington intends to end the confrontation through diplomacy or renewed military action — whether the president will embrace Israel's proposal for another concentrated air campaign, or keep pursuing an agreement through economic and diplomatic pressure.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Jerusalem Post
  • InvestingLive

link.title: Trump weighs renewed Iran strikes as military warns of strain on forces

entry.title: Denmark orders Russian defence attaché out over alleged assassination plot
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Denmark has ordered Russia's defence attaché to leave the country after its intelligence service said Moscow planned to assassinate a Ukrainian-American rapper during a concert near Copenhagen in September.

Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen announced the decision on Friday, saying he had summoned the Russian ambassador and told him the attaché must leave Denmark within seven days. Denmark is also considering suspending Schengen visas for Russian citizens.

According to PET, Denmark's security and intelligence service, three people were stopped in a car near the concert venue on 25 September, where police found firearms and knives. Two Danish men appeared in court near Copenhagen on Friday charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Court documents showed they were arrested five minutes before the concert was due to begin, and one of them had bought a ticket to the performance. The concert was cancelled.

PET suspects the banned street gang Loyal to Familia helped plan the attack. Danish public broadcaster DR identified the intended target as Kyivstoner, a rapper who holds both Ukrainian and US citizenship.

PET chief Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen said the case showed that Russian intelligence had tried to carry out a killing on Danish soil. "A Russian assassination attempt is not something we've seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia," he told journalists.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen echoed that warning, saying Denmark faced "a cornered Russia, acting more aggressively and with a greater propensity to take risks". European Council President António Costa called the alleged attempt "unacceptable" and said it "will not go unanswered", promising Denmark the European Union's full backing against what he called Russian hybrid attacks.

Moscow rejected the accusation. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen called the expulsion "vengeful" and said Denmark had presented no evidence of Russian involvement. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would give "an appropriate response". Russia's security service had previously accused the rapper of helping Ukrainian intelligence plan a drone attack on a defence facility near Moscow, an allegation he denied.

Denmark has blamed Moscow for other hybrid attacks — operations short of open war, such as sabotage and disruption. Drones shut down Copenhagen airport for hours in September 2025, and PET said in September that Russia was recruiting Danish citizens to help plan sabotage against defence firms with ties to Ukraine. Russia denies involvement in such operations.

What evidence Danish prosecutors hold beyond the arrests has not been made public, and the charges remain allegations to be tested in court. But the expulsion is already Denmark's sharpest diplomatic response to Moscow since the war in Ukraine began — a signal, in Rasmussen's words, that Copenhagen wants to send a "very, very strong" message without breaking off diplomatic relations entirely.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • CNN

link.title: Denmark orders Russian defence attaché out over alleged assassination plot

entry.title: Haiti turns to El Salvador to build three new prisons
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Haiti has announced an agreement with El Salvador to build three new prisons, deepening a security partnership that has already put Salvadoran troops on the ground against the gangs controlling much of the capital.

The announcement came on Friday from Haiti's Minister of Justice and Public Security, Patrick Pélissier, after an official mission to El Salvador. The first prison will be launched soon, with the prime minister ordering it to be expedited, and will be one of three built by a Salvadoran company working with a Haitian firm, the minister said.

Haiti's need for prison space is acute. Gangs control an estimated 70% of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and swaths of the country's central region. In 2024, gang raids on the country's two biggest prisons released thousands of inmates, and the system has struggled ever since to hold those arrested. Haiti's prisons have long been notorious for severe overcrowding, with human rights experts warning that prisoners sleep standing and that hundreds have died in recent years. A 2023 visit by The Associated Press to one of the prisons found inmates thirsty and starving.

Pélissier praised the Salvadoran maximum-security prison CECOT, which he toured during his visit to El Salvador for an international conference. El Salvador has been under a state of exception since 2022 that has imprisoned more than 90,000 people with no access to family visits. The United States has also deported Venezuelans and Salvadorans to CECOT, and some have denounced torture there after their release.

"Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again," Pélissier said of the facility.

The minister did not say how much the prison projects would cost, whether El Salvador would help finance them, or whether it would play any role in managing them.

The announcement came on the same day El Salvador's armed forces said two of its soldiers were killed and two others injured in a detonation while handling explosives at a camp in Haiti. The soldiers were among the 2,500 Salvadoran troops President Nayib Bukele has deployed in a military operation to rescue four technicians who disappeared on October 18 after coming under fire from gangs in the Croix-des-Bouquets area northeast of Port-au-Prince.

The deployment runs alongside a United Nations-backed gang suppression force, authorised by the Security Council in October 2025, that is meant to have 5,500 security personnel working to dismantle armed gangs, protect infrastructure and facilitate humanitarian access in collaboration with the Haitian National Police. The force replaced the Kenya-led multinational mission and has not yet deployed its full strength. Bukele's additional troops are not part of the UN-backed force, which unlike its predecessor has the power to arrest suspected criminals.

Haiti has not had an elected government since President Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in 2021. Elections are set to take place next year.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News

link.title: Haiti turns to El Salvador to build three new prisons

entry.title: Judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A Missouri judge has approved Bayer's $7.25 billion settlement of lawsuits alleging that its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer, a decision that could finally resolve litigation that has weighed on the company for a decade.

St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer granted final approval on Friday, finding the nationwide class settlement "fair, reasonable, and adequate" and describing the total as among the largest in the history of mass-tort personal-injury class actions. The order is subject to appeal.

The deal covers people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a form of cancer, after exposure to Roundup. Individual payouts will range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on the severity of the illness, the age at diagnosis, and whether the exposure happened at home or at work. It applies both to people who are already ill and to those diagnosed in the future: the settlement covers exposure before February 17, 2026, and a second group of people diagnosed within 16 years after final approval. Monsanto, Bayer's subsidiary, will fund it through declining capped annual payments over up to 21 years, totalling up to $7.25 billion including money already paid.

About 65,000 claims are pending in US state and federal courts from people who say they developed cancer after using Roundup. The settlement, announced in February, aims to resolve nearly all current and future claims in the United States. Around 200 cases consolidated in an ongoing federal proceeding are excluded, and Bayer says a recent Supreme Court ruling gives it strong defences in those.

The litigation has shadowed Bayer since its 2018 purchase of Monsanto, costing the company billions of dollars and weighing on its share price. Bayer spent about $10 billion in 2020 to resolve most of the lawsuits then outstanding, but it could not win court approval for a parallel $1.25 billion deal covering future claims — the gap this new settlement is designed to close.

The legal ground shifted in Bayer's favour this year. In June, the US Supreme Court ruled 7-2 in the Durnell case that federal pesticide law pre-empts state "failure-to-warn" claims, undercutting a central argument in many of the lawsuits. Judge Boyer cited that ruling in finding the settlement adequate, and in October a Missouri jury sided with Bayer in the first Roundup verdict since the decision.

Bayer continues to deny the claims, saying decades of studies show glyphosate, Roundup's key ingredient, is safe and does not cause cancer. Lawyers for plaintiffs who support the deal say it ensures people with cancer will actually be paid at a time when the litigation has become more uncertain than ever. Opponents argued it does not offer enough money and said it would trap current and future claimants who would rather pursue their cases in court.

Bayer chief executive Bill Anderson called the approval "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation." If the approval survives appeal, the long-running claims programme will begin paying out to tens of thousands of people — and bring the most expensive chapter in Bayer's history closer to an end.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement

entry.title: Federal court halts Army plan to detonate unstable lead explosive in Iowa
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal appeals court has blocked the US Army from detonating about five tons of unstable lead explosive at a munitions plant in south-east Iowa, halting a plan that alarmed residents and state officials over the toxic lead dust it would scatter.

The US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay on Thursday night, barring the Army from using an Environmental Protection Agency emergency permit to carry out the blast. The one-sentence order, signed by Judge Susan Bindler, came hours after the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter — represented by the advocacy group Earthjustice — sued to stop it.

At issue are 68 barrels holding roughly 9,700 pounds of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, near Burlington. The Army discovered in March that the compound, stored for about 20 years, was crystallising after the ethanol-and-water mixture meant to stabilise it had largely evaporated. Lead azide is used to set off munitions, and in its degraded state it is extremely sensitive to friction or movement.

The Army had planned two controlled detonations at about noon on Friday. Late on Thursday, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle postponed the operation to Monday, November 23, calling that the latest possible moment before a forecast temperature drop that could further destabilise the material. The Army says a controlled blast is safer than moving the material, which could detonate by accident in transit, and that it has been planning the operation since March under an EPA emergency permit issued on November 13.

But the blast would send a plume of lead particles into the air: larger ones would probably settle within about 20 miles, while finer dust could drift further, toward Iowa City and across the Mississippi River into western Illinois. Residents were told to stay indoors for a day or two and wash down surfaces afterwards. There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowa already has the second-highest cancer rate of any US state.

On Friday, the Justice Department told the appeals court it intends to oppose the environmental groups' request for a longer halt, and cited a federal regulation it said could allow the Army to treat hazardous explosive waste without an EPA permit in a qualifying emergency. The filing did not say the Army had decided to use that route, and the Army is not a party to the lawsuit. The EPA said it would file its own response by November 22.

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds activated the state's emergency operations centre on Friday, and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker pressed the Army for more transparency about the risk to his state. The Army, the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services said in a joint statement that they were working together to carry out the detonation "in the safest fashion possible." With the permit suspended, whether Monday's blast can go ahead is now for the court to decide; it has not said when it will rule.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Little Village

link.title: Federal court halts Army plan to detonate unstable lead explosive in Iowa

entry.title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's Andes, felt in Lima
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A magnitude 6.7 earthquake shook the Andes in central Peru on Friday evening, sending residents of the capital, Lima, rushing out of their homes and into the streets. Authorities reported no immediate casualties or major damage.

The US Geological Survey said the quake struck at 7:09 p.m. local time, with its epicentre in the Andes about 34 kilometres north of Junín, at a depth of 108 kilometres. Peru's Geophysical Institute put the epicentre slightly differently — about 30 kilometres north-west of Junín — and measured the depth at 129 kilometres. The shaking was felt across a wide area, including Lima, Huánuco, Callao and the Andean regions of Áncash, Ica, Ucayali and Cerro de Pasco.

Peru's Geophysical Institute said no damage or casualties had been reported in the hours after the tremor. The mayor of Carhuamayo, a town near the epicentre, told a local television station there were no reports of victims or material damage there. Later updates pointed to minor damage to some homes, power cuts and landslides in places near the epicentre, but still no injuries or deaths, as emergency officials continued monitoring vulnerable areas.

In Lima, hundreds of people evacuated buildings in the Miraflores district after the tremor, and television footage showed lawmakers leaving the Congress building as the shaking was felt in the capital. Peru's National Emergency Operation Center said the quake was felt with moderate to strong intensity.

Peru lies along the "Ring of Fire", a 40,000-kilometre arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin where most of the world's earthquakes occur. The country is no stranger to strong tremors: in August, a magnitude 6.7 earthquake in the southern Andes injured at least two people and damaged homes, health centres and schools in the Ayacucho and Cusco regions, and in July, a 5.5-magnitude quake in the Junín region killed six people and injured 30.

The depth of Friday's quake — more than 100 kilometres below the surface — likely helped limit the damage at ground level, even though the shaking was felt far from the epicentre. Authorities said monitoring would continue through the night.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • TRT World

link.title: Magnitude 6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's Andes, felt in Lima

entry.title: NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter halt science work after separate glitches
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two of NASA's Mars explorers have paused their science work after being hit by separate technical problems, the agency announced on Thursday. Engineers hope both spacecraft can return to normal operations by the end of November.

The Perseverance rover ran into trouble with its main radio link home. On October 30, the rover's main UHF downlink radio — the system it uses to send data back to Earth through Mars orbiters — stopped sending its usual "heartbeat" signals to the onboard computer. The rover switched to its backup radio on its own and entered a protective safe mode.

After the rover recovered from safe mode, engineers found the backup radio was transmitting at only about half its expected power, so they stopped using that one too. Perseverance is now talking directly to Earth through its high-gain antenna and NASA's Deep Space Network, a link with much lower data rates. With the team prioritising diagnostic data, science work — including camera observations — is on hold, and no new raw images have appeared on the mission website since November 7. NASA said the rover is stable and communicating.

The timing is a sharp turn of fortune. The glitch appeared just 19 days after Perseverance set a new off-Earth driving record on October 11, covering 28.10 miles (45.22 km) in a single drive and passing the mark of 28.06 miles set by NASA's Opportunity rover.

Meanwhile, the Mars Odyssey orbiter lost the use of one of its four reaction wheels, which keep the spacecraft pointed in the right direction. Three working wheels are required, and Odyssey had already lost one in 2013, making this its second wheel failure. The problem appeared on November 4, when the orbiter entered safe mode; it stayed there until November 6 while engineers diagnosed the fault.

Testing has at one point got the faulty wheel moving on command again, and further tests are under way to confirm whether it can be recovered. Although Odyssey left safe mode about two weeks ago, it has not yet resumed science or data-relay work. NASA's goal is for it to return to both in the last week of November.

If the wheel cannot be recovered, the team would have to steer the orbiter using thrusters alone — and Odyssey has only about one to two months of hydrazine fuel left for that. Odyssey arrived at Mars in October 2001 and is the longest-operating spacecraft at the Red Planet; among its contributions, it produced the first global maps of the Martian surface's composition.

Two unrelated problems striking both spacecraft at once is an unlucky coincidence for NASA's Mars fleet, but engineers say both vehicles are stable while the teams work through diagnostics and recovery.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Space.com

link.title: NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter halt science work after separate glitches

entry.title: UN states agree to keep talking on 'killer robots' — but binding rules are still years away
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A week of United Nations talks on lethal autonomous weapons has ended with a promise to keep talking — not with the binding rules that many countries wanted.

Delegates from the 128 member states of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons met in Geneva from Monday, and the negotiations ran past 4 a.m. on Saturday before a compromise was reached. The agreement pledges further discussions aimed at developing new rules within two years, by 2028. It does not say whether those rules will be legally binding.

Around 100 countries had backed a push for binding rules within a short timeframe, to govern weapons systems that can identify and engage targets with varying degrees of autonomy — sometimes called "killer robots". But major arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed that approach, and the final text was watered down as a result.

Russia's opposition shaped the outcome in more than one way. Diplomats said Russian objections to the rules of procedure forced the cancellation of some formal meetings, and negotiators spent hours overnight wrangling over a handful of words before the deal was struck.

The Swiss chair of the meeting, Julien Thoeni, called the agreement a significant achievement for humanitarian disarmament after more than a decade of talks. "It shows that even in today's deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results," he told reporters as the session closed.

Human rights groups were less convinced. "Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk," said Nicole van Rooijen, executive director of the campaign group Stop Killer Robots, speaking on the sidelines of the talks. One diplomat from a country supporting new laws described the outcome as "disappointing but could have been much worse".

The urgency behind the talks is not theoretical. Alarm has grown over the use of lethal autonomous weapons systems in conflicts including Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East. The UN secretary-general, the pope and the Red Cross have all called for strong and legally binding rules, and campaigners warn that technology is advancing faster than diplomacy.

That gap is now the central question. Because the current UN framework requires all 128 state parties to agree by consensus, some observers and former military officials say states should be prepared to consider a new process outside it. For now, though, the path chosen in Geneva is to keep negotiating — with the deadline for rules set two years out, and the question of whether they will bind anyone still open.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: UN states agree to keep talking on 'killer robots' — but binding rules are still years away

entry.title: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis — but the proof still needs checking
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A mathematician at Anthropic says he has used the company's AI system Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a problem about prime numbers that has resisted mathematicians since 1859. If the claim survives scrutiny, it would settle what many regard as the most important open question in pure mathematics. It has not yet been verified.

Levent Alpöge, a number theorist who works at Anthropic, announced the result on Friday in a four-page note on his personal website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote. He said the method also resolves a broader version of the problem known as the generalized Riemann hypothesis.

The hypothesis, first proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, concerns the distribution of prime numbers — the numbers divisible only by themselves and one. It conjectures that all the non-trivial zeros of a function called the zeta function lie on a single vertical line, the "critical line".

Alpöge did not publish a conventional paper. Instead, he released the argument as code in Lean, a programming language that lets computers check mathematical reasoning step by step. He said a full written version would be extremely long and that he had not yet mastered all of the mathematics involved.

Early checks have been encouraging. Within hours, mathematicians including Andrew Sutherland of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology downloaded the Lean code and reported that it compiled without errors. "Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero," Sutherland said. But a further check, known as a comparator run, is still under way to confirm the code does not redefine any of the symbols in the statement.

Reaction has been mixed. Brian Conrey, a leading specialist on the hypothesis, called it "a monumental moment in human history", while admitting he had not yet seen a manuscript. Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal, was more cautious, describing the released note as garbled and saying a clearer write-up should have come first.

The announcement came the day after Anthropic's record stock-market debut, which initially valued the company at $1.5 trillion. Alpöge said he had consulted chief executive Dario Amodei before announcing and acknowledged the timing could be viewed cynically, calling it "horrible" but saying he could not wait any longer.

The claim arrives two months after rival OpenAI said an AI model had solved another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, on the equations that govern fluid motion. That proof also awaits full vetting. The Riemann hypothesis carries a $1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute, but a solution must be published in a peer-reviewed journal and withstand two years of scrutiny.

In August, Anthropic said an unreleased Claude had improved a related result, raising the proven share of zeros on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2% — while stressing it had not proved the hypothesis. Whether this claim closes the gap is now for the mathematics community to decide.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Scientific American

link.title: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him prove the Riemann hypothesis — but the proof still needs checking

entry.title: U.S. stocks slide into correction as AI sell-off deepens
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

U.S. stocks fell sharply on Friday, dragging the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 into correction territory and wiping out the Nasdaq Composite's gains for the year, as a sell-off in artificial-intelligence stocks turned into a broad market rout.

The Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.9 percent, to 48,147.33, more than 10 percent below its record high in August. The S&P 500 dropped 265.44 points, or 3.7 percent, to 6,910.39, also more than 10 percent below its October peak. A correction is generally defined as a decline of 10 percent or more from a recent high. The Nasdaq Composite sank 1,261.47 points, or 5.3 percent, to 22,617.73, coming close to bear-market territory — a fall of 20 percent or more from its peak.

It was the worst week for American stocks in years. For the week, the S&P 500 fell 8.6 percent, the Dow lost 8 percent and the Nasdaq tumbled 10 percent, its worst week since March 2020. The S&P 500 has now fallen for seven straight sessions, its longest losing streak since February 2020, and members of the Nasdaq lost more than $4 trillion in market value this week alone. The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street's "fear gauge," jumped to its highest level this year.

The selling was led by the technology companies at the heart of the AI boom. Nvidia, whose chips power the data centres behind AI, plunged 14 percent on Friday to $125.53 and finished the week down 23 percent — about half its value since its October 6 record high. Investors are still unsettled by the sudden departure of chief executive Jensen Huang this month, and by questions about the financing behind the AI buildout.

Anthropic, the AI lab behind the Claude chatbot, also slid. Its shares fell 9.1 percent to $88.30, close to the $83 IPO price, after the biggest initial public offering in U.S. history failed to calm the market.

The rout spread well beyond technology. All 11 sectors of the S&P 500 fell by more than 1 percent this week, and retailers dropped on fears that a slump in AI investment and home prices could slow the wider economy. Analysts pointed to a pile-up of worries: rising financing costs for the AI buildout, persistent inflation and a Federal Reserve seen as inclined to raise interest rates, a strengthening dollar drawing liquidity out of markets, and Democratic victories in the midterm elections raising the prospect of heavier data-centre regulation.

Some traders called the sell-off a necessary reset as investors re-evaluate the companies that have driven market gains for nearly four years. Others worry the cracks in the AI story are now too deep to ignore. Either way, a market that spent most of 2026 climbing on the promise of artificial intelligence ended the week asking whether that promise was priced too high.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Wall Street Journal
  • MarketWatch

link.title: U.S. stocks slide into correction as AI sell-off deepens

entry.title: The 'me inside' may live in the brain stem, not the cortex, researchers propose
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Close your eyes and cover your ears. Much of the world disappears, but the feeling of being present — of being you — stays. Two researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem now argue that this basic feeling does not come from where most neuroscientists have looked for it.

Their paper, "Brainstem Theory of Consciousness," published in the journal The Neuroscientist, proposes that raw conscious experience — what the authors call the "me inside" — is generated by the brain stem, the stalk-like structure at the base of the brain that connects the upper brain to the spinal cord. Until now, the dominant view has placed conscious experience in the cerebral cortex, the folded outer layer responsible for language, recognition and planning.

The authors — veteran pain researcher Prof. Marshall Devor and neuroscientist Dr. Mark Baron, of the Hebrew University and Harvard Medical School's Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center — build their case on pain, brain injury and anaesthesia.

Pain is central to it. Detecting a harmful stimulus and feeling it hurt are different things, Devor told The Jerusalem Post: the nervous system can trigger an automatic withdrawal reflex, but pain also involves a subjective experience — it hurts. That feeling, they argue, does not depend on the cortex the way complex sights and sounds do. Extensive damage to the cortex can wipe out vision or hearing, yet usually leaves the experience of pain intact, or even stronger. Damage to particular regions of the brain stem, by contrast, consistently sends a person into a coma.

They point to one part of the brain stem, the mesopontine tegmentum, where earlier research located circuits involved in coma after brain injury and in losing consciousness under anaesthesia. In a 2001 rat experiment, tiny doses of anaesthetic delivered into one small node there rapidly and reversibly switched off pain responses and other signs of consciousness, while injections placed even slightly off target had no effect.

Under the theory, the cortex does the heavy computing — recognising a face, judging whether an animal might attack — while the brain stem acts as an adjudicator, filtering the flood of sensations and deciding which signals deserve conscious attention. "The cortex provides detailed information about the world, and brain stem mechanisms shine the light of subjective experience on those aspects that deserve conscious attention," Devor said.

The authors stress what they have not shown: the paper synthesises existing findings and clinical observations, proposing a framework for further investigation — not a proven mechanism. The precise mechanism remains unresolved, they say, though it is surely biological.

If the theory holds up, it could change how doctors assess consciousness in patients with severe brain injuries, coma or disorders of consciousness. Devor also suggests the capacity to feel pain arose early in evolution, before the mammalian cortex existed — perhaps in reptiles, even fish — though whether they have subjective experiences, he said, "we don't know."

Sources

  • The Jerusalem Post
  • Sci.News

link.title: The 'me inside' may live in the brain stem, not the cortex, researchers propose

entry.title: Signal blocks screenshots to keep AI agents out of your private chats
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Signal, the encrypted messaging app, is switching off screenshots inside its own app — not to stop people saving messages, but to stop the artificial intelligence built into their phones from reading them.

The change, announced on Friday by Signal president Meredith Whittaker, blocks screenshots by default on iPhones running iOS 27 and switches on screen protection on Android phones when an AI assistant tries to capture what is on the display. The target is the new generation of operating-system assistants — Apple's Siri AI, with its Onscreen Awareness feature, and Google's Gemini Intelligence — which scan whatever is on screen so they can answer questions and carry out tasks.

That scanning is the problem, Signal says. A message may be encrypted as it travels, but once it arrives it is decrypted and shown in plain text on the screen. When an AI agent reads the screen, it captures that text and can store it locally or send it to a remote server — entirely outside Signal's control, and unseen by the other people in the conversation.

Users can switch the protection off under Privacy, then App Security, in the app's settings. Signal warns against doing so: turning it off can expose not only your own messages but also those sent by your contacts, and it breaks the app's privacy guarantee.

The move follows a similar step last year, when Signal blocked Microsoft's Recall feature from taking periodic screenshots of its app on Windows 11. But the company is candid that blocking screenshots is only a partial answer. It does not stop AI agents reaching app data through other routes, such as files stored on the device or notifications, and it offers no protection at all if the person at the other end of a conversation has switched the protection off. On macOS, Signal says it cannot implement the protection at all.

Signal also points to third-party agents beyond the built-in ones. It cites reporting by Reuters that Meta's Muse agent was able to read Signal messages by using the deep permissions users are encouraged to grant during setup — accessibility tools on a Mac and push notifications on Android — which Signal describes as a skeleton key meant to help people use their devices, not to hand their chats to an AI.

Rather than fighting each new agent one by one, Signal is asking Apple, Google and Microsoft for something more basic: a simple, well-documented way for developers to opt their apps out of AI data access — screen reading, file access and notifications — without breaking the app, plus clear documentation of how the agents actually work. Whittaker says the company is in conversation with Apple and Google and is cautiously optimistic.

She frames the stakes bluntly: the way AI agents are being woven into operating systems is an existential threat to Signal's mission, and to any developer trying to guarantee privacy in the app. Signal is the canary in the coal mine, the post says — but the problem, it argues, affects the whole ecosystem.

Sources

  • Signal
  • The Register

link.title: Signal blocks screenshots to keep AI agents out of your private chats

entry.title: Earth has a temporary second moon — a tiny asteroid called 2026 QQ8
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Earth has gained a second moon — but it will not stay. A tiny asteroid, roughly the size of a person, has been looping around our planet since April, and astronomers expect it to drift away in December.

The visitor is called 2026 QQ8. It measures only about 1–2 metres (3–6 feet) across, and it is so small and dim that it took astronomers several weeks to confirm what it was. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center formally named it in late October.

Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky, a research coordinator at the Konkoly Observatory who has found hundreds of near-Earth asteroids, first spotted the object in August. Only later, once its orbit had been calculated precisely, did its unusual nature become clear: it had been captured by Earth's gravity months earlier, in April, and had been circling the planet ever since.

For a while, astronomers could not rule out that it was a piece of space junk — a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. Only by watching how sunlight pressing on the object affected its motion over several weeks could they establish that it was a rock, not hardware. Observations from the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona and the University of Hawaii's 2.2-metre telescope on Mauna Kea settled the question.

The asteroid most likely came from the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, though its exact origin is still being studied. In April it drifted close enough, and slowly enough, for Earth's gravity — helped a little by the Moon's — to bend its path into a wide, looping orbit. At its closest it stays about 568,000 kilometres away, roughly one and a half times the distance to the Moon.

There is no danger. Even if it did fall towards Earth, it would burn up in the atmosphere. "At best, you would get a bright meteor in the sky and a bit of a bang," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center.

Earth's temporary companions are not as rare as they sound. Previous mini-moons include 2006 RH120, which stayed about a year, and 2020 CD3, which orbited for about three years. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," Payne said. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." Most are simply too small, too far away and too fast-moving for current surveys to spot.

2026 QQ8 is not expected to be captured again soon. It approaches Earth roughly once every ten years, but its next close pass, in 2058, is not expected to end in another temporary orbit. By early 2027 it should be back on its own path around the Sun — a journey that takes it about 359 days to complete.

About 40,000 near-Earth objects have been identified so far, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile is beginning a ten-year survey that should expand the catalogue of known solar system objects from about 1.5 million to 5 million.

Sources

  • CNN
  • BBC Sky at Night Magazine

link.title: Earth has a temporary second moon — a tiny asteroid called 2026 QQ8

entry.title: Trump calls Putin 'my friend' at APEC summit — and allies push back
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

At a summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, President Donald Trump pointed at Vladimir Putin, smiled, and called him "my friend" as the two men shook hands. The greeting came at the start of the first formal meeting of the leaders of the United States, China and Russia — a gathering Trump later rated "12 out of 10".

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen. Trump and Putin spoke face to face for about 40 minutes before joining their host, Chinese President Xi Jinping, for a 90-minute three-way session around a single table. Trump greeted Xi warmly too, telling him: "You're my friend and we have a very special relationship." Afterwards the three leaders issued a short "Declaration toward Peace". It made no mention of Ukraine, and it condemned the International Criminal Court, which has issued an arrest warrant for Putin over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children.

The reaction from America's allies was swift. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted on X: "God, protect us from such friends." His foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said the optics "cause us some concern", and asked whom Trump considered the closer friend — Putin or Poland. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the meeting "very incomprehensible", and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned against a rerun of the 1945 Yalta Conference, at which the victorious powers carved up Europe. In Washington, Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen called Putin a "war criminal and murderer", and Senator Tim Kaine said he is "no friend". Republican Senator Thom Tillis also criticised the summit. Asked about the remark at a news conference in Berlin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy only shrugged and walked off the stage.

Trump stood by the greeting the next day. At a White House news conference on Friday, he said his "fantastic relationships" with Putin and Xi kept the United States safe. Asked whether Putin was a friend to America, he replied: "I can't speak to America", pointing instead to their "very good relationship". He told Reuters it was "nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy", and repeated that Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the engagement, noting that the three countries hold the vast majority of the world's nuclear weapons, and that the idea of the three leaders not meeting regularly was "not just absurd, it's dangerous".

Putin's own message, however, was very different. Hours after the summit, he told reporters that Russia would not negotiate a partial ceasefire with Ukraine following Ukrainian strikes on the Crimean Bridge. Poland's defence minister said Russia had violated Polish airspace overnight with three objects, probably two missiles and a drone. Trump, meanwhile, called into a meeting of European leaders in Berlin and told them Putin was ready to end the war — a claim the events of the day did little to support.

Sources

  • NBC News
  • USA Today

link.title: Trump calls Putin 'my friend' at APEC summit — and allies push back

entry.title: MIT study finds the brain's nightly clean-out weakens with age
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

As people get older, sleep often gets shorter and more broken. Now MIT researchers have found a deeper change: the waves of fluid that flush waste out of the brain during deep sleep are significantly weaker in older adults.

The team, led by neuroscientist Laura Lewis, recruited volunteers in two age groups — 18 to 39, and 60 to 84 — and studied them as they fell asleep late at night inside brain scanners. Using standard functional MRI to track blood flow, a modified MRI technique Lewis developed to track cerebrospinal fluid, and EEG to measure brain waves, they watched what happened as volunteers drifted into deep, non-REM sleep.

In younger adults, slow brain waves grew stronger as they entered deep sleep, and the waves of cerebrospinal fluid grew larger with them. In the older group, the average fluid waves were significantly smaller. The difference was tied to a decline in the slow waves themselves — not simply to older people sleeping less.

The researchers also found the brain's blood vessels responded less eagerly in older adults. When volunteers looked at a flickering checkerboard image, neural activity rose as expected, but blood flow did not rise as much as it did in younger people. A breath-holding test showed the same pattern: a smaller increase in blood flow. A statistical model showed that weaker "neurovascular coupling" and smaller blood-flow responses explained much of the drop in fluid waves, though not all of it.

The work builds on a 2019 study from the same lab showing that slow waves during deep sleep generate the fluid waves that clear waste from the brain. None of the volunteers in the new study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder, but some older participants showed signs of grey-matter loss, which tracked with larger reductions in fluid flow.

The team now wants to find out whether weaker waste clearance raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, and whether the sleep patterns they measured could one day help identify people at greater risk. They also hope to test whether interventions can strengthen the process: in a recent study, short bursts of "pink noise" during sleep increased fluid flow in younger adults, but the approach has not yet been tested in older adults. The study appears in Nature Aging.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Boston Globe
  • MIT News
  • ScienceDaily

link.title: MIT study finds the brain's nightly clean-out weakens with age

entry.title: Russian cargo ship Sparta II hit by drones in Gulf of Finland
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A Russian cargo ship bound for the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad was hit by two drones in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, catching fire and drifting out of international waters and into Finnish territorial waters, Russian and Finnish officials said.

The vessel is the Sparta II, a Russian-flagged roll-on/roll-off cargo ship sailing from St Petersburg to Kaliningrad. Russian officials said the attack happened about three nautical miles from Russia's border, west of Gogland Island, in the eastern part of the gulf. Finland's defence ministry said its forces detected the strike at about 8:40 a.m. local time.

A fire broke out on board and the ship lost manoeuvrability. A photograph taken by a Finnish patrol plane showed flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the vessel. The Finnish Border Guard, which took charge of the rescue operation, set up a restricted area around the ship and said the situation posed no danger to other maritime traffic or to people.

By Saturday afternoon the ship had anchored in Finnish waters south of the town of Loviisa. The Border Guard said rescue units were on site, the crew had not been forced to abandon the vessel, and no environmental damage had been detected. Finnish officials said the ship's 16 crew members were evacuating into rescue craft, and that Russian rescue vessels were expected to arrive later in the day, with Russia intending to tow the ship back into its own waters.

Finland temporarily restricted air and sea traffic in the eastern gulf as a precaution, lifting the restrictions in the early afternoon. Separately, Finnish authorities said a Russian helicopter was suspected of entering Finnish airspace near Loviisa shortly after midday, reaching about four kilometres into Finnish territory. Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said the suspected violation was possibly connected to rescue or tracking operations around the damaged ship, and the Border Guard is investigating.

The Finnish Defence Forces said on Saturday afternoon that the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility. The Sparta II is known to Finnish authorities as a vessel with links to Russia's armed forces, and it is under US sanctions. Finnish officials said there was no confirmed information about what cargo was on board, and that military materiel could not be ruled out.

The incident comes barely a week after a similar strike in the same waters, when Finland said it detected an attack on a Russian warship in the gulf. It also underlines how exposed the Baltic has become: Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave wedged between Poland and Lithuania, depends on sea routes through the gulf, and the war in Ukraine keeps spilling into waters shared with NATO members.

Russia's Leningrad region governor, Aleksandr Drozdenko, said 80 drones had been shot down over the region and lifted a drone threat warning. Kaliningrad's governor, Alexei Besprozvannykh, said the incident posed no threat to supplies to the region.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Russian cargo ship Sparta II hit by drones in Gulf of Finland

entry.title: Mexico captures 'El Chapo Isidro,' one of the FBI's most wanted, after gunfight in Sinaloa
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Mexican military forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in a nighttime raid in Sinaloa on Friday, in one of the most significant cartel arrests in Mexico in years. Meza Flores, 44, was one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives; his detention set off hours of cartel violence across the state.

Mexico's defence ministry said special forces from the army and the National Guard, working with US intelligence, used "stealth and surprise" to surround a house in Guasave, a city in northern Sinaloa. As troops established a security perimeter, they came under attack with gunfire and explosives from suspected cartel gunmen, then entered the house and detained him. He was flown to Mexico City. Security officials identified the two others as German "N," known as "Serafin," said to be his second-in-command, and Jose "N," described as the organisation's financial operator.

Meza Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Los Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, according to Mexican authorities. The US State Department says he and his organisation spent more than 20 years moving heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States. The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, offering a $5 million reward, and he has been indicted in the US on drug-trafficking charges since 2012. Despite the shared nickname — "Chapo" means "shorty" — he is not related to Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman, the former Sinaloa Cartel leader now jailed in the United States.

The arrest set off a wave of violence across Sinaloa. Gunmen set up flaming roadblocks, torched cars, trucks and petrol stations, and attacked federal forces in several areas. In Guasave, crowds fled a baseball game as gunfire rang out, and videos showed helicopters circling over homes. Businesses were burned, including convenience stores, kiosks and pharmacies, according to local officials. Security Secretary Omar Garcia Harfuch said armed forces would remain deployed in the state to protect civilians, calling the detentions "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

The capture is the latest in a string of high-profile blows against Mexico's cartels. In February, the military killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as "El Mencho," the leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, in an operation that also set off a burst of violence. President Claudia Sheinbaum has pursued the cartels more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have fallen during her two years in office — but she is under intense pressure from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly threatened unilateral military action inside Mexico if her government does not do more against the cartels. The Mexican government said US intelligence helped in the Guasave operation but gave few details about how the two countries coordinated.

Meza Flores is wanted in Mexico on organised-crime and drug charges and is subject to a US extradition order. US agencies did not immediately comment on the detention, and no timetable for any extradition has been announced.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Mexico captures 'El Chapo Isidro,' one of the FBI's most wanted, after gunfight in Sinaloa

entry.title: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card rates
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he would work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates and fees, reviving an affordability proposal that stalled earlier this year.

In a Fox News interview on Saturday morning, Trump was asked whether a cap on card rates was something he could find common ground on with Democrats, who take control of both chambers in January. "I would do it," he said. "These credit card companies have made a lot — and the credit card fees that they charge. I'm all into it."

"The credit card companies, they're getting too much," he added. "The fees are too high and the interests are too high."

He framed it as fairness, not ideology, saying it was no question of free enterprise when a fee was set by "some guy... on Park Avenue" and decided was too high. "So I'm all for that," he said.

The proposal is not new. In January, Trump said on Truth Social that he would set a 10% cap on credit card interest rates for one year, warning lenders that did not comply would face legal consequences. Nothing came of that threat. Banks pushed back, saying a cap would force card cancellations for less creditworthy customers or sharp cuts to rewards. The idea also found little enthusiasm among Republicans, and the GOP-controlled Congress made no serious effort to pass it.

The politics have shifted since then. Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, who is expected to become the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has long backed a cap and recently said she is ready to work with Trump on a bill. Responding to Saturday's interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money."

The stakes are large. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. Researchers estimated a 10% cap would save Americans roughly $100 billion a year in interest. About 195 million Americans held cards in 2024 and paid $160 billion in interest, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

The industry's objections have not gone away. Banking groups say a cap would deny credit to millions by making lending too risky; credit unions put the figure at more than 47 million people losing access. Supporters counter that the industry would remain profitable even at lower rates, though rewards and other perks might be scaled back.

Whether it becomes law is unclear. Trump did not repeat the 10% figure on Saturday, no bill has been agreed, and it is not clear how high a priority Democrats will make the idea in January.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • Business Standard

link.title: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card rates

entry.title: Fiona, the hippo who beat the odds as a newborn, dies at 9 after swallowing a visitor's hat
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Fiona, the hippopotamus who became one of the world's most famous zoo animals after surviving a premature birth, has died at the Cincinnati Zoo at the age of nine.

The zoo announced her death on Thursday, November 19, eleven days after she swallowed a knit hat that had accidentally landed in her enclosure. "It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said.

The chain of events was, in the zoo's words, almost impossible. On November 8, a child visitor tossed a knit cap into the air in front of Fiona's habitat. A ceiling fan caught it and flung it through a one-foot opening above the 12-foot-high viewing windows, and it landed in the enclosure. Fiona ate it.

At first she seemed fine, and the care team hoped she would pass the hat naturally. Within days, though, her appetite began to fall away. Vets gave her fluids and medication, sedated her for a colonoscopy using a nine-foot scope borrowed from the Columbus Zoo, and even placed her on a vibration plate borrowed from a horse farm in the hope of moving the object along. An ultrasound showed her intestines bunching, a sign that something was passing through her small intestine — but the scope could not reach the hat.

Surgery was never a realistic option. At more than 2,000 pounds, Fiona was a full-grown hippo, and the zoo said a long open incision "would've been a death sentence." Instead the team provided round-the-clock supportive care and waited. It was not enough.

A necropsy later found the hat lodged in the middle of Fiona's small intestine, about 25 feet beyond her final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success," said Dr. Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health, "and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."

Fiona's story had been followed around the world since her birth in January 2017. Born six weeks early at just 29 pounds, she could barely walk and could not stand long enough to nurse from her mother. Keepers hand-raised her, and her progress — first steps, first swims, first solid food — was shared online until she became an internet celebrity, with fans, merchandise and even a statue outside the zoo. Her younger brother, Fritz, was born at the zoo in August 2022.

"We are in shock at the moment," zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

The news brought an outpouring of grief from fans who had watched Fiona grow up, and tributes from across Cincinnati, including the city's sports teams. The zoo has described the hat entering the enclosure as an accident, and the episode is a reminder for visitors to hold on to their belongings and respect the barriers around animal habitats.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Smithsonian Magazine

link.title: Fiona, the hippo who beat the odds as a newborn, dies at 9 after swallowing a visitor's hat

entry.title: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators in Berlin as Iran talks stall
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met senior Qatari officials in Berlin on Thursday to discuss mediation between the United States and Iran, Axios reported, citing two sources familiar with the meeting. The talks were the latest attempt to revive a ceasefire and restart nuclear negotiations — and, according to the report, they made no significant progress.

Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani and his envoy, Ali al-Thawadi, attended the meeting, the sources said. The session coincided with a visit to Germany by Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, who held talks with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and called for diplomatic efforts to de-escalate conflicts across the Middle East.

Qatar is the main mediator between Washington and Tehran and has spent weeks trying to broker a deal that would restore the ceasefire, restart nuclear negotiations and prevent a return to war. The Berlin meeting was part of a flurry of diplomacy in recent days: an Iranian technical delegation visited Doha earlier in the week, al-Thawadi met Iran's foreign minister in Turkey last week, and a Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday evening for talks with Iranian officials, according to Iran's deputy foreign minister.

Trump, in a brief phone interview with Axios on Thursday, signalled he is in no hurry to decide his next step. "We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," he said. At a White House news conference on Friday, he said Iran wanted an agreement but not one he could accept. "We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal," he said, adding that Iran could not be allowed to have a nuclear weapon.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Qatar and Pakistan are the only two mediation channels with the Trump administration. He said Tehran's two-day proposal — resuming a ceasefire, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and relaunching nuclear negotiations — remains on the table, and that Iran is open to shortening its timetable. Tehran's conditions include a ceasefire on all fronts, an end to the naval blockade, waivers allowing Iran to sell oil and the release of frozen Iranian funds. Araghchi said Iran will not allow its enriched uranium stockpile to leave the country, though he believes "a fair solution" can be found, and that Iran is prepared to hold expert-level talks.

The diplomatic push comes after the Qatari prime minister visited Washington last week and met Trump and Vice President JD Vance. After that meeting, Trump told reporters a renewed military campaign against Iran was "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Since then, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressed Trump to launch a new operation, Axios reported. No deal has been reached, and the mediators are still passing proposals between Washington and Tehran.

Sources

  • Axios
  • Dawn

link.title: Witkoff and Kushner meet Qatari mediators in Berlin as Iran talks stall

entry.title: Two tankers struck near the Strait of Hormuz as Iran's shipping crackdown deepens
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Two oil tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, British maritime authorities said, the latest attacks in a sharp escalation of Iran's campaign to control shipping through the vital waterway.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) said one tanker was hit on its stern about 20 kilometres north of Khasab, a port town on Oman's northern coast. A second tanker was struck in its engine room about 31 kilometres east of Khasab. No casualties were reported in either incident, and it was not immediately clear whether the two reports involved the same vessel.

Iran's navy said on Saturday that an oil tanker had caught fire after striking a naval mine in a restricted area east of the strait. In a statement carried by Iranian state television, the navy accused the vessel of ignoring warnings and travelling with its identification and navigation equipment switched off. That account could not be independently verified, and it was unclear whether the burning tanker was one of the vessels in the UKMTO reports.

The attacks followed a similar strike on Friday, when a tanker sailing out of the strait was hit by an unknown projectile about eight nautical miles north of Khasab and caught fire, according to UKMTO. No casualties were reported then either.

The incidents are part of a pattern that has intensified sharply over the past week. Citing statements from Iran's armed forces, Al Jazeera's correspondent in Tehran reported about 25 incidents since the previous Saturday — roughly three a day. Tehran says any ship passing through the strait must coordinate fully with Iranian authorities and follow lanes set by Iran, and warns that vessels that do not comply risk attack or striking sea mines laid by Iranian forces.

The confrontation is playing out against a war that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Before the conflict, the strait carried nearly a fifth of the world's crude oil. The United States has responded to Iran's restrictions by blockading Iranian ports and deploying naval vessels to escort tankers through the waterway. A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night for two hours of talks with Iranian officials, according to Iran's deputy foreign minister — the latest diplomatic effort as the standoff grinds on.

Maritime security analysts say the threat level remains severe. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf in its latest reporting period, and weekly transits through the strait have fallen. For the crews and companies still moving oil through the narrow passage, each crossing now carries a risk that was unthinkable before the war.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Reuters

link.title: Two tankers struck near the Strait of Hormuz as Iran's shipping crackdown deepens

entry.title: SEC turns its Nvidia inquiry to accounting as California subpoena lands
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is examining Nvidia's accounting practices, according to two people briefed on the matter, adding a new front to the legal troubles facing the chipmaker at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that the SEC was investigating Nvidia, without establishing the focus. The two sources told Reuters that enforcement staff are scrutinising potential accounting issues at the company. Neither the SEC nor Nvidia would comment. It is not known when the inquiry began or which accounting issues are under review.

The report landed on Friday, and Nvidia's shares fell about 14 percent to $125.53, extending a slide that has wiped more than a third off the company's value.

The accounting inquiry is only the latest of Nvidia's problems. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served the company with an investigative subpoena. His office is examining whether Nvidia or its former chief executive, Jensen Huang, allowed advanced chips or confidential information to reach China — and whether the company misled investors and the public about that risk.

"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.

The investigations follow Huang's sudden resignation on November 11, days after he admitted to extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a businesswoman US authorities suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. China has denied she is a spy. Alice Huang formerly led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm that was once a large Nvidia chip customer. US authorities have investigated Megaspeed since 2024 over alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China in breach of export controls, the Justice and Commerce departments said this week.

One area drawing renewed attention is how Nvidia reports revenue by region. Last year it switched to customer headquarters rather than billing addresses, removing Singapore from its geographical breakdown — even as sales booked through Singapore soared to almost half its global revenue, the Financial Times reported this week. It is not known whether that change is part of the SEC inquiry.

The Justice Department is also reviewing Nvidia's proposed $12.9 billion purchase of open-source platform Hugging Face as part of a broader antitrust investigation.

Nvidia's board has launched its own independent investigation and set up a committee on national security and export-control compliance. Colette Kress, the longtime chief financial officer, is interim chief executive, and Huang is due to testify before Congress on December 1.

Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing, and many close without enforcement action. But for the company whose chips power most of the world's AI data centres, the pile-up — an SEC accounting probe, a state subpoena, a federal export-control inquiry and a shareholder lawsuit — is now a test of how far investors still trust the AI boom's most important supplier.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Barron's
  • Barron's

link.title: SEC turns its Nvidia inquiry to accounting as California subpoena lands

entry.title: Princeton neuroscience student detained by ICE at Reagan airport after presenting her research
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A Princeton neuroscience doctoral student was detained by US immigration officers on Thursday at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she travelled home from a conference where she had just presented her research.

Eva Yi Xie, 24, a third-year PhD student at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, had presented a poster on how the brain makes decisions at the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. On Thursday, as she boarded a flight home, she was taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Her colleagues learned what had happened from a message Xie sent on Slack asking for help, then lost contact. Her research group, the Brody Lab, later confirmed she was being held at an ICE facility in Chantilly, Virginia.

Her adviser, professor Carlos Brody, posted on Bluesky and X that Xie is "a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist" who "went to a conference to present her work, and now she's in a detention center. She should be home."

Princeton has arranged legal counsel for Xie. Rodney Priestley, dean of the Graduate School, called the news distressing and said the university would stay in contact with her legal team and family: "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton."

Xie's lawyer, Kerry Doyle, told The Daily Princetonian that Xie is an asylum seeker with an immigration court date set for early 2028. Her lawyers have filed a habeas corpus petition in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, arguing the detention is illegal. On Friday, District Judge Anthony J. Trenga ordered that Xie not be removed from the judicial district without further direction, and required immigration officials to respond by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25.

The Department of Homeland Security has given a different account.
