It told Newsweek it conducted a targeted enforcement operation at Reagan National on November 19 to arrest Xie, whom it called "an illegal alien from China." The department said Xie was admitted in March 2016, was required to leave by September 2016, and never held valid authorisation to study. A pending application, it said, does not give her legal status, and she would remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.

Xie's lawyers dispute that reading. They say her pending asylum application allows her to remain in the United States legally while her case is heard, even though her visa had expired.

Xie, a 2024 MIT graduate, emigrated from China in 2016.

The detention has rattled foreign-born academics, who say the case crystallises fears that travelling to conferences has become risky. Xie is the first known Princeton student to be detained by ICE, according to The Daily Princetonian.

Why Xie was detained at this moment remains unclear: no reason was made public until the Homeland Security statement on Friday, and ICE did not answer repeated requests for comment. For now, the court order keeps her in Virginia while her lawyers challenge the detention.

Sources

  • Princeton Alumni Weekly
  • STAT

link.title: Princeton neuroscience student detained by ICE at Reagan airport after presenting her research

entry.title: NATO vows to defend 'every inch' of Poland as Trump calls earlier incursions a mistake
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

NATO's secretary-general pledged on Saturday to defend "every inch" of Polish territory, a day after Russian missiles and a drone came down in south-eastern Poland during a heavy bombardment of Ukraine.

Mark Rutte made the promise during a visit to Warsaw, telling Polish media he could guarantee the alliance would defend Poland, according to the Polish Press Agency. The head of NATO forces in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, would do everything necessary to identify threats and adjust deterrence if needed, Rutte said. NATO's North Atlantic Council, the alliance's main decision-making body, will discuss the incident in Brussels on Monday.

The pledge came after Polish officials said two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia's overnight attack on Ukraine on November 20. One missile, believed to be a Kh-101 cruise missile, came down near Nowy Lipowiec, about 50 kilometres from the Ukrainian border; a second suspected missile fell near Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone near Molodycz. No injuries or damage were reported in Poland.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the incursion appeared to be "an intentional provocation" by Russia, likely timed to coincide with the Coalition of the Willing military exercises under way in Poland. The multinational exercise, involving troops from 11 countries, is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine.

The response from Washington has been strikingly different. President Donald Trump, speaking by phone to Fox News aboard Air Force One on Thursday, said of Russia's earlier incursions: "Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake." The remark came hours before the latest objects fell — and it was aimed at Tusk's criticism of Trump for greeting Vladimir Putin as "my friend" at a summit in Shenzhen. Tusk had answered on social media: "God save us from such friends."

That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine, firing more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.

Poland has not invoked Article 4, the clause under which allies hold emergency consultations — it did so in September 2025 after Russian drones entered its airspace. Invoking Article 5, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, requires agreement from all 32 members, and analysts say the bar remains high: it would take a sustained attack on Poland, not a handful of stray weapons.

For now, Warsaw is asking for more NATO support under the alliance's Eastern Sentry mission, which already patrols the eastern flank. What form that takes — possibly an airborne early-warning aircraft — is still to be decided.

Sources

  • The Washington Post
  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: NATO vows to defend 'every inch' of Poland as Trump calls earlier incursions a mistake

entry.title: Honda and Toyota recall 1.6 million vehicles as Takata airbag risk resurfaces
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Honda and Toyota said on Friday they are recalling about 1.6 million cars, trucks and SUVs because the Takata airbag inflators in them could rupture when the airbag deploys.

Both carmakers said there have been no injuries or crashes linked to the vehicles being recalled, and no airbag inflator ruptures have been reported in them. The inflators will be replaced.

The recall covers 810,592 older Honda cars and SUVs in the United States and 790,000 Toyota vehicles worldwide, including 314,000 in the United States.

The Toyota recall includes the 2002–2010 Lexus SC430, the 2011 IS250, the 2017 GX460, the 2003–2008 Toyota Corolla, the 2005–2006 Tundra, the 2005–2007 Sequoia and the 2016–2017 4Runner. The Honda recall covers some 2013 Accord, 2012–2013 Civic and 2012–2013 CR-V models, along with the 2013 Acura ILX and 2013 Acura RDX.

The Honda recall applies to vehicles sold or registered in 14 states and territories known for high heat and humidity and large temperature swings: Alabama, California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, plus Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, the Northern Mariana Islands, Guam and American Samoa. Toyota did not specify which U.S. states its recall covers, but said it expects replacement inflators to be ready by early 2027.

What sets this recall apart from the earlier Takata recalls is the type of inflator involved. The inflators in these vehicles contain a moisture-absorbing material, unlike the millions recalled previously. Honda said long-term monitoring and analysis had revealed potential propellant degradation in certain inflators in specific regions. Toyota warned that degraded propellant could cause the inflator to rupture if the airbag deploys, causing serious injury.

The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said analysis and inflator-degradation simulation models run by independent testing groups had allowed the carmakers to act before the risk materialised. "Honda and Toyota saw early evidence of degradation risk in certain of their vehicles and are currently conducting proactive recalls of vehicles," the agency said late on Friday, adding that other carmakers continue to run inflator analysis and testing.

The Takata airbag defect is one of the biggest safety failures in automotive history. At least 28 people have died in the United States and more than 400 have been injured from defective Takata inflators since 2009, prompting the largest auto recall in U.S. history. All of those deaths involved inflators without a drying agent, and at least 20 of them were in Honda vehicles. Over the past decade, two dozen major carmakers have recalled more than 100 million vehicles fitted with Takata inflators worldwide, including about 67 million in the United States.

The inflators can explode on deployment, sending metal fragments into the cabin and killing or injuring drivers or passengers. The new recalls are a reminder that the problem is not fully closed: even inflators fitted with a moisture-absorbing material, long thought to be the fix, are now showing signs of degradation in hot, humid climates.

Sources

  • Newser
  • The Japan Times
  • Nikkei Asia

link.title: Honda and Toyota recall 1.6 million vehicles as Takata airbag risk resurfaces

entry.title: ICE officers arrest two passengers boarding Alaska flight in Seattle
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Masked immigration officers detained two passengers on a jet bridge at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning as they boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles, delaying the departure and prompting sharp criticism from the airline, the airport operator and Washington's governor.

The confrontation unfolded during boarding for Alaska Airlines Flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m. Video showed officers dragging away at least one person as a woman screamed that her daughter was being taken and that she has a work permit; officers were also seen struggling with a person on the ground.

The Department of Homeland Security said officers carried out a targeted enforcement operation against Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who, it said, had overstayed his visa. A second passenger, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was also arrested after, according to the department, she threw hot coffee at officers during the confrontation. The department said she had also overstayed her visa and will face federal charges of assaulting a federal officer. No criminal charge was mentioned for Mendoza. A department source told CBS News the two are father and daughter.

Alaska Airlines said immigration officers gave it no advance notice of the enforcement action, which took place during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. "We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said, adding that it recognised how distressing the incident had been for affected employees and guests. The airline said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see whether protocols were followed, and that it had raised concerns directly with the appropriate authorities.

The Port of Seattle said the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred.

Washington Governor Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, called the incident "just the latest example of ICE's deeply un-American tactics" and said the agency was "completely and totally out of control." He said he was outraged by masked agents who do not identify themselves dragging people off jetways as they board a flight.

Democratic Representative Adam Smith said masked agents detained at least one passenger and forcibly dragged the individual off the jet bridge. Representative Pramila Jayapal said she was disturbed by the reports and that her office was gathering more information.

The arrests come as immigration officers have stepped up enforcement at airports since the summer, focusing on visa overstays amid closer collaboration between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration — putting boarding gates and jet bridges at the centre of a growing political fight over where enforcement should happen.

It remains unclear how the two passengers were identified during boarding, or whether any airport protocols were breached. The episode is likely to add to scrutiny of the agency's tactics as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and investigate them.

Sources

  • CBS News
  • The Straits Times
  • South China Morning Post

link.title: ICE officers arrest two passengers boarding Alaska flight in Seattle

entry.title: SpaceX Dragon splashes down off Los Angeles with a hold full of science
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

An unpiloted SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles at 2:03 p.m. PST on Saturday, closing NASA's 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station and delivering more than 6,300 pounds of science back to Earth.

Dragon undocked from the station's Harmony module at 11:05 a.m. CST on Friday, after more than five weeks docked to the orbiting laboratory. The capsule had arrived at the station on October 15, two days after launching aboard a Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Its departure had been pushed back from Wednesday by unfavourable weather at the splashdown zone off the California coast.

Most of what came home is research. The returning cargo includes a blood vessel construct made with a 3D bioprinter, which scientists will use to study how blood vessels age and how cardiovascular disease develops, in space and on Earth. Frozen tumour organoids — small lab-grown clusters of cells that mimic a tumour — were treated aboard the station and frozen for the trip home, in work researchers hope will point to better cancer treatments and more personalised medicine. Scientists will also analyse frozen microbial samples to learn how bacteria that resist antibiotics survive, adapt and evolve during spaceflight.

A lighting system that spent more than three years aboard the station also returned, after researchers tested its potential to support astronauts' sleep and wellbeing on long-duration missions. The crew packed a wrist joint from the station's Canadarm2 robotic arm that failed in May, so engineers can examine it on the ground.

SpaceX said the capsule would announce its arrival with a brief sonic boom as it tore through the atmosphere faster than the speed of sound, before parachutes lowered it into the Pacific. NASA did not stream the splashdown, instead posting updates on its space station blog.

Dragon is one of the few vehicles that can bring experiments back intact, rather than leaving scientists to rely only on readings transmitted from orbit. The samples now head to laboratories on the ground, while the station's crew continues the research programme the resupply flights keep stocked.

Sources

  • NASA
  • NASA

link.title: SpaceX Dragon splashes down off Los Angeles with a hold full of science

entry.title: Trump signs law ending the penny after more than two centuries in circulation
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

President Donald Trump signed the Common Cents Act into law on Friday, formally ending production of the penny for general circulation and closing a chapter of American coinage that began in the 1790s.

Trump signed the bill in the Oval Office alongside Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, the measure's lead Senate sponsor. The legislation, H.R. 10167, passed both chambers of Congress without opposition — by voice vote in the House on September 14 and by unanimous consent in the Senate on September 28. Its sponsors spanned both parties: Lummis introduced it in the Senate with Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, James Lankford of Oklahoma and Ron Wyden of Oregon, while Representatives Lisa McClain of Michigan and Robert Garcia of California carried the companion bill in the House.

The law permanently ends production of the one-cent coin for everyday use. The U.S. Mint may still strike pennies for collectors, and the law authorises a new, lower-cost version of the nickel. It also requires the Treasury Department to give Congress 60 days' advance notice before discontinuing any other circulating coin.

The penny's end has been coming for some time. Trump directed the Treasury Department to stop minting the coin in February 2025, and the Mint struck its final circulating penny on November 12, 2025, at a ceremonial final strike at its Philadelphia facility. Friday's signing makes that halt permanent in law.

The driving reason is cost. It now takes nearly four cents to make a one-cent coin — the unit cost rose from 1.42 cents to 3.69 cents — and the Mint projects the change will save taxpayers $56 million a year. The fight to end the coin goes back nearly a decade, to the late Senator Mike Enzi's COINS Act, which first proposed suspending penny production.

What changes at the till is rounding. When a cash payment cannot be made with exact change, businesses may now round the total to the nearest five cents under a single national rule: totals ending in 1, 2, 6 or 7 cents round down, and those ending in 3, 4, 8 or 9 cents round up. Card, check and other electronic payments stay exact to the cent.

Existing pennies remain legal tender, and the roughly 114 billion already in circulation will keep changing hands for years — the Federal Reserve will keep recirculating them for as long as possible. The uniform rule matters most to businesses that still handle large amounts of cash: grocers, convenience stores and restaurants, which have been improvising rounding practices since production stopped. Nearly one in four purchases in restaurants are still made in cash, according to the National Restaurant Association.

The penny was first authorised by the Coinage Act of 1792 and first minted in 1793. The final strike last November closed a 232-year chapter. It will take many more years for the coin to cycle out of everyday use — but no new pennies will enter circulation to replace it.

Sources

  • U.S. Senate
  • ABA Banking Journal

link.title: Trump signs law ending the penny after more than two centuries in circulation

entry.title: COP31 climate talks stretch into a second day of overtime as fossil fuels stall a deal
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

United Nations climate talks in Antalya have stretched into a second day of overtime, with a standoff over fossil fuels threatening to derail any final deal at the COP31 summit in Türkiye.

The two-week summit was due to end on Friday. Instead, negotiators spent Saturday night in hasty meetings, bracing for another long stretch on Sunday as the presidency tried to bridge the conference's defining divide: whether the final agreement will mention coal, oil and gas at all.

Late on Saturday, COP31 President Murat Kurum told a plenary session that a third and final text would be put to delegates. "We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon," he said. Delegations had until 03:00 GMT on Sunday to raise objections, with a session at 06:00 GMT to begin approving the deal.

The dispute began with the draft agreement. An opening draft from Australia, which is leading the talks, called on Monday for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version released on Thursday removed every mention of them, after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected. The omission drew protests inside the venue and threats from several countries to walk away.

More than 130 countries want phase-out language restored. France and Panama led a late pushback on Friday; Panama's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said it was "not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it." The European Union warned the draft "risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit."

Other issues remain unresolved, including industrial carbon capture and storage, whether a push to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35 percent by 2035 should rely on renewables alone, and how much money richer countries will provide to help poorer ones adapt. An earlier draft dropped a $120 billion target for adaptation finance.

Pressure from outside the negotiating rooms has been blunt. On Saturday, 100 civil society groups wrote to the co-hosts warning they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs" the United Nations has ever held, with only hours left "to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations."

The stakes are plain. The United Nations said before the talks that the world would likely blow past the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial temperatures, and October 2026 was 1.8 degrees warmer than the mid-1800s. For the first time, the final agreement — the Antalya Accords — could acknowledge the 1.5-degree goal has been missed.

Expectations were already low amid an oil price shock and tensions over the war in Iran. If negotiators cannot agree, the summit could end with no deal at all and have to be suspended — leaving the question of fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, unanswered for another year.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Channel NewsAsia

link.title: COP31 climate talks stretch into a second day of overtime as fossil fuels stall a deal

entry.title: China's AI shares shed $1.7 trillion as the once-hot trade turns into a rout
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Chinese technology stocks have shed a combined $1.7 trillion in market value since the end of June, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, turning one of the year's hottest trades into a rout.

The three main tech-focused indexes have all given up their gains for the year, while major peers in the United States, Taiwan and South Korea remain in positive territory. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Tech Index, home to Alibaba and Tencent, has slumped to a two-year low. The onshore ChiNext Index reached a record high this summer but is now down 31% on the year, and the chip-heavy Star 50 Index has similarly wiped out a record rally.

The selloff is a sharp reversal for a trade that took off after DeepSeek showed Chinese firms could build competitive AI models far more cheaply than US rivals. Breakthroughs from Huawei and Beijing's drive for national tech self-sufficiency drew investors in. Now frothy valuations and a reliance on policy support have left the sector exposed as cracks appear in the global AI boom.

Investors are worried both about a slowdown in AI capital spending and about whether US-China supply-chain business can be sustained, according to Bush Chu, investment director of China equities at Aberdeen Investments, who said the year's wild swings and second-half selloff had left fund managers "pretty speechless".

The latest pressure comes from Washington. Draft rules released by the US earlier this month would effectively block Chinese firms from renting cutting-edge processors from Nvidia and others through overseas data centres, closing a vital backdoor for training next-generation models. Chinese AI is already slipping: none of the current 10 most advanced models in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index are from China, a sharp contrast with four months ago, when Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 rivalled OpenAI and Anthropic.

The chip crunch is reaching company results. Tencent warned in last week's earnings call that the next version of its HY4 model could be delayed, though it said the domestic supply chain should help over time. Alibaba said on Thursday that it expects cloud sales growth to slow to 30% to 45% next year before bouncing back above 50% in 2028. Chinese internet giants also face the same high AI development costs pressuring US hyperscalers, alongside sluggish domestic consumption and persistent price wars.

"The key issues are weak AI monetization, compute bottlenecks, intense competition and margin pressure," said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management.

A KraneShares exchange-traded fund tracking China's Star 50 gauge fell more than 4% in US trading. On November 20, China's four major A-share indexes all moved lower, with the Shanghai Composite down 1.41%, the Shenzhen Component down 1.71%, the ChiNext down 2.15% and the STAR Composite down 2.99%.

What happens next is unclear. It is not yet known whether domestic chipmakers can fill the gap left by US restrictions, whether Beijing will step in with further support, or whether the selloff deepens when markets reopen on Monday.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Bloomberg
  • The Edge Malaysia

link.title: China's AI shares shed $1.7 trillion as the once-hot trade turns into a rout

entry.title: BepiColombo reaches Mercury after an eight-year journey through the inner Solar System
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

After eight years in space, the European-Japanese BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury. The European Space Agency (ESA) announced on 21 November that the spacecraft had been captured by the planet's gravity, making it only the second mission ever to enter orbit around the Solar System's innermost planet, after NASA's MESSENGER, which circled Mercury from 2011 to 2015.

The arrival closes a journey that began with a launch on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou in French Guiana on 20 October 2018. Since then BepiColombo has travelled roughly 9.9 billion kilometres, using nine planetary flybys — one of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury itself — to shed speed. Mercury is a difficult destination: falling towards the Sun, a spacecraft must lose a great deal of energy before the planet's weak gravity can capture it, and the trip takes more energy than reaching the outer Solar System.

The mission nearly missed its window. In April 2024 engineers found that the transfer module's electric thrusters could not deliver full power, and ESA recalculated the route, pushing arrival back by almost a year from its original December 2025 date. The Mercury Transfer Module, which had powered and steered the spacecraft for most of the journey, separated from the two orbiters on 3 September 2026, more than 200 million kilometres from Earth.

For now the two orbiters remain joined together as one stacked spacecraft in an initial elliptical orbit of about 590 by 11,640 kilometres. They are due to separate on 9–10 December, when the mission becomes the first ever to fly two spacecraft around Mercury at the same time. ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) will gradually descend to a close polar orbit between 400 and 1,500 kilometres above the surface by March 2027, mapping the planet and studying its composition and interior. JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, known as Mio, will trace wider ellipses between 500 and 11,000 kilometres, sampling the magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind.

The long cruise was not wasted. En route, mission scientists tested the onboard instruments, pointing the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS) — the first X-ray imaging device sent on an interplanetary mission — at the Crab Nebula, the remnant of a supernova seen from Earth in 1054.

Mercury has long been the Solar System's oddity: a small, scorched world that nonetheless holds water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters and generates a magnetic field despite its size. MESSENGER showed its surface hides unexpected geological activity. With two orbiters working together, scientists hope to separate Mercury's own magnetic field from the short-lived fluctuations caused by solar wind and flares — a distinction a single spacecraft could not make cleanly — and to learn how a planet so close to its star formed. That matters beyond Mercury: most exoplanets found so far orbit very close to their suns.

Full science operations begin in April 2027, after months of manoeuvres to settle both orbiters into their working paths.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Nature
  • ESA

link.title: BepiColombo reaches Mercury after an eight-year journey through the inner Solar System

entry.title: Russian cargo ship burns in the Baltic after drone strike as Finland warns the war is spilling over
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A Russian cargo ship was still burning in the Baltic Sea on Sunday, a day after drones struck it in the Gulf of Finland, in an attack Finland says was probably carried out by Ukraine — and which Helsinki warns shows the war reaching into its own neighbourhood.

The Sparta II, a 121-metre Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by the shipping company Oboronlogistika, left St Petersburg on Friday bound for Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave on the Baltic coast. On Saturday morning it was hit by two drones in international waters west of Gogland island, about three nautical miles from Russia's maritime border, according to Russian officials and Finland's Defence Forces. The ship caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters, where it now sits at anchor.

Finland's coast guard said the fire burned through the night as several vessels sprayed the ship with water cannons, trying to douse the flames and cool the containers stacked on its deck. All 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. No casualties have been reported. Helsinki has imposed temporary aviation and maritime restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland to protect civilians and give its forces room to act if drones need to be intercepted.

"The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said on X. "Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor." Finland's military said it was likely Ukraine was behind the attack, though it was not clear why the vessel had been targeted. Kyiv has not commented.

The ship's background is part of the story. The Sparta II is subject to US sanctions imposed in 2022, and to Ukrainian sanctions imposed earlier this year. Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, and the vessel has been suspected of carrying weapons from Syria to Russia. Finnish border guard commander Ilja Iljin said there was no confirmed information about what cargo was on board, but that military materiel could not be ruled out.

The Baltic has become a flashpoint in the war. Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia's north-western Leningrad region this year, some straying into the airspace of nearby Baltic states. Finland and Sweden joined NATO in 2023 and 2024 in response to Russia's full-scale invasion. Estonia's navy commander said on Sunday that the risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland could not be ruled out, and hours after the strike a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace — an incident Helsinki said may be linked to the rescue operation.

Finland is leading the rescue operation, and its border guard says the plan is to enable the damaged vessel to be towed into Russia's area of responsibility. No environmental damage has been detected, and officials say there is no danger to maritime traffic or people.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Russian cargo ship burns in the Baltic after drone strike as Finland warns the war is spilling over

entry.title: South Korea's education minister resigns over AI-cheating chaos at college entrance exam
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

South Korea's education minister resigned on Sunday after last-minute rule changes meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the country's college entrance exam left students and teachers in confusion.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered to step down, saying he took responsibility for the disruption. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation about an hour later, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said.

"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi said in a statement released by the ministry. "Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation."

The exam at the centre of the row is the College Scholastic Ability Test, known in Korea as the Suneung. Held on Thursday, the annual nine-hour test is widely seen as a defining moment, with university admission heavily shaping career prospects.

The crisis began four days before the exam, when the top scorer on the national certified tax accountant exam admitted to cheating with a miniature camera, a smartphone and generative AI. The ministry had initially focused on smart glasses, then rushed out new rules in the final days before the test.

Two days before the exam, the government announced 8,400 extra staff, including about 1,800 to detect smart devices. The day before, the rules changed again: test-takers could bring only pencils into exam rooms, and marking pens, correction tape and erasers were banned. Students were also required to cover the buttons on their clothing with stickers, to block miniature cameras. During the exam, the authorities sent three emergency disaster alerts to mobile phones nationwide to help identify test-takers who had failed to hand in their phones.

The education ministry said on Friday that 111 suspected cheating cases involving electronic devices were detected during the exam. Its examination misconduct committee is reviewing the cases and will decide on penalties before scores are released on 11 December.

Choi also drew criticism for remarks he made in parliament ahead of the test. Asked by a lawmaker whether he was 100 percent confident that AI-assisted cheating could be detected, the 72-year-old replied: "I don't think I could, because of my age."

President Lee wrote on social media shortly after the resignation that concerns over AI-assisted cheating were spreading beyond the CSAT to essay-based admission exams and school tests, and that "the fairness of exams is a principle that can never be compromised." He said he would order a comprehensive inspection of exam management, and a review of marking question papers so their source can be traced if leaked.

The government and the ruling party have suggested extending the ban for AI-assisted cheating to 10 years, potentially applying it retroactively to this year's exam. Separately, a man who earned a perfect score on this year's law school entrance exam was found dead on Thursday after facing cheating allegations.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Yonhap News Agency
  • Channel News Asia

link.title: South Korea's education minister resigns over AI-cheating chaos at college entrance exam

entry.title: Waymo files two safety recalls days after California bars its robotaxis from freeways
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Waymo has filed two safety recalls covering its self-driving system, days after California regulators ordered its robotaxis off the state's freeways.

The Alphabet-owned company said on Friday that it had filed the recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration on Thursday. Both are software recalls for its automated driving system, aimed at improving how its cars handle closed freeway lanes and intersections where police or emergency workers direct traffic by hand.

The first recall covers situations in which a Waymo car may drive into a closed freeway lane and keep going. Waymo said no crashes or injuries had been reported in connection with those events, and that it was still developing the fix.

The second covers how the cars respond to manual traffic control at intersections. It follows a collision in which a Waymo car initially followed an officer's directions, but the officer was then temporarily hidden from the car's view. Waymo said the software update for that issue was finished on 6 November.

The recalls come a little over a week after the California Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo's driverless cars from all state freeways, for both testing and passenger service, effective 11 November. The regulator said the cars posed an "imminent hazard to public safety" after three of them entered an active construction closure near Burlingame, and a separate incident involving California Highway Patrol vehicles in San Francisco. Waymo said its cars continue to operate normally on surface streets, and it has paused freeway rides in every market where it offered them.

Waymo described the recalls as voluntary and said they do not require any vehicles to be taken off the road. A company spokesperson said Waymo holds its technology to high safety standards and acts proactively to improve it.

The recalls add to a difficult stretch for the company. Last week, NHTSA opened a separate recall query after reports that Waymo cars had passed stopped school buses, a probe covering nearly 3,000 vehicles. NHTSA and the National Transportation Safety Board are also investigating after a Waymo vehicle struck a child in January near an elementary school in Santa Monica.

What remains unclear is how many vehicles the two new recalls cover — no figure was given — and when the closed-lane fix will be ready or freeway rides will return. The California ban stays in place until Waymo shows its corrective actions work.

Illustration — not a photograph.

entry.title: Microsoft says a months-old bug and its own safeguards caused the global Outlook outage
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Microsoft has released its final report on last week's global Microsoft 365 outage, blaming a software bug that had sat dormant since July, testing that failed to catch it, and safety systems that spread the failure around the world.

The bug came from a Windows update Microsoft began rolling out in July to its network gateway, the servers in front of Outlook and Microsoft 365. It changed how those servers handle incoming connections: under heavy load, the connection process bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of memory and stopped responding.

The flaw hit hardest on the company's newer, more powerful servers, and for more than three months it caused no problems at all. One reason it went unnoticed is that Microsoft's testing did not match the real world: its labs mostly used older servers running a different mix of traffic. "Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident," the company acknowledged in the report, released Friday, a week after the outage was resolved.

The report lays out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Nearly 14% of the gateway's server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. About 15 hours earlier, a routing glitch on Teams' own gateway moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the email servers. Then the US workday began, with failures starting around 8 a.m. Pacific. Without the bug, the report says, all three together would have been routine.

What turned a local failure global was Microsoft's own protection. As servers stopped responding, its systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway's servers in North America were unresponsive, and within about two hours servers in every region were affected. Getting the service back was its own problem: as servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a "thundering herd."

The report also settles two questions that hung over the outage: it was not hackers, and it was not AI. "This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity," it says. "This change was not caused by AI tooling." Its first customer notice went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and no business email was lost.

The report lists 13 next steps, including production-like testing, due by the end of March; changing how traffic shifts between regions so a problem in one part of the world stays there; and splitting up the servers that handle email so a surge elsewhere cannot take email down. Some fixes are due by the end of the year or March; several have no date yet. Chief executive Satya Nadella told the Ignite conference this week that Microsoft has work to do on resilience.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • GeekWire
  • Chosun Biz

link.title: Microsoft says a months-old bug and its own safeguards caused the global Outlook outage

entry.title: As winter closes in, Kyiv's broken windows leave homes open to the cold
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

For weeks after a missile exploded in front of her apartment block, Oleksandra Horban kept finding pieces of glass in her small flat in Kyiv. She threw out her two-year-old son's soft toys, which were covered in shards. Outside her ground-floor home, mangled window frames were piled onto a mound of rubble, with glass mixed into the fallen leaves on the muddy ground.

"Even now we still find glass," she said.

As winter sets in, Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of replacement windows, with Russian missile and drone strikes continuing to damage buildings and leave residents exposed to the cold. Temperatures in Kyiv fell to minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 Fahrenheit) last winter. Government help can take months to arrive, skilled installers are in short supply, and replacement costs have soared — hitting low-income districts near industrial zones hardest.

Horban lives in a Soviet-era "groundscraper", an enormous horizontal apartment block in the Ukrainian capital. A missile blast in October damaged a vertical section of the building and shattered hundreds of facade windows. Most broken windows have since been covered over with fibreboard or tarps. Some boards have small openings fitted with Plexiglas, to let a little daylight into the flats behind them.

Replacing the windows in Horban's flat would cost about $1,700 — more than three times the country's average salary. Government compensation can take three to four months. Many residents cannot afford to wait: without proper windows, flats are left open to cold, damp and mould, above all during power cuts.

Housing damage is among the largest costs of the war. An estimated 3 million housing units were destroyed or badly damaged by the end of last year, adding $90 billion to Ukraine's reconstruction needs, according to the World Bank.

Ukraine's window manufacturers can keep up with demand. The bottleneck is the people to fit them. Factories can produce a window in about 10 working days, but installation can be delayed far longer while customers wait for a crew to become available. Mykhailo Orlenko, executive director of the Association of Ukrainian Manufacturers of Transparent Structures, said businesses had been unable to exempt their employees from military service, including many installers. "The market lost a large number of these specialists," he said.

The industry is now investing in training a new generation. A vocational college in Kyiv opened a European Union-funded facility in March, where 26 tenth-graders have started a three-year programme to become window, door and facade installers. The programme was set up after industry associations lobbied the government to formally recognise window installation as a profession, allowing the industry to access grants and run structured training courses.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • AsiaOne

link.title: As winter closes in, Kyiv's broken windows leave homes open to the cold

entry.title: Russian cargo ship burns through the night in the Gulf of Finland after drone strike
entry.content:
A fire aboard a Russian cargo ship struck by drones in the Baltic Sea burned through the night, Finland's coast guard said on Sunday, as firefighting vessels worked to douse the flames and cool the containers stacked on its deck.

The vessel, the Sparta II, was hit on Saturday morning in international waters west of Gogland island in the Gulf of Finland. It later drifted into Finnish waters, where it remains at anchor. All 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.

Finland's military said the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine, though it did not say why the vessel had been targeted. Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia's north-western Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries — raising fears that the war is spilling onto NATO territory.

The Sparta II is a 121-metre Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Oboronlogistika, a shipping company that provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company's website. The vessel is subject to US sanctions. It left St Petersburg on Friday, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.

What the ship was carrying remains unknown. The commander of the Finnish Border Guard, Ilja Iljin, said it could not be ruled out that military materiel was on board. The vessel had been damaged in its bridge and cargo area, and at least two drones struck it, according to Finnish officials. The governor of Russia's Leningrad region said the attack took place about three nautical miles from Russia's border.

Hours after the strike, Finland's defence minister said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace — an incident he suggested may have been linked to the rescue or monitoring of the damaged ship.

Finland's prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said the episode showed the war in Ukraine was spilling over. The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, cannot be ruled out, Estonia's navy commander told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.

Finland's military said last week it had also detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. Finnish authorities are leading the rescue operation while the ship sits in their waters, although Russian vessels may eventually tow it home. Officials said the incident posed no known danger to surrounding shipping, and no oil had been reported entering the sea.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Russian cargo ship burns through the night in the Gulf of Finland after drone strike

entry.title: Four supermoons in a row begin with November's Beaver Moon
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

November's full moon will rise on Tuesday, November 24, opening a run of four supermoons in a row that stretches into February 2027.

The full Beaver Moon reaches its fullest point at 9:53 a.m. EST on November 24, and it will look full on the nights of November 23 and 24. It is the first supermoon since January, and the second of 2026. Look for it climbing in the east around sunset, glowing near the Pleiades star cluster and the bright orange star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus.

A supermoon happens when a full moon lines up with perigee, the point in the moon's orbit where it comes closest to Earth. November's perigee falls about 30 hours after the full moon, on November 25, close enough for the moon to appear up to about 14 percent wider and 30 percent brighter than an average full moon. The difference in size is hard to spot with the naked eye, but the extra brightness is easier to notice, especially as the moon rises near the horizon.

The streak continues with the Cold Moon in December, which will be the closest full moon of 2026 at roughly 221,700 miles from Earth. It reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on December 23. The Wolf Moon follows on January 22, 2027, reaching its full phase at 7:17 a.m. EST, and the Snow Moon completes the run on February 20, 2027, at 6:23 p.m. EST.

Three or four supermoons occur most years, and they always arrive in consecutive months, because the full moon drifts gradually closer to perigee and then away again over several lunar cycles.

November's full moon is traditionally called the Beaver Moon, a name tied to the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and trappers once set their traps before the waters froze. No telescope or special equipment is needed to watch it — a clear sky and a view toward the eastern horizon at sunset are enough, and the moon stays visible all night.

Sources

  • USA Today
  • EarthSky

link.title: Four supermoons in a row begin with November's Beaver Moon

entry.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as countries fail to agree on fossil fuels
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The COP31 climate summit collapsed on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, after more than two weeks of negotiations ended without an overarching agreement — the first time United Nations climate talks have broken down without a deal since Copenhagen in 2009.

At the closing plenary, COP31 president Murat Kurum conceded that the draft "Antalya Pact" could not be adopted. "It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document," he told delegates. The summit had already run a record 44 hours past its scheduled Friday close, making it the longest climate conference ever held.

Fossil fuels were the breaking point. The first draft of the agreement, published on Monday, had called for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems." But every reference to coal, oil and gas was stripped from later versions after objections from Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers, despite a push by more than 100 countries to keep the language in.

The European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that refused to endorse the weakened text. Ireland's climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, said the bloc "will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya Pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change." "We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel," he added.

The draft also backed a major expansion of carbon capture technology, with a goal of capturing and storing one billion metric tons of carbon, and dropped a $120 billion target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change. The United States was not part of the talks, after the Trump administration pulled out of international climate action.

The failure stands in sharp contrast to COP28 in Dubai in 2023, when countries agreed for the first time to "transition away from fossil fuels." Delegates in Antalya did make progress on smaller technical matters, but without a cover decision the summit leaves the central question — how fast the world moves away from the fuels driving warming — unanswered, with the 1.5C target under the Paris agreement looming ever closer.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Arab News

link.title: COP31 climate talks collapse as countries fail to agree on fossil fuels

entry.title: Relativity rewrites a textbook rule of chemistry in heavy-element bonds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A rule of chemistry taught in classrooms for generations does not hold up when atoms get heavy enough, according to new research from Brown University. Chemists there have found direct experimental evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity can reshape the structure of a triple chemical bond — blurring a distinction textbooks treat as fixed.

The study, published in the journal Science, looked at molecules containing carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element. Using a technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the researchers measured the energy needed to knock electrons out of the molecules with laser light, revealing the underlying structure of their bonds.

In the standard textbook picture, a triple bond is made of three separate connections: one sigma bond, formed by electrons overlapping head-on along the axis between two atoms, and two pi bonds, formed by electron density extending to either side of that axis. That model works well for lighter elements. But in the carbon–bismuth molecules, the team found something different: instead of one sigma and two pi bonds, the bond showed one pi bond and two hybrid bonds that mix sigma and pi character.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore."

Why relativity enters the picture

Heavy elements have nuclei packed with protons, and their strong electrical pull can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At those speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity start to matter. One of the most important is spin-orbit coupling, in which an electron's spin — the quantum property that gives it a magnetic character — becomes tightly linked to its orbital motion. That linkage changes how electrons take part in bonding, and in heavy atoms it can wash out the clean split between sigma and pi bonds.

The idea that relativity matters in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s, Wang said, but the new work provides direct spectroscopic evidence for it in a triple bond. Doctoral students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, working with Wang and colleagues, produced the carbon–bismuth molecules and examined them at temperatures near absolute zero.

The finding could change how chemists describe bonds involving heavy elements, and it may matter beyond the textbook. Bismuth is being studied as a non-toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells, and the research could also help scientists working on quantum computing and quantum materials, where controlling electron behaviour is essential. The work was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation and the U.S. Department of Energy.

What the study does not do is overturn chemistry as a whole. The familiar sigma-and-pi picture still describes the bonds of lighter elements accurately. The result redraws the boundary instead: for the heaviest atoms, relativity is not a footnote to bonding — it is part of the bond itself.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceDaily
  • SciTechDaily

link.title: Relativity rewrites a textbook rule of chemistry in heavy-element bonds

entry.title: BepiColombo arrives at Mercury after eight years in space
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

After eight years crossing the inner Solar System, the European-Japanese BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury. The European Space Agency confirmed on Saturday 21 November that the spacecraft had been captured by the planet's gravity, making it only the second mission ever to enter orbit around the Sun's closest planet.

BepiColombo is a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). It carries two orbiters travelling together as one stacked spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, known as Mio. The only previous mission to orbit Mercury was NASA's MESSENGER, which circled the planet from 2011 to 2015.

The spacecraft was launched on 20 October 2018 aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana. Its route to Mercury was deliberately indirect, using nine planetary flybys to shed speed before the final approach. An electric-propulsion problem in 2024 pushed the planned arrival back by a year, and the mission shed its transfer module in September to begin the final leg.

For the orbit insertion itself, four of the MPO's thrusters fired to slow the spacecraft as it approached Mercury's south pole, easing it into an initial elliptical orbit of 590 by 11,640 kilometres. Flight controllers in Germany then waited through several anxious hours while data travelled the roughly 152 million kilometres back to Earth before they could confirm the capture had worked.

Two orbiters, one planet

The arrival is only the first step of a longer sequence. MPO and Mio are due to separate from each other on 9–10 December, after which BepiColombo will become the first mission to fly two spacecraft around Mercury at the same time. MPO will then fire its thrusters repeatedly over the coming months to descend to its final science orbit by March 2027. Science operations for both orbiters are set to begin in April 2027.

The pair will study Mercury from different vantage points. MPO will fly close to the surface, mapping craters, volcanic plains and mountain ridges, while Mio swings far out to sample the planet's magnetic field and how it interacts with the solar wind. Together they should help explain why Mercury, a planet barely bigger than the Moon, still has a magnetic field at all — and what its strange, dense interior reveals about how planets form close to their stars.

The mission is named after Giuseppe Colombo, the Italian mathematician who worked out how to use gravity assists to reach Mercury. It is the third spacecraft ever to visit the planet, and the first in more than a decade. For a world long dismissed as a dead rock, Mercury is about to get its closest look yet.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ESA — "BepiColombo entering orbit around Mercury"

entry.title: Sugar-based hydrogel gets stronger the more it bends
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Most materials wear out with use: bend a paper clip back and forth and it snaps. A team at Washington University in St. Louis has now built a material that breaks that rule: a sugar-based gel that gets stronger the more it is bent, and stronger in exactly the places that take the strain.

The work comes from the lab of Chenfeng Ke, a professor of chemistry, and is described in a study published in Nature Materials. The material is a hydrogel — a soft, water-absorbing solid — made from a biodegradable blend of sugar crystals and polyethylene glycol, a compound widely used in laxatives and other health products. It is patented and compatible with 3D printing.

Its secret is a sugar compound called cyclodextrin, which forms tiny ring-shaped structures. When the gel is stretched or bent, large clusters of these rings break apart, slide along the polymer chains, and reorganize into smaller crystalline structures as the material relaxes. The moving rings reinforce the zone under stress while the rest of the gel stays soft and pliable.

"We bent it 10,000 times, and the material performed just as we predicted," Ke said. "The polymers in the hydrogel become more uniform and organized, making it stronger in exactly the places where the strain is happening."

A lesson borrowed from the body

The design takes its cue from biology. Collagen, the protein that gives skin its strength and elasticity, also adapts to the forces placed on it, and the new gel works on a similar principle: reinforcement arrives only where it is needed. "Some of the most impressive smart materials are found in biology," Ke said. "We used nature for inspiration."

To test the idea, the team mounted the gel on a flexible, knee-like joint and bent it repeatedly. Instead of fatiguing, the material held up and reorganized itself, with its internal network growing more ordered at the points of greatest strain.

Ke sees medical uses first. Because the gel is made of sugar and polyethylene glycol, it is fully compatible with biological tissue, which makes it a candidate for supporting artificial joints or repairing damaged tissue. In either setting, the parts of an implant that never bear load would stay soft, while the stressed regions would firm up on their own.

Ke is a chemist, not an orthopedist, and he is quick to note that surgeons and medical-device specialists may see applications he has not yet imagined. His team is now looking to work with experts at WashU Medicine and elsewhere to explore the possibilities.

For now the material exists only in small batches, tens of grams at a time. But with the concept demonstrated, the researchers believe production could scale. "We've shown it's possible to produce smart materials with a 3D printer and the right chemistry," Ke said. "We see a lot of possibilities."

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • Washington University in St. Louis

entry.title: Explosion on Russian warship at Benghazi port blamed on suspected drone attack
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

An explosion and fire aboard a Russian warship docked at the port of Benghazi was likely caused by a drone attack, Libya's eastern-based government said on Sunday, in the latest incident to drag the war in Ukraine into the Mediterranean.

The government said a preliminary investigation indicated the blast happened aboard a Russian ship at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, and that a drone attack was suspected. The vessel had stopped at the port to refuel and resupply on its way back to Russia, under maritime cooperation agreements between the two countries.

Two Libyan military officials told the Associated Press that the damaged vessel was the Russian Navy corvette Merkury. They said several Ukrainian sea drones had been launched at the ship from a base in western Libya, and that at least four were intercepted before two struck the warship, severely damaging it and starting a fire. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity, and the account has not been independently verified.

Naval News, a specialist defence outlet, reported that the vessel was almost certainly destroyed by the blast and fire, though it was not clear whether it had sunk at its berth or burned out above the waterline. The ship had been at the port for several days while escorting a convoy, the outlet said.

Two medical sources told Reuters that no deaths had been reported, but that there were injuries. The number of people hurt and their nationalities were not immediately known. There was no immediate reaction from the Russian authorities, and no one had claimed responsibility for the suspected attack.

The eastern-based government said port and naval base facilities, including warehouses, were safe, and that normal operations would resume once the fire was brought under control and the site secured. It condemned the suspected attack as a violation of Libya's sovereignty and a threat to maritime safety, and said it would take legal and diplomatic measures against anyone found responsible.

"The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts," it said in a statement.

Not every account of the blast agrees. Services in Benghazi under the Libyan National Army, which controls the east of the country, attributed the explosion to a detonation at an ammunition depot inside the naval base rather than a direct strike on the ship. The exact cause remains unconfirmed.

The incident came a day after the Russian-flagged cargo ship Sparta II was hit by two drones in the Gulf of Finland on 21 November, in a separate attack that also remains unattributed. Together, the two strikes point to a widening campaign against Russian shipping far beyond the Black Sea, where Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Moscow's fleet.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

entry.title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeats longtime GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina recount
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Democrat Chuck Hubbard will unseat longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th Congressional District, after Foxx conceded the race on Sunday following a machine recount that left Hubbard ahead by about 330 votes out of nearly 287,000 cast.

Foxx, 83, chairs the House Rules Committee, one of the most powerful posts in the chamber, deciding which bills reach the floor and how they can be amended. She has represented the district since 2005 and is the longest-serving member of North Carolina's congressional delegation. Hubbard, 64, a former journalist, will be the first Democrat to hold the seat since 1995.

Foxx requested the recount after the initial count showed her trailing by 331 votes. The recount, which wrapped up on Saturday, barely moved the numbers: Hubbard finished with 139,769 votes to Foxx's 139,439, according to the Associated Press results, a margin of roughly one tenth of one percent. Foxx called Hubbard on Sunday to congratulate him.

"After a hard-fought and thorough election process, the voters of the Fifth Congressional District exercised their Constitutional rights and made their voices heard," Foxx said in a statement. "While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina."

The result was the last House race of the midterm elections to be decided, and it caps a sweeping Democratic performance in North Carolina and nationally. Democrats will control at least 259 House seats when the next Congress convenes in January, their largest majority since the early 1990s, according to CNN. One race remains uncalled, in Minnesota, where a recount is scheduled to begin on November 30, and runoff elections in Louisiana on December 12 will settle the final two seats.

Hubbard's win is a sharp reversal from two years ago, when he lost to Foxx by about nine points in the same district. He ran again this cycle in a year that saw Democrats flip seats in deeply Republican territory, and the contest tightened steadily after election night: Hubbard led by 99 votes in the unofficial returns, stretched the lead as provisional and cured ballots were tallied, and held on through the county canvasses and the recount.

The outcome still awaits formal certification by the North Carolina State Board of Elections, which is due to meet on Tuesday. But with Foxx's concession, the last outstanding question of the 2026 House map is effectively settled, and attention now turns to how the new Democratic majority will use its numbers in the 120th Congress.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN — "Republican chair of the House Rules Committee loses reelection in Democrats' largest majority this century"
  • Associated Press — "Chuck Hubbard defeats Rep. Virginia Foxx after a recount in their North Carolina House race"

link.title: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeats longtime GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina recount

entry.title: Delta outage delays more than 1,300 flights days before Thanksgiving
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

More than 1,300 Delta Air Lines flights were delayed across the United States on Sunday after the airline's automated system for calculating aircraft weight and balance failed, snarling travel at its Atlanta hub just days before the Thanksgiving holiday rush.

The system, known as ALIS, went down on Sunday morning. It performs the load calculations crews must complete before every departure, working out how passengers and cargo are distributed so an aircraft stays within safe limits and keeps a stable centre of gravity. Without it, Delta staff fell back on manual calculations, and departures slowed to the pace of work done by hand.

By early afternoon, more than 1,300 of Delta's mainline flights had been delayed, at least 40 percent of the airline's planned operation for the day, according to figures from the tracking service FlightAware. The heaviest disruption was at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the carrier's home base and the world's busiest airport, where FlightAware counted 1,044 delayed flights by the afternoon. Around 45 percent of Delta flights out of Atlanta were running late as of 1:30 p.m. ET.

The Federal Aviation Administration briefly halted Delta departures bound for Atlanta on Sunday morning before easing the restriction to a ground delay programme. The agency said the problem was confined to Delta's own technology and was not connected to federal air traffic systems.

"Delta teams are using manual workarounds this morning to safely get flights departed while work continues to restore automation," the airline said in a statement. Delta later reported that its automated systems were working again at about 3:30 p.m. ET, and apologised to customers for the delays.

Not all of the disruption at Atlanta came from the outage. Delta said about 70 percent of the airport's delays were caused by the system failure, with the rest linked to bad weather and air traffic adjustments in New York City and the Northeast.

The timing adds to the pressure on travellers. Thanksgiving week is one of the busiest periods in American aviation, and a day of manual operations leaves aircraft and crews out of position, meaning knock-on delays can linger into Monday even after the system itself is fixed. Delta advised passengers to check their flight status in the airline's app or on its website before heading to the airport.

Sunday's failure is the latest in a run of technology problems to hit American aviation. On November 13, a failure in the FAA's own communication systems grounded flights nationwide for about four hours, and a separate issue affected only United Airlines last Monday. The FAA stressed that Sunday's Delta disruption was unrelated to its systems.

Delta has not said what caused its weight-and-balance system to fail, and it gave no detailed account of the fault while restoration work was under way.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • USA Today — "Glitch delays Delta flights in Atlanta as Thanksgiving travel spikes"
  • The Points Guy — "Delta tech outage, bad weather fuels messy Sunday at airports"

link.title: Delta outage delays more than 1,300 flights days before Thanksgiving

entry.title: Tarik Skubal agrees to record $450 million deal with the New York Mets
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Tarik Skubal has agreed to a nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets, the richest deal ever given to a pitcher, landing the two-time Cy Young Award winner in Queens just days before baseball's offseason is expected to shut down.

The agreement was reached on Sunday, November 22, according to multiple reports, and had not yet been formally announced. The $450 million total shatters the previous record for a pitcher, Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract with the Dodgers, and carries an average annual value of $50 million, second only to Skubal's new teammate Juan Soto among Mets players.

The terms are heavily front-loaded. Skubal will receive a $45 million signing bonus, giving him a large sum up front before a potential work stoppage, and $30 million of the contract is deferred. Reports say the deal contains no opt-out clauses and includes full no-trade protection.

Skubal, who turned 30 on November 20, has been the best pitcher in baseball over the past four seasons. He has a career 3.02 ERA and 1.02 WHIP, and has posted an ERA between 2.39 and 2.80 in each of the last four years, winning the American League Cy Young Award in 2024 and 2025 with the Detroit Tigers. His fastball-changeup combination has produced 10.9 strikeouts per nine innings over that span.

He arrives in New York after a whirlwind four months. Detroit traded him to the Dodgers at the trade deadline, and he helped Los Angeles reach the National League Championship Series before the Brewers swept them out. The Mets will be his third team since July.

The signing continues the Mets' runaway spending under owner Steve Cohen. New York will have four players, Soto, Skubal and infielders Francisco Lindor and Bo Bichette, earning between $32 million and $51 million next season. Yet the spending has not yet bought success: the Mets have missed the playoffs in both seasons since Soto's 15-year, $765 million arrival, finishing last in the National League East at 74-88 this year.

The timing was deliberate. A lockout is expected to shut down all offseason activity on December 2, and Skubal's deal was completed before the freeze. The size of the contract is also certain to feature in the coming labour fight, with owners expected to use the Mets' payroll as evidence in their push for a salary cap.

Skubal now becomes the centrepiece of a rotation the Mets have been trying to build around Soto's bat, and the highest-paid pitcher in the game's history.

entry.title: Bay Area braces for highest king tides in 18 years as flood warnings begin Monday
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The San Francisco Bay Area is bracing for the highest king tides in 18 years, with forecasters warning of major to extreme coastal flooding through Thanksgiving week as unusually high tides combine with a storm and a surge of warm El Nino water.

The National Weather Service has issued a Coastal Flood Warning for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bays from 6 a.m. Monday, November 23, through 4 p.m. Thursday, November 26. A Coastal Flood Advisory covers the Pacific coast through Thursday. The warning means flooding of low-lying roads, trails, parking areas and other shoreline infrastructure is expected, along with coastal erosion.

The tides are driven by a rare alignment: the monthly king tide cycle, the strongest El Nino conditions in years, and warmer ocean water that lifts sea levels through thermal expansion. At the San Francisco tide gauge, high tide is expected to reach about 7.8 feet on Sunday, 8.0 feet on Monday, 8.4 feet on Tuesday, 8.6 feet on Wednesday and 8.2 feet on Thursday. The U.S. Coast Guard said water levels could run 1 to 2 feet above normal high tides, and higher where storm surge adds to the peak.

A second storm arriving Tuesday and Wednesday will make matters worse. Forecasters expect 1 to 2 inches of rain in the North Bay and up to an inch across much of the Bay Area, with runoff draining into bays already at historically high levels. The storm will also bring hazardous beach conditions, with breaking waves of 14 to 18 feet on Tuesday building to 18 to 24 feet on Wednesday, along with sneaker waves and strong rip currents.

Local agencies are already preparing. The Southern Marin Fire Protection District urged residents and businesses to protect property, review emergency plans and prepare for road closures, warning that moderate flooding is expected this weekend before major to extreme flooding develops during Thanksgiving week.

The timing adds pressure to one of the busiest travel periods of the year. The Weather Service said the storm and the flooding could delay travel on roads, railways and flights, and officials have urged residents to reconsider non-essential travel along the coast. The Coast Guard advised mariners and beachgoers to stay clear of the water, warning that king tides can bring dangerous surf and sneaker waves that catch people off guard.

The king tide season is only beginning. The Coast Guard said the highest tides of the season are expected around December 22 to 25, when observed heights could reach 7.8 to 8.2 feet, with another cycle following in late January.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • National Weather Service
  • U.S. Coast Guard
