entry.title: Australian music legend Molly Meldrum dies aged 83
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Ian "Molly" Meldrum, the music journalist and television presenter who shaped Australian popular music for more than half a century, has died aged 83.

Meldrum died peacefully at 5.30am on Monday at Epworth Hospital in Richmond, Melbourne, after a long period of ill health, his family said. A state funeral will be held to honour him, Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said, honouring a wish made by his family.

Born Ian Alexander Meldrum on 29 January 1943 in Orbost, in eastern Victoria, he began writing for the weekly music paper Go-Set in 1966. When the ABC launched Countdown in November 1974, he joined as talent coordinator. Within a year he was in front of the camera, and for almost 13 years, until the show's final episode in July 1987, he was its beating heart.

In the days before streaming and music video channels, Countdown was how Australians discovered new music. The show brought the world's biggest acts into living rooms, from ABBA, David Bowie and Elton John to AC/DC, Kylie Minogue and INXS, and gave homegrown artists their first national exposure.

Meldrum's enthusiasm could make or break a career. His catchphrase, "do yourself a favour", attached to a record or an act he believed in, could move sales and fill venues. He became a household name in his trademark Stetson hat, known for his bumbling charm, his unpredictable interviews and his undisguised love of the music.

That unpredictability produced some of Australian television's most famous moments, including a 1977 interview with the then Prince Charles in which he referred to the Queen as "your mum". He was also a record producer, and a passionate supporter of the St Kilda Football Club, where he helped start the cheer squad, and the Melbourne Storm, where he was the club's number one ticket holder for many years.

His health had been fragile since December 2011, when he was placed in an induced coma after a fall from a ladder while hanging Christmas decorations. In 2014 he was inducted into the ARIA Hall of Fame, together with Countdown, becoming the first non-artist to receive the honour.

Tributes poured in from across Australian music and television. His longtime friend and manager, Mark Klemens, called him a "true icon" who "opened doors for so many and entertained millions of people". Singer Kate Ceberano, who first sang in front of him as a judge at the age of 14, wrote: "He was the fan all artists wish to have." Marcia Hines thanked him for his contribution to the Australian music industry and worldwide.

Meldrum is survived by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, and his adopted son, Morgan Scholes. His family has asked for privacy as they grieve.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Australian Associated Press
  • Mumbrella

link.title: Australian music legend Molly Meldrum dies aged 83

entry.title: A hidden world up to twice Earth's mass may be lurking beyond Neptune
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Astronomers may be closing in on a hidden planet beyond Neptune, according to new research that models the outer Solar System across its entire 4.5-billion-year history.

The proposed world, nicknamed Planet X2, would be about 1.5 to two times the mass of Earth, orbiting at least 200 times farther from the Sun than our planet at its closest approach. Despite decades of mapping the Solar System, such a world could have remained undetected in the dark region beyond Neptune, where sunlight is faint and objects move slowly.

The idea comes from a study led by Patryk Sofia Lykawka, an adjunct associate professor at the University of Southern Queensland based at Kindai University in Japan, with co-authors Pedro Bernardinelli and Jonti Horner, published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. The team ran computer simulations testing how a hidden planet of different masses and orbital paths would shape the distant Solar System over billions of years.

Their preferred model, a planet of about twice Earth's mass on a wide orbit 350 to 500 times Earth's distance from the Sun, reproduced several puzzling patterns among the icy bodies beyond Neptune. It generated the detached population of objects that drift far from Neptune's influence, built up a reservoir of highly tilted orbits, and matched the orbital niches of extreme objects such as Sedna and 2012 VP113, whose stretched, elongated paths have long defied easy explanation.

The simulations also tested an alternative idea, that Mars- to Earth-sized embryos scattered early in the Solar System's history could explain the same patterns. That scenario failed: the embryos were typically flung out of the Solar System within a few tens of millions of years, leaving results much like models with no extra planet at all.

Planet X2 is not the same as the better-known Planet Nine hypothesis, which proposes a much larger and more massive world in the outer Solar System. The new model offers a smaller, closer alternative, and it comes with testable predictions: the researchers say upcoming surveys, including the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time, should be able to confirm or rule out the planet's existence.

Caution is warranted. The planet has not been observed, and the model does not match every known observation. The researchers themselves note a remaining discrepancy in the distribution of orbital sizes, an area for further work. Until a telescope spots it, Planet X2 remains a hypothesis, albeit one that now fits the evidence better than the alternatives tested.

If it exists, its discovery would rewrite the map of our own cosmic neighbourhood, showing that a world larger than Earth hid in plain sight at the edge of the Solar System all along.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • EurekAlert!
  • Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society

link.title: A hidden world up to twice Earth's mass may be lurking beyond Neptune

entry.title: More than 12,000 evacuated from Manchester arena after unknown substance released at concert
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from a concert in Manchester on Sunday night after an unknown substance was released into the crowd, police said.

The incident happened towards the end of a performance by US rapper Don Toliver at the Co-op Live arena, at about 22:00. Greater Manchester Police declared a major incident after reports of concertgoers suffering the effects of the substance, and emergency services moved in to clear the venue.

One person was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment, according to the North West Ambulance Service. More than 50 people were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms, and several were treated at the scene. Decontamination was carried out as a precaution, and the ambulance service deployed several emergency crews, including its Hazardous Area Response Team.

Assistant Chief Constable Steph Parker said the major incident declaration allowed emergency services to coordinate a safe response. Police said their priority was the safety of everyone at the concert, and thanked the crowd for its patience as the arena was emptied.

What exactly was released remains unknown. Police initially believed the substance to be tear gas, but that has not been confirmed, and officers said they would now work to establish what it was and how the incident came about.

The venue said it was working closely with police to identify the cause. In a statement, Co-op Live said the safety and security of visitors remained its priority and that it would share more information once it had an update from police.

Police advised anyone who had left the event and later became unwell to attend their local hospital, and the ambulance service gave the same advice to anyone who noticed side effects after leaving.

Toliver was performing in Manchester as part of his Nitrous tour. The show was stopped as the evacuation got under way, and footage shared on social media showed emergency services converging on the arena as concertgoers streamed out, some of them coughing.

The investigation is continuing, and no further details about the substance or how it was released have been given.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC

link.title: More than 12,000 evacuated from Manchester arena after unknown substance released at concert

entry.title: Rescuers pull seven-year-old alive from collapsed flats in Dymer
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Rescuers in Ukraine have pulled a seven-year-old boy alive from the rubble of a collapsed apartment building in Dymer, about 14 hours after a Russian strike hit the town in the Kyiv region.

The boy was in stable condition and was taken to hospital, Ukrainian authorities said. His rescue was confirmed by President Volodymyr Zelensky and by Ukraine's national police.

The strike hit the five-storey residential building at about 05:00 local time on Sunday, while families were still asleep, according to Ukraine's Minister of Internal Affairs, Ivan Vyhivskyi. The building's apartments collapsed across all five floors, and emergency crews have been searching the wreckage for survivors ever since.

At least 11 people were killed in Dymer, Ukrainian officials said. A 79-year-old woman was also pulled alive from the same building and taken to hospital. Six people were injured in the attack, according to Kyiv regional head Tymur Tkachenko, and others were still missing as the search continued.

More than 130 police officers, explosives experts, sniffer dog teams and medics are working at the site, Zelensky said, adding that the operation would continue until there was complete information about every person in the building. He said the rescue effort was being complicated by constant new air-raid alerts and renewed threats.

The Dymer strike was part of a wider overnight attack across the Kyiv region. A strike on a private home in Bila Tserkva killed one person and set the building ablaze, officials said. In Vyshneve, three people were killed and 13 were injured when a grocery store was hit on Sunday, and the town's mayor, Illya Dikov, said three children were among the injured.

Vyhivskyi said that by Sunday evening, more than 70 strikes had been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions.

The rescue in Dymer drew praise from Ukrainian officials, who thanked everyone involved in saving the boy's life. The search for people still trapped under the rubble was continuing on Monday.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Kyiv Post

link.title: Rescuers pull seven-year-old alive from collapsed flats in Dymer

entry.title: Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Asian stock markets opened the week with sharp losses on Monday, as doubts about the artificial intelligence boom deepened and last week's sell-off on Wall Street spilled into a new trading day.

South Korea bore the brunt. The Kospi index in Seoul slid as much as 5.8 percent in early trading before paring losses to close 3.3 percent lower. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the world's two largest memory chip makers and central players in the AI build-out, fell 3.1 percent and 2.5 percent respectively.

Elsewhere the picture was mixed. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index dipped 0.1 percent after falling nearly 2 percent earlier in the session. In mainland China, the CSI 300 edged up 0.1 percent, reversing a decline of more than 1 percent. Taiwan's Taiex recovered from an early fall to close 2.2 percent higher. Japanese markets were closed for Labour Thanksgiving Day.

The losses extend a rout that began on Friday. Wall Street's benchmark S&P 500 closed 3.7 percent lower, entering a correction, the term for a fall of 10 percent or more from a recent high. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.3 percent, erasing all of its gains for 2026. Across Asia on Friday, the Kospi, Japan's Nikkei 225 and Taiwan's Taiex each finished between 5.1 and 6.2 percent lower, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 1.9 percent.

At the heart of the sell-off is a question investors have been circling for months: whether technology companies can sustain the vast sums they are pouring into the data centres and computing power needed to train and run AI systems. Much of that spending is financed by debt. Research firm Gartner expects global AI-related investment to reach 2.7 trillion dollars this year and 3.6 trillion dollars in 2027, figures that have fuelled comparisons with the run-up to the dot-com crash of 2000.

Rajat Agarwal, an Asia equity strategist at Societe Generale, told Al Jazeera that investors were trying to judge whether the correction had gone too far after what he called a more than three-standard-deviation event in US tech shares on Friday.

Pressure on the sector is also building from politics and regulation. The Democratic Party's sweeping midterm win in the United States is expected to slow data centre construction in some states, while an alleged espionage scandal involving chip giant Nvidia has prompted calls for tighter limits on China's access to advanced chips.

There were signs the bleeding may be slowing. US equity futures pointed to a strong rebound on Monday, with S&P 500 futures up 2.2 percent and Nasdaq futures up 2.9 percent. Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, noted that South Korea reported very strong exports for the first 20 days of November, with semiconductor exports up 294.4 percent year on year.

Even so, Goh said AI concerns were likely to dominate trading for the rest of the week, as investors try to work out whether the bottom is near.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Asian stock markets tumble as AI bubble fears mount

entry.title: Ukrainian drones sink Russian warship off Libya, Zelenskyy says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Ukraine says its forces sank a Russian warship off the coast of Libya in a naval drone operation on Sunday, in Kyiv's furthest strike yet on Russian military assets beyond the Black Sea.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that seven Ukrainian-made naval drones sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest warships, and destroyed a Ka-27 combat helicopter carried on board. The attack took place in the port of Benghazi, in eastern Libya, some 2,400 kilometres from the front line in Ukraine.

"A exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war," Zelenskyy said in a post on X, praising the crews behind the attack.

The Merkury, a 1,800-tonne Steregushchiy-class corvette about 344 feet long, was commissioned in 2023, a year after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Libyan authorities said the ship had stopped in Benghazi to refuel and resupply while en route back to Russia. Video released by Ukraine showed sea drones speeding toward the vessel before a large explosion erupted at the dock.

Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also hit a second target, the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which he said Moscow used to transport weapons. Ukraine's security service said the drones were carried to the area aboard a mothership and launched from there, and that Russian forces tried to intercept them from the air, sea and shore.

Libyan officials said at least four drones were intercepted while two struck the corvette, and that at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded. Libya's eastern health ministry said all crew members had been rescued and were receiving treatment. Satellite images showed the warship smouldering and partially submerged in the water at Benghazi.

Russia made no immediate comment on the attack. There was no independent confirmation of the full extent of the damage to the two vessels, and the United Nations has called for an independent investigation into the drone attacks.

The operation is the latest in a series of long-range Ukrainian strikes on Russian assets far from the battlefield. The Merkury was the second Russian ship hit over the weekend, after a cargo vessel was struck in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, and the Russian Black Sea Fleet has lost more than 20 vessels since the start of the war.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Ukrainian drones sink Russian warship off Libya, Zelenskyy says

entry.title: NHS launches world's largest trial of AI in breast cancer screening
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The NHS has begun recruiting for the largest trial anywhere in the world of artificial intelligence in breast cancer screening, with nearly 700,000 women expected to take part across the United Kingdom.

The study, known as EDITH, will test whether AI can help specialists find cancers sooner and review screening images more efficiently. Recruitment has started at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of around 30 NHS screening sites that will join over the coming months.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women, with around 55,000 people diagnosed each year in the UK. The NHS screening programme invites women aged 50 to 71 for a mammogram every three years, carrying out about 2.1 million screenings a year and preventing an estimated 1,300 deaths annually.

At present, two specialists examine each mammogram for signs of cancer. The trial will test whether an AI-assisted tool working alongside a specialist can spot cancers too small to see or feel, so that most images need to be checked by only one specialist. If it works, the change could free hundreds of radiologists and other specialists to see more patients who need cancer tests and treatment, and help cut waiting lists.

The £10 million study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and led by the University of Warwick, the University of Cambridge and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, working with NHS England.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper, who visited the trial team at Addenbrooke's Hospital in Cambridge, called it the biggest AI breast cancer trial in the world. She said the technology could help women get a diagnosis and start treatment much more quickly, while stressing that proper safeguards must be in place so AI is used safely and effectively.

Professor Fiona Gilbert of the University of Cambridge, a co-chief investigator of the trial, noted that millions of women have a mammogram each year and fewer than one in a hundred will have cancer. Technology that makes reviewing those images more efficient, she said, would let specialist breast radiologists spend more time caring for patients with cancer.

Researchers will also track how many cancers the AI-assisted approach detects, how often women are called back for further tests, and whether screening quality and safety are maintained throughout. The trial was first announced in 2025; results will take several years to gather and will be published in a scientific journal.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Digital Health

entry.title: Wall Street steadies as futures climb after a bruising week for tech stocks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US stocks looked set to open sharply higher on Monday, November 23, as futures pointed to a rebound after one of the worst weeks for technology shares in years.

Futures tied to the S&P 500 rose about 2.3 percent ahead of the open, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 3 percent in premarket trading, according to the New York Times. Dow futures climbed roughly 1.9 percent. Nvidia, the chip maker at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom, rose about 7 percent before the bell, and Alphabet, Intel and Micron were each 4 to 5 percent higher.

The bounce followed a punishing week. The S&P 500 fell 8.6 percent over the week, its worst weekly performance since April 2025, when President Trump announced sweeping global tariffs. Friday was the sharpest day of the rout: the Nasdaq dropped 5.3 percent, erasing its gains for 2026, while the S&P 500 fell 3.7 percent. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow have now fallen more than 10 percent from their record closing highs, putting them in correction territory.

The sell-off was driven by growing doubt about the AI trade. Investors questioned whether the trillions of dollars pouring into artificial intelligence infrastructure would ever pay off, and those worries spilled into a broader market rout. Pressure built on Nvidia through the week amid leadership turmoil and reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into its accounting, and its shares fell about 14 percent on Friday alone. Anthropic, the AI company that began public trading last week after a record debut, also pulled back, while voters in several US communities rejected new data-centre projects.

Analysts cautioned that Monday's move looked largely mechanical, a bout of bargain hunting after an oversized fall, rather than a sign that doubts about AI spending had gone away. Asian technology stocks fell on Monday as traders there caught up with Friday's heavy selling in the United States, and authorities in China, Taiwan and South Korea rolled out measures to support their markets.

The week ahead is short. US markets close on Thursday for Thanksgiving and shut early on Friday. Bitcoin, which slid to about $55,500 over the weekend, climbed back above $61,000 on Monday as stocks steadied.

What is still unclear is whether the rebound holds once regular trading resumes, and whether the debate over AI spending deepens or fades in the weeks ahead.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • The New York Times
  • Reuters
  • CNN

entry.title: A flower smaller than a grain of rice hid in a museum rock for 130 years — it is 100 million years old
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A flower no bigger than a grain of rice lay hidden inside a museum rock for more than 130 years. When scientists finally saw it, they found it was about 100 million years old — the oldest palm flower ever discovered, and the oldest flower yet found showing the pattern shared by palms, lilies and orchids.

The flower, named Tomlinsoniella pedicellata, measures about 1.5 millimetres high and 1.2 millimetres across. It dates from the mid-Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs still walked the Earth. Its description was published in the American Journal of Botany.

The discovery was an accident. Paleobotanist Steven Manchester, of the Florida Museum of Natural History, had borrowed a sandstone specimen from the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History to examine a different fossil flower on its surface, known as Dakotanthus. He was scanning the rock with micro-CT — an X-ray technique that builds a three-dimensional picture of the inside of a sample — when he noticed a second floral shape completely entombed within it.

The specimen came from the Dakota Formation in Kansas, a geological unit famous for the plant fossils in its sandstones. It was collected in the 1870s to 1890s by Leo Lesquereux, a pioneer of American fossil-plant research. Nothing on the surface of the stone had given the hidden flower away.

The flower itself is long gone. After it fell into clay-rich sand, the clay hardened around it and the plant tissue decayed, leaving a cavity that faithfully replicated its shape — a fossil preserved in negative. Manchester and his colleagues scanned that void, built a three-dimensional model of it, and then inverted the model, turning the empty space into a solid object so the flower could be examined as though it had been picked yesterday.

What the scan revealed was a textbook monocot flower: three sepals, three petals, six stamens in two sets of three, and three carpels — every part repeated in threes, arranged in five concentric whorls. "Lots of monocots have gone on to evolve more complicated variants on this, but this exhibits the features of the basic monocot flower," said lead author Bruce Tiffney, a professor emeritus of paleobotany at UC Santa Barbara. "And we've got it a hundred million years ago."

The team's analysis found the flower fits most closely with the coryphoid palms, the lineage that includes fan palms. That makes it not only the oldest discovered palm flower, but the oldest flower showing the characteristic pattern of the entire monocot group — a group that today includes grasses, orchids, lilies and palms, and covers much of the plant life on Earth.

The authors are careful about what one tiny fossil can prove. More work is needed to place the flower precisely on the plant family tree, and a single specimen cannot settle how early monocots diversified. But as a window into the early history of flowering plants, a bloom that waited a century in a drawer to be noticed is a remarkable one.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • UC Santa Barbara
  • American Journal of Botany / PubMed

link.title: A flower smaller than a grain of rice hid in a museum rock for 130 years — it is 100 million years old

entry.title: Army to detonate unstable lead explosive in Iowa on Wednesday despite court pause
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The U.S. Army plans to detonate nearly five tons of degraded, unstable explosive at its munitions plant in south-east Iowa on Wednesday, despite a federal appeals court pausing the environmental permit for the operation. The Army told the court it can proceed under a separate emergency authority.

The blast at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown was first scheduled for Friday, November 20. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle postponed it to Monday, saying a forecast cold snap could further destabilise the material. The Justice Department then told the court the Army intended to act Tuesday, November 24 — before the Army said on Sunday evening the detonation would instead take place Wednesday, November 25, the day before Thanksgiving, "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced." No time was given.

On Thursday night, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay of the EPA emergency permit after the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter sued. In a Saturday filing, the government argued the stay only "suspends the authority the Permit conferred" and does not bar the Army from acting under a separate legal authority — an emergency exclusion for munitions and explosives in federal hazardous-waste rules. On Sunday, the government asked the court to lift the stay; as of Monday morning, no ruling had been reported.

A sworn declaration from Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the Army's 71st Ordnance Group, says the 68 drums hold 9,773.5 pounds of material, with deterioration found in 58 of them. The lead azide was found degrading in March, after the liquid meant to keep it stable had largely evaporated; the contractor had not checked it since September 2025. Degraded lead azide is extremely sensitive to friction or movement, and the Army says moving it would risk an accidental detonation.

Health officials in Iowa and Illinois have advised people in affected areas to stay indoors on Wednesday with windows closed for 24 to 48 hours after the blast. The detonation would send a plume of lead dust into the air, larger particles settling nearby and finer dust drifting further, toward Iowa City and across the Mississippi River into western Illinois. The paused permit required a plume estimate within six hours, sampling within 24 hours, and a final report to the EPA within 30 days; the Army says it intends to follow those terms even if the permit is not in effect.

The environmental groups that sued now concede the blast may be unavoidable. "It appears that detonation may be, at this point, the only feasible option due to how long this problem was allowed to persist," said Michael Schmidt, general counsel for the Iowa Environmental Council. But a retired EPA official countered that the forecast was comparable to conditions the material had already endured. The Army has not said whether the 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. window it gave one Middletown neighbourhood to leave on the original date will apply on Wednesday.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Military.com

link.title: Army to detonate unstable lead explosive in Iowa on Wednesday despite court pause

entry.title: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $43.9 billion all-stock deal, one of the largest in cybersecurity
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

CrowdStrike said on Monday it will acquire Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing the company at about $43.9 billion, one of the largest acquisitions in the history of the cybersecurity industry.

Under the terms, which both companies' boards unanimously approved, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 shares of CrowdStrike for each Zscaler share they own. Based on CrowdStrike's closing price on Friday, November 20, that implies a value of about $260.41 per Zscaler share, a premium of roughly 34 percent. CrowdStrike's existing shareholders would own about 84.1 percent of the combined company, with Zscaler holders owning the rest.

The deal pairs CrowdStrike's Falcon platform, built around protecting computers and servers, with Zscaler's zero-trust network security, which controls who and what can reach a company's systems. The combination would create one of the world's largest pure-play cybersecurity providers, with more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue. The companies said they are targeting $1 billion of annualised revenue synergies.

Investors reacted quickly. Zscaler shares jumped more than 13.4 percent in premarket trading on Monday, while CrowdStrike fell about 5 percent, a familiar pattern when a buyer pays in stock.

The timing reflects two pressures reshaping the industry. High-profile hacks and fast-evolving artificial intelligence threats have made digital defence a boardroom priority, and large enterprise customers are trying to cut the number of security vendors they use, favouring providers that can deliver several products through a single relationship. CrowdStrike estimates the deal will expand its addressable market by more than $185 billion in calendar 2029.

The announcement came just three days after Bloomberg and Reuters reported that CrowdStrike was in early-stage talks to buy Zscaler, with no agreement then signed. CrowdStrike unveiled the deal alongside its fiscal third-quarter results, which it said set company records for new business and cash flow, and held a joint call with Zscaler on Monday morning to discuss both.

The transaction is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028, subject to approval by Zscaler shareholders and regulators. The companies said they will continue to operate independently until then. Whether regulators scrutinise the combination closely remains to be seen, given its size and the overlap between two of the sector's largest vendors.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Wall Street Journal
  • Business Wire

link.title: CrowdStrike to buy Zscaler in $43.9 billion all-stock deal, one of the largest in cybersecurity

entry.title: NATO intelligence warns Russia is ready to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, German media report
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

NATO members' intelligence services have concluded that Russia plans to launch a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon into space this year, German media reported on Monday.

The report, by broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, said Western intelligence services — including Germany's foreign intelligence agency, the BND, and the German armed forces — had shared assessments showing the satellite, named Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is stationed in the Moscow region.

Russia's embassy in Germany, the BND and NATO headquarters in Brussels did not immediately respond to requests for comment, Reuters reported.

Asked about the reports on Monday, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance was constantly assessing its deterrence and defence. "I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory. And that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element," Rutte told reporters at a joint news conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Rutte said NATO had a variety of response options, even if the public did not always see them. "When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

The reports revive a concern that first surfaced publicly in 2024, when US officials said Russia was developing a weapon that could destroy enemy satellites by setting off a nuclear explosion in space. Russia denied the assertion at the time.

US officials have alleged for years that Moscow has been working on a nuclear weapon capable of destroying entire satellite networks, including SpaceX's Starlink internet system, which Ukrainian troops have relied on during the war.

A weapon of that kind would threaten the satellite networks that carry civilian communications, navigation and military data, which is why the reports drew a swift response from NATO's leadership. But much remains unconfirmed: no launch date has been made public, and the assessment rests on intelligence shared among allies rather than any announcement from Moscow.

For now, the alliance's public message is one of readiness rather than alarm: it is watching, it says, and it has options.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Reuters

link.title: NATO intelligence warns Russia is ready to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, German media report

entry.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok deepfakes, saying users were misled on safety
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Virginia and Oregon filed lawsuits on Monday against SpaceX's AI division, alleging its Grok chatbot generated non-consensual sexual images — including images depicting children — while the company misled users about how safe the tool was.

The two states are the first to sue over Grok, though several other attorneys general had already announced investigations. Both cases were filed under consumer protection laws and seek damages, penalties and court orders requiring the company to stop breaking state law.

At the centre of the complaints is a feature in Grok's image tools known as "spicy mode", which the lawsuits say lets a user turn an existing photograph of a person into a sexual or nude image or video. The states say SpaceX promoted it to attract users and gain ground on rivals, even though its safeguards were not strong enough to prevent abuse.

Virginia's complaint cites Center for Countering Digital Hate research estimating that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted millions of sexualised images on X, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

"In the absence of federal action, AGs have stepped into the breach," Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones told Reuters before the filings, describing state attorneys general as a regulatory force in a lightly regulated industry.

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield said the lack of needed safety measures "was considered a feature, not a bug". Virginia is asking for $2,500 for each wilful violation of its consumer protection law. Its case was filed in Richmond; Oregon's in Multnomah County.

The suits name SpaceX, the social platform X and SpaceX Super Intelligence, the AI subsidiary that now owns Grok. SpaceX acquired xAI, Grok's original developer, in February and renamed the AI division in October.

In a statement, SpaceX Super Intelligence said sexual content involving minors, whether real or AI-generated, "is abhorrent. It has no place on X or in Grok, and neither do explicit images of real people made without their consent."

The suits follow a backlash that began in January, after Grok's image-editing tools were opened to all users in December and it became clear they could create realistic fake sexual images of real people. The company tightened restrictions in mid-January, but Reuters reported in early February that Grok was still producing such images even when users said the subjects had not consented.

SpaceX already faces more than a dozen lawsuits from individuals who say Grok generated non-consensual sexual images of them, as minors or adults. In Britain, lawmaker Jess Asato is suing the company over sexualised images users generated of her; the company denies those claims. SpaceX is also suing at least two people in the US, alleging they misused Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

The two states say they worked together and hired the same outside firm to help litigate the cases. The filings mark an escalation: regulators are no longer just investigating AI image tools — they are asking judges to hold their makers to account.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Associated Press

link.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok deepfakes, saying users were misled on safety

entry.title: A black hole spinning near its limit could split in two, study suggests
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Black holes are famous for colliding and merging in some of the most violent events in the universe. A new theoretical study argues they might also be able to do the opposite: under extremely narrow conditions, a single black hole could split into two or more smaller ones.

The paper was published on October 22 in the journal Physical Review D. Its authors used several mathematical modelling methods to test whether the event horizon of a black hole, the boundary beyond which nothing can escape, could branch apart. They describe the possible shape with a homely image: a pair of pants, with one waist splitting into two legs.

For decades, physicists assumed that splitting was off the table. The reasoning rests on two obstacles. The first is entropy. A black hole's surface area cannot decrease, a result tied to Stephen Hawking's area theorem. Splitting a static black hole, the simplest kind, would break that rule, so it is strictly forbidden in ordinary four-dimensional general relativity. The second obstacle is motion: even if a split began, the fragments would be pulled back together and recombine almost immediately.

The new paper finds a possible loophole, and it depends on spin. A black hole spinning extremely close to the maximum rate allowed by general relativity carries an enormous store of rotational energy. The researchers argue that this energy could be converted into the motion needed to fling the fragments apart fast enough to escape each other. In that narrow regime, at the edge of what the laws allow, a split would not violate entropy or conservation of energy and angular momentum.

The idea changes again in more exotic settings. In models with more than four dimensions, the rules loosen. A black hole stretched into a long cylindrical form, sometimes called a black string, could pinch off into separate pieces, like beads breaking away from a string.

The fragments, if they existed, could be extraordinarily small. In one example calculated by the researchers, a black hole with ten times the mass of the Sun would favour fragments with masses comparable to a few Great Pyramids of Giza, compressed into a region smaller than a proton. Such fragments could help explain black holes too small to have formed through the usual routes, if they are ever found.

Nobody has observed a black hole splitting. The paper explores what the laws of physics permit; it is not a report of an event. The conditions it requires are so extreme that they may never occur in nature, and full simulations of the splitting process are still needed before the idea can be tested further.

Even so, the result redraws a boundary physicists thought was settled. Black holes can merge, and the mathematics now suggests that, in the rarest of circumstances, they might also be able to divide.

Illustration, not a photograph.

Sources

  • Live Science: "Black holes can split apart 'like pants' if they spin too fast, astrophysics study hints"

link.title: A black hole spinning near its limit could split in two, study suggests

entry.title: COP31 failure sparks calls to overhaul how UN climate summits decide
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The failure of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya has turned into a debate about the summits themselves, with former US vice-president Al Gore, the conference's own co-chair and leading scientists all saying the way the United Nations reaches climate decisions needs urgent reform.

The talks, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, ended late on Sunday without the sweeping "Antalya pact" they were meant to produce, after running more than two days past their scheduled Friday close — making COP31 the longest climate summit on record. Under the UN climate convention's rules, decisions can only be adopted by consensus. When a group of countries formally objected to the final text, the pact could not go through.

The draft that died had dropped every mention of fossil fuels — widely seen as a concession to oil-producing states. The EU, Panama, Belize, Vanuatu, the UK, the Marshall Islands and Norway were among those that refused to accept it. Ireland's Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, said the bloc would not endorse a deal that did not even name fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change.

Gore called the outcome an outrage and said significant reform was needed. "World leaders no longer want to settle for the lowest common denominator," he said, adding that most countries had come to Antalya in good faith and that it was time for a process reflecting the will of the majority.

Australia's climate minister Chris Bowen, who co-chaired the summit, pointed directly at the decision rule. "The fundamental root problem is that when Cops were created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only," he said. "That's a very tough ask when you also need consensus to change consensus."

The UN's chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, defended the consensus system, noting that it produced the 2015 Paris agreement and helped lower expected end-of-century warming from almost 5C to 2.6C. But he conceded it had fallen short in Antalya and said he was championing a review to seek outside advice on reform.

Other voices went further. Johan Rockström of the Potsdam Institute said the summits needed to move from "negotiating promises and commitments that we never deliver on" to holding countries accountable for what they have already promised. Tobias Holle of Shifting Advocacy said the process was "not fit for purpose any more". During the talks, Panama released an open letter calling for a path away from consensus toward simple majority voting.

Former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has called the decision to walk away a "sign of courage". China, India and many developing countries did not formally object, and later expressed disappointment that it failed. Ghana's delegation told the plenary: "Africa has always chosen to build multilateralism rather than walk away from it."

The question now passes to Ethiopia, host of next year's COP32 — along with an open argument over whether nearly 200 countries can keep deciding only when every one of them agrees.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • Channel News Asia

link.title: COP31 failure sparks calls to overhaul how UN climate summits decide

entry.title: Hegseth's former chief of staff says the defence secretary should resign
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Pete Hegseth's former chief of staff has publicly called on the defence secretary to resign, saying Hegseth has lost the ability to lead the Pentagon effectively.

Joe Kasper, who served as Hegseth's chief of staff during the first three months of the Trump administration, made the call in an interview with Politico published on Monday. He said Hegseth's capacity to do the job was nearly exhausted, and that it was time for him to step aside.

Kasper criticised Hegseth's handling of the war in Iran, his dismissal of dozens of senior military leaders, and his blocking of promotions for military officers. He also said Hegseth's standing with Congress had collapsed, arguing that the secretary had destroyed his relationships on Capitol Hill and would soon find himself unable to function in the role.

Kasper said he decided to speak out after an incident earlier this month at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery, where Hegseth and a group of his advisers were rebuked by an Army sentinel for breaking decorum. A day later, Hegseth awarded the soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, the Joint Service Commendation Medal for carrying out his duties.

Kasper, an Air Force veteran, left the chief of staff post in April 2025 and briefly remained at the Pentagon as a special government employee. During his tenure he oversaw the dismissal of three senior Pentagon officials, senior adviser Dan Caldwell, former deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll, a former chief of staff to the deputy secretary of defence, who were accused of leaking sensitive information to the news media. All three denied the accusations, and an administration official later told The Hill that Caldwell had been investigated and cleared, with no evidence released to suggest he had leaked anything.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to The Hill's request for comment. President Donald Trump has continued to stand by Hegseth, praising him for removing generals he described as "woke". The Hill also reported that Trump's decision to elevate adviser Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff is likely to help Hegseth, given the close relationship between the two men.

Kasper's intervention comes shortly after Hegseth survived an impeachment effort in the House led by outgoing Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican. The Hill previously reported that the failed effort followed the president asking allies and advisers about Hegseth.

It is not yet clear whether Kasper's criticism will change anything. Trump has shown no sign of dropping Hegseth, and the secretary himself has not responded directly to his former aide's call to quit.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Hill

link.title: Hegseth's former chief of staff says the defence secretary should resign

entry.title: Type 2 diabetes tied to 53% higher Alzheimer's risk in review of 27 million people
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

People living with type 2 diabetes face a 53 percent higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease, according to a major review pooling data from more than 27 million participants.

The Curtin University-led review brought together 40 studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis. It found that for every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes followed for a year, about 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease. After accounting for other factors, the adjusted relative risk was 53 percent higher than for people without the condition.

The researchers screened 9,431 scientific articles before selecting the 40 studies that met their criteria. The work was published on November 9 in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.

The findings sharpen a connection scientists have suspected for years. Earlier reviews often grouped different types of diabetes together, or lumped Alzheimer's in with other forms of dementia, which blurred the picture. This analysis looked specifically at type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease, and measured both how much the risk rises and how often new cases occur.

"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," said study author Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi, an investigator fellow at the Curtin School of Population Health. "Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur. Putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes."

The numbers describe an association, not proof that diabetes causes Alzheimer's. The review cannot say why the two conditions travel together. Possible explanations include damage to small blood vessels, chronic inflammation, and how the body handles insulin, which also plays a role in the brain. None of those mechanisms was tested here.

What the study offers is a firmer basis for prevention. The authors argue that the results support building cognitive risk checks into routine diabetes care, so memory problems are spotted earlier and patients get support sooner. For people living with type 2 diabetes, the conversation with a doctor may increasingly cover brain health as well as blood sugar.

The absolute risk remains small for any one person in a given year. About five new cases per 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes annually is modest on its own, but across a condition affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide, it adds up to many cases. That is why the authors say the burden matters for health systems, not only for individuals.

More work is needed to pin down who with diabetes is most at risk, and whether tighter control of blood sugar or blood pressure lowers the chance of developing Alzheimer's. For now, the review gives doctors and patients a clearer number to work with, and a reason to treat brain health as part of diabetes care.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceDaily
  • Alzheimer's Research & Therapy

link.title: Type 2 diabetes tied to 53% higher Alzheimer's risk in review of 27 million people

entry.title: NATO to send early-warning aircraft to Poland after Russian missiles land
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

NATO will send one of its AWACS early-warning aircraft to Poland after three Russian missiles landed in the country last week, Poland's deputy defence minister said on Monday.

Pawel Zalewski told reporters in Brussels that the aircraft would be made available to Poland following a meeting of NATO allies. "This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," he said.

Three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles came down in south-eastern Poland on Friday, during a large overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. Prosecutors confirmed the missiles had landed on Polish soil, adding to fears that the war in Ukraine could spill into NATO territory. No one was injured and no infrastructure was damaged, according to Polish officials.

NATO's AWACS fleet — 14 aircraft with distinctive nine-metre-wide radar domes — has served as the alliance's eyes in the sky since 1982. Based at Geilenkirchen air base in Germany, the planes have played a central role in surveillance along NATO's eastern flank since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. In a conflict, they can build a shared radar picture for allied fighters, ships and command centres, and direct combat jets to their targets.

The deployment is the first concrete allied response since the incursion. Poland had asked NATO for more help guarding its airspace, including AWACS aircraft and F-35 fighter jets, and the alliance's North Atlantic Council met in Brussels on Monday to discuss the incident. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte called the airspace violation a "dangerous incident" and said the alliance "will defend every inch of Polish territory."

The incident was the latest in a series of Russian weapons straying into the airspace of NATO's eastern-flank states during the war. Poland and the Baltic countries have been the most affected, and Warsaw revised its air-defence procedures earlier this year to let fighter pilots decide for themselves whether to shoot down intruding objects.

What happens next is not yet clear. Warsaw has not said when the AWACS aircraft will arrive or how long it will stay, and NATO has not announced any further reinforcements. Russia has not publicly commented on the missiles landing in Poland.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Kyiv Independent

link.title: NATO to send early-warning aircraft to Poland after Russian missiles land

entry.title: Drone attack hits Colombian police base in Cúcuta, injuring three civilians
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Explosive-laden drones struck a police headquarters in the Colombian city of Cúcuta early on Monday, injuring three civilians — including an 18-month-old baby — and damaging more than 60 homes, in what local reporting described as the first drone attack on a major Colombian city.

The attack hit the Norte de Santander police department, known as DENOR, in the Tasajero neighbourhood of Cúcuta, a city of about half a million people near Colombia's border with Venezuela. Police said the drones struck at around 2:30 a.m. local time. No officers were reported injured, and officials did not immediately say who was responsible.

The three injured civilians were a couple and their baby, hurt inside their home near the police compound, according to the Cúcuta metropolitan police commander. Local officials said more than 60 homes were damaged, most of them close to the headquarters. Reporting in Colombia suggested the police department's signal-jamming systems may have thrown the drones off course, so that some of the explosives fell on surrounding houses instead of the compound itself.

Cúcuta is a major trade hub and a centre for criminal groups that profit from the drug trade and other smuggling. Armed groups including the National Liberation Army (ELN) operate in the nearby Catatumbo region, where they tax local businesses and promote coca cultivation, and the ELN has carried out repeated drone attacks there. No group had claimed the Cúcuta attack by Monday, and no authority had named those responsible.

The Cúcuta strike was not an isolated incident. On the same day, drones also attacked a police station in the town of Curumaní, in the department of Cesar. And on Saturday, one soldier was killed and 12 others were injured when drones and rockets hit a military base in La Jagua de Ibirico, also in Cesar. Officials said both incidents remained under investigation.

The attacks come as Colombia's armed groups increasingly turn to small drones, homemade rockets and roadside bombs. President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative who took office in August, has stepped up military offensives against rebel groups and drug gangs, including more air strikes, and cancelled the peace negotiations his predecessor Gustavo Petro had been pursuing with rebel groups.

According to the Ideas for Peace Foundation, which monitors Colombia's conflict, illegal armed groups carried out 272 drone attacks during the first nine months of 2026 — a 71 percent increase on the same period last year. For years, drone strikes in Colombia were largely confined to rural areas and jungle fronts. Monday's attack on a city police headquarters shows the tactic has now reached an urban centre.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Colombia Reports

link.title: Drone attack hits Colombian police base in Cúcuta, injuring three civilians

entry.title: One shared code in the brain links 21 languages, MIT study finds
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The human brain may process every language through one shared code, according to a new MIT study published in Nature Neuroscience. Brain scans of people speaking 21 different languages — from Vietnamese to Lithuanian — revealed a common pattern in how the brain handles language, one that appears to be about meaning rather than grammar or sound.

Scientists have long known that all languages activate the same network of regions in the left hemisphere of the brain. What they did not know was whether the brain actually processes those languages in the same way. A team led by Andrea Gregor de Varda, a postdoctoral researcher at MIT, and Evelina Fedorenko, senior author and investigator at MIT's McGovern Institute for Brain Research, set out to answer that question with help from artificial intelligence.

The researchers used multilingual language models — AI systems trained to handle hundreds of languages at once — to build "encoding models" that predict how the brain responds to a sentence. They combined the models' numerical representations of language with brain scans of people listening to stories from "Alice in Wonderland" in their native tongues.

The lab already had brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages, including Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Marathi, Spanish, Tamil and Vietnamese. For the new study, the team recruited speakers of nine more — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin and Korean — bringing the total to 21 languages across several language families.

The encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in every language tested, even in Marathi and Lithuanian, for which the researchers had relatively little data. More striking still, a model trained on one language could predict brain activity in a language it had never seen. A model trained on French responses, for example, could predict how a Vietnamese speaker's brain would respond. That kind of transfer is only possible, the researchers say, if all the speakers' brains represent language in a shared way.

When the team picked apart which linguistic features drove that shared signal, the evidence pointed to meaning — the information and feelings people are trying to share — rather than word order or sound patterns.

The finding could matter beyond neuroscience. AI language tools are increasingly used to detect cognitive decline from brain activity during speech, but most are built for widely studied languages such as English. Showing that the brain's language code is shared across diverse languages could help extend those tools to far more speakers. Fedorenko also suggested the approach could one day help preserve endangered languages, by training a model in reverse — from a single speaker's brain activity back into language.

The researchers caution that languages also differ in clear ways, and those differences must be represented in the brain as well. Mapping them is the next step.

Sources

  • MIT News
  • Nature Neuroscience

link.title: One shared code in the brain links 21 languages, MIT study finds

entry.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A genuinely new web browser engine is a rare event, and one has just arrived. Ladybird, an independent browser built around an engine written from scratch, entered its first alpha on Monday, with test builds available for macOS and Linux.

Developer Andreas Kling announced the release after more than four years of development. Ladybird began as part of the SerenityOS project before spinning out into its own effort, and it is backed by a nonprofit whose stated goal is an independent, fast and secure browser that respects user privacy and fosters an open web.

What makes the release notable is what Ladybird is not: a fork. Nearly every browser in everyday use runs on one of three engines — Blink, which powers Chrome and Edge; Gecko, behind Firefox; or WebKit, behind Safari. Ladybird's engine was written from the ground up, making it the first browser in years to arrive with an entirely new one.

Kling is candid about the alpha's limits. He described the browser around the engine as "modest but functional," and warned that some websites will not work and the browser will sometimes crash. That is expected at this stage: the alpha is aimed at early adopters willing to test and report problems, and a broken site can be reported from inside the browser itself.

For now, the alpha is limited to macOS and Linux. A Windows version is planned for a later stage of the project, and the team says its JavaScript engine is already built and tested on Windows. The browser is free and open source.

The project is small by browser standards, with a small full-time engineering team supported by community testing and bug reports. Its bet is that the web needs a fourth engine that answers to no browser vendor — one built on web standards and free of the commercial interests that shape the existing three.

Whether Ladybird can survive contact with the real web, and with the attackers who probe every new browser, is the question the alpha is meant to answer. For now, anyone curious can download it and find out first-hand.

Sources

  • The Verge
  • Ladybird
  • Phoronix

link.title: Ladybird, the first new browser engine in years, is now available to test

entry.title: US adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist at the heart of the Nvidia chip scandal
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The United States has added Megaspeed, the Singapore data-centre company at the centre of the scandal engulfing Nvidia, to its trade blacklist — closing the door on its access to advanced American chips.

The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security placed Megaspeed International and six other firms in South-East Asia on its Entity List on Monday, in a filing to the Federal Register. The bureau said the seven entities had been found to be acting against the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.

The designation means American companies now need a government licence to ship the firms advanced technology, including Nvidia's top-end graphics processors used to train and run artificial intelligence systems. Such licences are generally denied. It is the first time since October 2025 that the Commerce Department has added new entities to the list.

The six other firms are MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Speedmatrix in Malaysia; Apex Enterprise Solutions and Swiftdata in Singapore; and Megaspeed in Thailand. All were linked to Megaspeed, according to a Commerce official.

The move came hours after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, less than two weeks after he resigned amid revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. President Donald Trump said he had personally urged Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged on the news of his return.

A listing long resisted

The blacklisting follows weeks of open disagreement inside the administration. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's department had declined to place Megaspeed on the Entity List even as the investigation into the firm deepened, drawing public criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and from lawmakers.

US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over suspicions that it diverted advanced Nvidia chips to China in breach of export controls. Last week the Justice and Commerce departments confirmed the criminal investigation and said they would pursue the matter to the full extent of the law.

US officials have accused Alice Huang, Megaspeed's controlling shareholder, of working with China's Ministry of State Security in an intelligence-gathering operation targeting the Nvidia chief. Beijing has rejected the claims as groundless. Megaspeed has previously denied wrongdoing and said it complies with all applicable US and local laws. It did not respond to requests for comment on the listing.

What is still unknown

The criminal investigation into Megaspeed continues, and it is not yet clear how strictly the licensing regime will be applied in practice, or whether any of the seven firms will seek exemptions. Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand have not yet commented publicly on the designations.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: US adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist at the heart of the Nvidia chip scandal

entry.title: Samsung sets December date and $899.99 price for its 1,100Hz Odyssey G6 monitor
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Samsung has put a price and a date on the fastest gaming monitor it has ever made. The 27-inch Odyssey G6, known as the G60H, will reach retailers across the United States in December priced at $899.99, the company announced on Monday.

The headline figure is a refresh rate of up to 1,100Hz — the number of times per second the screen can redraw its image. Samsung describes it as the first gaming monitor in the world to reach that speed. But the four-digit figure comes with a trade-off that buyers will need to understand: the monitor only hits 1,100Hz in HD mode, at a lower resolution. At its native QHD resolution of 2,560 by 1,440 pixels, the refresh rate tops out at 600Hz.

That split is the work of a feature Samsung calls Dual Mode, which lets players switch between the two settings depending on the game. A fast competitive shooter, where spotting movement a fraction of a second sooner matters, suits the 1,100Hz mode. A slower, visually rich open-world game suits the sharper QHD picture at 600Hz — itself far above the 144Hz or 240Hz most gaming monitors offer.

A new blur-reduction feature

The G6 also introduces Odyssey Clear Motion, a blur-reduction system that Samsung says keeps fast-changing scenes clear during critical moments of play. The company plans to bring the feature to more of its gaming monitors after its debut here.

The panel is a fast IPS display with a 1ms grey-to-grey response time, and it supports HDR10+ Gaming, which adjusts brightness and contrast in real time. It works with Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium to reduce tearing and stutter, and it connects through one DisplayPort 2.1 port and two HDMI 2.1 ports.

The launch has been a long time coming. Samsung first showed the monitor in December 2025, when the highest refresh rate it quoted was 1,040Hz. By August, at the Gamescom trade show, that figure had risen to 1,100Hz, while the QHD figure stayed at 600Hz.

The monitor arrives into a small but intensifying race. LG's UltraGear 25G590B tops out at 1,000Hz, and Samsung's new model undercuts it on price by about $100. Samsung says it has led the global gaming monitor market for seven consecutive years, from 2019 through 2025, according to IDC figures.

What buyers should check

Not every setup will reach the headline speeds. Samsung notes that macOS does not support Dual Mode or the 600Hz maximum, and that AMD FreeSync Premium does not operate at 1,100Hz. Older AMD Radeon RX 6-series cards and below cannot reach 1,000Hz or higher.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Samsung Newsroom
  • Digital Trends

link.title: Samsung sets December date and $899.99 price for its 1,100Hz Odyssey G6 monitor

entry.title: Ancient rift beneath Botswana shows signs of stirring back to life
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

In April 2017, a magnitude 6.5 earthquake shook central Botswana, where earthquakes were not supposed to happen: the middle of the Kalahari Craton, an ancient block of crust largely unchanged for billions of years. Nearly a decade later, scientists say they finally understand why. An ancient rift system beneath Botswana, dormant for around 180 million years, appears to be stirring back to life.

Published in the journal Tectonics, the findings come from researchers in Botswana and at Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, and suggest the forces slowly pulling Africa apart are reaching into ground long assumed to be unshakable.

A failed rift

A continental rift forms when tectonic forces pull Earth's crust in opposite directions until it fractures along large faults. Given millions of years, the process can split a continent apart and open a new ocean. But not every rift gets that far: some stall, leaving a failed rift frozen in the crust.

That is what the team believes happened in Botswana. They focused on the Khurutshe Fault, a major fracture linked to a 50-mile scar in the landscape, about 50 miles south of the 2017 quake. The fault's steep scarps hinted at past movement, so the team dug trenches across it and imaged the rock below with electrical currents.

The evidence points to a rift that first opened around 180 million years ago, during the Jurassic Period, when tectonic forces were stretching the region. It stalled before it could split the continent and lay dormant for millions of years. But the fault has also displaced younger Kalahari sand laid down within the past 2.6 million years, a sign movement has resumed recently. When exactly it reawakened is still unknown.

Why here

The researchers say it exploited an ancient seam inside the craton, an intra-cratonic suture zone formed billions of years ago when separate blocks of crust collided and joined. Even in a craton as strong as the Kalahari, such old seams stay comparatively weak, giving tectonic forces a place to grip.

"Whether rifts do propagate through cratons has been a really big question in geoscience," said Boniface Kgosidintsi, the study's lead author. His co-author Folarin Kolawole put it more plainly: "While cratons are regarded as strong old continental blocks, they do have inherent zones of weakness that can localize a new plate boundary. Maybe you need to reactivate the rift multiple times. You need to try multiple times before it actually succeeds."

It may also redraw the map of southern Africa's plates. The region south of the Okavango Rift Zone has long been treated as part of the San Plate, a microplate moving as one block. The renewed fault activity suggests it may instead be slowly breaking into two smaller plates.

Nobody is predicting a new ocean in Botswana: any breakup would unfold over millions of years. But the study shows continental breakup can reach into regions once written off as stable, and that splitting a continent may take more than one attempt.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Gizmodo
  • Columbia Climate School

link.title: Ancient rift beneath Botswana shows signs of stirring back to life

entry.title: Google's AI Mode can now read your Wallet, with Drive and Gemini chats to follow
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Google Search's AI Mode is getting a much closer look at its users' digital lives. Google announced on Monday that its Personal Intelligence feature, which tailors AI Mode answers using information from a person's own Google apps, is expanding to Google Wallet, Google Drive and the Gemini app. The Wallet connection starts rolling out now; Drive and Gemini support will follow in the coming weeks.

Personal Intelligence already draws on Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Photos; the three new connections extend that to spending, documents and chat history.

What Wallet adds

Connecting Google Wallet lets AI Mode use spending information to help map out financial milestones, find ways to trim everyday spending, and get more from credit card benefits, such as cash-back categories, travel perks and reward points, based on the cards linked in Wallet.

Google is explicit about the limits: the connection is read-only. AI Mode can look at information from a person's accounts, but it cannot move, manage or invest their money. The same Wallet connection also works in the Gemini app, so the context carries across both places.

Drive and Gemini come next

With Google Drive connected, AI Mode will be able to pull together information scattered across a person's documents, spreadsheets and PDFs. Google's example is a personalised tax-season preparation plan built from the files already in Drive.

The Gemini app connection works in both directions. If a person explores an idea in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search will have that foundation to build on, and vice versa, so a conversation does not have to start from scratch. According to 9to5Google, AI Mode will be able to draw on Gemini chats and material shared with the Gemini app, such as photos, files and attachments.

Still the user's choice

Every connection is opt-in. To turn them on, users open Search Personalization in their Google Search settings, select Connected Apps and choose which apps to link. Connections can be switched off at any time, and Google says a "Personalization" icon will soon let people see the context AI Mode is using below a tailored response. If something is wrong, users can correct it in the conversation, for example by telling AI Mode they are no longer vegetarian.

AI Overviews and AI Mode responses are also becoming more personally relevant, tailored to recent search context, so someone planning a trip can pick up where they left off instead of repeating themselves.

The feature is limited to adults with a personal Google account, and availability varies by country and language. Only the Wallet connection is rolling out for now; Drive and the Gemini app follow in the coming weeks.

Illustration — not a photograph.
