  • Google
  • TechCrunch
  • 9to5Google

link.title: Google's AI Mode can now read your Wallet, with Drive and Gemini chats to follow

entry.title: Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast travel as nor'easter may become a bomb cyclone
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A powerful coastal storm is set to strike the East Coast on Wednesday and Thanksgiving Day, bringing heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding as millions travel for the holiday — and forecasters say it could rapidly strengthen into a "bomb cyclone."

NOAA's Weather Prediction Center said it has high confidence in an impactful holiday storm, likely a nor'easter and perhaps a bomb cyclone, hitting the East Coast on Wednesday, November 25, and Thanksgiving, November 26. A bomb cyclone forms when a storm's central pressure falls by at least 24 millibars in 24 hours. The system is expected to develop off the Southeast coast and track north along the seaboard.

Heavy rain on Thanksgiving Day

The heaviest rain is forecast for Thanksgiving Day along the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast coasts: 1 to 4 inches in the Carolinas and the Mid-Atlantic, and 1 to 2 inches across the Northeast. Local flash flooding is still possible, especially in flood-prone urban areas.

Winds, outages and coastal flooding

Powerful winds will accompany the rain through at least Friday night, when the storm moves into the Canadian Maritimes. Gusts of more than 50 mph are forecast along the coast and above 40 mph inland into the Interstate 95 corridor, raising the risk of power outages and tree damage.

Strong onshore winds, high surf and high tides could also bring significant coastal flooding and beach erosion from Georgia through the Northeast. Forecasters warn of moderate to major flooding around Charleston, South Carolina, and Tybee Island, Georgia, on Wednesday, and at least moderate flooding along the Virginia Tidewater and Delaware coast at the Thanksgiving high tide.

Macy's parade balloons at risk

The storm also threatens the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, starting at 8:30 a.m. on Thursday with a record 100 inflatables. Under city safety rules, the giant balloons must stay grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph or gusts top 34 mph. Winds are expected to strengthen through the morning, and rain could arrive around parade time, though the exact timing remains uncertain. No cancellation has been announced.

A second storm on the West Coast

On the West Coast, record-high king tides are expected to coincide with an incoming Pacific storm, and the National Weather Service had issued coastal flood warnings from San Francisco to the southern coast of Washington as of Monday morning. That storm is expected to bring rain, high-elevation snow and dense fog to northern and central California.

More than 81 million Americans are expected to travel for Thanksgiving, and forecasters warn of expanding airline delays, first in Orlando and Miami from Tuesday into Wednesday, then in Atlanta and Charlotte on Wednesday. The National Weather Service urged travellers to monitor its forecasts and follow local guidance.

Snow is not expected to be a major issue, as temperatures are too warm for much to accumulate, though snow showers are possible on the back side of the system on Friday into Saturday, with only minor impacts likely.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • USA Today
  • Gizmodo
  • Fox Weather

link.title: Thanksgiving storm threatens East Coast travel as nor'easter may become a bomb cyclone

entry.title: Kagi takes on Gmail with a private email service in public beta
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Kagi, the company behind a paid alternative to Google Search and the Orion web browser, is taking on another Google service. On Monday it opened a public beta of Kagi Mail, a paid email service it describes as having "no surveillance, no ads, open standards, and no lock-in."

The launch puts Kagi in direct competition with Gmail, the world's most widely used free email service, and with paid privacy focused providers such as Fastmail and Tuta. Kagi acknowledged the crowded field in its announcement, saying it asked itself more than once whether the world needed another email service before deciding to build one anyway.

What Kagi Mail includes

Subscribers get an address at @kagimail.com, with support for unlimited aliases and their own custom domains. The service includes 50GB of storage and a built-in calendar, and it is built on Stalwart, an open source mail server. It supports open standards including IMAP, JMAP and CalDAV, so customers can use Kagi's own clients or a third party app such as Apple Mail or Thunderbird.

The service also includes an AI layer that draws on the user's existing Kagi allowance and can be switched off. A headline feature called Highlights flags messages that need attention, such as mail waiting for a reply or carrying a due date, rather than summarising the inbox automatically.

Price and what is still to come

Kagi Mail is available now with a 60-day free trial. After the trial it costs $99 a year plus sales tax as a standalone subscription, or it is included in Kagi Ultimate, the company's $25 a month bundle covering search, the Assistant and its other products.

Not everything is ready on day one. Kagi says contacts and a full address book are planned for the first quarter of 2027, with fuller integration of its Assistant around the same time. Native mobile apps are further out, scheduled for the third quarter of 2027. Customers who leave keep access to their mailbox for six months, with sending and receiving for the first 60 days and read and export access for the remaining four.

A paid model in a free market

The launch extends Kagi's strategy of charging users directly instead of selling advertising. The company, a small profitable team based in Palo Alto, has built its search engine and browser on the same user funded model, and it presents Mail as the third part of that lineup.

Whether enough people will pay $99 a year for email remains the open question. Gmail costs nothing and comes bundled with the rest of Google's services, while established paid providers already serve the privacy conscious market Kagi is targeting. Kagi's answer is that an email service should do its job and then get out of the way, and it is betting that a growing number of users agree.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Verge
  • Kagi Blog
  • Techaeris

link.title: Kagi takes on Gmail with a private email service in public beta

entry.title: China to launch Shenzhou-24 carrying its first foreign astronaut to Tiangong
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

China will launch its Shenzhou-24 spacecraft on Wednesday morning, carrying a Pakistani astronaut who will become the first foreign national to visit the country's Tiangong space station.

The three-person crew consists of commander Tang Hongbo, flight engineer Wu Yi and Pakistani payload specialist Zeeshan Ali. The spacecraft is scheduled to lift off at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT) aboard a Long March-2F rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, the China Manned Space Agency announced on Tuesday.

Ali's participation is part of bilateral cooperation under Beijing's Belt and Road Initiative, according to the agency. His flight marks the first time a non-Chinese astronaut has boarded Tiangong, a station China has operated with all-Chinese crews since it began hosting long-duration missions in 2021.

A short visit, then a handover

Ali is scheduled for a short-term stay rather than a full six-month rotation. He will return to Earth with two members of the outgoing Shenzhou-23 crew, while the third, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain in orbit for a year-long mission, authorities said.

Shenzhou-24 is the 41st flight mission of China's crewed space programme. Once in orbit, it will complete a handover with the Shenzhou-23 crew, and the new arrivals will carry out space science experiments alongside planned station research.

The mission is the latest step in a programme that has sent trios of Chinese astronauts to Tiangong for six-month stays since 2021, steadily expanding the station's role as a platform for science and for international cooperation.

A wider race to the Moon

The launch comes as the contest to return astronauts to the Moon accelerates. The United States has alleged that Beijing plans to colonise and mine lunar territory and resources, claims Beijing has strongly rejected.

China has not set out a crewed lunar landing date in its public announcements, but its space programme has moved quickly from building Tiangong to planning deeper exploration. For Pakistan, Ali's flight is a milestone of its own: a national first, achieved through a partnership with its closest regional ally.

The crew is reported to be in good condition, and launch preparations are complete, the agency said.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: China to launch Shenzhou-24 carrying its first foreign astronaut to Tiangong

entry.title: Sanofi to acquire Insmed in $41 billion deal
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

French drugmaker Sanofi said on Tuesday it has agreed to buy U.S. biotech Insmed for $41 billion in cash, its largest bet yet on respiratory medicine and one of the biggest pharmaceutical deals of the year.

Sanofi will pay $175 per Insmed share, a premium of about 46 percent to Insmed's unaffected closing price on November 18, the day before media reports of a possible transaction emerged. The deal values Insmed at roughly $41 billion, or €37.6 billion, and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

The acquisition gives Sanofi two marketed medicines and a late-stage pipeline asset, strengthening a respiratory business that is set to become more important as patent protection on its best-selling eczema and asthma drug Dupixent begins to run down.

What Sanofi is buying

The centrepiece is Brinsupri, the brand name for brensocatib, a once-daily oral drug approved in the United States, the European Union, Britain and Japan for non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition in which the airways widen and become prone to infection. It is the first drug of its kind approved for the disease.

Sanofi also gains Arikayce, an inhaled antibacterial used alongside other drugs to treat a serious lung infection known as MAC lung disease. Arikayce brought in $433.8 million in revenue in 2025, up 19 percent on the year before, according to Sanofi.

Behind the two marketed products sits treprostinil palmitil inhalation powder, known as TPIP, a once-daily inhaled treatment in phase 3 trials with potential uses across several rare respiratory diseases. Sanofi said the deal would add to its earnings per share by the end of 2028.

Why now

The deal follows a familiar pattern in the drug industry: large companies buying growth as their biggest products approach patent expiry. Dupixent, jointly developed with Regeneron, has been Sanofi's main growth engine for years, and the company has been building its respiratory and rare-disease portfolio to carry it beyond that franchise.

Reports of a possible Sanofi–Insmed deal surfaced last week, lifting Insmed's shares before Tuesday's announcement confirmed the terms. Sanofi will brief investors on the transaction at a conference call later today.

If the deal closes on schedule, Insmed's two commercial products and its pipeline will sit inside one of the world's largest drugmakers, with the resources to expand their reach beyond the markets they serve today.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Sanofi

link.title: Sanofi to acquire Insmed in $41 billion deal

entry.title: Trump held at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as chipmaker's chief gained White House access
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

President Donald Trump held at least $12 million in Nvidia shares at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News, making the chipmaker one of his three largest individual stock holdings.

The stake was worth between $12.5 million and $58 million at the end of last year, according to a CNBC analysis of the president's disclosures, up sharply from between $615,000 and $1.3 million a year earlier. The filings give holdings as broad dollar ranges rather than share counts, so the exact value is not public.

Trump's investment accounts have kept trading Nvidia since his return to the White House, buying or selling the stock at least 103 times in transactions worth a combined $27 million to $97.5 million, the CNBC analysis found. ABC News reported more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, based on separate periodic filings.

The pace of trading is a marked change from Trump's first term. His accounts disclosed more than 21,000 trades in 2025 alone, compared with roughly 500 during his entire first term in office, according to CNBC's analysis.

White House response

The White House maintains that the president does not direct the trading. A spokesperson said his stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions, held in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognised indexes.

The disclosures offer no evidence that Trump directed the trades, or that his advisers had access to classified intelligence, CNBC reported.

Why the holdings are in focus

The disclosure comes as Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang has become one of the president's closest business allies, meeting or appearing with Trump at least 15 times since he returned to office. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive last week following revelations about his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China and reports of affairs with company employees.

Trump stood by Huang as Nvidia's board weighed his future, urging him to fight to keep his job, and has since floated the idea of reinstating him. Nvidia's board is not considering a return, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.

Nvidia's rise has also been central to the market Trump points to as a measure of the economy. The chipmaker alone accounted for about 13.5 percent of the S&P 500's gains in 2026 through September, according to an analysis by Choate Wealth.

What is still unclear

Because the filings report holdings in wide value ranges and do not list share counts, Trump's current stake in Nvidia cannot be pinned down precisely. Based on the value he reported holding in August, the stake would have been worth between $4.5 million and $57.7 million at midday on Monday, with the stock priced around $157.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNBC
  • ABC News

link.title: Trump held at least $12 million in Nvidia stock as chipmaker's chief gained White House access

entry.title: US puts Alibaba unit and Megaspeed on trade blacklist over Nvidia chip fears
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The US Commerce Department has added Megaspeed International and Alibaba's Singapore subsidiary Apex Enterprise Solutions to its trade blacklist, escalating Washington's crackdown on suspected diversions of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.

Announced on Monday, November 23, the move places seven companies in Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand on the Entity List. Firms on the list need a US government licence to buy American exports, which is usually refused. The other five are linked to Megaspeed, including its owner Swiftdata and Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatrix.

Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company and Nvidia partner, has been under investigation by US authorities since 2024 over suspected diversions of AI chips to China. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security said the companies were added because of "the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorised end uses or end users."

The Alibaba connection

Apex, which buys computing power for Alibaba in Southeast Asia, paid around $4.2 billion to Megaspeed and others as prepayment to rent computing capacity there. Speedmatrix, its Malaysian subsidiary, pledged its entire business as collateral and held about $2.14 billion in assets at end-2024.

Alibaba rejected the decision. "Adding Apex Enterprise Solutions to the Entity List is erroneous because Apex has never diverted advanced computing chips subject to US export restrictions," the company said, adding that it would "seek all legal avenues to protect our rights and reputation."

Megaspeed says its business is legitimate and lawful and complies with US export controls. It said Alice Huang, a former executive at the centre of the scandal, left the company in August 2025.

A scandal that reached Nvidia's top

Megaspeed came under intense scrutiny about two weeks ago after reports that Nvidia chief Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. China has called the accusations groundless. Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief and has since been reinstated.

The department had faced growing criticism over its handling of the case. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly complained on November 13 that the company had still not been listed, and Senator Pete Ricketts said the department "still needs to explain to Congress why this took so long." Senator Maria Cantwell called for a broader investigation.

A separate rule unveiled last week requires data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to get a US licence before exporting advanced AI chips to customers there. The Justice and Commerce departments also said they would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred."

What happens next

Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Tuesday his country would continue its own investigation. US and Singapore law enforcement visited in 2025 and interviewed Alice Huang.

It was the first Entity List addition since October 2025, and it shows how far the fallout has spread.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNA
  • The Straits Times

link.title: US puts Alibaba unit and Megaspeed on trade blacklist over Nvidia chip fears

entry.title: Japan pays ICC contribution early as US sanctions threaten the court
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Japan will pay its full 2027 contribution to the International Criminal Court by the end of this year, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told the court's president on Tuesday, moving months ahead of schedule to shield the tribunal from American sanctions.

Takaichi informed ICC President Tomoko Akane of the decision during a 15-minute meeting at the Prime Minister's Office in Tokyo, and announced it in a post on X. "Japan has consistently supported the ICC and will continue to do so," she wrote. Akane, who had asked Tokyo for the early payment, thanked the prime minister afterwards and said the money would go toward staff salaries and keeping the court running.

Japan is the court's largest financial backer, covering about 15 percent of its budget — 4.6 billion yen, or roughly $28.9 million, in 2026 — followed by Germany, France, Britain, Italy, South Korea and Canada. Its 2027 contribution is expected to be roughly the same amount. Normally Tokyo sends its payment in April or later; paying in December hands the court its money before the sanctions bite.

The timing matters because the United States is pressing the court from two directions. Washington sanctioned Akane herself — the first Japanese national to lead the court — freezing her US assets and barring her entry in August, and broader American sanctions on the tribunal take full effect in April 2027. Reuters reported that the US is pushing to dismantle the body and encouraging member states to leave it.

The move puts Japan, one of Washington's closest security allies, publicly at odds with the American campaign against the court. It comes five days after Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin used their first three-way summit in Shenzhen to declare that the court "must not abuse" its jurisdiction — a statement aimed at an institution that has an arrest warrant outstanding for Putin.

Analysts say Tokyo's early payment could set an example. If other large contributors follow suit and pay early, the court could build a meaningful cash buffer before the sanctions take full effect, buying time while it fights for its funding and its future.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Kyodo News

link.title: Japan pays ICC contribution early as US sanctions threaten the court

entry.title: Trump's meme coin dinner went badly wrong for one VIP guest
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The dinner on Sunday was meant to reward the biggest holders of President Donald Trump's meme coin with an evening at his golf club. For one guest who had bought his way to VIP status, it ended outside in the rain.

Morten Christensen, a Dutch crypto investor who lives in Mexico and runs the website Airdrop Alert, attended the gala at the Trump National Golf Club in Potomac Falls, Virginia, with his sister Gabriëlle Felen. He had been to both previous dinners and said he bought enough of the coin to qualify as a VIP this time, with an email to prove it. But when he tried to enter the area reserved for the top guests, he was turned away — his name was not on the list.

Later in the evening he was approached and told to leave. He said he was told it was because he had been sharing pictures online and was in touch with the media. Organisers did not reply to NPR's email seeking comment. Christensen waited outside in the rain while his sister stayed inside.

Felen said Trump eventually appeared to cheers, but his speech jumped from topic to topic and made few important points, in her view. She was disappointed that VIP guests got a one-on-one selfie with Trump and probably a handshake — an opportunity her brother missed. Christensen said the evening will be his last Trump event.

Gift boxes for guests contained perfumes, a watch and a small golden statue of the president, and dinner was grilled filet mignon or pan-seared halibut. Kevin O'Leary of CNBC's Shark Tank, former boxer Floyd Mayweather and former NBA star Tristan Thompson all gave speeches, while mentalist Lior Suchard performed a trick for the siblings.

The event's website listed 185 qualifying wallets, with the top 29 invited to a VIP reception. It was the third such gala for the coin's top holders. Trump's meme coin, launched just days before his inauguration, has fallen from a peak of over $70 in January 2025 to less than $1, sharply reducing the cost of qualifying. Trump, who effectively has a royalty deal with the company behind the coin, earned more than $600 million from it last year, according to his disclosures.

The dinners have drawn sharp criticism. Anti-corruption activists say they effectively reward the largest coin buyers with access to the president, with the top buyers getting the closest access. Consumer group Public Citizen said about half of those who qualified for Sunday's event appeared to be foreign-based. Prominent Democrats, including Senator Adam Schiff of California and Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, have demanded more information about the latest dinner. The White House has defended the events as part of Trump's private business, not his public functions.

The dinner came weeks after corruption was a defining issue in the midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of Congress next year.

Sources

  • NPR

link.title: Trump's meme coin dinner went badly wrong for one VIP guest

entry.title: Break-in at William and Kate's Norfolk country home leads to two arrests
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Two men have been arrested after a break-in at the country home of Prince William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, in what police are treating as a burglary at one of Britain's most closely watched royal addresses.

Norfolk Constabulary said officers were called just before 6pm on Monday after a report of suspicious activity at a property on the Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England. The property was Anmer Hall, the couple's country retreat. Two men were arrested on the estate on suspicion of burglary and trespass and remain in police custody. The house was unoccupied at the time, and inquiries are continuing.

The Sun newspaper first reported the break-in, saying masked intruders had made their way into the house on Monday night. A search of the estate followed, involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, according to reports of the police operation.

Nobody from the family was at Anmer Hall when the incident happened. William, Catherine and their three children — Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis — were at their main home, Forest Lodge in Windsor, at the time. A spokesperson for William said the prince's office did not comment on security matters.

Anmer Hall is a ten-bedroom, Grade II-listed Georgian house set within the King's private Sandringham estate, where the royal family traditionally gathers for Christmas. The late Queen Elizabeth II gave the house to William and Catherine as a wedding present in 2011, and the couple use it for holidays and short breaks, while their main home is on the Windsor Castle estate west of London.

It is not yet known whether anything was taken from the house, or how the intruders gained access. Police said their investigation remains open, and the two arrested men have not been named.

The news emerged on Tuesday morning as William visited Prime Minister Andy Burnham at 10 Downing Street — a rare working visit by the heir to the throne to the prime minister's official residence. The timing turned a routine royal engagement into the backdrop for a security incident that will raise fresh questions about protection at royal homes outside London.

The Sandringham estate, in the east of England, is one of the monarch's private residences rather than a state-owned palace, and its grounds are patrolled by royal protection officers alongside local police. The break-in is the most serious security breach at a royal country home to become public in recent years, and it comes at a moment when the Wales family have made Forest Lodge their primary base, spending less time at Anmer Hall than they once did.

Police have asked anyone with information about suspicious activity around the estate on Monday evening to come forward.

---

Sources

  • CNN
  • Arab News

link.title: Break-in at William and Kate's Norfolk country home leads to two arrests

entry.title: Ukraine defends Libya drone strike on Russian ships as self-defence
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Ukraine has defended a weekend drone attack on Russian ships in Libyan waters as a legitimate act of self-defence, after Libya's government in Tripoli condemned the operation and said it would not accept being drawn into the war.

Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday that both Russian naval vessels and cargo ships carrying military equipment were valid targets, and that Ukraine's right to self-defence is set out in Article 51 of the United Nations Charter.

The operation sank the Russian naval corvette Merkury in the eastern port of Benghazi, according to Libya's Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, which condemned the attack on Monday. Benghazi is controlled by military commander Khalifa Haftar, whose Libyan National Army has ties with Russia, while the internationally recognised government in Tripoli controls western Libya.

"Ukraine is not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," Sybiha wrote on the Telegram messaging app. "Ukraine respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Libya. We emphasize that Ukraine's actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people."

Sybiha argued that international law does not limit the right to self-defence to the territory where the aggression takes place, saying it can also apply on the territory of the aggressor or in international waters. Russia, he said, was the one endangering third countries by using their civilian infrastructure for its military purposes.

The Institute for the Study of War said the corvette had stopped over for several days at Benghazi to refuel and resupply under a cooperation agreement, while escorting cargo ships capable of carrying military supplies to Russia.

The eastern government in Benghazi said on Monday there were indications the naval drones had been launched from western Libya, and asked the United Nations to investigate allegations that Ukraine has deployed military experts there. Russia's defence minister has not commented publicly on the attack.

In a separate development, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy confirmed in an interview published on Tuesday that Ukraine was responsible for a drone strike on Saturday on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, in the international waters of the Gulf of Finland. He said the vessel was a legitimate target because it was carrying weapons. Russia's Transport Ministry said on Tuesday that the damaged vessel had been towed back to the Russian port of St Petersburg.

The Libya operation marks a widening of the war's geography: a Ukrainian strike carried out far from the front lines, against Russian naval assets using a foreign port. How far Kyiv is willing to press that logic — and how Libya's rival governments respond — remains to be seen.

---

Sources

  • Reuters

link.title: Ukraine defends Libya drone strike on Russian ships as self-defence

entry.title: Court unseals records from search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's home
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A federal judge has ordered the release of 169 pages of court records from the search of Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., home, revealing a constitutional dispute between prosecutors and the judge who authorised the search — but shedding little new light on the investigation itself.

Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the partial unsealing on Monday, after more than a dozen news organisations, including The Associated Press, argued that the public has a First Amendment right to see the records. The documents, released in heavily redacted form, relate to the October 12 search of the Minnesota Democrat's home by Department of Homeland Security agents.

The filings show that U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, who authorised the search, raised concerns before signing off about the Speech or Debate Clause — the constitutional protection that shields members of Congress from executive-branch interference in their legislative work. Sharbaugh rejected the government's argument that the privilege applies only to official congressional offices and certain electronic devices.

"That logic does not hold," the magistrate wrote, according to the records.

Sharbaugh concluded that the government's law-enforcement interests had to be balanced against Omar's constitutional rights as a member of Congress. The government ultimately agreed to a search protocol allowing Omar to invoke the privilege over any legislative material before agents carried out the search.

What the records do — and do not — reveal

The released documents do not disclose new details of the investigation, which Omar has described as politically motivated. Federal authorities are examining potential fraud in her family's immigration paperwork and have issued grand jury subpoenas to some of her relatives, the AP reported last month.

According to The Wall Street Journal, one court brief states that the government believes Omar has committed crimes described only in redacted text "over decades," and that prosecutors sought evidence dating back to 1980. Omar, a naturalised U.S. citizen born in Somalia, has not been charged with any crime and has denied any wrongdoing.

Boasberg agreed with the government that it would be premature to unseal a 67-page affidavit supporting the search warrant, which contains sensitive details of the investigation. The warrant itself was not included in the release. The government argued last month that unsealing the records before a charging decision is made would jeopardise the investigation.

Omar has said agents seized 17 items from her home, including phones, notebooks, her passport, a Somali-language children's book and a vintage camera her husband had received as a gift.

The search took place less than a month before the November 3 midterm elections, in which Omar won a fifth term. The Justice Department has historically avoided public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of an election.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • The Wall Street Journal
  • USA Today
