entry.title: China places Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

China's anti-corruption watchdog has placed Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of Shanghai and a member of the ruling Politburo, under investigation — the most senior civilian official to fall in President Xi Jinping's widening purge of the party's top ranks.

State news agency Xinhua announced on Tuesday that Chen, 62, is suspected of "serious violations of discipline and law", the party's standard phrasing for corruption cases. The investigation is being conducted by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the National Supervisory Commission. No details of the alleged wrongdoing were given, and Chen could not be reached for comment.

Chen is the fourth member of the 24-member Politburo to be investigated since 2025, after generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia and former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui. The body, formed after the party congress in 2022, now has 21 active members. It is the largest purge at this level since 1976, according to The Wall Street Journal.

A rising star, now fallen

Chen had an unusual path to the top of Chinese politics. An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial College London and rose through Tsinghua University to become its president, before serving as Beijing's mayor. He joined the Politburo in October 2022 and took over as party secretary of Shanghai — China's largest city and financial centre — succeeding Li Qiang, who went on to become premier.

The Shanghai post is one of the most powerful in China and has traditionally been a stepping stone to the Politburo Standing Committee, the pinnacle of party power. Chen was widely seen as a candidate for promotion to that body at the party's next congress, scheduled for the second half of 2027, when Xi is expected to seek a fourth five-year term as party chief.

His last public appearance was last Thursday, when he inspected the headquarters of the state-owned shipping group China Cosco Shipping in Shanghai. On Tuesday evening, the Shanghai party committee's standing committee held an expanded meeting to brief officials on the investigation. No replacement for Chen has been named; the city's mayor, its number-two official, could stand in until a permanent appointment is made.

Chen is the first sitting Shanghai party chief to be placed under investigation since Chen Liangyu was removed from the post in 2006.

A widening campaign

The probe is the latest escalation in Xi's anti-corruption drive, launched after he took power in late 2012 and intensified in recent years. At the party Central Committee's fifth plenum in late October, the expulsions of 33 high-ranking members were formalised, nearly half of them military officers.

For officials of Chen's rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the discipline inspection commission generally signals eventual political downfall. What remains unknown is what specific conduct Chen is accused of, and how the party will fill one of its most important regional posts as it prepares for the 2027 congress.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: China places Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under investigation

entry.title: Anthropic slides below its $83 IPO price days after record debut
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Anthropic's shares slipped below their $83 initial public offering price on Tuesday, less than a week after the Claude developer's record-breaking Nasdaq debut — a swift reversal for the most anticipated listing of the year.

The stock was down 6.5% at $82 in premarket trading, according to Reuters, and later touched $80.10 shortly after the market opened. It is a steep fall from the November 19 debut, when shares opened at $111.50, reached $115.10 on their first day, and the company's fully diluted valuation briefly topped $2 trillion.

The drop came a day after Anthropic missed out on a broad rally in AI-linked stocks. Nvidia surged nearly 30% on Monday after reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive, but Anthropic barely moved. The shares fell sharply on Friday, their second day of trading, and have since spent most of their time below $90.

Filings also showed that chief executive Dario Amodei sold more than 3.37 million shares worth over $280 million on November 20, the day after the debut, at the $83 IPO price. The sale was disclosed late on Monday.

A record listing, quickly tested

Anthropic raised $93.5 billion in the largest IPO on record once underwriters exercised their option to buy extra shares, passing SpaceX's $85.7 billion listing in June. As the first frontier AI company to go public, it is widely seen as a proxy for the sector — which is why its slide has fed a wider debate about stretched AI valuations and the vast sums being poured into computing infrastructure, with rising interest rates threatening to push those costs higher.

The broader market has offered little shelter. The S&P 500 and the Dow ended last week in correction territory, and Nvidia posted its steepest weekly loss since 2008, underscoring the sell-off that has swept Anthropic along with it.

History offers a mixed guide

Anthropic is not alone among blockbuster listings in quickly giving up its early gains. SpaceX took about a month to fall below its offer price, while Facebook — now Meta — slipped below its offer price on its second trading day in 2012. The experience of past high-profile listings suggests an early break below the offer price is not necessarily a guide to longer-term performance.

Some support may be on the way. Index provider MSCI will add Anthropic to its global standard indexes at the November 30 close, and index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates passive funds could buy up to 30% of the shares offered by year-end.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Fast Company

link.title: Anthropic slides below its $83 IPO price days after record debut

entry.title: GTA VI drew 39 million PlayStation players in four days — and hundreds of millions watched
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest launch in PlayStation history, Sony said on Monday, with more than 39 million unique players playing the game on PlayStation 5 in its first four days.

Players logged 683 million hours between November 19 and 22 — about 17 hours each — and Sony said the game set a new record for the most players online at the same time on PlayStation. It was also the first game played on 70 percent of new PS5 consoles set up during launch week, and Sony said the release drove the largest single-day surge in newly connected consoles outside the year-end holidays.

The launch dominated streaming as well. According to streaming data from Streams Charts, reported by The Guardian, viewers watched 364.5 million hours of GTA VI content in the two days after release — roughly 41,000 years of footage. The game drew more viewership than the next three titles combined, and more than twice the launch viewership of Valorant, making it the most-watched game release on record.

The sales behind the players

The player counts follow the official sales figures Take-Two Interactive announced last week: $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales and 32.5 million copies sold before release, the biggest entertainment launch in history across any medium. The figures are the company's own estimates of what players paid in shops and online stores, and they replaced early third-party estimates of about $2.36 billion.

The two sets of numbers measure different things, and should not be added together. Sony counts players, not copies sold: its 39 million covers PlayStation 5 only, over four days, and counts unique accounts rather than purchases. Take-Two's $3.79 billion covers every platform on launch day alone. The company has not split its total by console or between digital and boxed copies.

Thirteen years in the making

The scale reflects both the wait and the spend behind the game. GTA VI is the first new entry in the series in 13 years, and Take-Two is estimated to have spent $1 billion or more developing it, making it one of the most expensive entertainment projects ever made. For comparison, its predecessor, Grand Theft Auto V, made about $800 million on its first day in 2013. Critics have been nearly unanimous as well: the game holds a 99 on review aggregator Metacritic, tying the highest score ever recorded there.

For now the game is available only on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with no PC version announced, and Take-Two has said little about the online multiplayer mode analysts expect in 2027. But whether measured in sales, players or viewers, the launch has already set records on every count released so far.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • Engadget

link.title: GTA VI drew 39 million PlayStation players in four days — and hundreds of millions watched

entry.title: Denmark's top court upholds 'ghetto law' evictions, backing hard line on immigration
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Denmark's Supreme Court has ruled that the eviction of "non-Western" tenants from a social housing estate under the country's so-called "ghetto law" was not discriminatory, handing the government a major legal victory for its hard line on immigration.

The court on Monday rejected an appeal by seven families whose leases were terminated in 2022 by the housing association Boliggarden. The families were among 91 households evicted from the Nøjsomhed estate in Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, most of them classed as "non-Western". Lower courts had already dismissed their claims.

At the heart of the case was whether the law's dividing line — between immigrants and descendants from "non-Western" countries, and everyone else — is effectively a proxy for ethnicity. The court said it was not: both groups contain people of many different ethnic origins, and people of the same ethnic origin can fall into either group. No information had been presented about the ethnic background of the evicted residents, and the court found no evidence that particular ethnic groups had been put at a particular disadvantage.

A law aimed at 'parallel societies'

The legislation, adopted in 2018 and officially known as the Parallel Society Act, targets social housing areas where more than half of residents are immigrants or descendants from "non-Western" countries, alongside at least two of four socio-economic thresholds covering unemployment, low income, low educational attainment and criminal convictions. Such areas must reduce the share of public family housing to no more than 40 percent by 2030, which can mean demolishing buildings, selling homes to private landlords or converting them — and relocating residents. Tenants' associations say some 11,000 people will be forced to leave their apartments and be rehoused elsewhere by 2030.

The government describes the law as a bid to promote integration and combat segregation in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Denmark officially stopped referring to "ghettos" in 2021, but the nickname has stuck. Housing Minister Jacob Mark said he was satisfied with the ruling, saying the law "strengthens security, social cohesion, and integration".

The decision is not the last word on the law's compatibility with European anti-discrimination rules. The EU's top court ruled last December that the legislation could amount to discrimination on ethnic grounds, but left the final determination to Denmark's courts. The Supreme Court has now made that determination — in the government's favour.

The families' lawyer, Eddie Khawaja, said the court had focused more on the wording of the law than on how it was implemented on the ground, and that in his view "non-Western" is "a proxy for ethnic origin". One of the plaintiffs, Riad, told AFP: "We're obviously disappointed."

Denmark has pursued a tough line on immigration for more than three decades, and the housing law — widely criticised by tenants and their associations — retains broad political support. Monday's ruling removes a major legal obstacle to it, and signals that the courts will not block policies that sort residents by origin, so long as the sorting is framed in terms of nationality rather than ethnicity.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • DW

link.title: Denmark's top court upholds 'ghetto law' evictions, backing hard line on immigration

entry.title: US jury convicts Huawei of trade-secret theft and bank fraud, but clears it of racketeering
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

A federal jury in Brooklyn has convicted Huawei of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks, ending an eight-year criminal case against one of China's most prominent technology companies — while clearing it of the most serious charge prosecutors brought.

Jurors on Tuesday found Huawei and three affiliates guilty on 10 of the 12 counts they faced, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud, wire fraud and violating United States sanctions. They acquitted the company of racketeering conspiracy, the charge that it operated as a criminal enterprise, and of conspiracy to obstruct justice. The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defence calling 15.

A two-decade pattern, prosecutors said

The case began in 2018, when US prosecutors alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business in Iran, allowing it to move money in and out of the country in violation of American sanctions. Charges added in 2020 accused the company of conspiring to steal trade secrets from US technology firms over two decades.

Prosecutors told jurors that theft was part of how Huawei grew into one of the world's largest suppliers of telecoms equipment. They presented evidence that it took source code from Cisco for its routers, antenna technology from the wireless firm Quintel, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by the semiconductor company CNEX. Jurors also saw video prosecutors said showed an employee slipping part of a T-Mobile testing robot into a backpack.

The defence: ordinary business, not conspiracy

Huawei's lawyers argued the government was criminalising normal competition. The banks knew about its business in Iran and were competing for its custom, they said, and prosecutors had cherry-picked unrelated incidents to support a claim of a 20-year conspiracy.

"It's about competition, not conspiracy; innovation, not theft; ordinary business dealings, not criminal misconduct," defence lawyer Brian Heberlig said, arguing Huawei had succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development."

The company welcomed the racketeering acquittal, saying it "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years." It added that the remaining charges lack legal or factual merit.

A case that began with an arrest in Canada

The prosecution emerged in December 2018, when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of its founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant. She had been secretly indicted for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's Iran business. She later entered a deferred prosecution agreement acknowledging the company had illegally conducted business in Iran, and returned to China. The charges against her were dropped.

US authorities have targeted Huawei for years, saying the company poses national security risks, and in 2019 placed it on a trade blacklist restricting its access to US technology. Experts say the case has nevertheless not undermined its business, as the company has diversified and become a key player in China's push into artificial intelligence.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: US jury convicts Huawei of trade-secret theft and bank fraud, but clears it of racketeering

entry.title: Astronomers find the most distant quasar ever seen, just 630 million years after the Big Bang
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Astronomers have found the most distant quasar ever seen, a blazing galactic core already shining just 630 million years after the Big Bang, when the universe was less than 5% of its current age.

Formally catalogued as J1504+6252, it appears as it was more than 13.1 billion years ago, beating the previous record holder, announced only in July, by about 40 million years — the largest single leap in the quasar record in nearly a decade.

A quasar is the fiercely bright heart of a galaxy, powered by a supermassive black hole feeding on gas and dust. As material spirals inward, it forms a disc heated to extreme temperatures, radiating so much energy that a quasar can outshine its entire host galaxy. That brilliance makes quasars visible across billions of light-years, and lets astronomers use them as beacons to study the early universe.

What startles researchers is the size as much as the distance. The black hole powering it had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun — roughly 90 times the Milky Way's central black hole. "Just 630 million years after the Big Bang, this black hole had already grown to about 360 million times the mass of the sun and was shining as a quasar," said Julien Wolf of the European Southern Observatory, who led the study.

Euclid, the European Space Agency's space telescope, first spotted it among millions of candidates in about 18 months of survey observations. Follow-up work with the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii and the Large Binocular Telescope in Arizona confirmed it and pinned down its distance: a redshift of 8.13, the first quasar found beyond redshift 8.

The team nicknamed it Dún Aonghasa, after a prehistoric stone fort on a cliff on Inis Mór, off Ireland's west coast, which looks out over the Atlantic much as the quasar stands at the edge of what telescopes can see.

It deepens a long-running puzzle: how did black holes grow so large so quickly? One possibility is that this one began as the remnant of one of the first stars, but it was feeding too slowly to have reached its size that way. The other is that it was born big, when a vast cloud of gas collapsed directly into a black hole. The team's calculations favour the second explanation.

It dates to the epoch when the first stars and galaxies were burning through the hydrogen fog left over from the Big Bang, making the universe transparent to light for the first time.

More may be coming: Euclid could yet find quasars even farther away, and models suggest the first quasars could date to 270 million to 470 million years after the Big Bang. "So in short: this is the furthest quasar we have ever seen, but maybe not the furthest there is to find," said study co-author Silvia Belladitta of the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • European Space Agency

link.title: Astronomers find the most distant quasar ever seen, just 630 million years after the Big Bang

entry.title: U.S. measles deaths reach 14 as cases near 6,000 in worst outbreak since 1991
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The United States has recorded 14 measles deaths this year, with the national case count nearing 6,000 — the worst outbreak the country has seen since 1991.

Pennsylvania reported its ninth death on Monday, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County, and Wisconsin reported its third death on Tuesday, an adult in Lafayette County. The two deaths, announced on consecutive days, pushed the national toll to 14, according to Ars Technica's tally of state health department reports.

Cases are now approaching 6,000 for the year, the highest annual total since 1991, when more than 9,600 were recorded. The virus has been reported in 47 states and jurisdictions. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, accounting for 96 percent of all cases, and four states have each recorded more than 500 cases. Pennsylvania leads the country with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalised nationwide.

The deaths have not been confined to the two hardest-hit states. New York reported the death of a 7-month-old baby, its first measles death in more than 30 years, and Virginia reported the death of a child aged between 0 and 4 on November 20. Wisconsin's earlier deaths were an infant and a child.

The rising toll comes a week after international health authorities formally revoked the United States' measles elimination status, which it had held since 2000. The Pan American Health Organization acted on November 17 after determining that measles had been transmitted without interruption for more than 12 months, meaning the virus is once again considered endemic in the country.

State tallies and the federal count do not agree. As of mid-November, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's official count listed six measles-related deaths, against 14 reported by state health departments. The gap has become a point of dispute: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has asked the CDC not to count the deaths in the official tally, questioning whether they were caused by measles, while state officials say they count a death as measles-associated when a person with confirmed measles dies within 30 days of developing symptoms, unless the death had an unrelated cause.

Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known, and it is preventable with the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine. Before widespread vaccination, the disease sickened 3 million to 4 million Americans a year and killed 400 to 500. Health officials say the current outbreak is concentrated in communities with low vaccination coverage, and that the reported case count is likely an undercount of the true total.

With cases still climbing week by week, officials expect the final tally for 2026 to keep rising — and the question of whether transmission can be interrupted before a second full year of endemic spread is now open.

Sources

  • Ars Technica
  • Milwaukee Journal Sentinel

link.title: U.S. measles deaths reach 14 as cases near 6,000 in worst outbreak since 1991

entry.title: UK warns companies supplying Ukraine to prepare for Russian sabotage
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Britain's defence ministry and its domestic intelligence service MI5 have warned companies providing direct support to Ukraine's military that they face a growing threat of sabotage from Russia, in an unusually public alert issued on Tuesday.

The warning came jointly from the Ministry of Defence and the National Protective Security Authority, the part of MI5 that advises businesses on security. It told firms to take action now to improve their defences against what it described as the risk posed by operatives acting for Russia.

"In recent months Russia has increased attempts to conduct sabotage against European defence-related facilities," the alert said. "This activity is typically characterised by the use of proxy actors employing low-sophistication sabotage methodologies, such as arson."

The warning applies broadly. Any organisation that supports military procurement or supplies equipment to Ukraine's armed forces could be a target, the alert said — including companies further down the supply chain. Firms were urged to reduce the chances that hostile actors can identify them or their people as targets, carry out reconnaissance, or attack their staff, sites and operations.

The advice is practical rather than dramatic. Companies were told to cut their digital footprint by reviewing publicly available information and removing unnecessary detail about their products, facilities and staff, since hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research. They were also urged to install visible protective security measures, train employees to recognise and report suspicious activity, and identify their most critical assets.

The government is holding closed-door threat briefings for chief executives from the defence sector and critical national infrastructure in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday, bringing together senior intelligence officials and ministers.

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said the recent attempts across Europe showed how serious the threat had become. "It's truly shameful that actors are seeking to disrupt our way of life and that of our allies, especially targeting organisations doing vital work in support of Ukraine," he said.

Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said Britain's adversaries were not limiting themselves to military targets. "They are prepared to use cyberattacks, espionage, sabotage and hostile reconnaissance against the companies, technology and supply chains that underpin our national security," she said.

The alert follows a series of suspected Russian sabotage operations across Europe. Estonia has investigated suspected sabotage targeting Milrem Robotics, a maker of unmanned military systems used in Ukraine, and in November said it had foiled an alleged attack directed by Russian military intelligence against drone manufacturer Threod Systems. Last year, a group of British men were jailed for an arson attack on a Ukraine-linked business in London that UK authorities said was carried out at Moscow's behest.

There was no immediate comment from Russia's embassy in London. The alert did not name specific companies or plots, and no details of individual incidents were published.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Kyiv Independent

link.title: UK warns companies supplying Ukraine to prepare for Russian sabotage

entry.title: Dow closes above 50,000 as Nasdaq slides in renewed AI sell-off
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 50,000 on Tuesday, gaining 423.39 points to finish at 50,018.70, while the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite both fell as technology stocks gave back part of Monday's sharp rally.

The Dow rose 0.85 percent, its second straight daily gain and its first close above the 50,000 mark in about a week. The S&P 500 slipped 0.50 percent to 7,201.09, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.48 percent to 23,733.54. The split session showed investors rotating out of the technology shares that had powered the previous day's surge and into defensive and value stocks instead.

The reversal was led by Nvidia, which fell nearly 6 percent on Tuesday after surging about 31 percent on Monday. The chipmaker's rebound a day earlier had been driven by the reinstatement of chief executive Jensen Huang, and it lifted the Nasdaq more than 6 percent and the S&P 500 nearly 5 percent in one of the strongest single-day rallies in years. On Tuesday, chip stocks fell broadly, with several semiconductor names among the day's biggest decliners.

Smaller companies fared better than the big technology names. The Russell 2000 index of small-cap stocks rose 0.57 percent to 2,684.94, suggesting the selling was concentrated in the large technology stocks rather than spreading across the whole market.

The Dow's advance was helped by gains in health care and consumer stocks, which investors tend to favour when they grow cautious about growth shares. MarketWatch reported that investors rotated into defensive stocks and away from technology, leaving the blue-chip index higher even as the broader market weakened.

Tuesday's session capped a volatile stretch for American equities. Markets have swung sharply in recent weeks as investors weigh the outlook for artificial intelligence spending, corporate earnings and the path of interest rates. The Dow's return above 50,000 gives the index a symbolic milestone, but the renewed slide in technology shares underlines how quickly sentiment can turn.

Attention now turns to the next round of corporate results, with Dell among the companies reporting, and to economic data due before the Thanksgiving holiday, when US markets close on Thursday and trade for a shortened session on Friday.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • MarketWatch
  • Sharecast

link.title: Dow closes above 50,000 as Nasdaq slides in renewed AI sell-off

entry.title: Dell revenue doubles as AI server sales surge, lifting its outlook again
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Dell Technologies more than doubled its quarterly revenue as demand for artificial intelligence servers surged, reporting record results on Tuesday and raising its full-year outlook for the third time this year.

Revenue for the fiscal third quarter rose 103 percent from a year earlier to $54.9 billion, comfortably ahead of the $49.3 billion analysts had expected. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $9.45, well above the $6.59 forecast, while net income rose to $5.67 billion.

The growth was driven almost entirely by Dell's infrastructure business, which sells servers, storage and networking gear to companies and cloud providers building AI systems. Revenue in that division nearly tripled to $42.0 billion. Sales of AI-optimised servers jumped 291 percent to $22.0 billion, and traditional servers and networking rose 235 percent to $15.0 billion.

Orders kept piling up faster than Dell could ship them. The company booked $60.2 billion in new AI server orders during the quarter and ended it with a record backlog of $132.3 billion. More than 7,500 customers are now deploying Dell's packaged AI systems, known as Dell AI Factories, which bundle servers, storage, networking and software for running AI models.

Dell now expects full-year fiscal 2027 revenue of $202 billion, up from its previous target of $192 billion and above Wall Street's estimate of about $194.5 billion. It also raised its adjusted earnings forecast to $29.68 per share, from $25.50, and lifted its projection for AI server revenue this year to $78 billion, from $74 billion. For the current fourth quarter, Dell guided to revenue of $56.3 billion and adjusted earnings of $8.40 per share, both above expectations.

The personal computer business, once Dell's core, grew far more modestly, rising 3 percent to $12.9 billion — a reminder of how far the company's centre of gravity has shifted toward data-centre infrastructure.

Dell also returned a record $4.9 billion to shareholders in the quarter through buybacks and dividends, and its board approved an additional $25 billion share repurchase authorisation. Shares rose about 3 percent in after-hours trading following the report.

The results underline how much of the AI spending boom is flowing through hardware makers. Dell's servers are powered largely by Nvidia chips, and enterprises and cloud providers are buying them to run complex AI workloads. The open question for investors is whether the $60.2 billion of orders booked in a single quarter converts into shipped revenue without straining Dell's cash, since the company must buy expensive components and fund assembly before delivery.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Dell Technologies

link.title: Dell revenue doubles as AI server sales surge, lifting its outlook again

entry.title: Shanghai's party chief falls under investigation in Xi's widening purge of China's top ranks
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

China has placed Chen Jining, the Communist Party chief of Shanghai and a member of its elite Politburo, under investigation — the fourth member of the party's top leadership body to fall since 2025, and the most senior civilian official yet caught in President Xi Jinping's widening anti-corruption campaign.

State news agency Xinhua announced on Tuesday that Chen, 62, is being investigated for "suspected severe violations of discipline and laws", the party's standard euphemism for corruption. The brief statement gave no details of the alleged wrongdoing.

Chen is the first serving Shanghai party secretary to be placed under investigation since Chen Liangyu in 2006, who was later jailed for 18 years. The post is one of the most prestigious in Chinese politics and has often served as a springboard to the very top: Xi himself briefly held it in 2007 before joining the Politburo Standing Committee.

His fall is striking because of the career it interrupts. An environmental scientist by training, Chen earned a doctorate from Imperial College London, rose through Tsinghua University to become its president, then served as China's environment minister and mayor of Beijing. He joined the Politburo in October 2022 and took charge of Shanghai, China's financial hub and largest city, the same month. Political watchers had seen him as a strong candidate for elevation to the Standing Committee at the party congress due in the second half of 2027, where Xi is expected to seek a fourth five-year term.

Before Chen, three members of the 24-strong Politburo formed in 2022 had already been removed: generals He Weidong and Zhang Youxia, both senior figures in the Central Military Commission, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary. With Chen under investigation, the body now has 21 active members.

Shanghai's senior party leadership moved quickly to endorse the probe. At a meeting on Tuesday evening, officials pledged loyalty to Beijing and said the investigation demonstrated the party leadership's determination, according to the city's official newspaper. No replacement for Chen has been named, and the city's mayor, its number-two official, could stand in until a permanent appointment is made.

Chen's last public appearance was on Thursday, November 19, when he inspected the headquarters of a Chinese shipping conglomerate.

The investigation caps a year in which Xi's disciplinary campaign has thinned the senior ranks. At the Central Committee's fifth plenum in late October, the party formalised the expulsions of 33 high-ranking members, nearly half of them military officers. Analysts say the pattern is unprecedented: the purge has now reached the civilian leadership of China's richest city, and it clears the way for Xi to reshape the ruling elite ahead of next year's congress.

What happens next is unclear. In past cases at this level, the announcement of an investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection has generally signalled an official's eventual political downfall. Whether Chen faces trial, and what charges if any are brought, has not been disclosed.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Shanghai's party chief falls under investigation in Xi's widening purge of China's top ranks

entry.title: Abrego Garcia leaves US voluntarily for Spain, ending 20-month deportation fight
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Kilmar Abrego Garcia left the United States voluntarily on Tuesday, boarding a flight to Spain and bringing to a close a legal fight that has lasted nearly 20 months and, at one point, reached the Supreme Court.

Abrego Garcia, a 31-year-old Salvadoran national who has lived in Maryland for years, departed under an arrangement approved by a federal judge, who had told him to leave the country by Tuesday. His departure was confirmed by a person familiar with his travel, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

His case became one of the defining sagas of the Trump administration's mass-deportation drive. He was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and flown to a maximum-security prison in El Salvador, even though a 2019 immigration judge had ruled he could not be returned there because he faced danger from a gang that had threatened his family. An administration official later described the removal as an "administrative error."

Facing public pressure and a court order, the administration brought him back in June 2025 — but only after securing an indictment charging him with human smuggling in Tennessee. A federal judge dismissed that case in May, finding that the prosecution had been designed to punish Abrego Garcia for challenging his deportation. The government is appealing.

The administration then moved to deport him to a third country, at various points naming Uganda, Eswatini, Ghana and, most recently, Liberia. Abrego Garcia argued that if he had to leave, it should be to Costa Rica, which had agreed to take him. But Todd Lyons, the former acting director of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, wrote in a March memo that sending him to Costa Rica would be "prejudicial to the United States," saying Liberia should be the destination because Washington had spent government resources and political capital negotiating for it to accept third-country nationals.

The case took an unusual turn on October 6, when lawyers for both sides walked out of a Maryland courtroom five minutes before a hearing on the planned Liberia deportation. When they returned, the hearing was cancelled without explanation.

Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who travelled to El Salvador last year to press for Abrego Garcia's release, welcomed the outcome. "I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free," he said in a statement, describing Abrego Garcia as "a free man" travelling to a country of his choice.

What comes next is not settled. The New York Times reported, citing his lawyers, that he ultimately plans to make his way to Mexico, and he may not remain in Spain long term. The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CNN
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Abrego Garcia leaves US voluntarily for Spain, ending 20-month deportation fight

entry.title: Physicists send a message through a brick wall using gravity alone
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Physicists at the University of Queensland have sent a message straight through a solid brick wall — not with radio waves, light or cables, but with gravity itself. The message was a single word: "Gravity."

The experiment, published in the journal Science Advances, used an unlikely transmitter: a 1950s elevator in the university's Parnell physics building. The lift's counterweight weighs about 1.8 tonnes. By moving the elevator between two floors, the researchers shifted that mass between two positions — one standing for the binary digit 0, the other for 1.

On the other side of the wall, in an adjacent bathroom, sat a gravimeter, an instrument sensitive enough to detect minute changes in gravitational pull. The counterweight came within about 70 centimetres of the detector, separated from it by brick. Each shift in position produced a distinct reading, and the team decoded the readings back into letters.

The signal was extraordinarily faint — roughly five-billionths of Earth's gravitational acceleration — but it was measurable, and every bit arrived intact. The word "Gravity" took 49 bits to encode, and at one bit per minute the transmission took about an hour. "Our lift was snail-paced — it's from the 1950s," physicist Andrew White said in a University of Queensland statement.

The researchers were not generating gravitational waves, the ripples produced by colliding black holes. They were nudging the local gravitational field — the same everyday force that keeps feet on the ground. Because no known material can block that field, the message is, in principle, unblockable: surround the receiver with steel or bury it in concrete and the signal would still get through.

The idea grew out of an earlier project to weigh passing trucks by measuring their gravitational pull without touching them. If a moving truck could produce a readable signal, the team reasoned, a deliberately moved mass could carry a message.

Practical uses are distant. Gravity is weak, and its pull fades fast with distance. The researchers calculate that faster machinery and better detectors could reach around 15 bits per minute, and that quantum sensors with heavier moving masses could in theory extend the range to about 500 metres. Possible niche uses include reaching sealed bunkers or facilities where ordinary wireless signals cannot penetrate. Study co-author Matthew Davis was candid about the limits, telling The Guardian: "At the moment, it's very hard to imagine how it could be practically useful."

For now, the point is the proof. With an old elevator, a bathroom and an hour of patience, the team showed that gravity itself can carry information — slowly, faintly, and through anything in its way.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ZME Science
  • ScienceDaily
  • Science Advances

link.title: Physicists send a message through a brick wall using gravity alone

entry.title: Russia's own records point to nearly 500,000 war dead
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

At least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the war in Ukraine began in 2022, according to Russian government statistics analysed by the BBC — a figure Moscow has never published itself.

The number comes from leaked records of Rosstat, Russia's federal statistics agency. BBC Russian obtained access to more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, after a hack by Belarus's Cyber Partisans and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Rosstat has admitted a cyber-attack took place, but denies that any protected information was leaked.

With the independent Russian outlet Mediazona, BBC Russian checked the files against its own list of confirmed military deaths, compiled from open sources. The two sets matched in 90% of cases.

The records show how deeply the war has reshaped mortality in Russia. In 2025, 65% of Russians aged 18 to 24 who died lost their lives in the war; for those aged 25 to 34, the figure was 59%. Only among 45- to 54-year-olds does another cause, cardiovascular disease, claim more lives.

The data also put numbers to the fighting in specific places. About 20,000 Russian soldiers died fighting for control of ten Ukrainian villages whose combined pre-war population was 12,000. In the fight for one small village, Andriivka, south of Bakhmut, 1,122 Russians died. Before the war, 74 people lived there.

The dead have grown older as the war has gone on: the average age of those killed was 34 in the first year and 40 by 2025, as prisoners and contract soldiers joined the ranks. The burden has fallen unevenly: men from some of Russia's poorest regions in eastern Siberia — Tyva, Buryatia and Zabaykalsky Krai — are 20 to 25 times more likely to die in the war than residents of Moscow and St Petersburg.

The files also counted at least 5,017 foreigners who died fighting for Russia, including 1,031 Uzbeks and 720 Tajiks. The BBC separately identified 2,304 North Koreans who died repelling Ukraine's 2024 incursion into Russia, from satellite imagery and photographs of a new memorial in Pyongyang.

Russia has released no public figures for its losses since February 2022, and two years ago Rosstat stopped publishing deaths from external causes, the figures analysts used to estimate losses. The Kremlin has not commented.

The 490,334 figure is a floor rather than a ceiling. The dataset covers only officially recorded deaths; it cannot count soldiers listed as missing, bodies never recovered, or men who died later of their wounds. BBC Russian and Mediazona's own open-source count of confirmed deaths stands at 290,012, and military experts cited by the BBC estimate that figure may represent only 45 to 55% of the true toll — putting it between roughly 527,000 and 644,000. Counting the missing as well, Meduza and Mediazona estimate the toll has likely passed 700,000. Ukrainian losses are contested too: Zelensky put them at about 50,000 in July 2026, while the open-source UA Losses list counts 115,952.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Le Monde

link.title: Russia's own records point to nearly 500,000 war dead

entry.title: UK energy bills to rise 26% from January as Ofgem lifts the price cap
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Household energy bills in Britain are set to rise sharply in the new year, after the regulator Ofgem announced a 26% increase in the price cap from January.

The cap sets the maximum suppliers can charge for each unit of energy on a standard variable tariff. For a typical household in England, Scotland and Wales on a dual-fuel tariff paid by direct debit, the annual bill would rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the new level were sustained for a full year. In practice, the increase applies for the first three months of the year, working out at roughly £37 extra a month over that period — about £126 for every £100 a household currently spends. What any family actually pays will still depend on how much energy it uses.

Ofgem said the rise was driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers, primarily linked to the war with Iran. The regulator's Neil Kenward also pointed to the continuing conflict across the Middle East. It is the largest increase since Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent energy prices soaring in 2022.

Millions of households will feel the change at the start of winter's coldest stretch. Charities and suppliers expect energy debt to climb and more people to need emergency support. Dame Clare Moriarty, the chief executive of Citizens Advice, warned of a "brutal winter" for households already struggling. People on prepayment meters are likely to feel the rise most sharply, because they pay for energy as they use it rather than spreading the cost across the year.

The government has announced measures to soften the blow. Millions of households will receive a £100 payment from 4 January, alongside an ongoing cut in VAT on electricity. The Warm Home Discount will also take £150 off the bills of six million households on benefits this winter. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people would be "deeply concerned" by another rise in their bills.

The increase lands at a difficult moment. Wholesale gas and power prices have been climbing through the autumn as the conflict in the Middle East has disrupted energy markets, and suppliers pass those costs on to customers through the cap. Ofgem reviews the cap every three months, so the January level is not the last word — the next announcement will show whether wholesale prices have settled or are still rising.

For households, the practical advice remains the same: check whether a fixed tariff would beat the cap, make sure any benefits or discounts are claimed, and contact a supplier early if bills become unmanageable. Suppliers are required to offer support, including payment plans, to customers who fall behind.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC News

link.title: UK energy bills to rise 26% from January as Ofgem lifts the price cap

entry.title: Solomon Islands signs treaty naming Australia its primary security partner
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The Solomon Islands has signed a sweeping treaty with Australia that names Canberra its primary security partner and declares that no foreign military or security base will ever be established on its soil.

Prime Minister Matthew Wale and his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, signed the agreement in Canberra on Wednesday. In a joint statement, the two leaders said the treaty "reflects Solomon Islands' sovereign choice of Australia as its primary security partner" and confirms that the archipelago, about 2,000 kilometres northeast of Australia, will remain free of foreign bases.

The signing follows reports that Honiara plans to end the secretive security pact it struck with China in 2022, which brought Chinese police trainers to the capital and raised fears in Canberra and Washington of a Chinese naval foothold in the South Pacific. Wale would neither confirm nor deny those reports at the press conference, saying the Chinese agreement contains a non-disclosure clause. "We have ongoing discussions with China," he said.

Under the new treaty, Australia will support the expansion and development of the Solomon Islands police and border force, and provide funding for education, health, infrastructure, energy and climate resilience. Honiara has also agreed to consult Canberra before striking deals on critical infrastructure — including airports, ports, energy and telecommunications — with countries outside the Pacific Islands Forum.

The agreement marks a sharp turn in the island nation's foreign policy. Wale, who became prime minister in May, has sought to reset relations with Australia, which frayed under his predecessor Manasseh Sogavare, while maintaining diplomatic and trade ties with Beijing. Sogavare signed the 2022 pact with China, which was never officially published; a leaked draft showed it could be extended in five-year blocks unless either side gave six months' notice to end it.

For Australia, the treaty is the latest in a run of Pacific security deals, following similar agreements with Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji. Canberra has spent four years trying to counter Beijing's growing influence in the region, and the Solomons deal — coupled with signs the China pact will be allowed to lapse — is seen by analysts as its most significant win yet.

The Solomon Islands parliament is expected to return in January to approve reforms tied to the treaty, including a pledge of free education. What remains unclear is how Beijing will respond, and whether the Solomons' parliament — where some members have close ties to China — will back the shift without a fight.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Reuters
  • CNN

link.title: Solomon Islands signs treaty naming Australia its primary security partner

entry.title: All hostages rescued as Colombian forces storm Cartagena supermarket
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Colombian security forces stormed a supermarket in the Caribbean city of Cartagena early on Wednesday, freeing the last 20 hostages held after a failed armoured-vehicle robbery turned into a day-long siege. One of the captors was killed in the assault, President Abelardo de la Espriella said.

The gunmen had tried to rob an armoured vehicle on Tuesday before fleeing into an Éxito supermarket in the La Castellana neighbourhood as police closed in. Security camera operators had alerted officers to the attempted robbery, and the men took about 30 staff and shoppers hostage inside the store. Police, troops and special forces surrounded the building and cut power to the area as negotiations began.

By nightfall, 10 of the hostages had been released, including five elderly women. Hours later, shortly after midnight, explosions were heard and security forces moved in. "In an extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the Armed Forces, all the hostages were rescued," de la Espriella said early on Wednesday. Cartagena's mayor said all of those freed were "safe and sound" and would be reunited with their families before undergoing medical checks.

De la Espriella travelled to the scene, appearing in fatigues and carrying a walkie-talkie as he met commanders from a specialist anti-kidnapping unit. He was quick to rule out the involvement of guerrilla or paramilitary groups. "It's not that a terrorist group carried out a kidnapping — no, these are criminals who were caught off guard, had no way out, and then kidnapped a group of people," he said.

The siege unfolded on the 10th anniversary of Colombia's 2016 peace deal with the FARC, and it adds to a run of high-profile security incidents facing a president who campaigned on a promise to crack down on crime. Former President Gustavo Petro weighed in on social media, blaming the violence on the collapse of the tourism sector. De la Espriella defeated Petro's handpicked successor, Senator Iván Cepeda, in a run-off election on June 21.

Cartagena, a Caribbean port famed for its colonial walled old town, beach resorts and cruise-ship tourism, was brought to a standstill for much of the day. The city's Rafael Núñez airport briefly suspended landings while the armed forces used one of its runways in connection with the operation.

Sources

  • Al Jazeera
  • Arab News
  • AFP via Kuwait Times

link.title: All hostages rescued as Colombian forces storm Cartagena supermarket

entry.title: Astronomers catch a dying star's final pulse, frozen in a ring of gas
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Astronomers using the world's largest radio telescope have captured the first direct evidence of a dying star's final thermonuclear pulse — a "final nuclear heartbeat" preserved as a ring of gas around a star 12,000 light-years away.

IRAS 06530-0213, in the constellation Monoceros, is in the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula. Observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) — 66 antennas in northern Chile — reveal a thin shell of gas about half a light-year wide encircling a young hourglass-shaped nebula still taking shape. The research, led by NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Raghvendra Sahai, was published on November 20 in The Astrophysical Journal.

By measuring how fast the gas is moving outward, the team estimates the shell was blown off around 6,500 years ago, during the star's last thermal pulse — a flare-up in which helium burning briefly intensified, flinging gas outward. Until now, such pulses had only been inferred from models. "We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas," Sahai said.

The images also let the team reconstruct what happened next. For roughly 2,000 years after the pulse, the star shed material slowly. Then, over the next 1,000 years, mass loss rose sharply, building a thick, lumpy shell now seen as a tangle of curved filaments. Their spiral shape may mean an unseen companion is orbiting the star, stirring the gas. Inside the shell, the hourglass nebula and a dense doughnut of gas around its middle formed within just the last 700 years — so the star left its red giant phase very recently in cosmic terms.

Two surprises turned up: an unexpected abundance of heavy isotopes of carbon, oxygen and nitrogen — a mix that does not fit current models of how such stars forge and spread elements. And ALMA found no dust disk around the star, although such disks are usually seen around dying stars with companions and have been used to explain hourglass shapes. The team suggests a disk may have existed briefly, driving jets that sculpted the hourglass before fading.

The finding matters because stars like IRAS 06530-0213 die the way the Sun will. In billions of years, the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf wrapped in a glowing shell. This is a physical snapshot of that process in action — and a sign the standard story is more complicated than assumed. "Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai said. "IRAS 06530 shows the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."

Unresolved: whether a companion is really there, why the chemical mix is so unusual, and how the hourglass formed without a surviving disk. The observations are part of PANORAMA, an ALMA survey of dying stars in transition; IRAS 06530-0213 is the first object from the survey to be presented in detail.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Space.com
  • National Radio Astronomy Observatory
  • Phys.org

link.title: Astronomers catch a dying star's final pulse, frozen in a ring of gas

entry.title: Brussels plans a €50bn fund to back European AI and quantum firms
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

The European Union is planning a new technology fund worth up to €50 billion (about $55 billion) to back European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies, in its biggest attempt yet to cut the bloc's dependence on American and Chinese technology.

The proposed Sovereign Tech Equity Fund was reported by the Financial Times on Wednesday, citing two officials involved in the discussions, and the European Commission formally presented it the same day alongside a draft law to boost quantum technology. The fund would take direct equity stakes, writing larger cheques, taking on more risk and holding investments for longer than the EU's existing financing schemes. Its main targets would be AI and quantum firms, with strategic semiconductor technology also potentially in scope. "We want to build a fund and our target scale is now 50 billion euros," EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen told a press conference at the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

The push reflects a chronic financing gap. Europe attracts only about 5% of global venture capital, against 52% in the United States and 40% in China, according to figures cited in coverage of the plan. In quantum, the imbalance is starker in private money: European start-ups raised €1.1 billion last year, against €7 billion in the US — even though about a third of the world's quantum companies are based in the EU, and European public quantum funding of €8.6 billion exceeded America's €5.3 billion, though it trailed China's €13.6 billion. The Commission's June 2026 tech sovereignty paper found Europe depends on non-EU providers for more than 80% of key digital products and intellectual property.

The fund was unveiled with the draft Quantum Act, which aims to make Europe a global leader in quantum technology by 2030. The draft law would push public authorities to favour European businesses in procurement tenders and sets out measures to turn the bloc's research strength into industrial leadership. It still needs to be negotiated with EU member states and the European Parliament before it can become law.

Much remains undecided. Operational details are expected in February, and it is not yet clear where the €50 billion would come from — the EU budget, member states, or the European Investment Bank. The Commission has confirmed the fund's name and its €50 billion target scale, but the final size and structure could still change. The Financial Times reported the Commission aims to attract private investors alongside the public money, targeting up to €6 of investment for every €1 committed.

The move follows the 2024 Draghi report, which warned that Europe was falling behind the US and China on innovation and urged far higher investment. If the fund reaches its target scale, it would dwarf the EU's existing financing vehicles — and test whether public money can keep Europe's most promising deep-tech companies growing at home instead of selling out or moving abroad.

Sources

  • Financial Times
  • Reuters

link.title: Brussels plans a €50bn fund to back European AI and quantum firms

entry.title: Claude artifacts can now be installed as desktop apps on Mac and Windows
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic said on Tuesday that Claude users can now turn the interactive tools the chatbot builds — known as artifacts — into desktop apps on Mac and Windows. The "Install as app" feature is rolling out in beta on every plan, including the free tier.

An artifact installed as an app gets its own icon and opens in its own window, instead of living inside a Claude conversation. The process is short: describe the tool to Claude, try it out as an artifact, then choose "Install as app" from the artifact's Share menu. No packaging, code signing or API key is involved, and the resulting app can be shared with other Claude users. The kinds of tools Anthropic points to are small and practical — a timer, a tracker, a tool that renames photos — rather than full-scale software.

Installed apps can do more than a web page could. They can send desktop notifications, register global keyboard shortcuts, float in an always-on-top window, and add an item to the Mac menu bar or the Windows system tray. They can also call on Claude and on services a user has linked to it, so a tracker that reads a calendar no longer has to live in a browser tab.

That extra reach is where the permission system comes in. Every installed app starts at the default level, where it can only do what it could do inside a browser. A second level, app permissions, lets it request desktop features such as notifications and shortcuts. The highest level, full computer access, lets an app run programs and read, change or delete files without asking each time. Anthropic says it does not review apps before they are installed, and full access is only available for apps a person built themselves — or, on Team and Enterprise plans, apps built by someone in their own organisation. Permissions are requested again after every update, including the owner's own edits.

There are limits to what the feature offers for now. An installed app needs an internet connection and an active Claude sign-in to open at all, and anything it asks Claude counts toward the user's plan usage limits. It requires Claude for Mac or Windows version 6.28899.0 or later. Document-style artifacts — Claude Docs, Slides and Sheets — cannot be installed, and Linux, the web and mobile are not supported at launch. For Team subscribers the feature is switched on by default, with full computer access off; for Enterprise subscribers it stays off until an administrator enables it. Organisations with HIPAA-ready configurations do not get it.

The move takes artifacts out of the chatbot and onto the desktop, where the small tools people build with Claude can sit alongside the programs they already use. It is the second Claude update this week aimed at people building with the tool.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac
  • MacRumors

entry.title: Cancer cells grown in orbit could help doctors predict which tumours will spread
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A photograph taken aboard the International Space Station shows clusters of human stomach cancer cells growing in three dimensions — something they rarely do in a laboratory dish on Earth. NASA published the image as its Image of the Day on November 23, 2026. It was captured on November 19 inside a miniaturised biochip, part of an experiment called Encapsulate-1.

The experiment studies tumour samples taken from patients, grown aboard the station to learn how cancer cells move and interact when gravity is effectively switched off. On Earth, cells in a dish flatten against the surface and behave differently from how they behave inside the body. In microgravity they float, clump together and form compact, three-dimensional structures that resemble real tumours far more closely. That gives researchers a clearer window into the process they most want to understand: metastasis, the spread of cancer from its original site to other parts of the body.

That is the experiment's goal, in NASA's own framing. The results could help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient's risk of metastasis and support more personalised cancer treatments. It is early-stage research, not a treatment: no drug has come out of this experiment, and the samples must return to Earth and be analysed before any conclusions can be drawn. What the image confirms so far is that the biochip works as designed and the cells are alive, growing and forming the structures the team hoped to see.

The work is a joint effort between NASA and Encapsulate Inc., a Connecticut-based medical startup that builds the biochips. The project received a $3.63 million grant last year through NASA's In Space Production Applications programme, which funds commercial research that can only be done in orbit. "This grant represents a bold step forward in how we approach cancer research," Encapsulate co-founder and chief executive Dr. Armin Rad said when the grant was announced.

The station, orbiting more than 200 miles above Earth, has hosted more than 4,000 experiments since it launched nearly three decades ago, and its biomedical workload keeps growing. A resupply mission launching on November 29 is set to carry further cancer research, including tests of a new class of antibody-drug conjugates on patient-derived tumour organoids, alongside studies of muscle loss and lab-grown liver tissue.

For now, Encapsulate-1 remains a study of behaviour, not a cure. But if watching cancer cells in weightlessness teaches researchers to predict which tumours will spread — and which will not — the payoff could reach far beyond the station: treatment decisions tuned to each patient's actual risk, rather than to averages.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NASA
  • PetaPixel
  • Newsweek

link.title: Cancer cells grown in orbit could help doctors predict which tumours will spread

entry.title: Nasdaq slides about 3% as AI sell-off deepens ahead of Thanksgiving
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US stocks fell sharply on Wednesday as the sell-off in artificial-intelligence shares resumed, wiping out much of the relief rally that followed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's return to the company two days earlier.

The Nasdaq Composite was down about 3 percent shortly after the opening bell, and closer to 4 percent in early trading, while the S&P 500 fell 2.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 900 points, or about 1.9 percent. The losses spread well beyond technology: chipmakers, optical-networking firms, industrial suppliers and energy companies tied to the AI buildout were all under pressure.

Nvidia led the decline, falling about 8 percent in early trading after sliding nearly 6 percent on Tuesday. The chipmaker had surged more than 30 percent on Monday — one of its best days on record — after its board reinstated Huang as chief executive, only for the rebound to fizzle within a day. Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, fell about 6 percent to around $77 a share, slipping further below its IPO price.

The renewed selling reflects growing doubt about whether the AI boom can sustain itself. Investors have questioned the scale of spending on data centres, much of it funded by debt, and the returns companies will earn from it. The cost of insuring technology companies' debt against default has risen, and credit spreads across AI-linked borrowers have widened — signs that lenders, not just shareholders, are growing cautious.

Two other worries added to the pressure. Fresh inflation data due on Wednesday morning fuelled expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again, and new tariffs on major US trading partners threatened to lift costs further. Gold fell below $3,500 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025, as traders braced for higher rates.

The slide caps a volatile week. Monday's rally had lifted the Dow by more than 1,000 points and the Nasdaq by about 7 percent; on Tuesday the Nasdaq gave back 1.5 percent to close at 23,733.54 and the S&P 500 slipped 0.5 percent to 7,201.09, even as the Dow rose 0.85 percent to 50,018.70 — its first close above 50,000 in about a week — on strength in health care and consumer stocks.

With US markets closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and trading ending early on Friday, investors face a thin, holiday-shortened stretch in which moves can be amplified. Whether the AI trade steadies or keeps falling may depend less on any single company than on the inflation data and the market's verdict on how much more the data-centre boom is worth.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN
  • Barron's

link.title: Nasdaq slides about 3% as AI sell-off deepens ahead of Thanksgiving

entry.title: AI replaces teachers at $75,000-a-year grade schools opening across Los Angeles
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A new kind of private school has opened in Los Angeles, where artificial intelligence — not a teacher — delivers the core lessons. Alpha School launched its first classes this year in Santa Monica, Playa Vista and Malibu, charging more than $75,000 a year, with no homework and no traditional teachers in the room.

The school's model compresses the academic day. Pupils spend about two hours working silently through personalised lessons on Alpha's software, called TimeBack, which adapts to each child's level and requires a score above 90 percent before they can move on. Alpha says those two hours cover what a conventional school takes six hours to teach. The rest of the day is spent on projects, field trips, coding, sport and practical workshops — building bookshelves, designing toy prototypes on 3D printers, even surfing.

The adults supervising are called guides, not teachers, and often have no formal teaching background. A University of Colorado policy centre estimated that about a third of Alpha's guides have education training or degrees. The lessons draw on AI systems from companies including Anthropic and OpenAI, although pupils do not chat directly with tools such as Claude or ChatGPT.

Alpha was founded in Austin, Texas, in 2014, and its biggest investor, tech entrepreneur Joe Liemandt, committed $1 billion to the school in 2022. The network has grown from 20 campuses to 50 this year, nine of them in California, and Alpha says its pupils learn twice as much as their peers in mainstream schools.

Education experts urge caution. They say the approach is experimental, that young children need a trained adult in the room, and that there has not yet been enough independent testing to know whether it works or is safe. "So much of learning happens collaboratively and in conversation with humans," said Anne Blackstock-Bernstein, a lecturer at UCLA. "Until we have more time with this sort of technology, it's going to be hard to know exactly what is lost when you do that with a machine." Morgan Polikoff, an associate professor at the University of Southern California, said Alpha should open itself up to rigorous external research. Alpha says it has given independent researchers access to its student data, though that research is still in its early stages.

The contrast with public schools is sharp. The Los Angeles Unified School District has placed a moratorium on generative AI on school-issued devices for this school year, and other Southern California districts bar younger pupils from consumer AI tools altogether. In the long term, Alpha hopes to bring its system into public schools, and it is planning further openings in Southern California, including Beverly Hills.

Two months into the school year, the parents who enrolled their children say they are happier — and free of homework. Whether a machine can replace a teacher at scale remains an open question, and one that educators across the country will be watching.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Los Angeles Times
  • DNYUZ

link.title: AI replaces teachers at $75,000-a-year grade schools opening across Los Angeles

entry.title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners as China faces the highest rates
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Trump administration has proposed a new round of tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union, in its latest attempt to rebuild the sweeping import taxes the US Supreme Court struck down earlier this year.

The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the duties on Wednesday after an eight-month investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a law that lets Washington penalise countries it finds are treating American businesses unfairly. The inquiry, which began in March, examined what the administration calls "structural excess capacity" — factories abroad producing far more steel, cars, computer chips and solar panels than their home markets can absorb, then selling the surplus cheaply overseas.

China faces the steepest charges. The US proposes a 20% excess-capacity tariff on Chinese goods, on top of roughly 25% in duties imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. That rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce between Washington and Beijing, due to expire on 10 January, falls apart. Vietnam faces up to 35% if its talks with Washington fail, or 20% if a deal is reached.

The other partners face lower rates, capped by trade deals already agreed with the administration. The European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland would be capped at 15%; Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh at 18%; India at 17% if a deal is finalised, or 25% if talks fail; and Singapore at 10%. Mexico and Norway were not targeted in this round. The USTR also proposed a 10% tariff on Brazilian Embraer commercial aircraft and higher duties on Brazilian sugar above import quotas.

The duties will not take effect immediately. They are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing scheduled for 25 January, and are not expected to come into force until next year. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the measures would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy."

The European Commission rejected the move, pointing out that tariffs on EU goods are limited to the 15% already agreed. The announcement also comes as the tariffs face growing political pressure at home: they have contributed to higher prices for American consumers, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the Republicans' midterm losses found 62% of respondents supported efforts to repeal them.

The new measures mark the administration's most determined effort yet to restore the "Liberation Day" tariffs it announced in April 2025, which the Supreme Court ruled illegal in February because they had been imposed under emergency powers. Section 301, the route chosen this time, is widely seen as harder to challenge in court — though the caps agreed in existing trade deals mean many countries may see only a modest rise in the cost of trading with the United States.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Reuters

link.title: US proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners as China faces the highest rates

entry.title: Sleep and anxiety drugs still reach one in three older adults with failing memory
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Older adults living with dementia or other cognitive disorders are especially vulnerable to the harmful effects of common anxiety and sleep medicines — and a new American study finds that nearly one in three of them are still taking drugs that could make their thinking worse.

The research, from the University at Buffalo and published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society, tracked the medication use of 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently. Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing about 29.7 million older Americans between 2011 and 2022.

The news was encouraging, up to a point. Exposure to potentially inappropriate medicines fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022 — a steady, decade-long improvement. But the researchers were clear that the remaining share is still too high. "One-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good," said first author Haowen Hsu, a postdoctoral fellow in pharmacy practice at the university.

The drugs in question act on the central nervous system: benzodiazepines such as Xanax, prescribed for anxiety, and sleep medicines such as Ambien. In older adults whose nervous systems are already compromised by cognitive disorders, they can impair memory and thinking, as well as balance and coordination. The potential consequences include more emergency-room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

To identify the risky medicines, the team used the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, a list of roughly 100 drugs that may pose risks to older adults. They then focused on those that present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

The answer, the researchers say, is not to stop medicines abruptly but to review them carefully. Older adults who have taken these drugs for years may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dose, or gradual discontinuation — a process the researchers call "deprescribing." In some cases a milder alternative can be substituted. They also suggest that care teams use tools such as the Drug Burden Index, which measures the combined effect of medicines acting on the central nervous system.

The work is part of Team Alice, an interdisciplinary initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety. It is named for Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 after being prescribed a muscle relaxant flagged as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognised, and she died after six weeks of preventable complications. Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared the story with university researchers in the hope of driving systemic change.

The findings land as the world's population ages rapidly. According to a recent US Census Bureau report, adults aged 65 and older now outnumber children from birth through age five worldwide for the first time in human history — and nearly 75% of those older adults live with at least two chronic health conditions, which often means taking more medicines.

The study did not examine what caused the decade-long decline in risky prescribing, though Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians. Further research is still needed to establish whether better medication use improves quality of life and reduces hospital admissions for older adults with cognitive difficulties. For now, the researchers say, thorough medication reviews at routine appointments are the simplest safeguard — because the patients least able to tolerate these drugs are the ones still most likely to receive them.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ScienceDaily
