entry.title: Fed's preferred inflation gauge climbs to 3.8% in October, locking in a December rate rise
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

US inflation picked up again in October, with the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge rising to 3.8% from a year earlier — nearly twice the central bank's 2% target — and all but guaranteeing another interest-rate increase next month.

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, published by the Bureau of Economic Analysis on Wednesday, rose 0.3% on the month. The annual rate climbed from a revised 3.7% in September, matching economists' expectations. Core PCE, which strips out volatile food and energy prices and is watched most closely by the Fed, rose to 3.3% from 3.1% — its highest level in nearly three years and slightly above forecasts.

The report was the last major inflation reading before the Fed's final policy meeting of the year, on December 8–9. Traders now price in a near-certain quarter-point increase, which would lift the benchmark rate to a range of 4% to 4.25%. The odds of a further rise in January stand at roughly 56%, according to the CME FedWatch Tool.

The figures land at an awkward moment for the central bank. The Fed held rates steady in October to get a clearer picture of price trends, after raising them by a quarter point in September. Instead of cooling, inflation has moved the other way, and the question facing policymakers is no longer whether to raise rates in December, but how far to go in 2027.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller has floated raising rates by a quarter point in both December and January, or by half a point in December alone. Others on the rate-setting committee have been more cautious, and the split reflects a wider tension: borrowing costs are already biting for households and businesses, yet price pressures have not been tamed.

Markets took the data largely in stride. Treasury yields slipped after a flurry of Wednesday releases, which also included a second estimate of third-quarter economic growth. Investors appear to have accepted a December rise as a done deal; the bigger open question is whether the Fed signals more tightening to come next year, at a time when stocks have already been sliding on worries about the artificial-intelligence boom.

The next reading of the Fed's preferred gauge is due on December 23 — two weeks after policymakers wrap up their final meeting of the year. Until then, the October numbers leave the central bank with little room to pause: inflation is rising, core pressures are at a near-three-year high, and the target is still a long way off.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • Barron's
  • FXStreet

entry.title: Lukoil's overseas assets sold to Boehly-led US consortium in a $10 billion share swap
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A US-led consortium headed by billionaire Todd Boehly has agreed to acquire the international energy business of Lukoil, Russia's second-largest oil producer, in a deal that gives Washington an ownership stake and ends more than a year of fraught negotiations over the sanctioned company's overseas empire.

The consortium — Boehly's investment firm Eldridge, the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), UAE-based Catena Investment Holding and US investment bank Xtellus Partners — announced a definitive agreement on Wednesday to buy LUKOIL International GmbH, the unit that holds the group's assets outside Russia.

No cash will change hands. Instead, the buyers will hand over Lukoil securities worth about $10 billion, bought from US and British funds and depositary banks that held them on behalf of retail investors. Those shares were frozen after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and written down as near-worthless in the West. Under the deal they will be held in a restricted custodial account in the United Arab Emirates for five years, or until sanctions are lifted.

The portfolio being sold is sprawling: oil and gas operations in 11 countries producing around 350,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day, three refineries in Bulgaria, the Netherlands and Romania, some 2,000 filling stations across 16 countries in Europe, North America and Central Asia, and an international trading business. Reuters reported the package is valued at roughly $16 billion. Boehly said closing the deal could take up to a year, and that the venture would be renamed.

The DFC's participation gives the US government an equity stake — its size undisclosed — entitling Washington to a share of future profits once the private investors have recouped their capital plus an agreed return, and a role on the company's governing board.

The sale was forced by sanctions. The US Treasury sanctioned Lukoil more than a year ago in a bid to cut off revenue funding Moscow's war in Ukraine. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London, told CNN the deal showed sanctions working: a company that spent decades building an international footprint is being made to give it up, removing both future earnings and a lever of influence over energy infrastructure in Europe and beyond.

It caps a long and messy sale process. An offer from Swiss commodities trader Gunvor collapsed after failing to win Treasury approval, and private equity firm Carlyle's provisional agreement in January lapsed in July without a Treasury decision; Carlyle walked away in October.

The new agreement is not yet done. It still needs conditional approval from the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which has previously rejected a similar share-swap structure, and it carries a 60-day exclusivity period to finalise terms.

entry.title: Hera reveals a stadium-sized crater on the asteroid NASA struck
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Four years after NASA slammed a spacecraft into an asteroid to test whether humanity could deflect a dangerous space rock, Europe's follow-up mission has shown what the blow actually did — and the damage is far greater than expected.

The European Space Agency released the first close-up images of Dimorphos on Wednesday, taken by its Hera spacecraft. The 151-metre-wide moonlet, which orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos, now has one side flattened into a crater the size of a sports stadium — a scar that spans the entire width of the face NASA's DART probe struck.

"The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width," said Patrick Michel, the mission's principal investigator.

The surprise was not only the crater. The rest of Dimorphos looks much as it did before the impact, its boulder fields apparently unchanged — yet the moonlet itself is now tumbling chaotically in its orbit, its steady spin knocked out of kilter by the blow.

Hera also found the asteroid pair surrounded by hundreds of boulders drifting in space, some just a few metres across, with more than 100 of them between the size of a football and a washing machine. The debris cloud is a hazard the mission team must now take into account as Hera moves closer.

DART — the Double Asteroid Redirection Test — hit Dimorphos on 26 September 2022 at about 22,500 kilometres per hour, shortening its 11-hour-55-minute orbit around Didymos by 33 minutes. It was the first time humans had deliberately changed the motion of a celestial body, a proof of concept for planetary defence: if an asteroid were ever found heading for Earth, a spacecraft impact might nudge it aside.

But until Hera arrived, scientists could only guess at what the impact had done to the asteroid itself. Hera, a car-sized spacecraft launched in October 2024, reached the system about three weeks ago and is now observing from 25 to 30 kilometres away. It will move to within about 13 kilometres next month, and in January it will release two shoebox-sized CubeSats to probe even closer — one to map the surface minerals, the other to peer inside Dimorphos with ground-penetrating radar.

The images were unveiled by mission manager Ian Carnelli in the dinosaur hall of Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde — a deliberate reminder of what an asteroid impact did 66 million years ago.

"NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit," Carnelli said. "Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself."

The Didymos system is currently about 193.5 million kilometres from Earth. What Hera measures over the coming months — the crater's depth, Dimorphos's exact mass, the structure of the rubble inside — will decide whether the deflection technique can be trusted the next time it matters.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • ESA
  • Reuters
  • CNN

entry.title: Israeli judges urge prosecutors to drop Netanyahu's most serious corruption case
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The judges hearing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's corruption trial told prosecutors on Wednesday that the most serious case against him should be dropped — a dramatic intervention in a prosecution that has run for more than six years.

The three-judge panel of the Jerusalem District Court summoned Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara to the hearing and said the bribery case, known as Case 4000, was unlikely to end in a conviction. The presiding judge, Rivka Friedman-Feldman, said the charge presented "considerable difficulties" and that the prospects of a conviction were low enough to justify reconsidering the case.

In Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours worth around 1.8 billion shekels — about $500 million — to the telecoms company Bezeq, and in return sought favourable coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, on the Walla news website, then controlled by Bezeq's former chairman, Shaul Elovitch. Netanyahu faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in the case, the most serious of the three against him.

The judges went further than they had before. They had twice previously urged prosecutors to reconsider the bribery charge, in June 2023 and again in June of this year. On Wednesday, they said their doubts extended to the fraud and breach-of-trust charges in the same case as well.

They also recommended that prosecutors reconsider a second case, Case 2000, in which Netanyahu is accused of negotiating an arrangement with Arnon Mozes, the owner of the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, under which he would receive more favourable coverage in return for legislation slowing the growth of a rival paper. The judges said they were not convinced the conduct described in the indictment amounted to a criminal offence.

On the third case, Case 1000, the judges struck a different note. That case concerns gifts, including cigars and champagne, that Netanyahu is alleged to have received from wealthy businessmen. The judges did not suggest dropping it; instead they said the prosecution and defence should try to reach an agreement and find a procedural path to bring it to a conclusion.

The court stressed that its comments were recommendations, not a verdict, and reflected its impressions at this stage of the trial. Baharav-Miara told the court she would review the judges' statements with the prosecution team. The judges also made clear that their assessment concerned Netanyahu alone; dropping the charges against him would not automatically end the prosecution of Shaul and Iris Elovitch, whose liability would need separate consideration.

Netanyahu, who was indicted in 2019 and whose trial began in May 2020, welcomed the development and said the trial "must end". He has denied wrongdoing throughout.

The hearing came after the completion of Netanyahu's own testimony, which the court said had brought the proceedings to a point requiring a fresh assessment. There is also a practical clock running: Friedman-Feldman, who heads the panel, is due to retire in March 2028.

No charges have been withdrawn yet. But the judges' message was unmistakable: two of the three cases may not be sustainable.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Times of Israel
  • The Jerusalem Post

entry.title: Russian refinery runs fall to lowest in more than 20 years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Illustration — not a photograph.

Russia's oil refineries are processing crude at their lowest rate in more than two decades, according to new estimates, as Ukraine's sustained campaign of strikes on energy infrastructure takes an increasing toll on the country's fuel supply.

Russian refineries were processing between 2.6 million and 2.7 million barrels of oil a day as of Monday, according to Rystad Energy, a Norwegian energy research firm. That is roughly half the level recorded on October 30, and below the previous multi-year lows seen during earlier waves of attacks this year.

The figures come from Viktor Kurilov, a senior oil analyst at Rystad, and were first reported by Bloomberg. Ukraine launched a new wave of strikes on Russian refineries at the end of last month, hitting plants almost daily. According to a Bloomberg tally, at least 18 refineries have been attacked since late October — though that does not mean all of their capacity has been knocked out. Some plants kept running at reduced rates after earlier strikes, while others restored production quickly.

The decline is already showing up at Russian petrol stations. Average retail gasoline prices rose 0.5% in the week from November 17 to 23, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service — the largest weekly increase since early September. The domestic fuel market has faced repeated shortages since the summer, and Moscow has responded by restricting gasoline and jet-fuel exports, allowing fuel imports, and redirecting supplies to the regions hit hardest.

Measuring the damage is difficult. Since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia has classified nearly all data on its oil industry. Rystad builds its estimates from oil supply chains, tanker movements, satellite imagery, and information from industry sources. Its latest figure does not yet include the effect of strikes on Wednesday against two refineries in the Samara region.

The squeeze on refining has had a knock-on effect beyond Russia's borders. Crude oil that Russian plants can no longer process is being redirected for export instead, adding to a surplus in global supply.

For Ukraine, the refinery campaign has become a central part of its strategy: by hitting the plants that turn crude into fuel, it aims to strain Russia's war economy and its domestic market at the same time. For Russian consumers, the cost is already visible in the price at the pump — and, with strikes continuing, analysts expect the pressure to persist.

Sources

  • Bloomberg
  • Ukrinform

link.title: Russian refinery runs fall to lowest in more than 20 years

entry.title: Dow claws back from a 1,100-point plunge to close higher in a wild pre-Thanksgiving session
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Wall Street staged one of its wildest turnarounds in years on Wednesday, as the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell more than 1,100 points in early trading and then recovered the entire loss to close higher — its biggest intraday reversal into positive territory since 2022.

The Dow finished up 164.25 points, or 0.33%, at 50,182.95. At its low of the day it had been down about 2.2%. The S&P 500 also clawed back most of its losses but still ended 0.25% lower at 7,182.78, after falling as much as 3.2% during the session. The Nasdaq Composite closed 0.62% lower at 23,585.80, having been down as much as 4.6% at its worst.

The selling began with a batch of morning economic data that gave investors two worries at once. The second estimate of third-quarter growth came in at a 4.3% annual rate, well above the earlier 3.4% reading, while the core inflation measure watched by the Federal Reserve hit a three-year high. Strong growth paired with sticky inflation raised doubts about further interest-rate cuts, and a fresh tariff threat added to the pressure.

Chip stocks bore the brunt of it. Nvidia, the market's most watched artificial-intelligence name, ended about 4% lower after a far steeper drop earlier in the day, and the technology sector was the only one of the market's eleven major groups to finish in the red — down just 0.8% after being off 5.5% at its low.

The turn came around midday, when bargain hunters stepped in. Eight of the eleven S&P 500 sectors finished higher, and advancing stocks outnumbered decliners by nearly three to one on the New York Stock Exchange. The breadth of the recovery was the session's most encouraging sign: most stocks rose even as the headline indexes stayed mixed, suggesting the selling was concentrated in the big technology names rather than spreading across the whole market.

The rebound also carried the Dow to a second straight close above 50,000, a level it had only recently reached for the first time.

Whether the calm holds is far from settled. The Nasdaq remains close to its lows of the correction, and the same questions that drove the selloff — whether spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and whether inflation will stay high enough to keep rates elevated — are still unanswered. Volatility stayed high, with the market's fear gauge, the VIX, up more than 7% on the day.

Trading now pauses for Thanksgiving. US markets are closed on Thursday and reopen for a shortened session on Friday, closing at 1 p.m. Eastern time.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • MarketWatch

entry.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade moves to Saturday in first postponement of its 100-year history
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not march on Thanksgiving Day. Organisers announced on Wednesday that the parade is postponed until Saturday, November 28, because of a major storm forecast for New York City — the first time in the event's history that it has been moved to another day.

The parade will now begin at 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday. It is the first postponement since the parade began in 1924. The only other times it has missed Thanksgiving Day were 1942 to 1944, when it was suspended during World War II — but it has never before been rescheduled because of weather.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.

The decision was driven by the giant balloons, the parade's signature feature. A strong coastal storm, or nor'easter, is expected to track up the East Coast through Thanksgiving Day, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and significant coastal flooding. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for New York City for Thursday into Friday, with gusts forecast to reach 50 to 60 mph.

City rules require the balloons to be grounded if sustained winds exceed 23 mph and gusts exceed 34 mph. That threshold was set after high winds sent a balloon crashing into a lamppost during the 1997 parade, seriously injuring a spectator. Weather has grounded all of the parade's balloons only once, in 1971.

This year's parade was set to be the biggest yet, with a record 100 balloons, performances from nine Broadway shows and appearances by musicians including Raye, Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Natasha Bedingfield and Keke Palmer. By Saturday the storm is expected to have cleared, with milder weather forecast for the rescheduled march.

NBC, which broadcasts the parade, will air a rerun of the 2025 parade on Thursday morning instead. The 2026 parade will be televised live on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET on NBC, Peacock and Telemundo.

For many Americans, watching the parade is as much a part of Thanksgiving as the meal itself, and millions line the Manhattan route each year. This time, the wait will be two days longer — and the 100th parade will make its debut on a Saturday instead.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • CNN

entry.title: Fuel tanker crash ignites deadly fire on Cairo ring road, killing 31
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

At least 31 people were killed and 21 injured after a fuel tanker overturned and caught fire on a major ring road near Cairo on Wednesday evening, Egypt's health ministry said.

The tanker, which was carrying petroleum products, crashed on the Ring Road in the Al-Warraq district of Giza, on the western edge of the capital. The fire broke out above a tunnel on the busy highway, which links the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia.

State-owned media reported that a high-voltage cable fell in front of the tanker, causing the driver to lose control. The vehicle crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire. The tanker belonged to a private contractor, according to the reports.

Thirty-nine ambulances took part in the rescue operation, the health ministry said. Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering from burns and smoke inhalation. Emergency crews worked through the night at the scene, and the highway was later cleared and reopened.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the death toll could still rise. DNA testing was under way to identify victims, after the fire left many of those killed unrecognisable.

The crash is one of the deadliest road accidents in Egypt in recent years. The country's roads have a long record of serious crashes, driven by speeding, poor road conditions and lax enforcement — a problem the authorities have repeatedly pledged to tackle, with limited success.

Investigators from the public prosecution are examining the circumstances of the crash, including the fallen cable and the tanker's condition. No official cause has yet been confirmed beyond the initial reports of the cable falling into the road.

For the families of those killed, the wait for identification will be agonising. For Cairo's commuters, the fire was a stark reminder of how quickly an ordinary evening journey can turn catastrophic on one of the region's busiest highways.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • BBC
  • Reuters

link.title: Fuel tanker crash ignites deadly fire on Cairo ring road, killing 31

entry.title: Judge blocks FCC's early review of ABC station licenses in First Amendment win for Disney
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal judge on Wednesday barred the Federal Communications Commission from continuing its early review of ABC's broadcast licenses, ruling that the agency's action appeared to be retaliation for programming critical of President Donald Trump.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction halting the review of the network's eight company-owned television stations. "This is not a close case," she wrote, adding that ABC had a weighty interest in vindicating its right "to be free of retaliation for (their) protected speech."

Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August after the commission ordered all eight stations to apply for license renewals years ahead of schedule. The stations' licenses were not otherwise due for renewal until between 2028 and 2031.

The timing was central to the judge's reasoning. The FCC launched the early review on April 28, one day after Trump criticised remarks by late-night host Jimmy Kimmel and called for his firing. The commission has maintained that the review was prompted by Disney's diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and its response to an investigation into the company's employment practices. AliKhan wrote that she did not find that explanation credible, and said FCC Chair Brendan Carr "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders."

The judge found that ABC was likely to succeed on its First Amendment claim and that the retaliatory proceedings themselves caused irreparable harm, even before any license was revoked. She also denied the FCC's motion to dismiss Disney's lawsuit.

A win with limits

The ruling does not end the dispute, and it does not stop the FCC from continuing its investigations into Disney's employment practices or its scrutiny of the daytime show "The View." AliKhan also declined ABC's request for a broader injunction barring the FCC from threatening the company over its editorial decisions.

"No one doubts that the Commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit," she wrote. "But in doing so, Defendants may not retaliate against or punish Plaintiffs and other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech."

The case has been closely watched as a test of whether a regulator can use broadcast licensing — a power that can, in theory, take a station off the air — as leverage over a network's editorial choices. Press advocates called the decision an important win not only for ABC but for all broadcasters.

What happens next

The FCC has until December 2 to report back to the court on its compliance with the injunction. Both sides are due to submit a joint proposal for the next steps in the case by December 9. As a condition of the injunction, ABC and Disney were ordered to post a bond of $1.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The New York Times
  • Reuters

link.title: Judge blocks FCC's early review of ABC station licenses in First Amendment win for Disney

entry.title: Pakistan's first astronaut boards China's Tiangong station in historic first
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

China's space station has welcomed its first foreign visitor. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan Air Force pilot, boarded the Tiangong station on Wednesday after his Shenzhou-24 spacecraft launched from the Gobi Desert and docked about three and a half hours later — a first for Pakistan, and a first for China's crewed space programme.

The Long March 2F rocket lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre at 8:18 a.m. Beijing time, carrying Ali alongside Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi. The spacecraft separated from its rocket roughly ten minutes after launch and entered orbit, and the China Manned Space Agency confirmed the docking later that morning. The three men entered the station on Wednesday afternoon, where the Shenzhou-23 crew already living aboard greeted them.

Ali is serving as a payload specialist on the mission. He is expected to spend around a week at the station — reports put the stay at five to ten days — running scientific experiments, including work in biotechnology and materials science, before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft. He is the first Pakistani to travel into orbit, and the first foreign national to set foot on Tiangong.

The flight is the product of a space cooperation agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025. Ali and his backup, Khurram Daud, have been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing since April. The mission also coincides with the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and Pakistan's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, congratulated the nation as the launch went ahead, saying Pakistan had begun its journey "beyond the stars."

For China, the mission extends a programme that has moved quickly since Tiangong became fully operational in late 2022. Shenzhou-24 is the country's 18th crewed spaceflight, and for Tang Hongbo it is a record of sorts: he has now visited Tiangong three times, more than any other astronaut.

Tiangong — "Celestial Palace" — has until now been crewed exclusively by Chinese astronauts, in contrast to the International Space Station, which has hosted visitors from many nations. Beijing has said it wants to open its station to international partners, and Ali's flight is the first concrete step: a guest astronaut, on a short stay, doing joint science rather than simply visiting.

What comes next is still open. Pakistan's space agency, Suparco, says Pakistani science payloads will now begin work in the station's Wentian and Mengtian laboratories. Whether other countries follow — and whether short guest missions become a regular feature of Tiangong — will be watched closely by space agencies weighing how to work with China's station in the years ahead.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • Dawn
  • Channel News Asia

link.title: Pakistan's first astronaut boards China's Tiangong station in historic first

entry.title: Anthropic chief says handing governance to AI would be 'a bad idea'
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has said it would be "a bad idea" for humanity to hand the job of governing society to artificial intelligence, rejecting the suggestion that he believes people should surrender their free will to machines.

Amodei made the argument in a lengthy post on X on Wednesday, responding to an Axios report that described a growing divide among leaders of the leading AI labs over how much authority superintelligent systems should be given. The report, citing people familiar with internal discussions, said some Anthropic employees believed humanity would safely hand authority to superintelligent systems — and often should — rather than fight to keep control.

"We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination on the altar of efficiency or security," Amodei wrote. "This argument against autocracy applies word for word to governance by AI, and I feel just as strongly that handing over governance to AI is a bad idea."

He called it "absurd" to suggest he held the opposite view, pointing to hundreds of pages of essays in which he has argued that AI must be governed through legitimate democratic processes. Political decisions, he said, should stay in human hands, and he rejected handing power to AI as firmly as he rejected autocracy.

Amodei drew a sharp line between governing and doing. Letting AI systems take on specific, complex tasks — driving a car, designing a cancer drug, writing software end to end — is a different matter from giving up free will in politics, he argued. That kind of automation is "clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives," he wrote, but it also has downsides, and in some areas it may not be worth it. In many cases, he added, people would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, "so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better."

He also set out where he believes the real safety line falls: recursive self-improvement, or AI systems building successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human oversight. Anthropic does not consider it safe for its Claude models to do that fully autonomously, he said, and safety research must keep pace with improvements in AI capabilities.

The post comes as the industry's leaders argue openly about the future. Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, has separately written that society should not accept a "handover" to AI. Amodei, meanwhile, criticised rival executives who repeat slogans about "human control and agency" while shipping products built for more and more automation.

Amodei also pointed to Anthropic's own record as evidence of where it draws lines. The company refused to allow its existing models to be used for autonomous weapons during its dispute with the Pentagon, he wrote — a refusal he said he was willing to risk Anthropic's future over, "even in the face of legal sanctions."

The debate is not abstract for Anthropic. The company went public on Nasdaq on November 19 in what has been described as the largest initial public offering in history, putting its stance on AI governance under sharper scrutiny from investors and policymakers alike. Amodei's message was that the company's position has not changed: AI can take on more of the work, but the decisions about how society is run are not its to make.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Decoder
  • TechCrunch

link.title: Anthropic chief says handing governance to AI would be 'a bad idea'

entry.title: Every American child to get two SpaceX shares in $18bn pledge, Musk says
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Elon Musk has said every child in the United States will receive two shares in SpaceX — one from the company and one from him personally — in a pledge worth more than $18 billion.

Musk announced the plan in a brief post on X on Wednesday, without giving details of how or when the shares would be delivered. "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," he wrote.

SpaceX had said earlier in the day that it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, and that Musk would personally match the number of shares the company donates. Trump Accounts are a government programme designed to give Americans born between 2025 and 2028 a stake in the stock market and help them build wealth from an early age.

With about 72 million children under 18 in the US, and SpaceX shares closing at $127.44 on Wednesday, the combined pledge is valued at around $18.35 billion. On the roughly 70 million active Trump Accounts reported by the White House, the figure would be about $17.8 billion.

"Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," Musk added in his post.

It is not the first such gift from inside SpaceX. President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband had already pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than two million children under the Trump initiative. Other companies have joined the programme too: Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell and his wife pledged a $6.25 billion cash gift.

The pledge is a small fraction of Musk's fortune, which Bloomberg estimates at about $813 billion, most of it tied to his SpaceX stake. He owns 849.4 million shares of SpaceX's Class A common stock, according to regulatory filings, alongside billions of Class B shares with greater voting power and a large holding in Tesla.

Some details remain unclear. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's personal share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts or come with any kind of lockup period — a restriction that would stop recipients selling the shares for a set time. Musk had already said last month that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America, and Wednesday's announcement turns that idea into a matching commitment from both the company and its chief executive.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Morningstar

link.title: Every American child to get two SpaceX shares in $18bn pledge, Musk says

entry.title: Google patent sketches an AI TV channel where you star in every show
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Google has sketched out a television channel with an audience of one: you. A patent application published by the US Patent and Trademark Office last week describes "My Channel", a feed of AI-generated shows tailored to a single viewer — with that viewer cast as the lead.

The filing, titled "Creating a Channel of Video Experiences Tailored to a User", was submitted on May 13, 2025 and published on November 19, 2026. It names two Google engineers, Aravind Reddy Ayuluri and Prameela Kavya Thummuru, as the inventors. The idea was first spotted by patent-tracking site Patentlyze and reported by 404 Media.

Instead of recommending shows that already exist, the system would ask a large language model to generate new video on the spot. It would draw on a viewer's watch history, preferences, demographic details such as age group, and device data such as language and location, and turn all of it into a prompt for the model. The result would appear as a channel on the TV home screen, labelled with the viewer's name and filled with tiles for shows made for them.

The filing goes further than tailored recommendations. In one version, the system would build a digital likeness of the viewer from their photographs and synthesise their voice, placing them at the centre of the story. A sample prompt in the application reads: "You are a customized video generating model. Generate a customized video for a user where the user will play the protagonist." The genres could range from romantic comedies to science-fiction adventures, following the style of whatever the viewer watches most.

Shows could be generated on request, or without any request — the filing describes automatic scheduling on a weekly, monthly or yearly basis. A second model could pull in current news, trends and sports scores to shape what gets made. And there is room for commercials: in one version, the video would be sent to an advertising server that inserts ads before streaming it to the TV.

There are two important caveats. First, a patent filing is not a product: Google has announced no plans to build My Channel, and the filing names no launch date. Second, according to Patentlyze, a patent examiner has already issued a final rejection of the application — though Google can still amend its claims or appeal.

Even so, the filing is a window into where television could be heading. YouTube, which Google owns, unveiled Custom Feeds earlier this autumn, letting viewers build hyper-specific homepages. A channel that generates its own shows would be the next step: no shared schedule, no shared hits, everyone watching something made only for them. As 404 Media noted, that could also mean fewer moments when many people watch the same thing and talk about it afterwards.

For now, the starring role is hypothetical. But the patent shows how much a TV knows about its owner — and how little stands between that knowledge and a show with your face in it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Gizmodo
  • Business Standard

link.title: Google patent sketches an AI TV channel where you star in every show

entry.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Andy Taylor, the guitarist whose riffs helped make Duran Duran one of the defining bands of the 1980s, has died at the age of 65.

Taylor died at home on Monday, surrounded by his family, after living with metastatic prostate cancer. His death was announced on Wednesday in a joint statement from his family and his former bandmates.

Taylor was diagnosed with the disease in 2018. He went public with it four years later, when his health prevented him from attending Duran Duran's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.

Born in 1961 in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, Taylor picked up the guitar at the age of 11 and left school to tour England and Europe with a series of bands. He moved to Birmingham and joined Duran Duran in 1980, a year before the group released its debut album. Global fame followed with 1982's Rio, and Taylor co-wrote some of the band's biggest hits, including "Hungry Like the Wolf", "Rio" and "Girls on Film", as well as "The Reflex".

His guitar work — muscular, melodic and unmistakably his own — gave the band's polished pop a harder edge, and helped carry Duran Duran from the Birmingham club scene to stadiums and the early days of MTV. The group went on to win two Grammy Awards, and Taylor was later inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with his bandmates.

Away from Duran Duran, Taylor recorded as a solo artist, releasing his debut album Thunder in 1987, and played in the supergroup The Power Station alongside Duran Duran bassist John Taylor and singer Robert Palmer.

In the family statement, his wife, Tracy Wilson-Taylor, said: "To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather."

The band's surviving members — Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes, John Taylor and Roger Taylor — said Taylor had been there "at the very beginning of our story", arriving in Birmingham from the north-east "with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become". He brought, they said, "an indelible fire and swagger to our music", and faced his illness "with courage, honesty and grace". Le Bon added that there was now "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

Tributes arrived quickly from across the music world, including from Sir Rod Stewart, who called Taylor a dear friend, and singer Belinda Carlisle. Taylor is survived by his wife, their four children and a grandson.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • People

link.title: Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor dies aged 65

entry.title: Webb finds the farthest 'little red dot' yet, from the universe's first 500 million years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have found the most distant "little red dot" yet discovered — a faint, compact object that appears to have existed just 400 to 500 million years after the Big Bang.

The object, named CW-LRD-z10, sits at a redshift of 10.36, meaning its light set out when the universe was roughly 450 million years old. The finding is reported in a new study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Little red dots are small, intensely red points of light that Webb first began detecting in 2022. Many are thought to be young supermassive black holes, still growing, wrapped in dense gas and dust. They have become a central puzzle because they suggest giant black holes were already in place far earlier than most theories predicted — yet until now, every one found had existed between 600 million and 1.5 billion years after the Big Bang.

The new object pushes that record back by a wide margin. The previous most distant little red dot with a measured redshift stood at 9.288.

The discovery was led by Takumi Tanaka, a graduate student at the University of Tokyo's Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe, working with professor John Silverman and an international team, using high-resolution infrared images from Webb's COSMOS-Web survey.

Finding it took a new approach. Webb's near-infrared camera can only study light at wavelengths between 0.6 and 5 micrometres, but light from such a distant object has been stretched far beyond that range by the expansion of the universe. The team combined data from the near-infrared camera, NIRCam, with the mid-infrared instrument, MIRI, to pick out the tiny object in its characteristic red.

The team then confirmed the distance with spectroscopy. The spectrum showed the Lyman-alpha break — the sharp drop in light caused by absorption from neutral hydrogen in the early universe — along with emission lines from hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and iron. It closely matches previously discovered little red dots, confirming CW-LRD-z10 as the most distant one yet.

One caveat remains: CW-LRD-z10 is still a candidate, not a confirmed black hole. The broad hydrogen lines that would clearly show a feeding black hole are stretched beyond this spectrum's reach, and the data cannot yet rule out that some of the light comes from star formation.

That uncertainty is part of why the object matters. If little red dots are the seeds of the supermassive black holes at the centres of most galaxies today, finding one this early narrows the window in which those seeds had to form. Theories have suggested such precursors could have appeared around 500 million years after the Big Bang — and now there is an object sitting almost exactly in that era.

Next, the team plans to study CW-LRD-z10 in more detail, examining its hydrogen emission lines for signs of black hole activity. Finding more little red dots from the same early epoch should help pin down when they first appeared and how they formed.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Phys.org
  • The Astrophysical Journal Letters

link.title: Webb finds the farthest 'little red dot' yet, from the universe's first 500 million years

entry.title: Judge declines to extend ban on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads, but says Democrats may yet win the case
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A federal judge on Wednesday declined to extend a ban on taxpayer-funded television ads that promoted President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, ruling that Democrats had not shown they were likely to win an immediate court order — even as she said they may ultimately succeed in proving the ads broke the law.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., refused a preliminary injunction sought by the Democratic National Committee, which sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. The DNC argued the spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda designed to promote the president's campaign message in the weeks before November's midterm elections.

AliKhan noted that her earlier temporary restraining order had been issued when the election was less than a week away. "But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone," she wrote. The DNC argued it could still be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections, or because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun. "At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded," she wrote.

She also rejected the party's argument that campaigns are effectively permanent. Taken to its logical conclusion, she wrote, that reasoning "would allow the DNC to seek preliminary relief in perpetuity because it could always point to the occurrence of some election somewhere in the country."

The Justice Department argued there was no threat of harm because the government had already stopped using public funds to air the ads and the midterms had passed. AliKhan's earlier order had blocked the administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through November 25.

The ruling follows a similar decision in a separate case in New York, where another judge also declined a long-term ban on the ads — though that judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to remove three of them from official government websites and social media accounts.

The decision is not the end of the case. AliKhan said the DNC was likely to succeed on its claim that using public money for the ads violated the law, and the lawsuits continue. For now, though, no court order stops the ads from airing again.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • AP News
  • AP via KSAT

link.title: Judge declines to extend ban on taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads, but says Democrats may yet win the case

entry.title: Japan unveils rover prototype to hunt for water at the Moon's south pole
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Japan's space agency has shown off a test model of the rover it plans to send to the Moon's south pole in search of water — a joint mission with India that is aiming for launch in 2028.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, JAXA, unveiled the four-legged test model to reporters in Tokyo on Wednesday, then put it through a demonstration run at its Chofu Aerospace Center. The rover moved slowly across a simulated lunar surface on caterpillar tracks fitted to its four legs, crossing rocks and a crater-shaped dip without difficulty.

The mission, known as LUPEX — Lunar Polar Exploration — is a partnership in which Japan is responsible for the rover and the H3 rocket that will carry it, while India is building the lander. The launch is planned for fiscal 2028 from the Tanegashima Space Center in Kagoshima Prefecture.

The target is water. The Moon's polar regions contain areas of permanent shadow that never see sunlight, and scientists believe water ice is likely to exist there close to the surface. Once it lands, the rover is expected to look for the most promising sites and drill up to about 1.5 metres underground to collect samples, giving scientists their first detailed data on how much water is there and in what form.

The reason goes beyond science. Water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen — the ingredients of rocket fuel — so a reliable lunar supply could one day let spacecraft refuel on the Moon instead of carrying everything from Earth. "We ultimately want to use lunar water for rocket fuel," project manager Takeshi Hoshino told reporters. He noted that more than 90 percent of the water aboard the International Space Station is recycled, but the water produced when rockets burn oxygen and hydrogen cannot be recovered — which is why producing fuel on the Moon matters for missions returning to Earth or heading onward to Mars.

The test model is being used to prove the rover can cope with the lunar surface, which is covered in fine dust called regolith. Engineers have tested it climbing slopes on a single leg, driving continuously on two legs, and moving under vacuum conditions. The flight version is still under development: JAXA's specifications put it at about 350 kilograms, roughly two metres long and 3.3 metres tall, carrying instruments including a water analyser and a drill.

The two countries agreed to pursue the mission jointly last year. India landed its Chandrayaan-3 spacecraft near the lunar south pole in 2023, and Japan made its own first soft landing on the Moon in 2024 with the SLIM probe, becoming only the fifth country to do so. Last month JAXA also launched a spacecraft to one of Mars's moons on a mission to bring back samples.

If LUPEX stays on schedule, the rover will explore the south pole for about 100 days after landing, with the results feeding into the US-led Artemis programme and longer-term plans for lunar bases.

Illustration — not a photograph.

  • The Japan Times
