entry.title: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest in nearly 30 years
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Net migration to the UK fell to 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, according to provisional figures published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) on Thursday — the lowest level since 1997, outside the coronavirus pandemic.

The figure is less than half the 204,000 recorded in the previous 12 months. An estimated 738,000 people arrived to live in the UK long term, down 17% from 893,000 a year earlier, while 661,000 left, broadly unchanged from 689,000. Net migration has now fallen by about 92% from its peak of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The fall was driven almost entirely by fewer arrivals from outside the EU. Net migration among non-EU nationals fell to 258,000, from 379,000 a year earlier, as work-related arrivals fell by 45,000, study-related arrivals by 33,000 and asylum-related arrivals by 19,000. Study remained the most common reason for coming to the UK, accounting for 257,000 arrivals, followed by work at 135,000 and asylum at 73,000.

More British and EU nationals left the UK than arrived. Net migration for British nationals stood at minus 137,000, with an estimated 245,000 British nationals emigrating during the year. Net migration for EU nationals was minus 45,000, and has been negative since the year to June 2022.

The figures reflect successive tightenings of immigration rules for workers, students and asylum seekers. The ONS said net migration had fallen to "levels not typically seen since the 1990s", as arrivals from outside the EU for work and study continued to decline.

The numbers are provisional and will be revised as fuller data arrives. The ONS warned that estimates for British nationals carry greater uncertainty than usual, because the latest registration data was unavailable for this release and the figures rest on a 15-month projection. Updated estimates are due in May 2027.

For now, the picture is a sharp reversal: after the post-pandemic surge that pushed net migration close to a million, arrivals and departures have nearly converged, leaving a net flow close to the levels of the late 1990s.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Office for National Statistics
  • The Straits Times

link.title: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest in nearly 30 years

entry.title: Cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa as first generic shipments land in Zambia
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The first shipments of a low-cost generic version of lenacapavir, a twice-yearly injection that prevents HIV infection, have arrived in Zambia, the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria announced on Wednesday.

A delivery to Uganda is expected in the coming days, and a further shipment financed by the Global Fund is due to reach Zimbabwe in early 2027. The arrivals come about a year after the branded version of the drug first became available in sub-Saharan Africa.

Lenacapavir is a long-acting form of pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP. Instead of a daily pill, it is given as an injection twice a year, and clinical evidence shows it is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection. The generic version is expected to cost about $40 per person per year, far less than the original drug developed by the US pharmaceutical company Gilead Sciences.

India's Hetero, one of the generic manufacturers, said on Thursday it had begun shipping the drug to Africa and plans to supply 300,000 vials to Zambia, Uganda and Zimbabwe. It plans to extend supply to 10 more African countries in early 2027.

Gilead has licensed six generic drugmakers, including Hetero and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, to manufacture and supply the drug in 120 low- and middle-income countries. The US Food and Drug Administration gave tentative approval to a generic version earlier this month, although it cannot be sold in the United States while Gilead's branded version, Yeztugo, remains under patent.

The rollout is moving fast. More than 189,000 people across 10 countries had received a first dose of lenacapavir as of November, according to the Global Fund, and 24 countries are expected to have received supplies by the end of 2026. The Global Fund and the US government aim to reach at least 3 million people with the drug by the end of 2028, and plan to deliver four times as much lenacapavir in 2027 as in 2026.

The evidence behind the drug is striking. In 2024 trials involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV. That result matters because daily PrEP pills, while effective, are hard for many people to take consistently — and a missed dose leaves a gap in protection.

For health systems across southern and eastern Africa, where the HIV burden remains highest, the arrival of an affordable twice-yearly option could change who gets protected. The question now is delivery: getting the injections from warehouses in Lusaka and Kampala into clinics, and from clinics to the people most at risk, in time to meet the 2028 target.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Global Fund
  • Reuters

link.title: Cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa as first generic shipments land in Zambia

entry.title: FedEx cargo jet runs off Miami runway on Thanksgiving eve; crew safe
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A FedEx cargo jet ran off the end of a runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday evening, forcing the airport to close all but one of its runways on the eve of Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year. No one was hurt.

The aircraft, a McDonnell Douglas MD-11 operating as FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis, overran runway 26R at about 8:40 p.m. local time, according to the airport. It came to a stop roughly 1,000 feet past the end of the runway, on grass near the airport's perimeter fence and short of a public road. The two crew members on board were unhurt and walked off the plane.

FedEx said the aircraft had "an issue upon landing" and that the company is cooperating with investigators. The Federal Aviation Administration said it will investigate the incident.

The disruption rippled through the airport quickly. The FAA issued a ground stop for flights heading to Miami, and all but one runway — 9R — was temporarily closed while emergency crews responded. Flights began moving again later in the evening, with the ground stop lifted at about 10:30 p.m. The timing was unwelcome: more than 500 flights at Miami had already been delayed before the incident, according to FlightAware figures, as millions of Americans travelled for the holiday.

Weather is likely to be part of the investigation. Thunderstorms and heavy rain were moving through the Miami area at the time, and a flood watch was in effect. Air Cargo News, citing meteorological data from the airport, reported rain and crosswinds around the time of the landing. What exactly caused the jet to run long remains unknown.

The incident is the second time in about three months that a cargo jet has overshot a runway at Miami. In September, an Amazon cargo jet overran a different runway, crossed a road and struck a van carrying a plane-cleaning crew, killing five people on the ground. Wednesday's jet landed on a different runway, but three of Miami's runways converge at the airport's west end, so it ended up close to the same area.

For travellers, the episode was a reminder of how quickly a single incident can snarl a holiday. For investigators, the focus now turns to the runway, the weather and the aircraft — and to why Miami, of all airports, has seen this happen twice in a season.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • People

link.title: FedEx cargo jet runs off Miami runway on Thanksgiving eve; crew safe

entry.title: FCC clears SpaceX to deploy one million satellites for data centers in space
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The Federal Communications Commission has given SpaceX permission to deploy up to one million satellites that would work as data centers in orbit, the first authorization of its kind in the United States. The decision, announced on Wednesday, hands Elon Musk's rocket company a regulatory green light for a project scientists say faces enormous technical obstacles.

The network, called Starmind, would be made up of "orbital compute modules" — satellites fitted with computer chips that process data in space for use back on Earth. SpaceX describes the idea as capturing solar energy in orbit to power low-cost, high-performance computing for artificial intelligence. The FCC called the authorization a historic first in the race to build AI infrastructure, saying the constellation would help meet rapidly growing demand for computing power.

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the decision "opens a bold new frontier" for the computing infrastructure needed to power American leadership. Musk welcomed the ruling on social media.

The license sets a long schedule: at least one satellite in orbit by November 2033, 100,000 by November 2035, half the constellation by November 2038, and the full one million by 2040. The company's chief financial officer has said it hopes to begin demonstrating the technology in 2027.

About 17,000 satellites currently orbit Earth, including just over 11,000 of SpaceX's own Starlink internet satellites. A full Starmind constellation would multiply that number roughly fiftyfold.

That scale is what worries scientists. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and author, called the prospect of launching a million satellites to run data centers "a fantasy." "It's not going to happen," he told the Associated Press on Wednesday.

One problem is heat: space is cold, but it is also a vacuum, which traps heat inside objects much like a thermos — and data centers generate enormous amounts of it. Becker said there are "basic physical limits" to radiating that heat away.

Other risks include atmospheric pollution from launches and reentries, and the chance of collisions in orbit. "You could end up with a cascading set of space junk collisions," Becker said, warning of a cloud of debris in low Earth orbit, where many weather and telecommunications satellites also fly.

The American Astronomical Society said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision, warning it would undermine decades of investment in astronomy and the public's ability to enjoy the night sky. The society, satellite operator Viasat, and Amazon's Kuiper Systems were among those that asked the regulator to deny the request. The FCC maintained that the constellation complies with its orbital debris rules, said the deployment serves the public interest, and set aside environmental concerns as outside its authority.

The authorization does not mean the network will be built. SpaceX itself cautioned in a filing ahead of its planned public offering that orbital data centers rely on "unproven" technology and "may not achieve commercial viability." For now, the one-million-satellite data center exists on paper — and on a fourteen-year deadline.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • NPR
  • Reuters

link.title: FCC clears SpaceX to deploy one million satellites for data centers in space

entry.title: Ukraine says its combat laser downed a Russian jet drone — a claimed world first
entry.content:
Ukraine says it has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a development Kyiv is presenting as a world first in combat air defence.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defence technology, announced the interception on Wednesday. He said the Blysk laser air defence system, developed and manufactured by the Ukrainian defence technology firm Carmine Sky, brought down the drone while protecting a critical infrastructure facility. No exact time or place was disclosed.

Beskrestnov described the strike as the first time anywhere in the world that a combat laser had destroyed a jet-powered drone. The claim has not been independently verified, and no Russian response has been reported.

The announcement matters because Russia's jet-powered drones have become one of the hardest threats for Ukraine to stop. Moscow began deploying them at scale earlier in 2026, and their higher speed makes them far more difficult to intercept than the propeller-driven attack drones that have pounded Ukrainian cities for years. In June, Ukraine was intercepting only about 57 percent of jet-powered drones, compared with about 90 percent of conventional Russian attack drones.

Russia has increasingly relied on its jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely producing some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones in that month alone, and it projected those numbers would keep growing.

A laser works differently from the missiles and guns Ukraine normally uses. Instead of exploding, it holds a beam on one spot of the incoming drone until the parts inside overheat and fail. That makes each shot far cheaper than a missile, but tracking a fast, twisting target with a beam is difficult, and bad weather can scatter the light before it reaches the drone.

The Blysk system is modest by the standards of directed-energy weapons, with a reported output of about four kilowatts and an engagement range of up to roughly one kilometre. It is being developed under Ukraine's government-backed Private Air Defense program, which about 100 companies across the country have joined. Ukraine began testing laser air defence systems over the summer of 2026.

Beskrestnov was careful not to overstate what the single interception proves. "It is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser," he said, adding that tests are continuing while the systems defend critical sites.

For now, the claim stands as a single reported success rather than a proven capability. If the system works as described, it could give Ukraine a cheaper way to defend its cities against the fastest drones Russia sends — but the technology remains experimental, and its effectiveness in large numbers is untested.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • CBS News
  • The Straits Times

link.title: Ukraine says its combat laser downed a Russian jet drone — a claimed world first

entry.title: Court upholds New York City rent freeze, handing Mamdani a win — with a sharp rebuke attached
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

A Manhattan judge on Wednesday upheld New York City's rent freeze, dismissing a lawsuit from landlords who argued that the city's signature affordability policy was the product of a rigged process. The ruling keeps the freeze in place for roughly one million rent-stabilized apartments — but the judge paired the victory for Mayor Zohran Mamdani with a blunt warning about how he campaigned on it.

Justice Brendan Lantry of the New York State Supreme Court ruled that the landlords had failed to show the freeze was unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious. In a 20-page decision, he found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board acted within its authority when it voted in late June to freeze rents on both one-year and two-year leases — the first time the board has frozen both lease types at once.

The freeze applies to rent-stabilized apartments, which account for about one million of the city's 2.3 million rental units, and covers leases up for renewal between October 1, 2026, and September 30, 2027. It has already been in effect for weeks, and the mayor's office says it affects more than two million New Yorkers.

The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, sued in July, calling the board's decision a "sham process." They argued that Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome by appointing board members who shared his pledge to freeze rents, and that the board relied on manipulated data. Lantry rejected those claims. "Elections have consequences, a premise that is the backbone of our democracy," he wrote, noting that Mamdani was fully empowered to appoint board members of his choosing and that their shared political views "does not indicate any level of collusion."

But the judge did not let the mayor off the hook. He called Mamdani's campaign promise to freeze rents "reckless and irresponsible," writing that the mayor of New York has no authority to raise, freeze or otherwise adjust the rents of stabilized units — that power belongs to the board alone. He also described communications between the board's chair and City Hall as "troubling," saying they cast "a dark shadow" on the board's claimed independence.

Mamdani welcomed the decision as "a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in." In a statement, he added: "Housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity. This holiday weekend, more than two million New Yorkers can breathe a little easier."

The landlords' lawyer, Randy Mastro, said the group was reviewing the ruling and considering its next steps, including an appeal. He noted that the judge had acknowledged the freeze could have "devastating consequences for small landlords" across the city.

The decision is Mamdani's second court victory this month, after an appeals court revived the city's tax on second homes valued at $5 million or more. The rent freeze sits at the centre of his affordability agenda, alongside a plan to build 200,000 affordable homes and preserve 200,000 more over the next decade. For tenants, the ruling means the freeze survives its first legal test; for the mayor, it comes with a judicial reminder that the promise was never his to make alone.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • The Wall Street Journal

link.title: Court upholds New York City rent freeze, handing Mamdani a win — with a sharp rebuke attached

entry.title: Kim Jong Un orders wider spread of battlefield nuclear weapons as talks with Trump stall
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has ordered his country to spread its battlefield nuclear weapons more widely, state media reported on Thursday, days after he ignored President Donald Trump's offer of a meeting during Trump's visit to Asia.

North Korea's official Korean Central News Agency said Kim inspected nuclear-material production facilities on Wednesday, including two factories — one newly built and one being expanded — along with a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute. The agency did not say where the sites are located.

Kim said production capacity for nuclear material was being systematically expanded and described North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state as "absolutely inviolable." He called the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons "across multiple domains for different missions" an important and urgent task, given what he called the inevitable reality of facing what he described as the most dangerous enemy state — a reference to South Korea.

Tactical nuclear weapons are lower-yield warheads designed for battlefield use, unlike strategic weapons built for longer-range strikes. North Korea has focused on developing them in recent years amid heightened animosity with South Korea. Photographs released by KCNA showed Kim and senior military officials walking between rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to enrich uranium, and touring halls displaying what analysts said looked like miniaturised warheads, including the Hwasan-31 design first shown in 2023.

Kim justified the buildup by citing what he called variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula "moment by moment." He accused the United States of pushing its regional allies toward nuclear-powered submarines and of committing to share nuclear weapons with them, and he called international demands for denuclearisation an infringement of sovereignty. He also warned that attempts to deny North Korea's nuclear status would amount to "an open declaration of war."

Analysts say the visit was meant to show off an evolving arsenal and to make clear that Kim will not discuss giving up his nuclear weapons in any future talks. The trip was his fourth visit to a nuclear facility since September 2024, and it came after a widely expected meeting with Trump failed to happen during the president's trip to China last week. The visit likely also served as a check on this year's progress in the nuclear programme ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defence Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and maintains firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under its alliance with the United States.

What remains unknown is where the facilities Kim visited are located. Outside experts have assessed that a uranium enrichment site North Korea disclosed in June is likely an additional facility at its main Yongbyon complex, and analysts are still studying the new photographs. There is also no sign of renewed dialogue: with the talks offer unanswered, the visit reads as Pyongyang setting its terms — recognition as a nuclear power, with no discussion of disarmament.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Reuters

link.title: Kim Jong Un orders wider spread of battlefield nuclear weapons as talks with Trump stall

entry.title: Europe picks Pablo Hernández de Cos to lead the ECB as Lagarde era ends
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

European leaders have agreed to nominate Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank, choosing a career central banker to steer the eurozone through a period of stubborn inflation and strained public finances. The 55-year-old Spaniard will succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down on February 7, several months before her term was due to end.

De Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, the Basel-based forum for the world's major central banks, and previously served as governor of the Bank of Spain. He will become the first Spaniard to lead the ECB, and its fifth president since the bank was founded.

The decision fell into place on Thursday after the Netherlands dropped its backing for its own candidate, Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank governor and the only other contender. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten agreed to support de Cos, EU officials said, clearing the way for a consensus nomination. EU ambassadors were due to meet on Thursday afternoon to launch the written procedure under which capitals formally sign off on the recommendation.

The nomination is part of a wider reshuffle of the ECB's leadership. The same recommendation names Laurence Boone to run the bank's market operations and Markus Brunnermeier as chief economist. European Council President António Costa confirmed the agreement, and French President Emmanuel Macron welcomed what he called a balanced trio for the euro area.

Formal approval still lies ahead. The European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council must endorse the candidacy, with a final seal from EU leaders expected at December's European Council summit. The Parliament's opinion is not binding, and with political agreement now in place, the appointment is widely seen as assured.

De Cos takes over an institution facing a difficult inheritance. Inflation in the eurozone is still running above the bank's 2% target, government debt tensions in France have unsettled bond markets, and the war involving Iran has added to uncertainty over energy and growth. He is also expected to advance the ECB's digital euro project, with a pilot planned for 2027. He is regarded as more dovish on interest rates than Knot, his rival for the post, but he also has a record of preaching fiscal discipline.

Markets took the news in stride. The euro edged up 0.12% to $1.0988, while German 10-year government bond yields, the benchmark for the wider eurozone, rose 5 basis points to 3.268%.

De Cos will oversee monetary policy for 21 member states and about 350 million people. His appointment closes a closely watched succession race and hands the eurozone's most powerful economic institution to a technocrat who has spent his career inside central banking — first as an economist at Spain's central bank, then as its governor, and most recently at the helm of the BIS.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Europe picks Pablo Hernández de Cos to lead the ECB as Lagarde era ends

entry.title: Michael Giles, the drummer who helped invent prog rock with King Crimson, dies at 84
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Michael Giles, the drummer and co-founder whose playing powered King Crimson's landmark debut and helped define progressive rock, has died aged 84.

Giles died on Monday, November 23, his record label Discipline Global Mobile (DGM) announced on Wednesday. No cause of death was disclosed. In a statement, the label called him a "visionary drummer, composer and co-founder of King Crimson" and praised his "extraordinary rhythmic imagination, musical sensitivity and highly inventive drumming."

Born on March 1, 1942, in Winton, Bournemouth, Giles began playing with guitarist Robert Fripp in 1967, forming the trio Giles, Giles and Fripp with his brother Peter. The following year, the group evolved into King Crimson, with Fripp, singer and bassist Greg Lake, multi-instrumentalist Ian McDonald and lyricist Peter Sinfield completing the original lineup.

The band's debut album, In the Court of the Crimson King, released in October 1969, became one of the defining records of progressive rock. Giles's drumming drove its opening track, "21st Century Schizoid Man," a jagged, jazz-inflected performance that set a new standard for what a rock drummer could do. The album reached the top five in Britain and has rarely left lists of the most influential records of its era.

Giles left King Crimson in 1970, shortly after the debut, but returned as a guest drummer on the follow-up, In the Wake of Poseidon. He went on to record the album McDonald and Giles with Ian McDonald in 1971, worked widely as a session musician, and later played with the 21st Century Schizoid Band, a group formed by former King Crimson members to revisit the band's early material.

His influence outlasted his brief time in the band. The precision and swing of his playing on those first two King Crimson records became a reference point for generations of progressive-rock drummers, and his work is still studied by musicians drawn to the band's early sound.

Fripp is now the only surviving member of King Crimson's original lineup. Lake died in 2016, McDonald in 2022 and Sinfield in 2024.

Tributes from fellow musicians and fans have focused on the same quality: a drummer who could be both fiercely powerful and remarkably musical, and whose playing helped turn a debut album into a genre's founding document.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • The Guardian
  • Rolling Stone

link.title: Michael Giles, the drummer who helped invent prog rock with King Crimson, dies at 84

entry.title: Trump demands probe after GDP growth is revised sharply higher to 4.3%
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

President Donald Trump has demanded an immediate investigation into the government's economic statistics, after the Commerce Department revised third-quarter growth sharply higher in the weeks after the midterm elections.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) said on Wednesday that the US economy grew at an annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, up from the 3.4% advance estimate it published on 29 October — five days before the 3 November midterms, in which Trump's Republican Party suffered heavy losses. The 0.9 percentage point upward revision was driven by stronger investment and consumer spending than first measured.

Trump seized on the revision in a post on his Truth Social network on Thursday, Thanksgiving Day, calling the figures published before the election "FAKE" and the revision a "massive, and purposeful, error". He offered no evidence for the claim that the numbers were deliberately understated.

"It was just revealed that the REAL Numbers on the Economy, published before the Election, were FAKE," he wrote. "Why wasn't the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation."

In the same post, Trump argued that the corrected figure showed the economy under his administration was "doing FAR BETTER than the good numbers already released", adding: "Third Quarter GDP Growth has now been corrected to be 4.3%, instead of 3.4%, a major difference!"

He returned to the subject in a second Thanksgiving post, wishing a happy holiday "even [to] those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late", and calling the revision a "RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated."

The BEA says revisions of this kind are routine. Its advance estimate for each quarter is based on incomplete source data, particularly on inventories, trade and consumer spending on services, and is updated as fuller figures arrive. The agency said this revision largely reflected upward adjustments to investment and consumer spending, after updates to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Producer Price Index showed stronger spending than first recorded.

The BEA publishes three estimates for each quarter — an advance, a second and a third reading — and the final third-quarter estimate is scheduled for release on 23 December. Economists note that revisions of close to a percentage point, while large, are not unusual when the advance estimate is based on partial data.

The episode comes as Trump has repeatedly questioned official figures that cut against his political interests, including in the wake of the midterm results. For now, there is no indication of what form any investigation would take, or which body would conduct it.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Axios
  • Reuters

link.title: Trump demands probe after GDP growth is revised sharply higher to 4.3%

entry.title: Two Italians killed in alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait; Tehran denies role
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Two Italian nationals were killed in Kuwait on Thursday when drones struck a military air-defence site, in an attack that Kuwait and Italy blame on Iran. Tehran denies any involvement.

The two men were technicians for Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of German defence group Rheinmetall. They had been maintaining detection antennas for the Skyguard air-defence system at the site when it was hit, Italy's foreign ministry said.

Kuwait's defence ministry said four people were wounded by falling debris as air defences intercepted incoming drones at what it called a "vital facility". Alongside the two Italians, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured. All four were taken to hospital, and the two Italians later died of their injuries.

Italy's foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, confirmed the deaths and told the Senate that "several drones of Iranian origin targeted Kuwaiti military installations", including an air-defence detection station. He said the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran, while noting that "numerous pro-Iranian militias operate in the region".

Iran rejected the accusation. Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, a spokesperson for Iran's armed forces, said no military or offensive operations had been conducted by Iranian forces in the region, and described the claims as a cover for further insecurity. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied Iranian involvement in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts, and offered a joint investigation into the incident.

The attack drew swift condemnation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for more pressure on Tehran, while Gulf Cooperation Council secretary-general Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi condemned what he called a "brutal" attack and a dangerous escalation.

The strike is the latest in a series of Iranian drone attacks on Gulf states since September. Gulf governments have said an attack against one of them is an attack against all, and the incident came as an Italian delegation — including the commander general of the Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, and Italy's ambassador to Kuwait — was visiting the country.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Jazeera

link.title: Two Italians killed in alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait; Tehran denies role

entry.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for the first time ever as storm bears down on New York
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

New York's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not march on Thanksgiving Day this year. Organisers have postponed the 100th edition to Saturday, the first postponement in the parade's century-long history, as a powerful storm bears down on the city.

Macy's announced the decision on Wednesday, after consulting city officials, saying the parade had been moved "out of an abundance of caution." The rescheduled parade will begin at 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, November 28.

The storm is a nor'easter expected to bring intense wind and heavy rain to the region through the holiday. The National Weather Service issued a high wind warning and a coastal flood warning for New York City for Thursday into Friday, with gusts potentially reaching 60 mph. City officials banned empty tractor-trailers from bridges on Thursday morning because of the wind.

The danger was clearest for the parade's giant balloons, which were already being filled on Wednesday when the postponement was announced; workers were then seen deflating them. High winds can push the balloons off course between Manhattan's skyscrapers and over the crowds below, and the city has long had rules for lowering or grounding them when the wind gets too strong.

At a news conference, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday's winds would be strong enough to snap tree limbs and bring down power lines, and that rescheduling was the right call. "I know that this change of plans will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first," he said.

NBC, which broadcasts the parade, said it would instead air a repeat of the 2025 edition on Thursday.

It was not immediately clear how much of the parade's large lineup could shift to the new date. Representatives for the Broadway shows "The Rocky Horror Show," "Wicked" and "Hamilton" said their performers would take part on Saturday, and the University of Connecticut's marching band, which had been due to perform in the parade for the first time, will also make the rescheduled event. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band, however, will head home to perform at a football game.

Macy's executive producer Will Coss said organisers were working with bands and other performers and were "optimistic that we're going to be able to maintain the parade that we set out to produce." A company spokesperson confirmed it was the first time the event had ever been postponed.

The parade began in 1924 and was suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II, but it had never before been moved because of weather. Its balloons have been grounded only once, in 1971. The city's wind rules were tightened after high winds sent a balloon into a metal pole during the 1997 parade, leaving a woman in a coma.

For at least one family, the delay was good news: Sarah Collins and her youngest son had not planned to see the parade because their flight from Florida arrives on Friday. Now, she said, it is part of their plans — and he is excited.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Associated Press
  • Reuters

link.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed for the first time ever as storm bears down on New York

entry.title: Two arrested in Germany over alleged plot to attack Cologne synagogue
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

German prosecutors said on Thursday that police had arrested two Iraqi nationals suspected of belonging to a terrorist organisation that plotted attacks on Jewish and other targets in Europe, including a synagogue in Cologne.

The two men, identified only as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J. under German privacy rules, were detained in Heidelberg and Cologne after officers searched 17 properties across the states of Baden-Wuerttemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia. Prosecutors said more than 250 officers took part in the operation.

Prosecutors say Mostafa Al-R. was closely associated with Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is facing terrorism charges in the United States and is described as a key figure in a pro-Iranian group known as Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyyah, or HAYI. Prosecutors believe the group is behind a series of attacks on US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe since March.

According to the arrest warrants, Al-Saadi and Mostafa Al-R. formed a separate organisation with others at the end of 2025 to prepare further attacks in Germany and elsewhere in Europe. Ameer J. was a member of that group, prosecutors said. The group raised funds and recruited people to carry out bomb attacks, according to the warrants.

The warrants say that on two consecutive nights in late March, unidentified people acting on the group's behalf travelled to a synagogue in Cologne and to another location in Europe, apparently carrying explosive devices. The attacks were not carried out, for reasons that remain unclear.

The two suspects were due to appear before a judge on Thursday, who will decide whether they remain in pre-trial detention. Prosecutors said the investigation was launched on intelligence supplied by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

In the United States, prosecutors unsealed an eight-count indictment earlier this month charging Al-Saadi and two other men with terrorism-related offences, in a case linked to the same network.

Jewish institutions in Germany are under heightened protection after warnings of threats linked to tensions in the Middle East, and Germany has faced a series of attacks and plots in recent years. Prosecutors have not said whether further arrests are expected.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Reuters
  • Al Arabiya

link.title: Two arrested in Germany over alleged plot to attack Cologne synagogue

entry.title: Nvidia pauses AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian nations as US chip curbs bite
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to pause shipments of AI servers to four Southeast Asian countries while it checks whether they are complying with new US export controls, according to reports published on Thursday.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia instructed partners including Dell and Super Micro to halt server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia for an unspecified period. The Financial Times, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported the same move, and said partners had told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia would not allow their orders to be shipped.

The pause follows a US Commerce Department rule issued on November 16 and in force since November 19, which requires a US export licence to send advanced AI chips to those four countries and to Brazil. The rule is aimed at a workaround Washington says Chinese companies have been using: renting computing power remotely from data centres abroad instead of importing the chips directly.

Those four Southeast Asian countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, whose direct export to China is restricted. The think tank Institute for Progress estimates that remote data centres of this kind supply about 24 percent of China's AI computing power, according to the Journal's reporting.

Under the new rule, cloud providers that were already supplying large amounts of computing power to companies in China or other covered locations have 90 days from November 19 to obtain a licence, by showing their end users do not include restricted entities.

It is not yet clear whether the halt is temporary. Nvidia declined to comment, and Dell and Supermicro did not immediately respond to requests for comment, according to the reports. Bloomberg reported that a $480 million loan sought by Singapore cloud company Aolani to buy Nvidia graphics processors for a data centre in Malaysia has been put on hold.

The disruption is already rippling beyond the chipmaker. Data centre operators in the region that had planned to sell GPU computing power to Chinese customers are reassessing projects, and financing tied to those plans is under pressure.

The halt comes days after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, on November 23. For buyers in the four affected countries, the immediate question is how long the pause lasts — and what compliance will look like when shipments resume.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • TechCrunch
  • Reuters

link.title: Nvidia pauses AI server shipments to four Southeast Asian nations as US chip curbs bite

entry.title: Duterte trial to open November 30 as ICC lays out schedule into April 2027
entry.content:
Illustration — not a photograph

The International Criminal Court has set out the full schedule for the trial of former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, with proceedings due to open on November 30 and evidence hearings running into April 2027, under an order issued by Trial Chamber III on November 26.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed immediately by the first prosecution witness. Prosecutors have been given two hours and 15 minutes for their opening statement, the Common Legal Representatives of Victims one hour and 30 minutes, and Duterte's defence one hour to outline its case. The court will sit until its judicial recess on December 18, then resume in the new year.

Each trial day will run in four one-hour sessions: 10 to 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., 1:30 to 2:30 p.m., and 3 to 4 p.m. Hague time. In Manila, that is 5 to 6 p.m., 6:30 to 7:30 p.m., 8:30 to 9:30 p.m., and 10 to 11 p.m. The timetable was adjusted on expert advice to build in regular breaks during the day.

The chamber has also fixed the first three blocks of evidence hearings for 2027: January 12 to February 19, March 1 to 24, and April 5 to 30. Dates for hearings after April 30 will be set in due course. Each side must provide a schedule of its forthcoming witnesses at least four weeks before a block begins, and the chamber has told the parties to organise appearances so there are no gaps between one witness finishing and the next beginning.

About 100 prosecution witnesses are expected to testify, the court's spokesperson, Oriane Huber Maillet, said on Tuesday. Duterte faces three counts of alleged crimes against humanity, tied to incidents during his time as mayor of Davao City and in the early part of his presidency. He was arrested on March 12, 2025, so the trial will open roughly 20 months later. His defence team has contested the charges.

The schedule gives both sides and the victims' representatives a clear runway for the first time since the case was confirmed. The opening statements on November 30 will be the first public test of how each side frames a trial that has been closely watched in the Philippines, where families of those killed during Duterte's drug war have been seeking justice at home and abroad.

Illustration — not a photograph.

Sources

  • Inquirer.net
  • ABS-CBN News

link.title: Duterte trial to open November 30 as ICC lays out schedule into April 2027
